He joined ESPN in September 2019 as an NBA reporter dedicated to the Midwest region before switching to his current role in April 2021. The Flint, Mich. native is a graduate of Western Michigan University and has authored/co-authored three books: "Wasted," "Ethan's Talent Search" and "All In: The Kelvin Torbert Story". He is a proud parent of one son, Ethan. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions DETROIT -- When Dan Campbell arrived for the NFL's annual league meeting in March, no one would have guessed he was three months removed from one of his most disappointing seasons as the Detroit Lions ' coach. Instead, those who saw him at the Arizona Biltmore in Phoenix were more preoccupied with his hair, which along with his goatee was considerably longer than anyone covering the team since 2021 could remember. "You know what? I just haven't cut it," Campbell joked. "I haven't cut it. I cut the sides, but I haven't." His relaxed look mirrored the calm confidence with which he discussed his team while answering questions from reporters alongside his coaching peers. He talked about his team heading into the 2026 season -- expressing his belief in the staff and the roster that he and general manager Brad Holmes had built. "We've been going. It's been fun. Been fun. Brad and I have been -- we've been back in the bunker just going at it," Campbell said. "It's been fun. It really has. Kind of a little bit of a rebirth, actually." His Lions were in need of the mini reset. They had won 15 games in 2024 and 12 the season before that, cementing themselves as one of the NFC's top contenders along the way. But in 2025, after losing both coordinators and eight coaches overall, they won just nine games and missed the playoffs for the first time since 2022. This offseason, some change was inevitable. The biggest: Campbell brought in former Arizona Cardinals offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to replace John Morton, whom the Lions fired in January after the first-time OC struggled to give Detroit an offensive identity. Detroit also put the finishing touches on a two-year renovation of the offensive line by moving All-Pro Penei Sewell from right tackle to left, adding Cade Mays in free agency and drafting tackle Blake Miller with the No. 17 selection. Otherwise, the team that enters the 2026 campaign is largely made up of the same nucleus that helped push the Lions to so much success. And Detroit has doubled down by locking down two of its young stars in running back Jahmyr Gibbs and linebacker Jack Campbell with lucrative contract extensions. Those signings followed new deals they've given to other homegrown talents over the past three years and raised their overall investment in extensions to more than $1 billion over that span. Dan Campbell said the commitment to the current roster, combined with the organization's recent track record of success, is why he and the Lions remain confident their championship window remains open despite last season's setback. "Our window is not closed. It's not closed. That was the whole reason why we did this. We fell short last year. But needed to get in [the playoffs], and now it's about the matchups, where you're playing and who you're playing," Campbell told ESPN of his team, which is favored by DraftKings to win the NFC North and have the fifth-best odds to win the conference . "We want to be able to do that every year, and sometimes, I'm just saying is what happens is, you want to go all-in for one player, well how do you know that one player doesn't get hurt? "Or how do you know the three players behind him don't get hurt and now you've got no depth. Whereas, let's just get a unit together that we feel like can compete every year and then it's about in that moment, we're making those plays and finding a way to win that game." And they are not alone in their assessment of the team. Asking about the Lions' prospects revealed a consensus from top coaches around the NFL -- from the Los Angeles Rams ' Sean McVay to the Green Bay Packers ' Matt LaFleur -- that the 2026 Lions are not the 9-8 team the league saw last season. Here's what the Lions and others around the league are saying about Detroit's Super Bowl worthiness in 2026. Part of the reason for Detroit's uncharacteristic 2025 campaign was the turnover on the coaching staff. After finishing 15-2 in 2024, the Lions most notably lost offensive coordinator Ben Johnson and defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn, who took head coaching jobs with the Chicago Bears and the New York Jets , respectively. Those two departures were big losses for the team. But an underappreciated aspect that contributed to its struggles last season was the sheer number of coaches Campbell had to replace. Campbell: "Well, you learn. But I don't think anybody necessarily tells you, 'Hey, be ready to lose [eight] coaches in one year.' Of course, that's the plan. You're going to lose some guys, you do it right and then the next guy, you can promote or you can go find guys. But when you're talking about [eight coaches], that's a tall task. But you owe it to the players, you owe it to the organization to find the best guy. "So, I feel like those pieces we added last year, for the most part, really fit what we're about and are good for us." McVay: "I think it's a champagne problem. When you end up losing coaches for the reasons that you're talking about with Dan, that means you're doing really well. People want to try to replicate. Or people in your building that are in leadership roles, they want to have them lead or take elevated steps in their career. "What I would say is it's a blessing. What I've really leaned into for us is what's been really fortunate is you get exposure to new people. New ideas." Glenn: "It's a really good problem to have because usually when you're losing coaches like that, that means you're doing well." LaFleur: "I do think that is a challenge, obviously. [Campbell] lost both of his coordinators, and there's a little bit of learning curve there and sometimes you have some growing pains, but I still think they're an elite team." In Johnson's three years as OC, the Lions established one of the NFL's most dangerous and prolific offenses. In 2024, his unit scored a franchise-record 564 points and led the league in scoring for the first time since 1954. Since 2022 -- the year Johnson took over playcalling duties midseason -- the Lions are tops in the NFL in scoring and total offense. While they still managed 481 points last season, they failed to establish an offensive identity outside of home run plays, and Morton, who replaced Johnson, was relieved of playcalling duties in November. In January, the Lions fired Morton and hired Petzing, who'd spent the previous three seasons as OC of the Cardinals. Campbell: "I feel like the addition with Drew Petzing is going to be great for us. I think it's going to get us centralized. Back to being centralized more on offense." McVay: "This league is so volatile, great coaches get let go every year and great coaches become available. And I think when you show your place is a developmental staff that'll invest in the human being and help them get to places that Dan and I were fortunate enough to get to, you attract high-caliber people and you've got to lean into it." The Cardinals ranked second in the NFL in rushing yards per attempt (4.92) and ninth in total rushing yards (6,399) during Petzing's three years of calling plays in Arizona. And while Detroit's average yards per carry remained steady from 2024 to 2025 (4.7 to 4.6), the team's attempts, rushes per game and rushes of 10 or more yards per game all dipped last season. Petzing, on what he wants from his offense in Detroit: "It needs to be physical, it needs to be tough, it needs to be difficult to defend and it needs to be multiple at times. "It's not going to all run through one person, it's not going to run through one personnel, it's going to change week to week. I think that's important in this league. Defensive coordinators, I think, do things at a really high level. They watch tape, they understand scheme. So, I think that's a big part of what we need to be on offense." Gibbs on Petzing: "He's nice. Smart. He's demanding of us, but he knows we can do it. He puts a lot on our plate, but like I said, he knows we can do it. We're smart, we're really good football players. I like him. He's cool. That's my dog." Campbell enters his sixth season with the Lions having helped lead the franchise to unprecedented heights in the Super Bowl era. Despite missing the playoffs last season, Detroit's 9-8 mark gave it a winning record for a fourth consecutive season -- the longest such streak in more than 50 years and tied for the second longest in team history. Cincinnati Bengals coach Zac Taylor: "This is his sixth year, so I would have complete trust that Dan and those guys have a great plan. We played them last year, and they're a great team from top to bottom. They certainly got the best of us, and I'm happy we don't play Detroit this year because I've got a lot of respect for Dan and Detroit and the job they've done there, and [quarterback Jared] Goff . ... I haven't studied them as much this offseason or going into next year, but I would imagine they're going to continue to have success." LaFleur: "Oh yeah, Dan Campbell's a stud. He is an unbelievable football coach. Got a ton of respect for him. What he's been able to establish here, the culture that they have. You know you better strap it up when you're going to play the Detroit Lions ." Buoying Detroit's hopes in 2026 is a roster brimming with talent on both sides of the ball. Since 2021, his first year in charge, Holmes has drafted more players who have been named All-Pro (six) than any other GM or franchise over that span, according to Elias Sports Bureau. And Holmes, as part of his draft-and-develop strategy, has signed many of those players to extensions, ensuring the Lions -- projected by ESPN's Mike Clay to win 12 games this season -- will have its core group of stars together for years to come, which has contributed to the organization's strong sense that a Super Bowl in 2027 and beyond is a very real possibility. Lions president and CEO Rod Wood: "When you look at us top to bottom and I think we've got elite players in some of the most important positions. [Offensive tackle] Sewell, [All-Pro wide receiver Amon-Ra] St. Brown , [defensive end] Hutch [ Aidan Hutchinson ], and there's a lot of teams that would trade for that. ... [Sam] LaPorta at tight end, and Gibbs at running back, Goff at quarterback. So, you put it all together and I think that we've got a team that can compete. "Not to compare, but I don't think that too many people are assuming that the window's closed on the Chiefs , and they only won six games last year. So, it can come back just as fast as it went the other way, but I'm very confident." St. Brown: "I think Dan's 100% right. I think our Super Bowl window is still wide-open. I think our nucleus is still here. ... The guys that are important key players are still here. There's so many guys on our team that are core pieces that are still with us, so I feel like that changes that we've had, every team is going to go through changes. You win games, your corners, they leave and you've got to bring new guys. We've got more changes this year, and I think it's going to be good for us. "I think we, as a team, are going to be hungrier than ever because of what happened last year and how disappointed we were just as a team internally. We feel like we had way bigger goals than what we did last year and what happened. For us, it's like, we know what we got; we've just got to put it together and just keep working towards the biggest goal." Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell: "Yeah, it's no excuses, and I feel like everybody here knows that. Our roster has more than enough talent to get it done. We've just to go out there and do it, and it comes down to the players. "So, I don't know if that's pressure or whatever, but again, it doesn't matter. You've just got to be yourself. Each and every player is here on this roster for a reason."

He has more than 20 years of experience working in NFL analytics and is the creator of the DVOA and DYAR metric. He also serves as the Chief Analytics Officer at FTN Network. Follow on X , Ben Solak Close Ben Solak ESPN Ben Solak joined ESPN in 2024 as a national NFL analyst. He previously covered the NFL at The Ringer, Bleeding Green Nation and The Draft Network. , Louis Riddick Close Louis Riddick NFL ESPN NFL Analyst 12-year NFL scout and Director of Pro Personnel Played in the NFL for six years Graduated from University of Pittsburgh Follow on X , Seth Walder Close Seth Walder ESPN Analytics Seth Walder is an analytics writer at ESPN, specializing in quantitative analysis. You can follow Seth on X via @SethWalder. Multiple Authors Aug 17, 2026, 06:20 AM ET Email Print Open Extended Reactions The 2026 NFL season kicks off in less than a month, and we'll have plenty of coverage about the race to Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles. But we're also in the business of trying to predict the future. In our annual Future Power Rankings, we're not focused on the outcome of this season. Instead, we're ranking all 32 teams by who is primed to be among the league's best from the 2027 through 2029 seasons. To do so, we asked our panel of experts -- analysts Louis Riddick, Aaron Schatz, Ben Solak and Seth Walder -- to rate each team's quarterback situation, remaining (non-QB) roster makeup, front office and coaching staff using this scale: 100: A+ (elite) 90-99: A (great) 80-89: B (very good) 70-79: C (average) 51-69: D (very bad) 50 and below: F (disastrous) After averaging the results from the panelists, each of the four categories was weighted to create the overall score: quarterback (20%), roster (30%), front office (25%) and coaching (25%). The result is a comprehensive ranking based on how well each team is positioned for the future. Our experts then picked out reasons for optimism, reasons to worry, crucial stats/nuggets to know and bold predictions for all 32 franchises over that three-year span. Jump to a team: ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND JAX | KC | LV | LAC | LAR | MIA | MIN NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF SEA | TB | TEN | WSH Note: Overall scores are rounded to the nearest 10th of a point. 1. Seattle Seahawks (Overall score: 88.7) Reason for hope: The league has been looking for a young defensive counterstrike to the ascent of offensive masterminds Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan, and the Seahawks have finally found it! Coach Mike Macdonald has a stellar track record of defensive player development, and the emergence of WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba , OT Charles Cross and QB Sam Darnold sets a high floor in Seattle for years to come. -- Solak Reason for concern: The relationship between Darnold and former OC Klint Kubiak was an obvious net positive for the organization. For the future, what does that real-time relationship look like between Darnold and new OC Brian Fleury? Fleury is not just calling plays for the first time on the NFL level but also doing it with a roster that is set up to contend into the future. -- Riddick Nugget to know: Including the postseason, the 2025 Seahawks finished with the highest DVOA of any team since the 2007 Patriots. The top-12 teams by DVOA since 2010 finished with an average of 10.9 wins the following season (prorated for a 17-game season). However, these numbers are dragged down by two injury-riddled 49ers teams (2020 and 2024). Remove those teams, and the average is 11.9 wins. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Darnold will not be on the Seahawks in 2028. He started last season red-hot and finished fairly strong in Seattle's Super Bowl run. But from Weeks 10 to 18, he ranked 27th out of 30 quarterbacks in QBR. The Super Bowl win certainly will buy Darnold time. But if he stumbles in 2027, I don't think there are guarantees that he will be re-signed . -- Walder 2. Philadelphia Eagles (Overall score: 88.1) Reason for hope: Even in an offseason of tumult, with A.J. Brown traded and the transition to a new offensive system, the Eagles rank very highly in our future outlook. Why? Because general manager Howie Roseman has proved over the past decade that nobody builds contenders more quickly. The Eagles' star-studded young defense is proof alone. -- Solak Reason for concern: Decision-makers in Philadelphia clearly believed the offense needed to evolve philosophically, and the change was made to bring in offensive coordinator Sean Mannion. His ability to teach, develop and use the skills of QB Jalen Hurts -- without fully neutralizing what has made him a Super Bowl-winning QB -- will shape this organization over the next several years. -- Riddick Nugget to know: The Eagles project to have the league's youngest defense if we look at their top-12 projected defensive players (starters in both base and nickel). The average age is 25.6; Jonathan Greenard and Zack Baun are their only starters over 27. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: The Eagles will trade Jalyx Hunt or Nolan Smith Jr . ahead of the 2027 season. They will be entering the final year of their deals and are the second- or third-best pass rusher on the Eagles, in some order, with Greenard aboard. Trading either player could net Philadelphia draft capital going forward -- and save some money if it's Smith. -- Walder 3. Detroit Lions (Overall score: 86.2) Reason for hope: As GM Brad Holmes begins paying the legendary 2023 draft class that galvanized this Lions turnaround, future contention becomes tougher and tougher in Detroit. But between Holmes and coach Dan Campbell, the Lions' leadership is unquestionable. And Detroit's group of young stars entering their primes (RB Jahmyr Gibbs , LB Jack Campbell , OT Penei Sewell and WR Amon-Ra St. Brown ) is as deep as any. -- Solak Reason for concern: I still have concerns about the Lions' ability to rush the passer at a championship level (26th in pass rush win rate last season), although rookie 2026 second-round pick Derrick Moore could lessen some of the burden on Aidan Hutchinson . What is of more concern is the secondary, where Brian Branch is trying to come back from an Achilles tear and Kerby Joseph is rehabbing a knee injury . Both are among the best in the league at their position, so it would be a major blow if they can't get back to their top form. -- Riddick Nugget to know: Detroit has reset its offensive line with youth, and only Miami now has a younger average age among its five projected starters for the 2026 season. The Lions' starting linemen range in age from right tackle Blake Miller (22) to center Juice Scruggs (26), who replaces the injured Cade Mays (27). -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Hutchinson will win Defensive Player of the Year. His five pre-injury games in 2024 always stick out in my mind, when he had 7.5 sacks and an obscene 35.0% pass rush win rate at edge ( Danielle Hunter led qualifiers that year at 26.1%). Of course, that was a small sample. But Hutchinson has the capability to be an elite -- even the best -- edge rusher over a whole season. -- Walder 4. Denver Broncos (Overall score: 85.6) Reason for hope: Across the 53-man roster, there is perhaps no team deeper than Denver. And the Broncos' coaching staff, with Sean Payton and Vance Joseph, features two of the league's preeminent schemers over the past decade. The continued growth of QB Bo Nix and the final addition of WR Jaylen Waddle could push this team into one of the three Super Bowl matchups in question. -- Solak Reason for concern: Last year , I expressed my concern about whether Denver's RB room could make this offense complete. I'm not as worried about that now, as I think the addition of fourth-rounder Jonah Coleman (an absolute tank ) next to RJ Harvey gives the Broncos the perfect 1-2 punch over the next few years. My concern now is whether new coordinator Davis Webb can create a balanced offense to go along with their lights-out defense. -- Riddick Nugget to know: The Broncos are set up well for the future, but age on the offensive line is an issue. Starters range in age from Quinn Meinerz (28) to Garett Bolles (34). Guard Kage Casey , a 2026 fourth-round pick, is the only offensive lineman Denver has selected in the past two drafts. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Ja'Quan McMillian will become the highest-paid nickel back in 2027 -- with Denver or another team. McMillian is an excellent slot corner on a good defense, allowing 1.0 yards per coverage snap (average) and minus-19 expected points added on targets (fourth best). He also spent 17% of time in tight coverage (third best), per NFL Next Gen Stats. -- Walder 5. Los Angeles Rams (Overall score: 85.3) Reason for hope: The Rams are tricky to rank because we don't know for certain whether coach Sean McVay, who has contemplated retirement, will stay in Los Angeles after quarterback Matthew Stafford hangs up the pads. The team is well positioned with so many good young players, and the duo of McVay and GM Les Snead duo has worked so well for so long. Even if the Stafford era ends soon, it'll likely end only on a Super Bowl run. -- Solak Reason for concern: Different season, same concern. Stafford now has an MVP award after what was in many ways the best statistical season of his career. But he is still year-to-year as far as the future goes. And though I am a big believer in the Rams' succession plan with Ty Simpson , the transition will not be easy. -- Riddick Nugget to know: The Rams already ranked eighth last season in pass rush win rate (40%) and first in run stop win rate (34%). Now, they'll have reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett (and possibly former DPOY Aaron Donald). -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: The Rams will lead the NFL in light offensive personnel in 2028. After shepherding the league into heavy usage of multiple tight ends, McVay will pivot again once the rest of the NFL -- and its defenses -- has caught up. By 2028, he'll presumably have a new quarterback and will need new advantages for him. One can only guess at what that will be, as McVay seems to find value in zigging when the rest of the league zags. -- Walder 6. New England Patriots (Overall score: 84.6) Reason for hope: Teams with elite quarterbacks on rookie contracts will never fall far down this list, and that's exactly what the Patriots have with Drake Maye . Throw in more blue-chip players at elite positions, such as cornerback ( Christian Gonzalez ) and defensive tackle ( Milton Williams ), and the Patriots have a wonderful bedrock to remain high in these rankings for the next decade. -- Solak Reason for concern: The 2025 season could not have gone much better, given the magnitude of the organizational reset that took place during the offseason. With the foundation now in place, the concern has to do with a specific area of the roster: the pass rush. If players such as second-rounder Gabe Jacas hit big, and Mike Vrabel's defensive staff can develop a diamond in the rough, such as seventh-rounder Quintayvious Hutchins , this team can continue to contend for Super Bowls. -- Riddick Nugget to know: After adjusting for era and schedule, Maye finished eighth among second-year quarterbacks in my DYAR (defense-adjusted yards above replacement) metric. The quarterbacks above him, in order, were Dan Marino, Patrick Mahomes , Lamar Jackson , Daunte Culpepper, Brock Purdy , Justin Herbert and Peyton Manning. Boomer Esiason was ninth. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: The Patriots will have a top-six pass-protecting offensive line, in terms of cumulative pass block win rate over those three seasons. It's a big leap for a unit that was a concern for New England. But the Patriots could have a strong O-line if Will Campbell and Caleb Lomu develop, Alijah Vera-Tucker stays healthy and Jared Wilson settles in at center ( Mike Onwenu is already established as a solid guard). -- Walder 7. Green Bay Packers (Overall score: 84.4) Reason for hope: Green Bay's yearly investment in young starters always leaves the Packers well-positioned for the future. Jordan Love is emerging into a Tier 2 quarterback alongside guys such as Dak Prescott and Justin Herbert , and Love's pass catchers ( Tucker Kraft , Christian Watson , Jayden Reed , Matthew Golden ) look as dangerous as ever. With a couple of hits on young offensive linemen ( Anthony Belton , Jordan Morgan ), Green Bay's passing attack should, once again, be one of the league's most potent. -- Solak Reason for concern: I remain concerned about the dependability and availability of those Love depends on, namely the wide receiver group. But the real elephant in the room is the availability of edge rusher Micah Parsons . What level of play will he return to after his ACL tear ? Green Bay has nobody on the roster who comes close to matching his physical profile. -- Riddick Nugget to know: For the second straight season, the Packers were the youngest team in the NFL by snap-weighted age in 2025. They ranked 30th on offense, 31st on defense and 29th on special teams. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Parsons will break Myles Garrett's single-season sack record . He has never exceeded 14.0 sacks in a season. But since he entered the league in 2021, he has a 29% career pass rush win rate -- much higher than the second-best player, Garrett, at 24.9%. If Garrett can record 23 sacks on the Browns, Parsons can exceed that on a better team in the Packers. -- Walder 8. Houston Texans (Overall score: 84.3) Reason for hope: The Texans were one of three elite defenses last season (along with Seattle and Denver), and almost the entire starting 11 were homegrown players under coach DeMeco Ryans. If you can set your watch to Ryans and GM Nick Caserio building a great defense, then the Texans can be a perennial team in the top 10 of these rankings. -- Solak Reason for concern: Though I am still concerned (as I was a year ago) about the future effectiveness of this revamped offensive line, it's quarterback C.J. Stroud who has to answer some questions. His playoff performance in 2025 was unacceptable from a decision-making, ball security and accuracy standpoint. Until he makes people forget what he put on tape to end the 2025 season, the concern will exist. -- Riddick Nugget to know: Despite being regarded as having one of the finest pass rushes in the NFL, the Texans finished a shocking 21st in pass rush win rate last season (35%) after ranking No. 1 in 2024 (49%). -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Cornerback Kamari Lassiter will earn more first-team All-Pro honors than cornerback Derek Stingley Jr . between 2027-2029. Both cornerbacks are amazing, but Lassiter is more underrated. He spent a higher percentage of time in tight coverage last season (22.3% of the time, sixth best among corners with at least 300 coverage snaps) and is an excellent run defender. -- Walder 9. Baltimore Ravens (Overall score: 83.7) Reason for hope: The Ravens haven't signed Lamar Jackson to an extension just yet, but it's fair to assume that the two-time MVP will remain a Raven and keep the team in a yearly contention conversation. And the infusion of new coach Jesse Minter could be just what Baltimore needs to get over the Lombardi hump. -- Solak Reason for concern: John Harbaugh was fired because the organization seemed to lose belief in his ability to guide the Ravens to postseason success. Now, the focus shifts to Minter. Can he return the defense to the levels of greatness of years past? In 2025, the Ravens couldn't rush the passer with consistency (28th in pass rush win rate) or prevent explosive plays of 20-plus yards (31st in NFL). -- Riddick Nugget to know: Wide receiver Zay Flowers accounted for 36.9% of all the Ravens' receiving yards last season, second in the NFL behind Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: The Ravens will trade Rashod Bateman in 2027. Other than a solid 2024 season (756 receiving yards), Bateman hasn't really lived up to his hype. Right now, the Ravens need him. But they have a slew of young players -- Ja'Kobi Lane , Devontez Walker and Elijah Sarratt -- who could ascend and take his targets. -- Walder 10. Los Angeles Chargers (Overall score: 83.5) Reason for hope: With an elite young passer in Justin Herbert and an elite coach in Jim Harbaugh, the Chargers are set up well for the future. How well Harbaugh and GM Joe Hortiz operate in lockstep is underappreciated. The lack of playoff success keeps Los Angeles lower on this list than it could be, but that should be rectified this season. -- Solak Reason for concern: For the past two seasons, I have been concerned about how the quality and upside of the receivers room has affected Herbert's career. Though I still have questions, my focus has shifted to the health and durability of the offensive line. If the starters can stay available, their league-worst pass block win rate and second-worst run block win rate should improve dramatically in future years. That's a must to keep Herbert from taking the hits he absorbed in 2025 (54 sacks, second most). -- Riddick Nugget to know: The Chargers have a young offense (average age of projected top-12 players is 25.5, second youngest) but an old defense (average age of projected top-12 players is 28.8, tied for oldest). -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Cornerback Tarheeb Still will earn first- or second-team All-Pro recognition at some point. The 2024 fifth-round pick has been impressive in the first two years of his career. Last season, he allowed just a 12% target rate and 0.7 yards per coverage snap. -- Walder 11. Kansas City Chiefs (Overall score: 83.2) Reason for hope: How far can a team with Patrick Mahomes at quarterback really fall? Questions abound regarding GM Brett Veach's recent drafting and head coach Andy Reid's antiquated scheme, but the Chiefs will always be Super Bowl contenders so long as No. 15 is healthy and under center. Such is the benefit of employing a generational talent. -- Solak Reason for concern: As great as Mahomes is, he needs a lot more help than what he has received over the past two seasons. I think Veach fixed the RB situation with Kenneth Walker III , but I am concerned about the WR position. My hope is 2026 fifth-rounder WR Cyrus Allen elevates into a primary target. Second-year receiver Jalen Royals could also develop into a bigger role. It's critical that this position becomes a more dependable and productive group. -- Riddick Nugget to know: The Chiefs led the NFL last season in playing man coverage, according to ESPN Research (58% of passes). That makes young cornerbacks, such as Mansoor Delane (22) and Nohl Williams (24 in September), very important to Kansas City's future. -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Mahomes will throw for 5,000 yards in a season again. No one -- let alone Mahomes -- has done it since he threw for 5,250 in 2022. This is just a little blind faith in the Chiefs finding their groove again in the passing game. -- Walder 12. Chicago Bears (Overall score: 82.8) Reason for hope: The Cardiac Bears proved last season what an elite coach (Ben Johnson) and ascendant young quarterback ( Caleb Williams ) could achieve at their peak. General manager Ryan Poles still needs to prove he can solve the defensive talent issues, but Johnson and Williams alone will keep the Bears in a strong position for all future projections -- especially if the third-year quarterback takes another step forward. -- Solak Reason for concern: The defense. Coordinator Dennis Allen is charged with improving a unit that was 29th in yards per play allowed and 31st in pass rush win rate last season. The Bears desperately need some 2026 rookies -- such as first-round safety Dillon Thieneman , fourth-round cornerback Malik Muhammad and sixth-round defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg -- to immediately make an impact. -- Riddick Nugget to know: The Bears ended 18.6% of defensive drives with a takeaway last season, the highest rate since the 2019 Steelers got a turnover on 20.3% of drives. (This is a stat that tends to regress toward the mean from year to year.) -- Schatz Bold prediction for 2027-29: Chicago will reach the Super Bowl at some point. I'm worried that the Bears are a little overhyped in 2026 because of the defense and Williams' accuracy issues last season. But I want to buy as much Johnson stock as I can. At some point in this window, the Bears will combine a good enough defense with a strong offense to win the NFC. -- Walder 13. Jacksonville Jaguars (Overall score: 82.6) Category Score NFL rank Overall Roster excluding QB 80.5 8 Quarterback 85.75 12<

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions LOS ANGELES -- The Dallas Cowboys and New Orleans Saints have each been fined $500,000 for multiple fights that occurred at Tuesday's joint practice. The NFL said on Tuesday that the Competition Committee has made sportsmanship a point of emphasis over the years, including sportsmanship at joint practices and the league told every team about that emphasis this summer. "All clubs were reminded by memo prior to training camp of their responsibility in preventing unsportsmanlike behavior at joint practices that has the potential to result in injury," a league spokesperson said in a statement Thursday. Fights occurred on both fields after the teams split up to work their offenses and defenses against each other. Punches were thrown on both fields, and play had to be stopped multiple times on one field due to Saints offensive players and Cowboys defensive players rushing over to join the fray. One player tossed a helmet in one instance and in another skirmish, a player was body-slammed to the ground. Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer and Saints coach Kellen Moore discussed at one point whether to call practice early, but they decided to end the session on time. Schottenheimer said earlier on Tuesday that the NFL had requested the film of the practice to review the altercations. Team fines are appealable. "Obviously there was a lot of non-football stuff in that joint practice unfortunately," Moore said on Thursday. "We had a clean one today [against the Rams], we had a clean one with Jacksonville last week. We had some really good work overall. Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones called the fine "stiff," although he said the club will appeal the penalty. "[The fine] does make the point that it's a serious matter and it starts with everybody at all levels of a club -- and the clubs in this case where two are practicing together," Jones said Thursday. "It really emphasizes the league's intent to control it from the very top, which when they start dealing out those kinds of fines, they get your attention." While there were two NFL officiating crews on hand for the practice, Jones said the lack of consequences in a practice can lead to things getting out of hand. "This game is physical and it's easy to get involved with aggressive temperaments," Jones said. "All of that makes it a real focal point in the league to stay within good sport. And taking of helmets off and swinging and hitting and that type of thing is not good for anybody and it's certainly not what we want to represent to our fans as a league or as a team. So it's understandable how they're coming down with a real severe fines." Jones said the Cowboys would fine their individual players, which is allowable under the CBA, that were involved in the fracases. Donovan Ezeiruaku was thrown out of practice for throwing a punch. It was the second time he was ejected for throwing a punch in training camp. "You have to have consequences and that needs to register," Jones said. "In other words, we all know whether you're playing a game or out here in society, if you aren't sensitive about the consequences of your behavior, then you'll get brought to your knees quick. This is something that, knowing him, I think he has the capability of being sensitive to consequences." ESPN's Todd Archer contributed to this story.

The Flint, Mich. native is a graduate of Western Michigan University and has authored/co-authored three books: "Wasted," "Ethan's Talent Search" and "All In: The Kelvin Torbert Story". Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ALLEN PARK, Mich. -- Sam LaPorta 's status for the Detroit Lions ' regular-season opener is unclear after he suffered a hip injury. The star tight end sustained the injury during a recent practice and has missed multiple practices this week. Lions coach Dan Campbell said the team will rest LaPorta to let things "calm down," acknowledging he is unsure if the four-year veteran will be available in Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints on Sept. 13. "It flared up a little bit, it's a little aggravated," Campbell said Thursday. "But we feel good long-term about him. We'll rest him for a little bit here and letting it calm down." Campbell was asked whether LaPorta's injury could potentially linger into the regular season. "I don't know," he said. "I feel like we'll be OK, but I don't know." LaPorta is expected to be a big part of the offense under new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing after returning from a season-ending back injury in 2025, when he missed eight games. He underwent surgery in November to repair a fully herniated disk but wasn't feeling any lingering pain throughout camp before suffering the recent hip injury. Lions quarterback Jared Goff has enjoyed having LaPorta back at practice throughout the majority of this camp, and Detroit won't rush him back to the field. LaPorta finished last season with 40 receptions for 489 yards and three touchdowns.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Aug 20, 2026, 02:11 PM ET Email Print Open Extended Reactions MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- Multiple players from Thursday's joint practice between the Miami Dolphins and New York Giants were pulled for throwing punches or their physical actions during a fight-filled workout. Dolphins offensive tackle Austin Jackson and Giants right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor were among those to be taken off the field. Jackson and Eluemumor were each replaced for at least a series. Quarterback Jameis Winston was also removed for a couple plays after being in the middle of a scrum. Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said before practice that any player who threw a punch would be kicked out, and that he'd be "very, very disappointed" if it came to that. The Giants and Dolphins had a handful of fights interrupt practice on the two fields at the Baptist Health Training Complex. At one point, scuffles occurred moments apart, with Giants coach John Harbaugh and Hafley shuffling fields to break them up. "In this sort of an environment, you have these rules of engagement that aren't really rules of the game, and then somebody else goes over the line or they do go over the line and somebody needs to protect somebody and that's where it goes. And I think as long as it doesn't get out of control, where it gets a violent-type situation, it's fine, you know?" Harbaugh said. "And we decided that anybody that threw a punch in those scrimmages would be treated like the game. That's why Jermaine didn't practice toward the end. He didn't really throw a hard punch, but it was to the face mask. And that'll get you in the game. That's a 15-yarder at least." Jackson threw a punch at Giants rookie linebacker Arvell Reese , and was shoved to the ground by Giants linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux immediately after making contact with Reese's helmet. In adherence to Hafley's rules, Jackson was removed from team drills and replaced by recently added offensive lineman Caedan Wallace . However, Jackson's removal was short-lived; he returned to the Dolphins' lineup during the final period of team drills. Miami's defense was extra-physical from the start, knocking multiple Giants players to the ground at the end of plays. It seemed to signal the way this joint practice was headed, on both sides of the ball. "I don't know which way Jeff's going to go about it, but we try to hold our composure as much as we can," Dolphins center Aaron Brewer said. "But when you out here playing football, it get chippy. As I said before, people are out there competing, taking it all the way to the edge. We didn't try to initiate anything, but if somebody come at you, you got to hold your ground." The Giants had a similar approach in a practice in which outside linebacker Brian Burns declared his unit "dominant." He said they had more than six sacks of quarterback Malik Willis during the practice. Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart also had one of his best practices of the summer, hitting several passes downfield and finding tight end Isaiah Likely consistently for solid gains. Dart also almost got into the mix after Winston was chirping during a fight and took a punch from a Dolphins defensive player. "I didn't see what happened," Dart said. "I just looked over and saw the red 19 jersey [Winston] and I was like, 'I gotta go. I gotta go help my boy! I don't know what's going on over there.'" The situation was quickly defused. It just temporarily stopped the action. Still, both sides thought it was a productive practice. "I think we leave the practice a better team than when we came in," Harbaugh said. "That was our goal."

She joined ESPN in 2016 to cover the Green Bay Packers for ESPN Milwaukee. She then moved to Houston to cover the Texans. She came to ESPN after working as a writer and editor for Sports Illustrated. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions LOS ANGELES -- Rams head coach Sean McVay said he anticipates more workouts from Aaron Donald before the defensive tackle decides whether to come out of retirement. Donald worked out at the Rams' Woodland Hills facility Saturday, his second time working out for the team this training camp. McVay said Donald has "earned the right" to take the time needed to make the decision but said he'd "love to be able to have all of this stuff kind of figured out." "I know he's feeling good and he will continue to work out and I'm hopeful that we'll have some answers on that sooner than later for you guys," McVay said. All training camp -- since McVay first acknowledged that Donald was going through a "very strict, regimented process" to determine whether he wanted to play for the Rams this season -- the head coach has been clear that this will take place on Donald's timeline. When asked about Donald's decision last week, McVay said: "I don't want to say too much or put some sort of invisible deadline on something that doesn't exist in my mind for him." Donald, who spent his entire 10-year career with the Rams before retiring in March 2024, first began to consider the option of returning to football after Los Angeles traded for reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett in early June.

She started covering the Bucs for ESPN in 2016, but she has covered the team since 2009. Jenna is a former cheerleader at the University of South Florida and speaks to the consistency of the program as being one of the top best in the nation. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions TAMPA, Fla. -- For Vita Vea , it was always Tampa -- even when he requested a trade and stood on the sideline as an observer for mandatory minicamp and the first 22 days of Tampa Bay Buccaneers training camp. "They say home is where the heart is. I feel like my heart is in Tampa," said Vea, who received a $6 million boost in pay for 2026 and a one-year extension worth $30 million in guaranteed money in 2027 . "I always wanted to be a Buc, and I wanted to be a Buc for life." Vea, who will make $48 million over the next two years, was asked to address his hold-in and trade request. "Yeah, it's just all part of the business," Vea said Thursday, his first public comments since the deal was finalized. "I got drafted here. I made it my home. I made Tampa my home. I love it here. The guys on the team are like brothers to me. We look at each other as family. So I didn't want to leave that behind and switch teams and get traded." Vea emphasized that leaving the Bucs was "never the end goal for me," adding that he "always wanted to be here." "It's just one of those things," he said. "They took a chance on me in the draft, and I've been here ever since. And I fell in love with Tampa. I fell in love with my teammates. I love the organization. Everybody who works here. I walk around every day with a smile on my face." The agreement came together Wednesday afternoon, and Vea signed the contract Thursday morning. But this was after three weeks of no movement, and after his agent Collin Roberts told the Tampa Bay Times that he didn't see how this could end in any other way but a trade. Bucs general manager Jason Licht said the front office did take calls from other teams but conveyed they had no intentions of trading him. The first preseason game against the New York Jets came and went. He traveled to New Jersey for joint practices but was a nonparticipant. The Bucs began their preparations for the second preseason game hosting the Kansas City Chiefs , a game in which all starters -- including quarterback Baker Mayfield -- will see anywhere from eight to 15 plays, coach Todd Bowles said. Vea won't see action Saturday, but at least the two-time Pro Bowler will play in 2026. That's the goal right now, Bowles said -- getting Vea ready for Week 1 of the regular season at the Cincinnati Bengals on Sept. 13, while nursing a back injury that he sustained during the team's conditioning test on July 28. "We're going to start working him in next week slowly, preparing him for Cincinnati," Bowles said. "There's no way he plays against Jacksonville [in the third preseason game] or anything like that, but we're going to acclimate him and kind of work him in, trying to get him ready for opening day." Vea, one of the most critical players on Bowles' defense and a key piece of their Super Bowl LV championship, was originally set to earn $18 million in 2026. But compared to a defensive tackle market that had virtually exploded the last couple of years, the 347-pound Vea saw his deal fall well below market value. Things had changed dramatically from the time Vea inked that four-year, $71 million extension in January 2022 -- fifth among interior defensive tackles at the time -- to the end of last month. At that point, roughly 18 to 19 players were making more money. Vea also no longer had any guaranteed money remaining on the deal. In 2024, Chris Jones re-signed with the Chiefs for five years and $158.75 million, averaging $31.75 million per season. At the beginning of 2026, Jeffery Simmons re-signed with the Tennessee Titans for three years and $105.8 million, averaging $35.28 million per season. Then in July, Quinnen Williams signed an extension with the Dallas Cowboys for three years and $105.9 million, averaging $35.3 million per season. Next came Jalen Carter , re-signing with the Philadelphia Eagles for four years and $152 million, averaging $38 million per season. Vea said he's happy for his peers. "It feels really good to get that recognition. Hats off to those guys," Vea said. "They're hell of a players. But in today's game, I feel like a lot of the work we do -- we do a lot of the dirty work. So it feels good to get recognized for it." Vea has done a lot of work behind the scenes in camp too -- from assisting teammates with blocking drills to his daily encouragement of cornerback Benjamin Morrison . The 2025 second-round draft pick has been navigating his second hamstring injury, on top of undergoing bilateral hip surgery just before the draft, and Vea too dealt with injuries early on in his career. "He's dealt with a lot in the past year or so," Vea said. "And as an older guy in this league, you look at his game, it's like no one's going to leave this game unscathed, everybody deals with injuries. "So it's just, you understand the process of everything. So being able to see and understand what he's going through, I think just being there for someone like that and just trying to help him out through this process. I'm just trying to be there for my teammates and be able to give them a path to help them be the best they could be." Vea conveyed just how deep his level of loyalty is not only to the team, but also to Bowles, who helped him sharpen the mental side of his game. "We had a level of understanding," Vea said. "Every day we talked. It'd mainly be about football. Sometimes when you're not practicing, you see a lot more of everything that's going on. So it's basically just being able to pick his brain and see what he's thinking on certain plays and able to help me out in the long run with when we get things rolling here in the season." Vea even went as far as linking their careers when asked to explain what he thought led to Tampa Bay's 8-9 finish last year, saying: "The day [Bowles] retires is the day I retire." But ultimately, Vea is grateful to have the contract dispute behind him. His teammates certainly were too, as were other coaches, dapping him up before and after practice. Mayfield is all that's left for the front office to work out, but at least he's set to play in 2026, as is Vea. "It's just one of those things, you'd love to get compensated and feel that your work is appreciated," Vea said. "Obviously in this league, the market goes up and that's what happened. So we just had to work some things out and we ended up getting it resolved."

Nick has covered the San Francisco 49ers since 2016, having previously covered the St. Louis Rams for 12 years, including three years (2013 to 2015) at ESPN. In over a decade with the company, Nick has led ESPN's coverage of the Niners' 2019 and 2023 Super Bowl run, Colin Kaepernick's protest, the Rams making Michael Sam the first openly gay player drafted to the NFL, Sam's subsequent pursuit of a roster spot and the team's relocation and stadium saga. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- After wrapping up his reunion with the San Francisco 49ers early in free agency, linebacker Dre Greenlaw quickly turned his attention to recruiting. More specifically, Greenlaw thought the offense could use an enforcer similar to him. He soon reached out to wide receiver Deebo Samuel Sr ., who, like him, had once been a focal point of the 49ers' culture, departed for one season and was a free agent. Greenlaw's message was simple: There's unfinished business in San Francisco, and he and Samuel can help the team finish it. "[I said] 'Let's have a reunion, let's do this thing together,'" Greenlaw said. "This place is just about football ... Sometimes you got to go and go see what's out there, but once you go, you realize, hey, it ain't nothing like San Fran." Although Samuel didn't re-sign with the Niners until July 30, the warm reception he got when he returned to the building was similar to the one Greenlaw got when he arrived for the offseason program in April. "It felt like I never left," Samuel said. "They were happy. I was happy. We were ready to get the ball rolling." Both Samuel and Greenlaw are slated to slot back into their prominent roles for the 49ers. Greenlaw will start at weakside linebacker, which was further solidified when the 49ers traded away his replacement ( Dee Winters ) in April. Samuel will again have a varied role at receiver, running back and kick returner for a depleted skill group. And while they might not be as impactful as they were in their first stint with the team, there's no denying the intangible boost that San Francisco sought in adding Greenlaw and Samuel back into the fold. "Those are two just bullies on the offense and the defense," fullback Kyle Juszczyk said. "Guys that set the tone, guys that really motivate others just by the way that they play, the physical nature that both of them play with. And I'm so happy to have both of them." It was about a year and a half ago that Samuel and Greenlaw, both members of the 49ers' 2019 draft class, departed for other opportunities. The Niners attempted to keep Greenlaw in free agency, but he ultimately opted for a three-year, $31.5 million deal with the Broncos. Samuel, meanwhile, had requested a trade after a turbulent 2024 season, and he was eventually traded to the Commanders for a 2025 fifth-round pick. Neither player necessarily found the grass to be greener elsewhere. In Denver, Greenlaw again dealt with injuries. He missed eight games of quadriceps and hamstring issues, and he served a one-game suspension in Week 8 for unsportsmanlike conduct toward a referee. Greenlaw called the season "real tough" and acknowledged that he often found himself longing for what he had in San Francisco alongside Fred Warner , his close friend and fellow linebacker. By the end of the regular season, Greenlaw had 43 tackles, a sack, an interception and a forced fumble while playing 38.6 snaps per game. The Broncos released him on March 12, and he agreed to a one-year, $7.5 million deal with the Niners the next day. There's never been a question of Greenlaw's impact -- including the postseason, the 49ers were 52-24 and allowed 20 points per game when he played -- but injuries have long been an issue. He missed 36 games in his first six seasons with the team because of various injuries. After tearing his Achilles during Super Bowl LVIII, Greenlaw only made two more appearances for San Francisco before departing for Denver. The 49ers have been accordingly cautious with Greenlaw in hopes of having him healthy to open the season. "I haven't felt this good since about a month before the Super Bowl," Greenlaw said. "It's been just one [injury] after one after another, one after another. And I just been playing catch up the whole time. But now I just feel like I'm where I need to be now as far as just body, health wise, everything." Samuel's lone season in Washington was more fruitful than Greenlaw's in Denver. Samuel played in 16 games, leading the Commanders in catches (72), receiving yards (727) and receiving touchdowns (five). Of course, he made an impact on the ground with 17 carries, 75 rushing yards and one rushing touchdown. Despite the Commanders letting him walk, Samuel had nothing negative to say about his time in Washington but made it clear he was happy to be back with the 49ers. Over the past couple of seasons, questions about Samuel's conditioning have arisen as he's struggled to produce consistently. According to left tackle Trent Williams , one of Samuel's closest friends who was in contact with him weekly throughout his time in Washington, that could change this season. Samuel returned to the Niners in what Williams calls "probably the best shape I've seen him in since I've known him." "I know he's coming from a situation where he feels people doubt his ability," Williams said. "You put that extra doubt to him, that extra fuel to his fire, I think he's going to be a lot better." Throughout the preseason, those who have played with Samuel and Greenlaw before recognize many of the tone-setting traits they brought to San Francisco the first time. They also see a renewed chip on the shoulder, in no small part because of San Francisco's inability to win a Super Bowl, that should only further inflame the fuel Williams mentioned. "The good thing about it, they got something to prove," safety Ji'Ayir Brown said. "Deebo has something to prove. Dre has something to prove. And not to nobody else, not to no outsiders, more to themselves." In this training camp, Samuel has lined up at running back again and got the ball in space in a variety of ways. He is also taking on the kick return role, which he only did sparingly in his first stint but featured in for the Commanders last season (30.1 average yards per return). Greenlaw has resumed his role as the enforcer, though age (29 years old) has brought the wisdom to know when to pump the brakes. At one practice, he hit star running back Christian McCaffrey near the sideline. McCaffrey took exception, threw the ball and shoved Greenlaw back. Greenlaw didn't retaliate, realizing what he'd done and who he had pushed. McCaffrey didn't mind and counts Greenlaw among his favorite players in the league. That's a sentiment shared by the entire team, which is looking forward to Samuel leading them out of the tunnel pregame and Greenlaw flying around the field unafraid to take on anyone who tries him or his teammates. "To be able to bring back some enforcers like that who play exactly how we want everybody to play, those are two special dudes," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "I haven't been around two people like that in my career, really, who play that way. That stuff's huge. Just knowing they're in here gets guys pumped up. They've been away for a year, but to see them out there, they look exactly like the guys I remember."
