New England Patriots 2d Mike Reiss What we're hearing and seeing at Browns training camp: Watson delivers a must-see throw in practice vs. Bills Cleveland Browns 1h Daniel Oyefusi Cowboys: Jerry Jones shares camp thoughts as team leaves Oxnard Friday 56m Todd Archer Seahawks: CB Diggs talks for first time since signing 56m Brady Henderson Patriots: Maye pleased after two practices with Eagles 56m Mike Reiss Giants: Jaxson Dart's best performance of the summer? 1h Jordan Raanan Fantasy football rankings: Eric Karabell's RB tiers 13h Eric Karabell Fantasy football rankings: Eric Karabell's WR tiers 13h Eric Karabell Solak: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense is much more than just Caleb Williams Chicago Bears 2d Ben Solak Hallmark, hot dogs and touchdowns: The Colston Loveland story Chicago Bears 2d Courtney Cronin NFL Future Power Rankings: We stacked all 32 teams based on expectations for 2027 to 2029 Kansas City Chiefs 4d Louis Riddick, +3 More NFL preseason on NFL Network, ESPN: How to watch, schedule 20d ESPN play What is the state of the Browns' QB competition? (1:24) Dan Graziano Aug 20, 2026, 06:30 AM ET Close Dan Graziano is a senior NFL national reporter for ESPN, covering the entire league and breaking news. Dan also contributes to Get Up, NFL Live, SportsCenter, ESPN Radio, Sunday NFL Countdown and Fantasy Football Now. He is a New Jersey native who joined ESPN in 2011, and he is also the author of two published novels. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions While everyone else is predicting who's going to start at quarterback for various teams next month, we're looking beyond this entire 2026 NFL season to figure out where the QB questions are going to be next year . Several of the NFL's teams are entering critical seasons with their quarterback situations. Some have no idea how they'll make it through this season with what they have on the roster. Some feel confident about this season but don't know how things will shake out for 2027. The smart teams are thinking ahead, even as they prepare for 2026. So every year, we try to pick a dozen or so teams whose long-term QB situations appear to be in flux and examine what's most likely to happen in the short and long terms. We try to stay away from situations in which contracts make change extremely unlikely. For example, you might say this is an important year for Dak Prescott to break through in the postseason for Dallas. And in some ways you might be right. But in terms of Prescott's long-term future with the team, that is not the case. He's signed through 2028, he has $45 million in fully guaranteed salary for 2027, and various restructures have created a dead-money situation that makes him virtually uncuttable or untradeable. He's not on this year's list. Lamar Jackson wasn't on last year's list , because at the time he had three years left on his contract with the Ravens, and there wasn't any doubt he'd be on the team in 2026. This year, however, he has two years left on his deal. And while the Ravens said they wanted to get him extended this offseason, they could not reach an agreement. That ratchets up the uncertainty on Jackson for 2027 and beyond, so we included him just to flag the circumstances and examine them a bit. If Jackson signs a new extension with the Ravens in the next few days, things change. But unless and until that extension gets done, we have license to wonder. That's just a fact. Last year we started with Arizona ... and we're starting there again. Jump to a team: ARI | ATL | BAL | CAR | CLE | DET HOU | IND | LAR | MIA | MIN | NYJ PHI | PIT | SEA | TB Arizona Cardinals Current starter: Jacoby Brissett Signed through: 2026 The Cardinals have a new head coach in former Rams offensive coordinator Mike LaFleur. He inherits Brissett, who finished the 2025 season as Arizona's starter and played well under previous offensive coordinator Drew Petzing. But Brissett and the Cardinals spent the spring and summer in a contract standoff that resulted in a roughly $10 million raise over the roughly $5 million he had been scheduled to make this season under his previous deal. The team also signed seven-year NFL veteran Gardner Minshew II in free agency and drafted former Georgia/Miami quarterback Carson Beck with the first pick of the third round of this year's NFL draft. Of those three options, the only one under contract beyond 2026 is Beck, who played well in the Cardinals' first preseason game before sitting out the second because of a rib injury . The Cardinals have won four or fewer games in three of their past four seasons and are projected for the second-lowest win total (5) in ESPN's Football Power Index projections for 2026. Most likely outcome: They start the season with Brissett and struggle. They switch to Beck at some point during the season to give him an audition and find out whether he can be part of the long-term solution. They secure a very high pick in the 2027 draft and use it on one of the highly touted quarterbacks in that class -- someone they believe can be a franchise cornerstone. Long-shot outcome: Some combination of Brissett and Beck keeps the Cardinals competitive, even in a division where the other three teams each won at least 12 games last season (and one won the Super Bowl). They don't end up with a high draft pick, and they see enough from Beck to open 2027 with him as the starter. Atlanta Falcons Current starter: Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr . Signed through: Tagovailoa, 2026; Penix, 2027 plus a team option for 2028 The Falcons are ostensibly having a competition this summer for their starting job between Penix, who was the eighth pick in the 2024 draft, and Tagovailoa, who was released by the Dolphins this offseason. The Falcons were able to sign Tagovailoa for a veterans minimum salary because the Dolphins are on the hook for nearly $55 million in guaranteed salary for this year. Penix was their starter at the beginning of 2025 but is coming off a torn ACL . Because Penix hasn't been cleared for 11-on-11 team drills, this "competition" hasn't really gotten off the ground. And unless Penix gets out there soon, Tagovailoa will become the Week 1 starter by default. Tagovailoa wasn't good in the Falcons' first preseason game last weekend, but the new coaching staff under Kevin Stefanski likes his fit in the offense and believes Atlanta can get him ready in time for Week 1. No matter what happens, though, there's uncertainty beyond this season. Tagovailoa signed for only one year. Unlike Kyler Murray , who was in a similar situation when Arizona cut him with guaranteed money left on his deal and signed with Minnesota, Tagovailoa doesn't have a clause in his contract prohibiting his new team from using its franchise tag on him after this season. So if Tagovailoa played well and the Falcons wanted to keep him, they could -- but they aren't committed to it. play 1:10 Canty on Browns QB battle: Shedeur should start Week 1 of regular season As for Penix, the Falcons have to decide by the first week of May 2027 whether to pick up (and fully guarantee) his option for 2028. They'll need more information than they currently have on him before making that decision. Ideally, they'll see him play at some point this season. It's also worth noting that both of these players have significant injury histories. Tagovailoa has missed 20 games because of injury over the course of his six-year NFL career, and Penix suffered four season-ending injuries during his college career and then another last year in the NFL. Most likely outcome: Tagovailoa starts the season but struggles with health and/or performance, and the Falcons turn to Penix once he is healthy to continue their assessment of whether he can be their long-term answer. The new front office and coaching staff that took over following the 2025 season selects a QB early in the 2027 draft, either to develop behind Penix or to replace him if Atlanta has decided he isn't the answer. Long-shot outcome: Tagovailoa turns out to be an excellent fit for Stefanski's offense and has a good year. The Falcons win the NFC South for the first time since 2016 and make the playoffs for the first time since 2017. After the season, the Falcons and Tagovailoa agree on a Daniel Jones - or Baker Mayfield -style contract extension that keeps him there a couple of years more. Baltimore Ravens Current starter: Lamar Jackson Signed through: 2027 Two-time league MVP Jackson is making $52 million this year and $52 million in 2027, though none of the 2027 money is guaranteed. His contract contains void years in 2028 through 2030 for cap accounting purposes, but it voids after the 2027 season. It also includes a no-trade clause and a clause prohibiting the team from designating him its franchise or transition player. So if Jackson plays out the current deal and doesn't extend it, he'll hit free agency in March 2028, and the Ravens wouldn't be able to do a thing about it. Baltimore tried to do an extension with Jackson this spring in an effort to lower his 2026 cap hit, but it was unable to get a deal done. So it ended up lowering that cap hit by about $40 million through a simple restructure . As a result, his cap hit for 2027 is now projected to be $84.3 million, which means the Ravens have to either extend him or restructure the contract again next spring in order to save cap room. Jackson is coming off a down year by his own lofty standards, as he missed four games because of injury, and his 62.7 QBR was the second lowest he has posted in any season since his 2018 rookie year. The Ravens finished under .500, missed the playoffs and fired longtime head coach John Harbaugh. The new head coach is former Chargers defensive coordinator Jessie Minter, who brought in first-time offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. Jackson, according to multiple sources, has been all-in this offseason, showing an enthusiasm for Doyle's offense and what he can do in it. Again, he could sign a contract extension any day now. We just don't know. Most likely outcome: Jackson stays healthy and has a great year under Minter and Doyle. The Ravens return to the playoffs, everyone's feeling good and refreshed, and Jackson and the team get together next spring to do a brand-new contract extension that makes Jackson the highest-paid quarterback in the league. All of this worry turns out to have been for nothing. Long-shot outcome: The season doesn't go the way Jackson or the Ravens hoped, and extension talks next spring get testy. Armed with the leverage of the no-franchise-tag clause, Jackson drives a hard bargain, and the Ravens decide they don't want to meet his price. They're forced to decide whether to let him play out the final year of his contract and hit free agency in 2028, or to trade him before 2027. Even in this latter case, Jackson would still hold the cards; he has that no-trade clause and could dictate his preferred destination. Carolina Panthers Current starter: Bryce Young Signed through: 2027 The Panthers picked up Young's 2027 fifth-year option for the price of $25.9 million -- a no-brainer because it means they have to pay him a total of only $32 million over the next two seasons. What comes next for the No. 1 pick of the 2023 draft is the question. Young was eligible for an extension this offseason, but he still doesn't have one, and indications are the team wants to see continued development in 2026 before deciding what to do long term. The Panthers aren't the only team taking this approach (see: Houston Texans , a little further down this list), but it does result in some level of uncertainty when we talk about what's to come after this season. Young has shown a lot of improvement since being benched early in the 2024 season, and he played well down the stretch last season as the Panthers won the NFC South and lost a close game to the Rams in the wild-card round of the playoffs . Both publicly and behind the scenes, the Panthers have maintained their belief in Young and focused their past two offseasons on finding ways to build out the group around him to give him the best possible chance to be successful. If Young and Carolina each take another step forward in 2026, extension talks should get serious next spring. Most likely outcome: The Panthers have a season similar to 2025 (maybe a little bit better) but miss the playoffs because their division got stronger around them. Young continues to show signs that he can be the guy, and without another obvious option, the Panthers extend him next spring with a contract that falls closer to the Daniel Jones range in terms of average annual salary than it does to the Dak Prescott tier. Long-shot outcome: Young and the Panthers take a massive leap forward, winning the division for the second year in a row (with a winning record this time), and Young breaks the bank next summer with a contract extension that places him among the highest-paid players in the league. Cleveland Browns Current starter: Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders Signed through: Watson, 2026; Sanders, 2028 Watson has finally arrived at the fifth and final season of one of the worst contracts in NFL history -- the fully guaranteed $230 million deal the Browns gave him when they traded three first-round picks to Houston to get him in 2022. He has played a grand total of 19 games over the first four years of the contract, and not a single one since tearing his Achilles in October 2024. The Browns have restructured his contract every year for cap space, which means that if he plays out this season and they don't re-sign him, they'd be dealing with $86.2 million in dead money either next year or split up over the next two years. Watson has as many touchdown passes (19) as games played with Cleveland, and the team is 26-42 since acquiring him (9-10 in games he started for them). Sanders, meanwhile, started the Browns' final seven games as a rookie last season, throwing seven touchdown passes to 10 interceptions, posting an abysmal 18.9 QBR and going 3-4. He has been a lightning rod of debate since before he was drafted; many projected him to be a first-round pick, and his slide into the fifth round spawned countless theories and arguments that are still raging 16 months later. play 0:53 Why Daniel Dopp says Jared Goff's ceiling is capped in fantasy Watson has shown new head coach Todd Monken and his staff this offseason that he's healthy and can run the offense. Sanders has shown growth throughout the spring and summer, and he has impressed Monken with his improvement since the spring. Watson started the team's first preseason game last week, and Monken has said Sanders will get the opportunity to start this weekend's game against the Bills before the team decides which of them will start in Week 1. Most likely outcome: Watson opens the season as the starter, the team loses a lot of games, and Sanders takes over at some point. The Browns finish with one of the worst records in the league, and neither of these guys is in the mix to be their 2027 starter. Armed with two first-round picks, the Browns secure one of the top quarterbacks in the draft and reset once again at the position, hoping they've finally found their long-term answer. Long-shot outcome: Watson struggles early, leading to Sanders taking over. He plays well and leads the Browns into playoff contention, costing them a chance to pick high in the first round. (Their other first-rounder is the Rams' pick, which we also don't expect to be high.) The Browns go into the 2027 offseason trying to figure out whether Sanders has shown enough to be their long-term starter or whether they need to bring in competition for him. And in the end, they continue to wander the QB wilderness as they have all century. Detroit Lions Current starter: Jared Goff Signed through: 2028 Goff has been everything the Lions hoped and more since they acquired him as part of the Matthew Stafford trade following the 2020 season. He missed three games in his first season in Detroit but has started every game since -- and the Lions are 48-33-1 when Goff starts. They've had a winning record in each of the past four seasons, and they won the NFC North in 2023 (12-5) and 2024 (15-2). But they dropped to 9-8 last season and missed the playoffs. Goff is making $55 million this season. He's scheduled to earn $40 million in 2027, of which $18 million is already guaranteed. None of his $47 million compensation for 2028 is guaranteed. And Detroit's backups at the moment are veteran Joshua Dobbs and undrafted rookie Luke Altmyer . play 1:38 Daniel Jones to McAfee: I'm feeling good, no limitations Most likely outcome: The Lions, with a stacked roster and a soft-looking schedule, bounce back to the top of the division and make a playoff run behind Goff and their elite offense. Next offseason, they elect to keep Goff on his current contract and push off a possible extension to the 2028 offseason. Maybe they look to the draft for a developmental prospect, but at age 32 and still playing well, Goff remains their best and preferred option. Long-shot outcome: The defensive injuries are too much to overcome, and Goff and the offense hit a snag. The Lions fail to take advantage of that soft schedule and miss the playoffs for the second year in a row. Frustrated by their inability to cash in on what seemed like a Super Bowl window, the Lions decide to break things up. They move on from Goff and bring in a veteran whose situation elsewhere fell apart, such as Baker Mayfield or Jalen Hurts . Houston Texans Current starter: C.J. Stroud Signed through: 2027 Much of what we wrote about Bryce Young in the Panthers section above also applies here. Stroud was the second pick of the 2023 draft, and he is eligible for an extension for the first time this offseason. But the Texans, who are as aggressive as any team in the league with their veteran contract extensions, have not given him one. They did pick up his 2027 fifth-year option because it made sense, but they also seem to want to see more before handing him a long-term commitment. It's easy to see both sides. Stroud was Offensive Rookie of the Year in 2023. He led the Texans to the second round of the playoffs in each of his first three seasons. Including the postseason, the Texans are 31-21 in games he has started. There are quarterbacks who got top-of-market extensions to their rookie deals having accomplished far less than Stroud. However, he has yet to repeat the outstanding performance of his rookie season, and he missed three games last season because of injury. Plus, his play in the Texans' two playoff games was detrimental. He had an interception and five fumbles (two lost) in Houston's wild-card victory over Pittsburgh, then he threw four interceptions the following week in a season-ending loss at New England. The Texans have an elite championship-caliber defense. They have a deep and talented group of receivers, even after Jayden Higgins tore an ACL this week. They have continuity on the offensive line for the first time in Stroud's career, and the addition of David Montgomery this offseason has them believing they can also give Stroud a competent run game for the first time. This shapes up as a critical year for Stroud's future in Houston, and he appears to have what he needs to put the disappointment of last season behind him. Most likely outcome: The Texans are strong playoff contenders, maybe even winning their division for the third time in four years since drafting Stroud. He rebounds and looks more like his rookie self than his January 2026 self. Houston rewards him next year with a long-term contract extension. Long-shot outcome: Stroud totally flops in Year 4. Either because of injury or ineffectiveness, he finishes the season on the bench as Davis Mills steps in to replace him. Houston misses the playoffs and brings in someone else -- either a draft pick or a free agent -- to compete with Stroud in camp in 2027 as the extension talks remain on hold. Indianapolis Colts Current starter: Daniel Jones Signed through: 2027 A former Giants first-round pick, Jones signed with the Colts ahead of the 2025 season and played lights out. Through the first 10 weeks of the season, the Colts were 8-2 and had one of the best offenses in the league. Jones was winning with his arm and his legs, and things looked fantastic. Then, as he seemingly always has, Jones got hurt . At first, he played through a significant leg injury, and his performance suffered. Then in Week 14, Jones tore an Achilles tendon and had to miss the rest of the season. The Colts lost their final seven games of the season to finish 8-9 and miss the playoffs. However, Jones is back surprisingly quickly. He has been a full participant in training camp practices, and reports out of Indianapolis say he's playing and moving as if nothing ever happened. All signs point to him being ready to start the season, and the Colts re-signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract this offseason because they believe he can again do what he did over the first half of last season and make them contenders. play 1:37 Why Orlovsky doesn't blame Kevin O'Connell for Vikings' QB struggles Jones' deal included a $44 million signing bonus and $5.5 million in 2026 salary. He's slated to make another $38 million if he's on the team in 2027, but of that money, none is fully guaranteed and only about $10.5 million is guaranteed against injury. So, if the Colts wanted to cut a healthy Jones after this season, they'd have paid him $49.5 million for one year. If he were injured and the team wanted to cut him, he'd have cost $60 million for one season. Not ideal, certainly, but if things go badly and the Colts identify a better option in the offseason, they can work around it. Most likely outcome: I hate to say a thing like this, and we all hope it doesn't happen, but Jones' history tells us the most likely outcome is that he misses time again. Jones has played 16 games in a season exactly once in his seven-year career. He has had leg and neck injuries, and he's currently coming back from the extremely serious injury he suffered in December. Obviously everyone hopes he gets through the season healthy, but he almost never does. So, the most likely outcome is that Jones is in and out of the lineup throughout the season, and the Colts have to decide next offseason whether to bring him back or move on. Their final win-loss record, and whatever decisions ownership makes about the futures of the coaching staff and the front office, will likely determine Jones' future in Indianapolis. Long-shot outcome: Last season's first half was not a mirage. Jones completes a fully healthy season for the first time since 2022. The Colts win their division for the first time since 2014, and they give Jones a longer extension worth more than $50 million per year. Los Angeles Rams Current starter: Matthew Stafford Signed through: 2027 Stafford is 38 years old and turns 39 one week before the Super Bowl -- which the Rams are currently favored to win. He is the reigning league MVP, and he got a contract extension this offseason that ties him to the Rams through 2027 and guarantees him $40 million this year and $50 million next year. So ... why are the Rams in this piece? Well, again, because he's 38 years old, and he's going to take some time to decide whether he wants to keep playing each offseason from here on out. By all accounts, Stafford is healthy, rejuvenated and thinking about playing two more years. But he also has a degenerative back condition , has already won a Super Bowl and has made more money than he could ever possibly need. Stafford walking away after this coming season would not be the biggest shock in NFL history. And the Rams know they don't have much longer with Stafford, which is why they used their 2026 first-round pick on quarterback Ty Simpson . Most likely outcome: The Rams have the awesome season everyone is expecting of them after the splashy acquisition of Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and the looming possible addition of Aaron Donald. Maybe they win the Super Bowl, maybe they fall just short. But either way, Stafford gets to the end of the season feeling fine and decides to play again in 2027. Long-shot outcome: The Rams flop. Health issues plague Stafford and several of the other older stars on the roster. The Rams fall well short of the Super Bowl. Star wideout Puka Nacua never gets his contract extension, and the offseason opens with questions about whether he'll leave in free agency. The Sean McVay TV rumors percolate again. And a banged-up Stafford decides it's all too much and walks away with that one year left on his contract. Miami Dolphins Current starter: Malik Willis Signed through: 2028 Everything is new in Miami. The new GM (Jon-Eric Sullivan) and new head coach (Jeff Hafley) both come from Green Bay, where Willis was the backup quarterback to Jordan Love the past two years and played well when Love was hurt. They signed Willis to a three-year, $67.5 million contract , of which $45 million is guaranteed (including $21.5 million in 2027 salary). Willis is, however, still a speculative play. He has started a total of six NFL games across four seasons since the Titans selected him in the third round of the 2022 draft. He has plenty of talent, and the time spent in Green Bay with Matt LaFleur and that staff seemed to improve his game in many ways. But neither we nor the Dolphins know for sure whether he can hold up as a full-season starter. Add to that the fact that the Dolphins stripped down their roster a fair bit this offseason, including trading away receiver Jaylen Waddle and releasing receiver Tyreek Hill . Willis is left with an inexperienced receiving corps and a rebuilding team that's projected for a league-low 4.8 wins, according to ESPN's Football Power Index. If he flops, sure, that $21.5 million guarantee in 2027 won't be fun. But the Dolphins are taking massive dead-money cap hits this season in order to keep the books clean for future years. If Willis shows he's not up to this, moving on from him (or just benching him) in 2027 wouldn't be financially prohibitive. Most likely outcome: The Dolphins finish as one of the worst teams in the league, and while Willis has his moments, he doesn't do enough to dissuade them from picking one of the star quarterbacks in the 2027 draft class. Long-shot outcome: The season ends, and Lamar Jackson still doesn't have that contract extension with Baltimore. Negotiations between Jackson and the Ravens get ugly again, and Baltimore trades him to his hometown Dolphins next March. Minnesota Vikings Current starter: Kyler Murray Signed through: 2026 If you're the kind of person who reads articles like this, you probably don't need too much of a refresher on the Vikings' quarterback situation. After 2024 first-round pick J.J. McCarthy flopped in his first year as a starter, the Vikings brought in Murray, who was cut by the Cardinals. Because Arizona owed Murray about $37 million in guaranteed money, Minnesota signed him for a one-year, league-minimum contract . Murray's agent did, however, negotiate a clause into the deal that prohibits the Vikings from using the franchise or transition tag on Murray next offseason. So, if he plays well and the Vikings want to keep him around, they're going to have to fight off other teams to do it. McCarthy, meanwhile, is signed through 2027. The team holds an option for 2028, but unless McCarthy finds his way into enough games and plays well in them in 2026, it's hard to see on what basis they could pick that up. The team also brought back veteran Carson Wentz , who could be a candidate to back up Murray depending on what McCarthy is showing in practice. But Wentz is signed through only 2026. After this year, Minnesota's QB situation looks completely wide open. play 1:07 Orlovsky: Criticism of Jalen Hurts at training camp is 'outrageous' Most likely outcome: As with every quarterback other than McCarthy who has played for Kevin O'Connell in Minnesota, Murray plays well and has the Vikings in playoff contention. Dylan Buell/Getty Images Eric Karabell Aug 20, 2026, 06:37 AM ET Close Eric Karabell is a senior writer covering fantasy football, baseball and basketball at ESPN. Eric is a charter member of the FSWA Hall of Fame, a BBWAA baseball Hall of Fame voter and author of "The Best Philadelphia Sports Arguments." Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Fantasy football managers need all the help they can get with the frenetic pace of a draft and/or salary cap setting. Preparation is key, and one of the best ways to organize for success is to utilize a positional tiered system to find the so-called peaks and valleys of the available player list. Group players by expected production and distinguish where the talent -- really, the value -- drops off, then capitalize on limited supply versus demand. Prepare. Attack. Exploit. Command. Win. Simple rankings fail to discern how much better -- or more valuable -- one player might be from the next. A fantasy manager nearing his or her fourth-round pick sees a jumble of choices and must make a decision in a short amount of time. A tiered system might reveal one wide receiver left in a certain tier, compared to a crew of three or four at running back. Pick the wide receiver. Perhaps the most critical part of any tiered system is that the decisions are yours . Oh sure, one analyst's tiers at wide receiver appear below (here is that same analyst's RB tiers ), but these are your fantasy teams. Participate in myriad mock drafts , study and analyze however it is you study and analyze, look forward and not backward, recognize what you believe should determine the order for rankings and tiers. Then, dominate your drafts. Check out all of the tiered rankings: QB | RB | WR | TE Tier 1: Early first round 1. Ja'Marr Chase , Cincinnati Bengals 2. Puka Nacua , Los Angeles Rams 3. Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Seattle Seahawks 4. Amon-Ra St. Brown , Detroit Lions Some might quibble with the order, as Nacua outscored the others last season, or whether St. Brown belongs in this section, but these four players have distinguished themselves properly. Chase and Nacua are worthy No. 1 overall selections. Tier 2: Rounds 1/2 play 1:03 Liz Loza: Justin Jefferson is an 'incredible steal' at his lowest-ever ADP 5. CeeDee Lamb , Dallas Cowboys 6. Justin Jefferson , Minnesota Vikings 7. Drake London , Atlanta Falcons 8. Nico Collins , Houston Texans Question marks start earlier than usual at WR, as Lamb has missed several games in consecutive seasons, Jefferson had no chance with his quarterback play in 2025 and London might have difficulty with quarterback play this year . Still, few can argue the talent within this group. Tier 3: Round 2 9. Chris Olave , New Orleans Saints 10. Garrett Wilson , New York Jets 11. A.J. Brown , New England Patriots 12. George Pickens , Cowboys Brown, joining his third franchise, might seem set to slide a bit based on his prior achievements, but he remains reliable. Wilson should have better QB play this season. Pickens is the first of the No. 2 WRs on his own team to arrive, but he is worthy and motivated. Tier 4: Rounds 3/4 13. Zay Flowers , Baltimore Ravens 14. DeVonta Smith , Philadelphia Eagles 15. Davante Adams , Rams 16. Tetairoa McMillan , Carolina Panthers 17. Tee Higgins , Bengals Flowers might be a bargain after finishing seventh in WR scoring last season, but few regard him as worthy of a better tier. Enjoy the value. Smith moves up after the Brown trade. Adams was not traded, but he might be too TD-dependent. McMillan is an emerging star. Higgins might have his best season pending. Tier 5: Round 4 18. Rashee Rice , Kansas City Chiefs As with Christian McCaffrey at RB, just because these rankings fade a certain player so many rely on, that doesn't mean you must do the same. However, despite the statistical upside, there is also major risk in Rice, who for several reasons played in only 12 games over the past two seasons. His ranking/tier here might reflect a drop in safe, reliable WR2 options, too. Then again, things get even more dire at running back. Tier 6: Rounds 4/5 19. Emeka Egbuka , Tampa Bay Buccaneers 20. Ladd McConkey , Los Angeles Chargers 21. Terry McLaurin , Washington Commanders 22. Jameson Williams , Lions 23. Jaylen Waddle , Denver Broncos Managers will be relying on these players all season, and there is much to rely on. Egbuka was a rookie star during the first five weeks last season before leveling off. McConkey was a rookie star all season in 2024, but not in Year 2. Waddle joins a new franchise. There is a high floor for these options. Tier 7: Rounds 6/7 play 1:41 How much does Malik Nabers' health status affect his fantasy draft stock? 24. Malik Nabers , New York Giants 25. Mike Evans , San Francisco 49ers 26. Stefon Diggs , Commanders Here come some outliers. Nabers, when healthy, likely would fall safely in Tier 2, but there must be concern about his recovery from major knee surgery. If you believe all is well and covet Nabers (and/or Rice), go for it. With Evans and Diggs, older gentlemen who have more than proved themselves, they go to new situations where they should succeed. Evans was hurt last season, but Diggs was the No. 17 PPR WR! Don't be afraid to reach a bit for each. Tier 8: Rounds 7/8 27. DJ Moore , Buffalo Bills 28. Rome Odunze , Chicago Bears 29. Luther Burden III , Bears 30. Courtland Sutton , Broncos 31. Carnell Tate , Tennessee Titans Moore, pushed out of Chicago by the younger fellows ranked in this same tier, gets a slight nod over his former teammates (unless one believes one of the Bears will be significantly more valuable than the other). Sutton is being widely relegated to secondary status with Waddle arriving, though some might disagree. Tate is the first rookie listed, and therefore perhaps statistically overrated. It is OK to pass on him. Tier 9: Rounds 8/9 32. Michael Pittman Jr ., Pittsburgh Steelers 33. DK Metcalf , Steelers 34. Marvin Harrison Jr ., Arizona Cardinals 35. Michael Wilson , Cardinals 36. Christian Watson , Green Bay Packers 37. Matthew Golden , Packers So many teammates! The Bears started us off in the prior tier, and here are three other unclear situations, none led by a quarterback expected to challenge for QB1 status (unlike the Bears). It might be particularly painful to those who invest in this tier but guess wrong. Tier 10: Rounds 10/11 38. Parker Washington , Jacksonville Jaguars 39. Jakobi Meyers , Jaguars 40. Alec Pierce , Indianapolis Colts 41. Josh Downs , Colts These timeshare situations are a bit different. For one, the Jaguars boast a potential QB1 option in fantasy, but they also employ other notable WRs in Brian Thomas Jr . and Travis Hunter . Why do so many people think Hunter will play more offense than defense? As for the Colts, Pierce is recovering from ankle surgery, his Week 1 status problematic. Downs could benefit. Tier 11: Rounds 11/12 42. Wan'Dale Robinson , Titans 43. Brian Thomas Jr. , Jaguars 44. Jordan Addison , Vikings 45. Khalil Shakir , Bills 46. Xavier Worthy , Chiefs The surprising Robinson caught 92 passes last season, though it appears few believe he will repeat the achievement. Thomas caught 87 passes two seasons ago. Again, there are doubts. Worthy is a popular breakout option in his third season. Tier 12: Rounds 13/14 47. Chris Godwin Jr ., Buccaneers 48. Quentin Johnston , Chargers 49. Deebo Samuel Sr ., 49ers 50. Jayden Reed , Packers It wasn't so long ago that Godwin and Samuel were solid WR2 options. If we assume health, they are bargains here, but then again, we hardly can assume health. Johnston and Reed showing more consistency would be nice. Tier 13: Rounds 14/15 51. Makai Lemon , Eagles 52. KC Concepcion , Cleveland Browns 53. Denzel Boston , Browns 54. De'Zhaun Stribling , 49ers Rookies and Browns! Take your pick or simply rely on safer, proven veterans. Perhaps a rookie -- maybe even a Browns rookie! -- will emerge as a star. Tier 14: Later rounds/free agency play 1:41 Can fantasy managers trust Jalen McMillan to produce as a WR2 this season? 55. Romeo Doubs , Packers 56. Jerry Jeudy , Browns 57. Rashid Shaheed , Seahawks 58. Jalen Coker , Panthers 59. Jalen McMillan , Buccaneers 60. Calvin Ridley , Titans 61. Keenan Allen , Colts 62. Then, dominate your drafts. Check out all of the tiered rankings: QB | RB | WR | TE Tier 1: Top of the first round 1. Jahmyr Gibbs , Detroit Lions 2. Bijan Robinson , Atlanta Falcons No real need to dissect the order here. Most people agree these are the top options at running back. These two stand out among their peers. Tier 2: Mid-to-late first round 3. Jonathan Taylor , Indianapolis Colts 4. De'Von Achane , Miami Dolphins 5. James Cook III , Buffalo Bills 6. Derrick Henry , Baltimore Ravens 7. Chase Brown , Cincinnati Bengals Reasonable minds might disagree about who is missing in this tier, and that is fine. As for this group, people overrate the Miami situation. Achane is special. Cook is special, too, and it is not only touchdowns. He led the league in rushing yards. Henry was close, and he thrives every season, so don't bother looking up his birth year, not yet. Tier 3: Early second round 8. Christian McCaffrey , San Francisco 49ers We can acknowledge the 413-touch elephant in the room, yes? I wanted no part of McCaffrey, with his injury history, last season. OK, so I missed out, like really missed out. It changes nothing. I still want no part, even later in Round 1. Any player coming off this unsafe level of volume will step back statistically. Consider not only the upside, but the downside in investing in this player in Round 1. Tier 4: Rounds 2/3 9. Ashton Jeanty , Las Vegas Raiders 10. Saquon Barkley , Philadelphia Eagles 11. Omarion Hampton , Los Angeles Chargers Here are three options who should improve upon what happened a season ago. Barkley is the veteran here, and the Eagles seem intent on reestablishing him as the focal point of the offense. Jeanty and Hampton were disappointing as rookies, but both are in a better position to succeed. Tier 5: Rounds 3/4 12. Josh Jacobs , Green Bay Packers 13. Breece Hall , New York Jets 14. Kenneth Walker III , Kansas City Chiefs 15. Javonte Williams , Dallas Cowboys 16. Jeremiyah Love , Arizona Cardinals More question marks than the prior tier, but most notably (other than the first rookie) these are proven players. People sure love Love, but his situation looks a lot like what Jeanty dealt with (bad team, offensive line, confusing direction), and a high ankle sprain might compromise him for September. Walker and Williams might be better/safer options. Bottom line, though: If a fantasy manager doesn't have two running backs before this tier ends, they may regret it later. Tier 6: Rounds 5/6 17. Kyren Williams , Los Angeles Rams 18. Travis Etienne Jr ., New Orleans Saints 19. Quinshon Judkins , Cleveland Browns 20. Cam Skattebo , New York Giants Many will shout at this Williams falling to this tier, but the threat of compromised touches is real. The threat is real with all these players. Certainly Etienne might not catch as many passes in his new home. Judkins, returning from ankle surgery, didn't catch many passes as a rookie. Skattebo did in half a season, but health is far from guaranteed with his reckless style of play. Tier 7: Rounds 6/7 21. D'Andre Swift , Chicago Bears 22. Jadarian Price , Seattle Seahawks 23. Bhayshul Tuten , Jacksonville Jaguars 24. David Montgomery , Houston Texans More question marks. Swift and Montgomery are proven but a bit older, and they may be in annoying timeshares. Price, a rookie, and Tuten, beginning Year 2, are full of promise, but neither has been much of a pass catcher. Tier 8: Round 7 25. Rhamondre Stevenson , New England Patriots 26. TreVeyon Henderson , Patriots 27. Bucky Irving , Tampa Bay Buccaneers 28. Kenny Gainwell , Buccaneers Time for a few timeshares! Let's go against typical opinion here. Stevenson is quite good. Why do we assume the younger Henderson simply pushes him aside? Meanwhile, Gainwell proved he is quite good! Irving has major competition. For now, we rank Irving better, but I will simply wait a few rounds for Gainwell. Tier 9: Rounds 10/11/12 29. Tony Pollard , Tennessee Titans 30. Jaylen Warren , Pittsburgh Steelers 31. Rico Dowdle , Steelers 32. Aaron Jones Sr ., Minnesota Vikings 33. Jonathon Brooks , Carolina Panthers 34. Chuba Hubbard , Panthers Potentially productive players populate this tier, but these are unlikely to be safe RB2 choices. Roster them in case the numbers surprise, but rely on them mainly during bye weeks, if possible. Pollard seeks his fifth consecutive 1,000-yard rushing season, but the Titans need more. Guessing the hierarchy for the Steelers, Vikings and Panthers may be perilous. Tier 10: Rounds 12/13/14 35. Rachaad White , Washington Commanders 36. J.K. Dobbins , Denver Broncos 37. Kyle Monangai , Bears 38. Blake Corum , Rams 39. RJ Harvey , Broncos We finally see a Commander and Bronco. I happen to like White and Dobbins more than the ESPN projections recommend, but they are far from safe players. Monangai and Corum, younger than their team's starters, would hold far more appeal if they caught passes. Harvey does this. Tier 11: Rounds 14/15/16 40. Tyjae Spears , Titans 41. Jordan Mason , Vikings 42. Isiah Pacheco , Lions 43. Tyler Allgeier , Cardinals 44. Zach Charbonnet , Seahawks 45. Woody Marks , Texans 46. Alvin Kamara , Saints 47. Jacory Croskey-Merritt , Commanders 48. Chris Rodriguez Jr ., Jaguars This is a rather interesting collection of players who may be afterthoughts in your drafts. Spears and Kamara certainly catch passes, adding to their allure. Mason and Rodriguez do not, but they will play. Pacheco joins a top offense. Charbonnet may not play the first month as he recovers from knee surgery. Tier 12: Later rounds/free agency 49. Justice Hill , Ravens 50. Samaje Perine , Bengals 51. Brian Robinson Jr ., Falcons 52. Brown be more comfortable in the Patriots' offense? (1:14) Mike Reiss Aug 19, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close Mike Reiss is an NFL reporter at ESPN and covers the New England Patriots. Reiss has covered the Patriots since 1997 and joined ESPN in 2009. In 2019, he was named Massachusetts Sportswriter of the Year by the National Sports Media Association. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- The New England Patriots didn't even need to play a preseason game before meeting their new reality. The Indianapolis Colts arrived at the Patriots' practice fields last week -- where the energy of 10,000-plus cheering and booing fans put a palpable football buzz in the air -- and turned up the intensity. When Indianapolis intercepted quarterback Drake Maye on his final pass, then carved up the Patriots' top defense with ease to score a touchdown, the Colts celebrated as if they had won something big . "It's being able to go against the former AFC champions and measure where we are," Colts safety Cam Bynum explained. Ready or not, New England, this is what life is like at the top of the AFC. The Patriots are no longer the upstart; instead, just like the majority of the Bill Belichick/Tom Brady years, they are the team others in the conference are targeting after their surprise run to Super Bowl LX , which they lost decisively to the Seattle Seahawks 29-13. A lot has happened since then, including an offseason dominated by coach Mike Vrabel's personal travails , a long-rumored trade for star wide receiver A.J. Brown and nearly unprecedented roster turnover for a conference champion. It set the stage for the question many are asking: Are the Patriots primed to succumb to a tougher schedule or will Vrabel's relentless commitment to establishing team identity deliver another surprising run to the Super Bowl? "Having a taste of that game, being there, feeling that, feeling all the feels when you don't get what you want, it makes you hungry," New England linebacker and team captain Robert Spillane said of the Super Bowl defeat. "It makes you second-guess everything you've done. It makes you look for a little bit more of an edge." Indianapolis gave the Patriots an early taste of how opponents will be raising their intensity level against them, even if DraftKings Sportsbook doesn't view New England as the AFC favorite at +1600 (tied for third, behind the Buffalo Bills and the Baltimore Ravens ). But the Patriots have a chance to prove what kind of team they will be when they open the season in Seattle on Sept. 9 (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC). "Knowing where you are, and what type of team you are, is very important," said fifth-year cornerback and punt returner Marcus Jones . "We are the team being hunted. We have to wear that chip on our shoulder every time we get out there." MAYE SAT AT the interview podium for 16 minutes following February's Super Bowl loss in Santa Clara, California. His eyes welled up. His voice cracked at times. The first thing he said: "It hurts." The heartbreak set the stage for his offseason, which was already being mapped out that night. "That's what fuels you," Maye said. "I think that's the biggest thing about life. You're going to have times like this. It's how you bounce back." Vrabel kept repeating "307" to players in the aftermath, a reference to the number of days they had been together as a team and how far they had come in a short time. He told them to be prepared for a quick turnaround for the start of the voluntary offseason program in late April. By April, the Patriots were a much different team, a result of being aggressive spenders in free agency for a second straight year. Former Green Bay Packers wide receiver Romeo Doubs was a big catch and signed a four-year, $68 million free agent deal after the team released 2025 leading receiver Stefon Diggs . At outside linebacker, veteran Dre'Mont Jones (three years, $36.5 million) was prioritized over retaining pass rusher K'Lavon Chaisson (career-high 7.5 sacks in 2025), in part because Jones is a sturdier option against the run. Veteran safety Kevin Byard , who led the NFL with seven interceptions in 2025 with the Chicago Bears , was considered a coup and the reason the Patriots elected not to re-sign starter Jaylinn Hawkins (now with the Ravens). Guard Alijah Vera-Tucker also was brought aboard (three years, $42 million), which led to a trade of starting center Garrett Bradbury (1,072 snaps played) to the Bears and 2025 third-round pick Jared Wilson sliding over to replace him. Fullback Reggie Gilliam (three years, $10.8 million) was another early signing, which highlighted the desire to become a tougher, more physical team in the run game and on kickoff returns -- roles in which Gilliam excelled with the Bills. After what seemed like a successful free agency, the Patriots were preparing for the NFL draft when the discourse surrounding the team and its head coach took a turn. On April 7, the New York Post published pictures of Vrabel and The Athletic NFL reporter Dianna Russini at a luxury resort in Arizona, appearing to show the two, who are both married, embracing and holding hands days before the NFL spring league meetings. Russini resigned from The Athletic on April 14. One week later, Vrabel addressed reporters for the first time, calling it a "personal and private matter" and saying, "I've had some difficult conversations with people I care about -- with my family, the organization, the coaches, the players." As part of the fallout, Vrabel was away from the team on April 25, the third and final day of the NFL draft, as he said he was beginning the process of seeking counseling . The Patriots made six of their nine overall selections that day with the coach absent. They aren't relying on major contributions from their draft class, as Utah offensive tackle Caleb Lomu (first round, No. 28), Illinois outside linebacker Gabe Jacas (second round, No. 55) and Notre Dame tight end Eli Raridon (third round, No. 95) currently project as top backups and Wake Forest cornerback Karon Prunty (fifth round, No. 171) as a core special teams player. Vrabel's situation lingered throughout May before the Patriots made headlines once again -- this time trading for Brown, the Philadelphia Eagles ' star wide receiver. Speculation of a trade had been stirring for months, but it was officially announced June 1. The Patriots sent their 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick to deliver Maye a clear-cut No. 1 target and address perhaps the top deficiency on the roster. Brown, who grew up a Patriots fan, instantly shifted the energy around the team with his arrival. Smiling at the interview dais, he famously said, "Obviously, I know this ain't heaven, but it's close to it." Offensive tackle Morgan Moses , New England's oldest (35) and longest-tenured player (13th season), sounded optimistic that the Patriots can turn the page on last season and build with new additions. "You live and you learn. What we did last was successful, but obviously, we didn't walk off with the [Lombardi] Trophy like we wanted to," he said. "You gotta learn how to lose before you can win. I think we've digested that well over the offseason and coming together, adding new pieces." WITH PLENTY OF new faces in the locker room, Vrabel sought to continue what worked well in 2025: building a team identity. On Aug. 4 in the Patriots' new 160-seat auditorium, he stood in front of his players and talked about oranges and how the fruit relates to what he wants the 2026 Patriots to ideally become. Yes, oranges. Vrabel explained: When an orange is squeezed, everyone knows what it creates. So, when the Patriots are in the juicer, such as in a competitive game in a pressure-filled fourth quarter, can they become a team that oozes the ingredients most important to Vrabel? "Whatever you squeeze is what you are. That's you. He's trying to pull that out of us," veteran punter Bryce Baringer said. "He made the analogy if someone squeezes an orange, watermelon juice isn't going to come out. So, when we're squeezed, we have to be that team; it needs to be those four pillars of our identity." The four pillars haven't changed since last season: effort and finish; ball security and disruption; details, techniques and fundamentals; and making great decisions. But a significant number of the players hearing Vrabel's message have changed. Unlike most other conference champions, the Patriots have turned over nearly half their roster to create a rare mix: a significantly different team despite entering the 2026 campaign carrying the AFC's bull's-eye. Of the 91 players on the current roster, 43 weren't with the team last season. In comparison, of the 90 players currently on the Seahawks' roster, 25 weren't with the team last season. Furthermore, the Patriots lost 14 players who started at least one game for them last season. The Seahawks lost only five. If that holds in the regular season, it would be the fourth-most starters lost by a reigning AFC/NFC champion in the past decade, behind the 2020 Chiefs (20), the 2024 Eagles (19) and the 2017 Patriots (16), according to ESPN Research. With such turnover, it's no wonder Vrabel said he told the 2026 team the same thing he did the 2025 team at this time last year: The goal is to earn a role, build a team and prepare to win. "I don't think the messaging will be much different. It's got to be consistent," Vrabel said. "We have to be able to build each and every year, to start over and figure out the things that we do well, what we like and what the players have confidence in. And we have to be able to push the envelope on some things that we weren't very good at last year." In total, the Patriots have lost players who started a cumulative 104 games last season -- third most among the past 20 Super Bowl teams, behind the 2022 Eagles (116) and the 2020 Chiefs (105). Neither the 2022 Eagles nor the 2020 Chiefs returned to the Super Bowl the following season, which might be an ominous sign for New England. But at the same time, what makes the Patriots' roster turnover unique is that most of it was by choice. "We were very honest in our evaluations with what we needed even though we had a successful season last year," executive vice president of player personnel Eliot Wolf said on Sirius XM NFL Radio. "We were able to target and acquire some of the guys we coveted." The new and improved roster was built in Vrabel's image, which according to Wolf means "physical, tough, play through the whistle, block for the guy without the ball and who are great teammates." "[Vrabel] espouses that every single day; it's real and not just something he says. He wakes up every morning and thinks about this identity, and that permeates through the building," Wolf said in late July. "We all think that way now. We're not going to bring in guys that don't fit those characteristics or guys we don't think can improve in those characteristics. It's made our job easier on the scouting side." SINCE PURCHASING THE PATRIOTS in 1994, Robert Kraft has often said his expectation entering a season is to make the playoffs because anything is possible at that point. The 2001 New England team that shocked the Rams in Super Bowl XXXVI was the perfect example. Until Kraft noted a more recent occurrence in a July appearance on ESPN's "First Take." "If you make the playoffs, like we saw last year, no one would have predicted [the Patriots to have been in the Super Bowl]," he said. The Patriots have acknowledged playing in Super Bowl LX put them ahead of their own projection in Vrabel's first year as head coach. An MVP-worthy season from Maye and an improved defense was aided, in part, by playing a fourth-place schedule. The Patriots went 14-3 while playing the weakest schedule in the past quarter-decade in terms of opponents' combined records. Their 17 opponents (counting each divisional opponent twice) went a combined 113-176, for a .391 win percentage. Since 1980, New England was just the fourth team to play a schedule against teams that had a combined winning percentage of less than .400 and the first since 1999, when both the Rams and the Jacksonville Jaguars did it. In 2026, the Patriots will face the league's sixth-hardest schedule based on opponents' 2025 winning percentage. ESPN's Football Power Index (FPI), meanwhile, rates the schedule more favorably (23rd). Among the primary challenges are having seven of the first 11 games on the road. "You got something to chase, and I think that's one of the best things about experiencing it," Maye said of the heartache surrounding the Super Bowl, after which he had acknowledged receiving a pain-killing injection in his right throwing shoulder. "We have to be even better because our standard from last year, if we just play the same way, we won't make it there." The FPI, which is a measure of team strength meant to be the best predictor of performance going forward for the rest of the season, doesn't currently view the Patriots as likely to play next February. New England is ranked 14th overall and seventh in the AFC, behind the Bills (2), Ravens (3), Los Angeles Chargers (7), Chiefs (9), Cincinnati Bengals (12) and Houston Texans (13). Vrabel said he has yet to use those types of rankings as motivation for his team. Others view the Patriots among the elite with cornerback Christian Gonzalez , who is still negotiating a contract extension, headlining the defense and Maye -- runner-up for the NFL's 2025 Most Valuable Player Award -- running the offense. The quarterback enters his third pro season and second in coordinator Josh McDaniels' offense, which will prove critical for his growth. "Drake should have won the MVP last year," ESPN analyst Booger McFarland said. "You add A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs to what they already have ... and with Vrabes, he's one of the best coaches in football when it comes to X's and O's, techniques and the winning formula. For my money, he's the best there is." Former NFL executive Pat Kirwan, who visited Patriots training camp as part of his work on SiriusXM NFL Radio, said, "Most of the spring we all talked about, 'Well, Buffalo is going to take the [AFC East] division back.' I would be real careful about that one." How the Patriots respond to their standing as defending AFC champions, along with good fortune in terms of injuries, will be among the key factors. That's what Patriots Hall of Fame wide receiver Troy Brown remembers about the 2002 campaign -- the season the Patriots had turned from lovable underdogs to not-ready-for-the-bull's-eye AFC standard-bearer -- and how it caught some off guard. "There were things that were taken for granted, almost that we would be back in the Super Bowl again without realizing what the process was on that. That probably came with some immaturity, and it proved much more difficult than we thought it would be," Brown said of a 9-7 campaign in which the team didn't qualify for the playoffs. "You can play a team that is 0-6 and you're going to get their best shot. That's just the way it is." The present-day Patriots have talked about the importance of responding to that challenge. Now, they aim to prove it with actions. Marcus Jones, the slot corner and return specialist, believes they have the right mix in the locker room to deliver. "I feel like it's been a great response. We feel we need to prove more and more every single day," he said. "There's nobody in the building that thinks about complacency."
