records.new_body: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense works and 2026 expectations - ESPN Solak: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense is much more than just Caleb Williams --> Skip to main content Skip to navigation Solak: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense is much more than just Caleb Williams Chicago Bears 2d Ben Solak Hallmark, hot dogs and touchdowns: The Colston Loveland story Chicago Bears 2d Courtney Cronin NFL Future Power Rankings: We stacked all 32 teams based on expectations for 2027 to 2029 Kansas City Chiefs 4d Louis Riddick, +3 More NFL preseason on NFL Network, ESPN: How to watch, schedule 20d ESPN play Why Damien Woody loves Ben Johnson's goal to have 'highest-scoring offense ever' (0:44) Ben Solak Aug 19, 2026, 06:30 AM ET Close Ben Solak joined ESPN in 2024 as a national NFL analyst. He previously covered the NFL at The Ringer, Bleeding Green Nation and The Draft Network. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions When the Bears hired Ben Johnson last offseason, we had a pretty clear idea of who he was. The young coach had saved Jared Goff 's career and lit the Lions' offense aflame by grafting much of the old Sean McVay offense into a new approach in Detroit. His system included a ton of motion, play-action and intermediate in-breakers. All the classics ... with some new wrinkles, thanks to unique players such as Jahmyr Gibbs and Jameson Williams in the fold. So as Johnson took charge of second-year quarterback Caleb Williams , the burning questions were clear. How would Johnson reverse the arc for Williams, the 2024 No. 1 pick who had suffered as a rookie with late throws, missed targets, plenty of sacks and too many risks? How, if at all, could Williams play the pristine, timing-oriented ball that Goff had proved integral to Johnson's approach? Would Johnson lose patience with an oft-scrambling off-schedule playmaker? It's easy to look at the improvement of the Bears' offense in 2025 and say that our questions were well-founded. Williams' sack rate dropped from 10.0% to 3.8% (good job, Johnson), but his completion percentage fell from 62.5% to 58.1% (still inaccurate). The Johnson-Williams partnership must still be a work in progress. One with promise, but in progress nonetheless. Right? The scope here is too narrow. It commits the most frequent error of our modern NFL discourse and analysis. It looks at everything through the lens of the quarterback, believing that the entire offense will only go as he goes and that all innovation is meant to directly impact his life. The Johnson offense resurrected Goff and looks as if it might boost Williams to elite heights -- but that's not the only thing it's doing. In fact, much of Johnson's first year in Chicago was not about Williams' game at all. The Bears' offense was stripped down to the studs and rebuilt anew, in a process Johnson knew would be painful and slow. But it worked. It set up the Bears for total team success -- not only in 2025 with a revitalized quarterback but for years to come with a complete system. And it started not on the air but on the ground. Getting the run game going The Bears had the earliest possible bye week in 2025 -- Week 5 -- and were 2-2 entering it. There were big defensive issues to address (31st in success rate). On offense, they were about league average ... but with a major imbalance, ranking 12th in EPA per dropback and 31st in EPA per rush. "It was the running game," Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor told me. "We really needed to get the running game going." The running game is the lifeblood of Johnson's offense, and not in a trite, lip-servicey way -- a thing coaches say to placate their offensive linemen. Despite his new hat as the head coach, Johnson still installs the running game on a weekly basis himself, as he did in Detroit . "I haven't been around a playcaller, let alone a head coach, that installs his own running game," Bears tight end Cole Kmet said. "He has everybody in the room -- receivers, tight ends, backs, quarterbacks, linemen. We're all together as he installs." Johnson's heavy hand in the teaching of the run game is both a testament to its importance in his offense ... and its complexity. The Lions were notorious for running everything under the sun during Johnson's time as offensive coordinator, and he made a conscious decision before his first year in Chicago to install the offense as it was. Over three seasons in Detroit, Johnson's offense expanded in the stability offered by Goff, center Frank Ragnow and receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown . Fine adjustments are easier between longtime teammates, and new spinoffs of the playbook were written after the original chapters had long been internalized. Johnson didn't want to take the Bears' offense back to square one and rediscover those innovations, so he dumped it on their desks with the telltale thud of a thick textbook. But it was a lot to absorb in a short window, and through four weeks of Johnson's first season in Chicago, the running game proved difficult to stomach. The staff went back to the drawing board with their offensive linemen -- namely veteran guard Joe Thuney and center Drew Dalman. Thuney had played in two different offenses with different languages (New England and Josh McDaniels; Kansas City and Andy Reid) and could give Johnson and his staff honest feedback about the design of the rushing attack and how it was understood and communicated across the line. Dalman, as the center, was in charge of identifying the Mike linebacker -- off his point, the rest of the blockers would know their responsibilities. His understanding of the intent of the play and his authority to communicate it needed to be unquestionable. Here's a good snapshot of what it looked like pre-bye. In Week 4 against the Raiders, the Bears are down by five but in scoring range late in the fourth quarter. They want to run the clock as low as possible before they score a go-ahead touchdown. Before the snap, Raiders strongside linebacker Germaine Pratt (No. 57) is close to the line of scrimmage, and it has the Bears in an operational tizzy. Tight ends Kmet (85) and Durham Smythe (81) are requesting more information from the core of the formation, while both Dalman and Williams point. pic.twitter.com/oA2wJz9pxg Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) August 18, 2026 The Bears end up with three players (the center, left guard and left tackle) all on one defensive tackle while linebacker Devin White (45) runs unimpeded through the crease and meets D'Andre Swift behind the line of scrimmage. You can see the frustration from Thuney (62) and Dalman (52) after the play. Something got lost in translation. Remember, almost all of the Bears' offensive linemen were new to one another last season. A carousel of left tackles didn't help the building of chemistry -- but Thuney had never played beside Dalman, who had never played beside right guard Jonah Jackson , who had never played beside right tackle Darnell Wright . Kmet was a veteran at tight end, but fellow tight end Colston Loveland was a rookie. In fact, Jackson was the only one with experience in Johnson's offense. Though the old Lions running game accumulated over years of community growth, the Bears were trying to manufacture that in mere weeks. A lot of work in a little time can invite errors. In four games, the Bears had an appalling 11 pre-snap penalties (nine false starts, one illegal shift and one illegal motion). They were 31st in EPA lost on false starts and 30th in EPA lost on pre-snap penalties altogether. Not all of those penalties were on called runs, of course, but the Bears were actually breaking the huddle a whole second faster on called passes (19.6 seconds on the play clock) than they were on called runs (18.5 seconds). Many of Chicago's run calls were packaged with passes, and Williams could "can" one call to get to the other call. Again, no kid gloves on Johnson's offense. He wanted both calls available, and he was going to have them available. But the late assembly at the line, along with the time Williams needed to identify the defense and potentially change the call, was stressing a still-developing system. Johnson and his staff tried to alleviate the pressure by one-wording playcalls -- smashing each of them into one load-bearing keyword. "If we want to make this 10-word playcall into one word, we've still got to have something that's going to get the receivers the idea of where to line up, the line's going to understand the protection, the backs understand the action, the quarterbacks understand the read. It's on us to give as many mind taps as possible," Taylor said. "We came up with some pretty weird stuff." Every offense uses keywords like this to execute in the no-huddle. But to have up to 10 full playcalls on the one-word sheet for any given week -- calls in which the Bears could still motion, shift, kill a play, adjust an alignment, etc. -- and then to replace those with 10 new ones the following week was quite the task. Johnson, offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and Taylor all hailed from pretty wordy backgrounds, and it took a lot of brainstorming and outside research to get a workable one-word system. They also leaned on the players for help. Many of the Bears' younger players lived in codeword-style offenses in college, where one-word calls for the sake of tempo are far more commonplace. They gave ideas for clever mnemonics and enjoyed bullying Taylor during his Wednesday presentations on the absurd portmanteaus he had concocted. These one-worders weren't training wheels, mind you -- just better teaching. Just as Johnson had put the full onus of his playbook on his young offense, he also put the onus on himself to meet the players where they were -- to give them the offense in a language they could understand. The Bears' communication demons were not fully exorcised -- it was pre-snap confusion that led to an embarrassing playoff interception against the Packers -- but they were diminished. They got to the line faster. Johnson started putting more players in motion at the snap, especially in the running game (from 54.4% of runs pre-bye to 75.7% of runs post-bye). The many motions made run fits tougher on the defense. The running game didn't trickle out but exploded forth -- like water from an opened dam. Chicago ended the 2025 season second to only the Rams in both rushing success rate and EPA per rush. Solving the communication issues was one of several switches that were flicked in the Bears' off week. Another was directional. Through the first four weeks, the Bears ran as frequently to their left as they did to their right. But from Week 5 on, no team had a clearer directional tendency in the running game than the Bears, who saw a whopping 66% of their RB carries go to the offense's right side behind the mauling duo of Jackson and Wright. That would have been the biggest left/right skew of a full season over the past decade, according to NFL Next Gen Stats' numbers. It's rare to see a playcaller feed a tackle the way he might feed a star receiver, but that's what Johnson did for Wright. And he wasn't the only one. As running backs Swift and Kyle Monangai grew accustomed to the displacement that Jackson and Wright could create on the backside of zone runs, they began gravitating toward them. Not every run to the right was called to go that way, but water finds its level. And good backs find daylight. Wide receivers also have serious run-blocking demands in this offense (remember, they're also in the meetings). And Chicago became more intentional about who it asked to fill that role. DJ Moore , who had taken five snaps in a tight alignment through the first four weeks of the season, didn't get a single snap in tight alignments in the three weeks coming out of the bye; Rome Odunze saw his usage there take an accompanying leap. When Odunze went down because of a foot injury, it created more space for Luther Burden III , an admirable blocker in his own right. The Bears' running game, like the Lions units of Johnson's past, simply does not work without receivers who line up correctly, communicate with the tight ends and the quarterback for their assignment, understand how that assignment might change post-snap and dig their assignment out with legitimate effort. Without this commitment, the play-action passing game would never work to the level Johnson demands. Unleashing the explosive plays It's at this point in our understanding of what changed in the Johnson offense that we come to the easiest trap -- one that we absolutely must avoid: the idea that the run exists to set up the pass. Yes, it's true that Johnson uses the run to set up the play-action pass, like every other coach. Few, if any offensive designers are as committed to a marriage between the running and passing games. Johnson is notoriously hypersensitive to the splits of his receivers. A receiver's split -- how wide he lines up relative to the numbers or the hash -- is communicated by the formation, but it can be trumped by specific concepts called from that formation and adjusted again by the quarterback at the line of scrimmage. You simply can't get them wrong. If you do, the opposing defense might get a tip that it's run or pass, and that's not how this offense works. "Past offenses here, it used to be 'line up about where you should be and get to a spot,'" Loveland said, recalling conversations he had with Bears veterans as he entered the league and endured Johnson's geometric fastidiousness. "Here, if you're in the wrong split, you're going to know. If you're off by half a yard, they're going to know, and you're going to know." So the run sets up the pass. But that construction can trick us into thinking of the run as a jab, lulling the opponent into a predictable tempo and setting the reach for an inbound combination. The eventual incoming haymaker here is the play-action pass -- the payoff for all of those patient jabs. That is how some coaches think about the running game. Not Johnson. He is here to hit explosives, and that is exactly what his running game is designed to do. Only the Dolphins had a higher explosive run rate from Week 5 on last season. That Rams running game, which just barely beat the Bears in success rate? Not nearly as explosive. They live on between-the-tackles runs with the intent to stay ahead of the sticks. The Bears get outside of the tackles with misdirection, lead blockers, pullers -- anything to get a talented ball carrier with a runway. As Taylor said in a news conference last week, "We don't look at the run game as a way to stay on track. We look at the run game as a way to attack defenses and really be explosive and continue to just put our foot on the gas the entire game." The running game is not the jab. It's the haymaker. But the play-action pass is also the haymaker. The haymaker sets up the haymaker. Do you fear death? It's this paradigm of relentless attacking that helps us understand what is in store for the Bears in 2026. Again, the focus all offseason has been on the quarterback -- this time, his completion percentage. Williams completed only 58.1% of his passes last season -- 36th among 38 qualified quarterbacks. Johnson would certainly like to increase that number. He called it "something that we're going to emphasize." What he said right after was just as important. "We want to give these pass catchers -- we have so many talented ones -- opportunities to run after the catch. So we're being very critical on where we're putting that football with them." Nothing about taking more checkdowns. Nothing about risky throws or too many scrambles -- myths that have been spun about Williams and his fit in this offense since its inception. Just precise placement on YAC athletes who are on the move -- namely, over the middle of the field. Explosive plays. This has always been the point of the offense, even going back to the Goff days. Williams says he believes in explosives in the same way his head coach does, and he has the rare physical traits necessary to conjure them. He has the quickness and strength to escape the pocket, the anticipation of space and leverage down the field, and the flexibility to hurl deep shots while on the move. And he has the arm ... oh my heavens, the arm . Goff averaged 7.0 air yards per attempt on play-action passes through three seasons under Johnson; Williams was at 10.2 last season. This isn't just shot selection or scramble drill noise. It's a schematic choice. Goff averaged 9.0 air yards per attempt on in-breaking routes under Johnson. Williams is at 11.7. He had 12 completed in-breakers at least 20 yards downfield last season, whereas Goff had 17 such plays in three combined seasons. Williams is quite literally expanding the scope of the offense. Of course, there is some shot selection. Goff takes the checkdowns that Williams doesn't, because Williams was escaping pressure that Goff couldn't outrun. Williams can take more of those checkdowns, which will help the completion percentage -- but that's not the point. The point is to generate -- say it with me -- more explosives. "Two, three, four times a game, if you're just putting the ball in play a little bit quicker to the backs, we get three, four, five more calls to give you," Taylor said of Williams' increased focus on checkdowns in Year 2. "And we'll keep calling those. We'll keep unloading the clip." Williams has this in him. Here's a checkdown from Week 1 against the Vikings. With a lurking quarters safety who wants to drive on the dig route from Burden (10) and a middle linebacker sinking deep into the throwing window, Williams dumps the ball to the back on time for an easy first down. pic.twitter.com/QtHstdWAjg Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) August 18, 2026 The next time the Bears meet the Vikings, Williams has a similar concept with a similar lurking safety opposite the dig (this time to Odunze). But as the linebacker hasn't achieved nearly as much depth, Williams uncorks a laser beam that doesn't just tattoo Odunze on his chestplate -- it holds him in place to keep him away from coverage. pic.twitter.com/nDMEDnI4gu Good Clips (@MeshSitWheel) August 18, 2026 That second throw is a high-level pass that not many quarterbacks are making -- they simply don't have the arm to cash this check. Similarly, few coaches are calling a passing game as predicated on shot plays as Johnson -- they simply don't have the quarterback to cash the check. Our early perspective on Johnson and Williams focused on the ways that Williams is not Goff, and how he might fail to fit Johnson's offense. That view mistook Goff's precise footwork and picturesque timing as the goal of Johnson's offense, when it was really the vehicle. It was how Goff created explosives. He didn't have the huge arm or the magical scramble ability to do so otherwise. Williams does -- and he has the mentality of a big-play hunter. He and Johnson are of spookily similar mind -- two peas in a highly explosive pod. Anyone who thinks the Bears are going to throttle Williams' octane has learned the wrong lesson. They're going to keep banging that big drum. Explosiveness in the passing game is the hidden value that completion percentage fails to capture. We have better stats to measure down-to-down consistency (Williams was 23rd in dropback success rate). We have even better stats to measure who is creating big positive plays while avoiding big negative plays (Williams was 14th in EPA per dropback). More importantly, other players are seeing Johnson's vision and imitating Williams' devotion to it. As Williams has nailed down his details, fewer Bears practices are thrown into disarray by mistaken splits and forgotten motions. "It used to be, 'Man, these guys are just being jerks to me about every little thing,'" Taylor said, chuckling as he remembers that first summer of installs. "We have guys now that do understand. And when you see it and how challenging it is, you understand the beauty of it. Now, it's important to our guys. We have guys that love it now." What to expect for a 2026 encore Perhaps this is the biggest change in the Johnson offense entering the 2026 season. There were guys who trusted the process at this time last year -- but did they love it? Unlikely. Yet doubters become disciples when the scoreboard shows wins instead of losses. The cardiac Bears sure stole a game or two in an 11-6 season. But that does nothing to dull belief in the single-minded head coach. If anything, it sharpens it. Those impossible wins feel like the product of those fine details, those big plays so hard-earned in the exactness of little executions. That's the clever trick of the blurry game of football, and it's the way each Bear -- from Williams at the top of the depth chart all the way down -- carves out a slice of authorship over each unlikely win. The story will always be written as Williams "figuring it out" in the Johnson offense, and I get it. It has enough veracity to it, even if it is not complete and not satisfying. The victory of the Bears' offense is in so many ways beyond the quarterback. Johnson will be understood as a quarterback whisperer who fixed Goff, then fixed Williams. Again, it's not wrong, but it's not accurate. He's a wonderful offensive mastermind, the first real challenger to McVay's and Kyle Shanahan's dominance over the past decade -- but he is so because he's a running game designer and a one-word caller. He has built a running game around a right tackle in unprecedented ways. He has demanded new heights from his receivers as blockers. He has raised the bar for commitment to an explosive offense. Perhaps the fire will peter out in 2026 -- wilder things have happened in this league. The retirement of Dalman at 27 was an unwelcome surprise, and the left tackle position is still unsolved. Burden and Monangai are banged up. There's a lot that goes into making an offense good, and accordingly, there are a lot of inflection points at which it can go wrong. If you want to bet on regression, be my guest. Johnson called his team the "No. 1 regression candidate" this summer in a nod to that doubt. But I have no interest betting against this head coach and what he did in Year 1. In their second offseason under Johnson, the Bears have their first opportunity to take accumulated experience and parlay it into faster operations, better adjustments and perfect execution. They understand it now, the beauty of it.

AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh Courtney Cronin Aug 19, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close Courtney Cronin joined ESPN in 2017, originally covering the Minnesota Vikings before switching to the Chicago Bears in 2022. Courtney is a frequent panelist on Around the Horn and host of Best Week Ever and GameNight on ESPN Radio. She also co-hosts The Chicago Bears Podcast on ESPN 1000. She previously worked at the San Jose Mercury News as a multimedia sports journalist. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- In a Chicago Bears offense that features the Madden cover man in quarterback Caleb Williams and a high-profile coach in Ben Johnson, the celebrity of one young player is emerging from the shadows. From landing a role in the Hallmark Channel movie "Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story," to slinging hot dogs at the famous "The Wieners Circle" this summer, second-year tight end Colston Loveland is gaining attention on and off the field. "He can do everything," Williams said. After leading the Bears in receiving (58 catches, 713 yards, six touchdowns -- all team highs) as a rookie, Loveland is ranked the No. 3 tight end in fantasy by ESPN, behind the Arizona Cardinals ' Trey McBride and the Las Vegas Raiders ' Brock Bowers . "He can become the best tight end in the league," Williams said. "I think he is." But like with all elite players, Loveland isn't heading into Year 2 satisfied with his accomplishments. What's the best thing to order on our menu? Just ask Mr. Loveland pic.twitter.com/KaJlVugoEj The Wieners Circle (@TheWienerCircle) August 7, 2026 When Johnson popped by a special teams meeting early in training camp, he heard someone unexpected firing off questions at coaches. It didn't matter to Loveland that he wasn't likely to be on this specific unit given his sweeping role on offense. If there were ever a question about his responsibility on punt return or the field goal block team, Loveland made sure he would have the answers in his notes. "He's just a sponge right now," Johnson said. "He wants all the information. He knows all this knowledge is going to make him a better player, and he's going to continue to play faster." Once an install has been drilled down for the 10th time, Loveland will shift focus from his job at tight end to what's being asked of the wide receivers around him. He wants to know everything from the specifics behind route combinations -- even when he's not the primary target -- to the blocking rules for himself and the offensive line. "I don't want anyone to have an edge on me. Meaning, I want to study just as much or more than everyone," Loveland said. "I want to get as (many) touches, you know, whatever it may be. "So yeah, it's just like I see other people doing it, it's like, 'Why am I not doing it?'" That approach fuels Loveland on the practice field, where he routinely catches 100 passes from a combination of Bears quarterback and the Jugs machine before every camp session. One catalyst for Williams' hot start to training camp was the target he looked to most often. Get ready to see some familiar faces in Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story premiering Saturday October 17 on Hallmark Channel, streaming next day on Hallmark Plus! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/UvJvhIo6op Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) August 5, 2026 During a two-minute drill at the end of practice July 31, Williams found Loveland four times on a drive that started at the offense's 39-yard line and culminated with Loveland corralling a tight-window pass in the end zone for a 14-yard touchdown. That moment didn't teach Williams anything he didn't already know about the former No. 10 pick who turned eight catches into 137 yards and a critical 2-point conversion in the Bears' 31-27 comeback win over the Packers in the playoffs. Williams had long recognized Loveland's potential as a weapon who "can do everything," the type of player whose big-play prowess has bailed the Bears' offense out of a bind. In one of many furious late-game rallies that defined the Bears' 2025 season, Loveland turned six catches into 118 yards and two scores in Cincinnati, including a 58-yard walk-off touchdown. "Put it up there and give him a shot," Williams said. "He's such a big target, easy target, runs the right routes and nice routes, and then other than that he can run block and disguise things. He's an all-encompassing tight end." Loveland outperformed most veterans at his position last season, ranking second among all tight ends in receiving yards from Weeks 9-18 and generating a +44.6 receiving EPA, per Next Gen Stats, which was the highest mark by a rookie tight end since 2016. Like Sam LaPorta did in Detroit under Johnson's leadership, Loveland's impact on the offense sparked one of the league's most explosive passing attacks. His on-field contributions carried the Bears past a slow start in 2025 to their first playoff victory in 15 years. "He just got a lot of versatility," linebacker D'Marco Jackson said. "He's a good route runner, he's loose. He's really good at the catch point, his radius. "Man, he's a good all-around player and I feel like he's going to be a challenge in camp to keep working with and good preparation for the season." Loveland is such a good route runner that WR1 Rome Odunze said he has "learned a lot from him." "Rare," Odunze said when asked about Loveland's versatility. "A diamond. It's impressive just to see his route-running ability. It's incredible. And then you get him down blocking and he's holding his own like he's a tackle. "So his versatility is truly incredible. I'm super glad that he's on the crew, and I learned a lot from him as well just from his movement and his fluidity in and out of his routes."

New England Patriots 2d Mike Reiss What we're hearing and seeing at Browns training camp: Watson delivers a must-see throw in practice vs. Bills Cleveland Browns 1h Daniel Oyefusi Cowboys: Jerry Jones shares camp thoughts as team leaves Oxnard Friday 1h Todd Archer Seahawks: CB Diggs talks for first time since signing 1h Brady Henderson Patriots: Maye pleased after two practices with Eagles 1h Mike Reiss Giants: Jaxson Dart's best performance of the summer? 1h Jordan Raanan Fantasy football rankings: Eric Karabell's RB tiers 13h Eric Karabell Fantasy football rankings: Eric Karabell's WR tiers 13h Eric Karabell Solak: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense is much more than just Caleb Williams Chicago Bears 2d Ben Solak Hallmark, hot dogs and touchdowns: The Colston Loveland story Chicago Bears 2d Courtney Cronin NFL Future Power Rankings: We stacked all 32 teams based on expectations for 2027 to 2029 Kansas City Chiefs 4d Louis Riddick, +3 More NFL preseason on NFL Network, ESPN: How to watch, schedule 20d ESPN NFL Nation Aug 15, 2026, 11:06 PM ET Close NFL Nation is made up of 32 team-specific reporters who cover the NFL year-round across ESPN.com, ESPN television shows, ESPN Radio, ESPN+ and social media platforms. It was established ahead of the 2013 season. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions The first week of the 2026 NFL preseason kicked off Thursday, giving us our first look at rookies and players making debuts with new teams. It continued with three games Friday, with seven games being played Saturday. How did players in new uniforms perform? Who stood out? Which first-year players showed promise? Our NFL Nation reporters picked out what you need to know about top debuts and more as the NFL returns. Quick links: Full schedule | Where to watch Depth charts | Sign up to play fantasy Saturday's games Cowboys 17, Seahawks 7 Cowboys: The Cowboys will likely give both of Dak Prescott 's backups, Sam Howell and Joe Milton III , at least one start this preseason, but Howell, who signed a one-year deal worth $2.5 million as a free agent, got the call vs. Seattle and put together a solid first half. He completed 8 of 12 passes for 94 yards, including a 39-yard touchdown to undrafted rookie Camden Brown . Howell also ran twice for 15 yards, and he managed the game and kept the offense out of trouble, despite some inexperience around him. First-rounders Caleb Downs and Malachi Lawrence saw spot duty, although Downs' first appearance didn't even last through the opening drive of the game. Lawrence saw action at both edge positions and got caught inside on one pass rush, giving Jalen Milroe the chance to scramble for a decent gain. There are always some undrafted receivers who shine in camp practices but don't do the same in preseason games. Brown, from Georgia Southern, carried over his practice performance to Saturday's game. On his first touchdown, he pulled the ball away from Seahawks corner Shemar Jean-Charles . Brown's second touchdown was even prettier, a left-handed snare of a Milton pass on the opening drive of the third quarter. -- Todd Archer Next game: at Arizona Cardinals (Aug. 22, 10 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Seahawks: Safeties Bud Clark (three tackles) and Rodney Thomas II (five tackles) were the only newcomers who stood out, but not necessarily for plays they did or didn't make. That both were still playing well into the second half looks like further indication of where each stands on the depth chart. Clark, Seattle's second-round pick, does not appear close to wrestling away the starting job from Ty Okada , who got the night off along with virtually every other starter. The one-year deal Seattle gave Thomas, which included only $187,500 guaranteed, suggested the former Colts starter would likely be fighting for a roster spot. That still appears to be the case. Running back Jadarian Price did not play as Seattle's first-round pick continues to work his way back from what coach Mike Macdonald has described as lower-body soreness that should not keep him out long. -- Brady Henderson Next game: at Tennessee Titans (Aug. 23, 8 p.m. ET, Fox) Ravens 24, Eagles 7 Ravens: There was a familiar sight in the preseason opener: wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane in the end zone. With great effort after the catch, the rookie third-round pick dived across the goal line to score on a 16-yard touchdown in the second quarter. Lane finished with 38 yards on three catches, with the star of the Ravens' training camp shining brightly in the preseason. Tight end Matthew Hibner (fourth round) stretched the field on his first reception, catching a 29-yard pass on a wheel route. Hibner, who is looking to become the No. 3 tight end, led Baltimore with 61 yards receiving on five catches. Wide receiver Elijah Sarratt (fourth round), who has had struggles in training camp, fumbled in the third quarter. Running back Adam Randall (fifth round) scored on a 4-yard run in the fourth quarter but didn't run decisively. He finished with 46 yards on 12 carries (a 3.8-yard average). -- Jamison Hensley Next game: at Minnesota Vikings (Aug. 22, 1 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Eagles: The best rookie on the field for the Eagles was tackle Markel Bell , as has been the case all summer. The 6-foot-9, 346-pound third-round pick out of Miami got the start at right tackle and showed the power and poise (he drove a defensive lineman back 6 yards on one run play) that have fueled the organization's increasing confidence in him. With Lane Johnson coming off an injury-riddled season and likely entering his last NFL campaign, Bell's emergence appears right on time. Quarterback Cole Payton , the fifth-round pick out of North Dakota State, got the offense rolling late, using his legs to get into striking distance before throwing a TD pass to Erik Ezukanma . Philadelphia will need more patience when it comes to edge rusher Joshua Weru and defensive tackle Uar Bernard , who are products of the NFL's International Player Program. Both made their pro debuts and held their own, all things considered. Weru even registered a QB pressure and a tackle. -- Tim McManus Next game: at New England Patriots (Aug. 22, 7 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Jaguars 24, Saints 20 Jaguars: Rookie running back J'Mari Taylor got rolling in the second half. After 20 yards on seven carries in the first half, the undrafted player out of Virginia gained 58 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries in the final two quarters. The top three backs are set and the Jags are unlikely to keep four on the active roster, but Taylor made a solid push for a practice squad spot. Two rookie third-round draft picks -- defensive tackle Albert Regis and safety Jalen Huskey -- showed up the most on defense. Regis plugged up the middle and recorded a sack for a 14-yard loss. Huskey had a pass breakup and three solo tackles. He also had one of those hustle plays that coaches love: He chased down Saints kick returner Ty Chandler inside the 10-yard line after an 86-yard return on the opening kickoff, saving a touchdown. The Saints scored on the next play, but it's something that will stand out on film. Rookie receivers CJ Williams and Josh Cameron combined for three catches for 45 yards. Cameron also added a 25-yard kickoff return. -- Michael DiRocco Next game: vs. Carolina Panthers (Friday, 7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Saints: Several drafted rookies didn't play in this game, including receivers Jordyn Tyson and Bryce Lance , and defensive tackle Christen Miller left at halftime with an unspecified injury. Rookie wideout Barion Brown continued to be a camp standout and had a highlight-reel 28-yard catch down the sideline from Zach Wilson . Tight end Oscar Delp caught a 1-yard touchdown pass, and Jeremiah Wright saw significant time as the starting right guard with Cesar Ruiz and the rest of the starters sitting out the game. Undrafted rookie edge rusher Michael Heldman also put together a nice game after having several key moments in practices. -- Katherine Terrell Next game: at Los Angeles Rams (Aug. 22, 4 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Rams 20, Chiefs 12 Rams: All eyes were on rookie quarterback Ty Simpson , the Rams' first-round pick, as he faced a live pass rush for the first time in his NFL career. Heading into the game, Los Angeles coach Sean McVay said he wanted to see Simpson "consistently making good decisions" and "playing within the timing and rhythm" of the plays called. Simpson certainly checked those boxes Saturday, completing 21 of 25 passes for 190 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions. -- Sarah Barshop Next game: vs. New Orleans Saints (Aug. 22, 4 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Chiefs: Several Chiefs rookies had quality moments Saturday. Edge rusher R Mason Thomas displayed his burst off the edge, finishing with a pressure that led to a third-down stop inside the red zone, two tackles, a quarterback hit and a pass deflection. On offense, running back Emmett Johnson and receiver Cyrus Allen produced multiple highlights. Johnson ran around and through many tackles to lead the Chiefs with 59 rushing yards. He also reached the end zone, but his 4-yard touchdown was nullified by a holding penalty. Allen's best moment was when he made a leaping reception for a 13-yard gain. -- Nate Taylor Next game: at Tampa Bay Buccaneers (Aug. 22, 7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Vikings 13, Giants 10 Vikings: New quarterback Kyler Murray led the Vikings to a field goal on his only drive of the game. He finished with two completions on three attempts for 10 yards and no scrambles in a nine-play debut that seemed designed mostly to emphasize the Vikings' run game. Murray's best throw came on an 8-yard out route to receiver Jordan Addison to convert a third down. Of note, rookie running back Demond Claiborne -- a sixth-round draft pick -- got an extended look with 12 carries on 12 total snaps. He failed in two attempts to score from the 1-yard line but had already put his quick burst on display during runs of 7 and 9 yards earlier in the game. The Vikings lost new linebacker/safety Jamal Adams in the second quarter, after he played 11 snaps and produced one tackle for loss. Adams was carted off the sideline with an unspecified injury, and coach Kevin O'Connell said at halftime: "We're going to miss him." -- Kevin Seifert Next game: vs. Baltimore Ravens (Aug. 22, 1 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Giants: Odell Beckham Jr . made his return to MetLife Stadium in a Giants uniform for the first time in almost eight years. He caught a pair of passes for 6 yards and on several others was open downfield but didn't get the ball. The performance confirmed what the Giants have seen from him most of the summer. "He's had a good camp," general manager Joe Schoen said. "I'm impressed with how he's looked. He can still get open." The Giants' rookies also had their moments: Linebacker Arvell Reese , the No. 5 pick, flew through the line of scrimmage and stuffed running back Jordan Mason for a 1-yard loss on the third play of the game. Third-round pick Malachi Fields caught a TD pass from Jaxson Dart over a defender and finished with three catches for 34 yards. First-round OL Francis Mauigoa didn't stand out at first glance, which is good for a rookie lineman. -- Jordan Raanan Next game: at Miami Dolphins (Aug. 22, 4 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Bears 34, Browns 10 Bears: The Bears' run defense was solid in the preseason opener, highlighted by a third-down stop from free agent linebacker Devin Bush . Two Day 3 draft picks -- cornerback Malik Muhammad and defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg -- did the most with their reps. Muhammad started at nickel and recorded the second-most tackles (five) on the defense while Van den Berg notched three quarterback hits and a run stuff. Beanie Bishop Jr. was one of nine defensive backs who worked out for the Bears last week in the wake of so many injuries in the secondary. He intercepted both Shedeur Sanders and Dillon Gabriel . The best performances on offense came from wide receiver Kaden Davis and running back Salvon Ahmed . Davis had already made one of the best catches in training camp and added to his impressive offseason with a 41-yard reception. On Ahmed's 49-yard catch-and-run touchdown, it was Davis who sped in stride to lay down one final block to clear a path for the running back to reach the end zone. -- Courtney Cronin Next game: at Cincinnati Bengals (Aug. 22, 7 p.m. ET) Browns: The team couldn't have asked for a better preseason debut from its top picks on offense. Left tackle Spencer Fano played the entire first half and allowed two pressures but generally held up. Wide receiver Denzel Boston had one catch, but it moved the chains on a scoring possession. Wideout KC Concepcion turned heads the most, showcasing his versatility in the first half. Concepcion returned a punt 31 yards, caught three passes for 27 yards and scored his first NFL touchdown on a 14-yard jet sweep. -- Daniel Oysefusi Next game: vs. Buffalo Bills (Aug. 22, 1 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Bills 29, Panthers 14 Bills: DJ Moore 's first game with the Bills accomplished what the team was looking for from Josh Allen 's new No. 1 receiver. He caught three passes (four targets) for 61 yards on 10 snaps, including a 32-yard catch-and-run where 29 yards came after the catch. Moore did have his right leg looked at by trainers briefly but remained on the sideline, and the first-team offense did not return to the field. Other highlights included camp riser UDFA CB Kani Walker 's interception on a pass that went right to him from QB Kyle Trask , second-round edge rusher TJ Parker 's sack, free agent edge rusher Mike Danna 's two sacks and seventh-rounder Tommy Doman Jr . showing his lead in the punting competition and holding for all four of Tyler Bass ' field goal (made three) and point-after attempts (2-for-2). -- Alaina Getzenberg Next game: at Cleveland Browns (Aug. 21, 1 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Panthers: Several free agent additions made their debuts. Edge rusher Jaelan Phillips made an immediate impact with a sack and back-to-back pressures on the opening drive, forcing Buffalo to settle for a field goal. Inside linebacker Devin Lloyd had an excellent pursuit to running back James Cook III for a tackle for loss to begin the second series. Backup quarterback Kenny Pickett completed 16 of 19 passes for 92 yards and a touchdown. First-round pick Monroe Freeling looked sturdy in protection at right tackle in nine snaps. Undrafted defensive lineman Aaron Hall and returning outside linebacker Cam Gill flashed as pass rushers. Fifth-round safety Zakee Wheatley continued to do well as an open-field tackler and showed off his upside as a blitzer. -- Mike Kaye Next game: at Jacksonville Jaguars (Aug. 21, 7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN Unlimited) Friday's games Buccaneers 24, Jets 16 Buccaneers: As he has done throughout camp, undrafted free agent rookie cornerback Ayden Garnes made the most of his moment, picking off Bailey Zappe 's pass and returning it 47 yards for a touchdown. Second-round draft pick Josiah Trotter recorded two tackles. Outside linebacker David Walker , a 2025 fourth-round draft pick who missed all preseason last year because of a torn ACL, registered two quarterback pressures. Third-round pick Ted Hurst III hauled in two catches despite poor quarterback play from Connor Bazelak ; Jalon Daniels showed far better command of the offense. Tight end Bauer Sharp went 4-of-5 on targets, and wide receiver Dean Patterson went 5-of-7. First-round pick Rueben Bain Jr. will make his debut next week. -- Jenna Laine Next game: vs. Kansas City Chiefs (Aug. 22, 7:30 p.m. ET, ESPN) Jets: Fourth-round QB Cade Klubnik was the surprise starter after Geno Smith (ankle) was ruled out as a precaution. Klubnik strengthened his case for the No. 2 job, leading the starting offense to a field goal and touchdown in his only two series -- a curiously short outing. Coach Aaron Glenn arguably should have let the former Clemson star play the entire half. Facing the Bucs' backups, Klubnik (5-for-7, 56 yards) didn't make any big mistakes and kept the chains moving, hitting Garrett Wilson for two third-down conversions. It was a nondescript debut for edge rusher David Bailey , the No. 2 pick. Playing with the starters, he registered one tackle and one QB pressure in eight snaps, getting double-teamed on three of his six pass rushes. First-round wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr . got into the open field for a 26-yard reception while playing with the backups. He was leapfrogged on the depth chart by Isaiah Williams . It was a quiet night for the veteran newcomers, most of whom received limited action. -- Rich Cimini Next game: at Pittsburgh Steelers (Aug. 21, 7 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Broncos 27, Falcons 7 Broncos: On a team that returns 20 of 22 starters from the AFC Championship Game, there are not a lot of roster spots in play, but in Denver's win over the Atlanta Falcons , rookie fourth-round RB Jonah Coleman showed off his decisive running style with 24 yards on four carries. He also displayed the physicality the Broncos wanted to see while playing with the starters in the first half. Undrafted rookie wide receiver Cameron Ross , who has flashed athleticism in camp, had a 24-yard carry in the first half when the first- and second-team offense was on the field, a sign that he has already gotten the coaches' attention. Undrafted cornerback Sam Fresch prevented what would have been a Falcons touchdown when he knocked away a pass by Jack Strand with 1:54 to play in the game. -- Jeff Legwold Next game: vs. Green Bay Packers (Aug. 21, 9 p.m. ET, ESPN) Falcons: All eyes were on quarterback Tua Tagovailoa in his first start of any kind with the Atlanta Falcons . It was not an auspicious beginning. Tagovailoa looked uncomfortable and didn't get much help from his offensive line. He completed 3 of 5 passes for 22 yards. All four targets went to tight end Kyle Pitts Sr. , a result fantasy football enthusiasts might find interesting. It didn't get much better for the Falcons once Tagovailoa left the game. Veteran quarterback Cooper Rush , a recent signee, was 7-of-19 for 62 yards and two interceptions, including a 96-yard pick-six by Jahdae Barron . -- Marc Raimondi Next game: at Indianapolis Colts (Aug. 22, 1 p.m. ET) Commanders 20, Dolphins 7 Commanders: Linebacker Sonny Styles played in the first series, a 14-play Miami touchdown drive. Styles wasn't much of a factor, though he wore the green dot and called the plays. He finished with three tackles but looked like a rookie playing his first game, still getting comfortable. A few rookies had strong games. Undrafted free agent running back Robert Henry Jr . showed juice on his runs and scored from 22 yards out. He finished with 75 yards on 12 runs. Henry hit the holes fast and used good vision to knife through narrow openings. Center Matt Gulbin showed some power inside in the second quarter. Third-round receiver Antonio Williams caught one pass for 16 yards and didn't play until the third quarter. Running back Kaytron Allen doesn't have Henry's burst but managed 85 yards on 23 carries and a 1-yard touchdown. -- John Keim Next game: at Detroit Lions (Aug. 22, noon ET) Dolphins: Wide receiver Caleb Douglas shot up the depth chart during the Dolphins' first two weeks of training camp and showed why in his only snaps of the game. On third-and-5, quarterback Malik Willis hit Douglas on a slot fade. The rookie shook off defensive pass interference, tipped the ball to himself with one hand and corralled it in for a 28-yard reception. Second-round rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez finished with a tackle and a pressure in 13 snaps, and defensive end Max Llewellyn recorded half a sack. Willis, who signed a three-year deal with the Dolphins this offseason, was sharp in his lone series of the game -- a 14-play, 93-yard touchdown drive that spanned more than seven minutes. He completed 4 of 5 passes for 43 yards, adding 9 more yards on the ground. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques Next game: vs. New York Giants (Aug. 22, 4 p.m. ET, ESPN) Thursday's games Cardinals 27, Raiders 14 Cardinals: No. 3 draft pick Jeremiyah Love showcased his quick feet and power running during his time on the field Thursday night. It resulted in 11 carries for 58 yards, an average of 5.3 yards per carry. He showcased his ability to find holes and the strength to take on hits. He also had three catches for 14 yards with a long of 7 yards. Second-round pick Chase Bisontis left the game in the third quarter with a knee injury and did not return. He went down holding the back of his left knee and was rolling in agony as he was attended to by trainers. Wide receiver Reggie Virgil , Arizona's fifth-round pick, made an impressive one-handed catch for a 24-yard gain. -- Josh Weinfuss Next game: vs. Dallas Cowboys (Aug. 22, 10 p.m. ET, NFL Network) Raiders: The Raiders' quarterback battle between Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza was on full display. Cousins played only the opening drive, which resulted in a touchdown. After he completed a 10-yard pass to Jack Bech and a 16-yard pass to Tre Tucker , he found tight end Michael Mayer for a 13-yard touchdown, which capped off a 10-play, 68-yard drive to begin the game. Cousins completed 5 of 6 passes for 50 yards. As for the No. 1 pick, Mendoza, he showed off his resilience, a trait admired by the coaching staff. His first drive wasn't great -- he had two incompletions and the Raiders were forced to punt. His second was a different story. He completed a 19-yard pass to rookie wide receiver Malik Benson , fitting the ball through a tight window. Rookie running back Mike Washington Jr . then rushed for 53 yards before Mendoza zipped the ball over the middle to Bech for a 6-yard touchdown pass on third down. His third drive resulted in a three-and-out. But his fourth and final drive of the evening ended with him putting the Raiders into field goal range. He finished the night completing 10 of 16 passes for 97 yards. Mendoza did struggle against pressure. He was pressured on 38.9% of dropbacks, going 2-for-6 with 11 yards and a 42.4 passer rating. He was sacked once. -- Ryan McFadden Next game: at Houston Texans (Aug. 20, 8 p.m. ET, ESPN) Steelers 28, Packers 9 Steelers: Welcome to the NFL (kind of), rookies! Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions CHICAGO -- The Cleveland Browns dropped their preseason opener to the Chicago Bears on Saturday, but coach Todd Monken was pleased with the play of quarterback Deshaun Watson in his first game since the 2024 season. Watson, who is competing with Shedeur Sanders to be Cleveland's starting quarterback, started the first preseason game alongside the Browns' projected offense and played the first half. He completed 11 of 15 passes for 126 yards and led two scoring drives, the only points for Cleveland in the 34-10 loss . "It was awesome," said Monken, a first-year head coach. "It was so cool to watch him play. I get all of the frustration by fans, himself. But for him to come back and work like he did is an unbelievable credit to him. And then to go out there, he was having fun today. And that is so cool. And I thought he really functioned at a high level. Certainly we don't want to be taking timeouts. We sure as heck can't take delay of games, OK? But it was fun watching him play and watching us put the next step forward and see where we're at." The exhibition marked Watson's first game since he tore his right Achilles tendon in October 2024. Watson, who has been limited to 19 games because of suspension and injuries since being traded to the Browns in March 2022, sat out the 2025 season after undergoing a second Achilles surgery in January 2025. The Browns' opening possession was a quick three-and-out after three runs by Quinshon Judkins . On the second series, Watson completed his first four attempts, but his fifth was dropped by tight end Harold Fannin Jr . on a pass that would have resulted in a first down. Cleveland took a 3-0 lead on kicker Andre Szmyt's 50-yard field goal. Watson led a 10-play, 86-yard scoring drive on the next possession, a series that was capped by a 14-yard touchdown run from rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion . Watson turned the ball over on his fourth drive after he was strip-sacked on fourth-and-2, and the Bears recovered. His final two possessions resulted in punts. "I don't think [there is] anything that I doubt in myself," Watson said. "That's the reason why I worked hard these last two years to get back to that. Had some challenges with some injuries and suspension, and now being able to get a full offseason and continue to work my way back up, even though it takes time. But at the same time, I don't doubt myself in any way that I can't play at a high level." Sanders started the third quarter and played three series into the fourth quarter, completing 6 of 11 passes for 79 yards and one interception. His first two completions went for chunk gains on his opening possession, but he overthrew a pass to wide receiver Malachi Corley that led to the interception on his third and final series. Dillon Gabriel played the remainder of the game, completing 5 of 8 passes for 23 yards and an interception. "Obviously, turning the ball over and all that stuff is not great, and it won't survive a long time in the league doing that," Sanders said. "But as long as my eyes and my feet and everything were in the right place, being able to execute it, it just may happen. So, I look at the positive of things. I'm alive, I'm breathing. I'm able to come up here and talk to y'all. So, I can't be that down." The Browns will host joint practices with the Bills on Thursday, and Monken said Watson and Sanders will split first-team reps against Buffalo. Sanders will start the second preseason game against the Bills at home next Saturday and play in the first half. Watson will play in the third quarter, and Gabriel will play in the fourth quarter, Monken said. "Both of them had a turnover," Monken said of Watson and Sanders. "One was a fumble, but I was really pleased with our quarterback play. It's not going to feel like that. Turn it over three times, that's never going to be ideal. But to me, it felt like we are going to be able to throw the football, be effective in that, certainly do a better job coaching in the run game and protections and our play actions. And everything that we do we're going to get better at. But I was pleased with our quarterbacks."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Veteran defender Jamal Adams was taken to the locker room on a cart with a right knee injury Saturday shortly after his preseason debut with the Minnesota Vikings , who signed him to a one-year contract last month on the eve of training camp. Adams played 11 defensive snaps before going to the sideline medical tent. His final play was in pass defense on New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart 's 15-yard touchdown pass to Malachi Fields with 13 minutes, 32 seconds remaining in the second quarter. "Initial exam does not look good," coach Kevin O'Connell said after the Vikings' 13-10 win . "Don't want to confirm anything until we see the imaging on that." Adams, 30, was the New York Jets ' first-round pick as a safety in 2017. He has made three Pro Bowls but has struggled with injuries in the second half of his career. He played nine or fewer games in the 2022, 2023 and 2024 seasons. Adams moved to linebacker last season with the Las Vegas Raiders , but the Vikings have been using him at both positions during training camp.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions TEMPE, Ariz. -- Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love will miss the next week to let a sore ankle he injured in Thursday night's preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders heal, coach Mike LaFleur said Saturday. Love was more sore Friday than he was Thursday, said LaFleur, who added that the running back was "more sore than we were anticipating." "He was in great spirits even yesterday," LaFleur said. LaFleur said the Cardinals will reevaluate Love's ankle next week before deciding on a plan for the rest of the preseason. With Love not practicing this week, he also won't play in Saturday night's preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys . Love played 23 snaps Thursday night, rushing 11 times for 58 yards and catching three passes for 14 yards. With Love out this week, Arizona's running back rotation will start with Tyler Allgeier and continue with Bam Knight and Corey Kiner . LaFleur said running back Trey Benson , who has been dealing with a flare-up in his surgically repaired left knee, is "progressing," LaFleur said. "I can't give you an exact timeline when you guys will see him, but he's doing better than he was," LaFleur said. As for James Conner , who missed 14 games last season with a right foot injury and has not participated in 11-on-11 drills or played in the preseason, LaFleur said he is also "progressing." "I'm not going to give you a timeline on it because we don't know that timeline yet," LaFleur said. "And again, like I've said multiple times, he's played enough in this league and has earned the right to know when he is going to be able to return. And it's not return to play. It's return to performance. Anyone can get back out there, but if they don't feel like they can perform at the level that they're capable of, why put him out there? Particularly a vet like him who's done it at such a high clip for so many years. So I know he's eager to get back in due time. I think we'll see him."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Three-time Pro Bowl cornerback Devon Witherspoon and the Seattle Seahawks reached an agreement on an extension Saturday, with sources telling ESPN's Adam Schefter it's a four-year deal worth $132 million. The contract includes more than $101 million in guaranteed money, sources said, and makes Witherspoon the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history. The Seahawks announced the agreement but not the terms. The deal took longer than expected to complete given that the Seahawks turned their attention to extending Witherspoon right after making Jaxon Smith-Njigba the NFL's highest-paid wide receiver in March. One possible hang-up was that New England Patriots star cornerback Christian Gonzalez , who shares the same agent as Witherspoon, is also up for a top-of-the-market extension. But Witherspoon's deal was finished the day the Seahawks opened their preseason against the Dallas Cowboys . "It's a win-win," Seahawks general manager John Schneider told Seattle Sports 710-AM before Saturday's game. "It's a great deal for Spoon. It's a great deal for the organization. He'll be with us for the next ... six seasons. He's just such a great guy, such a high-end competitor. Obviously the instincts, the anticipation, but just the juice he brings, the way he treats everybody in the building, he's a special, special person." Witherspoon had been practicing throughout the offseason and into training camp despite not having an extension in place. "It feels good," Witherspoon said on the Seahawks' TV broadcast. "Long time coming ... I'm thankful. All glory to God. Shoutout to John and the people upstairs for making this happen. I'm just grateful, man." Coach Mike Macdonald recently praised Witherspoon's approach amid negotiations, saying he was "really impressed" by the cornerback's ability to compartmentalize the business side of things. In last week's season premiere of "Hard Knocks," Witherspoon said he was "not worried" about the contract talks, choosing instead to focus on getting prepared for the regular season. Witherspoon, 25, has made the Pro Bowl on the initial ballot in each of his first three seasons. He is one of the physical and emotional tone-setters for Seattle's defense, which allowed the fewest points in 2025 before leading the Seahawks to a 29-13 win over the Patriots in Super Bowl LX. Witherspoon was one of the stars of that game, recording a sack of Drake Maye and delivering the hit on New England's quarterback that led to a pick-six by Uchenna Nwosu . The Seahawks drafted Witherspoon with the fifth pick in 2023, which they acquired from the Denver Broncos in the Russell Wilson trade. Seattle took Smith-Njigba 20th that year. The two have since developed into franchise cornerstones for the Super Bowl champions. Witherspoon became the fourth player in team history to be named to the Pro Bowl in each of his first three seasons. Last year, as the Seahawks were commemorating their 50th season, they named him one of the franchise's 50 greatest players of all time. His résumé now includes a record-setting contract as well as the Super Bowl championship. In March, the Seahawks exercised Witherspoon's fifth-year option at a cost of roughly $21.2 million for 2027. He was set to make just under $5.1 million in 2026.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay said he thought rookie quarterback Ty Simpson had "good command" of the offense during his NFL debut Saturday in a 20-12 preseason victory over the Kansas City Chiefs . Simpson, the 13th pick and second quarterback selected in this year's draft, played the final three quarters, completing 21 of 25 passes for 190 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions. "I thought he took what the defense gave him," McVay said. "I thought he read the plays out, read with his feet. I thought he did a really good job overall. ... I thought he kept the ball in play. That's the biggest thing, is keeping the ball in play." Though he didn't know what to expect going into his first NFL game, Simpson said that after the first drive that it felt "just like playing in the backyard." Simpson is the first player with 190 passing yards and two touchdown passes in his preseason debut since Baker Mayfield did it with the Cleveland Browns in 2018, according to ESPN Research. Simpson completed passes to seven players, and both of his touchdown passes went to running back Dean Connors . Simpson received extended playing time in part because McVay doesn't play his starters or key backups during the preseason. Simpson didn't get significant reps during training camp, especially on days quarterback Matthew Stafford was practicing. Stetson Bennett IV , who is also competing to back up Stafford, started the game for the Rams. A 2023 fourth-round pick, Bennett compiled 4 of 6 passes for 38 yards in his two drives. After the game, Simpson was asked about the competition at backup quarterback but said he is focused on being "the best version" of himself. "I really don't get into that, honestly," Simpson said. "I really just try to be the best version of myself I can be and compete with myself. A lot of the time, people get caught up in 'who is better than who' and 'who is going to get this spot' and stuff. But at the end of the day, I'm just trying to prepare me for the future and try to stack days and [make] progress."

Raanan joined ESPN in 2016. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- Another game, another trip to the blue medical tent. And New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart isn't too happy about the reccurrence. After being checked for a concussion five times last year during his rookie season, Dart was sent to the medical tent after taking a big hit in Saturday's preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings . The request to undergo his latest concussion check left him "puzzled." Dart was cleared early in the second quarter of Saturday's 13-10 loss. He said he had the wind knocked out of him before being sent to the medical tent. "As far as the blue tent, I really respect the rules and the thought behind the NFL has of keeping players healthy and reviewing things," Dart said. "But at the same time, I'm still puzzled by it just feeling like every time that I get hit, I find my way in there, which, at times, I still try to wrap my head around." Dart was diagnosed with one concussion last year that cost him two games. This might be how he will be treated as a result. "If a normal QB takes that hit, I'm sure not much is going to be said about it," right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. "But, you know, when we play in New York and it's Jaxson Dart, I'm assuming people are going to make it bigger than it actually is. "I guess that is just the reality we live in right now. People are going to blow things up that don't really necessarily have to be blown up." When Dart was asked if this is his new reality, he said he was done addressing the situation. Dart was on the ground for a few seconds Saturday after the final play of the first quarter, when running back Tyrone Tracy Jr . missed a block. Coach John Harbaugh focused on what went wrong on the play. "My feelings in that moment was we need to block better," Harbaugh said. "That's what my feeling was." The Giants' medical staff checked on Dart in between quarters. The medical spotter in a booth high above called for the concussion check. It stunned Dart and Harbaugh. "Honestly, I was [surprised]," Harbaugh said. "But I would say that their job is to err on the side of player safety, so I can't argue with that either." Dart went into the blue tent for an exam. He was replaced by backup Jameis Winston for two plays, including a third-and-23 conversion. "I never thought that I was going to be taken out," Dart said. "So I'm going to keep playing until they tell me I'm not playing. I want to be out there." When Dart returned, he threw a touchdown on the first play. He scrambled left and threw sidearm against his body to rookie wide receiver Malachi Fields , who grabbed the ball over the defender's head for a 15-yard touchdown. It was the Giants' only touchdown in the contest. It was Dart's final play of the afternoon. "Was great. I don't know, in the heat of the battle, I didn't think too much about it," Harbaugh said of his quarterback throwing a touchdown pass on the first play after he returned. "But to see him go out there and throw a touchdown pass, I thought was pretty darn cool. I was excited about that. Made me happy." Dart finished 3-of-4 passing for 26 yards with a touchdown, and he was sacked twice. Harbaugh had no reservations about putting him back in the game after the big hit and being checked for the concussion. "No, he was fine," he said.

Courtney is a frequent panelist on Around the Horn and host of Best Week Ever and GameNight on ESPN Radio. She also co-hosts The Chicago Bears Podcast on ESPN 1000. She previously worked at the San Jose Mercury News as a multimedia sports journalist. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions CHICAGO -- An unexpected source brought the horsepower to the Bears ' 34-10 win over the Browns on Saturday. Bears wide receivers coach/assistant head coach Antwaan Randle El was handed playcalling duties for the second half of Chicago's preseason opener by coach Ben Johnson. The result was 24 unanswered points, 12 first downs and 235 yards as the Bears blew out the Browns at Soldier Field. "I thought he did a phenomenal job with [quarterback] Case [Keenum] taking the reins and then transition on over to [quarterback] Miller [Moss] just to see how he was trying to stay in their wheelhouse," Johnson said. "He was part of the quarterback meeting last night, and we were talking about what was on the call sheet and their favorites and all that. And I think it was a phenomenal experience for him, and I know our guys rallied around that as well." Randle El, a nine-year NFL wide receiver with Pittsburgh and Washington , has coached with Johnson since the two crossed paths in Detroit . He impressed Johnson and players alike with his game plan for the second half and how he put multiple offensive units in position to score. "I know he's going to be a head coach," Keenum said. "I think his demeanor in front of the team, his leadership qualities, are top-notch. Some of the best I've been around. His relatability to players? I mean, it's the fact that he's been there, done that with just about everything. And there's no, for lack of a better word, coachspeak to him. It's all real." Added quarterback Tyson Bagent : "Has anybody ever had a better first outing than Antwaan Randle El? That's just who he is. He's always prepared. He knows the ins and outs of the playbook. So really, it was not surprising, at least for us on the sideline." This is the second straight preseason where Johnson had allowed one of his assistants to take over calling plays for the offense, and Randle El might not be the last. Johnson said postgame that he might experiment with letting other Bears coaches call plays in the preseason. That's what he did in 2025 for Declan Doyle, who was Johnson's offensive coordinator during his inaugural season in Chicago. While Doyle did not call plays during the regular season, Johnson allowed his former OC to do so in preseason games. Doyle is now the offensive coordinator of the Baltimore Ravens , where he will call his own offense this season. That's something Johnson believes Randle El is capable of doing in the future. "Here's the thing about El, I think he's got a chance to be an offensive coordinator in this league," Johnson said. "I think he's got a chance to be a head coach in this league. I think he would do a phenomenal job in both those respects, and I don't know if he gets that type of credit around the league right now. So it's a good opportunity for him to get some recognition."
