Cockcroft play Why Field Yates expects a productive season for Emeka Egbuka in fantasy (0:44) Matt Bowen Aug 17, 2026, 11:23 PM ET Close Matt Bowen is a fantasy football and NFL writer for ESPN. He joined ESPN in 2015, writes regularly for ESPN+ and spent multiple years on "NFL Matchup." After graduating from the University of Iowa, Matt played safety in the NFL for St. Louis, Green Bay, Washington and Buffalo over seven seasons. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Editor's note: Saints rookie WR Jordyn Tyson is expected to potentially miss two months, so he has been removed from this column. I build a fantasy football draft board every summer. Mocks, film study, scheme trends, the numbers that translate to production, I look at it all. It's all part of the process. I draft players I like. Their traits, playmaking ability, the system fit. That includes the high-floor targets I can count on in my lineup, as well as the upside plays. You can take some risks here, too. Plus, everyone has their late-round fliers, the dart throws when the clock is running out in the 14th round. Take a shot. So, let's go through my board by position, focusing on some of my favorite targets in redraft formats heading into draft season later this month. (I play in four home leagues.) We'll do this in multiple tiers based on current ESPN average draft position (ADP). I'll also give you five targets to put on your radar for the later rounds. Have a great fantasy season. Let's win some leagues. Jump ahead Quarterbacks | Running backs | Wide receivers Tight ends | Later-round targets Quarterback Joe Burrow , Cincinnati Bengals (ADP: QB6) Landing Burrow as a mid-tier QB1 fits my philosophy on getting value at the position. Sure, there are availability concerns with Burrow (he missed at least seven games in two of his past three seasons). But in playing the full 2024 season, Burrow scored 21.9 fantasy PPG and threw 43 touchdown passes. That's who I'm drafting here, the league's best pocket passer, with two premier targets in WRs Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins . I think Burrow will produce top-three QB numbers this season. Caleb Williams , Chicago Bears (ADP: QB11) I'll take Williams all day as a fringe QB1. In 2025 (Williams' first season under head coach Ben Johnson), he scored 18.7 fantasy PPG and we saw how his natural playmaking ability leads to winning weeks (eight games with 20 or more points). With another year of development paired with Johnson's elite playcalling, I expect Williams to show even more growth as a rhythm passer. A big-time breakout looms here. Tyler Shough , New Orleans Saints (ADP: QB19) Drafting Shough as an upside QB2 fits if you carry two quarterbacks or play in a superflex format. In Weeks 13-18 last season, Shough had 117.5 fantasy points (QB4) and he scored at least 17 in each game. He's a timing-and-location thrower in Kellen Moore's system, plus he can create as a runner (186 yards rushing, 3 TDs). With a boost from the addition of rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson to play opposite Chris Olave , Shough has the skill set -- and the coach -- to push the QB1 line. Running back Jonathan Taylor , Indianapolis Colts (ADP: RB4) play 1:24 Why Jonathan Taylor's extension should put fantasy managers' minds at ease I'm taking Taylor (21.3 fantasy PPG in 2025) over both Christian McCaffrey and De'Von Achane if I'm picking in the middle of the first round. Taylor gives you high-end volume and scoring upside, as he led the league in both carries (323) and rushing touchdowns (18). Plus, Taylor can create explosive plays (36 carries of 10 or more yards), and his pass-game usage elevated last season (career-best 46 receptions). With QB Daniel Jones expected back for the start of the season, I'm all-in on Taylor as my RB1. Omarion Hampton , Los Angeles Chargers (ADP: RB11) An ankle injury limited Hampton to nine games as a rookie in 2025, and that Chargers offensive line was beat up. Still, Hampton had three games of 20 or more fantasy points and finished with 15.1 PPG. With a healthy and upgraded front in a new system under Mike McDaniel that uses heavy 21 personnel (2 RBs, 1 TE, 2 WRs) to create numbers and blocking angles, this Chargers run game can roll in 2026. I see breakout potential here for Hampton. Jadarian Price , Seattle Seahawks (ADP: RB26) Price is expected to share touches in Seattle's backfield with George Holani , Emanuel Wilson and Zach Charbonnet (once he's back from his ACL tear), but Price has the traits to emerge quickly at the start of the season. Price has the vision and instincts to find a downhill path, and he showed contact balance at the point of attack on his Notre Dame tape. Price averaged almost 6.0 yards per carry last season, and he can find the end zone (11 rushing TDs). He has the physical profile and speed to handle NFL volume. Jordan Mason , Minnesota Vikings (ADP: RB43) With Aaron Jones Sr .'s injury history (he missed at least five games in two of the past three seasons), Mason is on my board as a high-end insurance back. I'll try to land him in all my leagues. Mason had 23.6 fantasy points in the Week 3 game versus the Bengals last season, and he posted double-digit points in four of five starts. Plus, he's a strong fit for the zone run game in Minnesota. Draft Mason with the expectation that he starts some games for the Vikings this season. Wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Seattle Seahawks (ADP: WR3) The best receiver I saw on tape last season, Smith-Njigba scored 21.2 fantasy PPG in 2025 (second most among WRs) and led the league with 1,793 receiving yards. A true multilevel target, JSN can uncover at the short-to-intermediate areas of the field, plus he has third-level juice. Last season, Smith-Njigba's 18 receptions and 6.9 fantasy PPG on throws of 20 or more air yards led the league. The unquestioned No. 1 receiving option for QB Sam Darnold , Smith-Njigba gives you consistent volume and playmaking upside. Emeka Egbuka , Tampa Bay Buccaneers (ADP: WR18) With Mike Evans now in San Francisco, the door is open for Egbuka to emerge as the top target in Tampa Bay's offense. A detailed route runner who can create separation, Egbuka had four games with 20 or more fantasy points as a rookie, finishing with 68 receptions for 938 yards and 6 TDs. With the aggressive throwing mentality of Buccaneers QB Baker Mayfield , don't be surprised if Egbuka finishes as a top-10 wide receiver in 2026. Luther Burden III , Chicago Bears (ADP: WR28) Burden had double-digit production in three of his final four games last season, including the 27.8 points he scored in Week 17 versus the 49ers. With DJ Moore now in Buffalo, Burden should see a major boost in target volume, and coach Ben Johnson will deploy him as a playmaker. Burden suffered a groin injury in early August, which will sideline him for the preseason, but I'm still buying his outlook this season. You can draft Burden as a WR2/flex. You should expect some WR1 breakout weeks, too. Wan'Dale Robinson , Tennessee Titans (ADP: WR43) Robinson scored a career-best 13.6 fantasy PPG in 2025 and produced two games of 28 or more points. Robinson displayed more big-play ability, too, catching 13 passes of 15 or more air yards (after totaling four over his first three years as a pro). He should be a reliable slot target in Tennessee for QB Cam Ward and carries WR3 value in deeper leagues. Tight end Colston Loveland , Chicago Bears (ADP: TE3) I rarely jump at a tight end early in drafts, but Loveland is the one player I would make an exception for. Over his last five games as a rookie in 2025, Loveland scored 15.1 fantasy PPG (including 21 or more in two games) and his production continued in the Bears' two playoff matchups (12 receptions, 193 yards). With his formation flexibility and receiving traits, Loveland wins on schemed throws, plus he brings one-on-one ability to Johnson's offense. He can be a star in the league. Jake Ferguson , Dallas Cowboys (ADP: TE12) Ferguson has been my go-to in summer mocks, as it allows me to wait until the later rounds to draft a tight end. Ferguson scored 11.1 fantasy PPG last season, plus he's going to see the ball in scoring position. Ferguson had 23 red zone targets last season (including 10 end zone targets), and he finished with eight TDs, catching six on throws inside the 10-yard line. It has been a pattern, as Ferguson has 51 red zone targets (and 22 end zone targets) over his past three seasons. With that type of touchdown/scoring upside in an explosive Dallas offense, Ferguson is a quality starter for fantasy lineups. Isaiah Likely , New York Giants (ADP: TE14) Likely fits in deeper leagues as a sneaky sleeper candidate based on his skill set and projected usage with the Giants. Now removed from the shadow of Mark Andrews in Baltimore, Likely projects as the "move" player in New York's offense -- a versatile, multilevel target who can also be schemed on screens and unders. For his career, 47.4% of Likely's receiving yards have come after the catch. He has the ability to post low-end TE1 numbers this season if he sees consistent volume. Five late-round targets to put on the radar Jalen Coker , WR, Carolina Panthers Coker missed time to start last season due to an injury, but from Weeks 11-18, he averaged 11.0 fantasy PPG and had four games of double-digit production, posting a touchdown reception in three. Coker has the vertical stretch ability to win down the field, plus he can run the deep in-breakers or see the ball on three-step quicks underneath. Jalen Nailor , WR, Las Vegas Raiders Nailor is more than willing to work the middle of the field, and he has the quickness to separate on out-breaking routes. Nailor scored an impressive 10 TDs on 57 receptions over the past two seasons with the Vikings in a limited role, and someone must emerge as the perimeter No. 1 in the Las Vegas offense. Kaelon Black , RB, San Francisco 49ers If Black wins the No. 2 role behind McCaffrey, managers can target him late as an insurance play. A rapid accelerator, Black has the short-area speed to dart through daylight, rushing for over 1,000 yards and scoring 10 TDs last season at Indiana. Black had only eight receptions over his final two college seasons, but he can be utilized as an underneath outlet in the 49ers offense. Keep an eye on the competition in the San Francisco running backs room. Germie Bernard , WR, Pittsburgh Steelers The slot receiver in Mike McCarthy's system will see the ball, and while Bernard is not a vertical blazer, he showed the ability to uncover on his Alabama tape. Yes, Bernard has real competition for targets in Pittsburgh with DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr ., but he can be viewed as a bench stash, especially in 12-team leagues. There's potential upside here as a chain-mover for QB Aaron Rodgers . Kaytron Allen , RB, Washington Commanders I'd take a shot on Allen late in drafts. If the rookie out of Penn State can get some early-down carries -- and win the role as the primary goal-line back in Washington -- he'll have value in all scoring formats. Allen runs behind his pads, and his physical style shows up in tight quarters. That works when you need to get the ball into the end zone. He's a name to monitor through the rest of the preseason. var espn_ui = window.espn_ui || {}; var espn = window.espn || {}; es

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ATLANTA -- Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa was not pleased after his first game with the team. Preseason or not, Tagovailoa said the Falcons' 27-7 loss to the Denver Broncos on Friday night was "definitely not up to standard, not even up to par" for Atlanta. "Frustrated and disappointed at the way things happened tonight as we went out there," Tagovailoa said. Tagovailoa didn't play all that much -- just two series. He was 3-of-5 passing for 22 yards with all four of his targets going to tight end Kyle Pitts Sr. On his second snap, out of shotgun, Tagovailoa lost control of the ball and fumbled it before falling on it. He believes that set the tone for a lethargic start. The Broncos scored 24 unanswered points before the Falcons got on the board. "Just thinking about it, what we put out there is not a reflection of the hard work that we've put in the first two weeks into training camp, and it does no justice for the work that our coaches, as well, have implemented," Tagovailoa said. "So it starts with me. I got to be better with that. I thought off of that [second] play, [things] kind of got out of the rhythm." Tagovailoa is in somewhat of a competition with Michael Penix Jr. for the starting quarterback job. But Penix has not been cleared to practice fully. He cannot yet do 11-on-11 team sessions. So Tagovailoa is ahead of Penix at this stage mostly by default. He said he didn't think how he played Friday night did him any favors. "I'm competing," Tagovailoa said. "I'm wanting to go out there for points on the board, not go out there and we'll go three-and-out, three-and-out -- not be able to perform to the level that I know I'm able to do. So always looking at everything as a competition, but just got to be better." Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said it was tough to fully grade Tagovailoa's performance because the plan was to play him for only a series or two. Tagovailoa ended up getting nine plays, with just a single first down. "I evaluate the entire offense in that regard," Stefanski said. "So didn't move the ball well enough as an offense. Certainly, there's some things that we can clean up. We did drop a snap out there. So those are little plays that we will continue to work on. But hard to give a grade on that fewest amount of ... sample size." Tagovailoa and Stefanski are new faces in Atlanta. The Falcons hired Stefanski, general manager Ian Cunningham and president of football Matt Ryan in the offseason. That new regime then signed Tagovailoa, after he was cut by the Miami Dolphins , to a one-year, $1.3 million contract. "I thought it was great being in our building -- for a lot of us being in here for the first time, seeing what it's like in the building," Stefanski said. "I thought it was a great atmosphere for our players. I thought it just was exciting to be in front of our fans."

The dispute has become fodder for internet trolling. StubHub announced it would "no longer offer tickets in groups of 5." NASCAR Craftsman Truck Series team TRICON Garage said it would not be running No. 5 at a race Friday. After the win, which came against the Commanders' neighbor in MLB, the Mets posted a graphic saying they "Stopped at 4 out of respect for Jayden Daniels." He previously covered the NFL at The Ringer, Bleeding Green Nation and The Draft Network. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions NFL training camps are well underway across 32 teams as we transition to preseason games . And if training camp is school for NFL teams before the 18-week-long exam of the regular season, then we can't leave school without giving out some yearbook superlatives. Superlatives are, of course, rampant at this time of year, as training camp is a time to be superlative in our estimation of players and teams. Everyone is deserving of all the awards; every team will win every division. For these superlatives, I went after the true cream of the rising crop: the optimistic Bengals ... the ever-dramatic Browns ... and of course, the Branson Taylor - Kayode Awosika battle in Chargers camp. I have 10 fun awards and recognitions to hand out. From "most likely to succeed" to "best shape of his life," these are the players and teams that have made an impression on me over the early days of 2026 training camp. Jump to: Most likely to break your heart Best vibes | Biggest position battle Most cursed camp battle Most likely to succeed with new offense Most likely to succeed with new defense Best shape of his life Day 3 rookie everyone fell for Busiest medical tent | Preseason MVP Most likely to break your heart: Aaron Donald and the Los Angeles Rams Do I want to be the guy betting against the three-time Defensive Player of the Year and single best defensive player of my (and perhaps any) generation of football? No. But someone has to be the stick in the mud here. Training camp inevitably generates towering expectations, and the Rams are perfectly primed to stand atop the preseason mountain. Offseason trades for edge Myles Garrett and cornerback Trent McDuffie added star power to a defense punching above its weight in 2025. Sprinkle a little Donald on there, and we have what ...? The best defense in football? The best defense of the past decade? Maybe -- but probably not! First things first: Donald is not yet a Ram , and when he becomes a Ram, it is extremely unlikely he starts out playing 40 snaps per game. He is 35 years old. In the past five seasons, only Cameron Heyward and Calais Campbell have played at least 40 snaps per game as 35-plus-year-old defensive tackles. Widen it to 30 snaps per game, and you catch a John Jenkins year in 2024. Those guys were already at NFL-level conditioning, and it's going to take Donald (as unbelievably talented as he is) time to get there. When Donald joins Garrett and McDuffie in the Rams' astronomical effort to improve their defense, he will do his part elevating them from ... fourth in DVOA. The Rams were fifth in defensive success rate and sixth in defensive EPA per drive. This was a good defense last season. I admire the Rams' acknowledgement that it lacked star power -- a fact that did show up in the postseason -- and general manager Les Snead's willingness to take big swings to add blue-chip players to that side of the ball. But it's inaccurate to represent the Rams as a team that missed out on the Super Bowl because it lacked an elite defense. Los Angeles missed out because the Seahawks were very good and it lost in the brutally thin margins of professional football. The new additions will give the Rams an edge in the postseason, where elite, field-tipping players really show up in the game-planning process. But the Rams still have to get there, which means quarterback Matthew Stafford needs to stay healthy all season. It means the retirement of offensive tackle Rob Havenstein and potential suspension of Alaric Jackson can't hurt the pass protection too much. It means 33-year-old Davante Adams and the physical Puka Nacua , who could face disciplinary action because of the lawsuit filed against him in March , must stay on the field, as well. play 1:10 Canty on Browns QB battle: Shedeur should start Week 1 of regular season The NFL is not a run-it-back league. Injuries have too big of an impact in a 17-game season. Schematic changes force too much evolution year over year. And in the case of a defensive tackle returning from a four-year retirement, it simply is unreasonable to "run it back" on his impact. Donald is going to be a rotational player on a great defense, and if he makes just one game-changing play in the postseason, the juice will be worth the squeeze. But the Rams have to get to playoff football first, and he needs to get in a uniform to boot. The Rams are rightfully a huge preseason favorite, but as Bill Barnwell's column this week reminds us, their 1-in-8 chance to win the Super Bowl looks bigger now than it is in reality. Don't let the Reunion Rams break your heart with inflated summer expectations. Best vibes: Baltimore Ravens Here's the quick summary: Nnamdi Madubuike is back practicing after a neck injury threatened his career last season. No. 1 receiver Zay Flowers got a fat extension worth $34 million per year. According to ESPN Ravens reporter Jamison Hensley, rookie receiver Ja'Kobi Lane is having a training camp unlike any rookie he has seen in 27 years of covering the Ravens. Tyler Loop , who ended the Ravens' season with a missed kick against the Steelers, apparently can't miss this summer. New head coach Jesse Minter and defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver have the defense humming -- but QB Lamar Jackson and the rest of the Ravens' key offensive players are also gushing about new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. Calais Campbell is back , which is heartwarming. Even the first big threat to the immaculate vibes -- a left leg injury scare for top cornerback Nate Wiggins , who was carted off the field earlier this week -- ended OK, as sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport that testing revealed no structural damage. Training camp vibes have absolutely zero correlation with regular-season wins, of course. But it's better than having terrible vibes! Biggest training camp battle: Los Angeles Chargers left guard Can you name the five players who are competing for starting left guard in the Chargers' offense? (If you can, seek help!) They are as follows: rookie Jake Slaughter (a college center), 2022 first-round tackle Trevor Penning (acquired from the Saints last year), second-year pro Branson Taylor (a practice squad player for much of last season), veteran Kayode Awosika and veteran Trey Pipkins III . On Aug. 4, head coach Jim Harbaugh said he'd like to name a starter after the next 10 practices. That was six practices ago. To this point, no player has taken a lion's share of the snaps. Most teams are playing their first preseason game this week; there are plenty of other training camp battles underway across the league and there's plenty of time to declare a winner here. But any competition of five players indicates that there has been a lack of emergence -- that the staff is still fishing for someone to declare himself a cut above the rest. This is a particularly big issue for the Chargers' interior offensive line, which has been notoriously poor in the Justin Herbert era. Last season, after star offensive tackles Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater went down with injuries, the Chargers' offense became untenable. Herbert was hit 12.9 times per game last season, a preposterously high number usually reserved for true dual-threat quarterbacks, not occasional capable scramblers such as Herbert. New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel brings a quick-pass offense that should alleviate some of the concerns. But scheme can do only so much to hide a liability at guard on third-and-8. It's worth remarking that, while having Alt and Slater back will certainly help, the Chargers' other two interior positions will also feature new players. Former Patriots first-rounder Cole Strange follows McDaniel from Miami to start at right guard, and Tyler Biadasz (released by the Commanders this offseason) is the veteran at center. Both are improvements from 2025 but still are average starters. The interior will already be the part of the Chargers' line that opposing defenses attack, and uncertainty at left guard will only expand that bull's-eye. For the stakes at play and because of the sheer number of contenders, the Chargers' left guard spot takes our award for biggest training camp battle. Better luck next year, Bears left tackle. Most cursed training camp battle: Cleveland Browns quarterback It is exceedingly unlikely the Browns have a good starting quarterback on their roster. The contenders to start are veteran Deshaun Watson and second-year pro Shedeur Sanders . The last time we saw Watson -- who is coming off a torn (and then retorn !) Achilles tendon -- play was 2024. He averaged 4.03 yards per dropback that season -- 942nd out of 947 quarterbacking seasons (minimum 200 dropbacks) this century. And I've never known an Achilles injury to make a quarterback play better. Sanders' 2025 rookie season (5.55 yards per dropback) was 755th in the same sample -- better, but not anything to write home about. Among 70 rookie seasons since 2010 (minimum 150 attempts), Sanders was 68th in interception rate, 64th in EPA per dropback and 62nd in first down/touchdown rate. This is a small sample, of course. But Sanders was only a fifth-round pick and looked like it when he played last season. The chance that he can elevate his play to an acceptable starting level is mightily thin. Sanders might have a higher ceiling than Watson, in that he's a younger player about whom we know less. But Watson, who is in the final year of his deal, carries a (pre-June 1) dead cap hit of $86 million in 2026. That's a pretty penny. If the Browns can get palatable play from Watson, they're financially incentivized to keep him for another season and spread the cap hit out even further. So this competition might end up being decided not with on-field performance but rather on financial ramifications. That feels crummy. But it also might be good news that the competition won't come down to on-field performance, as both quarterbacks have been less than thrilling. As coach Todd Monken put it after a two-minute drill rife with pre-snap penalties at the end of a recent practice: "That was awful. That was s---ty football. play 1:00 49ers' Pearsall has knee surgery, targets 9-month recovery Most likely to succeed (with a new offense): Philadelphia Eagles Anyone else getting the big warm and fuzzies out of Philadelphia? Quarterback Jalen Hurts reportedly looks sleeker and faster, which is a big deal in and of itself. Last season, he had his fewest rushes (105) and rush yards (421) since his rookie season (2020), and when he ran, he produced his lowest yards per carry (4.0). Hurts isn't the only one reinvigorated in Philadelphia -- the new offense under coordinator Sean Mannion is an offense unlike any in which Hurts has played during his NFL career. Mannion, who coached under Matt LaFleur in Green Bay, is bringing the greatest hits of the Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan offense to Philadelphia: under-center alignments, pre-snap motion, wide zone runs, play-action fakes, etc. This offense will also ask Hurts to throw over the middle of the field -- something he has largely avoided as a pro but has done with some success so far in camp. There are two levels to the leap the Eagles could experience under Mannion. The first is addition by subtraction. The Eagles' shotgun-heavy, static pre-snap offense could have worked well last season. It worked under Kellen Moore and Shane Steichen in years past. But offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo didn't have the magic touch of those ex-coordinators (now head coaches), as offensive line injuries and the aforementioned diminished rushing of Hurts hamstrung the offense. Simply by moving on from Patullo and shedding some of the stale approaches of Hurts' past offenses, the Eagles should play better to their talent level on offense (which is pretty solid, even without receiver A.J. Brown , who was dealt to the Patriots). The second leap might come if Mannion has the goods as a coach. We don't know much about the former NFL backup quarterback who entered the coaching ranks in 2024. It might come if a new level is unlocked for Saquon Barkley in an under-center, wide zone rushing attack -- that's new to the running back, just as the play-action fakes and intermediate middle throws are new to Hurts. It might come if sixth-year receiver DeVonta Smith emerges in a new system and out from Brown's shadow the way Jaxon Smith-Njigba did for Klint Kubiak's Seahawks last season after the trade of DK Metcalf . And of course, that leap might come if Hurts takes to the new offense quickly. I cannot think of a modern quarterback who has improved more over his career (college and pro combined) than Hurts. The player who took snaps at Alabama was, at first, not a functional thrower for the college ranks. The young starter for the Eagles was turnover prone, late to respond to pressure and easily fooled by blitz looks. Yet Hurts has become better season over season thanks in part to trimming those aspects of his game in which he struggled, such as intermediate throws. If he's able to introduce those back into his menu, now as a more seasoned veteran quarterback, he'll reach another level of quarterbacking. I came into training camp willing to go either way on the Eagles' new offensive experiment. But all reports out of camp so far have me leaning positively for 2026. Most likely to succeed (with a new defense): Cincinnati Bengals It's hard for a defensive tackle to really make his presence felt in training camp. Most reps are not at full speed or taken to the ground, and the quarterback is certainly untouchable. It is a testament then to just how good Dexter Lawrence II has looked in his first season with the Bengals that he is the buzz of camp. He isn't the only one. Edge rusher Boye Mafe is winning against the Bengals' pair of starting tackles. Safety Bryan Cook is making plays against quarterback Joe Burrow . The Bengals entered the 2026 offseason with one big objective at the top of their to-do list -- fixing the defense -- and early reports are strong on their efforts. Of course, this isn't an entirely new defense, as Al Golden is in his second year running the unit. But with Lawrence, Mafe, veteran defensive tackle Jonathan Allen and second-round rookie Cashius Howell , four of the five leading snap getters on the defensive line might be new players. That has trickle-down effects. It will create a totally new picture for second-year linebackers Demetrius Knight Jr . and Barrett Carter , who both struggled mightily as rookies but now have a functional line to play behind. It will create a new chemistry for 2025 breakout defensive backs Dax Hill and DJ Turner II , as they can play more aggressively in coverage and expect the pass rush to get home after a reasonable period of time. As such, it seems like a new defense, built over two offseasons rather than one. And Burrow is even talking about his renewed belief in the Bengals' Super Bowl chances. The 'Best Shape of His Life' Award: Braelon Allen Every summer, we hear about numerous players who are apparently in the best shape of their lives heading into the new season. It's always tough to determine whose best shape of their life is the most best shape of their life. Are you grading against the other players' best shapes of their lives? Are you grading against each player's own previous best shape of his life? This is serious work! I had to give it to Allen. The Jets' backup running back opened minicamp in June by announcing that he was the "biggest I've ever been, the strongest, the fastest." He even went into greater specifics. "The most lean muscle I've had, the lowest body fat. Perfect symmetry in both my legs and arms." When you're talking about the best best shape, how can you not give extra points to perfect symmetry? Allen reportedly got close to 250 pounds this offseason after playing his injury-shortened 2025 season around 240 pounds. That would make him one of the heaviest running backs in the NFL, knocking on the door of Derrick Henry 's 252 pounds. I would like to give honorable mentions to: Texans running back David Montgomery , who just happens to be in the best shape of his life in the offseason he gets traded away (love when that happens). Vikings tackle Christian Darrisaw , who said he feels the best he has felt "in two years" (he's a blue-chip talent who has been limited by injury, so I'm rooting for that one). Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr ., who deserves a podium placement here for his offseason improvements after a disappointing 2025. Jaguars WR/CB hybrid Travis Hunter , who looks like he has been eating Popeye's spinach. Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter , who has shed weight and put his shoulder injuries behind him in the same offseason he signed a record-setting defensive tackle contract. The Day 3 rookie everyone fell for: Cyrus Allen It's impossible to choose between all the Day 3 darlings who are ripping up the second team and forcing their way into first-team reps. Vikings cornerback Charles Demmings is reportedly making the leap from FCS school Stephen F. Austin to NFL football with aplomb. Bears defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg is wreaking havoc; he picked up American football as a high school sophomore, so his ceiling is enticingly high. Raiders fifth-rounder Hezekiah Masses has broken into the first-team cornerback rotation, and it sounds like the Bengals might have a third receiver in the mix with fourth-rounder Colbie Young . But the buzziest Day 3 rookie by far must be Allen, a receiver drafted in the fifth round (No. 176) by the Chiefs. An undersized quickster, Allen (5-foot-11, 180 pounds) figured to fight for returner reps and rotational opportunities behind starting receivers Rashee Rice , Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton . But since Day 1 of training camp, Allen has made plays for Patrick Mahomes . "I think Pat's got some trust there," coach Andy Reid said after the first day of full-team practice in late July. Allen missed some time because of a left shin injury , but when he returned to camp, he was rotating with Worthy, Thornton and Rice as the top four receivers for Mahomes' training camp snaps. Allen's consistent separation against man coverage is of particular note, as Rice has been a great option against zone defenses but far less effective against man coverage over the course of his young career. It's worth remarking that the Chiefs are notorious for training camp hype from Day 3 offensive skill position players. Justyn Ross was an undrafted receiver in 2023 with plenty of buzz. Running back Brashard Smith seemed like a shoo-in for passing-down snaps behind Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt . Neither July/August performance materialized into meaningful regular-season snaps, as the Chiefs preferred to lean on veteran players. Still, training camp is a time for falling for the same gags over and over again. It's a season of unbridled hope, no matter how many times it burns us. Make sure to grab Allen in the last round of your fantasy drafts this year. Busiest medical tent: San Francisco 49ers As this week's viral "Hard Knocks" clip of Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald pulling linebacker Derick Hall out of practice for getting too rough near the quarterback reminds us, the most important part of training camp is emerging from it healthy. To that end, the 49ers -- who had the fifth-highest adjusted games lost last season -- are once again stumbling out of the gate. Cockcroft play Liz Loza: Justin Jefferson is an 'incredible steal' at his lowest-ever ADP (1:03) Eric Karabell Aug 15, 2026, 08:22 AM ET Close Eric Karabell is a senior writer covering fantasy football, baseball and basketball at ESPN. Eric is a charter member of the FSWA Hall of Fame, a BBWAA baseball Hall of Fame voter and author of "The Best Philadelphia Sports Arguments." Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen led his position with 364.62 fantasy points last season, and for six consecutive years, he has finished among the game's top two scorers at quarterback. However, quarterback is a deep position in 2026. One can make the case that nearly half the NFL teams have a QB worthy of starting for your fantasy team this season. Allen is awesome, but even last season he outscored vastly underrated Detroit Lions QB Jared Goff -- barely a top-10 performer at the position -- by only 67.56 points, or less than four points per week. Allen also spent quite a bit of time handing the football off (or throwing) to RB James Cook III , fantasy's No. 6 scorer at the position last season. Cook turned his 342 touches into 1,912 scrimmage yards and 14 touchdowns, and for the second season in a row he was a notable bargain in terms of ESPN average draft position. This season, Cook isn't such a bargain, as he is going early in Round 2, but he remains worth it. He isn't alone among running backs. In fact, this really is a year to invest a pick or two at running back early. If you don't, you might be quite disappointed in the options available later. In relation to Allen and his relatively slight superiority over other quarterbacks, for example, this narrative does not exist at running back. Standard fantasy starting lineups require one QB and two RBs, but -- considering the flex position -- many can and will play three RBs. Cook outscored the No. 20 RB, Denver Broncos youngster RJ Harvey , by 95.6 points. He outscored Chicago Bears RB Kyle Monangai , 30th among RBs, by 155.5. Fantasy managers cannot wait to build around running backs, so even if Cook, Baltimore Ravens star Derrick Henry , Omarion Hampton of the Los Angeles Chargers , Josh Jacobs of the Green Bay Packers , Chase Brown of the Cincinnati Bengals and others aren't what we would call "value picks," they are very much in demand because running back is not deep, unlike quarterback. We covet volume running backs, and there simply aren't enough. This is the year to secure a few in the early rounds, led by Cook, Henry and Hampton. As always, the annual "Do Draft" list focuses on players who keep ending up on my fantasy teams, either from valuable practice mock drafts or the ones that count, considering value versus standard ADP. I keep gravitating toward these players, either for strategic reasons -- such as waiting a long time to choose a QB or two -- or because the players make sense or seem undervalued. Cook might not be undervalued, since he has proved himself with 32 touchdowns and safe volume the past two seasons, but he is a player to build around because he is reliable. Allen is reliable as well, but the depth at quarterback and running back is hardly similar. Henry, one of my annual favorites, has been heavily featured in this "Do Draft" space for years, and he followed up his excellent 2024 season of 1,921 rushing yards and 18 total touchdowns with 1,595 rushing yards and 16 scores. Henry boasts double-digit touchdowns for eight consecutive seasons, and a top-10 fantasy finish at running back in six of the past seven. He is 32, and although that brings legitimate concern, there is no indication of decline. Henry is neither overvalued nor undervalued this season. Like Cook, he is someone to target. Every season I try many strategies of securing players, and how I feel about the results tends to direct how I approach the drafts that matter to me. This season, I covet a few volume running backs early even if that means ignoring my rankings of a WR with a late first-round pick. There is receiver depth. There is always quarterback depth. Try out some mock drafts and see how you feel! More at running back Dallas Cowboys starter Javonte Williams might belong in the same ADP range as Jacobs and Brown after an outstanding 2025 season with 1,201 rushing yards and 13 total touchdowns. Williams likely would have finished as the No. 10 RB if he had played in a meaningless Week 18 game. The Cowboys boast an electric offense and are committed to his volume. More than a few (maybe almost all?) of the RBs going in Round 5 and later scare me. Williams might be in a tier by himself, or perhaps bumped up with the others. New Houston Texans starter David Montgomery isn't necessarily safe or gleaming with upside, but he also doesn't cost you a high draft pick as he is going in Round 8. In the AFC for the first time, Montgomery begins the third chapter of an underrated career at age 29, and reasonable minds can debate what level of volume he will receive. Montgomery hasn't been a true featured back for years (through little fault of his own), but that doesn't mean he is incapable of a return to reliable RB2 range. The rushing yards and touchdowns should be there. This is a bargain player. I am generally not targeting first-year players, but Seattle Seahawks rookie Jadarian Price enters a positive situation with the defending Super Bowl champions. Kenneth Walker III is gone, and the Seahawks never seemed particularly concerned about replacing him. Price couldn't pile on the stats at Notre Dame with Arizona Cardinals pick Jeremiyah Love there as well, and he might not play much on passing downs, but I see a bruiser with 200-plus rushing attempts and double-digit touchdowns coming. I see an RB2 option lurking, and in his ADP range I want little part of the RB timeshares with the New England Patriots , Pittsburgh Steelers , Carolina Panthers and Minnesota Vikings . Kenny Gainwell boasts a strong chance of outscoring incumbent Bucky Irving with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , and I will reach a few rounds to grab him. I also will reach a bit for Broncos starter J.K. Dobbins . He might never appear in 17 games in a season, but perhaps this will be his first 1,000-yard rushing campaign. Harvey is the third-down back. Washington Commanders newcomer Rachaad White will be a popular in-season flex option as he steamrolls toward 70 receptions. Former Commanders option Chris Rodriguez Jr . should join him; he catches few passes but can earn early-down volume and approach double-digit touchdowns in Jacksonville. I will take a chance on New Orleans Saints pass catcher Alvin Kamara in the late rounds, too. Quarterback San Francisco 49ers starter Brock Purdy is going outside the top 100 in ADP. He was the No. 6 QB fantasy scorer in 2023 with 4,280 passing yards and 31 touchdowns, and he was on a similar scoring pace last year. Perhaps we cannot assume 17 games or pristine health for his targets around him, but I see a borderline QB1 option going as a clear backup in many leagues. Kansas City Chiefs star Patrick Mahomes (knee) is playing in Week 1 ... well, I believe he will. Don't expect the same rushing prowess as last season, but I would take the over on 4,000 passing yards and 30 TDs. How can one bet against Mahomes? Lions starter Jared Goff is rostered in barely 50% of ESPN leagues and is going 16th at his position despite finishing as a top-10 QB fantasy scorer in each of the past four seasons . No, really, it's true. What production! What consistency! I stop short of ranking him in the top 10, but as I write this section I wonder, "Why would it be so silly to do so?" Perhaps, as with Cowboys RB Williams, I need to move Goff up a tier. I continue to take chances (mainly in superflex formats) on new Vikings starter Kyler Murray and Saints sophomore Tyler Shough . I refuse to believe that the Miami Dolphins will be so embarrassingly bad on offense that new QB Malik Willis will fail, especially with his running ability. Wide receiver Vikings star Justin Jefferson might not reprise his 2024 numbers, but I bet he comes close. He doesn't need amazing QB play, he just needs competency there. Murray should be more than competent. Meanwhile, Vikings teammate Jordan Addison enters a critical season. His rookie numbers (70 receptions, 911 yards, 10 TDs) are in play, making Addison a bargain pick -- especially with an ADP below all of the Jacksonville Jaguars WRs fighting for targets. Newly paid Ravens starter Zay Flowers finished seventh in WR scoring last season despite underwhelming QB play, yet he is 17th among WRs in ADP. No, I don't rank Flowers as a top-10 WR, but something doesn't make sense here. I am fine with Flowers and a pair of reliable RBs among my first three selections. Lions starter Jameson Williams might never approach 100 receptions (75 is reasonable), so his value might be higher in non-PPR formats. Even so, his QB is durable and productive, the creative offense (usually) sings and Detroit's schedule this season might be the most favorable in the sport. This could be the TD breakout campaign. Williams easily boasts WR1 upside. I admit I might be too generous to 49ers newcomer Mike Evans , but he surpassed 1,000 receiving yards and scored 11 touchdowns (No. 7 WR fantasy scorer) only two seasons ago, doing so in 14 games. I don't expect quite that, but something like a reliable WR2 season makes sense. Indianapolis Colts starter Josh Downs is a wise breakout option after the team sent Michael Pittman Jr . to the Steelers. Downs enters his fourth season poised for his most targets, catches and, well ... everything. He and Alec Pierce are different. I like a healthy Pierce, but it seems he is not healthy (and Pittman over fellow Steeler DK Metcalf is a reasonable take, too). I don't get the ordinary projections for new Tennessee Titans starter Wan'Dale Robinson . I do get that the Titans grabbed rookie Carnell Tate in the draft to be their new top WR, but that scenario doesn't always work out initially. Throw Robinson into the slot and everyone enjoys 80-plus catches, even if they're somewhat hollow. That's valuable in PPR. Someone will catch passes in Miami. Relative fantasy afterthought Malik Washington can surprise. Tight end Nothing against the top options, but I still like to build with RBs and WRs. So, when thinking about TEs after Harold Fannin Jr . (whom I like) goes off the board, Packers breakout Tucker Kraft deserves a better ADP (perhaps in the Fannin neighborhood). Kraft is recovering well from the ACL tear, and it sure seems like he will play in Week 1. He is Green Bay's top receiving option. The good news is the Ravens' Mark Andrews outlasted now-New York Giant Isaiah Likely and earned his own contract extension. Andrews was disappointing in 2025, but there are no excuses now: His volume must rise. Andrews has been a top-five fantasy TE in five of the past seven seasons. It is hardly outrageous to expect a return to the top 10, and if he starts slowly, streaming is an option at the position. I bet the Vikings' T.J. Hockenson , Bills' Dalton Kincaid and Patriots' Hunter Henry outproduce their lowly ADPs, too.

New York Yankees 11h Erika LeFlouria Transfer rumors, news: Liverpool looking at Wharton as Jones replacement 3h ESPN Ranking the 25 best women's college basketball recruits right now UConn Huskies 11h Shane Laflin Rolando 'Rolly' Romero-Teofimo Lopez: Picks, predictions, more 12h Andres Ferrari MMA pound-for-pound rankings: Islam Makhachev a unanimous No. 1 ... still 1d play Dan Lanning opens up about Oregon this season: 'Boys are hungry' (1:25) Jordan Reid Aug 14, 2026, 06:20 AM ET Close Jordan Reid is an NFL draft analyst for ESPN, providing in-depth scouting on the nation's top pro prospects. Jordan joined ESPN in 2021 and also contributes to SportsCenter and ESPN Radio. He played quarterback at North Carolina Central University and then went on to coach there from 2014-18. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions We're only a couple of weeks away from the beginning of the 2026 college football season , and I'm pretty excited. We get to watch a lot of high-end prospects headed to the 2027 NFL draft class. But which colleges should NFL draft fans focus on when they turn their TVs on every Saturday? I have gone through my personal evaluations and talked to scouts and evaluators throughout the NFL to pick out the rosters loaded with potential 2027 draft picks. There's still a lot of time for players to rise and fall between now and when the draft starts next April in Washington, D.C., but I settled on 12 schools for draft fans to watch this season. I separated them into three tiers, considering the overall number of prospects and how many of them should be first-rounders. I also picked an under-the-radar program to watch -- I had eventual national champion Indiana in last year's version , but I'm going to the Big 12 this time around. Let's start with a stacked team looking to take the next step. Jump to a section: Tier 1 | Tier 2 | Tier 3 Under the radar Tier 1 Texas Top prospect to know: Arch Manning , QB Sleeper prospect to watch: Bo Mascoe , CB Game circled on the schedule: vs. Ohio State, Sept. 12 There's a strong argument that the Longhorns have the most impressive roster in the FBS. The fate and potential of the team starts with Manning. His first season as a starter began with immense expectations and got off to a rocky start, but he finished strong with 3,163 passing yards, 26 touchdowns and seven interceptions. Manning's mechanics, footwork and accuracy still need improvement, but if he can build on the momentum he generated late last season, he could be the No. 1 pick. Left tackle Trevor Goosby returns after contemplating entering the 2026 draft. At 6-foot-7, 325 pounds, he's a gangly, consistent blocker who has already received Round 1 grades from scouts. Also watch out for right tackle Melvin Siani . The 6-foot-6, 317-pound Wake Forest transfer could skyrocket up draft boards very quickly if he refines his considerable set of tools. Guard Brandon Baker is a Day 2 prospect who is transitioning from tackle, while center Connor Robertson is a late-round hopeful. Transfer wide receiver Cam Coleman is a Round 1 prospect who could vault into the top 10. He had 708 receiving yards and five touchdowns last season with Auburn but should flourish with Manning. WR2 Ryan Wingo is a Day 2 prospect whose speed and dynamic ability have already intrigued evaluators. His stock should rise if he catches the ball more consistently. play 0:16 Texas WR Cam Coleman makes a preposterous one-handed grab Hollywood Smothers and Raleek Brown are major upgrades at running back and viewed as midround prospects entering the season. The 5-foot-11, 193-pound Smothers is a smooth mover who can create explosive plays as a runner and pass catcher, while Brown is a determined ball carrier who can make defenders miss with ease. Colin Simmons is Texas' top-ranked defensive prospect. He has an electric first step, which helped him lead the SEC with 12 sacks last season. Simmons has the makings of a top-10 pick and could be the first defensive player off the board. Defensive tackles Hero Kanu , Ian Geffrard and Alex January carry late-round grades. Linebacker Rasheem Biles is an undersized but instinctive player who finished with 100 total tackles and two interceptions last season at Pitt. He carries a Day 2 grade, as does safety Jelani McDonald , who is a movable chess piece. And multiple scouts have mentioned Mascoe, a Rutgers transfer, as a potential riser this season. Predicted first-rounders in 2027: 4 Predicted total draft picks in 2027: 13 Oregon Top prospect to know: Dante Moore , QB Sleeper prospect to watch: Jerry Mixon , LB Game circled on the schedule: at Ohio State, Nov. 7 The Ducks are loaded after several players eschewed the draft to stay in school. The headliner is Moore, who enters the season as a prime contender to be the No. 1 overall pick. A natural thrower, the 6-foot-3, 210-pound quarterback experienced a breakout season in 2025, but scouts want to see him play better against high-quality opponents. Tight end Jamari Johnson steps in for Kenyon Sadiq , and there are evaluators who believe he's more well-rounded than the recent No. 16 overall pick. Johnson is expected to become a top receiving option for Moore, and if he takes another step in his development, he could be drafted higher than Sadiq. At wide receiver, Evan Stewart returns after missing last season with a torn patellar tendon , while UAB transfer Iverson Hooks could emerge as a late-round target. The offensive line is led by three prospects with late-round grades -- center Iapani Laloulu , guard Dave Iuli and tackle Michael Bennett III , a Yale transfer. Laloulu is a 6-foot-2, 329-pounder who could rise from his current Day 3 status. Oregon's defense is keyed by a defensive line full of potential draft picks, led by defensive tackle A'Mauri Washington . Washington is a player who could have been drafted high in 2026 and is viewed as a top-40 player in the 2027 class. He'll be joined by Bear Alexander , who is currently receiving Day 2 grades. On the edge, Matayo Uiagalelei and Teitum Tuioti are one of the better tandems in the country. Both have received Day 2 grades, with Uiagalelei seen to have a higher ceiling at the next level. Safety Koi Perich was a major addition after transferring from Minnesota . He is a fast-flowing, third-level defender who has received top-100 grades from scouts I've talked to despite an underwhelming sophomore season. Mixon and Devon Jackson are seen as Day 3 picks at linebacker, with Mixon being mentioned by multiple scouts as a potential riser because of his instinctiveness and consistency in coverage. Predicted first-rounders: 3 Predicted total draft picks: 11 Notre Dame Top prospect to know: Leonard Moore , CB Sleeper prospect to watch: Jordan Faison , WR Game circled on the schedule: vs. Miami, Nov. 7 The most recent draft saw Notre Dame have two first-round picks (RBs Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price ) for the first time since 2018. It could exceed that number and get three for the first time since 1994. Moore is the Fighting Irish's highest-ranked prospect and the top corner on my early board. At 6-foot-2, 197 pounds, he's an easy mover with excellent ball skills who finished with five interceptions last season while allowing only 12 receptions. Moore isn't the only Round 1 candidate in the secondary. Brauntae Johnson is my No. 1 safety after experiencing a breakout sophomore campaign that included four interceptions. Colorado transfer corner DJ McKinney is a long, agile corner who has received strong Day 2 grades despite an uneven 2025. Safety Adon Shuler and nickel Christian Gray are viewed as Day 3 options. Up front, edge rusher Boubacar Traore led Notre Dame in sacks (6.5) last season and has mostly received Day 2 grades. Linebackers Drayk Bowen and Jaiden Ausberry have late Day 3 grades. Quarterback CJ Carr thrived in his first year as the starter, finishing with 2,741 passing yards, 24 touchdowns and six interceptions in 12 games. With Notre Dame viewed as one of the early national championship favorites, many scouts will be paying close attention to Carr, who could cement himself in the first round. He'll be protected by guard Anthonie Knapp , who is on NFL scouts' radar, although his transition from tackle makes his exact projection uncertain. Faison steps into a crucial role and is getting early Day 3 grades. He'll be joined by Jaden Greathouse , who has NFL potential but is coming off an injury-plagued season. Predicted first-rounders: 3 Predicted total draft picks: 11 Miami Top prospect to know: Ahmad Moten Sr ., DT Sleeper prospect to watch: Marquise Lightfoot , Edge Game circled on the schedule: at Notre Dame, Nov. 7 Miami's defense lost two first-round edge rushers in Rueben Bain Jr . and Akheem Mesidor , but its defensive front is still strong. Moten enters the season as my top-ranked defensive tackle and his running mate, Justin Scott , is another early-round-caliber prospect. Edge rusher Damon Wilson II is expected to help fill the Bain/Mesidor void and is getting late Day 2 grades from scouts after finishing with nine sacks last season. Lightfoot and Armondo Blount are two more edges who could break out and jump into draft consideration. Darian Mensah is Miami's latest quarterback transfer and should join Cam Ward and Carson Beck as NFL draft picks. He finished with 3,973 passing yards, 34 touchdowns and six interceptions last season at Duke and is a polished passer who steps into a ready-made situation. He could even emerge into Round 1 consideration. Mensah's top target last season, wide receiver Cooper Barkate , also transferred to Miami, as did Vandrevius Jacobs (South Carolina). Both primarily have Day 3 grades. Tight end Elija Lofton steps into a full-time starting role and could rise. Running back Mark Fletcher Jr . surprisingly returned after a strong finish to 2025. He's a determined runner who has received a mixture of third- and fourth-round grades. The Hurricanes also have two draftable offensive linemen in guard Samson Okunlola and tackle Matthew McCoy . Miami's secondary is arguably the deepest in the country, with cornerback Romanas Frederique Jr . breaking out last season. He is a savvy technician with the potential to develop into a top-50 prospect if he can improve his durability and ball skills (one interception in two seasons). Fellow corner Xavier Lucas was more consistent than Frederique, earning mostly midround grades. Cornerback Ethan O'Connor and safety Zechariah Poyser , an aggressive downhill run stopper, are late-rounders. And linebackers Mohamed Toure and Chase Smith are late-round hopefuls. Toure is especially fascinating, as he enters his eighth season of college football. Predicted first-rounders: 3 Predicted total draft picks: 10 Tier 2 Ohio State Top prospect to know: Jeremiah Smith , WR Sleeper prospect to watch: Devin McCuin , WR Game circled on the schedule: at Texas, Sept. 12 Ohio State had a draft-high 11 players selected in 2026, including four in Round 1. The Buckeyes are loaded again and led by Smith, the No. 1 prospect on my board. Smith made an impact immediately upon arriving in Columbus and is among the best receiver prospects ever . At 6-foot-3, 225 pounds, he can win with speed or strength and is a constant headache for defenses. McCuin, who transferred from UTSA, and veteran Brandon Inniss complement Smith at receiver and are hearing Day 3 grades. Opinions are more mixed about Smith's quarterback, as Julian Sayin enters his second season as a starter after finishing last season with 3,610 passing yards, 32 touchdowns and eight interceptions. His 77% completion percentage led the FBS, as he's an efficient, point-guard-like distributor. New offensive coordinator Arthur Smith will give him more opportunities with NFL concepts and progressions. Some scouts are skeptical about Sayin's size (6-foot-1, 208 pounds) and arm strength, which could limit his ceiling. play 1:48 Why Ryan Day is excited for QB Julian Sayin's sophomore season Up front, Austin Siereveld is transitioning from tackle to guard. The 6-foot-5, 327-pounder is a heavy-handed technician who consistently generates movement at the point of attack. He's viewed as a Day 2 possibility. Center Carson Hinzman returns for his senior season with 35 career starts. He's seen as a mid-to-late Day 3 prospect. The Buckeyes' defense had five players selected in the top 65 of the 2026 draft, but there's still plenty of talent. The strength of the unit is in the secondary, led by Jaylen McClain . He's a rangy free safety with excellent coverage instincts; don't be surprised if he moves into the top 50. His running mate, Duke transfer Terry Moore , has received midround grades, though scouts are monitoring his recovery from a torn ACL. Florida State transfer Earl Little Jr . will occupy the nickel/rover spot as an aggressive, downhill thumper who is viewed as a Round 3 or 4 prospect. Cornerback Jermaine Mathews Jr . enters his second season as a starter and is in the late-round picture. The front seven is led by edge rusher Kenyatta Jackson Jr ., who had 6.5 sacks last season and carries strong Day 2 grades. Beau Atkinson and Alabama transfer Qua Russaw will be on the opposite edge and have late-round grades. Defensive tackle will be populated by three Day 3 prospects in returner Eddrick Houston and transfers James Smith

New England Patriots 2d Mike Reiss What we're hearing and seeing at Browns training camp: Watson delivers a must-see throw in practice vs. Bills Cleveland Browns 1h Daniel Oyefusi Cowboys: Jerry Jones shares camp thoughts as team leaves Oxnard Friday 1h Todd Archer Seahawks: CB Diggs talks for first time since signing 1h Brady Henderson Patriots: Maye pleased after two practices with Eagles 1h Mike Reiss Giants: Jaxson Dart's best performance of the summer? 1h Jordan Raanan Fantasy football rankings: Eric Karabell's RB tiers 13h Eric Karabell Fantasy football rankings: Eric Karabell's WR tiers 13h Eric Karabell Solak: Why Ben Johnson's Bears offense is much more than just Caleb Williams Chicago Bears 2d Ben Solak Hallmark, hot dogs and touchdowns: The Colston Loveland story Chicago Bears 2d Courtney Cronin NFL preseason on NFL Network, ESPN: How to watch, schedule 20d ESPN play Schrager: 'There's no excuse for Jordan Love' this season (0:59) Dan Orlovsky Aug 13, 2026, 06:20 AM ET Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions You're going to hear us talk about quarterbacks a lot on " NFL Live " over the course of the 2026 season . There will be debates about all of them, from the best in the game to the borderline starters. But for a third straight year , I'm narrowing the focus here in the preseason . Who are the best signal-callers in the NFL at individual skills? Does anyone boast a better arm than Josh Allen ? Does Joe Burrow or Matthew Stafford have the more refined mechanics? Is Lamar Jackson still the gold standard in QB rushing? I ranked the top 10 quarterbacks by seven different traits: arm strength, ball placement, mechanics, decision-making, pocket presence, second-reaction creativity and rushing ability. These lists are based on current performance and expectations for the 2026 season. It is how I would rank the QB group at this exact moment. I included only starters and leaned on what I see on tape to form the rankings. Jump to a section: Arm strength | Ball placement | Mechanics Decision-making | Pocket presence Second reaction | Rushing ability Arm strength 1. Josh Allen , Bills 2. Justin Herbert , Chargers 3. Caleb Williams , Bears 4. Matthew Stafford , Rams 5. Patrick Mahomes , Chiefs 6. Baker Mayfield , Buccaneers 7. Drake Maye , Patriots 8. Joe Burrow , Bengals 9. Lamar Jackson , Ravens 10. Dak Prescott , Cowboys There are different kinds of arm strength. Everyone immediately looks at deep balls -- the 60-yard Hail Marys down the sideline. It's all about who can throw the rock the furthest, right? You need a live arm to connect on those shot plays, no doubt. But I focus more on passes into tight windows in the intermediate areas of the field and the pure power throws from what I call "funny body" positions. Quarterbacks don't have the strong base to fall back on here; there is no loading up and driving through the pass. Instead, they need to rely almost entirely on their arm to get the ball where it needs to go with velocity. Allen is still No. 1 in this department. His ability to get zip on his throws from uncomfortable positions really stands out. He just flicks his wrist, and the ball is suddenly in his receiver's hands on a rope. Not every QB1 can do that, and yet he does it with consistency. But there are some challengers for his top spot this year. Herbert gets real pop on his throws by driving it. No one has completed more tight-window balls over the past five years than Herbert (162). Williams got legit consideration for No. 1, too. He made some miraculous passes from unorthodox positions in 2025, including a 40-plus-yard strike to the end zone late in the divisional round -- while back-pedaling. Mahomes can wing it with the best of them, and Stafford and Maye are both elite on downfield balls. Stafford completed 37 passes of 20 or more air yards last season, easily the most in the NFL. And I also want to call out Mayfield -- I still think he has the most slept-on arm in the NFL. The one quarterback I really wanted to get into the top 10 was Trevor Lawrence . He also has some underrated arm talent and makes difficult throws look easy. Hey, it's tough to limit these lists to just 10 guys. Ball placement 1. Matthew Stafford , Rams 2. Drake Maye , Patriots 3. Sam Darnold , Seahawks 4. Joe Burrow , Bengals 5. Jared Goff , Lions 6. Jordan Love , Packers 7. Josh Allen , Bills 8. Lamar Jackson , Ravens 9. Brock Purdy , 49ers 10. Dak Prescott , Cowboys How do you find the best quarterbacks in ball placement? Their receivers are never truly considered "covered." I say this every year in this space, but it's worth refreshing: Accuracy and ball placement aren't the same thing. Accuracy means putting the ball on the receiver so he can make the play. Ball placement means putting the ball on the receiver in the perfect spot so he can make the play -- and no one else can. The names at the top of this list -- including some MVP candidates last season in Stafford and Maye -- routinely keep the ball away from the defender. It's all about precision. Let's start by addressing a big shift at the top. Burrow was the top-ranked QB in ball placement on each of the past two lists I've put together. He's now No. 4. He's still extremely good in this area, able to pin the ball to his receivers. But injuries did cost him more than half of the 2025 season, and it opened the door for some others to move up the list a little bit. Fair or not, I'm factoring in time on task. And Stafford came out every Sunday and fired bull's-eyes with conviction. If you're looking at the stats, Maye would have a pretty good case to be the new No. 1, too. He settles for second here, but there's no knocking his league-best 72.0% completion rate and 9.1% completion rate above expectation (per NFL Next Gen Stats). And unlike every other QB in the top five, he wasn't playing with an All-Pro receiver. Maye was especially good with trajectory going downfield, dropping it in a bucket. I can't wait to see what he does with A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs in 2026. Goff is sneaky good in this trait, and we see it at all levels of the field. Purdy displays incredible touch, layering the ball in. His 10.7% off-target rate was fourth-best in the NFL last season. Love and Prescott have an impressive ability to float the pass in and set their receiver up for yards after the catch. It's another list that was hard to sort through at the bottom, but I think every name on here is deserving. Tua Tagovailoa has been a mainstay in the ball placement top 10, and he was all the way up at No. 2 in 2024 when I first started doing this annual project. But he has declined a bit here, and his QB1 battle in Atlanta disqualifies him, anyway. Geno Smith also slid out after making the list in back-to-back years; he didn't look like the same quarterback last season at 35 years old. Mechanics 1. Matthew Stafford , Rams 2. Joe Burrow , Bengals 3. Daniel Jones , Colts 4. Jared Goff , Lions 5. Dak Prescott , Cowboys 6. C.J. Stroud , Texans 7. Caleb Williams , Bears 8. Jayden Daniels , Commanders 9. Josh Allen , Bills 10. Lamar Jackson , Ravens It's neck and neck between Stafford and Burrow. Things that matter here: Clean, smooth throwing motions from start to finish Strong bases that keep the QB in rhythm and firm Repeatable processes that don't change from rep to rep, even when things get chaotic around the QB That last one is key for Stafford and Burrow. Defenses don't know what's coming because every throw looks exactly the same coming out. It's amazing consistency. The tight connection between Stafford's upper and lower body allows him to pull off all those no-look throws. Defenses can't tell the difference until his release, and bam, the ball is going somewhere unexpected. You might be surprised to see Jones at No. 3. I was, too. But watching the tape again, I was taken aback by how good his mechanics were in Indianapolis last season. The Colts ran many different forms of RPOs, and that means his mechanics need to be sound. They were. Goff, Prescott and Stroud are such pure passers, with beautiful, natural motions. Daniels' mechanics have shades of Stroud. And I was impressed with how much Williams improved here last season. He might be more known for the off-platform plays, but he's solid from a mechanics standpoint. I had a hard time leaving Justin Herbert off. He probably should be on the list. Aaron Rodgers was also a tough cut, even in Year 22. Decision-making with the football 1. Josh Allen , Bills 2. Matthew Stafford , Rams 3. Jordan Love , Packers 4. Drake Maye , Patriots 5. Jayden Daniels , Commanders 6. Dak Prescott , Cowboys 7. Lamar Jackson , Ravens 8. Joe Burrow , Bengals 9. Patrick Mahomes , Chiefs 10. Jalen Hurts , Eagles Here are the league's top problem solvers. Being a good decision-maker means making the right choice when things are going to plan, but it also means making the only choice when things are falling apart. Find the correct outlet, but avoid mistakes, turnovers and negative plays. Last year, I put Allen at No. 2 on this list and said that his "decision-making improved [in 2024] more than any other NFL quarterback improved in any trait." Well, he's moving up again. He makes good decisions both in and out of structure. He threw 10 interceptions and lost three fumbles last season, but his tape shows an ability to read the defense and avoid getting baited into trouble. Maye and Love leaped into the top five. They ranked Nos. 1 and 2 in EPA per dropback last season (Maye was first at 0.27, just beating Love's 0.22), and they were both in the top 10 in interception rate (Love was sixth at 1.4%, slightly better than Maye's 1.6% in 10th). Daniels, meanwhile, was already solid as a decision-maker, but he should keep growing in the new Commanders offense. I haven't really talked about Mahomes yet. Some might see decision-making as a question mark on his otherwise impeccable scouting report. But that would be discounting just how much is asked of him as a decision-maker in Kansas City. He threw 11 interceptions last season, but he was constantly trying to find plays when they weren't there. It was another list that could have included Trevor Lawrence . I also entertained Jared Goff , who threw eight picks all last season. Pocket presence 1. Drake Maye , Patriots 2. Joe Burrow , Bengals 3. Sam Darnold , Seahawks 4. Justin Herbert , Chargers 5. Dak Prescott , Cowboys 6. Lamar Jackson , Ravens 7. Caleb Williams , Bears 8. Brock Purdy , 49ers 9. Daniel Jones , Colts 10. Trevor Lawrence , Jaguars What I saw on tape matches the numbers here. Maye was No. 1 in QBR inside the pocket last season at 82.5. He was surgical, completing 74.9% of his throws from there for 9.2 yards per attempt -- both tops in the NFL. The quarterbacks on this list are great at navigating out of trouble and creating operational space. There's no panic to be found as they climb the pocket to maneuver out of danger. And Maye was tremendous in 2025, using his big, strong frame and movement traits to buy time and execute. Despite the injuries that derailed his season, I kept Burrow second on the list. I love watching him operate in a phone booth, with tiny adjustments to stay clean and deliver the ball in a composed manner over and over again. Darnold and Williams took big jumps in pocket presence; Williams even led the league in sack rate at 3.3%. Purdy displays the skills to deal with muddy pockets, and Herbert uses his big 6-foot-6 frame to stay firm. Herbert and Prescott were admittedly snubs from this list a year ago , and I couldn't let that happen again. This year, that will probably be Patrick Mahomes . I dropped him on a few lists as he comes back from a torn ACL . He's still one of the best quarterbacks in the world when he's healthy, and he'll be back here in short order. play 1:10 Andrew Hawkins pushes back on Patrick Mahomes decline talk Second-reaction ability 1. Josh Allen , Bills 2. Caleb Williams , Bears 3. Patrick Mahomes , Chiefs 4. Drake Maye , Patriots 5. Sam Darnold , Seahawks 6. Bo Nix , Broncos 7. Brock Purdy , 49ers 8. Lamar Jackson , Ravens 9. Jayden Daniels , Commanders 10. Baker Mayfield , Buccaneers The flip side is working outside the pocket. There's obviously always a plan when the ball is snapped, but NFL defenses are pretty dang good at derailing things. So, what happens when Plan A doesn't work? Can the quarterback pull something out of thin air and still make a positive play? I'm looking for creativity here, as well as the ability to throw from weird arm angles and platforms. You'll notice a lot of the strongest arms make this list, too -- that's obviously key. But mobility and field vision also matter in a big way. So, it's no shocker that I have Allen at No. 1. He shows all of those second-reaction traits, and he can obviously tuck and run if there's nothing else available. The creativity and off-schedule ability of Williams really jumped out in 2025, and Mahomes is always going to be on this list. Darnold led the league with 10.1 yards per attempt when moving at least 10 mph, per NFL Next Gen Stats (signifying throws on the move). And Purdy was atop the NFL in QBR on throws from outside the pocket (79.1). Nix surprised me. He really became a broken-play artist last season. His eight TD throws from outside the pocket tied for the second most in the league, and no one made more outside-the-pocket throws last season than Nix (133). It was a big part of his game. There were a bunch of guys who could have been on here, but I don't know who you could knock off that top 10 to make room. Jordan Love , Justin Herbert , Joe Burrow and Jalen Hurts all have good cases. Trevor Lawrence , too. I'd keep an eye on Cam Ward and Jaxson Dart -- if they take big steps in 2026, they could both be on this list in a year. Each passer has the traits to make those whippy throws on the move, but I want to see more consistency. Rushing ability 1. Lamar Jackson , Ravens 2. Josh Allen , Bills 3. Drake Maye , Patriots 4. Caleb Williams , Bears 5. Justin Herbert , Chargers 6. Jalen Hurts , Eagles 7. Patrick Mahomes , Chiefs 8. Baker Mayfield , Buccaneers 9. Bo Nix , Broncos 10. Jayden Daniels , Commanders I actually want to start with the guys not on the list. I would have loved to get Jaxson Dart in. He actually led quarterbacks in rushing yards per game last season with 34.8. But he needs to learn how to protect himself when he's on the move. I'd bet he makes the top 10 next year if he can stay on the field. Then there is Kyler Murray . I put this list together before he was named QB1 in Minnesota earlier this week, and it was tough to fit him in retroactively. Daniel Jones and Malik Willis also make sense. As for those who did make the list, I can't imagine many would argue for anyone over Jackson. His rushing numbers fell off last season, as he was limited to 67 carries for 349 yards and two ground touchdowns. But he still averaged 5.2 yards per carry, and he had reached at least 750 rushing yards in each of his past six seasons. Jackson's running ability opens things up for Baltimore, whether it be on designed carries or scrambles. He still has elite-tier speed, vision and suddenness. New coordinator Declan Doyle's system should capitalize on that more often. Allen and Hurts bring a more physical brand of QB rushing; Allen led all quarterbacks with 181 rushing yards after first contact. That helped him to a QB-high 14 rushing touchdowns in 2025, five more than the next best (Dart and Trevor Lawrence , potentially another hard snub). Maye hurts plenty of defenses with his legs, and Herbert runs at a high level when he's 100%. And Mahomes is the most impressive scrambler in the league. He scrambled 18 times for at least 10 yards in 2025 (tops in the NFL). I'll cap this with one general thought after looking at my seven lists: Lawrence is right on the cusp of so many. I considered him for about half of these but just barely left him off. Just something to keep in mind as he enters Year 2 with coach Liam Coen.
