Jamie Sabau/Getty Images Jamison Hensley Aug 13, 2026, 06:33 AM ET Close Jamison Hensley is a reporter covering the Baltimore Ravens for ESPN. Jamison joined ESPN in 2011, covering the AFC North before focusing exclusively on the Ravens beginning in 2013. Jamison won the National Sports Media Association Maryland Sportswriter of the Year award in 2018, and he authored a book titled: Flying High: Stories of the Baltimore Ravens. He was the Ravens beat writer for the Baltimore Sun from 2000-2011. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- About a week ago, quarterback Lamar Jackson was ticked off at Baltimore Ravens training camp, spiking his helmet down to the ground with both hands. Toward the end of a two-minute drill, Jackson hit tight end Durham Smythe down the seam to move the ball just outside the end zone with six seconds remaining. With the clock ticking, Jackson and the rest of his offensive teammates rushed to the line of scrimmage to get one more play off. But time expired and Jackson let everyone know his frustration. Jackson has experienced his share of ups and downs this summer while learning a new offensive system under coordinator Declan Doyle. There are plenty of practices where Jackson makes several great passes deep downfield and then throws an interception, including one to a 310-pound defensive lineman. But Jackson's track record suggests he will have more success in adapting to a new scheme than any of the other 21 teams that have a new offensive coordinator this season. Jackson has won the NFL Most Valuable Player award the past two times he has worked with a new offensive coordinator. In 2019, Jackson became only the second unanimous selection for MVP in his first season under Greg Roman. Four years later, he won MVP for a second time in his first season under Todd Monken. Now, under Doyle, Jackson has the opportunity to continue the trend where he embraces a new vision -- featuring a different alignment, cadence and targets -- to become the league's most acclaimed player again in 2026. "Lamar continues each and every year to push himself and learn and grow and find new ways to innovate," Ravens tight end Mark Andrews said. "Especially when you learn a new offense, you're able to kind of add some things to your repertoire and do some different things that other people haven't seen. He's the most adaptable, smoothest player in the league." In Doyle's offense, he stresses being physical and explosive. The biggest buzz word with Doyle is detailed. He wants his players to be students of the game, which starts with Jackson, or "L" as Doyle often refers to him. On every pass, the challenge for Jackson is to find where the defense is most vulnerable for a big play. Doyle believes, if Jackson is using the proper footwork and looking at the right spots, he will know where to distribute the ball. Doyle has emphasized making the plays as efficient and "schemed up" as possible. The Ravens are trying to take pressure off Jackson by limiting the number of times that Jackson has to go off script when a play breaks down. Jackson has been more engaged than ever. He attended the voluntary workouts in the spring. He's constantly talking with Doyle on the field, calling the first-time playcaller "a wizard." Doyle hasn't held back when coaching Jackson. During the spring minicamp, Doyle called out Jackson for pitching the ball instead of running a bootleg. "I feel like he is doing a great job at that [by] challenging us each and every play," Jackson said. "Even with the huddle, and how the huddle is set up, he challenges us to get to the line of scrimmage fast, execute, break down the defense and process everything fast so that it's a process of elimination when we get to the line of scrimmage." Jackson's teammates feel he has achieved a comfort level with the new offense this summer, just like he has done in the past. "Honestly, I do not know how he picks up on systems so fast," wide receiver Zay Flowers said. "It is crazy. I have to study a lot with this [system]. He just picks it up quick. I honestly do not know." THE LAST TIME Jackson took an extensive amount of snaps under center in games was youth football. That's likely to change this season. After primarily working out of the pistol or shotgun formations in his first eight NFL seasons, Jackson has been taking more snaps under center than any previous training camp. Jackson expects this change to continue into the regular season. "With this balanced type of offense, I feel like it will help us out a lot -- identifying the defense, really keeping the defense on their toes," Jackson said. Playing less in the pistol and shotgun will be a different look for Jackson, who has been under center for 5% of his career snaps in the NFL. Since 2018, Jackson's 226 snaps under center are the second fewest among quarterbacks with at least 50 starts behind Kyler Murray (202 snaps under center). Even though Jackson hasn't played under center much, he has been very effective when he does. Over the past eight seasons, Jackson has the highest QBR in the NFL (81.2) when under center, throwing 20 touchdowns and one interception. Jackson has looked natural under center in training camp, according to Doyle. "You would never notice that he hasn't been under there that much," Doyle said. "He has the ability to really do all three: He can be under [center], he can be in the pistol, [and] he can be in shotgun. There's a lot of versatility in his game." Doyle added, "You want to be able to mix all those things and make the defense have to deal with the multiplicity of those sets as [much as] you can. He provides us a lot of value in his ability to go under center and run some of the offense that way." KEEPING DEFENSES ON their toes goes beyond where Jackson lines up for the Ravens. Jackson's cadence can give an edge to Baltimore. Doyle has made the point that snap count is the one aspect that the offense knows and the defense does not. So, the Ravens have been working with Jackson's verbal and rhythmic sequence before the snap. "Lamar is a very quick learner when you start working with him, and so I have been happy with what we have done," Doyle said. "We are trying to kind of keep the defense honest, and yet, at the same point in time, there are times where cadence might provide an advantage to be able to try to create a big play. So, it all kind of ties together, but there is certainly an emphasis on the tempo in which we break the huddle [and] the cadence we use. That stuff is all a huge piece to what happens post-snap." Getting defenses to jump offside has been a struggle for Jackson and the Ravens. Since Jackson's first full season in 2019, Baltimore has drawn defenses offside 33 times. Only two teams have had fewer (New Orleans and New England). According to ESPN Research, that has resulted in 48 "free plays" for Baltimore -- when the flag is thrown on the defense and the offense knows any negative outcome can be erased by the penalty -- which is tied for the fifth fewest in that span. Jackson has one career completion on a free play: a 6-yard pass to Flowers in 2023 at the Browns. During this summer's training camp, there have been some hiccups along the way. On Sunday, the Ravens varied their cadences to get the defense off-kilter and it had the opposite effect. The offense was flagged for false start eight times. But, once Jackson and his teammates can get these cadences down, it can lead to the defense jumping into the neutral zone. And when Jackson sees that flag thrown, he is looking to take advantage of that more than he has in the past. "Free plays, free yards -- we need it all," Jackson said. We're trying to put points on the board." THIS YEAR'S DRAFT gave Jackson more than improved pass protection. He received more targets in the passing game. After selecting guard Vega Ioane with the No. 14 pick, Baltimore drafted two wide receivers ( Ja'Kobi Lane in the third round and Elijah Sarratt in the fourth) and two tight ends ( Matthew Hibner in the fourth round and Josh Cuevas in the fifth). Asked what advice he could give the rookies to mesh with Jackson, Flowers said, "If I am being honest, Lamar can adjust to everybody. He knows everybody is different. Everybody's play style is different." Flowers has noticed in training camp how Jackson has capitalized on Lane's leaping ability by throwing jump balls to him. "So, he kind of adjusts to you," Flowers said. "But at the same time, you can help him by just running. That is all you have to do. Just run." There should be plenty of chances for the first-year players to make an immediate impact. On the Ravens' current roster, there are two wide receivers (Flowers and Rashod Bateman ) and one tight end (Andrews) who have caught more than 10 passes from Jackson. "It's really important that we're evaluating these guys, we're correcting them and we're pushing them to get better," Doyle said. "But a core belief of mine is that players improve, they get better. If they didn't, then there'd be no reason for us to meet with them or work with them or any of that." Based on how Jackson has performed in new systems in the past, these new targets will benefit from a quarterback who believes his best football is still ahead of him. "Lamar's the best player in the league," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "When he's out there and he's obviously really engaged like he is, he makes everybody on the field better. So, he makes the offense better. He makes the defense better for having to defend that type of player." Minter added, "All he has to do is be himself. That's what he's proven that he is over the course of time. I do think sometimes when you're trying to learn new things, it really energizes you because you know that there's a requirement to get where you want to get between now and the game."

Raanan joined ESPN in 2016. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- John Harbaugh was admittedly nervous. He couldn't wait to address the New York Giants for the first time. The date was April 7. It had been 77 days since he was hired as their coach. And this was the first time he was allowed by rules to address the entire team. "I'm standing up here in front of the New York Giants. The New York Giants ," Harbaugh said while pacing the front of the meeting room at the Quest Diagnostics Training Center. "This is the New York Giants sitting in this room! The New York Giants! Wow! This is an honor." It was his first team meeting as coach of the Giants after 18 seasons with the Baltimore Ravens . Harbaugh was genuinely excited to be leading one of the NFL's marquee franchises considering the steep history and legacy. That was a massive part of his decision to take the job over several other options . When the team released a snippet of this speech last month to promote the impending "Giants Life: The Offseason" video series, some fans viewed it as old-school and real. They were pumped that this was the new Giants coach and liked the attitude he brought with him from Baltimore. But it was also met with some ridicule and chuckles for its hokeyness. Former NFL quarterback Cam Newton was among those especially critical of the speech. Speaking on his "4th&1" podcast, Newton questioned, "How could that be what inspires a group of grown men?" He said the silence was awkward, the message was off. Newton thought Harbaugh should be sharing his vision for the Giants, explaining his core values and mission. In reality, he did. Perhaps that just wasn't the ideal one-minute promo to showcase his oratory skills and ability to captivate the room. "It was the opening sentence of a whole meeting," Harbaugh told ESPN last week at training camp in West Virginia. "That was about a 30-minute meeting to kind of just kick things off and get to know each other and just kind of talk about stuff that presents a vision for where we were going. So that was just the opening line. After that, then the message came." Giants fullback Patrick Ricard , who previously played for Baltimore, defended Harbaugh's speech on Instagram. Tight end Isaiah Likely also thought the public reaction wasn't in line with the room in which it was spoken. "I think it was taken way differently," Likely said. That specific meeting was flush with introductions. First with the coaches and then the players, who each shared their identity and purpose. Harbaugh believed creating vulnerability would help team-building. On a bigger scale, the clip wasn't exactly an accurate depiction of what an everyday Harbaugh team meeting looks like. He specified that there are also different meetings for different times of the year. That was a first meeting ever with a team. A Harbaugh team meeting during training camp begins with something he calls "wise words." This is where individual players get up and share a daily message. It's inspiration or advice, and the order for who speaks is selected based on seniority. Harbaugh used "wise words" throughout his Ravens tenure. Just not always to start meetings. Often, it was after practices. He also employed something called "spotlight" in Baltimore during which a guy would tell his backstory to the team. Veteran wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr . used "wise words" last Tuesday to say: "Yesterday's touchdown doesn't win you today's game." His point being you can't rest on the laurels of a good practice. You have to bring it again the following day. Beckham had his second straight strong practice that afternoon. Likely went with: "Win your 1/11th and be where your feet are," which means take care of your own business first. Don't try to do too much. After the players offer their initial contributions at the team meetings, Harbaugh takes over. "Then I might have something for the day or I might not, based on whatever's kind of going on," he said. "A lot of times it's a story, like something happens or sometimes it's just whatever. It's whatever I'm kind of feeling. And then right now, this time of year, we go through practice. So I've got about 30-35 plays from the practice that I want to make coaching points on." If the previous day's practice was poor, such as last week when the Giants committed 14 penalties in one session, that's when you might get a "hard Harbaugh," according to Likely. Though it's rare to hear Harbaugh yelling over the music or other coaches during practice, he regularly coaches his players hard because he expects greatness every day and doesn't want to see the same mistake again. Then Harbaugh will outline the plan for that day's practice. "We'll go through situations, whatever the situations are. We try to detail those out," he said. "We teach every situation. We always have some sort of teach-the-game type of a deal, whether it's situations or it's field position or it's turnovers or it's ball security or it's how to get the ball north efficiently. There's always these fundamentals that we'll have something all through training camp." The Giants even ended a practice last week by practicing long drives. This is what Harbaugh calls the "opportunity of fatigue." He wants to see who can execute when they're tired and hot, when things are hard. The new coach isn't looking for his players to be perfect in this situation, just better than the guy lined up across from them. Harbaugh's messages at the team meetings vary by the day. They can be historical, famous quotes or even something that was texted to him that morning, maybe even by his mom or dad. There will also be a message for that specific practice. And Harbaugh has quite the catalog to choose from having been a coach for 40-plus years. "I've been doing it for a long time. Even as a special teams coach, I had that stuff," he said. "So I have a lot of messages that I've had and I rewrite them every year." Harbaugh has a computer file filled with messages and stories. He updates them to make them current and relevant. He hopes they're better now than they were 10 years ago, knowing it's important to evolve with the times. "Sometimes he'll quote family, family history. Or somebody texts him in the morning," Likely said. "He'll probably, if it goes with the message of his speech, he'll put it in a team meeting, let him know, read it out loud, stuff like that." Veteran defensive tackle DJ Reader said one day last week that Harbaugh used a message as simple as, "It takes what it takes." Reader liked that. He didn't view it as anything profound but enjoyed that it was simple and to the point. Just get it done was his takeaway. Harbaugh uses a lot of personal stories. He likes to come clean with his feelings. He believes guys like that best because it's authentic and shows the true, sometimes vulnerable, version of himself. "And you can tell he's wired a little bit different. Just in a quirky obsession type of way," Reader said. "He's obsessed with ball and doing things the right way. And you can tell it's him though. He can't shut it off. He's not up there faking it. And that's fun to see." Harbaugh seems to be a lot more like his brother, Jim, head coach of the Los Angeles Chargers , than most realize. Jim is known for his khaki pants and other quirks. John seems to suppress them more. In the meetings, the Giants get the real John Harbaugh. An offbeat unifier who has proved his approach can lead to winning games with his previous team. If it works, why change it? "He's all about having everyone on the same page, building a vision of what he sees the football team and how we all should be thinking," Ricard said of his years with Harbaugh. "So every day he'll give us a message and he'll give it to us either by quotes, stories, maybe even historical, and he'll try to relate it back to football and back to us as a team. And he just tries to have a vision. And then as the season goes on, even last year [in Baltimore] when we're losing games early on, he just kept telling us, 'We're not giving up. We're going to continue to fight. We're going down swinging no matter what.' "He's always just trying to keep everyone together."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions EAGAN, Minn. -- The decision to name Kyler Murray the winner of the Minnesota Vikings ' quarterback competition this week was "out of my control," former starter J.J. McCarthy said Wednesday. "Obviously, every competitor wants to play," McCarthy said. "But moving forward, it's just about continuing to work hard and just staying ready for when my number's called." Asked why he thought the competition was out of his control, McCarthy said: "There's so many things out of my control, like the heat today. And it's just really having the discernment to figure out which of the two [quarterbacks], and that was one of the things outside of my control. And me attacking and optimizing every opportunity, which was in my control, and that's all I was focusing on." Coach Kevin O'Connell said Tuesday that McCarthy is now the No. 2 quarterback. But the Vikings also have veteran Carson Wentz on the roster, and a trade could become a possibility. McCarthy, however, said his desire to remain with the Vikings -- who drafted him at No. 10 in 2024 -- hasn't changed. "This is the place I want to be," McCarthy said. "And I love every single person in this building. I love the state. I love the fanbase. And I'm going to continue to just do whatever I can for this team and this organization." The Vikings signed Murray in March, and O'Connell declared an open competition in response to McCarthy's difficult and injury-filled 2025 campaign. In practical terms, Murray was the heavy favorite; his uneven performance during training camp added a layer of complexity to O'Connell's decision. While making the announcement Tuesday, O'Connell said Murray had "shown enough" and that he was enticed in part by "what could be." McCarthy said at the start of camp he was "100%" convinced the competition would be fair and that he would have a legitimate chance to win it. Speaking Tuesday, McCarthy said he wasn't thinking about fairness "at all" during the competition. "I couldn't control anything during," he said. "I couldn't control anything after. The only thing I could do is focus on that next rep and keep at it." In the spring, McCarthy compared the Vikings' quarterback room to a high school classroom, where he would sit on one side of the room and Murray the other. Asked about his relationship with Murray now, McCarthy said: "Yeah, he's just one of my teammates that I care for and respect and just like all my teammates in that locker room. So, it's about just doing whatever I can for the room and this team and moving forward."

McCarthy? (2:09) Kevin Seifert Aug 11, 2026, 03:52 PM ET Close Kevin Seifert is a staff writer who covers the Minnesota Vikings and the NFL at ESPN. Kevin has covered the NFL for over 20 years, joining ESPN in 2008. He was previously a beat reporter for the Minneapolis Star Tribune and Washington Times. He is a graduate of the University of Virginia. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions EAGAN, Minn. -- No one should be surprised that Kyler Murray won the Minnesota Vikings ' quarterback competition. Murray demonstrated this spring that he had recovered from a foot injury that limited him last season with the Arizona Cardinals . From that point on, it was clear that his talent level represented a formidable obstacle for the Vikings' incumbent, J.J. McCarthy . Murray got a bit bogged down in a complicated offense toward the end of minicamp, which he noted was happening while getting only half the reps that a starter normally would, and then again during the second week of training camp. But at some point, coach Kevin O'Connell had to make a call. It came Tuesday . What went into the decision? Is Murray the Vikings' long-term answer, or could McCarthy one day reemerge? Let's take a closer look. Was Murray's win inevitable? No, but he was always a heavy favorite. This was a genuine competition in the sense that the best quarterback on the roster would start and neither would benefit from an off-field advantage. There would be no organizational inertia toward finances -- the Vikings are paying Murray the veteran's minimum of $1.3 million, while McCarthy is in the third year of his rookie contract -- nor toward draft status. The general manager who traded up to draft McCarthy No. 10 in 2024, Kwesi Adofo-Mensah, was fired in January. O'Connell was free to simply pick the best player, which turned out to be Murray, the No. 1 pick by Arizona in 2019. Murray faced some potential roadblocks given his recent injury history -- he has played fewer than 10 games in two of his past three seasons -- and the fact that McCarthy had a two-year head start on learning O'Connell's scheme. But once Murray showed he was healthy, his inherent skill set advantage was obvious to any objective observer. Did Murray perform well in camp -- or just better than McCarthy? This gets to the crux of the matter moving forward. It's one thing to be the best quarterback on a roster. It's quite another for Murray to have positioned himself to power an explosive offense during a regular season that will start with crucial games against two NFC North rivals, the Green Bay Packers and Chicago Bears , in its first two weeks. Murray had some intriguing days when he appeared to move through his reads in rhythm and find open downfield receivers, sometimes after breaking the pocket. He also demonstrated his ability to rescue broken plays with his speed and open-field running. But in the three practices leading up to O'Connell's announcement, Murray struggled. To top it off, he threw two interceptions -- and barely missed throwing a third -- during the Vikings' annual full-pads night stadium practice on Sunday. There were other days when his passes misfired, although usually it appeared less an accuracy issue than it was that he was still learning exactly where to place the ball. The most charitable way to put it is that through two weeks of practice, Murray has shown that he has a long way to go before anyone should believe he is ready to have the kind of season that would revitalize his career. So why did the decision come now? O'Connell had boxed himself in. He acknowledged Tuesday that his plan had always been to make a decision in this time period, about nine or 10 practices into training camp, to allow enough time for Murray and the offense to come together before the regular season begins. When that time arrived, neither quarterback had established himself. But O'Connell prioritized maximizing the time remaining before the start of the season. He also reiterated that part of the point of the competition was creating "a competitive environment filled with wildly capable players that could then obviously elevate our quarterback room through that process and in doing so elevate our team." To that point, while Murray has not had an eye-opening camp, it is more than reasonable to believe the Vikings would get better quarterback play from him this season than from McCarthy. Can Murray run the Vikings' offense? That remains to be seen, in part because the Vikings are perhaps coincidentally in the process of adjusting their offense in ways that would benefit him. They have been experimenting with more shotgun and pistol run plays after spending the third-most time (47%) under center during O'Connell's first four seasons in Minnesota. During Murray's time with the Arizona Cardinals , the team was under center at the league's third-lowest rate (18.3%). Murray has displayed superior arm talent to McCarthy in getting the ball to downfield receivers, a big part of O'Connell's offense. But in team drills during full-pads practices, when pass rushers are active, Murray has not always appeared to see whether receivers are open in the middle of the field. That will no doubt be a focus during the coming weeks. What does this mean for McCarthy? It's bad news, obviously, but in truth that news was delivered the moment the Vikings signed Murray. McCarthy finished the 2025 season on an upswing, ranking No. 7 in QBR (69.8) after Week 13. But he would have still needed to make significant progress this offseason and summer to mount a true challenge. Instead, his level of improvement was incremental at best. It was not nearly enough, and O'Connell's decision to end the competition at a down point in Murray's training camp performance was a reflection of how difficult it was going to be for McCarthy to win. He'll enter his third NFL season as a backup, and there is not much precedent for top-10 picks getting replaced in the offseason -- as McCarthy was, for all intents and purposes -- and then coming back to regain the organization's permanent starting job. O'Connell said he "absolutely" thinks McCarthy has a future with the organization. But the next opportunity might not happen unless Murray is injured, a possibility that merits a close eye due to recent history. Will the Vikings trade McCarthy? While O'Connell gushed over how McCarthy has handled training camp, and the months that preceded it, a trade can't be ruled out. The Vikings re-signed their 2025 backup, Carson Wentz , in March and he has worked as the No. 3 quarterback in camp. O'Connell confirmed that McCarthy will be the No. 2 quarterback, but Wentz's presence shouldn't be discounted. If the Vikings had deep conviction about McCarthy's future, they wouldn't have felt compelled to sign Murray and would have given McCarthy more than 10 starts to develop. What does this mean for WR Justin Jefferson and the rest of the franchise? Murray will be the Vikings' fourth different Week 1 starter in the past four seasons. After he struggled to reach 1,000 receiving yards in 2025, with McCarthy and then-rookie Max Brosmer starting 12 combined games, Jefferson has a better chance of elevating his production if Murray plays a full season. But Murray's ascension, and McCarthy's demotion, continues a decadeslong organizational tradition of plucking veteran quarterbacks for potentially short-term roles. During O'Connell's tenure alone, he'll be the ninth different quarterback to start a regular-season game. The Vikings agreed to a contract clause that prohibits them from using the franchise tag to retain Murray in 2027. So if he has a career season, he will have a clear path to the free agent market and a potential bidding war. If he struggles or is injured, it's hard to project the Vikings' interest in bringing him back.

Johnson outlined his goals for the 2026 season, his second as the Bears' head coach, as part of a wide-ranging profile published Wednesday by The Athletic. "You've got 31 other teams coming to training camp saying, 'Our goal is to win the Super Bowl.' I want more than that," Johnson told The Athletic. The Bears went 11-6 and won the NFC North title in their first season under the offensive-minded Johnson, who rose to prominence thanks to his success as the offensive coordinator and playcaller of the Detroit Lions from 2022 to 2024. Chicago finished sixth in the NFL last season in total offense (369.2 yards per game) and ninth in scoring offense (25.9 points per game) behind quarterback Caleb Williams and a group of talented playmakers. Johnson praised Williams during his interview with The Athletic, saying "it's just a matter of time" for the third-year star to unlock his full potential. As for the broader team, Johnson cited the Super Bowl-winning New England Patriots teams from 2003 and 2004, who at one point won 21 consecutive games between the regular season and postseason. "Why can't we do that?" Johnson said. "There has never been an undefeated season (since the NFL expanded its schedule to more than 14 regular-season games). "The moon is the Super Bowl, but we're shooting beyond that -- for the stars. And I want these players to feel that each and every single day they come in."

At the center of the dispute, according to a statement from Daniels' spokesperson to ESPN, is that the Tigers are allowing sophomore cornerback DJ Pickett to wear the No. 5 jersey that Daniels wore when he became LSU's third Heisman Trophy winner in 2023. While Daniels' jersey hasn't been retired by the Tigers, it's the first time a player has worn No. 5 since he left the program for the NFL. "The Daniels family is deeply disappointed and feels profoundly disrespected by LSU's decision to give Jayden's number to another player," the statement from Daniels' spokesperson said. "Jayden and his family had every reason to believe that his number would remain a meaningful part of his LSU legacy and would be honored and protected in recognition of his extraordinary contributions to the university." Pickett wore No. 3 during his first season with the Tigers in 2025 when he was named a freshman All-American. He led LSU with three interceptions to go with 37 tackles and one sack in 524 defensive snaps. Pickett was wearing No. 5 when the Tigers opened preseason practice last week, leading to questions about why first-year LSU coach Lane Kiffin had allowed the jersey swap to happen. "Jayden made it clear that he did not want his number given to another player, and he believed his wishes would be respected," the statement said. "His Heisman Trophy-winning season and everything he accomplished on and off the field cemented his place in LSU history. To see his number given to another player is incredibly disappointing and feels like a failure to honor the significance of what Jayden accomplished at LSU." The No. 9 jersey that Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow used at LSU hasn't been worn since 2019, when he won the Heisman Trophy and led the Tigers to a 15-0 record and College Football Playoff national championship. An LSU athletic department spokesman declined to comment when reached by ESPN on Wednesday. Kiffin told reporters Aug. 5 that Pickett had been promised he could wear No. 5 when he signed with the Tigers in December 2024. Pickett had worn that number as a high school star in Zephyrhills, Florida, where he was the No. 2 cornerback in the Class of 2025 by ESPN Recruiting. "DJ is in [No.] 5, and that was a situation that was promised to him in recruiting here, for him to sign here," Kiffin said. "I've done a lot of research on that with the family and the representatives and the people, so really I didn't have a decision to make. It was promised to the kid. It wasn't done for whatever [reason]. I'm not going to get into that. "I'm not going to judge something [that was done] when I wasn't here. But when a kid is promised something to come to a school, he should wear it. So at that point, I don't think that's really my decision. We should honor what he was told." Former LSU coach Brian Kelly told ESPN on Wednesday that he believed No. 5 was promised to Pickett during his recruitment, but Kelly chose not to issue it to him because Daniels wasn't on board with Pickett wearing his number. Kelly was fired on Oct. 26, 2025, after his teams compiled a 34-14 record in four seasons. "I just wasn't prepared to do it until we got a full commitment from another Heisman Trophy winner," Kelly said. "We didn't want to issue No. 9, so you can't treat one differently from the other." LSU has retired the jerseys of four of its former players -- halfback Billy Cannon (No. 20), defensive back Tommy Casanova (No. 37), halfback Jerry Stovall (No. 21) and running back Charles Alexander (No. 4) -- and plans to retire former quarterback Bert Jones' No. 7 jersey on Nov. 14. However, LSU's policy regarding jerseys being retired, which is published on its athletic department website, states that any number retired after Jan. 1, 2007, "does not preclude a current student-athlete in that sport from wearing the jersey number in that or any other sport, subject to the discretion of the head coach." The No. 20 jersey made famous by Cannon, who was the team's first Heisman Trophy winner in 1959, is the only number that can't be worn again by a football player. The jersey numbers worn by former LSU basketball stars Bob Pettit (No. 50), Pete Maravich (No. 23) and Shaquille O'Neal (No. 33) and former Tigers baseball coach and athletic director Skip Bertman (No. 15) have also been permanently retired in their respective sports. The LSU policy states that an athlete must have completed competition for five years before being nominated for jersey retirement and he or she must have "demonstrated truly unusual and outstanding accomplishments, such as winning a Heisman Trophy or National Player of the Year award and should be based on the total LSU career." In the cease and desist letter sent to Ausberry, attorney Adam Kenner noted that Daniels' contract with LSU permitted the school to use his name, image and likeness for 180 days beyond his final game in college. "Accordingly, LSU must immediately cease and desist from any further issue use, display, publication, distribution, promotion, commercialization, or other exploitation of Mr. Daniels' NIL in any manner or medium," Kenner wrote. "Any use of Mr. Daniels' NIL occurring after LSU's receipt of this notice will be deemed knowing and willful and will be pursued vigorously through all available legal and equitable remedies, without further notice." Sources told ESPN that LSU hasn't yet responded to the letter. Daniels, who spent three seasons at Arizona State before transferring to LSU, was named the Heisman Trophy winner after he passed for 3,812 yards with 40 touchdowns and ran for 1,134 yards with 10 scores while leading the Tigers to a 10-3 record in 2023. The Commanders made him the No. 2 pick in the 2024 NFL draft, and he was named the league's Offensive Rookie of the Year that season. Last season, Daniels labored through an injury-plagued season and appeared in only seven games.

(1:55) Rob Demovsky Aug 12, 2026, 02:30 PM ET Close Rob Demovsky is an NFL reporter at ESPN and covers the Green Bay Packers. He has covered the Packers since 1997 and joined ESPN in 2013. Demovsky is a two-time Wisconsin Sportswriter of the Year as selected by the NSSA. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions GREEN BAY, Wis. -- If this is indeed Aaron Rodgers ' final season, he will end his career without playing at Lambeau Field as a visitor, something he thought might happen this season. In advance of Thursday's Packers - Steelers preseason game in Pittsburgh, Rodgers said when he first heard the teams were slated to play this summer, he had hoped it would be in Green Bay. "100%, 100%," Rodgers told Packers reporters Wednesday during a Zoom call. "When I heard it was possible to play both my former teams, I was really hoping this one was going to be in Green Bay, not just to get back at Lambeau one more time, but to head out to Chives [restaurant] for a dinner and maybe head out to Green Bay Country Club for a quick nine or something. I was really hoping it was going to be in Green Bay for a lot of reasons. "It would have been strange, being in that [visitors] locker room and stuff, but I would have found my way over, like many former players have over the years ... and see some of the guys and see some of the trainers and equipment staff and all the people I really care about that still work there. Yeah, I was definitely bummed out that we weren't in Lambeau for this one." Rodgers spent 18 years with the Packers before he was traded to the New York Jets in 2023. The Jets did not play the Packers in either of Rodgers' two seasons there. After signing with the Steelers in 2025, Rodgers played against the Packers last season, but the game was at Acrisure Stadium. Green Bay won 35-25. At some point, Rodgers will almost certainly return to Lambeau Field. He has said this will be his last season, which means if he is a first-ballot Hall of Famer that his name would go up on the stadium facade in five years with the other former Packers in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. His No. 12 likely would be retired, and he could be inducted into the Packers Hall of Fame after four seasons of retirement. "Well, there first has to be an invite back," Rodgers said. "We'll see about that, but yeah, I'm always going to have such a strong tie to Green Bay and the organization. If that comes to fruition, that could be a cool deal." Throughout the 20-minute session, Rodgers spoke fondly about both the city of Green Bay and the Packers organization. Asked what he will miss the most when he is retired, Rodgers said: "Definitely the people I got to do it with." "That's what this game's all about," Rodgers added. "It's about the relationships, and I'm just most thankful for all the men and women, you know, who've been in my life through this game over the years. So many great people in Green Bay, in the entire organization, top to bottom. You know, just salt of the earth type of people. ... But the thing that actually lasts the longest is those people that impact your life, and there's been a lot of those, a lot especially in Green Bay, it had a huge impact on my life. So I think about those people a lot."

(1:55) ESPN Multiple Authors Aug 12, 2026, 08:43 PM ET Email Print Open Extended Reactions Veteran linebacker Elandon Roberts , who played in Pittsburgh during the 2023 and 2024 seasons, reached agreement with the Steelers on a one-year deal, his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, announced Wednesday. Roberts, 32, not only returns to a familiar place in Pittsburgh, but the one-year deal reunites him with Steelers defensive coordinator Patrick Graham, whom he played for in Las Vegas last season. Roberts' return adds depth and a run-stopping specialist to an inside linebacker group that also includes Patrick Queen and Payton Wilson . Roberts started in 16 of 17 games for the Raiders in 2025, serving as one of the veteran voices on the defense. Known for his aggressive, downhill playing style, Roberts totaled 90 tackles and 16 run stuffs. Roberts also spent three seasons with the Miami Dolphins after a four-year stint with the New England Patriots , who drafted him in the sixth round of the 2016 NFL draft. In 10 seasons, Roberts has collected 694 tackles, 14.5 sacks and five forced fumbles in 157 games (121 starts). ESPN's Ryan McFadden and Brooke Pryor contributed to this report.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa will start Friday night in the team's preseason opener against the Denver Broncos , coach Kevin Stefanski said Wednesday. Despite the decision to start Tagovailoa on Friday, Stefanski said it's still too early to tab a starting quarterback for the regular season. The Falcons travel to the Pittsburgh Steelers for Week 1 on Sept. 13. "We're not there to name a starter for Week 1," Stefanski said. "We'll cross that bridge when we get to it." Michael Penix Jr ., the third-year quarterback, is still not yet fully cleared from a torn ACL he suffered last season and unable to do 11-on-11 team sessions in practice. "I went and saw the doctor before camp started and he's like, 'This is an amazing ACL.' He's like, 'You should never have any more knee problems for the rest of your career." That's word for word what he told me," Penix said Wednesday. "So, it's like, OK, I hear that. But it's like, all right, now I'm like, 'Do I trust that?' Penix added that he feels good but he's not ready to take a hit. "I feel like I can do just about anything except for take a hit. And that's what we're trying to stay away from right now." Stefanski said Falcons starters will play the first series or about 10 plays -- whichever comes first -- and then come out. Veteran Cooper Rush will be the second quarterback used after Tagovailoa and undrafted rookie Jack Strand will finish out the game. "So, our guys are ready to play and looking forward to Tua getting his first action in a game in this system," Stefanski said. Stefanski said playing time Friday night will vary from player to player. Offensive coordinator Tommy Rees will call plays, as he will during the regular season. Stefanski said it'll be a "simple game plan" against the Broncos, so the Falcons can play fast. "I don't believe in showing a lot in the preseason and doing all sorts of exotic things and whatnot," Stefanski said.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions BEREA, Ohio -- Deshaun Watson will start the Cleveland Browns ' preseason opener against the Bears in Chicago on Saturday. Shedeur Sanders will start the team's second preseason game at home against the Buffalo Bills on Aug. 22. Browns coach Todd Monken informed the quarterbacks of his decision after practice Wednesday. Watson and Sanders have been alternating first-team practice reps in Cleveland's quarterback competition Saturday's exhibition will mark Watson's first game since he tore his right Achilles tendon in October 2024. He sat out the 2025 season after undergoing a second Achilles surgery in January 2025. Monken said before Wednesday's practice that he hoped to play whomever starts at quarterback for one half. The quarterback who does not start would then play in the third quarter. Watson said the preseason would be a "great opportunity" for him as he has played in only 19 games because of suspension and injuries since being traded to the Browns in March 2022. Since making his debut in Cleveland, Watson's 33.1 Total QBR would rank last among qualifying quarterbacks if he had enough starts to qualify. "I'm super excited," Watson said Wednesday. "I think all the hard work that I've put in with the training staff, with my team, my personal team, to get to this stage has been tremendous for myself. So, I'm super excited for those opportunities and can't wait for it." Sanders, the 144th pick in the 2025 NFL draft, started the final seven games of his rookie season. Sanders went 3-4 as a starter, throwing seven touchdowns to 10 interceptions. He also ran for a touchdown. Sanders recorded a 18.9 QBR as a rookie, the fifth-lowest mark among 696 quarterbacks with at least 200 attempts in the QBR era (since 2006). Coaches, though, have praised Sanders' pre-snap and post-snap development, dating to the offseason workout program. "We approach practice like a game," Sanders said Wednesday. "So it's the same amount of focus and experiences. So that's why I'm excited: to feel how similar does it feel to practice, honestly. Because it's a different type of intention and a mentality that we go out there every day with."

The 33-year-old playmaker spent last season with the Miami Dolphins working with new Panthers associate head coach/offensive specialist Darrell Bevell, who was Miami's passing game coordinator/quarterbacks coach. Waller came out of retirement in 2025 to join the Dolphins following a trade with the New York Giants . He battled multiple injuries in Miami, but in nine games he produced 24 catches for 283 yards and six touchdowns. Waller, a sixth-round pick of the Baltimore Ravens in 2015, has played nine seasons in the NFL but skipped the 2024 campaign for a retirement that proved temporary. He made the Pro Bowl with the Las Vegas Raiders in 2020 and has 374 receptions for 4,407 yards and 26 touchdowns in his career. Waller joins a tight ends room fronted by veteran Tommy Tremble , who is entering his sixth season in Carolina. The unit also features 2025 fifth-round pick Mitchell Evans and 2024 fourth-rounder Ja'Tavion Sanders , as well as veterans James Mitchell and Feleipe Franks . A source told ESPN that the Waller move was not because of an injury to one of the other tight ends on the roster. With Waller joining the team, Sanders, a former starter, might need to battle to keep his job in Carolina. Unlike Tremble and Evans, Sanders played in the Hall of Fame Game last week, even after suffering a minor ankle injury earlier in the week. Sanders has struggled with ankle injuries the past two seasons and underwent surgery for the most recent ailment last season. In 2025, the Panthers kept four tight ends on their 53-man roster -- Sanders, Evans, Tremble and Mitchell. With Waller aboard, the dynamic might shift, as Evans and Tremble are traditional tight ends, while Waller and Sanders are pass catchers, first and foremost. Franks, a former quarterback, is a special teams ace, while Mitchell struggled to find a consistent role on game days last year. When Waller, who turns 34 in September, officially signs with the Panthers, he will become the oldest non-specialist on the roster. The Panthers entered Wednesday with just three non-specialists over 30. The Panthers will need to make a corresponding move to add Waller to the roster. The team is currently at the 91-man limit, including an international exemption.

(0:46) John Keim Aug 12, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close John Keim covers the Washington Commanders for ESPN. He joined ESPN in 2013 after a stint with the Washington Post. He started covering the team in 1994 for the Journal Newspapers and later for the Washington Examiner. He has authored/co-authored four books. You can also listen to him on 'The John Keim Report', which airs on ESPN Richmond radio. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ASHBURN, Va. -- As soon as Washington Commanders coach Dan Quinn introduced the topic, one player began to feel the heat. Long-snapper Tyler Ott dreaded what would happen next on a spring morning before the team meeting began. And that's what Quinn wanted: to put his players under pressure, especially after a disastrous season that invited speculation about his own job stability. Within a minute, Ott was headed to the front of the room. For a spelling bee. "I had a feeling he'd pull up the Harvard guy," Ott said. "I probably felt more pressure doing that than coming out here to snap." For the next 20 minutes, the environment in the team auditorium shifted between tense silences and excitement. When Ott paused in the middle of spelling a word, teammates and coaches, watching intently, began to stir and murmur. At other times, the quiet was broken when he or coaching analyst Travis Ho, his spelling bee opponent on the day, spelled a word correctly -- the room erupting in applause and cheers. The pre-practice scene highlighted the mindset Quinn is trying to cultivate heading into the 2026 season. After a 5-12 campaign that followed a surprising run to the NFC Championship Game the previous year, Quinn spent the offseason searching for ways to sharpen a Washington team he felt had lost some of its edge last year. Through coaching changes, roster moves and an increased emphasis on competition in nearly every aspect of his program, Quinn has tried to inject more urgency into a franchise looking to rebound from one of the NFL's steepest year-to-year declines. This January, Quinn moved on from both coordinators, citing a lack of production on defense and a need for a change in philosophy on offense. In the offseason, Washington made scores of personnel changes, injecting youth and athleticism into what had been the NFL's oldest roster with the likes of edge rusher Odafe Oweh and top draft pick Sonny Styles , while also upgrading talent at positions of need, like the signing of Stefon Diggs to partner with No. 1 receiver Terry McLaurin last week. Despite the changes, Quinn heads into Year 3 leading a team projected by ESPN's Mike Clay to win 6.4 games and finish last in the NFC East. And that was prior to losing All-Pro left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a triceps injury Saturday. But Quinn insists his focus is not on outside expectations, but on rebuilding the standards he felt had slipped a season ago. "I don't feel under pressure," Quinn said. "I don't think in that kind of way." That's clear to those around him, whether it's players, coaches or acquaintances. Instead, one person who knows him well said Quinn, who hasn't had conversations about his job with team owner Josh Harris heading into this season, according to sources with knowledge of his situation, seems to have been invigorated by 2025's downturn. And he is focused on returning the Commanders to where they were entering last season, in part, by doubling down on the details and ramping up the energy levels in the building. Part of his plan has involved adding more competition to team meetings. At times that could mean having a basketball shooting contest between a player and a coach. It also could mean a table tennis match or even a friendship quiz -- when two sets of two players must answer questions about how well they know the other. One time two players competed to see who could finish song lyrics. Another time they played the trivia game Kahoot!, asking questions based on Washington's offensive and defensive systems. But, on the same spring day the National Spelling Bee was held in Washington, D.C., it was Ott vs. Ho -- Harvard vs. Vanderbilt. Ott misspelled "etcetera" and "miscellaneous" -- the word that made him pause -- and lost by one. "I don't know the last time I actually spelled miscellaneous," Ott said, shrugging his shoulders. "I was an Econ major." Regardless of the winner, the result was the same as every other competition this offseason: a team focused and full of energy as it prepares to take the field -- something, Quinn said, he didn't see enough of in 2025. "It gets you going," said safety Jeremy Reaves . "If you start the day with competition then the precedent is set." That, Quinn hopes, is the point. "There's something on the line all the time," Ott said. IN JUNE, QUINN said he spent time this offseason rewatching practices from 2025. He compared a practice from a 2024 OTA session with one at the exact same point in 2025. "I didn't love the urgency that I saw," Quinn said of last year's work. Coaches, players and others in the organization said they never sensed any big, noticeable slippage in the team's preparation last season that they feel directly led to their 5-12 record. Certainly, injuries played a major factor. But Quinn said, looking back, there were subtle signs that things were slightly off. "I could see in the spring, a little bit in the summer where all of a sudden you're just a little bit off," Quinn said. "And then you're a little more off and you're a little more and pretty soon you're like 10 degrees off and you're like, 'Why can't we swing this back?'" Quinn then showed his video findings to his coaches, then to the players who participated in both seasons. The offseason self-review stems from Quinn's longtime interest in introspection. In 2020, he underwent a 360 review that focused on his blind spots as a coach after being fired in Atlanta. When he examined last season, he arrived at the conclusion that little details slipped. In hindsight, the players agree. Sometimes the issues were seemingly minor. But looking back, the players knew they were telling, such as offensive linemen not always chasing the ball down the field after a running back broke through the line, or when a catch was made. Or when fellow offensive players didn't rush to defend Luke McCaffrey after the wideout was bumped hard to the ground by cornerback Mike Sainristil during an intrasquad scrimmage. On the first day of 2026 training camp, one defensive coach could be heard shouting at the players to get off the field faster. Before one practice in the spring, Quinn didn't like the energy as players broke a team huddle following their stretching -- and brought them together to voice his displeasure. "This year you can really tell they are being intentional with the work and it's being called out if we're not," offensive lineman Andrew Wylie said. To combat the complacency, Quinn placed extra emphasis on competition. He also installed a video leaderboard -- visible from the moment you walk into the facility -- that tracks categories such as ball security and takeaways, completion percentages, preparation and engagement in the meeting rooms. There's even a category for linebackers dubbed "intensity yards." "This is my first time letting my eyes and the numbers dictate, 'Hey, this is what I think excellent looks like. This is what I think below the line looks like.' And then I show them that." Every player is posted, not only the leaders, which leads to players getting loud, whether pointing out where they're at on the board or where a teammate stands. "I'm trying to see who's winning and who's not," Reaves said. "That's the nature of the business." All of this is meant to help produce a sharper and hungrier Commanders team in 2026. The team acknowledges slipping on the details wasn't the reason for last season's collapse. But Quinn and others believed those small lapses reflected a team that had grown too complacent. "We were just comfortable with what we did the year before. We thought we had arrived," said Reaves. QUINN KNOWS WHAT happens to coaches who don't win in the NFL. As the head coach of the Atlanta Falcons from 2015 to 2020, he guided the Falcons to the Super Bowl in 2017, where they famously blew a 28-3 lead in a loss to the New England Patriots . A 10-6 season followed, but then came consecutive losing years. When Atlanta started 0-5 in 2020, Quinn was fired. In Washington, Quinn said he has not been given an ultimatum leading into the 2026 season, according to multiple sources. Multiple people who have worked for Harris said that's not how he has operated in Washington or with his other pro teams, the NBA's Philadelphia 76ers and the NHL's New Jersey Devils. In 2023, his first full season as Washington's owner, he gave fourth-year coach Ron Rivera the entire season to show what he could do before making a move. The Commanders finished 4-13 and Rivera was fired after the season. But Quinn knows and multiple people in the organization have uttered the line "it's a results business" when it comes to an NFL coach's job security. According to one team source familiar with management's thinking, the owners love the culture in the building and the direction Quinn has provided. But, of course, they also want to see success. They want to see quarterback Jayden Daniels regain the path he was on as a rookie. They want to see the defense improve. They want the organization to have sustained success for the first time in decades. If they're healthy and struggle? That's when problems could occur and changes could result. But none of the people who were asked said there was a win total Quinn needed to reach. No one would say Quinn's seat is hot entering the season, and one source said any pressure Quinn feels is self-induced. "I think I would have been more worried in my earlier time as a head coach," Quinn said, "where you're like, 'What are they saying?'" But now, he said, his focus isn't on the result but, rather, on the coaches and the players. "I've been doing it a long time, so I have a lot of confidence in what we're doing and how we're doing it," said Quinn, who is entering his ninth season as a head coach. "You were asking about the pressure earlier. I do love it. I don't think of it any different when we're hitting all the marks and I don't think of it any different when we're not. "I just want to do a really good job for the coaches. I want to do a really good job for the players, and if I do that, man, I can put my head on the pillow knowing that like, man, I had really high standards. That's why last year bothered me so much when we didn't meet our standards of what we wanted to do." One longtime acquaintance said that perhaps Quinn didn't allow himself in Atlanta to think about what could happen. But, this person said, he understands what could happen -- but that last year "didn't change his demeanor. ... He was and still is an optimist. You can be aware of it, but what he's exceptional at is not letting it change his demeanor, not letting it change who he is." "You've been through hard things, you've been through it and I haven't wavered," Quinn said. "It was a very frustrating year and offseason, but I've got a lot of resolve. I like the energy and edge of the players." THE ENERGY WASN'T the only thing Quinn changed this offseason. In January, Washington parted ways with offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury and defensive coordinator Joe Whitt Jr. As one former member of the organization said, if Quinn felt like it wasn't working, he needed to make tough decisions -- or face regret for doing nothing and still getting fired if the season went south. "Two guys I regard a lot so it's definitely hard," Quinn said. "Making the hard calls is part of the gig. You don't like it, but if you have a big vision of what's going to be best then I do what I think is best for our team." Their replacements offer different visions and schemes. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones represents a departure from what Quinn has typically run in his career, using more three-man fronts and different pressure packages. "I like that he's on the front edge of some things," Quinn said. New offensive coordinator David Blough will run a more traditional offense than Kingsbury, with the quarterback more under center and with heavier emphasis on play-action passes. Multiple front office and coaching sources said Quinn would often talk in meetings about running the ball more often and having a better run-pass ratio. Another word used often this offseason by many in the organization was "collaboration." Several coaches said they have more of that on offense now. To help, Quinn organized coaching retreats in the offseason during which they'd listen to talks from leaders of various industries that focused on training people under pressure. Quinn's willingness to move on from both coordinators after two seasons together reflects the same mindset as the spelling bees, the leaderboards and the self-scouting in the offseason. He's unafraid to address any and every aspect that will help Washington win now. "When it's time for a change," Quinn said, "whatever the reason might be, you do what's best for the team at the moment."

He has covered the Broncos for more than 20 years and also assists with NFL draft coverage, joining ESPN in 2013. He has been a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame Board of Selectors since 1999, too. Jeff previously covered the Pittsburgh Steelers, Buffalo Bills and Houston Oilers/Tennessee Titans at previous stops prior to ESPN. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Sometimes when Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton begins to answer a question, his mind is already on things yet to come. There have been a few moments in training camp when he has mentioned the work to be done by quarterback Bo Nix in his "fourth year." Payton certainly knows Nix is actually in his third NFL season, but the accidental bobble fits since folks have been in a hurry to assess the 26-year-old quarterback from the moment the Broncos selected him with the No. 12 pick of the 2024 draft. Nix has been on the fast track since arriving in Denver. He was named the team's starter during his first NFL preseason and immediately found himself with the immense expectations that come from quarterbacking a franchise that has won three Super Bowls and been led by the likes of Hall of Famers John Elway and Peyton Manning. And as Payton has often said about Nix, "I'm glad he's on our team. ... I like where he's headed." But the clock is ticking for Nix and the Broncos, who have a 25-11 record (including postseason) in two seasons with him as the starter. They enter the third season of Nix's financially friendly rookie contract on a quest to win the franchise its fourth Super Bowl title. But that's not all that's on the line. The Broncos need to decide whether Nix is truly Denver's next franchise quarterback -- and if he's worthy of a big-money, long-term contract that will significantly alter the team's roster and salary cap situation. They have to juggle Nix's ability to win games and play at his highest level in the clutch with a growing list of ankle injuries and some red-flag moments in his play. For his part, Nix has remained calm, focused and quietly driven to make a giant step in where he wants his career to go this season. "Year 1, I'm trying to just not mess up for the team," Nix said. "I feel like Year 3, I'm trying to make plays for the team. It's just quite the different feeling. It's just a confidence-level thing." THE BRONCOS HAVE won 69.4% of their games with Nix as their starting quarterback. They have made playoff trips in his two seasons as a starter (after missing the postseason the previous eight seasons) and are the defending AFC West champions . And the Broncos went 14-3 last season, including an NFL-record 12 comeback wins and an 11-2 record in one-score games. Yes, the defense is elite. But Nix has done his part. He is only the third quarterback in league history to throw for at least 3,500 passing yards and 25 touchdown passes in his first two seasons (Manning and the Los Angeles Chargers ' Justin Herbert are the others). Nix has the most team wins, passing touchdowns, rushing touchdowns and total touchdowns among the six first-round quarterbacks selected in 2024, besting the likes of Caleb Williams , Drake Maye and Jayden Daniels . His QBR in the red zone last season also was fourth best in the league (82.6), and he led the NFL in winning drives (seven). He also embodies one of Payton's foundational principles in quarterback play: don't take sacks. Though Nix led the league in pass attempts (612) and dropbacks (667) last season, he was sacked the ninth-fewest times among the league's starters. And much of his late-game success is derived from his ability to move out of trouble and get a play to what Payton calls "the second act." "It's one of his superpowers," Payton said. "It's hard to sack some quarterbacks; he's one of them. That was something you saw on college tape. In our league when you take a sack, you just do the analytics on what your points become in that drive ... and it all drops dramatically." His ability to extend plays, his leadership style, day-to-day demeanor and overall approach to the job are among the first things his teammates list when asked why they believe Nix is "The Guy." "Bo just walks in the room like he's ready for anything," running back J.K. Dobbins said. "And he is. He ain't trying to walk like that, you know what I mean? That's just that thing about him. You're never going to feel you're out of it with Bo. People can say whatever they want about Bo, about this and that, but Bo's our guy. We all know it." How the Broncos built their roster shows how much their decision-makers agree with Dobbins. Since Nix was drafted, the Broncos have spent more than $300 million in guaranteed-at-signing money to secure standouts such as defensive tackle Zach Allen , guard Quinn Meinerz , edge rusher Nik Bonitto , wide receiver Courtland Sutton , cornerback Pat Surtain II and offensive tackle Garett Bolles to long-term extensions. They're returning 20 of 22 offensive and defensive starters from last season's AFC Championship Game , and they re-signed 17 of 21 players who were scheduled to be unrestricted, restricted or exclusive rights free agents. And when their internal reviews revealed a need in their passing game, they sent first-, third- and fourth-round picks to the Miami Dolphins in March to acquire wide receiver Jaylen Waddle . All of these moves were made to build the kind of depth chart around Nix "that can help a quarterback develop," as Payton has said. "The 'next step' is kind of cliché," the coach added when asked of Nix's progression. "He just finished winning 14 games and having a really good season. Do I think he's going to continue to improve? ... I think there are certain areas for us offensively that can help with the quarterback, a consistent run game throughout the year. There are some things that we can do to help him." THE BRONCOS SPENT what first-year offensive coordinator Davis Webb called "some long hours in the offseason" going through each Nix game of the past two seasons to evaluate what he has done well as a starter and the areas where progress needs to be made. Though Payton has consistently praised his QB's decision-making, processing and ability to avoid sacks and turnovers, Nix hasn't been particularly accurate, especially on downfield throws. He also resides near the middle of the pack among the league's starting quarterbacks in explosive pass plays. "We were really trying to evaluate ... the last two years, how his first read on plays marries up the second read, depth-wise, playcall-wise, where we are at that point in the game,'' Webb said. "... It's noticeable the strides he's making, hanging on [the first read], getting to two, to three." Nix was 26th in the league in completion percentage over expectation (minus-2.1%) last season, per NFL Next Gen Stats, and he was 12th in the league in completions of 20 or more yards (47 -- 25 behind league-leader Matthew Stafford 's 72). Nix also completed 44.1% of his pass attempts of 10 or more air yards, along with 36.1% of attempts for 20 or more air yards. Defensive coaches in the league have found other areas to exploit. Some who have faced Nix over the past two years say they want to present looks that force him to look toward the middle of the field, an area he hasn't shown comfort attacking. When his 2026 pass chart is fully separated into sections of the field, his lowest attempt totals come between the hashmarks (40 attempts). His highest volume comes outside the numbers (234 attempts). "We'll do that a lot in the spring self-scout," Payton said. "Then we'll look at -- 'All right, what are the things that maybe we need to be better at?' But yes, we'll look at hit charts, we'll look at the analytics." There are also questions about Nix's long-term health . He has shown exceptional durability so far, given that he started a then-record 61 college games in five seasons at Auburn and Oregon. He has sat out only one game as an NFL starter -- last season's AFC Championship Game. So by any definition, Nix has been reliable. But the fractured right ankle sustained in the Broncos' divisional round win over the Buffalo Bills means Nix has sustained ankle fractures in high school, college and the NFL. He has had three ankle surgeries in his two seasons with the Broncos, including a follow-up surgery in April to address bone spurs in the surgically repaired right ankle that Nix says he believes will head off future troubles. The ankle issues will at least be part of what the Broncos would consider when it's time for contract negotiations. But right tackle Mike McGlinchey spoke for most of his teammates when the barrage of questions about Nix's health were posed this summer. "I think Bo's healthy, ready to go," McGlinchey said. "He was here with us, there was a group of us that live here full time [in the offseason] that train here full time. I saw him every step of the way. He was checking all his boxes, he was attacking his rehab hard like he attacks everything." WHILE THE NFL salary cap continues to climb (it's currently at $301.2 million), the top 12 highest-paid quarterbacks have contracts that average $51 million per year or more, with the Kansas City Chiefs ' Patrick Mahomes and Dallas Cowboys ' Dak Prescott on deals that average more than $60 million per year . In a stark contract, Nix's $5.076 million cap charge in 2026 is the 19th-highest on the Broncos . But that is on the verge of changing. Nix is in the third year of his four-year rookie deal, and the Broncos hold a fifth-year option in 2028. So, his salary is bound to mushroom ... if Denver puts the checkbook behind its current belief that he is the franchise's long-term quarterback. "Obviously we want Bo here long term, but we're really focused on getting ready for this season, putting a competitive team on the field," Broncos owner/CEO Greg Penner said Tuesday. "I'll leave that, obviously, to [general manager] George [Paton] and Sean." An informal survey with several general managers and pro personnel executives revealed a couple of potential options with how the Broncos and Nix could move forward: Nix has a big season and guides the Broncos to playoff success. In that scenario, the Broncos, even after engaging the fifth-year option next spring, would try to negotiate what would be a big contract with Nix and his representatives. As the market value continues to balloon for QBs, a new deal probably would net Nix well over $100 million worth of fully guaranteed money (there are 11 quarterbacks who top $100 million in fully guaranteed money) and an average salary of more than $50 million. Nix's play levels out, and the Broncos fall short of expectations. In this scenario, the Broncos might be more inclined to pick up the fifth-year option but let Nix play out Year 4 of his deal in 2027, entering negotiations on an extension after that season concludes. How the Broncos proceed with Nix will affect their dealings with other players. The Broncos will face decisions next March on a long list of impending free agents, led by cornerbacks Riley Moss and Ja'Quan McMillian , safety Brandon Jones , guard Ben Powers and wide receiver/kick returner Marvin Mims Jr . For his part, Nix tries not to think about all that, preferring to keep his focus in the moment and not stray from the be-where-your-feet-are approach. "I think competitively, the way we are as players, you better treat every year as a year you have to prove," Nix said earlier in training camp. "You have to go out there and show the team that you're worth what you're putting in for you and what they're building around you. You can't ever let up and think that, 'I've made it. I've gotten to where I need to be,' because quite honestly, I'll never feel that way. "There's always the next season. There's always the next championship to go after. I think every year for every player is going to feel like a contract year because it should." But make no mistake: Since Nix was drafted, the Broncos have said -- from Penner on down -- that they believe he is their next franchise cornerstone quarterback. And as the championship clock ticks, Nix hopes to further prove that he is that player. "I think that question sort of answers itself," Nix said earlier this offseason when asked if he hoped the Broncos eventually make the long-term commitment to him. "I think everyone that's in the league wants that long-term extension and wants to play for their home team. For me, I love being here. I love where I'm at. I love this team. I'll play as long as they want to have me."
