(0:55) Mike Clay Aug 12, 2026, 06:47 AM ET Close Mike Clay is a senior writer for fantasy football and the NFL at ESPN. Mike is a member of the FSWA Hall of Fame. His projections power the ESPN Fantasy Football game, and he also appears on "Fantasy Football Now" and the Fantasy Focus Football podcast. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions Fantasy football leagues come in all shapes and sizes. In fact, I know this better than most, as none of the dozen or so teams I manage (not to mention countless best ball and mock drafts) are exactly the same, with a steady mix of seasonlong, dynasty, keeper, IDP, super-deep lineups and/or very creative scoring. One of my past leagues even had punters and head coaches. Yes, you can use both in the ESPN game ... and there are projections! I often get asked about how to adjust strategy based on these leagues, so without getting too into the weeds, here are ways I do just that. Dynasty leagues As much as I enjoy a good seasonlong draft, there is nothing I love more than dynasty leagues. It's the closest you can get to playing GM, as you retain your assets year to year and can make moves at nearly any point on the calendar. There are few better feelings in fantasy than hitting a home run on a rookie pick (just ask those who spent a late first-rounder on Justin Jefferson in 2020 or took a late flier on Puka Nacua in 2023) or watching one of your sleeper/bench stashes emerge (take a bow, stashers of Jalen Hurts , Chase Brown and Harold Fannin Jr . in years past). Oh, and the season never ends. Sure, it stinks to have a bad team, but if you fall out of contention in dynasty, the offseason begins -- at least for you -- and you can immediately begin making trades and waiver moves to set yourself up for future success. As odd as it sounds, sometimes that can be a more enjoyable ride than a stressful playoff run. And when it eventually leads to a title? There are few better feelings in this game. The best advice I can give as it pertains to dynasty is to consider perceived value. Dynasty managers love unproven youngsters and first-round draft picks much more than they like established veterans, excluding obvious superstars in their early prime. We get bored with guys who just get the job done year after year, and we are easily distracted by the shiny new toy. You can and should take advantage of this, and one way to do that in a startup draft is to go extremely young at the expense of winning in the short term. That might seem counterintuitive to what I just said, but bear with me. Aim for 20- to 24-year-old players (adjusting slightly by position) and do your best to fade everyone else. Not everyone you pick will pan out, but enough will, and within a year or two, your roster should be peaking, while the lineups of managers who drafted depreciating assets will be fading. Odds are, your slow start will also allow you to add another potential superstar via an early pick in the Year 2 rookie draft. This strategy sets you up with a good, deep roster of young players entering their prime and also an extremely attractive roster on the trade market. That reminds me of one of my championship-winning teams from back in 2020. Prior to that season, my roster was talented, young and deep, which allowed me to make a push for one more superstar. I traded Terry McLaurin , Raheem Mostert and a pair of future second-round picks for some guy named Davante Adams . That was fair market value at the time and proved to be a title-winning move. Speaking of dynasty trades, don't be afraid to trade rookie picks. I swap them often, especially if it lands me an established good player. We tend to overestimate the hit rate of rookies (like it or not, a lot of the rookies you're excited about right now will bust) and, as long as the player isn't "too old," turning what is essentially a lottery ticket into a weekly starter should be a no-brainer. I'm especially aggressive trading away picks if I expect my team to be good. (My picks would, in turn, be late in the round the next year.) Rookie drafts Perhaps the most important element of any dynasty league is the annual rookie draft. Unless you're a very aggressive trader, your roster isn't going to change a ton from year to year, with the largest impact coming via the rookie draft. These are fairly straightforward -- take the best players available -- but I do see people make avoidable mistakes quite often. One error is reaching in order to fill a positional need instead of taking the best player available. An even bigger one is not considering pedigree. As mentioned in the predraft playbook , most fantasy-relevant players were drafted on Day 1 or 2. It's easy to pick on GMs for occasional misses (Eagles GM Howie Roseman might never live down choosing Jalen Reagor over Justin Jefferson despite an incredible track record), but they are very good at their job, for the most part. Year after year, I see drafters in desperation for running back help reaching on Day 3 fliers with seemingly little competition for snaps in the short term over Round 1-2 wide receivers with a substantially better chance to be long-term fantasy starters. Not worrying much about position and taking the best prospect on the board is your best path toward building a powerhouse. Keeper leagues Do you prefer seasonlong leagues but hate the feeling of not getting to hang on to that amazing, late-round home run pick you made for multiple years? A keeper league is your new best friend. It's hard to give detailed advice here, as keeper leagues are known for having all kinds of rules and regulations pertaining to whom you're allowed to keep, how many players you can keep and, in many cases, which picks you must surrender in order to keep players. That said, I get a lot of keeper questions, and usually they are incredibly easy to answer. Look, if you're able to keep only a player or two or three, you're basically playing in a seasonlong league and should thus keep the players who help you in the short term, adjusting only slightly for age. The best advice in these scenarios is to consider ADP. A realistic question I get is something like, "Should I keep A.J. Brown for a second-round pick or Emeka Egbuka for a 12th-round pick?" Most agree Brown is the better short-term asset, but the players have a similar ADP. In this scenario, you keep Egbuka and you'll still get a player similar to Brown (if not Brown himself) when you're on the clock in the second round. I can't stress enough how easy it is to make keeper decisions simply by considering ADP. IDP: Individual Defensive Players There are some hardcore, serious IDP leagues out there, but I'd guess that most of you in a league with defensive players have a fairly normal set of starting slots at the offensive positions and then something in the range of one to six IDP starters. In this scenario (and assuming default scoring), you don't need to value defensive players very highly in your draft or on the trade market. Sure, a standout linebacker such as Jordyn Brooks can give you an edge and has middle-round value, but because IDP scoring is generally a step or two below offense, and because you're likely starting only one or two players at very deep positions, you're going to have plenty of good options both during the draft and on waivers during the season. Also, casual players know offense significantly better than defense, so identifying and finding good starters will generally be easier. In a nutshell, in leagues with basic IDP settings, you should focus on offense first and worry about IDP later. A quick reminder here on Travis Hunter . The Jaguars' second-year WR/CB has added a fun wrinkle to the fantasy football landscape. If you're in an ESPN fantasy league that uses only the standard positions, this won't affect you, as Hunter will get points only for non-IDP categories, same as all players. However, if you use defensive players, Hunter will get points for contributions on both sides of the ball. This makes Hunter an extremely valuable asset in IDP formats since he can be slotted into your lineup as a "CB" or "DB." Be sure to consider this when evaluating Hunter on draft day. Superflex Superflex means that your starting lineup includes a flex spot that can be filled with a quarterback (in ESPN leagues, this is the "OP" spot). Because the worst starting QB option in a given week is generally going to be projected to outscore the best flex options, this means that each team in your league ideally will be starting two quarterbacks. Needless to say, QB is significantly more valuable in this format. You should move all quarterbacks up your draft board and plan to roster an extra player or two at the position, as starting two good QBs each week needs to be your primary goal. Whereas top QBs Lamar Jackson , Josh Allen , Jayden Daniels , Drake Maye , Joe Burrow and Jalen Hurts are picked in the third- to sixth-round range in one-QB leagues, you can expect a handful of them to be off the board in the first round of superflex leagues. Knowing that the early QB run will lead to stars at other positions falling in the draft, my goal is almost never to open a superflex draft by picking two consecutive QBs. Instead, I'll aim for one star QB and then grab an elite back or wide receiver. Once the initial rush of QBs ends, it tends to quiet down significantly for several rounds, so I simply monitor the situation and eventually pounce on a good second QB when the opportunity presents itself (generally one ranked in the 8-to-15 range, though players in that tier are so similar in 2026 that you don't need to push it). I also make sure to grab either a reliable or upside third QB once the starters begin to dry up. You have to be careful to walk the line of not reaching too early and jeopardizing the rest of your roster while also not getting stuck with a really poor QB situation that handcuffs you all season long. In a perfect world, I have a very good QB1, a reliable QB2 (guys such as Justin Herbert , Bo Nix , Trevor Lawrence and Brock Purdy are strong QB2 targets) and then someone with upside. This season, you'll want to keep your eyes on Kyler Murray , Tyler Shough , Daniel Jones , Malik Willis , Cam Ward and Fernando Mendoza , for example. Best ball If you're not familiar, "best ball" means you simply draft your team, and then it requires no additional action. There are generally no trades or waiver adds, and your weekly starters are determined by your highest scorers at each position that week. For the most part, your strategy isn't changing massively from a normal league, but you do need to ensure you have more depth at each position since you can't trade or add players, even for injury. In a standard format, for example, you might draft 20 players, so you'd want 2-3 QBs, 5-6 RBs, 7-8 WRs, 2-3 TEs and 2-3 D/STs (these formats rarely use kickers and often don't include D/ST). I won't go too into the weeds here since league settings and contest structure matter, but if you're in a fairly standard league of 10-plus teams, you don't need to adjust your strategy much from the usual. However, in a tournament setting, you'll want to employ additional strategies such as stacking (drafting both Dak Prescott and George Pickens last season would've been a massive edge, for example) and considering matchups during championship week (almost always Week 17). Knockout leagues New at ESPN in 2026 are knockout leagues . In this format, the lowest-scoring team in the league is eliminated each week and that team's players are immediately placed on waivers. There are a few key differences from standard fantasy leagues. One is that you need to worry less about ceiling and more about floor. Posting the highest weekly score in the league earns you nothing, but posting the lowest score ends your season. Second, you need to be more aware of your team's schedule and bye weeks as one bad week can sink your entire season. An example in 2026 would be to upgrade Eagles players in your draft rankings as, although they face a brutally tough schedule during the fantasy football playoffs, they have perhaps the easiest slate during the regular season. You can put your Eagles to good use during the regular season and, assuming you keep advancing, load up your roster with better players with better matchups come playoff time. (P.S. Interestingly, the opposite is true in aforementioned best ball tournaments, as loading up on Eagles players could be costly come the all-important playoff run.) The other main difference is that you'll need to be a lot more active on waivers, as a handful of superstars will be available each week. Having a good game plan for spending your free agent budget (FAB) is half the battle. For more info on knockout leagues, check out this superb strategy piece from Tristan H. Cockcroft. 6-point passing TD I quickly want to touch on leagues that award six points for a passing TD, as opposed to the standard four points. Honestly, I don't adjust too much for this. As a whole, quarterbacks are more valuable, but there is still sufficient depth at the position, so we don't need to move them significantly up our ranks. The key is bumping up QBs projected to throw a lot of touchdowns at the expense of quarterbacks who do a lot of damage with their legs. The likes of Jaxson Dart , Jayden Daniels and Jalen Hurts take a hit, whereas Matthew Stafford , Joe Burrow , Dak Prescott and Jared Goff get a boost. A quick scan of projections and/or historical stats is your friend here. TE premium Leagues that award 1.5 or even 2.0 points per reception to tight ends are becoming more popular and have been common in high-stakes leagues for many years. It makes sense when you consider that the No. 2 TE in 1.0 PPR leagues last season (Kyle Pitts) scored 210.8 points, which would have ranked 17th at wide receiver, 19th at running back and 21st at quarterback. In a 1.5 PPR TE premium league, Pitts would've scored 243.9 points, which would've ranked seventh, 10th and 13th, respectively. Perfect? Perhaps not. Better? Of course. In this setup (this also applies to leagues in which you must start two tight ends), you'd bump up the value of all tight ends and could consider top options such as Brock Bowers and Trey McBride as early as late in the first round. You should also make it a priority to stash a tight end with breakout potential and/or upside on your bench ( Kenyon Sadiq , Isaiah Likely , Terrance Ferguson and Gunnar Helm come to mind). If you're interested in trying out this format, you can customize your league scoring by position in the ESPN fantasy game. Punters Just kidding. Or am I? I want punters from offenses likely to struggle, so I'm targeting the likes of Bradley Pinion (Dolphins) and AJ Cole (Raiders).

(1:01) NFL Nation Aug 12, 2026, 06:00 AM ET Close NFL Nation is made up of 32 team-specific reporters who cover the NFL year-round across ESPN.com, ESPN television shows, ESPN Radio, ESPN+ and social media platforms. It was established ahead of the 2013 season. Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions For NFL rookies, that first paycheck represents more than just a payday. After years of working toward the league -- which kicks off Thursday with a full slate of Week 1 preseason games -- many first-year players have used that money on long-awaited purchases and priorities. For some rookies, it's a new car. For others, it's a house or an opportunity to take care of their parents. And then there are those who aren't ready to spend a dime. Buffalo Bills fourth-round pick Skyler Bell , who said NIL money at UConn helped him buy his first car, is already eyeing his next ride -- "maybe like an AMG [Mercedes] or something." New Orleans Saints sixth-round pick Barion Brown has a different approach: "Nah, I'm a sixth-round guy, man. I've got to save every penny I can get!" Here's a look at what some of the NFL's top rookies told ESPN's NFL Nation they have done or plan to do with their first professional paycheck. Jump to a category: Savings, investing | Homes, goods Sports equipment | Apparel | Family Travel, vehicles | Electronics | Exotic pets Savings and investing Jeremiyah Love , RB, Arizona Cardinals Round 1, No. 3 | Age: 21 Love hasn't been shy about how he's going to spend his rookie contract, which is worth a fully guaranteed $53.9 million over four years -- or rather, how he won't be spending his rookie contract. Love said he plans to live off his endorsement money and not spend his NFL paychecks. He has deals with PayPal, New Balance and Celsius. Reports put Love's NIL valuation at Notre Dame at around $600,000, which Love said allows him to live off what he already makes and not new money. "I'm not going to touch the money," he said. "I'm probably going to put it all away and live normally like I've been doing now." Arvell Reese , LB/Edge, New York Giants Round 1, No. 5 | Age: 20 Reese also won't being spending big, even though his deal includes $47.8 million guaranteed. "I just signed it and then went to the hotel and then just got ready for the practice the next day," Reese said. "I don't really got [anything] to buy right now. I already got everything. I got a car and an apartment. So, I'm good right now." Malachi Lawrence , Edge, Dallas Cowboys Round 1, No. 23 | Age: 23 "I got a truck, a [Ram] TRX, that was my first purchase, but that was with NIL. It wasn't with my bonus," Lawrence said. So, what about his NFL money? "I haven't spent really any of that yet. I think like 70% of the players after the NFL go bankrupt or something like that, and I want to be in that 30%." Peter Woods , DT, Kansas City Chiefs Round 1, No. 29 | Age: 21 "I wouldn't say there is [anything specific I want to buy]," Woods said. "Nah, I'm just kind of letting my money make money right now. I had a pretty blessed college situation [at Clemson]. It's a different landscape [now]. It allows me to kind of be disciplined in that area. I'm not really worried about it, for real." Zachariah Branch , WR, Atlanta Falcons Round 3, No. 79 | Age: 22 The Falcons' rookie wide receiver wants to be frugal, the way his parents taught him to be. Branch said he has already spent "a little bit" of his NFL money but on an investment in the stock market. Specifically, S&P 500 companies. "I think I'm all good right now," said Branch, a third-round pick. "I don't think I'm in a position to get to doing certain things that's not smart. I'm trying to create generational wealth. So, whatever comes it may come, but right now I think I'm good on the investments and just food, family." Eventually, the Georgia product said he wants to get into real estate. His father, Sheva, is a prominent realtor in the family's hometown of Las Vegas. "Trying to get some properties and things like that to expand my real estate portfolio," Branch said. play 2:09 What does Kyler Murray being named Vikings' starter mean for J.J. McCarthy? Homes and household goods Blake Miller , OT, Detroit Lions Round 1, No. 17 | Age: 22 Miller isn't looking to purchase anything crazy but is looking to buy a home. "I'm trying to be smart with it and not be a big, big spender," Miller told ESPN. "But, I guess a place to live would be it." Miller, who was selected by Detroit as the 17th pick, learned the value of being smart with his finances from his parents and by managing his money at Clemson from 2022 to 2025, where he started all 54 games of his career. "Obviously being in college in the whole NIL era, that helped a little bit because I kind of was there when it was getting going and you get to see the progression of it," Miller said. "Like guys now, you don't just get a big chunk of money deposited in your account. You're still making good money, but it's not as crazy as it is now. So, I feel like that kind of helped me be able to deal with more and more money, and then my parents as well set a good example. They're always there with questions or anything, and they're really helpful." Jadarian Price , RB, Seattle Seahawks Round 1, No. 32 | Age: 22 With some of the $8.7 million in signing bonus money he received as the 32nd pick in the draft, Price bought his family a new house in his hometown of Denison, Texas. It was something he has wanted to do since he was young and his biggest goal once he reached the NFL. "Checked that off the list," he said. His family's reaction? "A bunch of smiles," Price said. Treydan Stukes , S, Las Vegas Raiders Round 2, No. 38 | Age: 24 "I actually got a house," Stukes said. "I went the real estate route. That was the big purchase, and everything else went into the savings [account]." Jacob Rodriguez , LB, Miami Dolphins Round 2, No. 43 | Age: 23 "I went and got a bed," Rodriguez said of his first purchase. "I went and got a mattress. So, you know, in college for a little bit, when I was a walk-on, I slept on the ground in my brother's apartment. And so, like, I'd never slept good when I was 13 and on, and so then I moved to the college, like 3-inch mattress or whatever. So I never bought a mattress until I was [drafted] because I always said my first purchase is going to be a bed. So, I bought a nice Tempur-Pedic." Brandon Cisse , CB, Green Bay Packers Round 2, No. 52 | Age: 21 Cisse's first paycheck wasn't his first payday. "I had mostly all my stuff already thankfully because of my NIL deals and stuff like that," he said. "But I was able to purchase a house for my family. At the time I purchased the house, I was having a daughter. Now she's here, so that's why I wanted to buy a house here in Green Bay." His daughter was born July 17, just before training camp opened. Antonio Williams , WR, Washington Commanders Round 3, No. 71 | Age: 22 The third-round pick from Clemson made one big purchase. "My first big purchase was a home about 10 minutes away from the [Commanders'] facility. I'm not a big spender. I feel that was a good investment. No cars, nothing crazy, man. I didn't want to make any dumb decisions." Sports equipment Caleb Lomu , OT, New England Patriots Round 1, No. 28 | Age: 21 "I'm not really a guy who spends too much money, but one of the first things I got was a new golf set," Lomu said. "I'm big into golf. I love playing some golf. I had to get some longer ones. I kind of outgrew my old set." Family support Jordyn Tyson , WR, New Orleans Saints Round 1, No. 8 | Age: 22 "I sent my dad some money. I looked at his USAA account. ... I was like, let me give Pops some money. [I didn't tell him.] When he saw me, he just gave me a hug," Tyson said. "For myself, I bought a house. I'd say that was the big thing." Zion Young , Edge, Baltimore Ravens Round 2, No. 45 | Age: 22 Young, who is the youngest of 11 siblings, used the money to help his parents. "My parents have [had] a house full of kids my whole life," Young said. "The first thing I wanted to do was put a little money in their pockets and pay for some [house] renovations." Now, Young is supporting his siblings. Each month, he selects one and pays their rent or mortgage. "I get a lot of thank-yous," Young said. Romello Height , Edge, San Francisco 49ers Round 3, No. 70 | Age: 25 Height didn't go on a massive spending spree. He said he helped out his closest family members and bought himself some streetwear. "I looked out for my mom a little bit, look out for my dad, sisters and brothers, and that's about it." Apparel Tacario Davis , CB, Cincinnati Bengals Round 3, No. 72 | Age: 21 Davis wants to save his money as best as possible. But he is eyeing one splurge -- a Rolex watch. "I feel like there's levels to it," Davis said. "When you're a kid, you want a chain. You don't ever want a watch. But watches start a conversation. Somebody will be looking [at you] and say, 'Nice watch, man!'" One model that caught Davis' eye -- an 18-karat rose gold Day-Date that carries a suggested retail price of $58,950. Travel and vehicles Denzel Boston , WR, Cleveland Browns Round 2, No. 39 | Age: 22 "A couple trips to Miami," Boston said of his first purchase. "Just was out there training. It was my sister's birthday, so just went to Miami and kicked it with her." Drew Allar , QB, Pittsburgh Steelers Round 3, No. 76 | Age: 22 Allar, a third-round pick, said he bought a car recently, but his first rookie check is going to "go to rent. Nothing too crazy yet." Electronics and toys Carnell Tate , WR, Tennessee Titans Round 1, No. 4 | Age: 21 Tate bought a Star Wars Lego Ultimate Collector Series set. He is an avid Lego collector and is currently working on the Titanic. He also said he purchased a house in Chicago, his hometown. Albert Regis , DT, Jacksonville Jaguars Round 3, No. 81 | Age: 23 Regis purchased a gaming PC (CyberPower) and gaming monitor (a 45-inch, curved LG monitor) with his signing bonus. "That was it. I didn't want to spend it on anything stupid," he said. "I bought those two things because those were two things that I really wanted, a really good gaming monitor and a really good gaming PC. I bought those, and that's it. That's all I spent my money on. It's a pretty good high-end PC. It gives me everything I need plus more, and I'm happy that I made those purchases and not something stupid." Exotic pets Caleb Banks , DT, Minnesota Vikings Round 1, No. 18 | Age: 23 In high school, one of Banks' classmates unknowingly prompted a lifelong obsession. The student mentioned that she likes koalas. "I'm like, 'Oh snap, all right, let me look into it,'" said Banks, who grew up near Detroit. "I started learning about koala bears a little bit, learning where they were from. Then I ended up figuring out where everything was in Michigan. And California and Florida, kind of like where it's different, where I'd never been. Then I fell in love with animals." He hoped to major in zoology when he arrived at Louisville in 2021, but the program was incompatible with his football schedule. At the very least, however, he knew one thing: He could amass an exotic pet collection. By the time the Vikings made him the No. 18 pick of the draft, Banks owned two bald pythons, a chameleon and a cane corso dog, among others animals. At the time, Banks said he planned to expand the collection when he moved to Minnesota. He arrived at training camp with an announcement: A tarantula and three more snakes had joined the family. "They're locked up, right?" a concerned reporter asked. "Maybe," Banks said with a smile.

She joined ESPN in 2021. Alaina was previously a beat reporter for the Charlotte Observer and has also worked for CBS Sports and the Dallas Morning News. She is a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- For decades, questions have lingered around Western New York: When and where would the Buffalo Bills move? Los Angeles? Toronto? The answer proved to be the other side of Abbott Road. The first public event held at the Bills' new Highmark Stadium was Saturday's training camp practice -- more specifically the annual "Return of the Blue & Red" night. It offered members of the team and 51,807 fans (a team record for a practice, per the Bills) a first look at the $2.2 billion stadium. The Bills' new home is now open after three years of construction. Saturday's practice was filled with blue, red and even some gray sights on what many described as a "bittersweet night." ESPN chronicled the evening through photographs. QB1's new look Quarterback Josh Allen 's first steps in uniform onto the new field was a highly anticipated moment. Photographers and videographers gathered by the tunnel more than a half-hour before he came out. Allen is known for wearing custom items for this particular stadium practice. But new year, new stadium, new look. Allen came out of the tunnel wearing the team's new alternate "Nickel City" uniform that has been surrounded in controversy. The quarterback vocally supported the look on the opening day of training camp. Before practice, Allen played catch with fans all the way around the track of the stadium. As he threw his final passes, a sign that read, "the house that Allen Built" was visible in the stands behind him. Backup quarterbacks Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele , as well as punter Tommy Doman Jr ., joined Allen in wearing the uniform, while the rest of the offense wore the team's home blue jerseys and the defense was in the away whites. "I don't know if your quarterbacks are always the best models to show how it looks like. I made fun of Kyle Allen," coach Joe Brady joked. "It's taken me a long time to let [the defensive line] know not to touch the red jerseys in practice. ... I said, 'Look, if you touch a gray jersey today, you don't have to worry about me being the mad one. There's 50,000 fans that are going to be pretty mad at you.'" The quarterbacks finished the practice unscathed. Hello, grass The new stadium features a big change that players are overwhelmingly in favor of -- going from artificial turf to natural grass. "Perfect," right tackle Spencer Brown said of the grass. "I love it. I might sleep out here tonight actually." The field is made up of Kentucky Bluegrass cultivated by Tuckahoe Turf Farms in New Jersey. While the night practice was held on a humid summer night (and was hit by a brief, but strong, rain shower) -- winter will come. When it does, the field's underground heating coils will activate to prevent freezing. There are also snowmelt systems on the artificial turf and track that surround it. There are four natural grass kicking areas cut into the artificial turf that surrounds the grass field. Those allow specialists to work from the sidelines on the same playing surface that is on the field. There were moments when players had to stomp grass chunks back into place, but the reception after the practice was all positive. "It's my No. 1 favorite thing, honestly," tight end Dawson Knox said. "I mean, people probably won't understand, but playing on grass vs. playing on turf is a huge difference. And I think I can speak for literally every player on this team, we love the grass. This is beautifully done. I mean, hats off to whoever did this grass, because it's perfect." The Family Circle The much-anticipated bison family statues were in place a month ahead of the practice, but this was the stainless-steel statues' time to shine, quite literally. Four hours before the practice, an orderly line of people waited for their chance to take a photo with the bison and the stadium behind. But soon after, the line broke apart and fans took photos from every angle. The bison reside in The Family Circle, where fans congregated and immersed themselves in signage. All of the members of the team's wall of fame from the previous stadium are recognized here -- outside of O.J. Simpson . There are also blank canvases, ready to honor current and future Bills. The team livestreamed the bison statues onto the jumbotrons in the stadium, and the statues were lit up in blue and red at the conclusion of the practice. 'Take it all in' Knox arrived at the stadium four hours early. He walked around the field, taking in all the sights or as he described, "taking myself on a little tour." The veteran tight end made sure to note all of the details. "It's the coolest place I've ever played football in," Knox said after practice. Other players and staff members took the field well ahead of the day's events with looks of awe and wonderment. Brady's goal with this practice was for his players to go through a game-like setting in the stadium. That's why a 7 p.m. start time was chosen. But he also wanted players to arrive early, as Knox did, to focus on practice when practice began. "The lights, how does the wind feel, just the grass, the environment, take it all in," Brady said. "So that hey, now when we get out to practice, we're not thinking about all the other potential distractions." The coach himself took some time before the practice to take in the field with his son, Jordan, 3, sporting a Josh Allen shirt, of course. "To get to run around with him, those are the moments that I made sure I tried to take that in," Brady said. "And then, all right, now it's time to go." A bag of Wegmans chips The old Highmark Stadium is largely erased from the Orchard Park skyline. What is left is the rubble from the upper deck as the underground portions of the stadium continue to be filled. Before the doors opened for practice, many fans took the opportunity to peer through the fence at what is left of the former home of the team. "Bittersweet" was uttered time and time again. The SanFilippo family sat by their car in the parking lot with the rubble of the past behind them and their eyes on the future. They had multiple sets of season tickets at the old stadium and ultimately kept just three seats total from their 1963 package that originated with Andy SanFilippo's father. Andy remarked how he can't look back at the old stadium that holds "great memories." He renewed his own season tickets when Jim Kelly came to Buffalo and kept them over the past couple of decades. Bills apparel in full display, Buffalo pride and Wegmans chips in hand, they all agreed on a sadness in seeing the old stadium go while also acknowledging that they were "excited' to see the new venue for the first time. Nods to Buffalo Bills owner Terry Pegula made very clear to the team's senior vice president of design, Frank Cravotta, what he wanted. "[Pegula] said, 'Frank, when you plop me down in my new stadium, I better know immediately that I'm in Buffalo,'" Cravotta said. "We have such a proud history. We have such great stories to tell." That includes placing the world's largest folding table in the 100 level, on which a fan placed a Josh Allen sticker during the event. There is the large-scale model of the Peace Bridge, which connects Buffalo to Fort Erie, Ontario, that fans can walk under. A full-size camper bus is on the 300 level. Food vendors are labeled with different Buffalo neighborhoods, and some represent local restaurants, such as Southern Junction, a BBQ restaurant with a South Asian influence. There is also an art program that includes more than 45 creators and teams who crafted pieces that are displayed throughout the stadium. The art depicts a variety of Bills-specific touches, and some reflect Western New York. 'Welcome to Highmark Stadium' The first fans heard warm greetings from a ticket scanner as they entered the gates near the M&T Club, phones up in the air to record their first steps inside. "Welcome to Highmark Stadium!" The event allowed personal seat license (PSL) holders to enjoy their new seats and get the lay of the land. The new stadium brought PSLs to Bills fans for the first time, and as part of the purchasing process, prospective buyers were shown virtual images of what the view from their seats would look like. Previously, the team used a season-ticket model for seats, but it now has transitioned to the PSL model that is common practice in the NFL. Just finding their seats was part of the fun. The navigation included discovering the nearest bathrooms and how steep the walkway to their seats is for those on the upper level. The stadium is nearly double the height of the previous stadium. Getting to the seats wasn't the priority for many, though. The concourses remained full of Allen jerseys and people exploring the new grab-and-go concessions while the heated lamps that thankfully don't need to be used just yet hung overhead. In the new parking lots, the infamous Bills Mafia tailgating experience had already taken shape -- even for a practice. Fans got to experience enlarged parking spots that allow more space for tailgating. "Kim and Terry [Pegula} said from the very beginning they wanted a building that was designed just to watch the game of football," Scott Radecic, former Bills linebacker and founding partner of architecture firm Populous, which designed the stadium. "First, you got the vibrancy of the seats. You got the stacked tiers. It's the closest upper deck in the entire NFL. ... There isn't another stadium in the National Football League where a general mission patron can stand on the field." "Everything about getting that intimacy and intimidation, getting the fans as close to the field as possible," said Jonathan Mallie, global director and managing director of Americas at Populous. As part of the stadium experience, closed captioning was highly visible next to the jumbotrons. But the event also exposed some of the venue's flaws. The sound system was difficult for some fans to hear. Debate over a variety of topics broke out online, including whether the advertised more than 60% of seats covered by the canopy held up in the rain. Many fans spoke highly of the views and experience, but some images have circulated on social media of railings or concrete obstructing views. The Bills said as part of a statement that, "We are currently addressing internal and external feedback regarding the facility's operation following the first event. We'll utilize the next six weeks to refine any details." A source told ESPN that the team has heard from less than 1% of its PSL holders regarding anything sightline related and that some of the seats circulated on social media by The Associated Press are not for sale for football events. 'One chapter ends, another begins' It was the swimming pool that stood out to Joe Andreessen . The Bills linebacker and Lancaster, New York, native has a unique perspective on the stadium change. He saw all sides of the old Highmark Stadium: the fan view and the player perspective. And now, Andreessen is trying to earn a roster spot with a new defensive coaching staff in his third season. As he checked out the facility Saturday, Andreessen's eyes were drawn to one spot in particular. "There's a hot tub, a cold tub, which is pretty standard training room stuff," Andreessen said. "But then there's just like a swimming pool. And I was like, 'Why do we just have a swim pool? That seems a little extra.' And they're like, 'Why not?'" Andreessen echoed what many said, also describing the move as "bittersweet." "I think being able to enjoy the last season at the old stadium and then being able to be a part of the first season at the new stadium is definitely a cool transition to be a part of," Andreessen said. "One chapter ends, another begins."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions OXNARD, Calif. -- The Dallas Cowboys and star defensive tackle Quinnen Williams agreed to a three-year extension worth $105.9 million, sources told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport on Monday. The deal includes $101 million guaranteed with $63.35 million guaranteed at signing, according to sources. Williams also received a signing bonus of $31.85 million, a source said. The $35.3 million annual average is the second highest among defensive tackles. Williams, 28, had been signed through 2027 in a four-year extension worth $96 million that guaranteed him $66 million from the New York Jets in 2023. He is now signed through 2030. The Cowboys acquired Williams from the Jets at last year's trade deadline for a second-round pick in 2026, a 2027 first-rounder and defensive tackle Mazi Smith . In seven games last year following the trade, Williams was credited with 20 tackles, 1.5 sacks, 33 quarterback pressures, two tackles for loss and a pass breakup. For his career, the four-time Pro Bowl selection has 342 tackles with 41.5 sacks, 60 tackles for loss, 134 pressures, 15 pass breakups, eight forced fumbles, three fumble recoveries and two interceptions. He was a first-team All-Pro in 2022 when he posted a career-best 12 sacks for the Jets. Williams is the fourth defensive tackle to agree to a deal averaging more than $30 million per season. The Philadelphia Eagles signed Jalen Carter to a four-year extension worth $152 million ($38 million annually), while Jeffery Simmons of the Tennessee Titans averages $35.2 million and Chris Jones of the Kansas City Chiefs averages $31.75 million. In March 2025, the Cowboys signed Osa Odighizuwa to a four-year, $80 million deal, which had been the largest in team history for a defensive tackle. Odighizuwa was traded to the San Francisco 49ers in the offseason for a third-round pick after the organization did not see him as a fit in defensive coordinator Christian Parker's new scheme. At the start of training camp, executive vice president Stephen Jones said the team wanted to get a long-term extension done with Williams. Williams' agent, Nicole Lynn of Klutch Sports, attended Saturday's practice, spending time with members of the front office. Two days later, a deal was agreed upon. "One, let's talk about what he does on the practice field," Jones said. "I mean he's a great player and he's one of the hardest practicing guys out there. Anytime he lines up, you feel him. He doesn't take anything for granted, doesn't say, 'Hey, I got this.' [It's,] 'Let my play do the talking when we play a game.' You see it. He's the best player on the field whenever he's out there. And so that was a big piece of it. And then the other thing is just what a man he is. He's a leader. We didn't have a lot of leadership on defense for the last couple of years. Now to have him and Kenny Clark and Rashan Gary , I think has really picked it up over there in terms of culture and the leadership." In the past year, the Cowboys have been able to get deals done early with Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith , Pro Bowl kicker Brandon Aubrey , tight end Jake Ferguson , cornerback DaRon Bland and fullback Hunter Luepke .

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print RENTON, Wash. -- Seattle Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said the team has interest in signing Terrion Arnold after meeting with the free agent cornerback over the weekend. Arnold was released by the Detroit Lions , who drafted him in the first round in 2024, in late June, less than a week after he was arrested in Tampa, Florida, on felony charges in connection with a robbery and kidnapping in early February. Seattle brought Arnold to team headquarters Sunday for a meeting that included a workout. It was listed as a tryout on the NFL's transaction wire. Macdonald was asked about the Seahawks' interest in Arnold on Monday. "It's enough right now that we had him in for a great visit, a great tryout," Macdonald said. "It's a situation where there's other things that are surrounding it. We're aware of that. But we're working through the situation right now. But it was a great visit. I really enjoyed meeting him, and I think he enjoyed being here, so we'll see where it goes." Arnold is accused of orchestrating the kidnapping and beating of three men whom prosecutors believe he wrongly suspected of stealing $100,000 in cash from him, along with luxury watches and bags. Arnold, through his representatives, has denied the allegations. He is facing four counts of kidnapping and four counts of armed robbery, which carry a potential sentence of life in prison. No trial date has been set. Arnold, 23, turned himself in to authorities June 24 and was released from custody June 30 after he posted a $1 million bond . Among the conditions ordered by a Hillsborough County (Florida) judge was that Arnold remain confined to his residence in Tallahassee, Florida, except for when he would be playing, training or traveling with the Lions, or making court-related appearances. The Lions announced his release June 29. "We're going to do our due diligence," Macdonald said. "There's a lot of people in Terrion's corner that we respect in terms of [their view of] the type of guy he is. So, we're going to work through all that, and I trust our people to make the best decision for us. We also think this is a great place to come work, too, and that people can be the best versions of themselves when given the opportunity, so it kind of works both ways." The Seahawks had strong interest in Arnold leading up to the 2024 draft, when the former Alabama star was taken 24th by Detroit. Karl Scott, the Seahawks' defensive backs coach and defensive passing game coordinator, recruited Arnold to Alabama while he was the Crimson Tide's DBs coach, though he left the school before Arnold's freshman season. No. 3 quarterback Jalen Milroe is among the current Seahawks who were college teammates with Arnold. "Karl recruited him, to my knowledge, but did not coach him, so it's not as big of a relationship as you might expect, but he's definitely a person that we would talk to," Macdonald said. "Anybody that has any relationship with anybody that we're going to bring in, we're going to seek that counsel." According to the NFL Network, Arnold also had a visit scheduled this week with the New Orleans Saints and previously visited the Houston Texans . After letting Riq Woolen leave in free agency, the Seahawks have Noah Igbinoghene and Nehemiah Pritchett battling for the No. 3 cornerback job behind Devon Witherspoon and Josh Jobe . Rookie third-round pick Julian Neal could enter that mix, but he's working his way back from an undisclosed injury that has sidelined him since early in training camp. "I have a ton of confidence in our defensive backfield room," Macdonald said. "This is a situation of, we're kind of in everything all the time. So we're always trying to make our team the best we can possibly make it. Whether or not Terrion ends up here or not or if it works out or it doesn't, we'll keep on rolling the way we know how." Arnold has one interception and 18 passes defensed in 24 career games. He played in only eight games last season while dealing with a shoulder injury that eventually required surgery. If the Seahawks sign Arnold, it's not clear when his legal situation would allow him to play. "I think we understand that anything is kind of on the table," Macdonald said when asked about Arnold's potential availability, "and that's where we're at in the process." ESPN's Eric Woodyard and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Bridgewater announced that he is retiring from the NFL for the second time Monday, a day after the Detroit Lions placed him on the reserve/retired list. "This time it's official," he wrote in an Instagram post . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Teddy Bridgewater (@teddyb_h2o) Bridgewater, 33, retired after the 2023 season only to return to the Lions late in the following campaign. He served as Baker Mayfield 's backup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2025 and then signed with the Lions in March. His retirement comes 10 years after he suffered a devastating knee injury on a noncontact play in training camp with the Minnesota Vikings that threatened to end his NFL career just two years after it began and one season after he was selected to the Pro Bowl. "It's so crazy 10 years ago around this time, I suffered one of the most gruesome knee injuries the game itself, it's players and some doctors had ever seen. Everything football related since 2016 had been fueled by the 'experts' predicting that I would never play football again," he wrote in his post Monday. "We really showed them by playing 10 more seasons! "However, this wheel of mine can no longer deal with something so simple as standing around on the turf field. This thing just doesn't recover the same way it did years ago so I rather officially hang it up. It's finally run its course and when the body speaks to me, I have to listen so that I can be in one piece and available for my children as they grow up. The game of football was beyond great to me and owes me nothing at all." Bridgewater finishes his NFL career with 15,182 yards passing, 75 touchdown passes and 47 interceptions, having started games for the Vikings (28), who selected him with the No. 32 pick in the 2014 draft; New Orleans Saints (six); Carolina Panthers (15); Denver Broncos (14); and Miami Dolphins (two). Lions coach Dan Campbell praised Bridgewater on Sunday when he announced the veteran quarterback was leaving the team. "I've known Teddy a long time, and the human being is unbelievable. Certainly, the player, everything that he's about. The type of teammate he is, the way he prepares ... always played the game up here and had a huge heart," Campbell said. "He's going to be missed." Before he returned to the NFL in 2024, Bridgewater took the job as the coach of his prep alma mater, Miami Northwestern Senior High School, and led the team led to a Class 3A state championship. However, he was suspended from the job for allegedly providing impermissible benefits to his players. Bridgewater posted on Facebook that he paid for Uber rides, meals and recovery services for his players during the 2024 season and self-reported his activity to the school. His suspension and public backlash to it ultimately led to a new law in Florida . Earlier this year, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the "Teddy Bridgewater Act" into law, allowing high school coaches in the state to use their own money to help their players with expenses such as food, transportation, physical therapy and rehabilitation services. ESPN's Eric Woodyard contributed to this report.

JOSEPH, Mo. -- Eric Bieniemy, the Chiefs' offensive coordinator, returned to the team Monday after a two-week absence following the shooting of his wife, Mia. Bieniemy missed 11 practices after traveling to Virginia to be with his wife, who was allegedly shot by the couple's son at the family's home . Mia Bieniemy, 57, was hospitalized July 26 and has remained in stable condition. "It's good to have EB back," coach Andy Reid said. "He's back in the fold and I don't think he missed a step, man. He was out there and getting after it. That's a positive for the offensive side." "I've talked to him several times a day, so I knew he was coming back if everything worked out the way he had been. The primary thing is that Mia is stable and in good hands and she's doing well." A few days after the shooting, Reid shared that Mia Bieniemy was released from the intensive care unit. Police in Loudoun County, Virginia, confirmed that a woman was being treated for "serious injuries" from multiple gunshot wounds but did not disclose her identity. Elijah Zion Bieniemy, 27, was arrested and charged July 27 with malicious wounding, use of a firearm in commission of a felony and discharge of a firearm inside of a dwelling, according to the Loudoun County Sheriff's Office. Sources told ESPN that Mia Bieniemy was shot in the chest and arm. Elijah Bieniemy is being held without bond at a detention center in Loudoun County. During Eric Bieniemy's absence, pass game coordinator Joe Bleymaier took over the offensive coordinator's duties. But Bieniemy remained in communication with the Chiefs. He was able to watch last week's practices via a live stream to take notes and to deliver messages back, and he called general manager Brett Veach to send a coaching tip to Reid for rookie running back Emmett Johnson . "That's the thing that is so refreshing to have back, to have that attention to detail," Veach said Thursday of Bieniemy, who rejoined the team after a previous stint as offensive coordinator from 2018 to 2022. "He demands that each player knows his assignment, and there's never a safe space with him." Bieniemy had his usual one-on-one coaching moments during Monday's practice, including the pass-blocking drill for the running backs. The entire group of offensive linemen greeted Bieniemy -- each one shaking his hand. "He's a great guy and very vocal," left guard Kingsley Suamataia said of Bieniemy. "He pushes us to our limits every day so we can be the best offense out there. It's been great."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart slid after a third-down run during Monday's practice. It's likely not something he would have done during his rookie year, when his unwillingness to get down possibly contributed to being examined on five different occasions for a concussion. The slide at practice drew quite the reaction, specifically from the Giants' defense. Dart slid near the sideline on which the defense was standing. "We've been begging him to do that for a while," Giants outside linebacker and defensive captain Brian Burns said. "So, I'm glad that he's starting to practice it." Coach John Harbaugh seemed to love it, as well. "I did," he said. "I clapped. I applauded. I applauded when he did that. It was great." It's notable after Dart was somewhat defiant last season about sliding or running out of bounds to avoid the big hit. The reckless style of play became a talking point that often overshadowed his accomplishments on the field. Coming out of Ole Miss, Dart was critiqued for his unwillingness to slide. On a Barstool Sports podcast, former NFL coach Jon Gruden predicted Dart would be in the blue medical tent often, getting checked for a concussion, if his approach wasn't modified. It wasn't, and that's exactly what happened, on a fairly regular basis, during his rookie season with the Giants. This is the latest evidence that perhaps some changes have been made. Dart said that during his first meeting with new quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan earlier this year, they watched tape of certain plays and discussed the risk. It seemed to resonate. "The most important thing I learned is I've got to be on the field," Dart said during a Giants Town Hall to fans in May. Dart said that on third and fourth down, and near the red zone, he would still try to run over defenders. But in other situations, such as first and second downs and early in games, he would reconsider. The situation in Monday's practice was one of those that demanded a slide. "Critical-situation drill. We were trying to get down a third or fourth down, but mostly third down, anywhere from 3 to 5 [yards] in a game where the offense can win the game in the fourth quarter with a conversion," Harbaugh said. "And so play calls and execution to get that first down, that is what that was. So we had a great play. It came open. He ran around the corner, got the first down, slid inbounds, kept the clock running. All those things were well done." The defense immediately erupted with some whooping and hollering. They know how important it is for Dart to learn when the right time is to slide or try to run over the defender. They need him on the field for the Giants to win games. This was the first time in 11 practices during training camp that Dart has slid. "As you can see, all the guys, the defensive players, were happy that he slid on that one play," wide receiver Darnell Mooney said. "So, he's being smart and, you know, he has his legs as well. So, all-around, great quarterback." Dart's mobility is a big part of his arsenal. He had nine rushing touchdowns last year, second most of any rookie quarterback in the modern era behind Cam Newton. Dart's 487 rushing yards were third most by a quarterback last season. But Dart was also regularly off the field, and the Giants won just four games. He officially suffered one concussion during his rookie season.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ALLEN PARK, Mich. -- Detroit Lions center Cade Mays suffered a wrist injury during a recent training camp practice and will miss a "significant period of time," according to head coach Dan Campbell. A source told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport that Mays fractured a small bone in his wrist that is expected to sideline him roughly eight to 10 weeks. Campbell wouldn't offer a timeline on Mays' return when he spoke to reporters but joked that "he'll be ready for the playoffs." Campbell also announced that Lions running back Isiah Pacheco is dealing with an MCL sprain and will miss some time. Campbell said he expects Pacheco to return before Detroit's Week 1 home contest against the New Orleans Saints and that he's "not concerned" about the injury. "Of course, you hate it. I hate it for him because I felt like he was having a good camp and he had grown so much in our system just since spring," Campbell said of Mays' injury. "In that regard, yeah, and for us, too, but at the same time, there, again, there's a reason why we have Juice [Scruggs ] here, too, and some of these other guys and they're going to get a look." This is a significant blow for the team as Mays was targeted in the offseason as an unrestricted free agent to help the unit after the Lions' offensive line struggled last season. He spent his first four seasons with the Carolina Panthers as a sixth-round selection in the 2022 NFL draft out of Tennessee. His 94.3% pass block win rate ranked 20th among qualified centers last season, while allowing just one sack. Without Mays, the Lions are expected to try Scruggs, Seth McLaughlin and Michael Niese at center as they attempt to find the best fit at the position before the season opener against New Orleans on Sept. 13. "Look, we're going to find the best five," Campbell said of the offensive line. "We will [identify] the best five and we're trying to find that before camp starts, but look, if this goes into the season it does, but at some point, we will find the best five and where they belong and they'll be ready."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- The Buffalo Bills have responded to a group of fans expressing some frustration with sightlines from certain areas of the team's new Highmark Stadium. The Bills hosted the first public event at the stadium Saturday night with the annual "Return of the Blue & Red" training camp practice. Personal seat license (PSL) owners were able to sit in their new seats for the first time. Posts from certain seats that either have portions of the stadium or elements of the stairways blocking part of view have gained traction on social media. The Bills said in a statement, "Thank you to Bills Mafia for setting a new attendance record with more than 50,000 fans at the Return of the Blue & Red. Saturday's practice was a great opportunity to test the new stadium. We are currently addressing internal and external feedback regarding the facility's operation following the first event. We'll utilize the next six weeks to refine any details as we prepare for the home opener on Thursday, September 17." A source told ESPN that the team has heard from "less than 1% of PSL holders" regarding any sightline issues at the stadium. The source added that some of the photos that are circulating show views from seats that are not for sale for football events. The team is planning to hold a variety of events at the stadium in the future. The team announced 51,807 fans were in attendance for the practice (capacity is 60,108). The Bills will host two preseason games and another open practice at the venue this month.

(1:12) Eric Karabell Aug 6, 2026, 06:29 AM ET Close Eric Karabell is a senior writer covering fantasy football, baseball and basketball at ESPN. Eric is a charter member of the FSWA Hall of Fame, a BBWAA baseball Hall of Fame voter and author of "The Best Philadelphia Sports Arguments." Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions The New York Giants , anything but a juggernaut NFL offense since the Eli Manning days, seem to have built something quite intriguing and potentially magical with QB Jaxson Dart , RB Cam Skattebo and WR Malik Nabers . The problem is that those young players -- two of them NFL first-round selections -- were barely on the field together last season (18 snaps), and those concerns continue in 2026. This is also the problem for fantasy managers considering early investment. We crave availability and covet statistics, but these promising Giants are question marks for the former and thus no lock to produce the latter. It seems trite, but availability really is the best ability. We don't get asterisks for missing the fantasy playoffs because potentially great players missed several games. Such is the risk that comes with securing these otherwise talented players, and because this is one of the NFL's higher-profile teams in its largest city (well, pretend it is New York City and not East Rutherford, New Jersey), value often becomes distorted. Nabers, the LSU product who dominated his rookie season (catching 109 passes for 1,204 yards and seven touchdowns), played only four games last season. He is the biggest question mark as he recovers from multiple surgeries on his right knee. His status for September action is still uncertain. Uncertain is a big problem for fantasy football, and as we welcome everyone to yet another NFL season and the latest (and often misunderstood) "Do Not Draft" list, the caveats in place bear remembering. Value is the key for fantasy drafts, especially in relation to average draft position (ADP) and expected statistical production. Few wide receivers offer the upside of Nabers, while Dart and Skattebo appear special as well. We all see it. The question is whether they are potentially special enough for this fantasy football season to warrant their lofty ADPs. It is a tough case to make. Nabers was seriously injured in Week 4 last season, suffering ACL and meniscus tears, and ordinarily, there would be relative confidence in him returning to full strength before the start of the following season. However, Nabers needed a follow-up procedure in the spring to remove scar tissue. The Giants have said the right things, claiming patience and optimism for a full recovery, but rumors of Nabers missing time at the beginning of the season still persist, even though he did not begin training camp on the PUP list. The Giants were noticeably active this offseason in adding depth to their wide receiver group. Judging Nabers as a top-10 fantasy wide receiver -- which was his initial ADP until recently, and it hasn't fallen far -- is dangerous. If one cannot properly define what someone's ADP should be, that's a decent indicator it shouldn't be too high. There is major risk with Nabers. The statistical upside we saw two seasons ago is immense. It isn't as immense, broadly speaking, for Zay Flowers of the Baltimore Ravens , Davante Adams of the Los Angeles Rams , Ladd McConkey of the Los Angeles Chargers or Denver Broncos newcomer Jaylen Waddle , among many other WRs expected or hoped to be WR2 options, but safety and security matter, too. With Dart and Skattebo, the upside is similarly inspiring, but these fellows must be out there on the field to achieve it. Dart, a late-first-round NFL draft selection in 2025, started 12 games, showing far more promise as a runner than as a pure passer. He missed multiple games with a concussion, and his occasionally reckless style makes him a prime candidate for more missed games. Quarterback is a deep position in traditional 10- and 12-team leagues. Perhaps the upside of Dart is worth it, but few could argue that Chargers starter Justin Herbert , among several examples, isn't safer. Speaking of recklessness, Skattebo, chosen in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL draft, became a fantasy star quite quickly, ramming into and through overmatched defenders to score seven touchdowns in eight games. He sure had the look of an RB1 option with high volume. Then it ended in Week 8 with a dislocated ankle. Skattebo might be a star, just like his offensive teammates. The pieces are in place for the Giants. It seems so obvious. Keeping everyone -- anyone? -- healthy is another matter. Then again, very few want to see backup QB Jameis Winston handing footballs off to Tyrone Tracy Jr . and Devin Singletary and throwing downfield to Darnell Mooney and Darius Slayton . Few offenses feature as much boom-or-bust injury potential. Here are other players I keep ignoring in myriad -- and I mean myriad -- mock drafts and real leagues this summer. Remember, none of this means Nabers will not be a productive player, just that the value in drafts is off. The Do Not Draft list is about fading players in relation to (over)popularity . Let's go! Quarterback Keeping with tradition in this space, Buffalo Bills star Josh Allen again gets featured because he tends to be the first QB off the fantasy draft board. Allen has finished among the top two QBs in fantasy scoring for six consecutive seasons. Nobody can match his production and durability. He is awesome! Still, is that worth a second-round pick in standard fantasy leagues (10 teams, one active QB)? I can't do it. The position is deep; opportunity cost matters. Give me all the productive RBs and WRs early, and one of several productive QBs much later. Sorry, Josh. It isn't you. It's me (and in this case, it is true). Drake Maye of the New England Patriots launched himself into stardom with 4,394 passing yards, 31 passing touchdowns, 450 rushing yards and four rushing touchdowns. Only Allen scored more fantasy points among QBs. Maye is 23. What about him could possibly scare us? Check New England's schedule. Maye didn't face a top-10 defense during the regular season. He will face a bunch of them this season. Expect production, but a repeat of 350 fantasy points? I'm fading top QBs anyway, and this great one stands out -- but perhaps only for this season. The Washington Commanders ' Jayden Daniels could not replicate his stunning rookie season in which he was a top-five fantasy QB. He played in only seven games last season, succumbing to injuries to a knee, wrist, hamstring and elbow. We love the running QBs when they are playing. Daniels, much like Dart with his immense tools, possesses a seemingly unlimited statistical ceiling, but the injury risk is real. Always beware of the rookies. Las Vegas Raiders building block Fernando Mendoza , the No. 1 pick in the NFL draft, might be a fantasy star in September if he pushes aside Kirk Cousins , or he might sit for months. He has little place in a standard fantasy draft (one QB, 10 teams) this season. For deeper formats, perhaps Indianapolis Colts reclamation project Daniel Jones really is recovered from a torn Achilles, but we cannot expect pristine efficiency or rushing touchdowns come September. Many fantasy managers overrate Green Bay Packers starter Jordan Love . There's a reason the Packers limit his passing attempts to fewer than 30 per game. Don't assume this will change. Love's low volume -- he doesn't run much, either -- limits him in fantasy. Do not speculate on the Cleveland Browns ' passers in fantasy. It's just not worth it. Running back San Francisco 49ers star Christian McCaffrey won Comeback Player of the Year honors, playing in all 17 games and easily leading the sport with more than 400 fantasy points. Congrats to him and those who invested! I didn't expect that, so I missed out. It was almost like the 49ers rostered McCaffrey in fantasy and were intent on him carrying their teams. It was wild. McCaffrey consumed more than 900 snaps and 400 touches, and I am going nowhere near him again in 2026. Running backs are mortal, especially this one who has demoralized fantasy managers in multiple seasons. Running backs cannot handle workloads to this degree in consecutive seasons. In fact, since 2000, there have been 13 instances of a running back logging 400 carries in a season (including playoffs), and none was among the top 10 RBs the next season. Saquon Barkley failed in 2025 (we were right about him, at least). This is a telling stat. McCaffrey, now 30, played all the games last season. It hardly means he can repeat the achievement. The 49ers will be far more cautious. New Kansas City Chiefs starter Kenneth Walker III comes off being named the Super Bowl MVP with the Seattle Seahawks , and most everyone presumes his best seasons are pending. Perhaps, but the Seahawks knew what they had in Walker, and he never finished better than 15th at RB in fantasy scoring during his four seasons. Even last season, Walker ranked 20th in rushing attempts as the Seahawks aimed to avoid injury until leaning on him in January. The Chiefs seem unlikely to make Walker a major part of the passing game. This one is about value: Walker in the third round is a bit much, at least for me. Los Angeles Rams backup Blake Corum averaged 5.1 yards per carry in his second NFL season. Starter Kyren Williams , with double-digit rushing touchdowns in each of the past three seasons, is going early in Round 5 in ESPN leagues. Perhaps Williams can sustain his production even as Corum continues to ascend, but it is likely Williams will take a statistical step back. Be careful about assuming Williams is a safe RB2 option again. Tampa Bay Buccaneers starter Bucky Irving starred as a rookie. His second season looked quite different. It is easy to blame it all on a shoulder injury that cost him nearly two months, but Irving rushed for one touchdown in 10 games, averaging 3.4 yards per rush. The Buccaneers signed Kenny Gainwell , an accomplished pass catcher (73 receptions in 2025!) who averaged 4.7 yards per rush with the Steelers. One can reasonably debate whether Gainwell simply outscores Irving this season, making Irving's sixth-round ADP while Gainwell goes in Round 13 feel silly. TreVeyon Henderson of the Patriots enters his second season with fantasy managers craving investment, even though productive veteran Rhamondre Stevenson remains very much involved in the offense. In fact, Stevenson, a power runner who can pass block, was the team's preferred choice during its January playoff run. As with Tampa Bay's Irving, this doesn't mean Henderson will disappoint in fantasy, but volume is critical in player evaluation, and it sure seems like the Patriots will share it in their backfield. Stevenson is the value pick multiple rounds after Henderson. I don't think we can assume that the Carolina Panthers will give Jonathon Brooks major volume, as the 2024 second-round pick barely played his first two seasons as he recovered from multiple knee tears, but there is enough doubt to worry about Chuba Hubbard being a safe RB3. Perhaps fading both of them is the play. New Orleans Saints acquisition Travis Etienne Jr . comes off his best season, but we must be wary of volume concerns. Alvin Kamara , one of the top pass-receiving RBs ever, is still here, and he caught 68 passes in 14 games two seasons ago. Etienne is not productive as a goal-line runner, and he is not catching six TDs again (he caught one in his first three seasons). I don't see a safe RB2 here. Tennessee Titans starter Tony Pollard will likely fall short of his fifth consecutive 1,000-yard rushing season. He's neither terribly efficient nor much of a pass catcher, and the Titans must do better. Again, perhaps Pollard is merely your flex option, but I'd prefer to aim higher. Wide receiver Chiefs starter Rashee Rice is more than an injury risk. He is a "games" risk. Rice has played in only 12 games the past two seasons, with injury and suspension derailing him, and if we must guess which narrative is a bigger problem moving forward, that is quite telling. Rice spent a month of his offseason knee surgery recovery in jail. When he is on the field, Rice is a statistical star, but we cannot presume anything close to 17 games considering his history. This is an unreliable player for you to use your second or third pick on. Perhaps you heard the news! The Patriots acquired former Philadelphia Eagles star A.J. Brown to be the No. 1 WR the offense lacked. I dunno, it was rarely discussed this offseason. Choose your reason for why Brown looked to be in decline last season other than a target-forced three-game stretch in November. He wasn't happy in Philadelphia. He might not be happy facing a tough schedule with the Patriots that is littered with shutdown cornerbacks. Draft Brown, of course, but not among the top 10 fantasy WRs. Arizona Cardinals disappointment Marvin Harrison Jr . might blossom one of these seasons, but we must stop blaming the organization or his quarterbacks for his ordinary numbers. Some still invest in Harrison because he was the No. 4 pick in the 2024 draft, and how can anyone with that pedigree not be truly awesome? Well, we are seeing it. Draft Harrison, but not as a definite WR2. If you must guess which Jacksonville Jaguars WR is going to be the most relevant -- three or four of them go in similar, albeit potentially bargain, ADP range -- that's usually a strong indicator to avoid them all. So I will. Especially the one who might play more snaps on defense. Rookie WRs look good on fantasy draft day in comparison to boring, uninspiring veterans because they haven't failed yet. College football games are different -- here's how Ohio State Buckeyes 6d Bill Connelly and Adam Rittenberg play Roddy Jones: Bet against UCLA coach Bob Chesney at your own peril (0:31) Paolo Uggetti Aug 10, 2026, 08:44 PM ET Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions UCLA is adding former Raiders and Saints quarterback Derek Carr as a special adviser to coach Bob Chesney, the team announced Monday. Carr, who spent 11 seasons in the NFL and earned four Pro Bowl selections, will assist Chesney and the Bruins' offensive staff with game-planning strategy while also working with UCLA's quarterbacks in a volunteer role. Carr announced his retirement from the NFL in May 2025. "We are excited to welcome Derek to our program," Chesney said in a news release. "He has played the quarterback position at a high level for more than a decade, and his experience, leadership and football knowledge will be an incredible resource for our coaching staff and student-athletes. What stands out most is his passion for the game and his commitment to developing young people. Derek will have a tremendous impact on our players and is a great addition to our program." While at Fresno State from 2009 to 2013, Carr overlapped with UCLA general manager Darrick Yray, who is in his first season with the Bruins. Yray spent four years as an offensive assistant and three as assistant director of football operations with the Bulldogs from 2008 to 2014. "I've known Darrick for a long time and have great respect for the work he's done throughout his career," Carr said. "The opportunity to help Coach Chesney, the staff and the quarterbacks at UCLA was one that really excited me. I'm looking forward to sharing my experiences and helping support the program in any way I can." Chesney is entering his first season as UCLA's coach following a 21-6 record in two seasons at James Madison as well as a Sun Belt title and an appearance in the College Football Playoff last season.
