He analyzes football on and off the field like no one else on the planet, writing about in-season X's and O's, offseason transactions and so much more. He is the host of the Bill Barnwell Show podcast , with episodes released weekly. Barnwell joined ESPN in 2011 as a staff writer at Grantland. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions The 2026 Rams are the closest thing we've had to a preseason superteam in several years. Sean McVay's group was already a popular pick to win Super Bowl LXI before the offseason began. But then L.A. traded for Trent McDuffie and signed Jaylen Watson , shoring up the secondary at the expense of a potential Super Bowl opponent in the Chiefs. The move to draft Ty Simpson as Matthew Stafford 's successor struck a curious tone, but general manager Les Snead responded with the mother of all high-stakes moves, trading Jared Verse and three picks to the Browns for reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett . Unsurprisingly, the Rams have become prohibitive favorites to win the Super Bowl after their aggressive moves this offseason. Picking any other team to win the Lombardi Trophy at this point would almost require coming up with some sort of explanation for what happened to the Rams along the way. And yet, we have to look back only one year to remind ourselves how NFL seasons can play out entirely differently once players get on the field. In 2025, 68 ESPN personalities picked their AFC and NFC champions, along with an eventual Super Bowl winner, before the season kicked off. Not a single person picked the Seahawks or Patriots. I predicted the Chiefs and Packers , who combined for exactly zero playoff wins. Preseason darlings like the Chiefs, Lions and Commanders each missed the playoffs altogether. Was 2025 just a weird year? And how often do heavily favorited superteams such as the 2026 Rams actually win the Super Bowl? I decided to take a more comprehensive look through history to get a sense of how confident we can be that Los Angeles will be the last team standing come Feb. 14 . Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' To do so, I'm going to look at the 15 largest preseason favorites since 1990 and see how their seasons played out. I'll be using the preseason odds compiled at Pro Football Reference from 1990 to 2025 and compare them with the odds posted for this season's Super Bowl at DraftKings . The Rams have odds of +550 at DraftKings to win the Super Bowl, while nobody else in the league is shorter than +1000. After we adjust for the vigorish and convert the betting lines into probabilities, the Rams have an implied 12.5% chance of winning this season's Super Bowl, putting them 5.1 percentage points ahead of the second-placed Bills and Ravens. While the absolute number might be a better sense of how the market views a particular team, I'm going to use the latter figure to sort through our top 15 teams (well, 16, if we're including the 2026 Rams). There were plenty of seasons in the 1990s where two or three superteams -- such as the 49ers and Cowboys -- were seen as significantly better than the rest of the competition. I want to get a sense of what it was like for the teams that truly separated from the pack before the season began, as appears to be the case for this Rams squad. Did those teams hold up to their preseason expectations? Was the market overconfident about their chances? Let's go team by team before using the lessons from those 15 earlier cases to talk about what it means for the 2026 Rams and their chances of winning McVay and Stafford their second title. Jump to: 2026 Rams | 2021 Chiefs | 2019 Patriots 2018 Patriots | 2017 Patriots | 2009 Patriots 2008 Patriots | 2007 Patriots | 2002 Rams 2001 Rams | 1998 Packers | 1997 Packers 1996 49ers | 1995 49ers | 1994 49ers | 1990 49ers Can this season's Rams win the Super Bowl? 2017 New England Patriots Implied odds: 19.8% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 11.5% Result: Lost Super Bowl LII to the Eagles, 41-33 I wouldn't have guessed that the 2017 Patriots stood out in terms of Super Bowl odds more than any other New England team from the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick era, but let's contextualize this. The Pats were coming off that legendary 34-28 win over the Falcons in Super Bowl LI . Brady was getting Rob Gronkowski back from injury after the star tight end missed the playoff run with a back ailment , while Belichick added a new star receiver to the mix in Brandin Cooks . After a 14-2 season and with Brady motivated by the four-game suspension he took for the Deflategate scandal, you could understand why the Patriots were heavy favorites to repeat as champs. Some things went as expected. Brady won the league MVP award. Cooks and Gronkowski each topped 1,000 yards. The Pats went 13-3 and took home the top seed in the AFC. Others did not. Belichick's team started 2-2 and needed a last-minute comeback win over a 4-12 Texans team to avoid opening the season 1-3. The Pats righted the ship quickly, but they were trailing by 10 points in the fourth quarter of the AFC title game and were down nearly three scores to the Jaguars, only for Myles Jack 's fumble recovery touchdown to be overturned. Two late touchdown passes to Danny Amendola controversially pushed the Pats into the Super Bowl. There, well, nothing went as planned. The Patriots defense had quietly been a mess all year, finishing the regular season ranked 31st in DVOA. The offense covered up the weakness by holding on to the ball and getting out to early leads. The Eagles were heavy underdogs with backup quarterback Nick Foles in for the injured Carson Wentz , and you know what happened next. Brady threw for 505 yards and three touchdowns, still the record for an NFL quarterback in a losing effort, but the defense couldn't stop Foles & Co. The Pats fell 41-33. 2007 New England Patriots Implied odds: 20.9% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 10.5% Result: Lost Super Bowl XLII to the Giants, 17-14 Are you sensing a trend? This was another Patriots team that rode offseason optimism about its offensive additions to high hopes before falling short in the Super Bowl. The 2006 Pats had blown a 21-3 lead to the Colts in the AFC Championship Game , but they also weren't far removed from winning three titles between 2001 and 2004. Brady had improved as a quarterback over that time, and during the offseason, Belichick had rebuilt the offense by trading for Randy Moss and Wes Welker and signing Donte' Stallworth. What happened next is one of the more notable seasons in NFL history. The Pats were caught spying on the Jets during a 38-14 blowout victory in Week 1, turning a team that had been the underdog favorites during their win over the Rams in 2001 into the villains of the NFL. On the field, the Patriots blew defenses away with their spread attack, as Brady produced arguably the greatest season in league history under center. The Patriots went 16-0 in the regular season, winning their average game by nearly 20 points. By the time the postseason came around, though, the cracks were beginning to show. Brady threw three picks in the AFC title game , but with Philip Rivers playing through a torn ACL and LaDainian Tomlinson limited by injury to three touches, the Chargers couldn't take advantage in a 21-12 defeat. And in the Super Bowl, again as heavy favorites, the Patriots were upset by a Giants team that was able to control Brady in the pocket with its pass rush. 1996 San Francisco 49ers Implied odds: 19.2% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 9.6% Result: Lost in divisional round to the Packers, 35-14 The 49ers were the preseason favorites to win the Super Bowl in 1994, 1995 and 1996. Their status as the third team on this list might have more to do with a lack of competition in the AFC than anything else. The Bills were among the Super Bowl favorites earlier in the decade, but after a 7-9 season in 1994 and a 10-6 campaign in 1995, they had fallen back to the pack. The Steelers had advanced to the Super Bowl the prior season, but starting quarterback Neil O'Donnell had signed with the Jets in free agency, turning things over to 34-year-old Mike Tomczak as the team's starter. And while the Chiefs were coming off a 13-win season, they had relied on a career year from journeyman QB Steve Bono and lost 10-7 to the Colts in the wild-card round. While there was no sure thing in the AFC, the 49ers seemed like the reliable option in the NFC. Though they had been bounced by the Packers in the divisional round the year before, George Seifert's team had won the Super Bowl in 1994. If the 49ers could make it past the Cowboys, who were the defending champs, they felt like an easy pick to win a Super Bowl against a random AFC opponent. Well, the good news is they never needed to worry about the Cowboys, who went 10-6 and lost to the Panthers in the playoffs in Barry Switzer's third year in charge. The team the 49ers did need to worry about, though, was the one that had beaten them the year before. The Packers beat their rivals in overtime during the regular season, which ended up giving Green Bay home-field advantage in the postseason. And when the two teams had a rematch at Lambeau in the NFC title game, Steve Young was already dealing with two broken ribs. The 49ers starter lasted two series, and after a Desmond Howard punt return opened the scoring, the Pack never looked back. Mike Holmgren's team won handily and then beat the Patriots by 14 points in the Super Bowl. We're 0-for-3 on favorites taking home the hardware. 2002 St. Louis Rams Implied odds: 15.7% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 7.8% Result: Missed playoffs Make that 0-for-4. Though Brady and the Patriots had upset the Rams in the prior year's Super Bowl , the Rams were easy favorites to return to the title game the following year. St. Louis was returning reigning MVP Kurt Warner and all of his key playmakers. Lovie Smith's defense had finished seventh in points allowed the prior season, leaving the "Greatest Show on Turf" with an expectation of dominance on both sides of the football. That never came together, in part because of injuries. Warner played only seven games and was uncharacteristically poor when he was on the field, throwing 11 picks to just three touchdowns. DB Aeneas Williams and OT Orlando Pace -- All-Pros the prior year -- combined to miss 16 games. Marshall Faulk, who had finished second to Warner in MVP voting in 2001, lost nearly a full yard per carry off the previous year's figure and never topped 1,000 rushing yards again. The Rams posted a minus-19 turnover margin and went 7-9, missing the playoffs entirely. 2009 New England Patriots Implied odds: 18.2% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 7.1% Result: Lost in wild-card round to the Ravens, 33-14 These have to be the shortest odds for a team that hadn't even made it to the postseason the prior year, but there's an easy explanation. The 2008 Patriots, who we'll get to in a minute, had lost Tom Brady to a torn ACL in Week 1. Though that team ended up missing the playoffs, this felt like an opportunity to get another shot on backing a team that had come within one Asante Samuel interception of a perfect year in 2007. While Brady was back and won Comeback Player of the Year, the legendary quarterback wasn't his usual self. Several key players from the 2007 defense were no longer on the roster, and Belichick wasn't able to coax the same sort of magic out of their replacements. The Pats went 10-6, losing Welker to a torn ACL during the final game of the season. New England still won the division and hosted the Ravens in the wild-card round, but running back Ray Rice scored an 83-yard touchdown on the first offensive snap of the game, Brady was strip-sacked to set up another short field, and the Ravens were up 24-0 before the end of the first quarter. The Pats got within two scores by the end of the third quarter, but a comeback wasn't in the cards. 1997 Green Bay Packers Implied odds: 18% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 6.5% Result: Lost in Super Bowl XXXII to the Broncos, 31-24 Well, this one is simple, right? The Packers had steadily worked their way up the ranks in the NFC, dethroning the 49ers before finally winning the Super Bowl against the Patriots the year before. Brett Favre was in the prime of his career and coming off back-to-back MVP trophies. Nobody in the NFC Central had been within three games of the Pack the prior year, and while the Cowboys had beaten Green Bay six times over the prior three seasons, there were questions about whether the Dallas dynasty was fading. As it turned out, the Cowboys weren't a threat, as they fell to 6-10 in Switzer's final year as coach. Favre won his third consecutive MVP award, splitting the honors with Barry Sanders. The Packers lost the top spot in the NFC to the 49ers on a tiebreaker, but Favre & Co. beat the Niners at Candlestick in the conference championship game, holding Young and the 49ers offense without a touchdown in the process. The favorites in the AFC were the Broncos, though, and while there might have been some skeptics unwilling to back a team that had lost three times in the Super Bowl with John Elway under center, Denver turned out to be the best team in football. The Broncos led the league in scoring, blew out the Jaguars and then beat the rival Chiefs with their run game at Arrowhead. Terrell Davis outran Jerome Bettis and the Steelers defense in the AFC title game , and while the Packers were 11-point favorites in the Super Bowl, a 157-yard, three-touchdown performance from Davis and a legendary "helicopter" run from Elway were enough to get the legendary quarterback his first title. 1990 San Francisco 49ers Implied odds: 14.3% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 6.3% Result: Lost in NFC Championship Game to the Giants, 15-13 One of those Broncos losses in the Super Bowl with Elway had come to these 49ers the prior year, with Joe Montana throwing for five touchdowns in a 55-10 shellacking. In some of the final seasons before the salary cap truly changed football, the 49ers were able to bring back an absolutely stacked roster and were blessed with Hall of Famers on both sides of the football. They were attempting to become the first team to successfully win three consecutive Super Bowls and were heavy favorites to pull it off. And for most of the year, the odds felt prescient. The 49ers started 10-0 before losing to the Rams, but a 7-3 win over the Giants helped lock up home-field advantage through the postseason. Montana's 8-1 record at home in the playoffs suggested that nobody was going to have much hope of beating the 49ers before the Super Bowl. The Giants, who were starting career backup Jeff Hostetler as eight-point underdogs at Candlestick, took that personally. They brutalized Montana, who eventually left the game with a bevy of injuries. Hostetler and the offense didn't score a touchdown, but with the 49ers trying to run the clock out, a Roger Craig fumble with three minutes to go handed the Giants a short field. Matt Bahr's fifth field goal of the game gave Bill Parcells' team a 15-13 victory before going on to beat the Bills on a missed field goal by Scott Norwood in the subsequent Super Bowl . 2008 New England Patriots Implied odds: 16.1% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 5.8% Result: Missed playoffs The 2008 Patriots understandably had better raw odds to win the Super Bowl than their 2009 brethren, but they didn't enjoy as significant of a gap with the rest of the field. This team was coming off the 17-0 campaign, and their hopes were immediately dashed by Brady's ACL tear in the season opener. Unheralded backup Matt Cassel took over and won 11 games, but for the first and only time in the 12-playoff team era, those 11 wins weren't enough for the Pats to make it to the postseason. Our search continues. 2026 Los Angeles Rams Implied odds: 12.5% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 5.1% Result: TBD Well, if you're a Rams fan, this might be a little worrying. Every single team that was projected to be more dominant versus the rest of the competition than the 2026 Rams failed to win the Super Bowl. Some made it to the title game and came very close to winning, of course, but we're currently 0-for-8. More on this season's Rams in a bit ... play 1:36 Andrew Hawkins: Donald return could make Rams an all-time great defense 1995 San Francisco 49ers Implied odds: 19.3% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 4.8% Result: Lost in divisional round to the Packers, 27-17 After going up 42-10 in the prior year's Super Bowl against the Chargers before winning by 23 points, you can understand why the 49ers were heavy favorites again in 1995. While the Niners had lost Deion Sanders to the rival Cowboys after one season in San Francisco, Dallas was stuck in an often-difficult NFC East. The 49ers were the kings of the NFC West, where no other team had posted a winning record in 1994. The 1995 49ers faced a new problem for our superteams: They were unlucky. While they had the point differential of a 12.7-win team, the Niners won only 11 games, the product of a 2-5 record in games decided by seven points or less. Though they managed to beat the Cowboys and were in position to clinch home-field advantage in the NFC during the final week of the season, they lost 28-27 to a Falcons team that relied on backup quarterback Bobby Hebert for most of the game. The loss dropped the 49ers to the second seed, so while they got a first-round bye, their opponents in Round 2 were the third-seeded Packers and soon-to-be MVP Favre. The 49ers couldn't stop Favre, who threw for 299 yards and two touchdowns. For all its experience and playoff savviness, San Francisco turned the ball over four times in a 27-17 defeat. 2021 Kansas City Chiefs Implied odds: 15.1% Gap to the rest of the NFL: 4.7% Result: Lost in AFC Championship Game to the Bengals, 27-24 It's our first Chiefs team from the Patrick Mahomes era. While Kansas City had lost to Brady and Tampa Bay in the prior year's Super Bowl , the Chiefs returned many of the key players from a 14-2 team that had been perpetually competing for a Super Bowl from the moment Mahomes took over as the full-time starter in 2018. The only other AFC team in the top six of that year's Super Bowl odds were the Bills, who couldn't seem to get past Mahomes when things mattered most. This wasn't a dominant Chiefs team. It was badly blown out 38-20 by the Bills early in the season, then finished October with a losing record at 3-4. Of course, from that point forward, the Chiefs won 11 of their next 13 games, including a legendary shootout with the Bills in the divisional round . The two losses were to the same team. The Bengals were nobody's idea of a Super Bowl contender given that they had gone 4-11-1 and lost Joe Burrow to a torn ACL the prior season, but the addition of Ja'Marr Chase and significant investments on the defensive side of the ball quickly turned things around. The Bengals started 7-6, but they began to believe after beating the Chiefs in a 34-31 barn burner late in the season. And while the Chiefs went up 21-3 on the Bengals in their conference championship rematch, a midgame gambit by defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo to drop eight into coverage flummoxed Mahomes and the Chiefs offense. Cincinnati scored the next 21 points to take the lead, and while Mahomes got the Chiefs in position to tie the game, he nearly blew the contest by taking an awful strip sack before the tying kick. A Mahomes interception in overtime handed the ball back to the Bengals, and an Evan McPherson field goal ended Kansas City's hopes. Archer has covered the NFL since 1997 and Dallas since 2003. He joined ESPN in 2010. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions OXNARD, Calif. -- The Dallas Cowboys have rediscovered the formula they used in the past regarding contract extensions for their key players. The three-year, $105.9 million extension agreed to Monday by Pro Bowl defensive tackle Quinnen Williams -- with an annual average of $35.3 million that is second highest among defensive tackles -- is yet another sign. The George Pickens contract situation ( franchise tagged for 2026 ) not withstanding, in the past 12 months the Cowboys have made Pro Bowl guard Tyler Smith the highest paid interior offensive lineman (subsequently passed by the Raiders' Tyler Linderbaum and Falcons' Chris Lindstrom ) at $24 million per season and Pro Bowl kicker Brandon Aubrey the highest paid ($7 million) at his position. They have also kept key players away from unrestricted free agency, including tight end Jake Ferguson and cornerback DaRon Bland , who signed deals that made each of them the eighth-highest paid player at their positions. Ferguson's deal averages $12.5 million a season, and Bland's checks in at $22.5 million. Add defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa to that list after he signed a four-year, $80 million contract in March 2025, though he was traded to the San Francisco 49ers before the draft. "Every deal's different. You just hit certain bumps in the road where things don't [work out]," executive vice president Stephen Jones said. "It's not because we don't want to. It's just getting the right deal for what we think, for the organization. I think that's the important part. "Obviously, no one thinks more of Dak than we do, but it's not easy to get one of the top quarterbacks in the league [done] and it can take time. Made a run at CeeDee the year before and it wasn't the right timing. So we put it on the backburner, never any hard feelings, then got it done." It was not too long ago that the Cowboys sweated out deals with Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb . In 2024, Prescott did not agree to his record-setting $60 million a year deal until the morning of the season opener, and Lamb sat out most of training camp before signing his deal that averaged $34 million and made him, at the time, the second-highest paid wide receiver. Last summer was dominated by the Micah Parsons ' saga. He was set to play last season on his fifth-year option when discussions went haywire after owner and general manager Jerry Jones thought he and the edge rusher agreed to an extension only to see Parsons say he would not sign a deal without involvement from his agent. Parsons went through a high-profile hold-in during training camp, eventually demanding a trade while in Oxnard. The week before the season started, he was traded to the Green Bay Packers for defensive tackle Kenny Clark and two first-round picks. If the Cowboys finish with a better record than the Packers in 2026, then Green Bay's first-rounder will be dealt to the New York Jets as part of the trade Dallas made with New York to acquire Williams in November. Williams is 28 and was signed through 2027. He is now signed through 2030. In the past, the Cowboys used major extensions to keep star players well away from free agency, including DeMarcus Ware , Tony Romo , Jason Witten , Terence Newman and more recently (2023) with Trevon Diggs , who was released in January. The Cowboys have a core of key figures under contract. Prescott and running back Javonte Williams are signed through 2028; Lamb, Ferguson and Bland are signed through 2029; Williams, Aubrey and Smith through 2030. Stephen Jones likes to say it takes two sides to get a deal done. At the start of camp, he said the organization wanted Williams for the long haul. Over the weekend, Williams' agent, Nicole Lynn of Klutch Sports, was at practice, perhaps jump-starting discussions. Perhaps Pickens' will be the next contract to get done, but that cannot happen until next offseason. He is playing this season on the $27.3 million franchise tag after the Cowboys declined to engage in extension talks this offseason. Jerry Jones said he has a long-term vision for Pickens. If he performs as he did in 2025 with career highs in catches, yards and touchdowns, will the talks get done as early and smoothly as the others have lately? Or will we see a return to sweating out a new deal? Stephen Jones is not thinking about how the Pickens' talks will go next offseason. "I'm worried about this season, tell you the truth," Jones said. "I want to go win some games."

Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions This week's " Fantasy Focus Mock Draft Monday" was a little bit different than our usual mock drafts. We decided to spice things up by making this a double-flex, superflex, mock draft. That's right, two flex positions plus an "OP" slot (often called superflex). Toward the end of the draft, the player pool becomes much thinner due to 12 teams drafting a total of 18 roster spots. As you'll see below, quarterbacks came off the board early and often, and it was no surprise that Josh Allen was the top pick. However, because of the QB-heavy nature of the early first round, that meant stars like Bijan Robinson , Jahmyr Gibbs , Puka Nacua were pushed to the back of the first round. How teams approached shoring up their QB2 spot was interesting, given the depth of the position. It's worth noting that, just before the start of the mock, Adam Schefter let us know that Luther Burden III will miss the entire preseason with a groin injury . Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. -- Twelve days, 10 practices, and it's time to get the heck out of West Virginia. The New York Giants got in their work, secluded, in the first summer under John Harbaugh. Mixed in have been team hangouts, dinners, golf at the beautiful Greenbrier and a trip to see "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." The experience was almost unanimously embraced. "Well, I think that what's really good about being here is that football is the main thing, and that's how it should be in training camp. So, I really love being here," quarterback Jaxson Dart said. "I know the guys have too because not only has it made us better on the field, but at the same time it's allowed us to make stronger connections off the field. So, just the more time we've been able to spend with one another I've loved, and I know all the other guys have felt the same way." The Giants truly believe they are leaving West Virginia better than when they arrived, even if their offense looked pedestrian and their defense better than most expected. The improvement is in the details. Here's what we learned about the Giants in West Virginia: Jaxson Dart & Co. are learning a new offense This seems to be getting overlooked by many. The Giants are running an offense that merges input from Harbaugh (from Baltimore) and Matt Nagy (from Kansas City and Andy Reid) with Greg Roman's intricate run concepts and Brian Callahan's modern West Coast concepts. Dart is learning to play under center more than ever and alter his footwork. It's a process. The coaching staff is learning what Dart & Co. do well. Dart is still learning and mastering the schemes and plays. It will take time. But at least the Giants' offense feels it made progress throughout training camp, especially with its corrections. "You're getting a big install each and every day," Dart said. "So, you just continue to learn, continue to get reps at things and have a lot of really valuable communication." As long as the Giants continue to improve as the summer progresses and wide receiver Malik Nabers returns soon (which is likely), the offense will be fine. The offensive line looks good. Long linebackers make a difference Harbaugh likes tall, physical players in the middle of the defense. So he added Tremaine Edmunds and Arvell Reese , who both stand at 6-foot-4, this offseason. It really does have an impact when the quarterback tries to throw to the second level. Reese looked every bit the No. 5 pick in West Virginia. Edmunds looked poised as the unit's signal-caller. Edmunds and Reese got their hands on passes all throughout the training camp. They made it hard to complete passes over their heads in the middle of the field. Expect this to be the case as the season progresses. "Hopefully more interceptions than tipped balls, but we're going to get our hands on them," Edmunds said. General manager Joe Schoen also noted their physicality will be vital to the Giants' ability to stop the run. That was a problem last season when the defense allowed a league-worst 5.3 yards per carry. OBJ is in midst of a roster battle Odell Beckham Jr . is proving that when healthy he can still play. He only got better as training camp went on, especially when getting some first-team reps. But he'll have his work cut out for him to secure one of the final wide receiver spots. Braxton Berrios had a strong camp as a receiver and brings value as a returner. Also, don't completely discount Dalen Cambre . He made a lot of plays in West Virginia and showed last year he can be an asset on special teams. Right now, it seems to be those three competing for one final spot. The CB shuffle Harbaugh rotates the defensive backs more than any other position. Paulson Adebo and Greg Newsome II began the summer with the first team. Adebo had a rough camp, and Deonte Banks was good. He was probably the team's best cover corner in West Virginia. As a result, he earned some first-team opportunities. "Oh, absolutely," Harbaugh said. "It's competitive, guys are competing. I've told you before, I really feel good about our corner depth. I think we've got some guys there. So, we're just going to let those guys keep competing and it brings out the best in everybody. I thought all the corners played well today." With slot corner Dru Phillips now sidelined for at least a few practices with a knee sprain, expect the cornerback shuffle to continue. Lots of opportunity for guys to win playing time and starting spots. The rookie leads the kicking battle Dominic Zvada remains in the driver's seat to be the Giants' kicker this season. He made 34 of 38 attempts at camp, and Ben Sauls hit 29 of 36. Both were solid, but Zvada appears to be Harbaugh's kind of kicker with his length and kicking stroke. Now he just has to do it in the preseason. Some big games upcoming later this month. Some standouts NT DJ Reader looked really good as a run stuffer in the middle of the defense. The Giants just need to keep him healthy. TE Isaiah Likely was Dart's favorite target with Nabers not participating in team drills. Likely had a strong camp and should fit nicely as the team's No. 2 receiver. If Nabers isn't healthy, Likely will be a favorite of Dart. Reese looked like he's going to make an instant impact with his physicality and athleticism in the middle of the Giants' defense. Don't expect him to come off the field much as new defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson finds ways to use his talents. S Jevon Holland looks primed for a bounce back. He was around the ball a lot this summer. DB Ar'Darius Washington looks natural in this defense. He's going to have a role as either a slot cornerback or safety. Maybe both.

He analyzes football on and off the field like no one else on the planet, writing about in-season X's and O's, offseason transactions and so much more. He is the host of the Bill Barnwell Show podcast , with episodes released weekly. Barnwell joined ESPN in 2011 as a staff writer at Grantland. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions How many Hall of Famers are playing in the NFL right now? It depends on when you're evaluating, of course. There are veterans near the end of their careers who have already proved themselves as locks to receive the game's highest honor one day, such as Aaron Rodgers and Derrick Henry . There are players in their prime who are well on their way, such as Justin Jefferson and Pat Surtain II . And then there are young players who haven't yet proved themselves to be Hall of Famers but could break out in the years to come, such as Caleb Downs or Arvell Reese from the 2026 draft. Go back to 2002, the first year with 32 teams. There are 54 players who suited up for at least one game that season enshrined in the Hall of Fame. That list doesn't include Tom Brady (who becomes eligible in 2028) or borderline candidates such as Steve Smith and Reggie Wayne, who could earn enough votes to cross the threshold in the future. At the very least, we can use 55 Hall of Famers as our gauge, which is just under 3% of the 1,839 players who suited up for at least one game that season. Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' Today, I'm going through each of the league's 32 teams and attempting to identify the players who either are on track or have a realistic hope of earning gold jackets one day. This will be my estimate of who is likely to make it using historical comparables as opposed to my opinion of who should or should not be enshrined at some point. Naturally, that includes positional preferences; voters have historically loved to honor quarterbacks, running backs and receivers, but the bar is higher for linemen. I won't attempt to pick among the rookies, whom we haven't yet seen line up for an NFL snap, but I'll work with everybody else and split the most notable candidates into one of five categories: Players listed as "in" have already done enough to earn enshrinement given their existing résumé. They could retire tomorrow and make it into the Hall of Fame after they become eligible. Those "on the cusp" have already done the vast majority of the work required and need only another season or two of solid play to get over the hump. As it stands, their résumé might already be enough to get in, but another successful season could push them into lock territory. The "keep it up" category is for players who are performing at a Hall of Fame level but haven't done so for a long enough time to guarantee their path to enshrinement. They need to play at or near their existing level for several more seasons to have a shot. Guys who have "work to do" aren't on track to make it to the Hall of Fame with their existing résumé and/or their most recent level of play. In some cases, that could be because injuries slowed their progress in 2025, or because they haven't played at a Hall-caliber level for long enough. They still have a shot, but something has to change. Finally, the "missing out" category is for veterans who are at the point where they don't have the existing résumé to make it to the Hall nor the time to reestablish themselves as viable candidates. Though anything's possible, it will be a serious surprise if any of these players end up in Canton one day. They're far more likely to end up in the Hall of Very Good. I usually start these all-32 columns with teams on the East Coast, so let's mix things up and begin out west. Jump to a team: ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND JAX | KC | LV | LAC | LAR | MIA | MIN NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF SEA | TB | TEN | WSH NFC West Arizona Cardinals On the cusp: S Budda Baker Baker has been stuck on some bad teams -- the Cardinals have one winning season across his nine years in the league -- but Pro Bowl voters have consistently seen him as an impactful and rangy difference-making safety. He has made eight Pro Bowls across that span. Every eligible player with at least 10 Pro Bowl appearances has been enshrined in Canton, so if Baker can earn two more, he should be a lock. One more might even be enough for the 30-year-old. Keep it up: TE Trey McBride The invisible force field that had kept McBride out of the end zone early in his career finally lifted in 2025, as he scored 11 touchdowns, nearly doubling his total over the prior three seasons combined (six). He's not quite as explosive or elusive after the catch as Travis Kelce was in his prime or Brock Bowers has been so far as a pro, but McBride makes up that for with great hands and massive target shares. Los Angeles Rams In: WR Davante Adams , Edge Myles Garrett , QB Matthew Stafford I don't think I need to do much convincing here. Garrett is one of the best defenders in league history, and Adams had a five-year peak as arguably the top wide receiver in football. The case against Stafford would have been that nobody had ever really seen him as the best QB in the NFL (or close to it) in any of his first 16 years ... but after winning MVP last season, that one's out the window. He's already in the top seven for career passing yards and touchdowns, and with an MVP and a Super Bowl victory, Stafford will waltz in. Keep it up: WR Puka Nacua Nacua already has 1,486- and 1,715-receiving yard seasons to his name by the end of his third pro campaign, which is remarkable, even given that those years are part of the 17-game era. Just for fun, the 2023 fifth-round pick is also one of the league's best blocking wideouts. The only questions are whether Nacua can stay on the field for full seasons at a time and whether there's any drop-off once Stafford is ultimately replaced by Ty Simpson . play 0:59 Evan Cohen is puzzled why Cowboys are in Super Bowl conversation Work to do: CB Trent McDuffie , DT Kobie Turner , Edge Byron Young The talented young linemen the Rams already had up front should get a boost from playing alongside Garrett. I thought Turner was the best of the bunch last season, but Young was devastating at times and parlayed his 12-sack, 29-knockdown campaign into his first Pro Bowl. I'm intrigued to see whether the Rams can afford to keep their DL standouts -- both of whom are pending free agents -- alongside Garrett for years to come. San Francisco 49ers In: WR Mike Evans , RB Christian McCaffrey , OT Trent Williams Evans and Williams are easy first-ballot selections. McCaffrey has struggled with injuries, but he has had multiple seasons as the best RB in the league and plays a position that the Hall is always looking to appreciate. On the cusp: TE George Kittle , LB Fred Warner Kittle is right on the borderline of being a lock, having made seven Pro Bowls over his past eight pro campaigns before he tore his right Achilles last postseason. I'd vote for Kittle given his dominance as a blocker and four 1,000-yard seasons, but tight ends can go underappreciated by the Hall at times. One more substantial season would push Kittle, 32, to the "lock" side of things. I'd argue the same for Warner, who had four first-team All-Pro nods over a five-year span before his own serious injury a year ago. Work to do: Edge Nick Bosa , QB Brock Purdy Bosa has a Defensive Player of the Year award to his name, but a pair of September ACL tears have essentially cost the 2019 first-round pick two of his seven pro seasons. He needs another great season and a couple more Pro Bowl-caliber campaigns to get back on the Hall track. Purdy's efficiency has slipped since that dramatic 2023 campaign, and he has suffered meaningful injuries in three of his four pro seasons. Missing out: FB Kyle Juszczyk Remember when I said a minute ago that every eligible player with at least 10 Pro Bowl appearances was enshrined in Canton? Well, Juszczyk will be a fascinating case to see whether that keeps up, given that he just earned his 10th consecutive Pro Bowl nod in 2025. Of course, while Juszczyk is a good player, it's fair to wonder whether he's racking up Pro Bowl appearances by virtue of being the most conspicuous player at a position where there simply aren't many others, just as Mike Alstott became a six-time Pro Bowler with the Bucs. Juszczyk plays only about half of the offensive snaps in a typical game, and it seems telling that the 49ers were willing to cut him this offseason before re-signing him , saving about $500,000 in the process. I'd be a little surprised if he made it in just given how the league has valued fullbacks. (Matthew Slater, who earned 10 Pro Bowl appearances as a special-teamer for the Patriots, will also test the 10-Pro Bowl rule.) Seattle Seahawks Keep it up: WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba , CB Devon Witherspoon It's pretty remarkable that the defending Super Bowl champions don't have a single player who is either likely to make the Hall of Fame based on his prior production or one who is a big year away, but that's a product of their unique roster build. Their stars are almost all young players, while their supporting cast is mostly veterans who have been solid players throughout their time in the NFL. The two cornerstones from John Schneider's 2023 draft are very clearly head and shoulders above the rest of the young players on the roster in terms of tracking for Canton. Smith-Njigba, 24, is coming off a career season that earned him an Offensive Player of the Year award. He seems set to stick as one of the league's best wideouts for years to come. Witherspoon has been named to the Pro Bowl in each of his first three seasons, becoming just the 10th defensive back in league history to start his career with those honors. Just three other players have managed it since 1980: Everson Walls, Charles Woodson and Patrick Peterson. Work to do: OT Charles Cross , S Nick Emmanwori , DT Byron Murphy II , G Grey Zabel Another great rookie class from Schneider makes its presence known here, as Emmanwori and Zabel produced Pro Bowl-caliber seasons in their debuts. Both play positions that can struggle to earn recognition. Cross appears to have settled in as a very good left tackle and, once Trent Williams retires, could benefit from seeing more honors head his way. Missing out: WR Cooper Kupp , DT Leonard Williams Williams went eight years between Pro Bowl honors, earning one for his time with the Jets in 2017 before returning in 2024 and again in 2025 with the Seahawks. He was one of the league's more underrated defensive tackles over that span, consistently producing impressive hurry rates without the significant sack totals that usually come along for the ride. He is deservedly getting plaudits for his work in Mike Macdonald's defense, but it would take something truly special throughout his 30s to get Williams into the Hall. Kupp's peak in 2021 through the first half of the 2022 season was truly spectacular, but there's a significant gap between those 18 months and what he has done over the rest of his career. NFC South Atlanta Falcons Keep it up: RB Bijan Robinson The Hall loves its running backs, and Robinson has been among the best in the league across his three-year career. The explosive plays that had curiously been missing from Robinson's profile appeared last season, and he nearly doubled his receiving totals from 2023 and 2024 with an 820-yard campaign in 2025. If Robinson can stay at or near this level while remaining healthy, he will earn a trip to Canton. Work to do: G Chris Lindstrom , WR Drake London , TE Kyle Pitts Sr . Lindstrom has made four straight Pro Bowls at right guard for the Falcons, but interior linemen typically need to be either earning first-team All-Pro honors or making double-digit Pro Bowls to find their way to the Hall of Fame. London has been saddled with inconsistent quarterback play, which hasn't helped his chances, but he just turned 25 in July and still might have his best football ahead. Missing out: S Jessie Bates III , OT Jake Matthews Here are two solid veterans who will end up landing in the Hall of Very Good. Matthews was unlucky to get stuck in the same conference as Trent Williams for most of his career. Bates has spent most of his time on subpar defenses, with that two-year run on the Bengals as they competed for Super Bowls as the exception. He's such an underrated player, and the Bengals haven't been the same on defense since he left in free agency in 2023. Carolina Panthers Work to do: DT Derrick Brown , CB Jaycee Horn , WR Tetairoa McMillan After struggling to stay healthy early in his career, Horn has mostly been able to stay on the field and earned back-to-back Pro Bowl honors for the Panthers. He has been a high-end cover cornerback at his best, although tackling can be an issue for him. McMillan got his career off to a solid start by winning Offensive Rookie of the Year, albeit amid a relatively weak class. Though a 1,014-receiving yard season was enough to earn the Panther the hardware, he'll need to be more productive to set his sights on a gold jacket one day. New Orleans Saints On the cusp: Edge Cameron Jordan I wrote about Jordan's Hall of Fame candidacy last week in my look at the defensive class of 2011 . I could see an argument that Jordan has already done enough to get in after a 10.5-sack season in 2025, and even a six-sack season in 2026 would surely be enough to get him over the hump. If he doesn't reach those marks, my guess is that Jordan will still earn enshrinement one day, but it might take a few years for the Saints legend to get in. Missing out: RB Alvin Kamara Kamara looked like he was well on his way to Canton after starting his career with five straight Pro Bowl appearances. Things haven't gone quite that way since then. Kamara averaged 5.0 yards per carry and 1,746 yards from scrimmage per season with Drew Brees at quarterback, but since Brees' retirement in 2021, Kamara has averaged 3.9 and 1,206. Kamara was able to come to terms on a restructured deal with the Saints, but he looks set to play in a split backfield alongside Travis Etienne Jr . for the next couple of seasons. Tampa Bay Buccaneers Keep it up: OT Tristan Wirfs Wirfs missed time with a knee injury last season and had more hiccups than usual in the weeks after returning, but he would still be the first pick if you were drafting any left tackle to dominate the league over the next decade. Let's hope that the hamstring injury he reportedly suffered at the start of training camp doesn't linger into the season. Work to do: S Antoine Winfield Jr . Winfield looked like he could be trending toward the Hall after a 2023 season with six sacks, six forced fumbles and three interceptions, but the second-generation pro missed half of the campaign that followed. Safeties typically need to stuff the stat sheet to have a shot at enshrinement, and Winfield's 2023 season has been an outlier relative to the rest of his career. He's also about to turn 28. Missing out: WR Chris Godwin Jr ., QB Baker Mayfield , DT Vita Vea There's another world where Godwin would have a realistic shot at the Hall. Maybe he'd have gotten a few seasons with Jameis Winston and Bruce Arians in that high-tempo, explosive offense from 2019. Things might have gone differently if Godwin hadn't torn an ACL at the end of an 1,103-yard season in 2021. And Godwin was on pace to approach 1,400 receiving yards in 2024, only for a dislocated ankle in garbage time to derail his season. play 1:41 Why Stephen A. won't count out the Chiefs as Super Bowl contenders NFC North Chicago Bears Keep it up: G Joe Thuney Long one of the league's most reliable guards, Thuney has finally gotten recognition for his steady and impactful work on the interior after turning 30; he has made it to four straight Pro Bowls and been a first-team All-Pro the past three seasons. Thuney's impact on deep playoff runs for the Patriots and Chiefs helps his case, but he'll need to win a few more All-Pro nods to get into the Hall. Work to do: CB Jaylon Johnson , TE Colston Loveland , QB Caleb Williams , OT Darnell Wright The young players on Chicago's offense have plenty of time to show what they can do. Wright took a major step forward in 2025 and was one of the league's best right tackles. Loveland didn't do much until November, at which point he became one of the league's most explosive tight ends. And Williams showed signs of the massive upside we saw from him as a prospect coming out of USC, often at the biggest moments for the Bears as they advanced to the divisional round of the playoffs. But these players have work to do to establish themselves as upper-echelon contributors. Missing out: DT Grady Jarrett , Edge Montez Sweat These are two good veteran linemen who don't have the sort of pass-rush production we associate with Hall of Famers. Jarrett could have won a Super Bowl MVP for his three-sack performance against the Patriots in Super Bowl LI had the defense not run out of gas in the fourth quarter. I'm not sure that would have been enough to swing a meaningful number of Hall of Fame votes, though. Detroit Lions Keep it up: WR Amon-Ra St. Brown , RB Jahmyr Gibbs , Edge Aidan Hutchinson , OT Penei Sewell Detroit's young stars, on the other hand, have already established themselves at elite levels for multiple seasons. If Wirfs isn't the first pick for best tackle of the next decade, it's probably Sewell, who will follow in Wirfs' footsteps this fall by attempting to make the move from right tackle to left tackle. Wirfs is one of the few to pull it off without a hitch, but I expect Sewell to follow in kind. Work to do: S Brian Branch , LB Jack Campbell , QB Jared Goff , S Kerby Joseph Injuries are sadly the reason Branch and Joseph have taken a step backward, with no clear timeline for either to return after Branch tore an Achilles and Joseph suffered a still-mysterious knee injury . Campbell was able to step in as a first-team All-Pro after Roquan Smith and Fred Warner went down with their own injuries last season, but it'll be difficult to hold onto those honors if the two standout linebackers are healthy again in 2026. Would Goff get serious Hall of Fame consideration? Not right now, although his résumé is better than you think. He has made five Pro Bowls and two deep playoff runs, but his limitations were on display in the Super Bowl loss to the Patriots. Goff is third in career passing yards through 10 seasons, trailing only Matt Ryan and Peyton Manning, both of whom played more games than him. Goff also hasn't missed a game to injury since 2021. If he stays healthy, he'll probably retire in the top 10 for career passing yards, and he could push to hit the top five. If there's playoff success and even a Super Bowl win along the way, he might have a shot. Green Bay Packers On the cusp: Edge Micah Parsons Parsons is facing a late start to the 2026 season after tearing his left ACL in December, but he was already well on his way to becoming a Hall of Fame lock. He has now started his career with five seasons of 12 or more sacks. Even if we lower the threshold to five 11-sack seasons to account fo

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- When the Denver Broncos formally introduced Russell Wilson as their new starting quarterback in March 2022, there were many with the team and around the NFL who believed Wilson already had a résumé worthy of the Pro Football Hall of Fame. In 10 seasons with the Seattle Seahawks , Wilson had won a lot. He led Seattle to eight playoff appearances and two Super Bowls, culminating with a Super Bowl XLVIII win over the Broncos to conclude the 2013 season. He also excelled individually, making the Pro Bowl nine times and having four consecutive seasons of 30-plus touchdown passes from 2017 to 2020, including a league-leading 34 in 2017 and a career-best 40 in 2020. Then Denver sent a package including two first-round picks to Seattle to acquire Wilson . The Broncos believed he could help break a then-six-season playoff drought and return them to Super Bowl contender status, showering Wilson with a franchise-record five-year, $245 million deal . Wilson was giddy in the introductory news conference , saying his goal was to play "10 or 12 more years and hopefully win three or four more Super Bowls." But Wilson struggled mightily in two seasons with the Broncos and two more with the Pittsburgh Steelers and New York Giants before retiring this offseason . And with the Hall's Class of 2026 -- a class that includes a first-ballot quarterback in Drew Brees -- set to be enshrined Saturday, Wilson's future Canton possibilities seem cloudy, with his late-career struggles casting doubt on whether he'll make it to the Hall. Wilson, who signed on to be an analyst for CBS after his retirement, now faces an uphill Hall of Fame climb because of a historic plunge in performance and a narrowing process for selection that has added difficulty for players to be enshrined, especially at a competitive quarterback position. Wilson won't be eligible to be inducted until the Class of 2031, but ESPN spoke to two dozen people -- some in the league and some involved with the Hall of Fame process -- to get an idea of where his case stands. WILSON'S PRIME WAS Hall of Fame level. His combination of passing ability, mobility and a penchant for late-game heroics was key to the Seahawks' considerable success in the 2010s. Along with eight 10-win seasons from 2012 to 2021 and nine playoff victories, Wilson also produced on the stat sheet. He threw for 4,212 yards and 40 touchdowns while rushing for 513 yards in 2020. He also ran for 849 yards in 2014, a season in which he rushed for 47 first downs. Wilson's 292 touchdown passes from 2012-21 was the second most in league history for a quarterback in his first 10 NFL seasons, behind only Peyton Manning's 306. And Tom Brady (324) and Aaron Rodgers (317) were the only two players with more touchdown passes than Wilson during his 10-year run in Seattle. Wilson's 113 wins as a starting quarterback (regular season and postseason combined) was the most for any NFL player in his first 10 seasons, too. But while quarterbacks typically see a drop in performance in the final years of their careers, Wilson barreled over a statistical cliff. The last four seasons of his career saw him frequently benched , and his teams went 17-27 in games he started. His production nosedived as his mobility waned. He was sacked an astounding 143 times in 47 games from 2022 to 2025, including 100 times in two seasons (30 starts) with the Broncos. Four of Wilson's five lowest yards per attempt totals of his career came after he left Seattle. Over his last five seasons, including his final one with the Seahawks, Wilson's completion percentage over expectation was in the negative three times, with a career-low minus-4.3% in 2022 in Denver. That rough finishing kick has made an impact on Hall of Fame voters. "Russell Wilson was a good quarterback for two-thirds of his career, a very good quarterback,'' longtime selector Ron Borges said. "[But] the Hall of Fame is not the Hall of Very Good, it is where the best to ever play their positions go. "Was Wilson ever considered the best of his era? If he was not, and I would argue he was not, how can he be judged one of the best of all time?" Sure, Wilson's counting stats are certainly Hall worthy. His 46,966 career passing yards ranks 16th (right behind Hall of Famer Fran Tarkenton), and his 353 passing touchdowns ranks 12th (ahead of Tarkenton and fellow Hall of Famer John Elway). But there is little precedent for the type of statistical drop-off Wilson had at the end of his career. "In short, can you play your way out of the Hall of Fame? His final four years are really bad, and they are made even worse by the whole move to force his way out [of Seattle] and prove himself,'' said Jason Cole, a selector for over a decade who says he believes Wilson is a Hall of Famer. "It exposed so many of the flaws that were covered up in Seattle. At the same time, his first 10 years are really pretty damn exceptional." Wilson was never a first-team All-Pro selection -- he was a second-team selection once -- and was not selected to the 2010s All-Decade team. And there is also the perception that the Seahawks' success was more a product of Seattle's "Legion of Boom" defense than of Wilson. The Seahawks' defense allowed fewer than 300 points in the first five seasons of Wilson's tenure (2012-2016), leading the league in scoring defense in four of those years (2012-2015). Players from that team's defense will be on the Hall ballot when Wilson becomes eligible for induction. One of them is former All-Pro cornerback Richard Sherman , who gave his thoughts on Wilson's legacy during a "Thursday Night Football" broadcast discussion with Tony Gonzalez last season. "I think you got to judge his career off when the Legion of Boom was there," Sherman said. Sherman is one of several high-profile Seahawks teammates who have levied public criticisms of Wilson, including him being potentially coddled by then-coach Pete Carroll . The Broncos' release of Wilson in March 2024 (and the then-record $85 million dead money hit that resulted from it) is also the type of thing that looms large in Hall of Fame discussions. Broncos wide receiver Courtland Sutton , who had a career-best 10 touchdown receptions in 2023 while playing with Wilson, said he believes the quarterback's approach and commitment to the game should matter in these discussions despite how things played out at the end. "He was a professional at every level, everything we did, how we met, how we practiced, how we spent post-practice, just to be able to see that from the perspective of being a receiver and being able to work with him,'' Sutton said. "People can say what they want to say about the outcome of how things went, I know what he gave to the game because I saw it day in and day out, how he prepared to go play." SO WHERE DOES all this leave voters and Wilson's case? Perhaps Kurt Warner (Class of 2017) might have the closest statistical profile in terms of drop in performance to Wilson's among enshrinees from the past three decades. Warner's career had peaks in the beginning and end of his 12 seasons -- with a five-year stretch from 2002 to 2006 in which he didn't exceed 10 starts in any season. But that middle was surrounded by two peaks in which Warner was a two-time league MVP and went to three Super Bowls, winning MVP of Super Bowl XXXIV after leading the St. Louis Rams to the championship. Wilson doesn't have the hardware of Warner, but he finished with a QBR of 60 or higher in nine of his first 10 seasons, finishing third behind Manning and Brady with a 74.8 QBR as a rookie in 2012 and fifth with a 71.8 in 2019. He combined for 65 touchdown passes in his final two seasons in Seattle after the Seahawks' Legion of Boom defense started to break apart. Those metrics have Wilson right in the middle of several recently retired quarterbacks in Cole's mind. "I kind of lump him in a group with Eli [Manning], [Philip] Rivers, Matt Ryan," said Cole, who added later that he believed Cam Newton was the best of the recently retired quarterbacks. Cole points out that this wouldn't be as much of a discussion if one play had just gone differently. That play, of course, is Wilson's pass at the end of Super Bowl XLIX. Wilson targeted Ricardo Lockette from the 1-yard line with 26 seconds left in the game for a would-be go-ahead TD. But the throw was intercepted by Patriots cornerback Malcolm Butler , clinching a New England victory. "If he had hit the goal-line pass in the Super Bowl -- or just not thrown it, thrown it away, or handed the ball to [Marshawn] Lynch -- I think he walks into the Hall of Fame without much discussion," Cole said. "He did some amazing things in that game that are all forgotten because of one play. "But there's this weird conversation about Wilson which all sort of emanates from that point. ... If he had just hit that one pass, we probably never talk about any of this." AN ARGUMENT CAN be made that it might be more difficult than ever to be enshrined into the Hall with its current guidelines. From 2007 to 2024, a maximum of five modern-era players (those in their 25-year window of eligibility after their retirements) were enshrined in all but one class (2009 being the exception). But the Hall's board of directors approved a change in the voting that altered the final stages of the voting process ahead of 2025. The last two Hall classes each included four modern-era finalists who were selected for enshrinement, instead of the maximum of five, as neither class included a coach or a contributor. They are the smallest back-to-back Hall of Fame classes since 2004 and 2005. These smaller classes will create an increased backlog. For players like Wilson with any questions, the road is more tricky under the current framework. Multiple selectors said privately over the past two weeks that players with more textured discussions or career fluctuations will have a far more difficult time with a tighter voting procedure. That's not the only logjam Wilson could face, as the quarterback field will get quite crowded. Two-time Super Bowl MVP Eli Manning has not been selected in his two years of eligibility and will be joined by Ben Roethlisberger (also a two-time Super Bowl champion) and Cam Newton (one-time NFL MVP) in 2027, Tom Brady (career passing leader, three-time NFL MVP and five-time Super Bowl MVP) in 2028 and Matt Ryan (one-time NFL MVP) in 2029. Philip Rivers (eight-time Pro Bowler) will be eligible the same year as Wilson. The upcoming retirements of Aaron Rodgers (who has said 2026 will be his last season ) and 18-year veteran Matthew Stafford will add even more quarterbacks to the pot. In short, Wilson will face a fight, not only at his position but with tighter voting restrictions in general, making his Hall of Fame case one of the most intriguing over the next decade or so. Sutton thinks not only that Wilson is fit for the Hall of Fame discussion but that his body of work makes his case strong. And that is what the selectors should consider. "At the end of the day, nobody can take away what he's done over the entirety of his career,'' Sutton said. "Not taking out three years, pointing out three years or four years of his career, the entirety of his career, the totality of his career, he has done amazing things, and I think he'll have a nod to be in that conversation to be a Hall of Famer."

Madison Beer/Instagram J.J. Post Jul 29, 2026, 04:36 PM ET Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions The NFL season hasn't started yet, but Justin Herbert already has a ring on his mind. On Tuesday, the Los Angeles Chargers quarterback announced his engagement to singer-songwriter Madison Beer. The couple shared the news Tuesday in a joint post on Instagram, captioned with a simple message: "Meet my fiancé." Herbert and Beer were first spotted together in August 2025 on the set of a music video Beer was shooting, which began to spark dating rumors. Beer would appear at Chargers games throughout the fall, with the dating rumors seemingly confirmed when the two shared a kiss on the sideline before the Chargers' Week 5 game against the Washington Commanders. The pair attended a Los Angeles Dodgers World Series game together later that autumn. The duo was also spotted sitting courtside at Crypto.com Arena supporting the Los Angeles Lakers . Herbert co-starred in the music video for Beer's song "lovergirl," which was released in May as part of her latest album "locket deluxe." View this post on Instagram Asked at the first day of Chargers training camp about whether he was more nervous about the proposal or his first NFL start, Herbert minced no words : "The proposal, for sure." His coach, Jim Harbaugh, said he felt great for Herbert, then mused about a unique quirk in the league's postseason calendar this year. "Valentine's Day. SoFi. ... Little hairs on your arms start standing up," he said . It's not the first time Harbaugh has chimed in with his support for the relationship. In May, Herbert missed the second phase of the team's voluntary offseason program to support Beer on tour. When asked about his reaction to the QB's absence, Harbaugh said he offered : "Do you need a ride to the airport?" Harbaugh also said then he was "happy" the quarterback was supporting Beer on tour. The couple's announcement post amassed more than 5.7 million likes on Instagram within an day of its posting, with the official NFL account among the well-wishers in the comment section.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions NEW ORLEANS -- Taysom Hill won't be returning to the New Orleans Saints for a 10th season, he confirmed in a statement posted to social media Wednesday night. Hill did not say whether he intended to retire, leaving the door open to playing elsewhere this season. In his first public comments since the end of the 2025 season, Hill thanked the Saints and their fans for his nine seasons in New Orleans, explaining that he has taken time this offseason to figure out what comes next. "I still don't have a clear answer about what the future holds, but I know that returning to New Orleans is not in the cards," Hill said in his post . "As training camp begins, I didn't want my silence to be misinterpreted, and as hard as it is to put into words, I wanted to express my gratitude." Hill was known as the "Swiss Army knife" during his time in New Orleans -- playing at quarterback, running back, tight end, wide receiver and on special teams -- and was considered one of the most versatile players in franchise history. "I had always heard, 'If you love New Orleans, New Orleans will love you back,'" Hill said in his post. "That could not have been more true. You exceeded every expectation I had of what it would be like to live and play in a city. The passion, loyalty, and support you showed my family and me over these nine seasons were truly one of a kind. "... I'm still working through what comes next, but I couldn't move forward without taking the time to say thank you." If Hill does not play again, he will retire as one of only five players in NFL history to score at least 10 touchdowns each via rushing, receiving and passing. He is the only player in the Super Bowl era to have at least 1,000 yards in all three categories. Saints general manager Mickey Loomis on Tuesday said he had recently talked to Hill, but he declined to share the details of that conversation. On Wednesday, Loomis praised Hill in a statement, thanking him for being a "great teammate, excellent leader and mentor." "We thank Taysom for all his great contributions, and we are positive that a day will come when all his accomplishments can be properly celebrated," Loomis said. Hill, who turns 36 next month, often drew comparisons to players from earlier generations because of his ability to play so many roles. When he caught his 10th career touchdown pass in 2023 to reach double digits in all three categories, he became the first player since Hall of Famer Frank Gifford to do so. Gifford accomplished the feat in 1957. Hill is less than two years removed from a serious knee injury sustained in December 2024. He began the 2025 season on the physically unable to perform list but returned to play 13 games. He caught 11 passes, threw one touchdown pass and ran the ball 52 times for 114 yards and a touchdown. A significant portion of those stats came in Hill's final home game Dec. 21. The Saints fed him the ball to try to get him 1,000 career receiving yards and also appeared to call plays that would get him in a position to score a touchdown, which he did on the final play of the game. "We had the touchdown, then the next play he tried to get me another one and then the next play he called the screen to me," Hill said after the game. "I was laughing in my head, and it was like, 'Kellen knows.' So those things don't go unnoticed." Hill became emotional after the game as he reminisced on his career, although he declined to say at the time whether retirement was on the horizon. The Saints claimed Hill off waivers from the Green Bay Packers before the 2017 season. He played in 118 regular-season games and six postseason games.

Nick has covered the San Francisco 49ers since 2016, having previously covered the St. Louis Rams for 12 years, including three years (2013 to 2015) at ESPN. In over a decade with the company, Nick has led ESPN's coverage of the Niners' 2019 and 2023 Super Bowl run, Colin Kaepernick's protest, the Rams making Michael Sam the first openly gay player drafted to the NFL, Sam's subsequent pursuit of a roster spot and the team's relocation and stadium saga. Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- After only three training camp practices, San Francisco 49ers receiver Ricky Pearsall did not participate Wednesday because of swelling in the posterior cruciate ligament in his right knee. That's the same injury that cost Pearsall all or part of 10 games last season. The Niners said Wednesday they have some "concern" about Pearsall's latest knee flare-up and they are "exploring all options" when it comes to the next step. That figures to include potential surgery solutions for an injury that has plagued Pearsall off and on since Week 4 of last season. Pearsall initially sustained the injury in a Sept. 28 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars . That followed a week in which he dealt with soreness in his left knee and was listed as questionable before playing against the Jaguars. From there, Pearsall sat out the next six games before returning Nov. 16 against the Arizona Cardinals . He played in the next four games before agitating the knee and an ankle against the Tennessee Titans . He sat out the next game against the Indianapolis Colts , returned against the Chicago Bears on Dec. 28 then sat out the next two games before returning in the NFC divisional round against the Seattle Seahawks . Pearsall had no catches or yards in that season-ending loss and finished his second NFL season with 36 receptions for 528 yards and no touchdowns over 10 games (including the postseason). With fellow receiver Christian Kirk dealing with a calf injury and also sitting out practice, the Niners are already down two of their presumptive top three wideouts. That leaves an opening for others, such as Demarcus Robinson , Jordan Watkins , Jacob Cowing and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling to get more opportunities as they did Wednesday. "They're getting better," offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. "I've just seen a lot of growth across the board. Those guys come out every day with the right mindset. They're on their assignments, they're working, they're competing. It's going to be fun to watch that room kind of become what it does over this next however many weeks of training camp. It's one of the positions where we have a lot of competition and I'm excited to see where it goes." Pearsall's injury wasn't the only one the Niners added to their growing list Wednesday. Safety Malik Mustapha , who is competing with Marques Sigle for a starting spot, is dealing with a hamstring strain, and running back Jordan James , the early leader to backup Christian McCaffrey , has a rib fracture. Both suffered injuries in Monday's practice and will sit out some time. Offensive tackle Vederian Lowe (high ankle sprain) and defensive tackle Gracen Halton (knee bone bruise) have already been out because of injuries sustained in previous practices.

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions LOS ANGELES -- Rams defensive end Myles Garrett said that he doesn't want to push defensive tackle Aaron Donald to come out of retirement but that if it does happen, "I think we can do great things." Donald, who retired in March 2024 after 10 NFL seasons, is going through a "very strict, regimented process" to decide whether he wants to play this season, Rams coach Sean McVay said last week. The Rams' trade for Garrett in June spurred talk about the possibility of Donald returning to play alongside the reigning Defensive Player of the Year. McVay said he and Donald first had a conversation about the possibility because he had reached out for Donald's opinion when the team was discussing the Garrett trade. "I don't want to push him in one way or another," Garrett said Wednesday. "If he's here, I'm going to be excited to be his teammate, his partner in crime. And I think we can do great things, but it's a difficult thing coming back, and I know he has a family. He has a lot of decisions to make." On Saturday, McVay said Donald is seeing how his body responds to the training he is putting it through in preparation to make a decision. Garrett was asked what he thought would be the toughest part of coming back after two years without playing. "Just getting back to that tempo," Garrett said. "As much as you can try to work yourself back into shape ... we get a small taste of it when you come back from the offseason and you've got to get your wind and your legs back underneath you. When you get on the field and things are flying around, you've got to find a way to get your conditioning back and slow down the game once more. "And someone who, as great as he is, I think he can definitely come back and do it. It's just whether he wants to do that for however many games he chooses to play." Garrett said he has a lot of respect for Donald and thinks "there's a lot we can learn from each other." "And I'd love to pick his brain on the kind of things he does to attack his matchups," Garrett said. "And I think the same could be said vice versa."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. -- Standout New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers took part in the individual portion of a full-team practice Wednesday for the first time since suffering a serious knee injury Week 4 of last season. Giants coach John Harbaugh said that Nabers "looked good" and that even though it will be a little while before he partakes in a full practice, this was a step in the right direction. Harbaugh and general manager Joe Schoen wouldn't commit to Nabers being on schedule for Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys . They're going to see how the knee responds and reacts and make a determination on his workload on a day-to-day basis throughout training camp. "We've got a really good plan for him," Schoen said. "The medical staff has a really good plan for him, and we're going to always say listen to the patients. So, we're going to see how he reacts. We got a good plan in place, so as long as everything goes as planned, we'll listen to Malik and his body. And, again, hopefully he'll be ready and we'll see how it plays out. But no predictions right now, just because we have a long way to go. Still a lot of camp." Nabers tore his ACL and needed a full meniscus repair in October. He needed a second surgery earlier this year to clean up scar tissue and eliminate some of the stiffness. That set his timeline back a bit and put Week 1 in jeopardy. But Nabers remained in New Jersey this summer and attacked his rehab aggressively. The Giants opted not to put him on the physically unable to perform list earlier this week for the start of camp. That was a step in the right direction. Nabers was stopping and starting, cutting and running routes with starting quarterback Jaxson Dart as the Giants took the field Wednesday for their first training camp practice of the summer. He was running without a limp or any noticeable discomfort. This was in stark contrast to the last time Nabers was seen trying to run at Brian Burns ' charity softball game in late May. His knee was stiff, and he moved with a significant limp throughout that event. Almost two months later, there has been significant progress. "It was great. You saw him. He looked good," Harbaugh said. "He's got a process going. Thought he looked good." The Giants didn't want to put a timetable on their No. 1 receiver. Dart and Burns even said they don't want to rush Nabers' return. The good news is that six-plus weeks remain before New York opens its season against the rival Cowboys. That seems like ample time to get Nabers ready. Barring a setback, he seems to be tracking toward Week 1. The Giants don't want to put that kind of pressure on Nabers. "Next will be tomorrow. We'll see where he's at," Harbaugh said. "That part of it will be that -- how It feels, how it responds, how it reacts, all those things. I want our guys, our trainers and staff, will be monitoring. See how the knee responds more than anything. Take it one day at a time. It was encouraging [Wednesday]." Dart and the Giants are well aware of the difference Nabers can make. He had 1,204 yards and seven touchdowns as a rookie in 2024. He was hurt four games into his sophomore season, in Dart's first game as the starter. Having Nabers on the field during training camp, even if it's limited, is important. Dart and Nabers didn't work together at all last summer with Russell Wilson as the Giants' first-team starting quarterback. They had just one week of practice and 23 snaps in game action before Nabers was injured. Dart sees the difference when his top playmaker is on the field. "Well, he definitely has a presence about him. There's an aura that he has on the field that is exhilarating," Dart said. "It makes me happy, everybody's happy, to see him out on the field. And I think for him, he's had a lot of positives. So, we're just going to continue to get him in slowly, and he's doing a great job with attacking his recovery."

Follow on X Multiple Authors Email Print Open Extended Reactions CINCINNATI -- Cincinnati Bengals defensive end Shemar Stewart was carted off the field Wednesday with a left leg injury suffered during the first day of training camp. As of Wednesday afternoon, the severity had yet to be determined following imaging done at Paycor Stadium. He was spotted in a protective leg brace on his left leg and was on crutches. Stewart, the team's first-round pick in 2025, battled injuries last season. He totaled one sack in eight games. Earlier in the week, Bengals defensive coordinator Al Golden spoke glowingly of the former Texas A&M player. "He gives us great versatility," Golden said. "We should see a huge jump with him, to be honest with you." The first day of Bengals training camp also featured a small skirmish and a flying helmet. Bengals wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase , who is no stranger to confrontation, got into a tussle with cornerbacks DJ Turner II and Jalen Davis during team drills. Chase ended up with Turner's helmet and proceeded to launch it into the air before he and Davis continued jawing. All involved parties finished the practice that was edgier than typical opening days of camp. "We just want to come out and have a different mentality," Davis said after practice. "And that's what came out." Cincinnati is coming off a six-win season and its third straight year without a playoff appearance. The defense, which has been much maligned for the last two of those seasons, received several significant upgrades, including defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II . Turner is coming off of a career year. By the end of last season, he was tasked with following the opposing team's best wide receiver. For Cincinnati, that guy is Chase, who was named an All-Pro selection for the second straight year. And for Turner, there was nothing to Wednesday's scuffle. "Everybody wants to win," said Turner, who also said that brothers fight all the time. "[It's] just competitive. That's all there is to it." Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow said Chase and Turner are two of the best players in the league at their respective positions and if that's what they need to sharpen their skills before the season opener, he's all for it. However, there is one caveat -- as long as it doesn't interrupt practice. "If you can maybe punch somebody in the face in maybe 15 to 20 seconds and then get back lined up, that's probably ideal," Burrow said.
