If you'd rather show the logo in full colour, delete the two filter declarations (one in the Subscribe to PFF+ Unlock every PFF grade, stat and premium tool Grades, advanced stats and premium tools (opens in new tab) Subscribe → Every NFL passing offense has its own nuance. Some teams rely heavily on one elite wide receiver, while others share targets, including to tight ends or pass-catching running backs. We’re ranking all 32 receiving corps entering the 2026 NFL season, evaluating the complete collection of pass-catchers each offense has at its disposal. 1. Detroit Lions The only offense in the league to boast both a wide receiver and a running back with PFF receiving grades above 90.0 last season, this unit is rightfully awarded the top spot. Amon-Ra St. Brown is one of the most well-rounded receivers in football, while Jameson Williams brings both downfield and cross-field elements few players can match. Jahmyr Gibbs has a case for being the most dangerous receiving back in the league. Don’t forget about Sam LaPorta either, who has hauled in a staggering 72% of his career contested targets; nobody else near his level of contested volume comes close to this success rate. The Lions are also expecting big things from second-year player Isaac TeSlaa , who caught six touchdowns as a rookie and didn’t drop a pass, albeit in limited play time. 2. Dallas Cowboys CeeDee Lamb is yet to rediscover his elite production from 2022 and 2023, but he’s still playing like a well-above-average starting receiver. George Pickens is fresh off a career year, and if the pair can click simultaneously in 2026, Dallas could propel to the top spot on this list. Jake Ferguson presents the team with an additional end-zone threat after collecting eight touchdowns last season. One of the only critiques of this unit is that no two pass-catchers have fumbled the ball more than Pickens or Ferguson over the last three seasons, with 16 collectively. 3. Cincinnati Bengals The recent numbers may suggest there are better receiving duos, but Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins still form a partnership worthy of Cincinnati ’s inclusion among the league’s elite. Chase leads the NFL in both receiving yards and touchdowns since entering the NFL, while Higgins posted a career-high 114.7 passer rating when targeted last season. The lack of proven depth behind this pair is the obvious knock on this unit. Also, running back Chase Brown ’s PFF receiving grades have worsened over each of his three NFL seasons. 4. Seattle Seahawks Jaxon Smith-Njigba was the breakout star of last season, but his six lowest-graded games all came after Week 13. This unit loses Kenneth Walker ’s average receiving presence, but returns veteran Cooper Kupp , Rashid Shaheed and tight end AJ Barner . Shaheed has long been regarded as a deep threat, but he has grown into a reliable target too. His 1.2% drop rate is the lowest of any player with at least 120 receptions since 2023. 5. Minnesota Vikings Many fans still consider Justin Jefferson the best receiver in the sport, and he will be hungrier than ever to make right on a very uncharacteristic down year in which issues at quarterback largely contributed to his lack of success. Jordan Addison is still only 24 years old, but his play really fell off toward the latter stages of last year, with a 57.0 PFF receiving grade from Week 10 onward. The addition of Jauan Jennings helps Minnesota stay ranked inside the top 10. He brings a true possession receiver presence, making 18 contested grabs last year. However, no NFL team got less receiving production from its non-wide receivers last year (1,012 yards). 6. Los Angeles Rams Puka Nacua has established himself as arguably the best receiver in football, and 33-year-old Davante Adams remains one of the most respected secondary options in the league. This receiving corps led the league by almost any metric last season, including PFF receiving grade. However, the unit’s success in areas like yards and touchdowns can be partially attributed to the outstanding supply it received from Matthew Stafford . 7. Atlanta Falcons Drake London is one of the league’s few true alpha receivers capable of winning contested catches at a high rate. His 52 catches in traffic since 2023 are tied for the most in the league. Kyle Pitts finished last season with a 91.8 PFF receiving grade over his last six games, so it’s easy to convince yourself this is his year in fantasy football once again. Then there is Bijan Robinson , who is good at everything, and therefore unsurprisingly one of the league’s best receiving backs. His 858 yards after the catch was the most of any offensive weapon last season. 8. Philadelphia Eagles PFF’s top-ranked receiving corps entering last season now loses A.J. Brown , with Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown and Dontayvion Wicks brought in as replacements. Whether DeVonta Smith can establish himself as a true WR1 is the central question. Dallas Goedert returns as well. This group has plenty of mouths to feed and will look to be more dynamic in 2026 — its 4.3 yards after the catch per reception last season ranked second-worst in the league. 9. New England Patriots The additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs give New England’s receiving corps a significant talent upgrade. TreVeyon Henderson also brings untapped potential as a receiving threat out of the backfield. Hunter Henry is also back following the most productive season of his 10-year career. This is a group with far more proven options than it had a season ago. 10. Jacksonville Jaguars Jacksonville posted the highest drop rate in the NFL last season (9.6%), which should statistically regress toward the mean. Travis Hunter may not be a major factor in this receiving room, and that is fine given the other options. Brian Thomas Jr. needs to rediscover his 2024 form, while Parker Washington will hope his strong finish to last season carries into 2026. He was the second-highest-graded receiver in the league from December onward. 11. Green Bay Packers This group was situationally strong last season with the NFL’s highest PFF receiving grade on third down. Its development may hinge on how Tucker Kraft looks coming back from a torn ACL. He was dominant early last year by averaging 10.8 yards after the catch, a full three yards more than the nearest eligible tight end. Christian Watson ’s return from injury was seamless, as he recorded an 88.3 PFF receiving grade over the second half of last season. A step forward in production from Matthew Golden would help this room. 12. Denver Broncos Courtland Sutton and newly acquired Jaylen Waddle bring complementary skill sets that give Denver’s passing game real versatility. The bigger question is whether Troy Franklin or Pat Bryant can emerge as a third option, or if the bulk of Bo Nix ’s targets will stay concentrated on his top two receivers. Trust may be running thin elsewhere, as Broncos running backs and tight ends led the league with 22 total drops last season. 13. San Francisco 49ers Ricky Pearsall ’s season-ending injury is a significant blow, but this team doesn’t always need wide threats to find aerial success. San Francisco’s 90.1 PFF receiving grade from running backs and tight ends was by far the highest in the NFL last year. George Kittle remains one of the most complete tight ends in the league, and Christian McCaffrey was the only running back to record 1,000 receiving yards in 2025. The addition of veteran Mike Evans gives this offense a proven outside contributor to help offset the loss of Pearsall. 14. Chicago Bears Tight end Colston Loveland impressed last season and is ready for an expanded role in Year 2. Luther Burden III ’s outlook is also trending upward after a slow start to his rookie campaign. The pieces are here for this group to take a real step this season and display more reliability. Despite coming up in the clutch several times last year, Bears receivers dropped seven targets beyond 20 yards downfield last season, the most of any offense. 15. Arizona Cardinals The Cardinals’ roster doesn’t do much right, but not many questions can be asked of their passing options. Trey McBride is statistically the best pass-catching tight end in football. Meanwhile, Michael Wilson caught six touchdowns in the last six games of last season, and rookie Jeremiyah Love will bring an additional receiving threat out of the backfield. This squad forced 94 missed tackles on receptions last year, 15 more than any other team. Uncertainty remains over Marvin Harrison Jr. ’s long-term prospects. 16. Pittsburgh Steelers Michael Pittman Jr. and DK Metcalf form a physically imposing combination, though it remains to be seen how well that fits a quarterback in Aaron Rodgers who is less inclined to push the ball vertically. Darnell Washington and Pat Freiermuth return at tight end, while Jaylen Warren delivered the best PFF receiving grade of his career last year (83.6). The Steelers led the NFL in average yards after the catch in 2025 (6.5). 17. Tampa Bay Buccaneers Losing Mike Evans leaves a significant void, both on the field and in the locker room. Emeka Egbuka steps into a larger role after getting close to a 1,000-yard rookie season, although his 68.5 PFF receiving grade doesn’t even rank among the top 30 rookies of the last five seasons. It’s tough to envision a vintage season from an aging Chris Godwin coming off multiple injuries. Jalen McMillan and Tez Johnson round out a group still finding its identity. 18. Houston Texans Nico Collins is a legitimate WR1 talent when on the field and healthy. Only Puka Nacua has averaged more yards per route run over the last three seasons. Sophomore receivers Jayden Higgins and Jaylin Noel are both capable of contributing more significant volume, which becomes especially important if Tank Dell is unable to make a full return from his career-threatening injury. This unit had the safest hands in the league last year with just a 3.6% drop rate, but that may have been helped by how shallow its receptions were: Houston was the only offense to amass 2,000 yards on throws within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage in 2025. 19. Los Angeles Chargers Under Jim Harbaugh, this remains a team built around the run despite having a superb talent at quarterback. Additions like Charlie Kolar and David Njoku will primarily support the ground game, though tight end Oronde Gadsden II already posted 664 yards last season, opening the door for passing out of heavier personnel groupings. Ladd McConkey needs to clear up a lingering hamstring injury if he wants to rekindle the rookie form that saw him compile 1,300 yards two years ago. 20. Buffalo Bills Despite acquiring DJ Moore , there is not much depth out wide beyond him. The rushing threat posed by James Cook and Josh Allen remains the beating heart of this offense. Josh Palmer and Khalil Shakir round out the receiver room, while a trio of tight ends in Dalton Kincaid , Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes could lead to some triple tight end sets this season. Kincaid was particularly brilliant, leading all eligible tight ends with 2.7 yards per route run in 2025. 21. Indianapolis Colts Alec Pierce was one of only two qualifying receivers to average more than 20 yards per reception last year, and now steps into a larger role following the Pittman trade. The big question is whether either he or Josh Downs has the talent ceiling to function as a true WR1, and until that is answered, this group carries lingering doubt. Tyler Warren will continue to dominate when collecting possession in shallow areas. His 487 yards after the catch ranked second among tight ends last year. 22. Carolina Panthers Tetairoa McMillan has been a major success so far, and Jalen Coker finished last season on a 1,000-yard pace. Beyond those two, there is very little proven talent to speak of in this receiving room. Tight ends Ja’Tavion Sanders and Tommy Tremble have combined for four straight PFF receiving grades in the 50.0s over the last two seasons. 23. New York Giants This is perhaps a little low for a side with Malik Nabers at its disposal. If he returns back to his best, this group could be propelled into the top half of the league. Darnell Mooney joins after a brutal 443-yard, six-drop season in Atlanta where he was the NFC South’s lowest-graded receiver. Meanwhile, Isaiah Likely adds a useful receiving option at tight end. 24. New York Jets The Jets owned the lowest PFF receiving grade in the league last season (60.3) and were the only offense to register fewer than 50 explosive passing plays, but they’ve attempted to put things right this offseason. Garrett Wilson looks to assemble a full, healthy season after missing over half of last year’s action. Breece Hall remains one of the league’s more underrated receiving backs. Rookies Omar Cooper Jr. and Kenyon Sadiq add athletic upside to a, dare I say, promising group. 25. Washington Commanders Luke McCaffrey , Jaylin Lane , Treylon Burks , Dyami Brown and Van Jefferson make for a fairly uninspiring group behind veteran Terry McLaurin , who leads the league in contested catches over the last five years. Third-round pick Antonio Williams could quickly work his way into starting reps if that room struggles to produce. Incoming running back Rachaad White was a proven passing game contributor in Tampa Bay, representing another option that can shoulder the load for Jacory Croskey-Merritt , who caught just nine passes in his rookie season. 26. Baltimore Ravens This is not a great spot to be in for Baltimore after down years from Rashod Bateman and Mark Andrews , the latter of whom failed to surpass a 75.0 PFF receiving grade for the first time in his career. Zay Flowers remains the clear WR1, and Baltimore will be hopeful that third- and fourth-round picks Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt can provide a spark behind him. 27. New Orleans Saints With first-round pick Jordyn Tyson expected to miss roughly two months with a hamstring injury, the Saints will once again be heavily reliant on Chris Olave , who has struggled to stay on the field himself. Alvin Kamara reworked his contract to remain in New Orleans, while the addition of Travis Etienne Jr. gives the Saints another option out of the backfield. Juwan Johnson is coming off a career year at tight end. No team produced more contested catches when its quarterback was under pressure last season than the Saints. 28. Kansas City Chiefs The definition of insanity may be trotting out Xavier Worthy , Rashee Rice and Travis Kelce again in hopes that this group finally clicks the way it is supposed to on paper. The talent is evident, but the on-field results have not matched as of late. Only the Jets posted a lower PFF receiving grade over the second half of last season. One major upgrade comes from the backfield, where Isiah Pacheco ’s league-worst 35.6 PFF receiving grade from last season has been swapped for Kenneth Walker ’s much more respectable 71.4 receiving grade. Second-year pro Brashard Smith remains a major asset in the passing game here too. 29. Tennessee Titans Calvin Ridley is the only returning starter in a group that caught the fewest touchdowns of any offense last year. Carnell Tate arrives with high expectations given his lofty draft selection, but the loss of Chig Okonkwo might be felt. Wan'Dale Robinson and Elic Ayomanor round out what is an underwhelming group of weapons. However, bonus points are in order for Tyjae Spears , who forced the most missed tackles on receptions of any running back last year. 30. Cleveland Brown s First-rounder KC Concepcion and second-rounder Denzel Boston should provide a boost here. Veteran Jerry Jeudy is still in the fold, although he tied for the most drops in football last year. Meanwhile, Harold Fannin Jr. looks poised for an even larger target share in his second season after forcing 22 missed tackles last year, second among tight ends behind Trey McBride . Running back Dylan Sampson is another source of optimism following an 80.6 PFF receiving grade in a rookie season which saw him finish third among running backs in yards per route run. 31. Las Vegas Raiders Brock Bowers was the highest-graded pass-catcher in the red zone last season and is the clear centerpiece of this passing attack. Ashton Jeanty does not carry a reputation as a big receiving producer out of the backfield, and there is very little to speak of at wide receiver. Jalen Nailor , Tre Tucker , Jack Bech and Dont’e Thornton Jr. would struggle to see the field in a number of other offenses around the league. 32. Miami Dolphins This may be one of the worst wide receiver corps in recent memory on paper, since Miami did not meaningfully address this severe need this offseason. The Dolphins were the only team in football without 500 passing yards against man coverage last year. Tutu Atwell , Jalen Tolbert and Malik Washington sit atop the depth chart. None of these players have ever registered a single-season PFF receiving grade above 75.0, nor have any of them achieved 700 yards in a season. There is a chance for someone to emerge from nowhere, but the outlook here is bleak. records.new_body: 2026 NFL running back unit rankings: Falcons top the list All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 2026 NFL running back unit rankings: Falcons top the list By PFF.com Posted Aug 20, 2026 7:35 am EDT The Falcons come in No. 1: Led by the NFL's highest-ranked running back and with a competent backup, Atlanta has an edge in the run game. Detroit ranks second: Jahmyr Gibbs has averaged more than 5.0 yards per carry in each of his first three seasons, with Isiah Pacheco joining the backfield. Philadelphia rounds out the top three: Saquon Barkley leads a deep Eagles group that also features Tank Bigsby, Dameon Pierce, Elijah Mitchell and Will Shipley. through . NOTE ON THE LOGO: the is forced to solid white via filter:brightness(0) invert(1) so it reads on the blue panel no matter what colour the source PNG is. If you'd rather show the logo in full colour, delete the two filter declarations (one in the Subscribe to PFF+ Unlock every PFF grade, stat and premium tool Grades, advanced stats and premium tools (opens in new tab) Subscribe → PFF's 2026 NFL position rankings continue with all 32 running back groups. The position remains one of the league's most polarizing, with some teams leaning on every-down workhorses, while others spread the workload across multiple contributors. We begin in Atlanta, where Bijan Robinson headlines the NFL's top-ranked backfield. 1: Atlanta Falcons Bijan Robinson is the best running back in football, and by virtue of that alone, the Falcons have the best running back room in the league as long as he stays healthy. Robinson’s 86 missed tackles forced and 0.3 missed tackles forced per carry were each the best in the league. He was also one of just two running backs to average over 4.0 yards after first contact. Tyler Allgeier has moved on, so Atlanta proactively addressed the need for a relief pitcher and brought in Brian Robinson , who should see a similar workload to his 400-yard season with the 49ers last year. It's unlikely that any of the depth options behind the two Robinsons see meaningful play time. 2: Detroit Lions Jahmyr Gibbs is one of the most electrifying players with the football in his hands. He has posted three consecutive seasons with over 5.0 yards per carry to start his career. Isiah Pacheco had a rough final season as a receiver in Kansas City, but his power running isn't up for debate. His 9.3% stuff rate was the lowest of any running back with 100 carries last year, a testament to how Pacheco simply gobbles up early yardage. He's a fitting replacement for David Montgomery and should help rekindle the “Sonic and Knuckles” pairing in Detroit. 3: Philadelphia Eagles Only one back in Philadelphia's room started his career there: Will Shipley . The group is headed by Saquon Barkley , who is coming off his lowest-graded season since 2021 after being stuffed on almost a quarter of his carries. However, he was also the only running back to take 300 handoffs last year without a fumble. The additions of Dameon Pierce and Elijah Mitchell carry tangible prior NFL success if Barkley happens to miss time. Tank Bigsby , acquired via trade last September, is probably the main roster lock behind Barkley. His 0.31 missed tackles forced per attempt since 2024 ranks second among qualifying running backs. 4: Baltimore Ravens The success of PFF’s top-ranked running back unit from a year ago once again faces the age-old question: Is this finally the year Derrick Henry begins to slow down? His 79.4 PFF rushing grade from 2025 was his lowest since 2021, but Henry has a track record of following up down years with more dominance. As time marches on, the need for a legitimate secondary option behind Henry grows stronger, and it'll be Justice Hill again this season. Keep an eye on fifth-round rookie Adam Randall out of Clemson , who has drawn hype so far this offseason. 5: San Francisco 49ers Christian McCaffrey remains the best aerial threat at the running back position in the NFL, as proven by his 91.7 PFF receiving grade last year. His career receiving yards already rank sixth all time among backs. However, now at age 30, McCaffrey is coming off his lowest yards-per-carry season since his rookie year. This is a quietly stacked group behind him though, provided they can stay healthy, with rookie Ka elon Black battling Jordan James for the second-string job, and also dealing with preseason injuries. The aging wonder that is fullback Kyle Juszczyk also boosts San Francisco's standing here. 6: Miami Dolphins De'Von Achane proved he's one of the best players in football last season with a 90.5 PFF rushing grade and 5.7 yards per carry, 4.1 of which came after contact — the highest rate in the league. Behind him, Ollie Gordon is a big power back who should serve as a nice change of pace from the explosive Achane. However, he was one of only two running backs to average fewer than 3.0 yards per carry on 50 or more handoffs last season. Jaylen Wright rounds out the room. Achane already possesses a blistering burst of acceleration, but playing alongside a legitimate dual-threat quarterback for the first time may only unlock more of his danger as defenders hesitate on read option plays. 7: Los Angeles Rams It’s an unchanged backfield in Los Angeles led by Kyren Williams , with Blake Corum and Jarquez Hunter ready when called upon. At ages 26, 25 and 23 to begin the season, this is a well-rounded group with all three backs in or near their peak years. Williams and Corum each finished inside the top 10 in yards before contact last season. 8: Buffalo Bills It'll be the James Cook show once again after accruing 348 carries for almost 1,800 yards last season. Cook’s 734 yards before contact were over 200 more than the next-closest running back. This backfield is as close to a one-man operation as it gets in the NFL, and even Cook's fumbling issues aren’t enough to keep him off the field for a prolonged period. Ty Johnson and Ray Davis sit in reserve. 9: Indianapolis Colts Like Buffalo, this is also close to a one-man show with 2025 rushing touchdown leader Jonathan Taylor hoping he can rekindle the same MVP-caliber play from early last year. Only Derrick Henry has more rushing yards and touchdowns than Taylor over the last five years, and the pair have tallied identical yards before contact. DJ Giddens and incoming rookie Seth McGowan do little to elevate a backfield that has leaned on the same player for years now. 10: Arizona Cardinals Just like in our receiving corps rankings, running back is another area where the otherwise lackluster Cardinals aren't devoid of talent. The luxury selection of Jeremiyah Love pushes them inside the top 10 of the league's rankings, as this was frankly a respectable group even before that pick. Tyler Allgeier , James Conner and even Trey Benson could all reasonably take snaps anywhere in the league. Arizona had the most pass-heavy offense in football last year, running the ball on just 30% of plays by virtue of trailing so often. 11: Kansas City Chiefs Super Bowl 60 MVP Kenneth Walker III is an outstanding upgrade at running back after posting a league-best 91.5 PFF rushing grade last season. The Chiefs also have seventh-round pick from a year ago Brashard Smith, who carries plenty of potential as a receiving back, while Emari Demercado , who averaged 7.1 yards on 44 handoffs in Arizona last season, deserves to see more of the field. 12: Pittsburgh Steelers Expect the Steelers to lean on this backfield again in 2026 with Aaron Rodgers returning under center. The room has gotten crowded behind Jaylen Warren , who recorded his first 1,000-yard season a year ago. The free-agent addition of Rico Dowdle and the late-draft selection of Eli Heidenreich add depth. Don't forget about Kaleb Johnson , an exciting draft prospect a year ago who barely showed a glimpse of that upside as a rookie. On top of all that, the Steelers brought in Travis Homer for good measure. 13: New England Patriots It feels like New England will always have a handful of backs it can lean on, to the point where one missing a few weeks wouldn't be overly noticeable. Rhamondre Stevenson continues as the power back having amassed 13 explosive runs over seven games in the lead-up to the Super Bowl. Also, big things are expected from TreVeyon Henderson in year two. 14: Green Bay Packers Josh Jacobs had a down year in his second season in Green Bay, but he still posted his sixth 1,000-yard season in seven years. Significant contributor Emanuel Wilson has left for Seattle, while 2024 third-round pick MarShawn Lloyd has taken just six career handoffs amid a litany of injuries. His NFL career hinges on staying healthy for a prolonged stretch for the first time since college. Chris Brooks is an underrated piece of this unit and one of the better pass-protecting backs in the league, ranking sixth in PFF pass-blocking grade last year. 15: Chicago Bears The Bears don't have a standout star like some of the groups above, but D'Andre Swift was the third-highest-graded running back in the league over the latter half of last season. Second-year player Kyle Monangai converted over 60% of third- and fourth-down runs last year, and Roschon Johnson somewhat surprisingly returns after seeing just four snaps through the first half of last season before he was placed on injured reserve. Last year, Chicago’s 15.1% explosive run rate trailed only the Ravens . 16: Los Angeles Chargers Poor offensive line play did rookie Omarion Hampton no favors last season. He still managed respectable numbers while also working through multiple injuries. With a clean bill of health and reinforcements in the run game via added tight end depth, Hampton is an obvious breakout candidate. If not, Jim Harbaugh must lean on Keaton Mitchell or Kimani Vidal to shoulder the load. Hampton and Vidal had the second- and third-worst stuff rates in the league last season among qualifying running backs. 17: Las Vegas Raiders It's going to be all about Ashton Jeanty once more in the Vegas backfield, as it should be given the draft capital invested in him. His offensive line did him no favors last season, as he managed just 0.6 yards before contact per carry, the third-worst mark among all players with 100-plus carries. As a whole, the Raiders recorded the lowest PFF rushing grade in the NFL. Fourth-round rookie Mike Washington Jr. wasn't especially productive in college, but he's one of the most athletic backs the league has seen, running a 4.33-second 40-yard dash at 223 pounds. 18: Cincinnati Bengals This is a fairly standard, if not uninspiring, group headed by Chase Brown . Brown enters a contract year having posted almost identical back-to-back seasons with 4.3 yards per attempt in both years, along with differences of just nine carries, one missed tackle forced, three first downs, 12 yards after contact and one touchdown between 2024 and 2025. Veteran Samaje Perine retains his backup role, and no clear third option has emerged behind the duo. 19: New York Jets Fresh off a career-high 83.7 PFF rushing grade and a three-year extension, Breece Hall has a real case as a top-10 back in the league, with age on his side relative to names like Barkley and Taylor. Braelon Allen , a bruising change of pace, won't turn 23 until after the upcoming regular season, but he has forced just one missed tackle per every 10 carries since he was drafted. 20: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Rachaad White has moved on, replaced by Kenneth Gainwell , who moved the chains on 30% of his handoffs last season — the most of any running back with 100-plus carries. He should see respectable playing time to help keep Bucky Irving fresh. Irving's best football may still be ahead of him after a prolonged injury absence stunted his progress in 2025. The third-year back remains the highest-graded and most productive of any NFL running back aged 23 or below. 21: Dallas Cowboys The lowest-ranked unit in this exercise last offseason has enjoyed a nice bounce-back, namely thanks to a career year from Javonte Williams . Entering his sixth NFL season, Williams won’t turn 27 until next April. He delivered the fourth-most chain-moving runs on first down last season. Behind him, former fifth-round pick Jaydon Blue will hope for an expanded role in Year 2. 22: Tennessee Titans It's mostly as you were in the Titans backfield with Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears returning. Pollard has the eighth-most yards after contact of any running back over the last two years. As the league’s fourth-most pass-heavy offense last year, Tennessee is far more concerned with getting its aerial attack up and running, though both backs can contribute there as well. Behind them is rookie Nicholas Singleton out of Penn State , no stranger to a committee role after operating alongside Kaytron Allen throughout college. 23: New York Giants Cam Skattebo ‘s eagerly awaited return to action will see him reassume the lead role in an unchanged backfield, which was ranked second-worst in this exercise ahead of last season. When Skattebo featured between Weeks 2 and 7, his 82.2 PFF rushing grade ranked fourth in the league. Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary round out the platoon. We've seen plenty of each of these players in recent years — they have combined for 1,000 carries over the last four seasons. 24: Denver Broncos J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey return, with fourth-round rookie Jonah Coleman snapping at their heels. Coleman has an extremely compact build at 5-foot-8, 220 pounds. Dobbins remains productive when healthy, but availability has long been his biggest concern. Depth option Tyler Badie posted the top PFF pass-blocking grade in the league among qualifying running backs last year. 25: Cleveland Brown s This might feel a little high, but the Browns have youth on their side in the backfield, with second-year players Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson both in the fold. Sampson struggled with just 2.7 yards per carry but showed promise in the passing game. Judkins leans more on power than speed compared to former teammate TreVeyon Henderson , and several aspects of his game project well to a key every-down role moving forward. Browns running backs totaled just 134 yards before contact last season, comfortably the lowest in the league. 26: Houston Texans With a stacked defense and suspect ball security at quarterback, expect the Texans to lean on the run in 2026. David Montgomery is a like-for-like replacement for Nick Chubb , with a bit more youth. Montgomery is coming off a slight down year, but he finished strong with an 85.0 PFF rushing grade from Week 14 onward. Montgomery will likely continue to split reps as he did in Detroit. There isn't much competition behind Woody Marks as his running mate. 27: Carolina Panthers Chuba Hubbard , Trevor Etienne and AJ Dillon are all recognizable names, but collectively, the group lacks standout explosiveness. Hubbard failed to build on his highly productive 2024 campaign. He received double-digit carries only three times after Week 4 of last season. Question marks remain over the health of Jonathon Brooks , who has taken just nine handoffs since he was drafted 46th overall two years ago. 28: Seattle Seahawks The team with the highest PFF rushing grade in the league last season lost Kenneth Walker in free agency but has reloaded thoroughly. Zach Charbonnet is returning from a torn ACL, and the signing of Emanuel Wilson , who posted the second-lowest stuff rate in the NFL last year, is a strong one. Adding Jadarian Price in the draft turns this into one of the more exciting committee backfields in football. If the Seattle defense continues to dominate, expect plenty of opportunity for all three pieces. 29: Minnesota Vikings At 31 years old, Aaron Jones is still a viable threat, closing in on 10,000 career rushing yards. However, his PFF rushing grade dipped below 70.0 for the first time in his career last season. Jordan Mason is one of the more established secondary options in the league. This group could have trouble staying healthy again. Improvements up front are the first step toward Minnesota fielding a competitive rushing attack. 30: New Orleans Saints Travis Etienne is a strong upgrade for PFF’s second-lowest-graded rushing attack from last season. Veteran Alvin Kamara returns in what should be a passing game-focused role despite his career-low 39.5 PFF receiving grade last season. Kendre Miller and Devin Neal are the other options on the roster. 31: Washington Commanders The offseason additions of Rachaad White and Kaytron Allen, along with second-year pro Jacory Croskey-Merritt ‘s continued development, materially improve the health of this backfield. Croskey-Merritt ran for 805 yards as a rookie, and his receiving chops remain relatively unexposed. We aren't factoring the rushing threat of quarterbacks into this ranking, but the option Jayden Daniels presents is sure to add hesitation for defenders at the mesh point. 32: Jacksonville Jaguars Bhayshul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez blend speed and power on paper, just not a particularly dangerous version of it. Rodriguez’s 3.5 average yards after contact was among the 10 highest marks in the league last year, but aside from that, there isn't much to get excited about with this pairing of former Day 3 draft picks. records.new_body: Ranking every international game on the 2026 NFL schedule All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Ranking every international game on the 2026 NFL schedule By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 20, 2026 7:30 am EDT 49ers – Rams is a doozy: The second game of the season, and the first ever in Australia, will offer lots at stake. A high-level showing in Rio de Janeiro: Lamar Jackson and the Ravens take on Dak Prescott and the Cowboys in a clash between two revamped playoff hopefuls. Two tough matchups for the Jaguars: Jacksonville's consecutive London games offer two difficult opponents in the Eagles and Texans. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) The NFL has hosted 55 international regular-season games over the last two decades. Teams and their fanbases back home may understandably dislike how these games can throw their season out of rhythm with excessive travel and unfamiliar surroundings in a foreign country. However, with nine international games on the calendar this season, including the NFL’s first expedition to Australia, the overseas slate will only continue to grow over the coming years. London, the league’s regular outpost, has become a relatively safe bet for travelling teams. Having hosted 42 international games since 2007, the NFL has refined the voyage across the Atlantic down to a fine art, even if growing pains will remain as the league expands into first-time host nations. Before ranking this year’s games, it’s worth asking whether these contests actually play out any differently from those on U.S. soil. International matchups have developed a bit of a reputation for the wacky and wonderful over recent years. They’ve also garnered a reputation for serving up underwhelming matchups between teams with losing records. In terms of offensive output, though, these games are totally ordinary. Yards per play, plays per game, conversion rates and points scored all closely mirror what we see during a typical Sunday in the United States. What about how teams approach the game itself? Do they slow down the tempo, lean more heavily on the run or empty the playbook with trick plays? Not really. Coaches generally stick to what they tell reporters all week by “approaching this like any other game.” There is no overseas voodoo causing more footballs to be dropped or more field goals to be missed. With that myth put to bed, let’s rank the 2026 international slate. 1. San Francisco 49ers vs. Los Angeles Rams Melbourne, Australia | Thursday, Sept. 10 The most audacious offering on the international calendar is also the first, and the best. It’s one of only two international fixtures matching up teams who are inside the top 10 in preseason Super Bowl odds, and it doubles as an NFC West showdown that could decide the order in the sport’s most stacked division. The loser of this game will receive the benefit of the doubt given the logistics involved. Both teams will travel roughly 16 hours, and cross the International Date Line to play a game at approximately 10:30 am on a Friday morning. The football itself should be worth the trip, though. The Rams and 49ers finished first and third in PFF offensive grade last season, respectively, while also boasting PFF’s top two run-blocking units. With Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan on opposite sidelines, this is clearly the tactical highlight of the international schedule. The big matchup worth watching comes in the trenches. Trent Williams and Myles Garrett have only faced one another twice in their careers, on just 32 total passing snaps. Garrett certainly holds the upper hand, having generated eight pressures and a sack during those opportunities. That works out to a 25.0% pressure rate. For reference, Williams has surrendered pressure on just 4.5% of his pass-blocking snaps across six seasons with San Francisco. 2. Detroit Lions vs. New England Patriots Munich, Germany | Nov. 15 The other matchup featuring two teams inside the top ten in preseason Super Bowl odds lacks the divisional stakes of the Melbourne opener, but it occurs much closer to the business end of the season. It also showcases two of the NFL’s most efficient passing attacks. The Patriots and Lions ranked first and fifth, respectively, in passing yards per attempt last season, and this is a game where both offenses can easily trade scores into the 30s. Both franchises have enormous fanbases in Central Europe — the Patriots due to their success during the boom of football in Europe, while Amon-Ra St. Brown ’s German lineage has attracted swathes of supporters new to the sport. 3. Dallas Cowboys vs. Baltimore Ravens Rio de Janeiro, Brazil | Sept. 27 Star power alone earns this game a place near the top of the rankings. The name brand of these franchises also make it an easy sell before even considering the atmosphere a first-time game in Rio should provide. One key to the showdown will be Dallas’ ability to limit explosive runs from Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry . Last season, 15.1% of Baltimore’s rushing attempts gained at least 10 yards, the highest explosive run rate in the NFL. Meanwhile, Dallas surrendered gains of 10 or more yards on 15.8% of opposing rushing attempts, the third-worst mark in the league. Dallas has invested additional bodies into its run support, including Rashan Gary and first-round pick Caleb Downs, but major question marks remain. 4. Jacksonville Jaguars vs. Philadelphia Eagles London, England | Oct. 11 No active player has become more synonymous with international football than Trevor Lawrence . The Jaguars quarterback is set to take his 500th career snap in London this October. Almost 10% of all snaps Lawrence has played in the NFL have taken place in London. Lawrence has generally performed well overseas too, posting a 78.5 PFF overall grade across his London appearances. Jacksonville’s familiarity with the annual trip may be becoming a genuine competitive advantage rather than just a novelty. The challenge this time, however, is considerably steeper. The Eagles once again field one of the league’s deepest rosters and are among the highest-quality opponents Jacksonville has drawn on the international stage since the London series began. 5. Jacksonville Jaguars vs. Houston Texans London, England | Oct. 18 It may feel like the quintessential London NFL fixture, but these AFC South rivals have only brought their divisional matchup overseas once before, with Houston cruising to a 26-3 victory back in 2019. The top defensive performer in international games over the last decade belongs to, perhaps unsurprisingly, Josh Hines-Allen . His 39 pressures and 90.7 PFF pass-rushing grade in overseas contests both rank first among active players. Jacksonville’s pass protection will certainly be tested over its two-week London stay. Both of the Jaguars’ opponents ranked inside the league’s top six in total pressure rate last season. Whether remaining in London between games proves beneficial for the Jaguars will be interesting. This is the fourth consecutive year where a team will remain in Europe between games, and such sides are currently 3-0 in the second matchup. through . --> Read more Read more 2026 NFL defensive line rankings: Rams lead the league, Steelers and Texans open in top three By Gordon McGuinness (opens in new tab) → 6. New Orleans Saints vs. Pittsburgh Steelers Paris, France | Oct. 25 Paris finally joins the NFL map this season with a game that features an interesting clash of offensive identities. With Aaron Rodgers returning at quarterback, the Steelers are expected to continue leaning on a quick passing game designed to create yards after the catch. Pittsburgh averaged 6.5 yards after the catch per reception last season, the highest figure in the NFL. The Saints sat at the opposite end of the spectrum. They averaged just 4.3 yards after the catch per reception, the league’s lowest mark, instead relying on Tyler Shough to generate far more of the offense through the air. D.K. Metcalf has only played in two international games but has already made quite the impression. His 90.0 PFF receiving grade and 197 receiving yards both rank among the best overseas performances by any active receiver. 7. San Francisco 49ers vs. Minnesota Vikings Mexico City, Mexico | Nov. 22 This Nov. 22 meeting is the latest an international game has appeared on the NFL calendar since 2013. By that stage of the season, playoff races are beginning to take shape, making the scheduling decision a slight gamble. The league is probably approaching the latest point at which it can comfortably stage international games without the risk of sending a mathematically eliminated team abroad for what would effectively become a glorified exhibition. From a travel perspective, it’s also among the least disruptive trips of the year. Minnesota faces less than five hours in the air and no time-zone adjustment whatsoever. Yet Mexico City’s altitude presents a different challenge. The stadium sits roughly 2,300 feet higher above sea level than Denver’s Empower Field at Mile High, making conditioning arguably the toughest test. Justin Jefferson is also closing in on a unique milestone. He needs just 12 more receiving yards to become the first player in NFL history to reach 500 career receiving yards on foreign soil. 8. Washington Commanders vs. Indianapolis Colts London, England | Oct. 4 This game quietly offers one of the more intriguing schematic contrasts on the schedule. Washington played at breakneck speed throughout last season. The Commanders’ 58.6% no-huddle rate was more than double that of every other offense in the league, forcing opposing defenses to communicate without a chance to substitute or regroup. Indianapolis played vastly differently. The Colts reserved their up-tempo offense for obvious two-minute situations, preferring to huddle and control the pace for the vast majority of the game. Whether either side adjusts its usual rhythm after traveling across the Atlantic will be worth monitoring, even if history suggests neither coaching staff is likely to reinvent itself for one week. 9. Atlanta Falcons vs. Cincinnati Bengals Madrid, Spain | Nov. 8 It feels slightly unfair ranking any game last considering Joe Burrow is involved. Madrid should provide another spectacular backdrop, and Burrow alone gives this contest plenty of entertainment value. But compared to the rest of this year’s international slate, it is slightly lacking. One player with an excellent overseas résumé is Falcons guard Chris Lindstrom . He is the highest-graded active player in international games, having appeared in three overseas contests with Atlanta. Lindstrom has produced an outstanding 92.8 PFF overall grade in those affairs. records.new_body: 10 highest-graded NFL players entering contract years in 2026 All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 10 highest-graded NFL players entering contract years in 2026 By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 20, 2026 7:15 am EDT The Rams have decisions to make after 2026: Stars like Puka Nacua , Kevin Dotson , Davante Adams and Byron Young are all on expiring deals entering this upcoming year. Will the Cowboys commit to George Pickens ?: The All-Pro will play this year on the franchise tag, although what happens this spring is unknown. The Colts could try to keep Quenton Nelson at home: The 2018 draft pick has only suited up for Indianapolis but will be a free agent in 2027. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) Every offseason brings a fresh group of players heading into contract years, and 2026 is no exception. Below are the 10 highest-graded NFL players going into the final year of their current deal based on PFF grading from the 2025 season. For some, an extension already feels inevitable and could get done prior to this season getting underway. For others, there is almost no sign of a deal in sight, so 2026 will be a major season for each player to prove their worth to both their current team and other potential suitors around the league. One interesting thing to note is that of our 10 highest-graded players still waiting on contracts beyond this season, none are actively in the process of holding out throughout training camp. 1: Puka Nacua , Los Angeles Rams (96.1) There is still no word on a contract extension for Nacua, who heads into the final year of his rookie deal after the Rams took him in the fifth round out of BYU in 2023. His 96.2 PFF grade from last season set a new single-season record for a wide receiver. Nacua dropped only five of 158 catchable targets, hauled in 30 contested catches and averaged 3.57 yards per route run, a figure that’s nearly unmatched in PFF history. Whether the Rams move toward an extension soon remains unclear, and it may be Nacua’s off-field headaches rather than anything happening on Sundays that keeps Les Snead from locking him up long term. Snead has a long shopping list of upcoming free agents to negotiate with, but Nacua is evidently the pick of the bunch. 2: Kevin Dotson , Los Angeles Rams (87.3) The Rams go into 2026 with their strongest roster in years, but with it comes the reality that several key players beyond Nacua are set to hit free agency once the season ends. Four of the five projected starters on the offensive line fall into that category, and Dotson would be the most damaging loss among them. Atlanta just handed Matthew Bergeron a lofty extension, which makes it hard to see the Rams affording both Dotson and the younger Steve Avila . If Dotson reaches free agency in 2027, he will obviously draw real interest. Turning 30 is not the concern for guards that it is at other positions. Dotson is one of four Rams to appear on this list, and the franchise tag is unlikely to be the answer for him specifically. The tag groups all offensive linemen into one number, which makes it a poor proposition for an interior player who would effectively be paid tackle money. 3: Antonio Johnson , Jacksonville Jaguars (86.8) At 24 years old, Johnson is the youngest and perhaps least well-known member of this list. The former fifth-round pick enjoyed a career year in 2025, salvaging his chances of a major second contract after a putrid 43.8 PFF grade in 2024 almost led to him losing his job while still on his rookie deal. Johnson was the highest-graded safety in the league last season in coverage thanks to five total interceptions along with three pass breakups. Opposing quarterbacks had a passer rating of 53.4 when throwing into Johnson’s coverage. With just one season of real success under his belt, Johnson needs a similarly strong 2026 campaign to prove his worth to the Jaguars or another potential candidate in need of a safety next offseason. He appears to have bulked up since we last saw him, with reports coming out of camp that a role closer to what we have seen from Nick Emmanwori in Seattle could be in the pipeline for Johnson entering Year 4. 4. Joshua Uche , Miami Dolphins (86.0) Uche may prove to be one of the bargain signings of the offseason for the Miami Dolphins , who landed the veteran edge defender on a one-year, $1.4 million deal. How did a player who earned an 86.0 PFF grade at a premium position come this cheaply? Playing time is the obvious factor. Uche logged just 244 snaps last season and eventually lost his place in a deep Eagles rotation around midseason, but he quietly produced at an excellent level when given opportunities. Uche generated 25 pressures on just 142 pass-rushing snaps, with his 17.6% pressure rate ranking 11th among all edge defenders. Now on his fourth team in as many seasons, Uche should have an opportunity to play a much more prominent role in Miami. The last time he saw significant playing time came with New England in 2022, when he earned an 87.8 PFF pass-rushing grade. Highest pressure rate among edge defenders since 2022 Player Pressure Rate Micah Parsons 19.7% Nick Bosa 18.2% Will Anderson Jr. 17.9% Myles Garrett 17.7% Joshua Uche 17.7% 5: George Pickens , Dallas Cowboys (85.9) Quinnen Williams got his extension from Jerry Jones. George Pickens has not, and he will play 2026 under the franchise tag with his long-term future in Dallas still unresolved. It remains unclear whether the Cowboys can retain him once this season ends, particularly after committing big money elsewhere. Among receivers entering contract years, only Nacua graded higher than Pickens, and Pickens ranked second in yards, receptions, contested catches and yards per route run as well. If he ends up waiting for free agency to get paid, whoever signs Pickens will be getting a receiver who has only just turned 26. An uneven start and finish to his 2025 season should not overshadow the stretch in between. From Weeks 4 through 13, Pickens was close to unguardable, averaging over 100 yards a game. He returns to a perfect situation working with Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb . 6: Quenton Nelson , Indianapolis Colts (85.5) Nelson says he has not had any conversations about his expiring contract as he heads into Year 9 with the Colts at age 30. The sixth overall pick in 2018 signed a four-year, $80 million extension ahead of the 2022 season. His play dipped somewhat from 2021 to 2023, with three consecutive grades hovering near 70.0. But he has since returned to his earlier form, posting grades of 84.7 and 85.5 the past two seasons. Since entering the league in 2018, only Joel Bitonio and Joe Thuney have logged more snaps at interior offensive line than Nelson’s 8,643. He is a beacon of quality and consistency along the offensive interior, and emits the vibe of a one-franchise player who could eventually retire for the same team that drafted him without ever leaving. 7: Davante Adams , Los Angeles Rams (85.2) The next in a long line of expiring contracts on the Super Bowl favorites, Adams will be 34 years old when his deal expires at the end of this season, making him the oldest player on this list. His huge haul of touchdowns courtesy of MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford propelled Adams to seventh all-time in receiving scores. Simply an average 2026 season in the same offense should see him collect five more and surpass Larry Fitzgerald for sixth. Another contract for Adams entering his 14th NFL season would see him continue to chase the leaders on this list, but also pursue a much-deserved ring if he is unable to do so with the Rams this upcoming year. Now 33, Adams just delivered his highest-graded season since his first campaign with the Raiders in 2022. However, only 16% of last year’s yardage came after the catch. That number was as high as 42% during his prime years in Green Bay, and this signifies how Adams has adapted and evolved to prolong his career well into his elder years. 8: Zach Charbonnet , Seattle Seahawks (85.1) Only De’Von Achane and former teammate Kenneth Walker III posted higher PFF rushing grades than Charbonnet last season. He forced a missed tackle on one in every four carries, which ranked sixth-best in the league. The primary concern with Charbonnet, of course, is that he is rehabbing from a torn ACL sustained in the postseason and won’t be expected to return in the early parts of his contract year. With Walker departing in free agency, the Seahawks picked up Emanuel Wilson , and stopping there would’ve boded well for Charbonnet’s chances at a new contract. But investing a first-round draft pick in Jadarian Price may have been a death knell in Charbonnet’s chances of returning to Seattle. Holding both a high-paid back in his prime alongside a first-round running back on the same roster is virtually unheard of. 9: Byron Young , Los Angeles Rams (83.7) Young is set to receive a healthy payday at the end of this season, but whether or not that is with the Rams will depend on where Les Snead’s priorities are regarding the rest of this roster. He entered the league as an older rookie in 2023, so although he has only three seasons under his belt, the next team to sign Young will be getting a 29-year-old edge defender. The acquisition of Myles Garrett arguably doesn’t help Young’s chances of remaining with the Rams, who may no longer feel the need to shell out money for a premier edge defender for a few years at least. Young told reporters this offseason that it would be “nice to get a contract right now.” However, he is fully participating in all team activities. Young has shown material progress throughout his career. His pressure rate has grown from 10.2% as a rookie to 14.9% in Year 2 and 16.4% 2025. With it, his sack production has also steadily improved. He finished with 12 in total last season — tied for ninth in the league. 10: Mike Jackson , Carolina Panthers (83.5) Jackson enters the season with plenty to prove despite producing the best campaign of his career in 2025. Approaching age 30 and with only three seasons as a full-time starter behind him, another strong year could be crucial to his chances of securing a significant contract in free agency. His recent play suggests he is capable of earning one, considering Jackson finished last season as one of PFF’s 10 highest-graded cornerbacks and saved some of his best performances for Carolina’s toughest opponents. Jackson earned a season-high 92.0 overall PFF grade against the eventual Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks before delivering again in the Panthers’ playoff appearance against the Rams. In that wild-card defeat, Jackson broke up four passes and intercepted Matthew Stafford in the end zone as Carolina threatened an upset, ultimately producing a 90.4 overall PFF grade. The Panthers used a fourth-round pick on Will Lee III, giving them a younger option in the secondary and reducing the likelihood of committing significant money to Jackson beyond this season. However, cornerback is an eternal need, and as long as Jackson can play, somebody will pay. records.new_body: Biggest concern for every NFL team entering the 2026 season All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Biggest concern for every NFL team entering the 2026 season By Gordon McGuinness Posted Aug 20, 2026 6:30 am EDT Several contenders face major offensive questions: Buffalo lacks a true No. 1 wide receiver, Philadelphia must replace A.J. Brown and Detroit enters 2026 with uncertainty across its offensive line. Quarterback concerns could define multiple seasons: Joe Burrow ’s availability, C.J. Stroud’s decline and Bo Nix’s continued development are among the biggest issues facing their respective teams. Key defensive losses create significant holes: Cleveland must adjust to life without Myles Garrett, Dallas needs to rebuild its pass rush and Green Bay opens the season without Micah Parsons. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) Every NFL roster also enters 2026 with a problem it has yet to solve, whether it’s Miami fielding what, on paper, is the league’s worst receiving corps, Carolina heading into the season without either starting tackle or Cleveland adjusting to life after Myles Garrett . Here is the biggest concern facing each of the NFL’s 32 teams. Arizona Cardinals: A defense short on high-end talent The Cardinals had just three defenders play at least 300 snaps and earn a PFF grade above 70.0 last season, and none of them topped 80.0. One of those players, Calais Campbell , is no longer on the roster, while the only projected new starter, Roy Lopez , earned a PFF grade below 70.0 in 2025. In short, this defense lacks high-end talent. If Arizona is going to take a meaningful step forward in 2026, it will need young players such as Walter Nolen , Will Johnson and Denzel Burke to develop quickly and join edge defenders Josh Sweat and Zaven Collins as reliable, high-level contributors. Atlanta Falcons: Receiver depth behind Drake London The Falcons signed wide receiver Drake London to a long-term extension this offseason, with the former first-round pick out of USC having earned a PFF receiving grade above 85.0 in three of his first four NFL seasons. Despite missing time in 2025, London still earned an 89.9 PFF receiving grade, racked up 919 receiving yards and averaged 2.34 yards per route run. The concern is that Atlanta doesn’t have much else to get excited about at the position. Free-agent additions Jahan Dotson and Olamide Zaccheaus both earned PFF receiving grades below 60.0 and averaged fewer than 1.00 yards per route run in 2025. They do have Kyle Pitts at tight end and Bijan Robinson at running back, who combined for 213 targets last year, but don’t be shocked to see rookie third-round draft pick Zachariah Brand finish fourth on this team in targets. Baltimore Ravens: The interior offensive line The interior of the offensive line is still a question mark. On one hand, Vega Ioane and John Simpson should be upgrades over Daniel Faalele and Andrew Vorhees , but Ioane’s lack of NFL experience means the Ravens may have to accept some growing pains. They also lost center Tyler Linderbaum to the Raiders in free agency. While the addition of Pocic helps, he is still a step down from a player who ranked fifth among all centers in PFF overall grade last season. Buffalo Bills: No true No. 1 receiver It’s not that there isn’t talent around Allen, but he does lack a true No. 1 target at wide receiver. Khalil Shakir led the Bills ’ wide receivers in yards per route run last season at 1.80, but that ranked just 30th among NFL wide receivers. They do have Dalton Kincaid at tight end, who led all players at the position in yards per route run(2.70), but it’s unlikely Buffalo ’s wide receivers will strike much fear into opposing defenses in 2026. That doesn’t mean the offense can’t be successful. Rather, it suggests the passing game will continue to flow through the middle of the field. Carolina Panthers: Both tackles are out The Panthers are currently without both starting offensive tackles. Left tackle Ikem Ekwonu suffered a ruptured patellar tendon in the wild-card loss to the Rams , while right tackle Taylor Moton is sidelined with blood clots. It remains unclear when either will return in 2026, but both appear likely to miss at least the start of the season. That makes the additions of Rasheed Walker and Monroe Freeling through free agency and the draft even more important. Walker earned a 69.3 PFF pass-blocking grade in 2025, while Freeling was one of college football’s top pass protectors, allowing just two pressures on 469 pass-blocking snaps. Still, losing both starting tackles is a significant concern, and for all of Freeling’s potential, he has yet to play an NFL snap. Chicago Bears: Replacing 23 interceptions, and the pass rush The Bears recorded 23 interceptions across the regular season and playoffs last year, but only four came from players still on the roster. Replacing that level of turnover production will not be easy, particularly after Kevin Byard accounted for seven interceptions. Coby Bryant and Dillon Thieneman will need to make an immediate impact to help fill that void. The lack of a true difference-maker off the edge is also a concern for Chicago’s defense. Montez Sweat generated 65 total pressures, but his 13.5% PFF pass-rush win rate ranked just 38th among edge defenders with at least 100 pass-rushing snaps. His career best came in 2022, when his 15.0% pass-rush win rate was tied for 24th at the position. Cincinnati Bengals: Joe Burrow’s availability Optimism about the offensive line should be tempered, given the small sample size of its late-season improvement, and it is not outside the realm of possibility that the unit regresses in 2026. Burrow has played 10 or fewer games in three of his six NFL seasons, and the Bengals need to keep him healthy in 2026 if they are going to contend. Responsibility is shared between Burrow and the offensive line. The pass protection has not been good enough for much of his career, and Burrow has never posted a pressure-to-sack rate below 19.0% in a season. If he stays healthy throughout the 2026 season, the Bengals will have a legitimate chance to compete for a championship. Cleveland Browns: Life without Myles Garrett, and the quarterbacks The loss of Garrett means it’s entirely possible that the Browns ’ roster is worse than the one that went 5-12 last season. There is talent here, but much of it lacks experience at crucial positions, and Cleveland could wind up fielding seven offensive starters who have no more than one year of NFL experience. Then there’s the quarterback problem. Shedeur Sanders earned a 44.1 PFF grade as a rookie, and Deshaun Watson earned a 63.1 PFF grade in 2024, the last time he took an NFL snap. Explore PFF Premium Stats The most advanced NFL and college football statistics — player grades, WAR, TIPP, and more. Filter by position, team, season, and snap count. NFL Premium Stats (opens in new tab) College Premium Stats (opens in new tab) Dallas Cowboys: The pass rush Trading Micah Parsons before the 2025 season left a massive void in the Cowboys ’ pass rush, and the free-agent departures of Jadeveon Clowney and Dante Fowler only compounded the issue. Dallas is now counting on Rashan Gary to rediscover his best form, Donovan Ezeiruaku to take another step forward and rookie Malachi Lawrence to make an immediate impact. Denver Broncos: Bo Nix’s development The Broncos simply don’t have many weaknesses on either side of the ball. If you were being picky, you could argue that an offensive line as good as theirs would benefit from having a truly elite running back behind it. What will likely define their season, though, is how big of a step forward Bo Nix can take in his third year. He has already improved his PFF passing grade from 73.8 as a rookie to 76.1 in Year 2, while his big-time throw rate climbed from 3.7% to 5.0%. Another jump in 2026 could be what takes an already talented Broncos roster to the next level. Detroit Lions: The offensive line The Lions finished the 2025 season with PFF’s 12th-ranked offensive line, but there are question marks or inexperience at every position entering 2026. Sewell is coming off a career-best 95.1 PFF grade, though his elite production has historically been driven more by his run blocking than his pass protection. While he has never earned a PFF pass-blocking grade below 69.4 and is coming off a career high in that facet as well, his transition to left tackle will be worth monitoring. Mays projects as a solid option at center but has played more than 500 snaps just once in his career. At left guard, Christian Mahogany earned a 40.7 PFF pass-blocking grade last season. Tate Ratledge impressed as a rookie, posting a 70.3 PFF grade at right guard, but he will line up next to rookie Blake Miller in 2026 after spending last season alongside Sewell. Green Bay Packers: Micah Parsons’ ACL recovery Micah Parsons was outstanding in his first season with the Packers , generating 79 total pressures on 436 pass-rushing snaps while earning a 92.9 PFF pass-rush grade. Through five NFL seasons, he has never posted a PFF grade lower than 91.6. However, because he suffered an ACL injury so late in the season, he will not be ready for Week 1. He is set to return by mid-October, leaving a significant void in Green Bay’s pass rush. Outside of Parsons, Lukas Van Ness and Devonte Wyatt were the only Packers defensive linemen to earn PFF pass-rush grades above 70.0 last season, posting marks of 71.3 and 71.4, respectively. Houston Texans: C.J. Stroud’s decline C.J. Stroud impressed as a rookie in 2023, leading all rookie quarterbacks and ranking 13th among all qualified quarterbacks in PFF grade (83.2). His performance has declined in each of the past two seasons, however, as he finished 15th in PFF grade in 2024 before falling to 32nd in 2025. That leaves the Texans facing both short- and long-term questions at the position. In the long term, they must determine whether Stroud has shown enough to warrant a lucrative extension in a market where 12 quarterbacks already earn more than $50 million annually. In the short term, the question is whether he can put together the kind of sustained stretch needed to lead Houston on a playoff run. As a rookie, Stroud posted four straight games with PFF grades above 80.0. In his second season, he produced another promising stretch, earning grades above 80.0 in three of four games. At just 24 years old, Stroud still has ample time to develop into the quarterback the Texans envisioned when they drafted him. But if Houston is going to realize its Super Bowl aspirations, he will either need to take another step as a passer or produce the type of postseason run that quarterbacks such as Joe Flacco and Nick Foles rode to Super Bowl titles. Indianapolis Colts: Daniel Jones’ inconsistency The Colts ’ commitment to Daniel Jones is relatively low risk, with his contract tying him to the team for only the next two seasons. Even so, it is fair to question whether he is the long-term answer at quarterback. Jones opened 2025 strongly, ranking 10th among quarterbacks in PFF grade (80.3) through Week 8, but he fell to 32nd from Week 9 onward. Over the full season, his 3.1% big-time throw rate ranked 34th among the 45 quarterbacks with at least 100 dropbacks, while his 3.9% turnover-worthy play rate was tied for the 13th highest. Jones’ career body of work offers little reason to expect a dramatic turnaround. Across seven NFL seasons, he has produced a higher big-time throw rate than turnover-worthy play rate just once, and his career 2.9% big-time throw rate would have ranked only 36th among those 45 qualifying quarterbacks in 2025. Jacksonville Jaguars: The interior offensive line The Jaguars return two projected starters on the interior offensive line who struggled in pass protection last season. Center Robert Hainsey earned a PFF pass-blocking grade below 60.0 and ranked 34th among the 40 centers who played at least 300 snaps, while right guard Patrick Mekari also finished below the 60.0 mark, ranking 67th out of 81 qualifying guards. Jacksonville is in much better shape at both tackle spots, but the interior of the offensive line projects as one of the weaker units in the NFL entering 2026. Kansas City Chiefs: Wide receiver production Part of the reason for the Chiefs ’ struggles in 2025 was a lack of production at wide receiver. Marquise Brown led the group with just 587 receiving yards, while Rashee Rice ’s 77.2 PFF receiving grade was the best among the team’s wide receivers. Xavier Worthy also took a step back from his rookie season, with his PFF receiving grade falling from 71.6 to 66.3 and his yards per route run dropping from 1.51 to 1.25. Rice is expected to be available in Week 1 after missing significant time in each of the past two seasons. His career average of 2.29 yards per route run highlights his status as Kansas City’s most productive wide receiver, but the Chiefs need him to stay on the field in 2026. through . If you'd rather show the logo in full colour, delete the two filter declarations (one in the Subscribe to PFF+ Unlock every PFF grade, stat and premium tool Grades, advanced stats and premium tools (opens in new tab) Subscribe → Las Vegas Raiders: A thin receiving corps The Raiders have done a nice job adding talent at the skill positions in recent years, selecting tight end Brock Bowers and running back Ashton Jeanty in back-to-back NFL Drafts, but wide receiver remains a weakness. None of their returning wide receivers who saw at least 30 targets last season averaged more than 1.20 yards per route run. Their biggest addition at the position was Jalen Nailor, who averaged just 1.06 yards per route run last season. In fact, none of the wide receivers currently on the roster ranked better than 78th among the 111 players at the position with at least 30 targets in the regular season. That leaves 2025 second-round pick Jack Bech as perhaps their best hope for a breakout at the position. He showed flashes as a rookie but saw just 28 targets, giving him an opportunity to earn a much larger role in Year 2. Los Angeles Chargers: Change on the defensive side of the ball Former defensive coordinator Jesse Minter is now the head coach of the Baltimore Ravens, with Chris O’Leary taking over the Chargers’ defense. O’Leary is highly regarded after an impressive 2025 season at Western Michigan , and the scheme should remain largely similar, but replacing Minter still introduces some uncertainty. The Chargers also lost Odafe Oweh , who led the team with an 81.0 PFF pass-rush grade during his stint in Los Angeles after arriving from Baltimore via trade. Between Oweh’s departure and the transition from Minter to O’Leary, there is reason for some caution with this defense heading into 2026, even if there isn’t necessarily reason for pessimism. Los Angeles Rams: Left tackle Starting left tackle Alaric Jackson will face a suspension for violating the NFL’s Personal Conduct Policy, and David Quessenberry is currently in line to replace him. Quessenberry enjoyed a strong season with the Tennessee Titans in 2021, earning a 79.2 PFF grade, but he hasn’t earned a grade above 65.0 since. He also hasn’t played more than 400 snaps in a season since then. Miami Dolphins: The receiving corps On paper, this is the worst receiving corps in football. The Dolphins ’ top three pass-catchers by PFF receiving grade from the 2025 season — wide receivers Jaylen Waddle and Tyreek Hill , and tight end Darren Waller — are no longer on the roster. Among returning wide receivers and tight ends, Greg Dulcich led the group with just 335 receiving yards last season. There is hope for the future after Miami selected three wide receivers within the first five rounds of the draft. Right now, though, the top of the depth chart consists of Jalen Tolbert , Tutu Atwell and Malik Washington . None of the three earned a PFF grade higher than 60.9 last season, and they combined for just 712 receiving yards across the regular season and playoffs in 2025. Minnesota Vikings: The pass rush The Vikings traded away edge defender Jonathan Greenard, who led the team with 47 total pressures last season. Defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ scheme relies heavily on the blitz, so linebacker Eric Wilson could once again rank among the team’s leaders in total pressures. That approach also reduces the need for a true difference-maker off the edge compared to many other defenses, but the lack of an edge defender with a PFF pass-rush grade above 75.0 does limit the unit’s flexibility. New England Patriots: No dominant edge defender The Patriots have talent throughout their defense, but if there’s one area to criticize, it’s the lack of a truly dominant edge defender. Gabe Jacas could develop into that player, and the addition of Dre’Mont Jones gives them another versatile piece they can move around the defensive front. Jones ranked just 25th among edge defenders in pressures (51) during the regular season last year, while Harold Landry tied for 28th in his first season in New England despite battling a lingering knee injury. The Patriots don’t lack capable edge rushers, and they can manufacture pressure through scheme, but they would benefit from a more consistent difference-maker off the edge. New Orleans Saints: The defense Outside of Chase Young on the edge, there are few proven difference-makers on the Saints ’ defense. Just one New Orleans defender who played at least 300 snaps earned a PFF grade above 80.0 last season: linebacker Demario Davis , who has since departed for the New York Jets . Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry did take a step forward in his second NFL season, with the 2024 second-round pick ranking 29th among cornerbacks with a 71.4 PFF coverage grade. The Saints also added linebacker Kaden Elliss , who provides another pass-rushing threat after his 30 pressures ranked second among linebackers last season. Beyond Young, McKinstry and Elliss, however, this is a defense that desperately needs some of its younger players to emerge in 2026. New York Giants: Ten new starters Including Patrick Ricard at fullback, the Giants are projected to have 10 new starters between offense and defense. Given how well they have drafted in recent years, combined with the arrival of Super Bowl-winning head coach John Harbaugh, there is reason to believe the franchise is headed in the right direction. At the same time, the sheer scale of the roster turnover illustrates just how much work was needed. It would not be surprising if the rebuild still requires another season before the Giants are ready to make a serious push for the postseason.
