NFL Premium Stats (opens in new tab) College Premium Stats (opens in new tab) New York Jets: Quarterback PFF grading dates back to the 2006 season, and in 20 years of data, the Jets have never had a quarterback earn an 80.0-plus PFF grade. Aaron Rodgers came closest in 2024 at 77.6. Their best hope of ending that streak is 35-year-old Geno Smith , who is coming off one of the worst seasons of his career. They are also projected to have eight new starters on defense, meaning they’ll need to get on the same page quickly this summer to avoid a slow start. Philadelphia Eagles: Replacing A.J. Brown Trading A.J. Brown made long-term sense for the Eagles , netting them a first-round pick in the 2028 NFL Draft, but there’s no replacing a player of his caliber in the short term. Even in what was widely viewed as a down season, Brown still topped 1,000 receiving yards in 2025. His departure should lead to a larger target share for DeVonta Smith , but it also places greater expectations on newcomers Dontayvion Wicks and Makai Lemon. Pittsburgh Steelers: Aaron Rodgers is not the quarterback he was The system and the players need to fit around Aaron Rodgers because he’s not the same quarterback he once was. His 68.0 PFF grade in 2025 was his lowest in any season in which he played at least 100 snaps. His 6.6-yard average depth of target was also the lowest of his career. The positive to take from that is he should push the ball downfield more in 2026 with Pittman at wide receiver and McCarthy as head coach. San Francisco 49ers: Misses on the defensive line The 49ers need much more from their first- and second-round picks on the defensive line this season. Last season, Mykel Williams played just 385 snaps before suffering a season-ending injury, earning a 54.7 PFF grade and generating only 19 pressures on 245 pass-rushing snaps. Alfred Collins stayed healthy and logged 550 snaps, but his 35.0 PFF grade was tied for the second-lowest among the 94 interior defenders who played at least 300 snaps. San Francisco still has plenty of talent on defense, but not enough to absorb misses on premium draft picks along the defensive line. Both Williams and Collins will be expected to take significant steps forward in 2026. Seattle Seahawks: A new offensive coordinator The Seahawks did lose offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak, who left to become the Las Vegas Raiders’ head coach. Brian Fleury replaces him after spending the past seven seasons with the San Francisco 49ers , where he served as run game coordinator and tight ends coach in his final year. With Sam Darnold still at quarterback and the talented receiving corps around him, Seattle has more than enough talent to remain one of the NFL’s better offenses. Even so, a transition to a new playcaller could bring some early growing pains. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: The defensive interior Outside of Vita Vea , there are significant question marks along the Buccaneers ’ defensive interior heading into 2026. Calijah Kancey missed most of his third NFL season and has earned PFF grades below 50.0 in each of his first three years. He has flashed as a pass-rusher, but his PFF pass-rush grade, pressure rate and total pressures all declined from his rookie season in 2023 to 2024, with his pass-rush grade falling again over a limited sample in 2025. Veteran A'Shawn Robinson provides experience alongside Vea and Kancey, but he has not earned a PFF grade above 65.0 since 2021, leaving Tampa Bay with plenty of uncertainty beyond Vea on the interior. Tennessee Titans: The offensive line, especially left tackle Peter Skoronski has developed into a reliable presence on Tennessee’s offensive line, leading the team with an 84.5 PFF pass-blocking grade last season. Right tackle JC Latham also showed encouraging improvement down the stretch, but there are still significant questions across the unit, particularly at left tackle. The Titans signed Dan Moore Jr. ahead of the 2025 season in the hope he would solidify the position, but he allowed 48 total pressures, tied for the third most among all offensive linemen. Austin Deculus was added in free agency to provide competition, though after earning a 36.5 PFF grade — the third-lowest among qualifying offensive linemen in 2025 — he is unlikely to pose a serious challenge for the starting job. Washington Commanders: Receiver depth behind Terry McLaurin Terry McLaurin remained productive when healthy in 2025, averaging 2.22 yards per route run despite an injury-shortened season. Beyond him, however, Washington lacks a proven receiving threat who consistently challenges opposing defenses. Treylon Burks has averaged fewer than 1.00 yards per route run in each of the past three seasons, while Dyami Brown has never topped 350 receiving yards in a regular season across his five-year career. Luke McCaffrey showed promise, averaging 1.90 yards per route run last season, but he has seen just 42 targets through his first two NFL seasons. If rookie Antonio Williams can make an immediate impact, it would provide a significant boost to what is, on paper, one of the league’s weaker wide receiver groups. records.new_body: 5 NFL units that could take a step back in 2026 All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 5 NFL units that could take a step back in 2026 By Bradley Locker Posted Aug 20, 2026 6:15 am EDT Dolphins pass-catchers have done an about-face: Jaylen Waddle , Tyreek Hill and Darren Waller are all gone from a unit that ranked 10th in PFF receiving grade. The Chiefs ‘ secondary has lots to replace: With no more Trent McDuffie , Jaylen Watson and Bryan Cook , Andy Reid will need players like Mansoor Delane to step up. Can the Bears ‘ offensive line play similarly?: Chicago lost center Drew Dalman to retirement and got a clean bill of health on four of five starters in 2025. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) With the NFL preseason entering its second week, the regular season is fast approaching. A fresh start is naturally accompanied by enormous positivity; after all, almost anything can happen when the pads come on for real in September. However, some of that optimism has already been dashed by a wave of injuries, a number of which look very difficult to overcome. On top of that, certain coaching staffs are presumably finding out in real time that their individual position groups may not be up to par relative to where they thought. Every season, certain units fall as others rise — whether due to absences, a new coaching staff or simply worse play from returning participants. These five contingents are ones to circle for some possible regression in 2026. Miami Dolphins receiving corps First-time head coach Jeff Hafley joins a Miami team staring down a rather bleak outlook for the 2026 campaign after gutting its roster. Arguably the biggest impact of that will be felt in the pass-catching room. Last year, the Dolphins placed 10 th in team PFF receiving grade. The star of the show was Jaylen Waddle , whose 85.2 receiving mark ranked eighth among receivers with at least 90 targets. Yet others also produced next to Waddle, with Darren Waller , Tyreek Hill and Greg Dulcich all reaching at least an 80.0 such grade. New general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan completed an overhaul this offseason by trading Waddle to the Broncos , cutting Hill and letting Waller walk. Now, Miami enters the 2026 season with one of the worst receiving corps on paper, starting players such as Malik Washington , Tutu Atwell and third-round rookie Caleb Douglas. It’s safe to say that Dolphins pass-catchers likely won’t get anywhere close to matching their efficacy from last year. Carolina Panthers offensive line Carolina has quietly built an above-average offensive line in recent seasons, but injuries and exits have already taken a toll — and are casting real doubt about how strong the unit will be in 2026. In 2025, the Panthers’ starting five placed eighth in overall PFF grade, finishing at least that high for the second straight year. The team received no worse than a 70.9 overall PFF grade across at least 950 blocking snaps from each of Taylor Moton , Ikem Ekwonu and Damien Lewis . Likewise, role players Austin Corbett (66.0) and Brady Christensen (72.5) were very capable fill-ins. However, Ekwonu is expected to miss the majority of the season after suffering a ruptured patellar tendon in the playoffs, while Moton will be sidelined into the starting slate due to blood clots in his lung. Also, former starting center Cade Mays headed to Detroit, while Corbett is now in Buffalo. The Panthers did locate replacements in the form of first-round pick Monroe Freeling, former Packer Rasheed Walker , ex-Saint Luke Fortner and fifth-round selection Sam Hecht. However, the team is likely to usher in three new starters — and it’s especially unknown how each rookie would fare off the bat if they both win first-team roles. Kansas City Chiefs secondary After a highly unusual season, the Chiefs have regrouped for a pivotal 2026 campaign. Part of what Andy Reid will have to sort out is how to replace tremendous production in his defensive backfield. While Kansas City was maligned at numerous spots last season, secondary wasn’t one of them. Indeed, the Chiefs registered the fifth-best overall PFF grade by team for cornerbacks and safeties — including sitting in the top eight for both coverage and run defense. Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson each ranked in the top 11 for overall PFF grade by cornerbacks, while Bryan Cook ’s 83.3 mark was the fourth-highest for qualifiers at safety. The dilemma is that all three are now gone. General manager Brett Veach was able to find new options like sixth overall pick Mansoor Delane and free-agent safety Alohi Gilman , but that’s a ton of well-rounded talent to lose in one fell swoop. Delane and second-year cornerback Nohl Williams (75.6 PFF coverage grade) boast tremendous potential, and the Chiefs can also call upon players like Chamarri Conner , Jaden Hicks and Jadon Canady. Nonetheless, a drop-off should inevitably be expected for this group this season, even if Steve Spagnuolo can work some magic. Minnesota Vikings defensive line The Vikings’ defense has been a hallmark under Brian Flores, earning two straight top-seven finishes in EPA per play. Doubting the defensive mastermind Flores carries risk, but his defensive line is also reshuffled entering this season. Although the Vikings’ big-ticket free-agent signings didn’t pan out, the team’s defensive line still ranked 10 th in overall PFF grade. That included sitting 13 th in PFF pass-rush grade and 11 th in PFF run-defense mark. Six separate Minnesota defensive linemen generated at least 25 pressures, and five of those secured no worse than a 65.5 overall PFF grade. The biggest loss confronting this unit is edge rusher Jonathan Greenard , whose 131 pressures since 2024 are the 13 th -most at the position. The Vikings do bring back Dallas Turner and Andrew Van Ginkel , but they’ll have their work cut out for them to individually step up — and there’s minimal depth behind them. The interior of Minnesota’s defensive line is even greener, with rookies Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange poised for significant roles next to Jalen Redmond . A coach like Flores has the acumen to mask a weaker defensive line, especially given his blitz-heavy scheme. But how well the Vikings’ front four can rush the passer and stop the run looms as a defining element of their season. Chicago Bears offensive line Like Flores, Ben Johnson has established himself as one of the foremost minds in football — reflected, in part, by his offensive turnaround with Chicago in only Year 1. However, the guru will have to confront multiple new pieces along his starting offensive line. The Bears’ offensive line was one of the anchors of the team’s success, securing the sixth-best team overall PFF grade at the position. Much of that was rooted in continuity, as four of five starters played at least 1,227 snaps. Newcomers Joe Thuney , Drew Dalman and Jonah Jackson combined to produce the fourth-best interior grade, while All-Pro right tackle Darnell Wright sat above a 74.6 in both pass- and run-blocking. Dalman’s sudden retirement this offseason left the Bears to trade for former Patriots starter Garrett Bradbury , who has finished below a 63.0 grade in six of his seven career seasons. On top of that, uncertainty mounts at left tackle in the wake of Ozzy Trapilo ’s ruptured patella tendon, although he was recently cleared. Further, Jackson has failed to reach 900 snaps in three of the past four seasons, prompting some concern about his availability despite the fact he remained healthy in 2025. Chicago retains two certified cornerstones in Wright and Thuney, with Jackson also impressive if he can stay on the field. Yet the performance of Bradbury (or rookie Logan Jones ) on the inside, coupled with what happens at left tackle, pose questions about whether or not this offensive line will turn in an encore. records.new_body: Fantasy Football: Perfect draft strategy, round by round for 2026 Hero RB builds All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting Premium Content Sign Up Fantasy Football: Perfect draft strategy, round by round for 2026 Hero RB builds By Nathan Jahnke Posted Aug 20, 2026 5:30 am EDT Draft Brock Bowers in the second round: The advantage of a hero-RB build is that it allows you to target one of the elite tight ends or quarterbacks in the early rounds. A healthy Jonathon Brooks should lead the Carolina Panthers backfield: The former second-round pick is finally healthy, and if he proves he can stay on the field, he has a clear path to becoming Carolina's lead back. He is the ideal second running back option for a hero build. Start with an elite running back: Jahmyr Gibbs is the top first-round target for a hero-RB build after averaging at least 21 PPR points per game in each of the past two seasons. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) This perfect draft strategy for 12-team, single-quarterback, redraft PPR fantasy football leagues is built on a consensus of current average draft positions (ADPs) from ESPN, Sleeper and Yahoo. It's your round-by-round guide to building a winning roster. While I wouldn't necessarily advise a hero running back strategy this season, this is how to best execute one to maximize your chances. Round 1, Picks 1-12: Draft a running back By definition, a hero-RB build needs one star running back to anchor the roster. While that player can occasionally be found early in the second round, it is generally safer to secure your hero back in the first round and then avoid the position for several rounds. Top Target: Jahmyr Gibbs Gibbs is the only running back to average at least 21 PPR points per game in each of the last two seasons, combining elite rushing efficiency, double-digit touchdown production and over 500 receiving yards. David Montgomery ‘s departure removes the main factor that had previously capped his goal-line ceiling. Detroit’s offensive line is the primary concern after dropping from second to 13th in PFF run-blocking grade last season. Two more starters were replaced this offseason, adding further uncertainty to an area central to Gibbs’ production. New offensive coordinator Drew Petzing has shown a willingness to feature a lead back heavily, so a dramatic shift in usage is unlikely. The same talented supporting cast that creates slight competition for touches also helps Detroit remain one of the league's best offenses. The other elite running backs at a similar ADP carry comparable or greater uncertainty, which keeps Gibbs at the top of the position. Possible Targets: Bijan Robinson , Christian McCaffrey , Jonathan Taylor , De'Von Achane , James Cook III Round 2, Picks 13-24: Draft a tight end The primary advantage of a hero-RB build is that it allows you to prioritize tight end and quarterback early, eliminating the need to spend additional draft capital on backups at either position. records.new_body: 2026 College Football Preview: Oklahoma Sooners All NFL Fantasy College - current NFL Draft DFS Betting 2026 College Football Preview: Oklahoma Sooners By Max Chadwick Posted Aug 19, 2026 12:52 pm EDT Oklahoma’s defense remains its biggest strength: The Sooners enter 2026 with PFF’s No. 5 linebacker unit, No. 10 defensive line and a top-15 secondary. John Mateer’s rebound could define the season: Mateer earned a 50.3 PFF grade from Week 7 onward after his performance declined following a throwing-hand injury. David Stone anchors an elite defense: The 315-pound defensive tackle posted an 80.7 PFF run-defense grade and a 13.0% run-stop rate last season. Explore PFF Premium Stats The most advanced NFL and college football statistics — player grades, WAR, TIPP, and more. Filter by position, team, season, and snap count. NFL Premium Stats (opens in new tab) College Premium Stats (opens in new tab) It’s been a roller-coaster four years for Brent Venables as Oklahoma’s head coach. After going 6-7 in 2022, the Sooners improved to 10-3 in 2023, fell back to 6-7 in 2024 and rebounded to 10-3 last season. In 2025, Oklahoma made its first College Football Playoff appearance in six years before losing at home to Alabama in the first round. The defense fueled the Sooners’ success, ranking seventh nationally in EPA per play, while an offense that ranked just 100th in the same metric ultimately held them back. Notable Transfer Portal Additions WR Trell Harris ( Virginia ) WR Parker Livingstone ( Texas ) OT E’Marion Harris ( Arkansas ) TE Hayden Hansen ( Florida ) TE Rocky Beers ( Colorado State ) Notable Transfer Portal Losses WR Javonnie Gibson ( Cincinnati ) RB Jovantae Barnes ( Kentucky ) OT Jacob Sexton ( Oklahoma State ) LB Sammy Omosigho ( UCLA ) CB Gentry Williams ( Georgia ) through . --> Read more Read more Top-10 returning players at every position By Max Chadwick (opens in new tab) → Biggest strength: Defense should remain elite Oklahoma should once again field one of the top defenses in college football. The Sooners boast our No. 5 linebacker unit, No. 10 defensive line and a top-15 secondary. The star of the group is defensive tackle David Stone, who enters the season as a projected top-10 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. Biggest question mark: Can they find greater consistency on offense? Oklahoma’s defense did an incredible job of carrying an inconsistent offense last season, particularly after John Mateer returned from his hand injury. Mateer was one of the least accurate quarterbacks in the country after returning, while the Sooners’ running backs combined to average just 4.2 yards per carry and force only 23 missed tackles all season. The offensive line and receiving corps also struggled to find consistency outside of Isaiah Sategna III. The offense needs more reliable production across the board in 2026, but if it can take a significant step forward, Oklahoma has the defense to emerge as a legitimate SEC title contender. Quarterback: John Mateer Before injuring his throwing hand last season, Mateer appeared to validate the hype that surrounded his arrival in the transfer portal. His loose, sidearm delivery and crafty rushing ability helped him earn a top-20 PFF grade nationally through Week 4. His performance dropped off dramatically after the injury. From Week 7 onward, Mateer earned a 50.3 PFF grade, one of the lowest marks in the country. His accuracy was clearly compromised, while his footwork became increasingly unsettled behind a shaky offensive line. If Mateer can recapture his early-season form, Oklahoma has the pieces to contend for a College Football Playoff berth. If his late-season struggles carry into 2026, the Sooners could fall well short of those expectations. through . The former Arkansas transfer possesses blazing speed, reaching 22.5 mph according to player-tracking data, and that explosiveness makes him especially dangerous with the ball in his hands. Sategna’s 524 yards after the catch ranked fifth among Power Four receivers, as did his 22 forced missed tackles. Defensive Player Spotlight: DT David Stone Stone is a freakish athlete at 315 pounds and one of the best defensive tackles in the country. His quick first step and natural violence make him a dominant run defender. His 80.7 PFF run-defense grade ranked 10th among qualified SEC defensive tackles last season, while his 13.0% run-stop rate ranked second nationally, trailing only Ohio State’s Kayden McDonald. Many draft evaluators view Stone as the top interior defensive line prospect in the 2027 class. With more discipline and a more refined pass-rush plan, he has the talent to prove them right. Bottom Line Oklahoma’s defense should be good enough to keep the Sooners firmly in the top-15 conversation. How much the offense improves will ultimately determine whether they can take the next step and compete with the best teams in college football. records.new_body: 2026 College Football Preview: Ole Miss Rebels All NFL Fantasy College - current NFL Draft DFS Betting 2026 College Football Preview: Ole Miss Rebels By Max Chadwick Posted Aug 19, 2026 11:31 am EDT College football’s best backfield leads the way: Ole Miss pairs PFF’s No. 4 quarterback, Trinidad Chambliss, with No. 2 running back Kewan Lacy entering 2026. Offensive line remains the biggest concern: The Rebels lost both starting tackles to the NFL, while all three returning interior starters earned PFF grades below 65.0 last season. Kewan Lacy returns after a massive 2025 season: Lacy led the FBS with 307 rushing attempts and all Power Four running backs with 24 rushing touchdowns. Explore PFF Premium Stats The most advanced NFL and college football statistics — player grades, WAR, TIPP, and more. Filter by position, team, season, and snap count. NFL Premium Stats (opens in new tab) College Premium Stats (opens in new tab) The 2025 season was a roller coaster for Ole Miss. The Rebels finished the regular season 11-1 and secured the first College Football Playoff berth in program history, only for head coach Lane Kiffin to leave for LSU before the playoff began. Defensive coordinator Pete Golding was promoted to head coach and kept the season on track, leading Ole Miss past Tulane in the first round before an upset of Georgia in the quarterfinals. The Rebels’ storybook run ended in the final seconds of their semifinal matchup with Miami (FL). Ole Miss finished No. 3 in the AP poll, its highest final ranking since 1962. Notable Transfer Portal Additions WR Darrell Gill ( Syracuse ) WR Johntay Cook II (Syracuse) CB Jay Crawford (Auburn) LB Luke Ferrelli (California) LB Keaton Thomas (Baylor) Notable Transfer Portal Losses ED Princewill Umanmielen (LSU) WR Cayden Lee ( Missouri ) ED Da’shawn Womack ( Auburn ) WR Winston Watkins (LSU) LB T.J. Dottery (LSU) through . --> Read more Read more Top-10 returning players at every position By Max Chadwick (opens in new tab) → Biggest strength: The best backfield in college football After winning an injunction against the NCAA that granted him another season of eligibility, Trinidad Chambliss returns to lead Ole Miss and enters 2026 as our No. 4 quarterback in the country. He’ll be joined in the backfield by Kewan Lacy, the cover athlete for EA Sports College Football 27 and our No. 2 running back in the nation, giving the Rebels one of the best quarterback-running back tandems in college football. Biggest question mark: Can they continue to thrive despite a below-average offensive line? Ole Miss’ offensive line was good enough for Trinidad Chambliss and company to work around last season, but the unit lost both starting offensive tackles to the NFL. Delano Townsend, Brycen Sanders and Patrick Kutas return on the interior, though all three earned PFF grades below 65.0 in 2025. There are also questions at tackle, where Terez Davis and LSU transfer Carius Curne are among the unproven options. As talented as the Rebels’ backfield is, the offensive line could become a significant issue against the SEC’s better defensive fronts. Quarterback: Trinidad Chambliss Chambliss came out of nowhere to become one of college football’s biggest revelations last season. After replacing the injured Austin Simmons, he never relinquished the starting job, winning SEC Newcomer of the Year and leading Ole Miss to the College Football Playoff semifinals. His 87.3 PFF grade ranked 13th among qualified FBS quarterbacks, and he committed just four turnovers all season. His Russell Wilson -esque playmaking style and ability to thrive under pressure became defining traits down the stretch. With Chambliss running the offense, Ole Miss has a chance to beat anyone on its schedule. through . Including the postseason, he led all Power Four interior defenders with 765 snaps and 35 defensive stops last season. He also showed a knack for disrupting passing lanes, batting down six passes at the line of scrimmage. Echoles’ 79.3 PFF grade ranked fifth among qualified SEC defensive tackles in 2025, and he should continue to produce at a high level this season. Even without Lane Kiffin, the Rebels have enough talent to remain among the SEC’s top contenders. records.new_body: Grading all 32 first-rounders: 2026 NFL preseason Week 1 All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Grading all 32 first-rounders: 2026 NFL preseason Week 1 By Mark Chichester Posted Aug 19, 2026 10:08 am EDT Ty Simpson could not have scripted a better debut: The No. 13 pick completed 21 of his 25 passes for 190 yards and two touchdowns without a turnover-worthy play, earning a 78.1 PFF grade. Arvell Reese needed only 12 snaps to make his case: The Giants linebacker posted an 88.2 PFF grade — the highest of any 2026 first-rounder — behind an 82.4 PFF run-defense grade. Positions appear set: Francis Mauigoa played right guard, Kadyn Proctor lined up at left guard and Keylan Rutledge took every snap at center. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) The 2026 rookie class has officially taken the field. Preseason Week 1 is the first look at how this group is being deployed — where they line up, how much rope they've been given and which ones have already climbed the depth chart. As always, we'll track their progress, PFF grades and workloads all season long. Two caveats worth stating up front. Sample sizes are tiny — several first-rounders played fewer than 15 snaps — so the snap counts and the alignment data often tell you more than the grades do. And seven first-round picks did not take a snap in Week 1. We've noted them below without reading anything into it. One early theme: the offensive line reshuffling. Three first-round blockers are already playing somewhere other than where they were drafted, with Francis Mauigoa taking every snap at right guard, Kadyn Proctor kicking inside to left guard and Keylan Rutledge lining up at center. 1. QB Fernando Mendoza , Las Vegas Raiders Snaps: 31 PFF Grade: 66.7 Key Stat: 10-of-16, 97 yards, 1 TD, 0 INT, zero turnover-worthy plays Mendoza's first NFL action was a clean, unspectacular one. He earned a 67.2 PFF passing grade across 18 dropbacks against the Cardinals , producing five first downs and a touchdown without a single turnover-worthy play. His 3.13-second average time to throw was on the slow side, and he took a sack on one of the six pressures he faced. He also attempted four passes of 10-plus air yards, producing two completions for 33 yards. 2. EDGE David Bailey , New York Jets Snaps: 8 PFF Grade: 63.3 Key Stat: One pressure and one defensive stop on eight snaps The Jets gave Bailey a cameo against the Buccaneers — eight snaps, all of them aligned outside the tackle. He made them count, generating a hurry on six pass-rush reps and recording a stop on one of his two run-defense snaps. 3. RB Jeremiyah Love , Arizona Cardinals Snaps: 24 PFF Grade: 61.7 Key Stat: 48 of 58 rushing yards came after contact Love handled a legitimate workload — 11 carries and 14 total touches — and immediately showed the contact balance that made him the highest-drafted running back in years. He averaged 4.36 yards after contact per attempt, forced three missed tackles and recorded two runs of at least 10 yards. The production extended to the passing game, where Love ran 11 routes and caught all three of his targets. 4. WR Carnell Tate , Tennessee Titans Snaps: 16 PFF Grade: 53.5 Key Stat: Zero receptions on three targets Tate’s debut was a quiet one. He ran nine routes against the 49ers but failed to haul in any of his three targets — and that's because he wasn't given a chance to. One target was contested, and they were all charted as uncatchable. His usage was perhaps more notable than the lack of production. Tate ran 90% of his routes from out wide and logged just one snap from the slot. 5. LB Arvell Reese , New York Giants Snaps: 12 PFF Grade: 88.2 Key Stat: Highest PFF grade of any 2026 first-round pick Reese was the story of Week 1 among this class. He played all 12 of his snaps off the ball against the Vikings and dominated the reps he got, earning an 82.4 PFF run-defense grade with two tackles and a stop while missing none. 6. CB Mansoor Delane , Kansas City Chiefs Snaps: 0 Delane missed Kansas City’s preseason opener against the Los Angeles Rams with a shoulder injury, but the rookie cornerback appears to be nearing a return. He recently shed the non-contact yellow jersey and returned as a full participant in 11-on-11 team drills, putting him on track to potentially make his preseason debut against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. 7. LB Sonny Styles , Washington Commanders Snaps: 14 PFF Grade: 71.1 Key Stat: 65.5 PFF coverage grade across seven coverage snaps Styles turned in a tidy 14-snap debut against the Dolphins , earning a 65.6 PFF run-defense grade and a 65.5 PFF coverage grade without missing a tackle. His playing time was split evenly between run defense and coverage, and the team even lined him up on the edge for two snaps. 8. WR Jordyn Tyson , New Orleans Saints Snaps: 0 The New Orleans Saints have confirmed that rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson suffered a hamstring injury during their joint practice with the Jacksonville Jaguars and will miss around two months. 9. T Spencer Fano , Cleveland Browns Snaps: 33 PFF Grade: 58.4 Key Stat: Two pressures allowed on 20 pass-blocking snaps Fano logged all 33 of his snaps at left tackle against the Bears . He held up reasonably well in protection, earning a 70.8 PFF pass-blocking grade while surrendering a hit and a hurry. His work in the running game let him down a touch, as his 47.1 PFF run-blocking grade across 13 reps dragged his overall mark down to 58.4. 10. T Francis Mauigoa , New York Giants Snaps: 30 PFF Grade: 66.5 Key Stat: Zero pressures allowed on 15 pass-blocking snaps Mauigoa, a college tackle, took all 30 of his snaps at right guard. He looked comfortable there, allowing zero pressures and earning a 73.5 PFF pass-blocking grade across 15 pass-blocking snaps. He also graded out at a respectable 62.7 in the run game, giving him the second-best PFF overall grade among first-round offensive linemen in Week 1, a tick behind Detroit's Blake Miller. 11. S Caleb Downs , Dallas Cowboys Snaps: 7 PFF Grade: 63.2 Key Stat: Zero targets in his direction across three coverage snaps Dallas gave its top pick a seven-snap look against the Seahawks and got him off the field. Six of those seven came at free safety, with one in the slot. There's essentially nothing to evaluate — no targets, no tackles, no plays made in either direction. The 63.2 PFF overall grade is a placeholder. What matters is that the Cowboys deployed him deep, which is where they'll need him. 12. G Kadyn Proctor , Miami Dolphins Snaps: 22 PFF Grade: 49.7 Key Stat: 80.9 PFF pass-blocking grade with zero pressures allowed Proctor took all 22 of his snaps at left guard against the Commanders . He allowed no pressures on 12 pass-blocking snaps and earned an 80.9 PFF pass-blocking grade, the best mark of any first-round blocker in Week 1. The run blocking was a different story, as he managed a 44.9 PFF run-blocking grade across 10 reps, which pulled his overall grade down to 49.7. 13. QB Ty Simpson , Los Angeles Rams Snaps: 39 PFF Grade: 78.1 Key Stat: 91.3% adjusted completion percentage Simpson earned a 76.6 PFF passing grade against the Chiefs while completing 84% of his attempts for 190 yards and two scores, generating a further eight first downs and a 125.0 passer rating without a turnover-worthy play. He was barely bothered, facing just three pressures on 25 dropbacks and taking zero sacks. The one caveat is the depth chart on his throws: a 5.3-yard average depth of target means much of that efficiency came underneath. 14. G Vega Ioane , Baltimore Ravens Snaps: 15 PFF Grade: 49.1 Key Stat: Two pressures allowed on 10 pass-blocking snaps It was a slightly rough first outing for Ioane, who played all 15 of his snaps at right guard against the Eagles . He gave up two hurries on 10 pass-blocking reps, and the resulting 24.6 PFF pass-blocking grade was the lowest of any first-round blocker in Week 1. The run blocking held up better at 56.8, and 15 snaps is a small enough sample that one bad rep swings everything. 15. EDGE Rueben Bain Jr. , Tampa Bay Buccaneers Snaps: 0 Bain did not play a snap in Tampa Bay’s 24-16 preseason-opening win over the New York Jets. Head coach Todd Bowles opted to sit the rookie first-round pick after seeing enough from him during training camp practices. 16. TE Kenyon Sadiq , New York Jets Snaps: 0 Sadiq did not play a snap in the Jets’ preseason opener against the Buccaneers as he continues to work his way back from hernia surgery and a subsequent setback during training camp. New York has taken a cautious approach with his recovery, with head coach Aaron Glenn targeting the regular-season opener for his return. 17. T Blake Miller , Detroit Lions Snaps: 39 PFF Grade: 66.6 Key Stat: 24 pass-blocking snaps, two hurries allowed, no sacks Miller played the second-most pass-blocking snaps of any first-round lineman in Week 1 and handled the volume well. All 39 of his reps came at right tackle against the Bengals , where he posted a 68.6 PFF pass-blocking grade. Just as encouraging, he graded at 63.3 as a run blocker — the best mark of any first-round lineman — making him one of the few rookie linemen in this class to grade positively in both phases. 18. DI Caleb Banks , Minnesota Vikings Snaps: 25 PFF Grade: 30.4 Key Stat: Zero pressures on 12 pass-rush snaps Banks played 25 snaps, split almost evenly between pass rush and run defense against the Giants , but he struggled to make an impact. He failed to generate a single pressure on 12 pass-rush reps, and his 32.0 PFF run-defense grade left him with a 30.4 PFF overall grade, the lowest of any first-rounder in Week 1. He did line up in a variety of spots, taking 16 snaps in a B-gap alignment plus seven over the tackle. 19. T Monroe Freeling , Carolina Panthers Snaps: 10 PFF Grade: 53.1 Key Stat: Two pressures allowed on seven pass-blocking snaps Freeling saw the lightest workload of any first-round offensive lineman, logging just 10 snaps at right tackle against the Bills. He allowed two hurries across seven pass-blocking reps, resulting in a 39.4 PFF pass-blocking grade. There is little to take away from a 10-snap sample, particularly when only seven came in pass protection. Freeling did earn a 57.7 PFF run-blocking grade, one of the better marks among this rookie group, but the first-rounder simply needs more reps before any meaningful conclusions can be drawn. 20. WR Makai Lemon , Philadelphia Eagles Snaps: 0 Lemon did not play a snap in Philadelphia’s 24-7 preseason-opening loss to the Baltimore Ravens. The rookie wide receiver was sidelined with a hamstring injury, delaying his preseason debut. 21. T Max Iheanachor , Pittsburgh Steelers Snaps: 0 Iheanachor did not play in Pittsburgh’s preseason opener against the Green Bay Packers after suffering neck and shoulder injuries during training camp practice in early August. 22. EDGE Akheem Mesidor , Los Angeles Chargers Snaps: 9 PFF Grade: 80.9 Key Stat: 74.6 PFF pass-rush grade on five pass-rush snaps Mesidor’s box score was empty — no pressures and no tackles — but his underlying performance told a different story. He earned the second-highest PFF grade among first-rounders in Week 1, including a 74.6 pass-rush grade and a 63.9 run-defense grade across nine snaps against the Texans. The pass-rush reps were particularly encouraging. Mesidor won two of his five opportunities for a 40% pass-rush win rate, even though neither win resulted in pressure. 23. EDGE Malachi Lawrence , Dallas Cowboys Snaps: 17 PFF Grade: 80.1 Key Stat: Two defensive stops and a pressure on 17 snaps Lawrence was the most productive first-round edge defender in Week 1 relative to his workload. Against the Seahawks, he recorded two defensive stops, generated a hurry on nine pass-rush reps and missed no tackles, finishing with a 72.5 PFF run-defense grade and a 69.7 PFF pass-rush grade. 24. WR KC Concepcion , Cleveland Browns Snaps: 25 PFF Grade: 77.6 Key Stat: 1.80 yards per route run Concepcion caught three of four targets for 27 yards against the Bears — including his lone contested target — and added a 14-yard touchdown run on his only carry, forcing a missed tackle and picking up eight yards after contact on the play. Fourteen of his 16 receiving snaps came from the slot, and he ran a route on 93.8% of Cleveland's pass plays while he was on the field. 25. S Dillon Thieneman , Chicago Bears Snaps: 14 PFF Grade: 52.4 Key Stat: Targeted once, allowed zero receptions Thieneman was thrown at once against the Browns and gave up nothing, holding opposing quarterbacks to a 39.6 rating in his direction. Chicago used him primarily as a deep defender, with nine snaps at free safety and five in the box. He added a tackle without a miss, which produced a 74.8 PFF tackling grade. 26. C Keylan Rutledge , Houston Texans Snaps: 12 PFF Grade: 61.4 Key Stat: Zero pressures allowed on eight pass-blocking snaps Rutledge played all 12 of his snaps at center against the Chargers. The early returns in protection were clean: no pressures allowed and a 77.6 PFF pass-blocking grade. 27. CB Chris Johnson , Miami Dolphins Snaps: 18 PFF Grade: 56.7 Key Stat: Two targets, one reception allowed for 14 yards Johnson saw the most work of any first-round defensive back in Week 1, playing 18 snaps against the Commanders with nine in the slot and eight on the boundary. He allowed one catch on two targets for 14 yards and a 72.9 passer rating in his direction. 28. T Caleb Lomu , New England Patriots Snaps: 43 PFF Grade: 55.1 Key Stat: Zero pressures allowed on 27 pass-blocking snaps No first-rounder played more snaps in Week 1 than Lomu, who logged all 43 of his at right tackle against the Colts and did not surrender a single pressure across 27 pass-blocking reps. However, he was beaten on two reps that didn't result in QB pressure, which explains his 60.5 pass-blocking grade. 29. DI Peter Woods , Kansas City Chiefs Snaps: 25 PFF Grade: 35.5 Key Stat: Zero pressures on 15 pass-rush snaps Woods drew the second-lowest PFF overall grade of any first-rounder in Week 1, ahead of only Minnesota ‘s Caleb Banks. He played 25 snaps against the Rams — 15 of them rushing the passer — without generating a pressure or recording a tackle, finishing with a 37.4 PFF run-defense grade and a 53.6 PFF pass-rush grade. 30. WR Omar Cooper Jr. , New York Jets Snaps: 21 PFF Grade: 61.0 Key Stat: 2.58 yards per route run, best among first-round receivers Cooper was the most efficient rookie receiver in Week 1 on a per-route basis, turning 12 routes into two catches for 31 yards against the Buccaneers, including a 26-yard gain. He averaged 4.0 yards after the catch per reception and generated an average target depth of 14.3 yards. 31. EDGE Keldric Faulk , Tennessee Titans Snaps: 30 PFF Grade: 72.5 Key Stat: Most defensive snaps of any 2026 first-round pick Faulk was trusted with more work than any other first-round defender, playing 30 snaps against the 49ers with 22 of them rushing the passer. He converted that into a quarterback hit, two tackles and a stop, grading at 72.4 against the run and 62.7 as a pass-rusher. 32. RB Jadarian Price , Seattle Seahawks Snaps: 0 Price did not play a snap in Seattle’s 17-7 preseason-opening loss to the Dallas Cowboys. The rookie running back was held out due to upper-leg soreness. records.new_body: Highest-graded NFL rookies after Week 1 of the 2026 preseason All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Highest-graded NFL rookies after Week 1 of the 2026 preseason By Gordon McGuinness Posted Aug 19, 2026 5:30 am EDT Kamari Ramsey leads all rookies: The Texans safety earned a 94.8 PFF grade and recorded an interception and pass breakup in his preseason debut. Matthew Hibner tops the offensive rookies: The Ravens tight end earned a 92.6 PFF grade after catching five passes for 61 yards on 12 routes. Carson Beck leads the quarterbacks: The Cardinals rookie posted a 91.7 PFF grade after recording three big-time throws and no turnover-worthy plays. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) With the first full slate of NFL preseason games in the books, it’s time to take stock of the rookies who made the strongest first impressions. We’ll update these rankings each week throughout the preseason, raising the snap threshold as the sample grows. For Week 1, players must have logged at least 15 snaps to qualify. Here are the NFL’s highest-graded rookies after Week 1 of the preseason. 1. S Kamari Ramsey , Houston Texans : 94.8 A fifth-round pick in April, Ramsey was the NFL’s highest-graded rookie in the opening week of the preseason, driven by a 94.7 PFF coverage grade. Across 14 coverage snaps, he didn’t allow a reception as the primary coverage defender and recorded both a pass breakup and an interception. 2. TE Matthew Hibner , Baltimore Ravens : 92.6 The 133rd overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft was the league’s highest-graded offensive rookie in the opening week of the preseason. Hibner ran just 12 routes but caught five passes for 61 yards, averaging an impressive 5.08 yards per route run. 3. LB Jacob Roberts , Minnesota Vikings : 92.6 Roberts was the highest-graded undrafted free agent in the opening week of the preseason, earning a 75.8 PFF run-defense grade and a 91.4 PFF coverage grade. He didn’t miss a tackle, recorded two defensive stops and added an interception in coverage. 4. S Jacob Thomas , Minnesota Vikings : 92.5 Like fellow Vikings undrafted free agent Roberts, Thomas made a strong first impression in his NFL debut. He didn’t miss a tackle and recorded an interception, helping him earn a 91.6 PFF coverage grade. 5. CB Ayden Garnes , Tampa Bay Buccaneers : 91.8 Garnes allowed a 26-yard reception against the New York Jets, but it was the only catch he surrendered across 17 coverage snaps. He more than made up for it by returning an interception for a touchdown. Garnes did miss two tackles, however, so his strong overall grade was driven largely by the pick-six. 6. QB Carson Beck , Arizona Cardinals : 91.7 Beck missed the Cardinals’ second preseason game, but his performance in the Hall of Fame Game still has him as the NFL’s highest-graded quarterback this preseason. Against the Panthers , he went 15-of-19 for 188 yards and a touchdown, recording three big-time throws and no turnover-worthy plays. 7. WR Camden Brown , Dallas Cowboys : 91.5 Brown made an immediate impact in his debut after signing as an undrafted free agent out of Georgia Southern . He ran 15 routes and caught three passes for 62 yards and two touchdowns, averaging 4.13 yards per route run. 8. TE Jack Endries , Cincinnati Bengals : 91.4 Endries averaged just 8.3 yards per reception on three catches against the Detroit Lions , but his average depth of target was only 1.0 yard. He did most of his damage after the catch, forcing three missed tackles on a 17-yard catch-and-run. 9. G Anez Cooper , New York Jets : 90.9 Cooper was the highest-graded rookie offensive lineman in the opening week of the preseason. The sixth-round pick out of Miami earned PFF grades above 85.0 both as a run blocker and in pass protection, allowing no sacks, hits or hurries across 20 pass-blocking snaps at right guard. 10. DI Christen Miller , New Orleans Saints : 90.5 The Saints’ second-round pick made an immediate impact in his preseason debut, earning the highest grade among rookie defensive linemen. He did his best work against the run, recording three defensive stops on just eight run-defense snaps, while also adding a hurry on nine pass-rushing snaps. 11. WR Malachi Fields , New York Giants : 90.3 Fields made an impact on just 10 receiving snaps against the Minnesota Vikings, catching three passes for 34 yards and a touchdown while averaging 3.40 yards per route run. He also showcased one of his best traits coming out of the draft, with two of his three receptions coming on contested catches. 12. CB Michael Coats Jr. , Cleveland Browns : 90.0 An undrafted free agent out of West Virginia , Coats was targeted five times across just 14 coverage snaps but held his own. He allowed two receptions for 13 yards while recording both a pass breakup and an interception. 13. EDGE Caden Curry , Indianapolis Colts : 89.5 The former Ohio State standout was the highest-graded rookie edge defender in the opening week of the preseason, driven by a 92.1 PFF pass-rush grade against the New England Patriots. Across 17 pass-rushing snaps, he generated four pressures, including a sack and two quarterback hits. 14. WR Kaden Wetjen , Pittsburgh Steelers : 88.0 Wetjen made the most of his 13 receiving snaps in his NFL debut, averaging 6.08 yards per route run thanks largely to a 74-yard catch-and-run that nearly went for a touchdown. He also contributed as a returner, which likely represents his clearest path to the field early in his NFL career. 15. CB Kenneth Harris , New England Patriots : 86.1 Harris was targeted three times across 16 coverage snaps, allowing just one reception for six yards. He also recorded a pass breakup, finishing with an 87.9 PFF coverage grade and allowing a 42.4 passer rating on throws into his coverage. records.new_body: 10 NFL players who turned heads in their 2026 preseason debuts All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 10 NFL players who turned heads in their 2026 preseason debuts By Bradley Locker Posted Aug 18, 2026 6:15 am EDT Martin Emerson Jr. looked lockdown for the Saints : The former Browns starter notched three pass breakups in limited work. Malachi Fields impressed for the Giants : The third-round pick caught two contested catches in his preseason debut and might be New York's WR2. Keshawn Banks could be a real pass-rusher for the Falcons : Atlanta's need for edge rushers might be satiated by Banks given his 90.2 overall PFF grade in Week 1. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) The onset of the NFL preseason means the return of live action and new results, including fresh PFF grades. After a six-month hiatus, it sure feels good to be back. It can be easy to overreact to preseason showings one way or the other given that most games feature players who are hoping to simply make a roster, not to mention more basic schemes. However, one unwavering part of the August schedule is names making strong impressions with their performances — a level of play which, if sustained, can genuinely translate into regular-season snaps. The 10 players below all made a very strong first impression during the opening window of the preseason, potentially opening the door for larger roles as September arrives. CB Martin Emerson Jr. , New Orleans Saints The Saints enter 2026 with big aspirations, but real questions confront the defensive side of the ball, especially their secondary. If his first outing was any indication, Emerson could be an answer. The former Brown was excellent in Week 1, compiling a 91.3 PFF coverage grade across 24 total snaps. Emerson broke up three passes on only 13 coverage snaps and was charted with allowing just one catch, putting his ball skills and instincts on full display. The Saints figure to start Kool-Aid McKinstry and Quincy Riley at boundary corner to begin the season. But if Emerson — who played well in 2022 before struggling and tearing his Achilles prior to last season — keeps it up, it’ll be very tough to keep him off the field in Brandon Staley’s defense. G Kayode Awosika , Los Angeles Chargers While optimism abounds for a revamped Chargers offense and offensive line, worries linger about the starting guards. Awosika staked his claim to get a bigger opportunity in his first game appearance of 2026. Against the Texans, Awosika flashed with a 90.1 overall PFF grade. His 85.5 PFF run-blocking grade is the ninth-best of any guard to play in the preseason thus far, and he also yielded zero pressures on nine pass-blocking snaps. The former undrafted free agent will have to fend off names like Trevor Penning and rookie Jake Slaughter to win the left guard job, but reports suggest he’s earned more playing time with Los Angeles’ first-team offense. If the 27-year-old keeps repeating this type of showing, he’ll leave Jim Harbaugh and Mike McDaniel with a fairly easy choice. WR Malachi Fields, New York Giants As a third-round selection, Fields already came into the NFL with legitimate upside. However, his first taste of the pros might suggest he’ll garner a bigger workload than expected right away. Fields was masterful against the Vikings, securing an 88.5 PFF receiving grade by hauling in all three of his targets for 34 yards and a touchdown. Impressively, two of those were charted as contested receptions, and he generated a nearly-perfect 153.5 passer rating when targeted. The Giants’ receiver room is crowded with the returning Malik Nabers as well as veterans like Darius Slay ton , Darnell Mooney , Calvin Austin III , JuJu Smith-Schuster and even Odell Beckham Jr. Yet the 22-year-old Fields may establish himself as a core part of John Harbaugh’s offense in short order if he turns in encores. Dl Gracen Halton, San Francisco 49ers The 49ers’ defensive line should receive several boosts this season in getting back key contributors. That resurgence could include the rookie Halton. The team’s fourth-round pick enjoyed a fruitful first game in San Francisco, notching a 73.6 overall PFF grade across 30 snaps. Halton was at his best in the run game, earning a 75.0 PFF run-defense grade while tallying four run stops and missing zero tackles. Last season, 49ers interior defensive linemen produced a league-worst 27.0 PFF run-defense grade, with rookies Alfred Collins and CJ West especially underwhelming. If Halton can sustain his run-stuffing work, he could see the field next to newcomer Osa Odighizuwa earlier than anticipated. CB Keyon Martin, Baltimore Ravens All eyes are on the Ravens’ defense as Jesse Minter takes over as head coach. While Baltimore ushers in plenty of star power on that side of the ball, an unsung contributor has also generated attention in Martin. Martin looked terrific against the Eagles in Baltimore’s first preseason showdown, accruing a 90.0 overall PFF grade with 76.0-plus marks in all of coverage, run defense, tackling and even pass-rushing. The former undrafted free agent notched a sack on his only pass-rushing attempt and showcased his blend of closing speed and physicality in multiple dimensions. The Ravens seem to have their starting cornerbacks set in Marlon Humphrey and Nate Wiggins , but Martin’s emergence could force his way into the lineup — especially considering Humphrey’s woes last season. After all, Minter has a track record of developing lesser-known defensive backs, and the second-year Martin could be next in line. EDGE Keshawn Banks , Atlanta Falcons The Falcons enter the regular season in rapidly uncertain territory, including with their quarterback situation. Atlanta’s pass rush looks especially worrisome given injury and suspension, but Banks might be an internal answer. Playing 24 snaps against the Broncos, Banks secured a 90.2 overall PFF grade. The former undrafted free agent collected two pressures and four pass-rush wins on only 10 attempts. Banks also added a strong 79.0 PFF run-defense grade. Down Jalon Walker to a torn ACL and James Pearce Jr. to an eight-game suspension, the Falcons are fairly desperate for edge-rushing solutions. The team feels likely to try to add outside help, but Banks — who played in the UFL this spring — could work his way into a thinner-than-expected rotation if he continues to thrive. EDGE Ahmed Hassanein , Detroit Lions The Lions have been in pursuit of secondary edge rushers next to Aidan Hutchinson for years. Detroit poured more resources into the unit this offseason to try to locate a real Robin, but Hassanein also impressed with his first preseason showing. The team’s 2025 sixth-round pick generated five pressures and two sacks against the Bengals, good for a 90.6 PFF pass-rush grade. Also encouraging was Hassanein’s 18.2% pass-rush win rate on true pass sets. It seems probable that Detroit will let free-agent signing D.J. Wonnum and second-round pick Derrick Moore get most early reps working next to the All-Pro Hutchinson. Yet if Hassanein keeps affecting the quarterback like this, he’ll have a real shot to not only make the roster, but also to factor into the Lions’ defensive line rotation. S Jaden Hicks , Kansas City Chiefs Following multiple offseason departures, the Chiefs will feature a different-looking secondary in 2026. A large part of that equation could be Hicks, at least if the preseason is any indication. The former fourth-round pick was all over the field for Kansas City against the Rams, earning an 88.3 overall PFF grade across 33 snaps. Hicks’ 79.9 PFF coverage grade led the team, allowing only two yards into his coverage. On top of that, he didn’t miss a tackle and chipped in with a 72.8 PFF run-defense mark. Hicks has played 914 defensive snaps over his two seasons in Kansas City thus far. With Bryan Cook now in Cincinnati , the 24-year-old Hicks could work his way into the starting safety rotation next to Alohi Gilman and Chamarri Conner . T Charles Grant , Las Vegas Raiders The hope is that the Raiders’ offense can show signs of life as it begins the Klint Kubiak era. The team’s first preseason game was a step in the right direction, particularly for Grant. Grant played 31 snaps against the Cardinals and was highly effective, meriting an 82.4 overall PFF grade. The 2025 third-round pick held his own on the ground with a 90.8 PFF run-blocking grade, a figure that trails just Dion Dawkins and Garett Bolles among all tackles through the first week of the preseason. Grant also didn’t permit a sack across 20 pass-blocking snaps, although he surrendered two quarterback hits. Las Vegas projects to start Kolton Miller and D.J. Glaze at tackle to begin the season. However, Grant could very well get a nod at right tackle if Glaze struggles and Grant plays up to par throughout the rest of the month. TE Matthew Hibner, Baltimore Ravens Tight ends dominated the flow of the 2026 NFL Draft, particularly in the middle rounds. While conversation has oriented around new names on other teams, Hibner is making sure he isn’t overlooked. The Ravens’ fourth-round pick starred in his pro debut with a 92.6 overall PFF grade, the fifth-highest of any offensive player in the early going. Hibner caught all five of his targets for 61 yards, amassing a 93.6 PFF receiving grade while averaging an impressive 7.6 yards after the catch per reception and securing four first downs. He also recorded a 74.2 PFF pass-blocking grade, albeit on just two such snaps. With Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar both departing this offseason, the Ravens are certainly in search of more reliable playmakers at tight end behind Mark Andrews . The SMU product Hibner has made a good case already to supplant Durham Smythe as the team’s No. 2 option. records.new_body: Breakout candidates for all 32 teams All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Breakout candidates for all 32 teams By Gordon McGuinness Posted Aug 18, 2026 6:00 am EDT Young players headline the breakout list: Walter Nolen , Deone Walker and Dylan Fairchild are among the second-year players positioned to take another step in 2026. Expanded roles create opportunities: Josh Downs , Isaac TeSlaa and Gunnar Helm could benefit from clearer paths to increased playing time or opportunities. PFF Grades highlight emerging talent: Armand Membou earned 70.0-plus PFF grades in pass protection and run blocking as a rookie, while Kelvin Banks Jr. led first-year offensive tackles with a 73.5 PFF grade. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools Subscribe For Full Access (opens in new tab) Some of the most important players of the 2026 season aren’t yet household names. From second-year linemen poised to take a leap to rotational pass-rushers and receivers stepping into larger roles, every roster has a player capable of breaking out. Here is one breakout candidate for each of the 32 NFL teams. Arizona Cardinals: Walter Nolen Nolen showed some encouraging flashes during his rookie season in Arizona, but he played just 169 snaps, limiting his overall impact. He generated 15 pressures on 99 pass-rushing snaps, earned an 80.1 PFF pass-rush grade and recorded at least three pressures in three of the four games in which he had 15 or more pass-rushing snaps. The key for Nolen will be staying on the field, but if he can, there’s a chance he emerges as Arizona’s best defensive player by the end of the season. Atlanta Falcons: Matthew Bergeron Left guard Matthew Bergeron enters the final season of his rookie contract with an opportunity to earn a significant payday with a strong 2026 campaign. He has already played more than 3,000 snaps in his career and has earned PFF overall grades above 70.0 in back-to-back seasons. Bergeron has consistently graded better as a run blocker than in pass protection, but he has also earned PFF pass-blocking grades above 65.0 in each of the past two seasons. He allowed 28 pressures across 519 pass-blocking snaps in 2025. Baltimore Ravens: Teddye Buchanan Linebacker Teddye Buchanan had started to impress before a season-ending injury derailed his rookie campaign. After taking over a starting role in Week 2, the 2025 fourth-round draft pick earned a PFF overall grade above 60.0 in five of his final six games and ranked 31st among linebackers in PFF run-defense grade (70.8). Buffalo Bills: Deone Walker A fourth-round draft pick last season, Deone Walker showed some encouraging flashes during his rookie campaign. Despite what you might expect from a player his size, the former Kentucky Wildcat made his biggest impact as a pass-rusher, earning a 78.3 PFF pass-rush grade while generating 20 pressures on 283 pass-rushing snaps. A full NFL offseason should give him the opportunity to take another step forward and make an even bigger impact along the interior of the Bills’ defensive line. Carolina Panthers: Jalen Coker The Panthers have already demonstrated their belief in former undrafted free agent Jalen Coker, signing him to a three-year, $34 million extension this offseason. Through his first two NFL seasons, Coker has earned PFF receiving grades above 70.0 and averaged at least 1.60 yards per route run in both years. With Tetairoa McMillan established as the primary target, Carolina does not need Coker to lead the passing game. Instead, 2026 presents an opportunity for him to earn more recognition as a versatile secondary option who can make plays both from the slot and out wide. Chicago Bears: Kyle Monangai Luther Burden III could play a significant role in the Bears ’ offense, but the same is true of fellow 2025 rookie Kyle Monangai at running back. The seventh-round pick averaged 4.5 yards per carry as a rookie while forcing 30 missed tackles. His 75.2 PFF rushing grade ranked 30th among the 65 running backs with at least 50 carries across the regular season and playoffs, and he formed an impressive backfield tandem with D'Andre Swift . Cincinnati Bengals: Dylan Fairchild The Bengals drafted guard Dylan Fairchild with the 81st overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, and the former Georgia Bulldog started 15 games as a rookie. Over the final eight games of the season, his 74.3 PFF pass-blocking grade ranked first among rookie guards and fourth among all rookie offensive linemen. He is capable of developing into the Bengals’ best offensive lineman by the end of the 2026 season. Cleveland Browns: Harold Fannin Jr. Tight end Harold Fannin Jr. followed up an impressive college career by finishing fourth among all rookies in receiving yards (731). He earned a 76.4 PFF receiving grade, trailing only Colston Loveland , Luther Burden III and Tetairoa McMillan among rookies to see at least 20 targets. Fannin fell in the draft because he was just an OK athlete, but his 3.77 yards per route run in his final college season was always a sign he could be a star in the NFL. Dallas Cowboys: Donovan Ezeiruaku Expectations are high for Donovan Ezeiruaku entering his second NFL season. He generated 36 pressures on 343 pass-rushing snaps as a rookie, showing flashes while earning a 66.8 PFF pass-rush grade. If he can develop into a consistent threat off the edge, it would go a long way toward easing concerns about the Cowboys’ ability to pressure opposing quarterbacks. Denver Broncos: RJ Harvey Rookie running back RJ Harvey had a solid debut season, earning a 69.6 PFF rushing grade across 165 carries while showcasing his big-play ability with runs of 38, 40 and 50 yards. He also contributed in the passing game, with his 1.40 yards per route run ranking ninth at the position. With J.K. Dobbins and rookie Jonah Coleman sharing the backfield, Harvey is unlikely to take on a true workhorse role. However, he has the talent to emerge as Denver’s best running back in his second NFL season. Detroit Lions: Isaac TeSlaa Isaac TeSlaa flashed impressive ball skills as a rookie, with five of his 16 receptions in 2025 coming on contested catches. He also did not drop a single catchable target, and with Kalif Raymond no longer on the roster, there is a clear path for him to emerge as the No. 3 wide receiver in the offense. Green Bay Packers: Edgerrin Cooper Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper has impressed since entering the NFL as a second-round draft pick in 2024, earning PFF grades above 75.0 in both seasons. In his first year as a full-time starter, he ranked 17th in the NFL with 45 tackles resulting in defensive stops during the regular season. Another strong campaign could put him firmly in the conversation as one of the league’s top linebackers, behind only Fred Warner of the San Francisco 49ers. Houston Texans: Aireontae Ersery Aireontae Ersery made 17 starts as a rookie for the Texans, including 16 at left tackle. Heading into his second season, he is firmly established as the team’s starter, and there were plenty of encouraging signs during his rookie campaign. Excluding his lone start at right tackle, Ersery earned a 69.1 PFF pass-blocking grade, tied for 42nd among the 86 offensive tackles who played at least 300 snaps last season. If he builds on that foundation, he has the potential to finish 2026 as one of the NFL’s top 20 tackles. Indianapolis Colts: Josh Downs Michael Pittman’s departure should create more opportunities for Josh Downs in a contract year. The 2023 third-round pick has recorded at least 500 receiving yards in each of his first three NFL seasons while dropping just 4.3% of his catchable targets over that span. In 2024, Downs averaged 2.20 yards per route run and saw 102 targets. With a clear path to the No. 2 receiver role in Indianapolis’ offense, he has a strong chance to return to that level of production in 2026. Jacksonville Jaguars: Parker Washington Parker Washington thrived in an expanded role after Travis Hunter’s injury, though his breakout season was somewhat overshadowed by the arrival of Jakobi Meyers at the trade deadline. Washington averaged 2.19 yards per route run in 2025, 0.61 more than any other Jaguars pass-catcher. He also caught fire down the stretch, recording 507 receiving yards over Jacksonville’s final five games, including the playoffs — more than double any of his teammates during that span. Kansas City Chiefs: Kingsley Suamataia After a difficult rookie season at left tackle in 2024, Kingsley Suamataia made significant strides following a move to left guard in 2025. Across 1,090 snaps, he earned PFF grades above 60.0 as both a pass blocker and run blocker, while his 64.9 overall grade represented a significant improvement from the 37.9 mark he posted across 198 snaps as a rookie. Suamataia still allowed 35 pressures, so there is plenty of room for improvement. Given the progress he made in his second season, though, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see him take another significant step forward in 2026. Las Vegas Raiders: Ashton Jeanty It’s an easy choice, but the addition of Tyler Linderbaum at center gives Ashton Jeanty an excellent opportunity to take a step forward in Year 2. Jeanty was solid as a rookie, earning a 73.1 PFF rushing grade that ranked tied for 33rd at the position. However, the struggles of the offensive line contributed to him finishing just 18th with 975 rushing yards, despite his 815 yards after contact ranking eighth. With an improved offensive line in front of him and a better situation at quarterback, Jeanty should have an easier time producing at a higher level in his second season. Los Angeles Chargers: Charlie Kolar Tight end Charlie Kolar is coming off a career-high 77.5 PFF grade and has the skill set to be a complete player in the Chargers’ offense. He is unlikely to lead the team’s tight ends in targets, but his 1.70 yards per route run shows that he can still contribute as a receiver. Kolar’s biggest strength, though, is his blocking. His 71.5 PFF run-blocking grade ranked 10th among tight ends in 2025, giving the Chargers an effective in-line option who can provide a boost to the running game. Los Angeles Rams: Kobie Turner Kobie Turner is set to hit free agency after the season, and if the first three years of his career are any indication, he’s about to earn a massive payday. He has earned PFF pass-rush grades above 80.0 in two of his first three seasons while generating 181 pressures, including 50 sacks and quarterback hits, on 1,654 pass-rushing snaps. With opposing offenses now likely to devote extra attention to Myles Garrett off the edge, Turner could see even more favorable one-on-one opportunities as a pass-rusher. Miami Dolphins: Kenneth Grant Defensive tackle Kenneth Grant endured a rough start to his NFL career, earning a 30.4 PFF grade over the first five weeks of the season. He steadily improved as the year went on, though, and his 62.0 PFF grade from Week 6 through the end of the season ranked third among the 14 rookie interior defensive linemen who played at least 200 snaps during that span. His 16 defensive stops over that stretch also ranked second in the group. With a full NFL offseason under his belt, expect Grant to continue that upward trajectory in 2026. Minnesota Vikings: Jalen Redmond An undrafted free agent in 2023, defensive tackle Jalen Redmond earned a 72.8 PFF grade across 793 snaps in 2025. It marked his second straight season with a PFF grade above 70.0, but it came over a significantly larger sample. He also developed into a more well-rounded player, generating 35 pressures on 369 pass-rushing snaps, with nine resulting in combined sacks and quarterback hits, while earning a 72.7 PFF run-defense grade. New England Patriots: Craig Woodson A fourth-round pick out of Cal in the 2025 NFL Draft, safety Craig Woodson played 1,202 snaps across the 2025 regular season and playoffs as a rookie. His 89.7 PFF run-defense grade far outpaced his 63.0 PFF coverage grade, making him better suited to playing in the box. The addition of Kevin Byard III in free agency should allow him to continue to thrive in that role. Even a modest improvement in coverage could see Woodson begin to earn more recognition. New Orleans Saints: Kelvin Banks Jr. Rookie Kelvin Banks Jr. led all first-year offensive tackles in PFF grade in 2025 (73.5), performing well both as a run blocker and in pass protection with grades above 70.0 in each facet. He enters his second season with more than 1,000 NFL snaps under his belt and an improved situation alongside him following the addition of left guard David Edwards . Banks earned PFF grades above 70.0 in six of his final nine games, and if that late-season progress carries into 2026, he could begin to establish himself as one of the league’s better young offensive tackles. New York Giants: Tyler Nubin Tyler Nubin put together a promising rookie season in 2024, earning a 65.8 PFF grade across 789 snaps. His overall production dipped in Year 2, though he did improve in coverage, raising his PFF coverage grade from 58.1 to 60.0. Entering his third NFL season, don’t be surprised if Nubin generates more buzz, particularly if he can recapture the level of run defense he showed as a rookie. New York Jets: Armand Membou Right tackle Armand Membou hit the ground running as a rookie, with the seventh overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft becoming one of just 22 offensive tackles to earn 70.0-plus PFF grades both in pass protection and as a run blocker. He improved as the season went on, allowing just two pressures on 146 pass-blocking snaps over the final four weeks of the regular season. Don’t be surprised if he establishes himself as one of the best tackles in football by the end of his second season. Philadelphia Eagles: Moro Ojomo With former first-round picks Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter also on the defensive line, it’s easy for a former seventh-round pick like Moro Ojomo to fly under the radar. The former Texas standout has quietly developed into one of the Eagles’ most reliable interior pass-rushers, earning PFF pass-rush grades above 70.0 while generating 93 pressures over the past two seasons. As he enters a contract year, don’t be surprised if Ojomo starts to draw much more attention if he maintains that level of production. Pittsburgh Steelers: Darnell Washington The Steelers rewarded tight end Darnell Washington with a contract extension for his solid performance over the first three years of his career, but 2026 could be the year he gets more national attention as one of the better players at the position. He set a career high with 1.72 yards per route run last year and ranked seventh among tight ends in PFF run-blocking grade (73.1). San Francisco 49ers: Dominick Puni Dominick Puni impressed at right guard as a rookie in 2024, earning an 80.5 PFF grade that ranked sixth among qualified guards. He took a slight step back in 2025, with his 69.2 PFF grade ranking 27th at the position. Even with that regression, Puni has already put together two seasons as an above-average starter. Entering his third NFL season, he has a chance to establish himself as a top-15 guard before heading into a contract year in 2027. Seattle Seahawks: Derick Hall Derick Hall took a significant step forward in his third NFL season, setting career highs with a 73.9 PFF run-defense grade and a 72.6 PFF pass-rush grade. The Seahawks rewarded him with a contract extension before he could reach free agency, and with Boye Mafe departing this offseason, Hall is in line for an even larger role in 2026. His career high is 45 pressures in a season, but if he continues on his current trajectory, reaching 60 is well within reach. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Tykee Smith After two solid seasons to begin his NFL career, 2026 could be the year Tykee Smith starts to receive more league-wide recognition. The 2024 third-round pick out of Georgia has earned PFF grades of 72.0 and 65.8 in his first two seasons. Smith is at his best playing close to the line of scrimmage, and his 23 tackles resulting in a defensive stop in 2025 ranked 21st among safeties. Another step forward in Year 3 could establish him as an important piece of Tampa Bay’s defense. Tennessee Titans: Gunnar Helm There were plenty of encouraging flashes from rookie fourth-round pick Gunnar Helm in 2025. The former Texas Longhorn earned a 69.3 PFF receiving grade in his first NFL season, and while his campaign was overshadowed by several standout rookie tight ends, his 1.45 yards per route run ranked 23rd among all players at the position. With Chigoziem Okonkwo no longer on the roster after seeing 76 targets in 2025, Helm has a clear opportunity to take on a much larger role. A jump to 100-plus targets is well within reach, and that workload would have ranked among the NFL’s top 10 tight ends last season. Washington Commanders: Trey Amos A broken leg cut Trey Amos ’ rookie season short in Week 10, but there were encouraging signs before the injury. Although he finished with a 58.8 PFF coverage grade, he earned a grade above 70.0 in four of his 10 starts. Amos also entered the NFL off an outstanding final season at Ole Miss, allowing just 280 receiving yards on 515 coverage snaps in 2024.
