PFF's fantasy football recap focuses on player usage and stats, breaking down all the vital information you need to achieve fantasy success in 2026. There are only a few days left to take advantage of the PFF Early Bird Sale . Use code earlybird by Aug. 17 to save $40 on a PFF+ annual subscription and get all the data, tools and expert insights you need for fantasy draft season and beyond. Carolina Panthers @ Buffalo Bills Jonathon Brooks starts for Carolina: Brooks played in his first NFL game since December 2024. Carolina moved on from Rico Dowdle this offseason, knowing Brooks would return to join Chuba Hubbard and Trevor Etienne in the Panthers’ backfield. Hubbard entered training camp as the starter, but there has been plenty of speculation that Brooks could eventually take over the job if he plays well enough, particularly given that Hubbard has lost playing time to other backs in the past. Brooks’ ADP began to skyrocket after Hubbard was declared week-to-week with a hamstring injury . The initial expectation was that Brooks could take over at some point during the season, but Hubbard’s injury has created a path for Brooks to potentially start as early as Week 1. His usage with the starters in this game was nearly ideal, as he played in every situation except third-and-long, when Etienne took over. Once Carolina turned to its backups, Brooks’ day was done and Etienne became the every-down back. Carolina’s decision to use Brooks on early downs and in short-yardage situations offers a strong indication of how he could be deployed during the regular season. Hubbard has played in all situations throughout his career, so a two-man backfield could push more of his work toward passing downs while Brooks handles the bulk of the rushing opportunities. That type of split would likely make Brooks the more valuable fantasy back of the two. Brooks may no longer qualify as a clear value in fantasy drafts given his rapidly rising ADP, but his potential workload gives him a legitimate chance to spend much of the season as a fantasy starter. Bills use a four-man wide receiver rotation: The addition of DJ Moore has shaken up Buffalo’s wide receiver room. Buffalo utilized several wide receivers last season, with injuries and inconsistent play leading to a constantly changing rotation. The Bills added Moore to bring some stability to the position. He joins Khalil Shakir as the only wide receivers with seemingly secure roles near the top of the depth chart, while Joshua Palmer and Keon Coleman are competing for playing time behind them. Buffalo experimented with several receiver combinations in this game and rotated players more frequently than we should expect during the regular season. That included some snaps in 11 personnel without Shakir, something that should be rare once the games count. The Bills also tried several combinations in 12 personnel. While Coleman primarily played X in previous seasons, he, Shakir and Palmer all saw notable snaps in the slot. The one constant was Moore lining up at X whenever he was on the field. Moore has played multiple roles throughout his career, but he was the Bears’ X receiver last season and also played there for the Carolina Panthers when Joe Brady was on the coaching staff. The Bills pulled most of their starters after the first two drives, including Moore and Shakir, while Palmer and Coleman re maine d in the game. That provides another indication that neither Palmer nor Coleman has secured a full-time starting role. Ultimately, this game shouldn’t have a significant impact on the ADP of any Bills wide receiver. The Bills consolidate their tight end rotation: Jackson Hawes played just one snap with the starters after playing 43% of Buffalo’s offensive snaps last season. Buffalo retained its top three tight ends from last season in Dalton Kincaid , Dawson Knox and Hawes. Kincaid was typically on the field in clear passing situations, while Knox and Hawes were the primary tight ends in 12 personnel. That rotation changed significantly in this game. Buffalo ran five plays out of 12 personnel with the starters, and Kincaid and Knox were on the field for all five. Hawes’ only snap with the starters came in 21 personnel. Kincaid and Knox also split the snaps in 11 personnel. Kincaid still might not play as much as a typical fantasy starting tight end, but this usage suggests his playing time could increase from last season, particularly in 12 personnel. Buffalo has also been cautious with Kincaid in previous preseasons, so the fact that he played as extensively as he did is an encouraging sign for his health and role. Kincaid is an ideal target for fantasy managers who wait at tight end. Miscellaneous Notes Bills backup wide receiver Tyrell Shavers remains on the PUP list as he recovers from the torn ACL he suffered in the playoffs last season. Third-down back Ty Johnson and rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell were among the other Bills players who didn’t play. Johnson suffered a knee injury in practice earlier this week. It’s unclear why Bell was held out, but several Bills beat reporters noted that he was not in uniform during warmups. With Johnson out, both James Cook and Ray Davis took snaps in third-and-long situations with the starters. Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker played 100% of snaps with the starters while Xavier Legette joined them in 11 personnel. This is how the Panthers used their wide receivers at the end of last season. While it has been widely reported that the Panthers will sign veteran tight end Darren Waller , the move is not yet official, so Waller did not play. Without Waller, Carolina used all three of their tight ends with the starters. Tommy Tremble and Mitchell Evans split 12 personnel snaps and early 11 personnel snaps. Ja’Tavion Sanders played on only third downs and in clear passing situations. Waller is expected to take Sanders’ snaps, and potentially other 11 personnel work. Cleveland Browns @ Chicago Bears Quinshon Judkins takes 80% of the snaps with the starters: The Browns’ backfield has gone from a three-man rotation to a two-man committee. Last season, Judkins handled the early-down, short-yardage and goal-line work, while Jerome Ford served as the third-down and two-minute-drill back. Dylan Sampson was the primary backup in most situations. Ford departed in free agency, and Cleveland didn’t make any substantial additions at running back, condensing the rotation to Judkins and Sampson. The Browns played two drives with all of their starters before beginning to mix in backups on the third. Judkins played eight snaps, handling 100% of the early-down and short-yardage situations, while Sampson took both third-and-medium or third-and-long snaps. The smaller rotation should lead to a substantial increase in playing time for both backs. The starters didn’t have any goal-line snaps in this game, but Judkins handled only 60% of those snaps last season. That rate could approach 100% this year. The biggest remaining question is how Cleveland will divide the two-minute-drill work, as both backs saw snaps in those situations last season. Judkins ended last season with a dislocated ankle and fractured fibula. While he has been practicing, it was reassuring to see Cleveland comfortable enough with his recovery to play him in a preseason game. Judkins is being drafted as a low-end RB2, but his expected volume gives him a strong chance to finish as a mid-range RB2. First look at the Browns’ wide receiver rotation: Rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston have already worked their way into the starting lineup. The Browns had the lowest-graded wide receiver unit last season, prompting the team to spend two early draft picks at the position. Boston was already named a starter earlier in the week, while Concepcion was also listed with the first team on Cleveland’s unofficial depth chart . They joined Jerry Jeudy on the first two drives. As expected, Boston lined up at X, Jeudy at Z and Concepcion in the slot. Concepcion primarily played in 11 personnel, but he also took one snap in place of Jeudy in 12 personnel with the starters. Jeudy left after two drives, while Boston and Concepcion remained in the game. Isaiah Bond replaced Jeudy, and the three receivers rotated in 12 personnel. Cleveland’s willingness to use Concepcion in two-receiver sets is encouraging, as it gives him a path to more playing time than a typical slot receiver. If he plays well enough, he could eventually take a larger share of those snaps from Jeudy. The later rotation also reinforced Bond’s standing as the top backup. He primarily played in the slot as a rookie but lined up outside throughout this game. If any of Cleveland’s top three wide receivers misses time this season, Bond appears most likely to see a significant increase in snaps. Boston and Concepcion are both intriguing mid-round fantasy picks. Their ADPs are unlikely to move much based on this game, however, as their usage largely confirmed expectations entering the preseason. Bears begin in 14 personnel: While most teams keep their personnel groupings relatively vanilla in the preseason, Chicago gave opponents something extra to think about. Chicago shifted toward more 12 personnel last season after adding Colston Loveland , using the grouping on 34.4% of its plays. After seeing the Los Angeles Rams succeed out of 13 personnel last season, Chicago spent a third-round pick on Sam Roush , suggesting we could see Loveland, Cole Kmet and Roush share the field frequently. The loss of D.J. Moore provides another reason for Chicago to lean further into multiple-tight end sets. Roush was the most notable Bears skill-position player to appear in this game. While he is unlikely to carry much fantasy value himself, his usage provided another indication that Chicago could lean even more heavily into multiple-tight end formations. The Bears opened the game with four tight ends on the field, a personnel grouping they didn’t use at all last season. That could point toward Chicago keeping a fourth tight end on the roster while rarely taking Loveland or Kmet off the field. From a usage standpoint, it may be useful to think of Loveland as closer to one of Chicago’s wide receivers, with Kmet operating as the more traditional tight end. Miscellaneous Notes The Browns announced before the game that fullback Michael Burton , wide receiver Cedric Tillman and tight ends Joe Royer and Jack Stoll wouldn’t be playing. It’s unclear whether Tillman’s absence is related to an undisclosed injury, but reporters have speculated a trade may be imminent . Royer has been away from the team throughout training camp for an undisclosed personal reason. Burton and Stoll have recently missed practice time due to injury . Tight end Harold Fannin Jr. played nine of 10 snaps with the starters, and left the game at the same time as Quinshon Judkins and Jerry Jeudy . The one play he was off the field was a short-yardage situation. Bears lead wide receiver Luther Burden III suffered a groin injury a week ago, which will likely keep him out of the entire preseason. There is optimism he will be ready for the start of the season. Rookie Zavion Thomas was also absent from this game after suffering a knee injury that isn’t expected to be serious. Chicago rested the rest of their starters and key backups, including quarterback Caleb Williams , running backs D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai , wide receivers Rome Odunze and Kalif Raymond and tight ends Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet . Minnesota Vikings @ New York Giants Vikings have unexpected wide receiver usage: Tai Felton played ahead of Jauan Jennings , while Jordan Addison spent more time in the slot. Last season, Justin Jefferson served as the Vikings’ X receiver, with Addison at Z and Jalen Nailor joining them in the slot in three-receiver sets. Nailor left for the Las Vegas Raiders in free agency, leading Minnesota to eventually sign Jennings. While Jennings most recently played X for the San Francisco 49ers , he began his career in the slot, making him a logical candidate to replace Nailor there. Jefferson had the day off, and Felton replaced him at X in both two- and three-receiver sets. The 2025 third-round pick caught only three passes as a rookie, so seeing him play ahead of Jennings was somewhat surprising. That doesn’t necessarily mean Felton is ahead of Jennings on the depth chart, as Felton continued playing with the backups while Jennings’ day was done. It does, however, suggest Felton is Jefferson’s direct backup, meaning Jennings might not see a significant increase in playing time if Jefferson misses time. Minnesota spent most of its time in two-receiver sets, with Jennings joining Felton and Addison when the Vikings went to three receivers. Surprisingly, Addison moved into the slot more often than not, while Jennings lined up outside. Addison has averaged 1.19 yards per route run from the slot in his career compared to 1.66 out wide. Jennings has averaged 1.86 yards per route run from the slot over the past three seasons compared to 1.55 out wide. However, this came over a sample of only four plays, and the Vikings weren’t entirely consistent with their alignments during those snaps. This will be a situation worth monitoring throughout the preseason, as a shift into less familiar roles could impact the fantasy production of both Addison and Jennings. The Giants’ committee at running back: Cam Skattebo , Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary all received work with the starters. New York retained the same top three running backs from last season despite bringing in a new coaching staff. While many expected Skattebo to emerge as the clear lead back, head coach John Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy have long histories of utilizing committees at the position. That uncertainty was reflected on the Giants’ first unofficial depth chart, where both Skattebo and Tracy were listed as starters . Skattebo started the game and played the first two snaps before Tracy took over on third down and remained on the field for the final four plays of the drive. Singletary opened the second drive with the starters, followed by Tracy and then Skattebo, with all three rotating heavily for the remainder of the drive. The one consistent trend was Skattebo coming off the field on third downs, but he still played only five of 12 early-down snaps. Skattebo is returning from a season-ending injury, and a new coaching staff has reason to give all three backs opportunities during the preseason. There is still plenty of time for him to establish himself as the clear lead option on early downs. However, there is also a chance Skattebo won’t be fully back to form this season, and this rotation raises the possibility that none of the three backs will consistently play more than 50% of the offensive snaps. That uncertainty makes Skattebo difficult to justify at his current ADP, particularly when other players in the same range have more secure roles in their offenses. The Giants’ wide receiver room is wide open: New York made several changes at wide receiver this offseason, but it remains unclear who will be in the starting lineup in Week 1. New York retained Malik Nabers and Darius Slayton from last season but added free agents Darnell Mooney and Calvin Austin III early in the offseason, followed by Odell Beckham Jr. , JuJu Smith-Schuster and Braxton Berrios later in the offseason. The Giants also drafted Malachi Fields in the third round. The Giants were without Nabers (knee), Smith-Schuster (knee) and Jalin Hyatt (leg) for this game. Of those three, Nabers is the only one assured of a starting role when healthy. New York used a consistent four-man rotation of Slayton, Fields, Mooney and Austin with the starters. Austin played exclusively in 11 personnel and typically lined up in the slot. The other three receivers all saw snaps at X, while Mooney also played five snaps from the slot. That leaves several possibilities once Nabers returns. Any of Slayton, Fields or Mooney could start at X, while Austin or Mooney could handle the slot role. If Nabers isn’t ready for Week 1, any of the four could also line up at Z. All four receivers remained in the game for the third drive, when Beckham and Berrios began to mix in. That suggests Beckham and Berrios are no higher than sixth on the depth chart at this point. Smith-Schuster and Hyatt appear to face an uphill battle to make the roster, as their injuries have prevented them from competing for spots during the preseason. Until the rotation becomes clearer, Nabers is the only Giants wide receiver worth drafting in most fantasy leagues. Isaiah Likely ’s troubling playing time: Likely played only six snaps with the starters, all in 11 personnel. Likely spent the first four seasons of his career in a tight end rotation with the Baltimore Ravens — where Mark Andrews was typically the primary receiving tight end, and Charlie Kolar handled much of the blocking work. Likely followed John Harbaugh to the New York Giants , where he was expected to emerge as the primary tight end. However, New York retained Theo Johnson , its top receiving tight end from last season, as well as its top blocking tight end in Chris Manhertz . The Giants ran 10 plays out of 11 personnel, with Likely playing six and Johnson playing four. All six of Likely’s snaps were pass plays, while three of Johnson’s four were runs. Johnson and Manhertz handled both snaps with two tight ends on the field, while Manhertz was the primary tight end in 21 personnel. That usage suggests Likely could remain in a rotation similar to the one he experienced in Baltimore, except he would now occupy the Andrews role, with Johnson filling something closer to Likely’s old role. It’s worth noting that the Giants ran only one play out of 12 personnel, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about Likely’s role in that grouping. New York also rotated heavily at running back and wide receiver, so plenty could change between now and the start of the regular season. One encouraging sign was that Likely’s day ended after two drives alongside several other starters, while Johnson and Manhertz remained in for the third. Still, this is a situation worth monitoring, and it would have been more encouraging to see Likely on the field more frequently with the starters. Miscellaneous Notes The Giants were without wide receivers Malik Nabers (knee), JuJu Smith-Schuster (knee) and Jalin Hyatt (leg). Jaxson Dart exited the game for two plays after taking a big hit, but he was able to return to the game and complete the Giants’ second drive. The Vikings rotated Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason every one or two plays, regardless of situation. We occasionally see this kind of rotation in the preseason, but rarely in regular-season practice. We can generally expect Jones to play more in passing situations and Mason more in rushing situations once the regular season starts, with this game giving us minimal indication how close to 50-50 that split will be. Minnesota’s tight end rotation largely resembled last season, with T.J. Hockenson playing in 11 personnel, Josh Oliver playing in 21 personnel, and the two sharing the field for 12 personnel. There was one exception with Oliver playing in 11 personnel on a run play. Los Angeles Rams @ Kansas City Chiefs Chiefs wide receiver depth chart takes shape: Kansas City appears to have a clear top five wide receivers, with players fighting for playing time. Kansas City had five different wide receivers play between 350-650 snaps last season in Rashee Rice , Xavier Worthy , JuJu Smith-Schuster , Hollywood Brown and Tyquan Thornton . Smith-Schuster and Brown left for the NFC East in free agency. Kansas City is replacing them by expecting 2025 fourth-round pick Jalen Royals to be a part of the rotation as well as fifth-round rookie Cyrus Allen , who has received significant praise throughout training camp. Rice and Worthy sat out this game, leading Kansas City to use Thornton and Royals on the outside, and Allen in the slot on its first drive. After the first possession, Kansas City subbed out some key players, including Thornton and tight end Noah Gray . It appears Kansas City is already comfortable with Allen in the slot, because after the first drive, he started playing specifically in 12 personnel on the outside to give him more experience in those situations. Royals continued to play with the backups, but only in 11 personnel. 2025 undrafted wideout Andrew Armstrong joined them on the outside, while Nikko Remigio played in the slot. Allen started seeing more playing time again in 11 personnel in the slot closer to the two-minute drill. The Chiefs' wide receiver rotation was a little unique, as most teams will just play some players and then move on to players further down the depth chart. Of the three wide receivers who played in this game, Allen has the most upside. While it would have been nice to see him exit the game after one drive with the starters, it’s understandably rare for a fifth-round rookie to already be held in that high regard after one preseason game. It was good to see Kansas City use Allen in different roles on offense, suggesting the team could see him play multiple roles in the regular season. However, both Allen and Royals continued to play into the third quarter, which is longer than you would like to see for players who might have fantasy value this season. An initial pecking order for the Kansas City backup running backs: Brashard Smith played with the starters, while Emari Demercado didn’t play until the fourth quarter. Kansas City completely re-worked its running back room this offseason, adding Kenneth Walker and Demercado in free agency, drafting Emmett Johnson in the fifth round and retaining 2025 seventh-round pick Smith. Walker is undoubtedly the lead back who will see a high percentage of snaps. Chances are, there will be some plays, particularly in passing situations, where Walker will need a break. There is a question to who will be that receiving back, which all three other players could fill, as well as who would be the lead back if Walker suffers an injury. It’s unlikely we will have a great answer heading into the season. Under Andy Reid, Kansas City has consistently played its running backs in all situations in the preseason, playing one player for some snaps and then moving on to the next. Smith and Johnson spent the first three quarters taking a drive or two at a time. Demercado was playing on special teams throughout the game, and didn’t see his first offensive snaps until the fourth quarter. This would suggest that Demercado is a distant fourth on the depth chart. However, he was listed on second on the unofficial depth chart, putting some doubt in the order of the running backs. It’s worth noting we saw Isiah Pacheco high on the depth chart for a preseason game in his rookie season, and that didn’t play out until the middle of that year. Last year, Elijah Mitchell was high on the depth chart in the first week of the preseason, and Carson Steele was the primary backup to Pacheco in the second game. None of these backup running backs should be drafted in most redraft leagues. Whoever has the most early down snaps outside of Walker in Week 1 could be a sneaky waiver wire pickup. Xavier Smith could fall down the Rams depth chart: Smith was the one notable Rams skill player who played in this game. The Rams largely kept the same skill players from last season. The only players who played a snap who are no longer on the roster are sixth-string wide receiver Tutu Atwell and fifth-string tight end Nick Vannett . Every other player who took a snap was among the Rams players who were resting, except for Smith. Smith was rarely involved in the offense early in the season, or in their 13- or 12-personnel packages, but from Weeks 13-17, he played 63.1% of snaps in 11 personnel. Los Angeles drafted CJ Daniels in the sixth round, and Daniels joined Smith in the starting lineup for this game. This opens the door for Daniels to surpass Smith on the depth chart. Anyone who rests for Los Angeles in the first week of the preseason typically rests for the other two games, with a few names joining that list as the preseason goes on. It will be interesting to see if Smith or Daniels join that list at some point this preseason, which would likely secure their spots on the roster. Miscellaneous Notes The Rams announced before the game they wouldn’t play quarterback Matthew Stafford , running backs Kyren Williams , Blake Corum and Ronnie Rivers , wide receivers Puka Nacua , Davante Adams , Jordan Whittington and Konata Mumpfield and tight ends Terrance Ferguson , Tyler Higbee , Colby Parkinson and Davis Allen . 2025 fourth-round running back Jarquez Hunter remains fourth on the depth chart, and he appears to be a distant fourth considering Rivers is among the players who didn’t need to play. Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes didn’t play because the team is being cautious about his knee after tearing his ACL and LCL last season. Usually, Kansas City will play its starters. But with Mahomes out, the team opted not to play wide receivers Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy and tight end Travis Kelce . Running back Kenneth Walker only played on the first play of the game, and then his day was done. The only skill player to not dress for this game due to injury was backup wide receiver Jimmy Holiday . Jacksonville Jaguars @ New Orleans Saints First look at the Jaguars' rookie tight ends: Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol have already worked their way to second and third on the depth chart. Brenton Strange was the Jaguars' starting tight end last season, but they had a few veteran backups in Johnny Mundt , Hunter Long and Quintin Morris , with none maintaining a consistent role. Jacksonville saw the success of the Los Angeles Rams using multiple tight end sets and wanted to replicate some of that, by adding Boerkircher and Koziol in the draft. Boerkircher and Koziol were the only skill players in this game who are likely to see significant playing time this regular season. This gave us a look at how the Jaguars might use their tight ends in the regular season, particularly if Strange were to miss time due to injury. The Jaguars ran seven plays out of 11 personnel, nine out of 12 personnel and one out of 13 personnel with the starters. The two rookies were joined by Hunter Long in 13 personnel. The two played most 12 personnel snaps together, with Long taking one snap from Koziol. In 11 personnel, Boerkircher played five snaps to two by Koziol. Koziol spent more time lining up in different positions, including one snap in the backfield, one out wide and three in the slot. Both tight ends continued to see playing time after Nick Mullens was done, with Koziol starting to see more opportunities. We should expect Boerkircher to join Strange in 12 personnel in the regular season, but it’s unlikely he will have much fantasy value. If Strange suffers an injury, it will be debatable which of the two rookies has more fantasy value with this usage. Boerkircher would likely run more routes, but Koziol would see more targets per route. Oscar Delp makes his Saints debut: New Orleans also added a rookie tight end, who could see value if there is an injury to Juwan Johnson . The Saints similarly have a lead tight end in Juwan Johnson , but opted to make several changes to their backups. They added veteran Noah Fant and drafted Delp in the third round. This led Delp and 2025 seventh-round pick Moliki Matavao to be the two tight ends for the Saints in this game. Over the first three drives, Delp played more in receiving situations and Matavao more in blocking scenarios, although this left a few passing plays where Delp was off the field. Delp spent a third of his snaps lined up in the slot, which is similar to the rate of Johnson last season. This suggests Delp will be a direct backup to Johnson, while Fant will likely join Johnson in 12 personnel. It’s also possible Matavao or a different blocking tight end could take Johnson’s place in 12 personnel. Johnson will be turning 30 before the start of the season, and Johnson’s PFF grade has been 67.0 or less in each season of his career. There is an opportunity for Delp to take over as the lead receiving tight end if he plays well enough, but that is unlikely to happen in 2026. Miscellaneous Notes Saints backup wide receiver Mason Tipton remains on the PUP list. Tipton is currently recovering from tibia surgery. The Saints didn’t play quarterback Tyler Shough , running backs Travis Etienne Jr. , Alvin Kamara , Kendre Miller and Devin Neal , wide receivers Chris Olave , Jordyn Tyson and Devaughn Vele and tight ends Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant . Fourth-round rookie wide receiver Bryce Lance was also among the players not playing. Typically, this would mean Lance is simply fourth on the depth chart and was among the key players not participating. However, healthy Day 3 rookies typically suit up in the first week of the preseason no matter how highly they are thought of. Jacksonville rested quarterback Trevor Lawrence , running backs Bhayshul Tuten , Chris Rodriguez Jr. and LeQuint Allen , wide receivers Parker Washington , Brian Thomas Jr. , Jakobi Meyers and Travis Hunter and tight end Brenton Strange . Philadelphia Eagles @ Baltimore Ravens Eli Stowers starts fourth on the depth chart: Stowers appears unlikely to make a significant impact as a rookie. Philadelphia drafted Stowers in the second round with the expectation that he could become its tight end of the future. Dallas Goedert is 31 and restructured his contract this offseason, ensuring he will remain with the Eagles this year, but he is entering the final season of his deal. Ideally, Stowers would have positioned himself to contribute as a rookie before potentially taking on a larger role next season. The buzz surrounding Stowers has been relatively negative since the draft, as he hasn’t made much of an impact during OTAs or training camp. He is known primarily as a receiving tight end, which makes his path to the No. 2 job more difficult because backup tight ends often need to contribute as run blockers. There is still room for Stowers as a receiving-oriented third tight end who could serve as Goedert’s backup, but he doesn’t appear to have secured that role yet. Philadelphia rested Goedert for this game, along with Mundt, who has spent much of his career in a blocking role. Grant Calcaterra was also retained and played well ahead of Stowers. Calcaterra logged 12 of 13 snaps over the first four drives, compared to five for Stowers. Stowers replaced Calcaterra for one snap in 11 personnel, while Cameron Latu replaced Stowers for one snap in 12 personnel. Calcaterra’s day ended after that stretch, while Stowers continued playing into the second half. There is still plenty of time for Stowers to move ahead of Calcaterra on the depth chart, but his dynasty value will continue to trend downward until he starts making more of an impact in training camp or preseason games. Ravens wide receivers compete for playing time: Rookie Ja’Kobi Lane and Devontez Walker both received significant playing time in the first half. Baltimore retained its top two wide receivers from last season in Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman . The Ravens opted not to re-sign veterans DeAndre Hopkins or Tylan Wallace , opening the door for a new No. 3 receiver to emerge. Walker, a fourth-round pick in 2024, 2025 sixth-round pick LaJohntay Wester , and 2026 mid-round picks Lane and Elijah Sarratt have all been in contention. Walker and Lane were listed with the second team on the unofficial depth chart, while reports from training camp have suggested Lane has begun to separate himself. With Flowers and Bateman out, Lane and Walker opened the game as Baltimore’s top two wide receivers, with Wester joining them in three-receiver sets. Lane primarily lined up at X, while Walker spent more time at Z. Although Tyler Huntley played only two drives, Baltimore kept the same three receivers on the field for each of its first four drives. Sarratt didn’t enter until the fifth drive, suggesting he is unlikely to have a significant role early in the season. This game didn’t provide a definitive answer on Baltimore’s No. 3 receiver, but it did make clear that Lane and Walker are the primary contenders. Both caught three passes, with Lane adding a touchdown, while Wester was held without a reception. Ideally, Baltimore will play more of its starters later in the preseason, giving us a clearer indication of whether Lane or Walker has the edge for the third receiver job. Miscellaneous Notes Eagles wide receiver DeVonta Smith has been dealing with a hamstring injury and didn’t play, although he went through warmups . First-round rookie Makai Lemon has also been sidelined with a hamstring injury . Backup wide receiver Johnny Wilson ( knee ) and running back Dameon Pierce ( hamstring ) also missed the game due to injury. Philadelphia rested several starters, including quarterback Jalen Hurts , running back Saquon Barkley , wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks and tight ends Dallas Goedert and Johnny Mundt . Second-string running back Tank Bigsby played three snaps on third-and-5 or longer with the starters, matching his total in those situations from the entire 2025 regular season. Free-agent addition Hollywood Brown played on the first two drives before leaving ahead of the rest of the Eagles’ starters, providing further evidence that he is fourth on the wide receiver depth chart. Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers (quadriceps) returned to team drills Thursday after missing a few days. He didn’t play in this game, although he likely would have been held out even if fully healthy. Backup running back Rasheen Ali and undrafted rookie wide receiver Octavian Smith were also sidelined by injuries. Baltimore also rested quarterback Lamar Jackson , running backs Derrick Henry and Justice Hill , wide receiver Rashod Bateman , and tight ends Mark Andrews and Durham Smythe . While it may have been surprising to see rookie Josh Cuevas and Matthew Hibner still playing in the fourth quarter, they were the only two tight ends active. Baltimore has only four tight ends on its roster, with Andrews and Smythe both resting. Dallas Cowboys @ Seattle Seahawks Jaydon Blue appears locked into the backup running back role: Blue dominated the first-half snaps, suggesting the No. 2 job is his to lose. When Blue was drafted in the fifth round last season, there was some thought that he could compete for the starting job with veteran free-agent additions Javonte Williams and Miles Sanders . Instead, Blue began the season as a healthy inactive, with Williams and Sanders atop the depth chart and fullback Hunter Luepke capable of handling halfback duties in an emergency. Blue received opportunities after Sanders suffered a season-ending injury, but Malik Davis eventually emerged as the primary backup. Dallas didn’t re-sign Sanders and largely kept the same group of backups, including 2025 seventh-round pick Phil Mafah , who missed nearly all of last season due to injury. Although Davis finished last season as the primary backup, the Cowboys have made it clear they want Blue to win the job. Blue played 20 of 26 snaps in the first half of this game, coming off the field only for stretches of longer drives when Mafah rotated in. Davis didn’t enter until the second half. Williams remains the unquestioned starter, but Blue appears to have established himself as his primary handcuff. In deeper leagues where most backup running backs are rostered, Blue should be drafted. In typical redraft leagues, he is right on the fringe of being worth a pick in the final rounds. Elijah Arroyo is closer to a breakout: Arroyo saw time in both 12 and 22 personnel with the starters in this game. AJ Barner won the starting tight end job last season and remains firmly atop the depth chart, leaving Arroyo in a backup role. Seattle also retained its top three tight ends from last season, including blocking specialist Eric Saubert . Saubert’s presence has limited Arroyo’s opportunities, but Arroyo has consistently made plays throughout training camp. Barner was among the starters who rested in this game, giving Arroyo opportunities in situations he typically wouldn’t see during the regular season. Saubert remained the primary tight end in 21 personnel and handled a few early-down snaps in 11 personnel, but Arroyo played in passing situations while also seeing significant work on running plays. The less encouraging sign was that Saubert exited after the first quarter, while Arroyo remained in the game throughout the second quarter in an every-down role. It will be difficult for Arroyo to become fantasy-relevant as long as Barner is healthy, but this game provided a glimpse of the role Arroyo could inherit if Barner misses time. If that happens at any point this season, Arroyo would immediately become a priority waiver-wire target. Miscellaneous Notes The Cowboys rested their starters throughout last year’s preseason, and head coach Brian Schottenheimer has said he plans to do the same this year. That includes quarterback Dak Prescott , running back Javonte Williams , wide receivers CeeDee Lamb , George Pickens , Ryan Flournoy and KaVontae Turpin , and tight end Jake Ferguson . Backup tight end Luke Schoonmaker played each of Dallas’ first eight offensive snaps before exiting ahead of the rest of the Cowboys’ starters. Seahawks running back Zach Charbonnet remains on the PUP list after tearing his ACL in the divisional round of the playoffs. He is reportedly ahead of schedule in his recovery but is still expected to miss the start of the season. First-round rookie running back Jadarian Price has been dealing with soreness. He recently returned to practice but sat out this game. Emanuel Wilson also missed the game due to injury. The Seahawks also rested several established starters, including quarterback Sam Darnold , wide receivers Jaxon Smith-Njigba , Rashid Shaheed and Cooper Kupp , and tight end AJ Barner . Wide receiver Tory Horton has returned to practice after ending last season on injured reserve, but he didn’t play in this game. records.new_body: Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza delivers efficient, mistake-free preseason debut All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza delivers efficient, mistake-free preseason debut By Mark Chichester Posted Aug 15, 2026 5:00 am EDT Las Vegas Raiders Fernando Mendoza delivers a clean NFL debut: The No. 1 overall pick completed 10 of 16 passes for 97 yards and a touchdown while avoiding a turnover-worthy play across 31 snaps. Intermediate throws provide an early bright spot: Mendoza went 2-of-3 for 33 yards on passes traveling 10-19 yards downfield, earning a 76.1 PFF passing grade at that depth. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. Fernando Mendoza ’s first taste of NFL action offered the Las Vegas Raiders plenty to build on. The No. 1 overall pick of April’s NFL draft played 31 snaps in the Raiders ’ 27-14 preseason loss to the Arizona Cardinals , completing 10 of his 16 attempts for 97 yards and a touchdown. He earned a 66.7 PFF overall grade and a 67.2 passing grade in his professional debut. Mendoza entered after veteran Kirk Cousins led the starting offense on a touchdown drive and initially appeared to be adjusting to the speed of the game. But the rookie settled in on his second possession, eventually finding Jack Bech for a 6-yard touchdown on third-and-goal. Mendoza earned four positive play-level grades against just one negative grade across his 31 snaps, with the lone negative coming on a missed throw to Malik Benson. He finished the night without a big-time throw, but more importantly, he avoided recording a turnover-worthy play. Mendoza stays efficient from a clean pocket The rookie did his best work when Arizona couldn't disrupt the pocket. Mendoza dropped back 12 times without pressure, completing eight of 11 attempts for 77 yards and his touchdown. He earned a 70.6 clean-pocket passing grade while averaging 7.0 yards per attempt and producing a 122.2 passer rating. His adjusted completion percentage climbed to 80.0% on those throws, and his average target traveled 8.1 yards downfield. As with almost all quarterbacks, that efficiency dipped when Arizona generated pressure. Mendoza faced pressure on six of his 18 dropbacks, completing two of five attempts for 20 yards and taking one sack. His passing grade fell to 57.8, while his adjusted completion percentage dropped to 50.0%. Still, there was no disastrous mistake. Mendoza didn't record a turnover-worthy play from either a clean pocket or under pressure. Click here for Mendoza's passing report Intermediate passing provides an early bright spot Las Vegas didn't ask its rookie quarterback to consistently attack deep downfield, but Mendoza found success when he worked the intermediate level. He completed two of three attempts between 10 and 19 yards downfield for 33 yards, averaging 11.0 yards per attempt and earning a 76.1 passing grade — his best mark at any depth. Most of his work came underneath. Nine of his 16 attempts traveled between 0 and 9 yards downfield, and he completed seven for 58 yards and his touchdown. Those throws accounted for 56.3% of his total attempts and earned him a 65.3 passing grade. Mendoza attempted just one pass of 20-plus yards, an incompletion 26 yards downfield. Two of his other incompletions were throwaways. Raiders keep the passing game relatively simple Kubiak and the Raiders didn't dress up Mendoza’s debut with an extensive menu of quarterback-friendly concepts. Play action accounted for only three of his 18 dropbacks, and Las Vegas didn't call a screen while he was on the field. Mendoza operated without play action on 83.3% of his dropbacks, completing eight of 14 attempts for 72 yards and his touchdown while earning a 65.1 passing grade. The limited play-action sample did produce some encouraging results. Mendoza completed both of his attempts for 25 yards, averaging 12.5 yards per attempt and earning a 67.0 passing grade. Arizona also blitzed him on five dropbacks. He completed two of four attempts for 25 yards in those situations and earned a 57.0 passing grade. When the Cardinals didn't blitz, he went 8-of-12 for 72 yards and his touchdown, earning a 70.9 passing grade. Mendoza was considerably harder on his performance than his grading profile suggested. “Unfortunately, I let my teammates down today,” Mendoza said. “But it’s a growing experience. I feel like we’re all growing and it helped me show that I need to grow a lot.” There is room for that growth. Mendoza didn't produce a big-time throw, and he struggled somewhat when Arizona created pressure. But the first night was largely clean. He protected the football, found success from a clean pocket and finished 18 dropbacks without putting the ball in harm’s way. For a rookie quarterback taking his first NFL snaps, that represents a solid place to start. records.new_body: NFL Preseason Week 1 Recap: Immediate fantasy football takeaways from Friday's games All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting NFL Preseason Week 1 Recap: Immediate fantasy football takeaways from Friday's games By Nathan Jahnke Posted Aug 14, 2026 8:08 pm EDT Breece Hall could see a larger role: The New York Jets running back signed a new contract and dominated playing time with the starters, unlike last preseason. The Miami Dolphins have their wide receivers: Caleb Douglas and Malik Washington appear to be the top wide receivers on the Dolphins' depth chart. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. PFF's fantasy football recap focuses on player usage and stats, breaking down all the vital information you need to achieve fantasy success in 2026. There are only a few days left to take advantage of the PFF Early Bird Sale . Use code earlybird by Aug. 17 to save $40 on a PFF+ annual subscription and get all the data, tools and expert insights you need for fantasy draft season and beyond. Denver Broncos @ Atlanta Falcons Jahan Dotson is the Falcons’ second wide receiver: The former Philadelphia Eagles receiver played 100% of the snaps with the starters. Eight different wide receivers drew a target for the Falcons last season, and only Drake London and backup Dylan Drummond remain on the roster. Atlanta replenished the position by signing Dotson and Olamide Zaccheaus in free agency and drafting Zachariah Branch in the third round. Reports throughout OTAs and training camp indicated that Dotson was the favorite for the No. 2 wide receiver job, and this game provided further evidence. He played every snap with the starters over two drives, lining up primarily at X. Zaccheaus joined him for every snap in 11 personnel, typically operating out of the slot. London played the first two snaps before exiting ahead of the other starters. Chris Blair replaced London, suggesting he could be London’s primary backup and a potential waiver-wire option if London misses time this season. Blair also has the most similar measurables to London among Atlanta’s other wide receivers. Branch played one snap with the starters, joining Dotson in 12 personnel. He returned with the backups and primarily lined up in the slot. If Branch earns significant playing time during the regular season, it will most likely come at the expense of Zaccheaus. That leaves Dotson not only firmly in a starting role but also facing minimal competition for playing time. Dotson hasn’t produced much over his NFL career, but his opportunity in Atlanta gives him a chance to put together his best season yet. He is worth a late-round pick in deeper leagues. Jonah Coleman is already third on the depth chart: The fourth-round rookie was listed sixth on Denver’s unofficial depth chart. Denver utilized a three-man running back rotation last season, with J.K. Dobbins handling the early-down work, RJ Harvey serving as the primary backup and Tyler Badie operating as the third-down back. All three remain on the roster, but Denver added Coleman in the fourth round to shake up the rotation. Unofficial depth charts can often be misleading, and the Broncos’ was particularly deceptive, with all of their rookies listed at the bottom. The Broncos played three drives with their starting offensive line. Harvey handled all six snaps on the opening drive and the first five snaps of the second before his day ended. Coleman replaced him to finish the drive and then played all 11 snaps on the third. Jaleel McLaughlin became the primary running back from that point forward, with Badie mixing in. This game offered little indication of how Denver will divide its backfield work during the regular season, but it did provide evidence that Coleman is already ahead of both McLaughlin and Badie. That was expected to happen at some point before the season, but seeing Coleman already occupy that spot in the pecking order is an encouraging sign. Pat Bryant is ahead of Troy Franklin: The Broncos were without Jaylen Waddle and Marvin Mims Jr., but this game still provided some clarity on the wide receiver rotation. Waddle hasn’t been practicing due to muscle tightness and didn’t play, while Mims has also been dealing with an undisclosed injury . That left Denver with a clear top three for this game in Courtland Sutton, Bryant and Franklin. The trio played together for the first two drives, taking all five snaps in 11 personnel. In 12 personnel, Sutton and Bryant were always the two wide receivers on the field, while Bryant and Franklin split snaps opposite Sutton in 21 personnel. Bryant frequently lined up in the slot, with Franklin and Sutton primarily playing outside. While several starters remained in the game for Denver’s third drive, Sutton and Bryant were done for the night. Franklin continued playing alongside Lil’Jordan Humphrey, Cam Ross and Dane Key. That usage suggests Bryant is ahead of Franklin on the depth chart and should see significant playing time in three-receiver sets alongside Sutton and Waddle. Sean Payton has historically utilized a deep wide receiver rotation, however, so Franklin should still have a role. There is also a chance Bryant cuts into Sutton’s playing time, as both are natural X receivers. The fact that Sutton and Bryant exited the game at the same time is at least an encouraging sign for Bryant’s standing in the offense. Miscellaneous Notes Lead running back J.K. Dobbins left practice on Monday with a soft-tissue injury , but he was able to return on Tuesday . Denver’s tight end rotation looked similar to last season, with Evan Engram seeing more work in passing situations and Adam Trautman handling more snaps on rushing plays. However, Engram played more frequently in 12 personnel over the first three drives than he did last season, an encouraging sign that his overall playing time could increase this year. The Broncos ’ preseason rotations under Sean Payton have often been poor indicators of how players will be used once the regular season begins. Last preseason, for example, J.K. Dobbins primarily handled third-down work before becoming an early-down back in the regular season. The same disconnect has shown up at wide receiver. Marvin Mims Jr. played 37 of 40 snaps with the starters last preseason, well ahead of Troy Franklin at 20 and Pat Bryant at two. Two years ago, Tim Patrick played 26 of 32 snaps with the starters, only to be released on cutdown day. Samaje Perine was used as the third-down and two-minute-drill back that preseason and was also released before the season. The Falcons rested star running back Bijan Robinson . Free-agent addition Brian Robinson is the unquestioned backup, and he took every snap with the starters. While it was a small sample size of eight plays, it was reassuring to see Kyle Pitts play 100% of snaps with the starters, with Charlier Woerner only playing in 12 personnel. Tampa Bay Buccaneers @ New York Jets Breece Hall handles an impressive workload: The Jets’ lead running back played 10 of 11 snaps on New York’s opening drive. Head coach Aaron Glenn emphasized last offseason that the Jets wanted to utilize all three of their running backs. That approach was evident in the preseason, when Hall played only 16 of 28 snaps with the starters, as Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis rotated in. The committee carried over into the regular season, with Hall playing fewer than 60% of the offensive snaps in two of the first three games. However, a season-ending injury to Allen eventually opened the door for Hall to take on a larger role. This offseason, New York appears more focused on making Hall the focal point of the running game. That was apparent on the first drive of this game, as Hall carried the ball four times over 11 plays and came off the field just once, on a third-and-long. More importantly, he remained on the field for two other third downs after not playing a single third-down snap with the starters last preseason. Davis didn’t play because of a knee injury . He served as the Jets’ primary third-down back last season, but Hall’s usage in this game suggests he could handle more of that work this year. Hall enters the season as a high-end RB2 with a path to RB1 production if the Jets’ offense exceeds expectations. Omar Cooper Jr. doesn’t play with the starters: New York’s rookie wide receiver appears to be fourth on the depth chart. New York’s wide receiver room was in constant flux last season, particularly after Garrett Wilson suffered a season-ending injury. The Jets’ primary additions at the position this offseason were Cooper through the draft and veteran Tim Patrick in free agency. The Jets opened this game with Wilson and Adonai Mitchell as their top two wide receivers, which has been the expectation throughout OTAs and training camp. Mitchell was already worth a late-round pick before this game, and his usage on the opening drive further solidified his role. Isaiah Williams served as New York’s slot receiver in 11 personnel. Williams has been a standout during training camp and is expected to maintain a role in the offense during the regular season. Wilson, Mitchell and Williams all left the game after the first drive. Cooper took over in the slot on the second drive, with Patrick and undrafted rookie Malik McClain lining up outside. Notably, Cooper remained on the field in 12 personnel. Even if Cooper eventually overtakes Williams as the primary slot receiver, it will be difficult for him to earn enough playing time to become a reliable fantasy option. He remains a late-round possibility, but several wide receivers being drafted after him have clearer paths to significant playing time this season. Don’t read into Sean Tucker ’s extensive playing time: The Buccaneers rested nearly all of their fantasy-relevant players, with Tucker being a notable exception. Tampa Bay rested its top two running backs, Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell . Tucker recorded 86 carries last season and saw significant work near the goal line, helping him score seven touchdowns. Given that role, his extensive playing time in this game might initially appear to be a negative sign for his involvement this season. However, the Buccaneers have only five running backs on their roster. Every other team outside of Tampa Bay and the Las Vegas Raiders has at least six. Teams typically use at least four running backs over the course of a preseason game, but with Irving and Gainwell resting, Tampa Bay had only three available. That context helps explain why Tucker, despite entering his fourth season, was still on the field alongside undrafted rookies. Miscellaneous Notes Jets starting quarterback Geno Smith did not play due to foot soreness, which was announced roughly an hour before the game. Smith had been expected to play before experiencing the soreness and would have suited up had it been a regular-season game, according to Mike Garafolo on NFL Network’s pregame show. Mason Taylor , a second-round pick of the 2025 draft, served as the Jets’ primary tight end with the starters, sitting out just three plays. Two of those came in 12 personnel, with Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods taking the field instead. First-round rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq also didn’t play as he continues to recover from a hernia procedure in May . He took a step forward in his recovery this week, as he was spotted running on the side during practice. Tampa Bay rested quarterbacks Baker Mayfield and Jake Browning , wide receiver Chris Godwin Jr. and tight end Cade Otton . Buccaneers wide receiver Emeka Egbuka missed this game due to a toe sprain. Tampa Bay is optimistic that he will be available for Week 1, and he likely would not have played in this game even if healthy. The Buccaneers were also without Jalen McMillan ( knee ), Tez Johnson ( groin ) and David Sills V ( knee ). Third-round rookie Ted Hurst III received significant playing time in the first half with five of the team’s other top six wide receivers sidelined. Hurst projects primarily as an X receiver and spent most of his snaps there, though he also saw considerable work in the slot. Miami Dolphins @ Washington Commanders The Dolphins have their wide receivers: Caleb Douglas and Malik Washington were the clear top two wide receivers with the starters. Miami moved on from longtime wide receivers Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle this offseason. Washington was the primary holdover, while the Dolphins added free agents Jalen Tolbert and Tutu Atwell and drafted Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman. Two months ago, the competition appeared wide open. Since then, Douglas and Washington have received the most praise throughout training camp. Miami’s starters played one long drive and utilized a variety of personnel groupings. Douglas and Washington played 100% of the snaps in 11, 12 and 21 personnel, while Douglas also played both snaps in 22 personnel. Washington’s usage was particularly noteworthy because he played 93.4% of Miami’s 11-personnel snaps last season but only 37.6% of the snaps in two-receiver sets, often competing with Nick Westbrook-Ikhine and Cedrick Wilson Jr. in those groupings. It was surprising to see Jalen Reagor serve as the third wide receiver in 11 personnel. The former first-round pick spent his first two seasons with the Philadelphia Eagles before bouncing between three teams over the next three seasons, recording single-digit receptions each year. He spent part of last season on the Los Angeles Chargers practice squad and didn’t sign with Miami until June 2. Tolbert and Atwell took over on the second drive, with Tahj Washington joining them in 11 personnel. Considering the opening drive lasted 16 plays, it would have been understandable for Miami to give Douglas or Washington a play or two off. Instead, both remained on the field throughout the drive, suggesting there is a sizable gap between them and the rest of the wide receiver room. Both Douglas and Washington are worth late-round picks, as one of the two will likely lead Miami in targets this season. Don’t give up hope on Greg Dulcich yet: Dulcich has been a popular late-round target, but his usage in this game initially appeared concerning. Miami re-signed Dulcich to a $3.25 million deal this offseason while moving on from Darren Waller , Julian Hill and Tanner Conner . The Dolphins replaced them with Ben Sims and rookies Will Kacmarek and Seydou Traore . Dulcich played a part-time role last season, but his 2.31 yards per route run ranked third among tight ends. The turnover in the tight end room, combined with uncertainty at wide receiver entering the offseason, made Dulcich a prime sleeper candidate. Dulcich played only eight of a possible 14 snaps with the starters, fewer than Kacmarek, but the raw snap count is less concerning once you look at how Miami deployed them. Dulcich was also wearing a red non-contact jersey last week because of a hand injury before returning to full practice this week. More importantly, Dulcich played 100% of the snaps in 11 and 12 personnel, while Kacmarek played 100% of the snaps in 12, 21 and 22 personnel. Those roles continued after the starters left, with Cole Turner joining Kacmarek in 22 personnel. Because 21 and 22 personnel are typically more run-heavy groupings, Dulcich’s role should keep him on the field for a high percentage of Miami’s passing situations. The Dolphins experimented with a variety of personnel groupings and ran both pass and run plays from each with the starters, which likely made Dulcich’s overall snap rate look worse than it would under typical regular-season usage. There are still reasons for concern. Miami’s wide receiver hierarchy appears more settled than it did earlier in the offseason, and there are rumors that Jonnu Smith could return to the Dolphins. Still, Dulcich’s usage in passing-oriented personnel groupings leaves a path for him to emerge as one of this season’s top sleeper tight ends. Kaytron Allen plays ahead of Jerome Ford : Allen handled the early-down work, while the two split opportunities on third downs. The Commanders made several changes to their running back room this offseason. They retained Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Jeremy McNichols , added free agents Rachaad White and Ford, and drafted Allen in the fifth round. Of those five backs, only Allen and Ford played in this game. Allen played 100% of the first- and second-down snaps with the starters. Washington faced three third downs during that stretch, including one third-and-short when both running backs were on the field. Allen and Ford split the other two third-down snaps. This usage suggests Ford could be on the outside looking in for a roster spot. White is expected to handle third-down work, while McNichols filled that role last season. Washington has little need for three backs who specialize in passing situations, potentially leaving Ford and McNichols competing for the fourth running back spot. Even if Ford makes the roster, his path to fantasy relevance appears limited, even if injuries strike elsewhere in the backfield. Allen has a clearer path to playing time, although he will still need to compete with Croskey-Merritt and potentially White for early-down work. The buzz surrounding Allen has also quieted during training camp after he impressed during OTAs. Early leaders emerge in the Commanders’ wide receiver battle: At least six wide receivers are competing for playing time behind Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs . Washington has used mid-round picks in each of the past three drafts on receivers who can play in the slot, selecting Luke McCaffrey , Jaylin Lane and Antonio Williams . The Commanders have also taken chances on several veteran receivers, including Treylon Burks , Dyami Brown and Van Jefferson . For most of the offseason, it appeared those six were competing for two open roles at Z and in the slot. The recent addition of Diggs, who can play both positions, has effectively reduced that competition to one open spot. Washington opened the game with Brown at X, Burks at Z and McCaffrey in the slot in 11 personnel. None of the other three receivers played on the first two drives. That gives Burks and McCaffrey an early edge to join McLaurin and Diggs in three-receiver sets. Neither would carry much fantasy value while the starters are healthy, but either could emerge as a waiver-wire option if Diggs misses time. Brown appears to be the favorite to back up McLaurin, which makes sense given his experience at X. He would be the most logical pickup if McLaurin were to suffer an injury. McCaffrey moved outside to X for his third drive, with Jefferson at Z and Lane in the slot. Williams appeared to be a favorite for a prominent role early in OTAs, but the buzz surrounding him has faded. He didn’t enter the game until later in the second quarter. There is still plenty of time for Williams to move up the depth chart, and he appears likely to make the roster, but his early-season playing time could be limited. If Washington keeps six wide receivers, McLaurin, Diggs, McCaffrey, Burks, Williams and Brown currently appear to have the inside track. That could leave Jefferson and Lane on the outside looking in. Miscellaneous Notes The Commanders announced before the game that they would rest several starters, including quarterback Jayden Daniels , running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt , wide receivers Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs , and tight ends Chig Okonkwo and John Bates . Running back Rachaad White also didn’t play despite not appearing on the team’s list of players being rested. Ben Sinnott served as Washington’s primary tight end throughout the first half. There had been some speculation that Sinnott could also see time at fullback this season, but Washington consistently used only one player in the backfield during the first half. Commanders backup running back Jeremy McNichols did not play due to a quad injury. He is competing for one of the backup running back spots on the roster. Miami’s third-round rookie wide receiver Chris Bell remains on the non-football injury list as he recovers from the torn ACL he suffered last December at Louisville . Bell isn’t expected back anytime soon, and while he is expected to return at some point this season, Miami will likely ease him into action once he is cleared. The other three stats exclude these plays. • Targets may differ from official NFL sources. The most likely discrepancy is a clear thrown-away pass, where the NFL may give the target to the nearest receiver, while this data will not. • Carries are only on designed plays. Quarterback scrambles won’t count for the total number of carries in the game. records.new_body: 10 NFL players whose final season may come in 2026 All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 10 NFL players whose final season may come in 2026 By Bradley Locker Posted Aug 14, 2026 7:07 am EDT Likely the last season for Lane Johnson : The Eagles tackle owns the second-most Wins Above Replacement at the position since 2017 but played under 500 snaps in 2025. An uncertain future for Cameron Heyward : The Steelers great has reached a 90.0-plus grade in each of the past two seasons, but how much longer he'll play remains tenuous. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. The NFL preseason is now in full swing, building up more and more excitement for what looks to be a riveting 2026 regular season. While the preseason is often about showcasing young, rising players, it can also mark the last August appearances for veteran players about to call it quits. Some of the players listed below have already signified that the 2026 campaign will be their last, potentially starting the clock for Hall of Fame enshrinement in 2031. Meanwhile, other names are continuing to battle either Father Time or mounting injuries despite their riproaring career production. No matter what, even seeing these 10 players take the field this season is something that shouldn’t be taken for granted, because it might never happen again after January. Note: Players who aren’t actively on teams but might play their final season ahead — like Bobby Wagner and Tyreek Hill — were excluded. QB Aaron Rodgers , Pittsburgh Steelers As he enters his 22 nd pro season — which Rodgers has repeatedly mentioned will be his last — he’s assembled a resume that few can match at the position. The four-time league MVP, four-time first-team All-Pro, Super Bowl champion and 10-time Pro Bowler is indisputably one of the best quarterbacks in league history. His advanced work is just as decorated, earning an 80.0-plus overall PFF grade in a gaudy 11 seasons and laying claim to the highest-graded quarterback campaign ever . Rodgers’ first season in Pittsburgh showed serious signs of regression, with his 68.0 overall and 68.8 PFF passing marks both his lowest in a full year in his illustrious career. His 4.8% big-time throw rate was one of his worst rates yet, and his 2.60-second average time to throw was Rodgers’ second-fastest due to his inability to withstand pressure. The 42-year-old will look to turn back the clock one last time on a Steelers team that reunites Rodgers with longtime guide Mike McCarthy as well as several assistants. T Lane Johnson , Philadelphia Eagles Point blank, Johnson has established himself as one of the premier tackles of the era. The five-time All-Pro and two-time Super Bowl champion has never earned worse than a 71.9 overall PFF grade across his decorated 13-year career, in which 10 seasons have sat above a 75.0. Further, Johnson is the second-most-valuable tackle by PFF Wins Above Replacement since 2017, trailing just Trent Williams . The 2025 season was a bit of an unfortunate one for Johnson, who played only 449 snaps due to a foot injury. The 36-year-old is clearly still capable of playing at a high level — reflected in his 80.4 PFF pass-blocking grade last season — but he surmised that 2026 figures to be his swan song. Johnson’s ability to stay on the field looms as an X-factor on an Eagles offense with several big questions. EDGE Cameron Jordan , New Orleans Saints Jordan has enjoyed an incredibly fruitful career after being a first-round pick by the Saints in 2011. Playing all 15 seasons in New Orleans, Jordan has racked up eight Pro Bowl bids and three All-Pro nods, not to mention nine seasons with at least a 75.0 overall PFF grade. Fascinatingly, one of those years came in 2025. Although Jordan’s efficiency as a pass-rusher has been below-average since 2022, he’s re maine d a strong run defender, ranking fifth among edge defenders with an 82.1 PFF run-defense grade last season. The franchise legend has seemingly indicated that he’ll call it a career after 2026, but at least he’ll get a proper farewell — and potentially one more playoff appearance — by sticking around in black and gold. TE Travis Kelce , Kansas City Chiefs Kelce is inarguably one of the best tight ends to ever play pro football. The 11-time Pro Bowler, four-time first-team All-Pro and three-time Super Bowl champion earned an 83.3-plus overall PFF grade in eight straight seasons and is easily the most valuable tight end by PFF WAR since 2018. As Kelce has gotten into his late 30s, he’s remained a solid player but hasn’t quite looked the same. Last year, Kelce’s 1.47 yards per route run were a career low, and his 8.4% drop rate was his second-worst yet. However, the 36-year-old still sat in the 67 th percentile in yards after the catch per reception and the 70 th percentile in separation rate against single coverage. Kelce hasn’t given any firm designation yet about the 2026 season, only signing a one-year contract to return to Kansas City. But following an offseason wedding and with his career already tenuous on a season-to-season basis, it’s fair to wonder if this will be it for the future Hall of Famer. QB Matthew Stafford , Los Angeles Rams Stafford has gone from respectable quarterback on a bad team to one of the league’s best. The No. 1 overall pick in the 2009 draft has reached an 80.0 overall PFF grade in eight seasons, with his zenith coming in 2025 — when he led the league (92.0) and claimed his first career MVP at age 37. The Rams star can clearly still spin it, although it’s worth wondering how much longer he’ll lace up the cleats. Los Angeles invested the 13 th overall pick in quarterback Ty Simpson to kickstart its succession plan, and Stafford seemingly dealt with a serious back issue before his award-winning campaign. The 38-year-old is under contract through 2027 after agreeing to an extension this offseason, but there’s a real chance 2026 will be his last year — especially if the Super Bowl-favorite Rams win the title in Los Angeles. through . --> Read more Read more PFF Hall of Fame Monitor: Which active NFL players are on track for Canton? By Bradley Locker (opens in new tab) → EDGE Khalil Mack , Los Angeles Chargers Mack has quietly compiled an excellent career across three teams, being named a four-time first-team All-Pro while winning Defensive Player of the Year. Nine of Mack’s 12 career campaigns have finished with at least an 85.0 overall PFF grade, which is extremely remarkable. Although Mack played only 478 total snaps with the Chargers last year, he was still impactful with a 79.2 overall PFF grade, 77.2 PFF run-defense mark and 42 total pressures. The 35-year-old has seemingly flirted with retirement in each of the past few offseasons but has elected to come back to Los Angeles thus far. With the Chargers picking Akheem Mesidor in the first round in April, it could signify that this season might be Mack’s curtain call. Dl Cameron Heyward , Pittsburgh Steelers Heyward’s career has mixed dominance with longevity. The 16-year veteran is a four-time first-team All-Pro who ranks third among positional counterparts in PFF WAR since 2018. Heyward has especially defied the aging curve by producing a 90.1-plus overall PFF grade in each of the last two seasons, including sitting above an 84.0 in both pass-rushing and run-defense in 2025. Like Stafford, Heyward also agreed to a one-year contract extension this summer, although there was genuine uncertainty whether or not he would return following Mike Tomlin’s departure as head coach. The Steelers great is still performing like one of the better defensive linemen in football, but the 37-year-old isn’t guaranteed to suit up beyond 2026. Dl Calais Campbell , Baltimore Ravens Campbell’s career has spanned nearly two decades and witnessed tremendous production for five separate teams, being named a Pro Bowler six times and an All-Pro in three campaigns. His best six-year peak is Canton-worthy, achieving an 82.5-plus grade from 2014-2019. The NFL’s oldest active defensive player, Campbell will turn 40 before the 2026 season begins. Although he’s more of a rotational interior option at this point, Campbell remains a useful player with a 9% run stop rate and 65.1 PFF pass-rush grade in 2025. Campbell has staved off retirement thus far, but a promising individual and/or team year in Baltimore could propel him to stroll into the sunset. T Morgan Moses , New England Patriots Moses doesn’t boast the accolades of his counterparts on this list, actually never even making a Pro Bowl or an All-Pro team. Yet he’s been a quality and reliable tackle for nearly a decade, posting six seasons with at least a 75.0 overall PFF grade. The 35-year-old was a major reason why the Patriots’ offensive line took a leap last season, earning a 78.8 PFF run-blocking grade while allowing only two sacks across 781 pass-blocking snaps and a career-high 1,294 total plays. However, the fact that New England selected tackle Caleb Lomu in the first round suggests that the hourglass may be ticking on Moses’ career — although he is under contract through 2027. QB Kirk Cousins , Las Vegas Raiders There were a number of players in contention for this final spot, but Cousins felt like the most recognizable and probable to walk away. The former fourth-round pick has vastly outperformed his draft slot, being named to four Pro Bowls and reaching an 80.0-plus overall grade six times in a memorable career. Cousins showed he can still perform at a solid level last season with a 75.0 PFF passing grade, but his 3.2% big-time throw rate and 72.3% adjusted completion percentage both placed 31 st out of 43 qualifying passers. On top of that, Cousins played just 289 dropbacks while operating as Atlanta’s backup. The former Vikings standout will occupy much of the same role in Las Vegas, presumably starting the season as the Raiders’ top option before handing the reins to rookie Fernando Mendoza. The almost-38-year-old could remain a steady backup or bridge option for the next several years, but the effective 2027 free agent very well may hang up the cleats this winter.
