records.new_body: Fantasy Football 2026: Injury and status updates for veterans All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting Fantasy Football 2026: Injury and status updates for veterans By Nic Bodiford Posted Aug 14, 2026 6:30 am EDT The Jaguars ’ running back rotation is still unknown : Questions remain as to how trustworthy the position’s usage was at Friday’s scrimmage. WR Luther Burden III , Chicago Bears : Burden has a chance to play in Week 1 after suffering a groin injury over the weekend. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. NFL training camps have been underway since late July. While some NFL veterans are safely set to take on clear-cut roles, others enter fantasy-relevant training camp battles and injury-related obstacles. The article below breaks down need-to-know information and recommended storylines to track in the coming weeks regarding NFL veterans in 2026. Jacksonville Jaguars running backs Jacksonville Jaguars second-year running back Bhayshul Tuten reportedly delivered consistently “ terrific ” performances in spring and summer practices while free-agent signee running back Chris Rodriguez rehabbed following spring foot surgery. Fellow second-year running back LeQuint Allen (80.8 PFF pass-blocking grade) remains entrenched as the third-down back, having graded out as the best pass protector among 35 NFL running backs with at least 50 pass-protection snaps in 2025. He is the only qualifying player to clear a 71.0 PFF pass-blocking grade. Tuten operated as the starter at last Friday’s scrimmage but eventually began rotating with Rodriguez, who took over in the green zone and “got most, if not all, of the goal-line type reps .” However, Sports Illustrated’s John Shipley believes “it is dangerous to use the scrimmage as a data point” because Jaguars head coach Liam Coen deployed former Jaguars and current Philadelphia Eagles running back Tank Bigsby as the team’s starter in last year’s scrimmage. Shipley has not yet identified the team’s two-minute-drill running back. Earning this role would meaningfully boost Tuten’s weekly fantasy-scoring potential. Running between the 20-yard lines is a fantasy-unfriendly role. Tuten can earn passing game involvement in that area, and even lead the backfield in targets, given Allen’s role as a pass protection-based player. If Tuten can at least force a split with Rodriguez for scoring position duties, Tuten can return RB2 value. Like all three-player backfields, this is, however, a precarious situation. Tuten earned a 66.7 PFF rushing grade and a 52.9 PFF receiving grade last year. By comparison, Rodriguez posted a 78.4 PFF rushing grade and a 47.7 PFF receiving grade. RB J.K. Dobbins , Denver Broncos Denver Broncos coach Sean Payton patted his right hamstring as he told reporters that running back J.K. Dobbins suffered a soft-tissue injury at Monday’s practice. Dobbins, 27, has an extensive injury history and notably tore his hamstring along with three knee ligaments and his meniscus in 2021. He earned an 80.8 PFF rushing grade, a career-worst 46.6 PFF receiving grade and a 60.3 PFF pass-blocking grade before suffering a season-ending Lisfranc injury in Week 10 last year. As detailed in “ Top 3 receiving running back prospects for fantasy football ,” fourth-round rookie running back Jonah Coleman is the best post-catch producer in the 2026 class, fares well in pass protection and profiles as a three-down back. He compiled an 82.1 PFF offense grade last year, and “his 5-foot-8, 220-pound fire hydrant frame yields a 33.4 body mass index (BMI) rating.” He has received positive reviews and will compete for the starting role if Dobbins is sidelined in the regular season. Second-year running back RJ Harvey registered a 69.4 PFF receiving grade, and may be best-suited to a pure pass-catching role. Dobbins resumed practicing on Tuesday, but re-injury remains a risk until details on the injury are made clear. WR Luther Burden III , Chicago Bears Chicago’s presumed No. 1 wide receiver and No. 2 pass-catcher , Burden suffered a groin strain on Saturday. He is expected to sit out for “about a month.” Burden has a chance to be ready for Week 1, with reporting language ranging from hope to belief . Playing in an exceptionally well-schemed offense , his elite upside keeps him in “ must-draft ” territory. He earned a 77.7 PFF receiving grade last year. Bears head coach Ben Johnson recently said he believes it is Burden’s “destiny to be one of the best wide receivers in the league,” comparing him to Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and former Miami Dolphins wide receiver Jarvis Landry , players Johnson coached with his prior teams. St. Brown earned a 92.8 PFF receiving grade while leading the team in targets (592) during Johnson’s 2021-24 tenure. Meanwhile, Landry recorded a 90.5 PFF receiving grade while also pacing the team in targets (552) in their four seasons together. Encouragingly, Burden exhibited a normal gait on Monday. He remains a WR2 with WR1 upside. His recovery must be closely monitored. WR Alec Pierce , Indiana polis Colts The Athletic’s James Boyd reported on Monday that Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce required a second PRP injection in his surgically repaired left ankle “to alleviate soreness and speed up his rehab.” Colts head coach Shane Steichen said he does not “have a timetable on his return.” The Colts signed Pierce to a four-year, $114 million extension this offseason. On Tuesday, Colts general manager Chris Ballard refuted Boyd’s reporting regarding the second injection in a statement to FOX59’s Mike Chappell, yet revealed that Pierce’s heel was also addressed surgically. Boyd stands by his reporting and left aspects unexplained. Colts wide receiver Josh Downs ( groin ) resumed practicing on Tuesday. Pierce did individual work with trainers and appears to show left calf atrophy . The situation is murky. A free-agent wide receiver signing would be a negative indicator. Pierce should be avoided in drafts at this time. He earned an 81.0 PFF receiving grade last year, while Downs played to a 77.4 PFF receiving grade. records.new_body: 2026 NFL Preseason Week 1 Recap: Immediate fantasy football takeaways from Thursday's games All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting 2026 NFL Preseason Week 1 Recap: Immediate fantasy football takeaways from Thursday's games By Nathan Jahnke Posted Aug 13, 2026 8:31 pm EDT Germie Bernard makes his case to start: The second-round rookie for the Pittsburgh Steelers led the Steelers' offense throughout the first half, primarily making plays out of the slot in a position that D.K. Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. don’t typically occupy. Tyler Allgeier and Jeremiyah Love split-first quarter carries: The Arizona Cardinals were one of a few teams to play their starters on Thursday night. Love got the first nod, but Allgeier also saw three carries on their first drive. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. PFF's fantasy football recap focuses on player usage and stats, breaking down all the vital information you need to achieve fantasy success in 2026. Detroit Lions @ Cincinnati Bengals Colbie Young plays with the starters: Young took two snaps on the first two drives in place of Tee Higgins while Joe Burrow was still playing. The Bengals spent the last two seasons with Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins as their top two receivers, with Andrei Iosivas joining them in three-receiver sets. The Bengals are one of the top teams in 11-personnel usage, leading to Iosivas playing over 75% of snaps each of the last two seasons. His snap rates have been helped by Higgins missing a few games each of the last two years. Young was drafted in the fourth round, and appears to have already passed players like Mitch Tinsley on the depth chart. One of Young’s snaps with the starters was in 11 personnel, but he also took a snap in place of Higgins in 12 personnel, rather than Iosivas taking the 12 personnel snap. Often, when starters leave the game, key backups are included. The Bengals' top two running backs and top two tight ends left the game, but Iosivas kept playing with the backups. This suggests Iosivas' job as the third wide receiver might not be secure. If Young plays well enough and Chase or Higgins suffers an injury, it’s possible that Young, instead of Iosivas, could be the player to pick up off the waiver wire. The Detroit Lions reworked their wide receiver room: The Lions' backup wide receiver room looks very different from last season. Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams are locked in as the top two wide receivers on the Lions' depth chart, and they were both among the starters who didn’t play in this game. Last season, Isaac TeSlaa , Kalif Raymond , Tom Kennedy , Dominic Lovett and Jackson Meeks were the top backups. Raymond is now with the Chicago Bears , while free agent addition Greg Dortch was expected to take his place. The Lions added to that depth by adding veteran Cedrick Wilson in May after not adding to the room in the draft. It was no surprise that TeSlaa was one of the primary receivers for this game, but Wilson appears to have overtaken all of the other backups, as he played all 15 snaps on the first three drives. Detroit used 11 personnel for all 15 snaps and deployed a rotation of Dortch and Meeks for the third spot. Both Wilson and Dortch stopped playing at the end of the first quarter, making it seem like their roster spots are secure. TeSlaa played on the first drive of the second quarter, which was odd considering he’s the favorite for the third spot, and two other receivers already stopped playing. Kennedy and Levett, who were two of the top backups last season, didn’t suit up until the middle of the second quarter, suggesting their roster spots are in jeopardy. While TeSlaa is still the clear favorite for the third receiving spot, the fact that he played so much in this game while other starters didn’t suggests his role isn’t as locked in as it could be. Miscellaneous Notes Detroit didn’t play most of its starters, including quarterback Jared Goff , running back Jahmyr Gibbs , wide receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams and tight ends Sam LaPorta and Brock Wright . The Lions were without running back Isiah Pacheco with an MCL sprain , but he is expected to be ready for the start of the season. Projected third-string running back Sione Vaki suffered a broken nose and eye injury a week ago, which has held him out of practice. The Bengals used running backs Chase Brown and Samaje Perine over the first two drives. Their usage was extremely similar to last season, with Brown playing more on early downs and Perine more on third downs. Brown took a third-and-short snap, and Perine received some time on early downs during a long drive. Neither of those exceptions was abnormal. While Bengals tight end Erick All is expected to be ready for Week 1, he was held out for this game . All missed all of last season, but should see significant playing time, replacing Noah Fant as an early down tight end for Cincinnati. Cam Grandy took All’s place in this game, with Drew Sample playing his usual early-down blocking role, and Mike Gesicki continuing his third-down role. It is very unlikely that Gesicki will see enough playing time to be fantasy-relevant this season if he wasn’t playing in early downs even with All out. Green Bay Packers @ Pittsburgh Steelers Matthew Golden plays in 12 personnel: Golden took both snaps out of 12 personnel with the starters over Jayden Reed . Green Bay had a crowded receiver room when everyone was healthy last season, with Christian Watson , Romeo Doubs , Dontayvion Wicks and Golden typically working outside. Reed has spent his entire career in the slot in 11 personnel, rarely taking snaps in other groupings. Doubs signed with the New England Patriots and Wicks was traded to the Philadelphia Eagles , and the Packers made no significant additions this offseason, instead letting Savion Williams and Bo Melton move up the depth chart. That led to speculation Reed could see more work in 12 personnel, or even start over Golden. The starters played one drive and largely stuck with 11 personnel, with Watson and Golden outside and Reed in the slot. The Packers ran only two snaps of 12 personnel, and Reed was off the field for both. Williams took one snap with the first unit, replacing Watson in 11 personnel rather than appearing in the heavier grouping. That makes Reed unlikely to be the primary receiver in 12, which caps his ceiling, though it doesn't rule out more of those snaps than usual. Watson and Golden should both play more than they have in the past, but neither is likely to hold above 90% of the offensive snaps, which leaves Reed in position to be the first man off the bench for either. Starting in 12 personnel helps Golden's fantasy ceiling. He is likely fourth in the target order behind Watson, Reed and tight end Tucker Kraft , but there is room to climb if he plays well. Pat Freiermuth remains in a tight end rotation: Freiermuth played less than half of the offensive snaps with the starters, primarily playing in passing situations. Freiermuth was a top-10 fantasy tight end as recently as 2024, but the emergence of Darnell Washington mixed with the addition of Jonnu Smith led Freiermuth to play 50.6% of snaps last season, culminating in a TE25 performance. Smith is no longer on the Steelers , and Pittsburgh didn’t make a significant addition to its tight end room. Reports suggested the Steelers wanted to make an effort to get Freiermuth more involved in the offense this season. He and Washington played two drives with the starters, with Washington playing more on early downs, and Freiermuth more on third downs. Unlike last season, Pittsburgh has a fullback in fifth-round rookie Riley Nowakowski , leading to a notable decrease in 12 personnel usage relative to last season. Washington was used in a mix of run and pass situations, while Freiermuth was only on the field in more obvious passing situations. While it’s possible for a tight end to become a fantasy starter in this kind of rotation, it typically needs to be in a better offense. While Freiermuth could be a bye-week replacement, it’s unlikely he has a significant bounce-back this season. Germie Bernard makes a case for the third wide receiver spot: Bernard was the Steelers' primary source of offense throughout the first half. D.K. Metcalf has been the top Steelers wide receiver since last season, while Pittsburgh traded for Michael Pittman Jr. to be the second option. When Bernard was drafted in the second round, it was generally expected he would win the third spot. Throughout training camp, third year receiver Roman Wilson has been playing ahead of Bernard. Metcalf and Pittman have been missing practices due to injuries and didn’t play in this game. This means we didn’t find out which of Wilson and Bernard are currently ahead, as they were the two primary receivers. One hint that Bernard might be further in the pecking order is that he played more than twice as many snaps as Wilson out of the slot. Both Metcalf and Pittman have spent their careers as outside receivers, so it’s likely that Bernard or Wilson will play primarily out of the slot this season. Bernard caught four passes for 51 yards, while Wilson only caught one pass for 7 yards, although they were catching passes from backup quarterbacks instead of Aaron Rodgers . The fact that both receivers played the entire first half after several starters exited the game suggests there is no clear winner at this point. It’s unlikely the winner of this battle will have much fantasy value this season, unless injuries continue to impact Metcalf or Pittman. In that case, one of these receivers could finish second on the team in targets. Miscellaneous Notes Green Bay running back Josh Jacobs is dealing with a groin injury , which will keep him out at least this week. Backup Chris Brooks recently returned from a hamstring injury , he was held out of this game. MarShawn Lloyd started for Green Bay, took every snap on the first drive and played every snap on the second drive with the backups. While this doesn't mean much in terms of where he sits relative to Brooks on the depth chart, it was good to see him used on all three downs. Packers backup tight end Luke Musgrave remains on the PUP list. While Tucker Kraft is no longer on the PUP list and he has been practicing, he was held out for this game. Josh Whyle was the Packers' primary tight end on the first drive, only sitting out the first play in a run situation. He didn’t play with the backups, suggesting Green Bay views him as a key member of the offense. Reports suggest Whyle could be the second tight end on the depth chart, ahead of Musgrave. Pittsburgh chose to sit quarterback Aaron Rodgers as well as running backs Rico Dowdle and Jaylen Warren , but most other healthy starters on offense and defense played. 2025 third-round pick Kaleb Johnson didn’t receive his first offensive snap until the middle of the third quarter, playing well behind both Travis Homer and Lew Nichols , making it seem very unlikely Johnson makes the 53-man roster. Indianapolis Colts @ New England Patriots DeMario Douglas is locked into the third wide receiver spot: Douglas was among the starters who rested, while others ahead of him on the depth chart last season played. The Patriots had a crowded wide receiver room last season, with Kayshon Boutte as the X receiver, Mack Hollins as the Z and Stefon Diggs in the slot, while Kyle Williams and Douglas were the top backups. New England released Diggs, signed Romeo Doubs in free agency and traded for A.J. Brown . In practice, Brown has been the primary X receiver, Doubs the Z and Douglas the slot. There has still been some rotation, including Boutte coming in at X, allowing Brown to move around. While Boutte and Hollins were starters last season, they had to play with Williams and Efton Chism III among the backups in this game. This suggests that Douglas is the clear third wide receiver on the depth chart. Chism was consistently the slot receiver, while the other three rotated on the outside. Boutte remains the subject of trade rumors, and it’s likely that one of Boutte, Hollins or Williams won’t make the roster unless the Patriots keep seven wide receivers. It will be difficult for any wide receiver in New England to have fantasy value this season outside of Brown, considering the depth at receiver and the likelihood that there will still be more rotation than most such rooms. The Colts' wide receiver depth chart has a clear order: Ashton Dulin was among the Colts starters who didn’t play in this game. Indianapolis’ wide receiver room has been straightforward in recent seasons, with Alec Pierce at X, Michael Pittman Jr. at Z and Josh Downs in the slot. Pittman was traded to the Pittsburgh Steelers , opening the door for Downs to play more snaps, but also for a third receiver to emerge in 11 personnel. Indianapolis didn’t make any significant additions to its wide receiver room, adding Nick Westbrook-Ikhine in free agency and Deion Burks in the seventh round of the draft. The Colts rested their starters in this game, including both Downs and Dulin. This suggests Dulin might not be competing for playing time at this point. His primary competition was expected to be Laquon Treadwell and Nick Westbrook-Ikhine . Both Treadwell and Westbrook-Ikhine started this game, with Treadwell at X, Westbrook-Ikhine at Z and 2025 undrafted player Coleman Owen joining in the slot. Treadwell was taken out after one drive, while Westbrook-Ikhine kept playing for an additional two possessions, suggesting Treadwell is ahead of Westbrook-Ikhine. There has been rampant speculation the Colts will add a free-agent wide receiver, with Keenan Allen at the top of the wish list. This game doesn’t rule out the possibility Indianapolis adds someone, but it also suggests the team is reasonably happy with Dulin and Treadwell. Miscellaneous Notes New England rested its starters, including quarterback Drake Maye , running backs Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson , wide receivers A.J. Brown , Romeo Doubs and DeMario Douglas and tight end Hunter Henry . Patriots backup running back Terrell Jennings landed on injured reserve on Thursday, ending his season. He was the favorite for the third running back spot. JaMycal Hasty was signed to take his place on the 90-man roster. Hasty played 15 games for the Patriots in 2024. Seventh-round rookie Jam Miller appears to be the favorite for the third receiver role. Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce remains on the active PUP list. Backup running back D.J. Giddens is dealing with a hamstring injury, which is likely why he didn’t play. He is competing with Seth McGowan for the backup running back spot, so this game gave no indication of where the two sit relative to each other on the depth chart. Indianapolis also rested most starters, including quarterback Daniel Jones , running back Jonathan Taylor , wide receivers Josh Downs and Ashton Dulin and tight ends Tyler Warren and Mo Alie-Cox . Drew Ogletree only played on the first drive with the starters for Indianapolis, suggesting he is locked in to the third tight end spot. Arizona Cardinals @ Las Vegas Raiders Jeremiyah Love makes his NFL debut: Love played 16 of 22 snaps over two drives. Arizona drafted Love third overall but also signed free agent Tyler Allgeier in free agency. Allgeier was listed first on the unofficial depth chart, and head coach Mike LaFleur has made it clear he doesn’t want to overwork one running back , preferring to keep his backs fresh. This has led to some concern about whether Love would see as much playing time as a typical early first-round running back. Love started this game, suggesting he is already ahead of Allgeier on the depth chart. He took each of the first six snaps before Allgeier replaced him and ran the ball on three straight plays. Love then returned to finish the first drive. Arizona took out most of its starters after the opening drive, but both running backs continued to play. Love dominated the snaps on the second drive, eight to three. Love continued playing for a third drive, while Allgeier’s day was done after two. Love played eight of 10 snaps on that drive, while Bam Knight played the other two. The fact that Love started despite the unofficial depth chart was encouraging. He played 75% of the offensive snaps over the first three drives, which is on the high end of the typical snap-rate range for a starting running back. However, it would have been nice to see Love pulled from the game at the same time as Allgeier — or, better yet, at the same time as the other starters. For a coach who doesn’t want to overwork his running backs, giving Love 14 touches in a preseason game was surprising. It’s possible Allgeier cuts into Love’s playing time a little more in the regular season and Arizona simply wanted to give its rookie an extended first look at the NFL. If anything, this game should help Love’s ADP rather than hurt it. Michael Wilson played only seven of 11 snaps with the starters: Wilson played fewer snaps than free-agent addition Kendrick Bourne . Wilson emerged as a breakout star last season, scoring six touchdowns over his final five games and recording two games with more than 140 receiving yards in the second half of the season. He has typically played the Z receiver role, but much of his breakout came at X receiver while Marvin Harrison Jr. was injured. Arizona strengthened its wide receiver room in the offseason by adding Bourne, who spent four seasons working with new Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur with the San Francisco 49ers . Arizona played Harrison, Wilson and Bourne together for one drive before taking all three out of the game. Harrison lined up at X, Wilson at Z and Bourne in the slot. Surprisingly, Wilson played only seven snaps, with Jalen Brooks replacing him for four plays. However, it’s worth noting that Wilson caught a pass early, came out for one play shortly afterward and then made an 18-yard catch before taking a few running plays off. While Bourne played more snaps, all of his playing time came in 11 personnel. While it would have been encouraging to see Wilson play X more frequently, his snap count in this game shouldn’t concern fantasy managers. It would become more noteworthy if Wilson continues to come off the field more often than he did last season. The Raiders’ new wide receiver rotation: Las Vegas has a clear plan for its wide receiver rotation after making several changes at the position this offseason. Las Vegas’ only constant at wide receiver last season was Tre Tucker in the Z role. Rookie Dont’e Thornton and Jack Bech split time at X, with neither able to secure the job. Jakobi Meyers served as the primary slot receiver until he was traded, after which veteran Tyler Lockett took over the role. Lockett was not re-signed this offseason, while Las Vegas added Jalen Nailor from the Minnesota Vikings . Nailor took over as the X receiver for this game, while Bech moved into the slot. Thornton has been missing practice due to injury , but it appears unlikely that he will be among the starters. Bech was better suited to play at Z or in the slot coming out of college and was playing out of position at X last season, while Thornton’s natural fit was at X. Nailor and Tucker played in both two- and three-receiver sets and rotated in 13 personnel, while Bech was limited to 11 personnel. While Brock Bowers is expected to lead the team in targets, either Nailor or Tucker could emerge as a fantasy-relevant option if the Raiders’ offense exceeds expectations. Miscellaneous Notes Cardinals star tight end Trey McBride and Raiders star tight end Brock Bowers each played the first offensive snap for their respective teams before calling it a day. It’s not uncommon for star players to make a brief, one-snap appearance in a preseason game. Arizona backup running backs James Conner and Trey Benson missed the Hall of Fame game, and both are still out with injury. Rookie quarterback Carson Beck didn’t play in this game due to a rib injury. Cardinals backup tight end Tip Reiman remains on the PUP list. Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty played the first seven snaps of the game before his day ended, departing before the rest of the Raiders’ starters. The game didn’t reveal much about how frequently Mike Washington Jr. could rotate in during the regular season, but it did help confirm that Washington is the No. 2 running back on the depth chart. Los Angeles Chargers @ Houston Texans Good news and bad news for Oronde Gadsden : The Chargers tight end was active, while newcomers Charlie Kolar and David Njoku didn’t play. Gadsden served as Los Angeles’ primary receiving tight end for most of last season, while some combination of Tucker Fisk , Tyler Conklin and Will Dissly handled early-down snaps. None of those three tight ends were retained this offseason, while Kolar and Njoku were added. The Chargers also brought in new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who consistently utilized a three-man rotation as head coach of the Miami Dolphins . The general expectation is that Kolar and Njoku will play more on early downs, with Gadsden seeing more work in clear passing situations, but the rotation appears to remain fluid. Ideally, Gadsden wouldn’t have played in this game if the Chargers already viewed him as an established starter. However, it’s worth noting that Los Angeles has only five tight ends on the roster, including two undrafted free agents, so it’s understandable that the team wanted three tight ends active for this game. Gadsden is also the youngest of the group and is likely to benefit most from the additional experience. Notably, much of that needed experience comes as a run blocker. Gadsden was used primarily in passing situations, both during the regular season and in the preseason last year. He played on each of the Chargers’ first three drives in this game, marking the first time he has been used in all situations. Gadsden’s floor remains very low this season, as Los Angeles could settle on a two-man rotation featuring Kolar and Njoku. However, if Gadsden improves as a blocker, he could earn more playing time than he saw last season. Still, it will be difficult to draft Gadsden in most standard-sized leagues until there is some indication that he will play beyond clear passing situations during the regular season. Kimani Vidal plays while Keaton Mitchell rests: While Mitchell and Vidal appeared to be in a competition for the second running back spot, Mitchell appears to be in second. The Chargers leaned heavily on both Omarion Hampton and Vidal last season before adding Mitchell in free agency. Mitchell has been among my top sleepers because of his strong play with the Baltimore Ravens and his similarities to Mike McDaniel’s former running back, De’Von Achane . The fact that Mitchell didn’t play while Vidal did suggests Vidal is a clear third on the depth chart. Unlike at tight end, where Los Angeles had only three players active, the Chargers had four healthy running backs and could have gone into the game with only three if they wanted to. Vidal played every snap on the first two drives before his day ended, earlier than several other players who started the game. While Vidal could see some work in clear passing situations this season, it seems unlikely that he will be a significant part of the rotation. Overall, this game was slightly encouraging for fantasy managers drafting Hampton or Mitchell. Jaydin Higgins sits while Xavier Hutchinson plays: The two spent all of last season rotating as the Texans’ Z receiver. Houston had a crowded wide receiver room last season, with Nico Collins at X, Higgins and Hutchinson at Z, and Christian Kirk and Jaylin Noel rotating in the slot. Higgins has been viewed as a breakout candidate this season, but for him to reach his potential, he needs to consistently hold down the Z role. While it remains unclear how much Tank Dell could stand in the way of a Higgins breakout, Hutchinson may not pose as much of a threat. Hutchinson playing in this game suggests he is further down the depth chart than Higgins, and he also ran more routes from the slot than any other receiver on the first drive. There have been reports that Hutchinson could see more work in the slot, and his usage in this game lends some support to that possibility. The complication is that Houston used all three of its wide receivers in the slot on the opening drive, so Hutchinson doesn’t appear likely to play there exclusively. It will be difficult for fantasy managers to go all-in on Higgins until there is more clarity on Dell’s role this season, but this game was a slight positive for the former second-round pick. Miscellaneous Notes The Chargers rested quarterback Justin Herbert , running backs Omarion Hampton and Keaton Mitchell , fullback Alec Ingold , wide receivers Ladd McConkey , Quentin Johnston , Tre Harris and tight ends David Njoku and Charlie Kolar . Los Angeles’ wide receiver depth chart appears to be set. Fourth-round rookie Brenen Thompson played the X role throughout the first half, KeAndre Lambert-Smith the Z, and Derius Davis the slot. All other wide receivers below them on the depth chart are recent undrafted players with minimal NFL experience. Houston didn’t play quarterback C.J. Stroud , running backs David Montgomery and Woody Marks , wide receivers Nico Collins and Jayden Higgins , and tight end Dalton Schultz . Wide receiver Tank Dell has recently returned to team drills , but he wasn’t ready to play in this game. Jaylin Noel was activated from the non-football injury list on August 7th. He potentially didn’t play because he hasn’t practiced enough, although it’s possible he didn’t play because he’s considered a starter. Backup running back Jawhar Jordan and tight end Brevin Jordan were out due to injuries. The Texans used Marlin Klein and Foster Moreau exclusively over the first two drives, with Klein playing more on both early and late downs. Moreau kept playing into the third quarter, while Cade Stover didn’t enter the game until the second quarter. It’s unclear where Jordan will fit into the backup rotation, but for now, it appears Klein could start the season as the second tight end. Tennessee Titans @ San Francisco 49ers Tyjae Spears out-snaps Tony Pollard : The running back rotation in this game suggests the Titans could be moving closer to a 50-50 split after two seasons of Pollard leading the backfield. Pollard and Spears have shared the Titans’ backfield for the past two seasons. Last season, when both were healthy, Pollard played roughly 70% of the early-down snaps, while Spears handled roughly 80% of the third-down and two-minute-drill snaps. The two split short-yardage and goal-line situations. They remain the top two running backs on the depth chart this season, but they are now playing under a new coaching staff. New offensive coordinator Brian Daboll has typically utilized a running back rotation outside of his time with a healthy Saquon Barkley . Pollard started this game and played six snaps on the first drive, while Spears played five. Spears then took all five snaps on the second drive before the two split the third drive with three snaps apiece. There was no clear early-down or third-down back like there has been in the past. Both running backs recorded four carries, with Spears breaking off a 25-yard run and Pollard scoring a touchdown. Teams don’t always rotate their running backs the same way in the preseason as they do in the regular season, so Pollard could still lean more toward early-down work and Spears toward third downs. Still, the frequency with which they rotated — combined with both leaving the game at the same time — suggests this backfield could be much closer to a 50-50 split than it has been in past seasons. Spears’ consensus ADP is 92 picks later than Pollard’s, but based on this game, the gap between the two should be considerably smaller. Carnell Tate takes the Z receiver role: Tate had been expected to serve as the Titans’ X receiver this season. The Titans revamped their wide receiver room this offseason, drafting Tate with the fourth overall pick and adding Wan’Dale Robinson in free agency. Calvin Ridley is also back healthy, pushing Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike from starting roles into backup spots. The general expectation was that Tate would play X, Ridley would line up at Z and Robinson would operate out of the slot. Robinson played in the slot as expected, but on the first drive, Ridley primarily lined up at X and Tate at Z. Ridley played only the first seven snaps before his day ended ahead of the other starters, with Ayomanor taking over at X for the remainder of the starters’ playing time. The starters played three drives in total, with Dike also mixing in exclusively in place of Tate at Z. The amount that Ayomanor and Dike mixed in with the starters is somewhat concerning for the fantasy value of the Titans ’ receivers. It was particularly notable for Robinson , who played exclusively in 11 personnel. All four other receivers logged multiple snaps in two-receiver sets. Robinson played in 12 personnel for most of last season, so he is expected to see a decline in routes this year. While Tate lining up at Z was somewhat surprising, it’s notable that Malik Nabers played the same role in the Giants ’ offense when Brian Daboll was head coach. If that usage carries over to Tate, it could be a positive sign for his fantasy value. Slow the hype on Gunnar Helm : The second-year tight end split playing time with Daniel Bellinger tonight. Helm spent last season as a backup for the Titans, but his playing time increased as the season progressed. Tennessee didn’t re-sign Chig Okonkwo , suggesting Helm could emerge as the clear starter this season. However, the team signed Bellinger, who has spent his entire career playing under Brian Daboll. The two shared the field in 12 personnel, but only for five plays. This appears to be an offense that will utilize 11 personnel more frequently than most teams. In 11 personnel, there was a general tendency for Helm to play in passing situations and Bellinger to handle more blocking work, but Helm was still on the field for only 64.3% of the Titans’ passing plays. It’s possible for a tight end to be fantasy-relevant with that level of playing time, but it generally requires a high target rate and a productive offense. Helm hasn’t shown that he can consistently command targets at a high rate, and there are still questions surrounding the Titans’ offense. For now, Helm should be left undrafted in most redraft leagues. De’Zhaun Stribling shines over three drives: Stribling caught seven passes for 63 yards on 15 routes. The 49ers drafted Stribling in the second round, and there has been significant speculation about how he could be used this season. His most natural position appears to be at X, where Mike Evans is expected to play. The 49ers’ biggest need may be in the slot, so Stribling has also seen some practice time there. With Ricky Pearsall out for the season, there has also been some speculation that Stribling could play at Z, even after the addition of Deebo Samuel . Most of San Francisco’s key players were out for this game, either due to injury or because the team elected to rest them. Even so, we received some indication of how Stribling could be used this season. He lined up in the slot on 14 plays compared to just eight out wide, suggesting his most direct path to playing time could be overtaking Demarcus Robinson and Christian Kirk for the slot role. When Stribling lined up out wide, he played more at Z than at X. However, he caught three passes for 47 yards on only five routes from an outside alignment, compared to four receptions for 14 yards on 10 routes from the slot. This game was encouraging for Stribling simply because of how heavily he was featured. His usage could also be good news for Evans, who may not have to worry as much about Stribling cutting into his playing time this season. Miscellaneous Notes 49ers tight end George Kittle and backup running back Isaac Guerendo remain on the PUP list. Running backs Christian McCaffrey (soreness), Jordan James (ribs), Kaelon Black (thigh), Kyle Juszczyk (finger) and wide receivers Mike Evans (quadriceps) and Christian Kirk (calf) are all dealing with various injuries . San Francisco also rested quarterbacks Brock Purdy and Mac Jones , wide receivers Deebo Samuel Sr. and Demarcus Robinson , and tight ends Jake Tonges and Luke Farrell . Table Notes Snaps include plays called back due to penalties, such as offensive holding or defensive pass interference. The other three stats have these plays removed. Targets may differ from official NFL sources. The most likely discrepancy would be from a clear thrown-away pass, where the NFL may give the target to the nearest receiver, while this data will not. Carries are only on designed plays. Quarterback scrambles won’t count for the total number of carries in the game. By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 13, 2026 10:03 am EDT Preseason defenses are more vanilla: Cover 1 accounted for 25.6% of league-wide preseason coverages in 2025 compared to 17.6% during the regular season. Chicago changed its coverage tendencies the most: The Bears posted a league-high 37.3% Coverage Tendency Difference, shifting away from Cover 0 and Cover 1 toward more zone coverage once the regular season began. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. Every August, we hear that you can glean absolutely nothing from how an NFL team lines up in the preseason. We’re told to take every standout offensive performance in the preseason with a grain of salt because opposing defenses are running vanilla schemes and refusing to show their true hand before the regular season. Likewise, when a defense gets carved up in August, many are quick to come to the defense of their coordinator, arguing that he was simply calling a basic game plan while saving his best ideas for games that actually matter. It’s a logical opinion, but how accurate is it? Are coaches really calling preseason games in an entirely different way to what they’ll call in September? After all, the preseason provides valuable live reps for playcallers, too. They still want to build good habits, communicate calls effectively and make the right decisions in a real game environment. On the opposite end of the spectrum, there is the theory that some teams deliberately lean into unusual tendencies in an attempt to throw early-season opponents off the scent. My guess is that very few NFL coaching staffs are spending hours dissecting every snap that their Week 1 opponent played in August, but they’re certainly watching the tape. Only five of the 16 Week 1 matchups this year are divisional games, meaning 22 teams are preparing for relatively unfamiliar opponents and must gather whatever information they can. That becomes even more relevant in years like this one — when 10 teams have hired new head coaches and several more have switched playcallers on at least one side of the ball. Whatever a defense looked like the previous season can no longer be treated as gospel. Suddenly, preseason film carries a little more value. So how much do teams actually disguise what they’re doing? For this study, we’ll focus solely on defense using PFF data from the 2025 preseason and regular season. The most obvious place to start is coverage usage. By comparing each team’s coverage distribution between the preseason and regular season, we can measure just how much their approach changed once the games counted. It should be acknowledged that a three-game preseason is a small sample. A handful of drives can noticeably skew the numbers. Expanding the study across multiple preseasons would increase the sample size, but it would also blur the results by mixing different coaching staffs, personnel and defensive philosophies. For that reason, we’ll stick with the 2025 season. Coverage Tendency Difference To make that comparison, we’ll use a metric called Coverage Tendency Difference. At its simplest, the metric conveys how many of a team’s preseason coverage calls we would have to change to match their regular-season usage. For example, imagine a defense played Cover 1 on 40% of its preseason snaps but only 20% during the regular season. That 20-percentage-point gap contributes to the overall difference between the two versions of the defense. We repeat that comparison across every coverage type to produce one number representing how much the team’s overall coverage tendencies changed. A score of 0% would mean the defense used each coverage at the same rate in the preseason and regular season. A score of 20%, for example, means 20% of its coverage calls would need to be reallocated from one coverage type to another for the two sets of tendencies to match. The lower the number, the more representative the preseason was of the team’s eventual defense. The higher the number, the more its coverage usage changed once the regular season began. Coverage Tendency Difference — Top Five NFL Rank Team Total Variation Distance 1 Chicago Bears 37.3% 2 Atlanta Falcons 29.1% 3 Detroit Lions 28.6% 4 Cincinnati Bengals 28.0% 5 Jacksonville Jaguars 27.6% These defenses gave away relatively little about how they would play once the regular season arrived. The Chicago Bears stand well clear of the field. They called Cover 0 on 14.4% of preseason snaps before reducing that figure to just 5.6% during the regular season. Their Cover 1 usage also dropped from 33.3% to 22.2%. Those snaps were largely redistributed into zone coverages. Chicago more than doubled its Cover 3 usage while exactly tripling its Cover 2 rate. The defense looked completely different. That is particularly notable given it was Dennis Allen’s first season running the unit. Rather than spending August repeatedly drilling his preferred coverages, Allen appeared comfortable keeping some of his tendencies under wraps. Was this an intentional strategy? It’s impossible to be sure. If so, did it work? No, it did not. The Bears allowed 0.187 EPA per play across their opening two games, 29th in the NFL, surrendering 79 points before eventually finding their footing. However, those games came against division rivals, who were already familiar with much of Chicago’s personnel. Jacksonville is an interesting example of a defense that entered the season as a total unknown. Anthony Campanile, entering his first season as an NFL defensive coordinator, adjusted his schemes at the fifth-highest rate of any play caller between August and the remainder of the year. In particular, Campanile barely called Cover 6 during the preseason before using it on 21.8% of regular-season snaps, the second-highest rate in football. Jacksonville opened the year against Carolina in a cross-conference matchup. Bryce Young threw three interceptions, including one against Campanile’s Cover 6 and another against quarters presented with a Cover 6 look before the snap. While it’s impossible to say preseason tendencies directly influenced those turnovers, Jacksonville certainly looked different once the games counted. Now let’s take a look at the opposite end of the spectrum. Coverage Tendency Difference — Bottom 5 NFL Rank Team Total Variation Distance 28 Dallas Cowboys 13.8% 29 Cleveland Browns 13.6% 30 San Francisco 49ers 12.7% 31 Los Angeles Chargers 11.4% 32 Miami Dolphins 6.5% The league average was 19.8%, so teams sitting in the low teens aren’t necessarily giving everything away. Miami, however, stands out as the outlier here. The Dolphins ’ coverage profile barely changed between preseason and the regular season. They led the NFL in Cover 2 usage at 24.3%, and the preseason pointed opponents clearly in that direction. They also played relatively little Quarters coverage throughout the year, another tendency that was already visible in August. Defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver was dismissed along with the rest of Miami’s coaching staff from last season, and head coach Jeff Hafley now takes over defensive duties. Hafley’s Packers ranked almost exactly league average in total variation during his final season in Green Bay. Looking at coverage usage across the league, there is clear evidence that defenses are indeed more vanilla during the preseason. The biggest indicator is Cover 1, which accounted for 25.6% of all coverages in the preseason compared to just 17.6% during the regular season. That’s a substantial increase in one of football’s most basic coverages. No coach embodied the basic nature of the preseason more than Dan Quinn. Washington already played Cover 1 at a relatively healthy 20.5% clip during the regular season, but that figure was comedically high at 44.4% during the preseason. Whether that reflected a desire to keep things simple or to evaluate players in straightforward assignments, it was one of the clearest examples of a team stripping its defense back to the basics. Another interesting angle is how coverages are disguised. PFF cannot identify every disguised coverage in football because the number of possible intricacies is effectively endless. However, rotating a safety immediately before or at the snap remains one of the league’s most common methods of disguising coverage. Across the 2025 regular season and playoffs, defenses rotated a safety on 30.2% of snaps. And that figure was very slightly higher during the preseason at 32.8%. This may seem counterintuitive, but one likely explanation is tempo. Regular-season offenses are more likely to hurry to the line, leaving defenses with less time to rotate at the snap. Preseason games generally unfold at a much slower pace, naturally affording defenses more opportunities to move safeties around before the snap. Finally, we must take a look at blitz rates. Blitzing can be employed for any number of reasons, but on the whole, it essentially increases both the potential reward and the potential risk of any defensive call. With little on the line in August, it isn’t surprising that the league-wide blitz rate dipped slightly compared to the regular season. The Steelers were the clearest example of a team holding back their blitz packages. They blitzed on just 19.8% of preseason snaps, ranking 28th in the league. Once the regular season began, that figure jumped to 37.1%, the third-highest blitz rate in football. You could take this study much further by examining personnel packages, fronts, simulated pressures, situational playcalling or even individual down-and-distance tendencies. But even with relatively simple metrics, the overall picture becomes fairly clear. NFL defenses are not treating the preseason as an elaborate deception exercise. Most teams trial plenty of their regular-season tendencies in August, and the average difference in coverage usage is smaller than most fans might expect. That said, a handful of coordinators clearly do keep something in reserve. While others showed almost exactly who they were from the very beginning. Who will those teams be this time around? Well, we won’t know until October at the earliest. By Bradley Locker Posted Aug 13, 2026 6:39 am EDT Fewer rookies are extending a great preseason into meaningful regular-season contributions: Of the 45 rookies with an 80.0-plus overall preseason grade last year, just one reached a 70.0 grade in the regular season. Disappointing players thrived as first-year preseason players: Names like Jermaine Burton and Ennis Rakestraw suggest that little relationship exists between a great August and a strong rookie season, let alone a worthwhile career. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. The NFL made a triumphant return last week with the 2026 Hall of Fame Game, a 33-30 thriller between the Panthers and Cardinals to kickstart the preseason action. As the remaining 30 teams get set for their openers this weekend, excitement is in the air, even though formal football is still nearly a month away. The annual onset of the league’s preseason brings about numerous constants, one of which is previously unknown players turning heads. That’s especially the case for undrafted or low-selected rookies attempting to claw their way onto rosters. At the same time, even those picked much earlier want to establish a strong tone for their careers with a promising preseason. Of course, every new player wants to begin by dominating in August, but only a select few can actually make that come to fruition. Yet how much stock should we as a football collective actually put into an excellent preseason for a rookie? Not much. Utilizing both overall PFF grade and snap counts in the preseason and regular season for first-year players allows us to understand not only how good a player was in the preseason, but how much that translates to both playing time and effectiveness later on. The sample of this data is the 2021-25 campaigns, which is the window in which the league reduced the number of preseason games (for all but two teams) from four to three contests. Let’s start most recently with last preseason. Across all the August action, 45 total rookies posted at least an 80.0 overall PFF grade on either offense or defense while playing a minimum of 25 snaps. That was actually the highest number within this five-year sample by a wide margin, suggesting that rookies are flourishing more than ever in their first taste of professional football. However, that initial dominance didn’t yield much of anything in the regular season. The only player out of that 45-name group to record a 70.0-plus overall PFF grade while playing a minimum of 250 snaps was Chargers safety R.J. Mickens , who burst onto the scene late as a sixth-round pick. Likewise, only 23 of these 45 players even experienced 100 snaps during the regular season, which isn’t a high number in and of itself. Incredibly, neither of the two highest-graded preseason rookies on both sides of the ball — the Rams ’ Willie Lampkin on offense and the Chargers ’ Eric Rogers on defense — played even one snap in the regular season. Highest-graded 2025 preseason rookies and their regular seasons Player Team Preseason PFF Grade Regular-Season Defensive Snaps Regular-Season PFF Grade Eric Rogers Chargers 97.0 0 N/A Andrew Mukuba Eagles 95.7 672 57.6 Jordan Burch Cardinals 90.9 504 49.0 R.J. Mickens Chargers 90.7 353 71.0 Antwaun Powell-Ryland Eagles 90.2 0 N/A Brandon Crossley Patriots 90.1 0 N/A Keyon Martin Ravens 90.0 144 53.4 Chandler Martin Ravens 89.2 0 N/A Jay Higgins Ravens 88.8 7 45.6 Nikko Reed Chargers 88.4 50 71.9 It can be easy to isolate 2025 as a potential aberrancy, but last preseason underscores a growing trend. Fewer and fewer rookies are converting flashy preseasons into top-notch regular-season campaigns. What’s striking is that the proportion of rookies to reach both the snap and grade criteria from September through January is dominated by first-round players. For instance, names like Jayden Daniels , Micah Parsons , Bo Nix and Will Anderson Jr. registered great preseasons and rookie seasons, but all were really expected to do so given their top-12 draft slots. Even other players occupying the list like Nick Herbig , Nate Hobbs and Dadrion Taylor -Demerson were typically no worse than a fourth-round selection, representing players who are already anticipated to contribute in some form as a first-year player. By comparison, seeing an undrafted free agent not only make a roster, but suddenly turn into a regular (and good) contributor is very rare. As the 2025 preseason revealed, having a fruitful August stretch doesn’t guarantee much of anything in terms of real snap shares. Last year’s 51.1% rate of good preseason rookies earning at least 100 regular-season snaps was the highest since 2022, and the number peaked in the first year of this span. A significant proportion of the rookies with an 80.0-plus preseason grade didn’t play whatsoever in their first NFL season, and a large chunk have rarely (if ever) seen the field throughout their careers. Similarly, many of these newbies only played a handful of snaps, and typically later in the season. A significant number of those who even appeared were players drafted in the earlier rounds as well. Why aren’t these dominant preseason rookies even walking onto the field much in the fall and winter months? The most logical explanation is that they are typically buried on a depth chart if they even make a roster, needing injury or very poor performance from starters to even have a chance at playing. Trotting out an impressive rookie over an initial starter — especially a first-year player in whom the team didn’t invest a lot of capital — would probably be considered taboo for a lot of coaching staffs and front offices. On the contrary, plenty of rookies have shined in the preseason as a means of catalyzing not only wonderful rookie campaigns, but also top-tier careers. These findings don’t necessarily mean that a good preseason holds no weight, especially for those picked near the top of the draft. But by the same token, some rookie preseason standouts in recent seasons include Jermaine Burton , J.J. McCarthy , Trevor Penning and Ennis Rakestraw , all of whom have generally failed to develop as expected over their careers. Perusing the list of a year’s top preseason rookie performers on each side is more of a Remember him? exercise than the harbinger of a tremendous pro tenure. To reiterate, this research definitely doesn’t nullify the preseason as a whole. It still holds legitimate value as a warm-up for players and coaches, especially as it allows first-year names to experience a faster and more physical game of football. By the same vein, a very good or bad preseason showing isn’t worth ignoring altogether. However, this recent data serves as a strong indicator that rookie preseason darlings probably won’t experience the same success as the calendar turns to September — if those players are even lucky enough to play in a few games. In simpler terms, it’s better not to overreact to a great individual preseason, because it guarantees almost nothing. records.new_body: Fantasy Football: Breakout quarterbacks for 2026 drafts All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting Fantasy Football: Breakout quarterbacks for 2026 drafts By Nathan Jahnke Posted Aug 13, 2026 5:15 am EDT Tennessee Titans Miami Dolphins New Orleans Saints Malik Willis scrambles more than anyone: Willis led all quarterbacks in scrambles per dropback over the past two seasons and now has a starting job with the Miami Dolphins . Tyler Shough is a great late-round option: Shough averaged 17.6 PPR points per game from Week 9 on last season, 12th among quarterbacks, yet he is going in the 13th round in fantasy drafts. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. Each season, some players take their game to another level while greatly improving their fantasy production along the way. Most of the 32 starting NFL quarterbacks have found at least some level of success from a fantasy perspective, leaving few options for potential breakout candidates. However, among the pool of young quarterbacks who haven't yet been consistent fantasy starters, here are the few most likely to become fantasy starters by the end of the season. Malik Willis , Miami Dolphins (ADP: 13.03) Willis spent two seasons as a backup for the Tennessee Titans but received only three starts. Tennessee drafted Will Levis 33rd overall a year after taking Willis 86th, which made the latter expendable. The Packers traded for Willis to serve as a backup, and over two years, he made three starts and saw notable playing time in three other games. Willis has dropped back to pass just 118 times over the past two years, but his 79.9 PFF passing grade ranks 15th among all quarterbacks. Most important for fantasy, he scrambled on 15.1% of his dropbacks over that span, which leads all quarterbacks. That was notably ahead of Jayden Daniels , Tyrod Taylor , Justin Fields , Drake Maye and Jaxson Dart . Willis signed with the Miami Dolphins to be their starting quarterback this season. Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley and general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan were both with the Packers before joining Miami. Some passing regression is fair to expect, since Willis won't have the same weapons in Miami that he had in Green Bay. Defenses will also be better prepared for him, since his appearances in Green Bay were often a surprise; because he plays so differently from Jordan Love , defenses weren't ready for him. Even if Willis’ scrambles per dropback regress somewhat, he should remain among the league leaders in quarterback rushing production, which is a big plus for his fantasy value. Extrapolating his rushing attempts per start and yards per carry in Green Bay, he would have posted 119 rushing attempts and 738 rushing yards over a season, both of which would have led all quarterbacks last year. It's fair not to expect numbers quite that big in Miami, but he could be a fantasy starter if he holds the job and scores enough touchdowns. Willis is a strong option for anyone willing to wait before adding a second quarterback in redraft leagues. Tyler Shough , New Orleans Saints (ADP: 13.04) Shough was drafted 40th overall by the Saints in 2025 and took over as the team's starter partway through Week 8. From Weeks 9 to 18, he averaged 17.6 PPR points per game, 12th among quarterbacks. He had the right combination of volume as both a passer and runner, along with good efficiency for a rookie. He benefited from an easier-than-average schedule. He faced a bottom-five defense against fantasy quarterbacks three times and posted two top-10 finishes in those games. In three more games against teams in the bottom half of the league at limiting quarterback fantasy points, he had his other top-10 finish. His remaining three starts came against top-half teams, and he failed to crack the top 10 in all three. The Saints leaned heavily on Shough last season. Alvin Kamara and Kendre Miller were both hurt for most of his time as a starter, and the team had traded away Rashid Shaheed and cut Brandin Cooks , leaving it thin at two important positions. New Orleans signed Travis Etienne and drafted Jordyn Tyson , which should help Shough's passing efficiency but could also push the Saints to run more. Shough's ADP is relatively low because there's usually a reason to prefer other quarterbacks, whether it's more experience at a high level, a better supporting cast or more rushing upside. The likeliest outcome is that he regresses somewhat despite the upgraded weapons, but there's a chance Etienne and Tyson lift the offense to a new level and Shough improves on his 17.6 PPR points per game. He is a clear example of how deep the quarterback position is this year and a reason it makes sense to wait at quarterback in single-quarterback leagues. Shough can be drafted in the later rounds and slotted into lineups when the matchup is right. Cam Ward , Tennessee Titans (ADP: 15.09) Ward was selected first overall by the Titans and stepped immediately into the starting lineup. He was expected to have a trio of veteran receivers at his disposal in Calvin Ridley , Tyler Lockett and Van Jefferson , but Ridley played only five full games, catching five passes for 131 yards and two touchdowns in his last healthy one. Head coach Brian Callahan was fired after the sixth game of the season, and Lockett lasted seven games before requesting his release. That understandably put a damper on Ward's rookie season. The good news is that he threw for two touchdowns in each of his final four full games after managing just seven across his first 12. He similarly posted his three best PFF grades near the end of the season. Ward will have a fresh slate this season, with more options. Tennessee drafted Carnell Tate fourth overall to be its new X receiver and signed Wan'Dale Robinson to play the slot. Ridley is also expected to be healthy, shifting from the clear top option to the third read in the passing game. Brian Daboll is the new offensive coordinator. In single-quarterback leagues, Ward isn't worth drafting in most redraft formats, but he could easily become a top waiver-wire target with a strong start. In superflex leagues, there are a few veterans he should go ahead of simply for his upside in a new opportunity. records.new_body: NFL Preseason 2026: Second-year players to watch All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting NFL Preseason 2026: Second-year players to watch By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 12, 2026 10:18 am EDT Vernon Broughton has an immediate opportunity: Bryan Bresee's season-ending ACL injury could open a meaningful role for Broughton after a hip injury limited the 2025 third-round pick to 24 rookie snaps. Jalen Milroe enters a key developmental year: Milroe saw minimal action behind Sam Darnold as a rookie after posting a 42.8 PFF passing grade during his first NFL preseason. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. Some top draft picks didn’t get to feature as much as they would have liked in their rookie seasons. In some cases, that was due to injury. Others found themselves stuck behind established NFL stars, proving that the “best player available” philosophy is alive and well across the league. This article takes a look at players drafted in the first three rounds of the 2025 NFL Draft who played fewer than 100 snaps during their rookie seasons. Eight of these nine players were selected in the third round, and all, of course, remain with the organization that drafted them just 15 months ago. DI Vernon Broughton , New Orleans Saints Broughton takes up the first spot on this list due to the recent news that Saints defensive tackle Bryan Bresee tore his ACL in training camp and will miss the entirety of the 2026 season. Drafted 71st overall in 2025, Broughton entered the league with legitimate expectations of contributing as part of the defensive line rotation before a season-ending hip injury in Week 2 cut his rookie campaign short after just 24 snaps. The former Longhorn has competed at the highest level of college football for several years and is already 25 years old. While some rust is to be expected after such a lengthy absence, the Saints will hope he can step straight into a meaningful role. First, though, he has to prove he belongs this August. RB Kaleb Johnson , Pittsburgh Steelers Johnson generated legitimate late first-round buzz out of Iowa during the pre-draft process before ultimately falling to the Steelers with the 83rd overall pick. A costly mistake on a kickoff return in his second career game — when he allowed the ball to settle in the end zone and gift the Seahawks a touchdown — derailed any early momentum and he never managed to carve out a larger role during his rookie season afterward. Johnson played just 51 offensive snaps, earning a 40.2 overall PFF grade. He averaged only 2.6 yards per carry while picking up just two first downs on his 29 rushing attempts. He also dropped one of his two targets in the passing game and was beaten on all reps in pass protection. Steelers fans will rightly argue that such a small sample size is nowhere near enough to judge Johnson’s talent. He does, however, remain in a crowded backfield that became even deeper after the addition of Navy ’s Eli Heidenreich in this year’s draft, paired with the free-agent acquisition of Rico Dowdle . QB Jalen Milroe , Seattle Seahawks Milroe unsurprisingly played the fewest snaps of any top-100 offensive draft pick, spending his rookie season behind Sam Darnold as Seattle went on to win the Super Bowl in his first season. The dual-threat quarterback left something to be desired last preseason, posting a 42.8 PFF passing grade without recording a single big-time throw despite an aggressive 10.1-yard average depth of target. He also held onto the ball for an average of 3.3 seconds. One area where nobody questions Milroe’s ability is as a runner, although there is room for improvement here, as well. He rushed for 104 yards last preseason but lost two fumbles in the process. Milroe should look to Malik Willis as a blueprint for how his career could develop. Willis has now earned a starting opportunity in Miami after spending several years proving himself as one of the league’s most reliable backup quarterbacks. WR Tai Felton , Minnesota Vikings Felton was drafted 102nd overall by the Vikings but played just 46 offensive snaps as a rookie, instead becoming a key special teams contributor with 293 snaps, the fourth-most on the team. After the free-agent addition of Jauan Jennings , Felton is still likely to begin the season as Minnesota ’s fourth receiver. However, he has already begun turning heads in training camp, taking first-team reps and hauling in plenty of passes from J.J. McCarthy . Felton’s 4.37-second 40-yard dash speed should add an explosive element to a Vikings passing attack that desperately needs it after producing just 28 explosive passing plays from Week 11 onward last season, the fewest of any team not named the Jets . WR Savion Williams , Green Bay Packers Williams was drafted 87th overall as a do-it-all offensive weapon with rare athletic ability. The 6-foot-5 receiver lined up out wide, in the slot, in the backfield and even took snaps as a Wildcat quarterback over the course of his rookie season. A nagging foot injury, combined with Green Bay’s depth at receiver, limited Williams to just 91 offensive snaps during his rookie season, although he did get great exposure to numerous roles within the offense. With Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks both gone elsewhere, a larger role should be available for Williams if he’s able to prove himself during the preseason. T Charles Grant , Las Vegas Raiders The 99th overall pick played just 59 offensive snaps as a rookie, with nearly all of them coming after the Raiders’ season was effectively over. Even so, Grant impressed in limited action, earning a 77.7 PFF pass-blocking grade while allowing just one pressure across 26 pass-blocking snaps. Grant entered the league from FCS William Mary, so this preseason should provide a much better indication of how comfortably he has adjusted to NFL competition. The Raiders hope Grant can become a long-term answer at one of the tackle spots protecting quarterback Fernando Mendoza. However, he has played almost exclusively at left tackle, where franchise stalwart Kolton Miller currently remains entrenched. LB Nickolas Martin , San Francisco 49ers The 75th overall pick played just 15 defensive snaps before suffering a season-ending concussion in Week 13. He also logged 76 snaps on special teams. At 5-foot-11 and 220 pounds, Martin is undersized even by modern NFL linebacker standards. He makes up for some of that with 4.53 speed and outstanding explosiveness, but his size will always leave him fighting an uphill battle, particularly on a roster featuring Fred Warner, who rarely comes off the field. Martin will be competing for the SAM role within Raheem Morris’ defense. However, the 49ers played base personnel on just 20.2% of snaps last season, the fifth-fewest in the league. Morris has already spoken in glowing terms about Martin’s potential. ED Landon Jackson , Buffalo Bills Jackson was one of the SEC’s top edge defenders during his time at Arkansas, earning first-team All-SEC honors in each of his last two years. From 2022 through 2024, only four SEC defenders recorded more sacks than Jackson. His rookie season in Buffalo never really got off the ground. Jackson did not make his debut until Week 5, played only 30 snaps over the following month and then suffered a season-ending torn MCL in Week 10. He has since added significant muscle and returned to training camp looking noticeably bigger than he did as a rookie, and Bills fans are optimistic that Jackson can show his talent this August before emerging into a rotational role. CB Jaylin Smith , Houston Texans The 97th overall pick finds himself buried behind one of the NFL’s strongest cornerback groups, with Derek Stingley Jr., Kamari Lassiter and nickel corner Jalen Pitre all ahead of him. Smith played just 32 defensive snaps before a hamstring injury ended his rookie season. He spent his first three years at USC primarily in the slot before moving outside during his final season, and he continued playing on the perimeter during last year’s preseason. Across those 70 preseason snaps, he posted an impressive 85.9 PFF run-defense grade. DeMeco Ryans has the versatility to deploy Smith wherever he sees fit, but unless injuries strike the Texans secondary, meaningful opportunities may be hard to come by for the 22-year-old.
