records.new_body: 2027 NFL Draft: The toughest matchup for every top prospect All NFL Fantasy College NFL Draft - current DFS Betting 2027 NFL Draft: The toughest matchup for every top prospect By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 12, 2026 9:23 am EDT Jeremiah Smith draws an elite one-on-one test: PFF's top prospect faces Oregon cornerback Brandon Finney Jr., who allowed a 42.3 passer rating into his coverage last season. Julian Sayin gets another shot at Indiana: The Hoosiers held Sayin to a 70.2 PFF overall grade in last season's Big Ten Championship Game, and they sacked him five times. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. The college football season is loaded with marquee matchups, but not every game carries the same weight for NFL evaluators. A top prospect running up their stats against FCS opposition means relatively little once the draft evaluation process kicks into gear. Top NFL decision-makers will be paying much closer attention to matchups between similarly talented players. Using PFF’s 2027 NFL Draft Big Board , we’ve picked out the toughest regular-season matchup for each of our top eight prospects. Seven of PFF’s top eight prospects play in either the SEC or Big Ten, so it’s no surprise that most face daunting tests throughout the season. While several will almost certainly add to their résumés in the College Football Playoff, these are the regular-season matchups that stand out most. 1. WR Jeremiah Smith, Ohio State Toughest matchup: CB Brandon Finney Jr., Oregon Smith will face four of PFF’s seven highest-ranked returning cornerbacks this season, and he’ll be the toughest assignment each of them sees. That has been the case for two years now, but it has rarely mattered. Finney was still in high school when Smith torched Oregon for seven catches, 187 yards and two touchdowns in the Rose Bowl, so this will be their first meeting. Unlike fellow Big Ten standouts Jyaire Hill and Jamari Sharpe, Finney hasn’t yet had to deal with Smith’s unmatchable combination of size, speed and ball skills, but he may be the most athletically equipped cornerback to cope with Smith. Finney allowed a 42.3 passer rating into his coverage last season, the lowest among qualifying Big Ten perimeter cornerbacks. Dan Lanning’s defense also plays a healthy amount of man coverage, which should give us plenty of true one-on-one reps between two of the nation’s premier talents. 2. QB Julian Sayin, Ohio State Toughest matchup: Indiana defense Three road trips to Iowa, Indiana and USC in the month of October could be a sneakily tough stint for Ohio State’s offensive operation, with the matchup against the Hoosiers likely serving as the most difficult of the trio. Sayin’s 70.2 PFF overall grade against Indiana in last season’s Big Ten Championship Game was the second-lowest of his career. Indiana took away the easy throws, forcing Sayin to hold the football for an average of 3.42 seconds — comfortably the longest time to throw of his career — and he was sacked five times as a result. The Hoosiers have retained 58% of last year’s defensive production, a higher figure than more than half of the Big Ten despite coming off a national championship win. That continuity, combined with an already proven blueprint for disrupting Sayin, makes this his toughest test of the regular season. 3. QB Dante Moore, Oregon Toughest matchup: Ohio State’s defense Moore avoids Indiana this season but instead must travel to Columbus in November to face another elite defense. He has yet to take a snap against Ohio State, and the late-season timing of this one may not work in his favor. November weather conditions in Ohio are one thing, but it goes deeper than that. The Buckeyes return only two full-time defensive starters after losing five defenders in the first two rounds of the NFL Draft, including three inside the top 11 selections. That naturally points toward a transition year, but by the tail end of the regular season, it’s reasonable to expect several of Ohio State’s talented sophomore defenders to have settled into prominent roles. Matt Patricia leads this production line of elite recruiting talent, and history suggests Ohio State will develop a few superstars among this crop. By the time Oregon visits Columbus, Moore is likely to face a unit playing with far more confidence than it will early in the season. 4. EDGE Colin Simmons, Texas Toughest matchup: T Cayden Green, Missouri Unlike many edge rushers, Simmons doesn’t stay fixed to one side of the formation. His alignment depends on factors such as which hash the ball is on, meaning he sees left and right tackles in fairly equal measure. Green presents one of the toughest individual assignments on Texas’ schedule. A converted guard, he allowed just seven total pressures last season. Simmons’ explosiveness is unquestioned, but at 6-foot-3 and 240 pounds, his relative lack of size can occasionally allow powerful offensive tackles to engulf him. The giant Cayden Green matches that profile perfectly. Simmons posted a 91.7 PFF pass-rushing grade last season, while Green earned an 89.6 PFF pass-blocking grade. Something has to give in what could be one of the season’s most intriguing trench battles between early first-round-caliber players. 5. CB Leonard Moore, Notre Dame Toughest matchup: Miami’s receiving corps Malachi Toney entered the season as PFF’s second-ranked returning wide receiver behind Jeremiah Smith, while Miami transfer Cooper Barkate also received an honorable mention. Together, they’ll give Leonard Moore (or indeed any cornerback) his biggest challenge of the year. Nobody doubts Moore’s ability to mirror receivers vertically or make plays at the catch point. But Toney tests corners differently. His ability after the catch forces defenders to tackle consistently in space rather than simply win downfield. Toney led the FBS with 841 yards after the catch and forced 33 missed tackles last season. Moore’s 17.0% missed-tackle rate over the past two years is one area scouts will want to see improve before next April, making this an especially valuable chance to solidify his draft stock. 6. QB Arch Manning, Texas Toughest matchup: LSU’s defense I’ve opted against picking the Ohio State defense for reasons stated earlier about its transition to a new crop of players, which is sure to produce some early-season growing pains. In addition, that matchup takes place at home for Texas and Arch Manning, and any improvement on their lackluster seven-point display from last season will be seen as an improvement. The more fascinating matchup for Manning comes with a trip to Death Valley to face an LSU defense that is garnering some hype as possibly the best unit in the SEC. Edge rushers Jordan Ross and Princewill Umanmielen headline an impressive transfer haul, with Umanmielen producing 51 pressures last season, third most in the SEC. Linebacker Whit Weeks and safety Ty Benefield are potential All-SEC players, while 6-foot-5 cornerback DJ Pickett could be the ideal matchup against Manning’s primary target, Auburn transfer Cam Coleman. Few environments are tougher for quarterbacks than Baton Rouge at night, making this the regular-season game scouts will circle. Expect a big crop of general managers in the stands for this one. 7. EDGE Dylan Stewart, South Carolina Toughest matchup: T E’Marion Harris, Oklahoma Stewart’s schedule is surprisingly favorable. South Carolina avoids matchups against each of PFF’s top three returning SEC offensive tackles — Trevor Goosby, Jordan Seaton and Cayden Green. His toughest battle may genuinely come against teammate Jacarrius Peak in practice. Stewart rushed over the right tackle on 95.2% of his snaps last season, yet South Carolina faces only one SEC right tackle who logged more than 300 snaps at the position last year. That’s Harris, who transferred from Arkansas. Harris isn’t flawless, allowing 24 pressures and three sacks last season, but he still represents Stewart’s best opportunity to prove himself against an experienced tackle. If South Carolina can stay competitive and force opponents into obvious passing situations, Stewart should have every chance to dominate this year. 8. T Carter Smith, Indiana Toughest matchup: EDGE John Henry Daley, Michigan Indiana avoids several of the nation’s deepest defensive fronts, including Oregon’s, while Ohio State enters the season without the same established edge talent of recent years. A trip to the Big House provides Carter Smith with his biggest challenge. John Henry Daley arrives from Utah after posting a nation-leading 93.4 PFF pass-rushing grade among returning edge defenders. He aligned over left tackles on 92.4% of his snaps last season, so assuming Michigan keeps him in a similar role, we’ll get a full afternoon of reps against one of the draft’s premier offensive tackle prospects. Playing on the road in Ann Arbor, where Indiana ’s offense will need to operate on a silent count for much of the afternoon, only makes the assignment more difficult for Smith against Daley’s already-explosive get-off. records.new_body: 5 storylines to watch during the 2026 NFL preseason All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 5 storylines to watch during the 2026 NFL preseason By Bradley Locker Posted Aug 12, 2026 6:00 am EDT At least two more teams still need to figure out a starting quarterback: The Browns will decide between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders , while the Falcons will pick between Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. Preseason darlings can become impactful during the regular season: Rookies like R.J. Mickens and Jahdae Walker turned strong early showings into real contributions late in the 2025 campaign. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. Believe it or not, football is back. Last week’s Hall of Fame Game marked the official onset of the 2026 season, with organized action happening in 24 of the next 25 weeks. If last Thursday’s thriller is any indication, the 2026 preseason will be compelling throughout. It’s true that defenses may not be entirely up to snuff, and that games won’t regularly feature the league’s best players. But following an offseason that has been filled with all sorts of twists and turns, even this year’s mid-August slate feels that much more exciting. Below are five key elements to watch as every team finally returns to play this week. Lingering quarterback battles Although the Vikings put the kibosh on their quarterback duel by naming Kyler Murray the starter , multiple other teams still need to decide on primary passers for at least Week 1 — if not longer. The Browns are in the strongest spotlight as Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders duke it out to be Todd Monken’s first option. Watson missed all of 2024 with an Achilles tear, while Sanders finished with the worst PFF passing grade (42.3) among the 38 quarterbacks with at least 200 dropbacks as a rookie. No matter who wins the initial job, it feels like the door will be open for the other to still get reps, especially if Cleveland struggles. Likewise, the Falcons need to determine their QB1 in Kevin Stefanski’s first season. The current favorite appears to be ex-Dolphin Tua Tagovailoa , who led qualifiers with a 5.4% turnover-worthy play rate during a cataclysmic 2025 season. Meanwhile, former first-round pick Michael Penix Jr. has yet to be fully cleared for contact, although a good (and healthy) preseason could merit additional opportunity. In addition to work in camp practices, preseason games against actual opponents figure to loom large for both the Browns and Falcons. Likewise, although the Cardinals and Raiders have essentially committed to Jacoby Brissett and Kirk Cousins , respectively, good showings for rookies Carson Beck and Fernando Mendoza may very well provide them the chance to start earlier than expected. Old faces in new places If it felt hard to keep up with all of the moves this offseason, you’re not alone. The last six months have brought drastic change in terms of where some of the NFL’s best suit up, and we’ll get to see many of those debuts at long last. On the trade market, veterans like Myles Garrett , Dexter Lawrence , A.J. Brown , Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Waddle all figure to play at least a smattering of snaps for their new teams in the preseason. It won’t feel the same as in Week 1, but even seeing such stars don nascent colors is something to recognize. The same principle applies to free agency. Big-ticket players that will play for newfound franchises include the Ravens’ Trey Hendrickson , Chiefs’ Kenneth Walker III , Dolphins’ Malik Willis , 49ers’ Mike Evans and Raiders’ Tyler Linderbaum . To reiterate, these standouts are all likely to play no more than 30 or so snaps, a far cry from what early September will showcase. At the same time, this small sample can still offer a window into how game-changers might be deployed differently by their new squads — such as a different route tree, new run concepts or even a distinct defensive alignment. Players stepping up in light of injury With training camp comes an unfortunate inevitability: Players suffering serious injuries. That’s already been the case in the onset of a young camp this summer. One consequence is getting a first look at those who will be called upon to replace veterans. The Commanders endured a massive blow when tackle Laremy Tunsil suffered a torn triceps, leaving Washington without the fifth-most-valuable tackle by PFF Wins Above Replacement for possibly all of 2026. The team could opt to sign a veteran like Taylor Decker , but the early indication is that Brandon Coleman will assume starting duties. After sporting a 64.6 overall PFF grade last year, how Coleman fares in August could be telling. The NFC South has also been especially gutted, with players such as Taylor Moton , Jalon Walker , Nic Scourton and Bryan Bresee out for weeks or the entire campaign. Those losses have swiftly propelled youngsters like Monroe Freeling, Christen Miller, Harold Perkins Jr. and Princely Umanmielen into elevated roles. How they perform during the preseason could decide whether or not such teams make additions or roll the dice on their upside. Other position groups to watch in light of injuries are Bears safeties without Coby Bryant , Lions centers down Cade Mays and 49ers receivers. Schematic shifts Not only did a myriad of players change teams, but so too did coaches. The preseason will give fans and analysts alike an appetizer of what they might expect to see once the calendar turns to September. This offseason, a whopping 10 teams welcomed in new head coaches. Matchups in mid-to-late August could indicate wholesale changes from veterans in different spots like Mike McCarthy and John Harbaugh. Meanwhile, rising leaders like the Ravens’ Jesse Minter and Raiders’ Klint Kubiak will also set the tone for what they hope to get out of preseason, including how long they play starters. Many of the same tenets also apply to coordinators now in adjusted colors. For instance, the Chargers’ offense should rise from 18 th to near the top of the list in motion rate with Mike McDaniel now calling the shots, potentially as soon as the preseason. First-time coordinators Christian Parker and Jim Leonhard will also begin to lay the foundation for their units in Dallas and Buffalo, including maybe establishing a coverage or blitzing backbone. The preseason is often decried due to very vanilla schemes and play styles, and rightfully so. Yet there’s always information to be learned, and reading the tea leaves this early could be at least some harbinger of what we’ll watch stylistically in the regular season. Unsung players carving out a role While the preseason can be laden with criticism, one of its main purposes is affording a platform for underrated players to shine. Year over year, low- and/or undrafted players earn chances because of what they achieve across those three weeks. The Hall of Fame Game was already a step in that direction. Consider Panthers quarterback Haynes King, who produced a 75.1 overall PFF grade and scored the game-winning touchdown in the waning seconds. The undrafted free agent certainly opened some eyes, and his chances of making a roster — whether Carolina’s or another — have likely increased. Year after year, rookies carve out meaningful snaps during the regular season by dominating in the preseason. A season ago, the Chargers ’ R.J. Mickens and Steelers ’ Yahya Black played their way into starting lineups despite being selected in the fifth round or later, rendering themselves tough to ignore by dominating in August. Likewise, Bears undrafted wideout Jahdae Walker reached the 53-man roster after posting an 87.0 PFF receiving grade in the preseason — and that faith was rewarded by scoring two touchdowns in Chicago’s final three games. It’s true that the preseason is fundamentally considered a tune-up for starters, but its real value lies in letting under-the-radar players make headlines. At least a handful of names on roster bubbles will sway staffs with their preseason play, and that accomplishment is always something to celebrate. In fact, those players should be remembered down the line — because they could turn out to be an important part of a team’s season. records.new_body: 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers open in top three All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Broncos, Eagles and Buccaneers open in top three By Gordon McGuinness Posted Aug 12, 2026 5:45 am EDT Denver opens at No. 1: The Broncos return all five starters from PFF's top-ranked 2025 offensive line, led by Garett Bolles and Quinn Meinerz. Philadelphia remains among the NFL's elite: The Eagles rank second with their entire starting five returning, including Lane Johnson, who has earned a PFF pass-blocking grade above 80.0 in six straight seasons. Tampa Bay rounds out the top three: Tristan Wirfs earned a career-high 92.7 PFF grade in 2025, while Luke Goedeke didn't surrender a sack or hit across 416 pass-blocking snaps. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. The offensive line is arguably the most important unit in football, and even one weak link can quickly derail an offense. Throughout the 2026 season, I’ll rank all 32 offensive lines each week, adjusting the rankings as we learn more about individual players and as starting lineups change due to injuries and players returning to the field. To grade each offensive line, I assigned every projected starter a score from 5.0 to 10.0 in 0.5-point increments. Those scores are based primarily on PFF grades from the past three seasons, where applicable, with added weight given to pass protection. I then calculated an average for each offensive line, with slightly more weight given to the two tackle spots, to produce an overall score out of 10. For the first four weeks of the season, the rankings will only change based on lineup adjustments. Four games is still a relatively small sample, but as the season progresses and we get a better picture of each player’s 2026 performance, those results will begin to factor into individual scores and move offensive lines up or down the rankings. 1. Denver Broncos LT: Garett Bolles LG: Ben Powers C: Luke Wattenberg RG: Quinn Meinerz RT: Mike McGlinchey The Broncos return the same five starters from an offensive line that ended 2025 as PFF’s top-ranked unit, and there is no reason for change at the top. Left tackle Garett Bolles earned a 91.0 PFF pass-blocking grade last year, the highest among all offensive tackles, and didn’t allow a single sack across 802 pass-blocking snaps in the regular season. On the other side of the line, right guard Quinn Meinerz was the highest-graded guard in football, with his 91.0 PFF run-blocking grade trailing only Atlanta's Chris Lindstrom among guards. 2. Philadelphia Eagles LT: Jordan Mailata LG: Landon Dickerson C: Cam Jurgens RG: Tyler Steen RT: Lane Johnson The big change on the offensive line for the Eagles this season is the departure of former offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland, but like the Broncos in the top spot, they return the same starting five. Right tackle Lane Johnson has indicated that this is likely to be his last season in the NFL, so we only have one more year to marvel at one of the finest pass blockers to play in the NFL since PFF began grading. Johnson has earned a PFF pass-blocking grade above 80.0 in six straight seasons and allowed just seven total pressures from 262 pass-blocking snaps a year ago. 3. Tampa Bay Buccaneers LT: Tristan Wirfs LG: Ben Bredeson C: Graham Barton RG: Cody Mauch RT: Luke Goedeke Injuries hurt the Buccaneers’ offensive line at points in 2025, but this is a really strong unit heading into the new season. Left tackle Tristan Wirfs set a career-high with a 92.7 PFF grade in 2025 and has yet to earn a PFF pass-blocking grade below 80.0 in a season. Opposite him, Luke Goedeke has improved throughout his career and didn’t allow a sack or hit on 416 pass-blocking snaps last year, while the return of Cody Mauch and the continued emergence of center Graham Barton give them the chance to be the best offensive line in football this season. 4. Indianapolis Colts LT: Bernhard Raimann LG: Quenton Nelson C: Tanor Bortolini RG: Matt Goncalves RT: Jalen Travis The 84.7 PFF grade earned by left guard Quenton Nelson was the best he has produced since 2020, and he pairs well with Bernhard Raimann to form one of the best left sides in the league. Tanor Bortolini took a huge step forward as a run blocker in 2025 at center, and right guard Matt Goncalves held his own in his first full year as a starter, earning a 65.8 PFF grade. Jalen Travis started the team’s final four games and earned a 72.2 PFF grade as a rookie, and takes over as the starter at right tackle in 2026. 5. Chicago Bears LT: Braxton Jones LG: Joe Thuney C: Garrett Bradbury RG: Jonah Jackson RT: Darnell Wright The Bears were dealt a blow with the sudden retirement of Drew Dalman , but this is still a strong unit overall. Braxton Jones will open the season as the starter at left tackle, but there has been optimism recently that second-year player Ozzy Trapilo could return from injury at some point during the season. He earned a PFF grade above 70.0 in four of seven starts on the left side of the line as a rookie. Right tackle Darnell Wright just signed a huge contract extension, having earned PFF grades of 79.3 and 80.3 in his second and third years in the league. 6. Buffalo Bills LT: Dion Dawkins LG: Alec Anderson C: Connor McGovern RG: O'Cyrus Torrence RT: Spencer Brown The strength of the Bills’ offensive line is on the outside, as Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown are one of the best duos in the league. Dawkins has earned a PFF pass-blocking grade above 75.0 in all nine of his seasons in the NFL, while Brown has emerged as one of the best run blockers at the position. Alec Anderson looks set to start at left guard and has just 542 snaps to his name, but the Bills did add veteran insurance behind him in Austin Corbett . 7. Los Angeles Chargers LT: Rashawn Slater LG: Jake Slaughter C: Tyler Biadasz RG: Cole Strange RT: Joe Alt Rashawn Slater is reportedly still on track to be good to go when the regular season begins despite a brief injury scare in training camp, and, all being well, we will get a full season of him and Alt bookending this line for the Chargers. Slater ranked second among all offensive tackles with a 90.9 PFF grade in 2024 before missing all of last season, while Alt had allowed just seven pressures from 118 pass-blocking snaps before his injury last year. The guard spots are a bigger question mark, but the health of their tackles will drive their success in 2026. 8. Kansas City Chiefs LT: Josh Simmons LG: Kingsley Suamataia C: Creed Humphrey RG: Trey Smith RT: Jaylon Moore Left tackle Josh Simmons looks good to go ahead of the 2026 season, coming off a rookie season in which he earned a 75.5 PFF pass-blocking grade on 367 pass-blocking snaps. His arrival allowed them to kick Kingsley Suamataia inside to left guard, where he earned a much more respectable 64.9 PFF grade on 1,090 snaps in his second year after earning a 37.9 PFF grade on 198 snaps as a rookie. They also have the best center in the league in Creed Humphrey, who has led all centers in PFF grade in four of his five seasons in the league. 9. Atlanta Falcons LT: Jake Matthews LG: Matthew Bergeron C: Ryan Neuzil RG: Chris Lindstrom RT: Jawaan Taylor The departure of offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford is a blow to this group, but they retain some of the best players at the position. Chris Lindstrom is a monster in the run game, having earned PFF run-blocking grades above 90.0 in three of the past four seasons. Jake Matthews is 34 years old now but remains a good pass blocker, earning PFF pass-blocking grades above 80.0 in each of the past four seasons. 10. San Francisco 49ers LT: Trent Williams LG: Connor Colby C: Jake Brendel RG: Dominick Puni RT: Colton McKivitz Trent Williams was still dominant at 37 years old, earning a 91.1 PFF grade for the fifth time in six seasons with the 49ers. This line’s ranking is highly dependent on him retaining that level of play, though, with Connor Colby earning a 52.4 PFF grade on 454 snaps at left guard next to him last year. If Dominick Puni can bounce back after a sophomore slump that saw his PFF grade drop from 80.5 as a rookie to 69.2 in Year 2, then he can form a really strong right side with Colton McKivitz. 11. Los Angeles Rams LT: Alaric Jackson LG: Steve Avila C: Coleman Shelton RG: Kevin Dotson RT: Warren McClendon Jr. Eleven guards earned PFF grades of 75.0 or better in 2025, and Steve Avila and Kevin Dotson were the only two teammates in that group. Avila has improved throughout his three seasons in the league and could make himself some serious money with another strong campaign in a contract year. There are still some lingering questions about whether Alaric Jackson will face a suspension for violating the league’s personal conduct policy, and that would be a big blow to this group. 12. Minnesota Vikings LT: Christian Darrisaw LG: Donovan Jackson C: Blake Brandel RG: Will Fries RT: Brian O'Neill Christian Darrisaw has missed significant time over the past two seasons but was one of the best left tackles in football when healthy between 2022 and 2023. If he can stay healthy, he could form one of the best left sides of the line in football with Donovan Jackson at left guard if the second-year player can develop as expected. Jackson earned a 59.4 PFF grade as a rookie, with his 65.7 PFF pass-blocking grade ranking second among rookie guards. 13. New England Patriots LT: Will Campbell LG: Alijah Vera-Tucker C: Jared Wilson RG: Mike Onwenu RT: Morgan Moses The Patriots made a big splash in free agency with the addition of Alijah Vera-Tucker. He has missed extensive time throughout his career but, when healthy, has been one of the best guards in football, earning a 77.7 PFF grade in 2024. The big question will be how left tackle Will Campbell responds after a tough end to the 2025 season. The fourth overall selection in the 2025 NFL Draft earned a 66.7 PFF grade as a rookie but closed out the year with three straight games with a PFF grade below 55.0 in the playoffs. If that was exclusively down to playing through injury, then there’s not much to worry about here, but his play should answer that question quickly in 2026. 14. Pittsburgh Steelers LT: Troy Fautanu LG: Mason McCormick C: Zach Frazier RG: Spencer Anderson RT: Dylan Cook Both Troy Fautanu and Mason McCormick are kicking over from the right side of the line to the left, and both have shown enough in their first two seasons in the league to suggest they can be an above-average duo at worst. The line is headlined by one of the best centers in the league in Zach Frazier. He allowed just 11 pressures from 673 pass-blocking snaps in 2025 and looks to be on the cusp of stardom. 15. Seattle Seahawks LT: Charles Cross LG: Grey Zabel C: Jalen Sundell RG: Anthony Bradford RT: Abraham Lucas If left guard Grey Zabel can show the improvement that we see from many highly drafted guards in their second year in the league, he can help power this unit beyond the middle of the pack. He finished the year strong with PFF grades above 68.0 in four straight games and looked much more comfortable as the year went on. Right guard Anthony Bradford is the weak spot, having failed to earn a PFF grade above 55.0 in three straight years, but the rest of the unit is strong enough to survive that weak link. 16. New Orleans Saints LT: Kelvin Banks Jr. LG: David Edwards C: Erik McCoy RG: Cesar Ruiz RT: Taliese Fuaga Rookie left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. had a strong season, leading all rookie offensive linemen with a 73.5 PFF grade. They added left guard David Edwards, who earned a 70.3 PFF grade with the Buffalo Bills in 2025, and with Erik McCoy returning at center, they just need right tackle Taliese Fuaga to take a step forward in his third year in the league for this to be a really strong group. 17. Dallas Cowboys LT: Tyler Guyton LG: Tyler Smith C: Cooper Beebe RG: Tyler Booker RT: Terence Steele The Cowboys could quite easily have the best interior offensive line in football in 2026. Left guard Tyler Smith has earned PFF grades above 70.0 in all four of his NFL seasons so far, while right guard Tyler Booker led all rookie guards with a 72.0 PFF grade. The question marks are on the outside, particularly at left tackle. Tyler Guyton did show some signs of improvement in his second season in the league, with his PFF grade improving from 49.4 as a rookie to 57.5 last year, but there is still a lot of improvement needed. 18. Las Vegas Raiders LT: Kolton Miller LG: Spencer Burford C: Tyler Linderbaum RG: Jackson Powers-Johnson RT: DJ Glaze The Raiders made Tyler Linderbaum by far the highest-paid center in football, and he should have a huge impact on their ability to run the football. The former first-round draft pick has earned PFF pass-blocking grades below 65.0 in each of the past two seasons but PFF run-blocking grades above 80.0 in three of his four seasons in the NFL. Left tackle Kolton Miller looked set for a career year before a season-ending injury after just four games. Look for this to be an ascending group in 2026 and one with serious potential to move up these rankings throughout the season. 19. Detroit Lions LT: Penei Sewell LG: Christian Mahogany C: Juice Scruggs RG: Tate Ratledge RT: Blake Miller The injury to new starting center Cade Mays drops the Lions from a team that would have ranked 13th on this list to just inside the top 20. Penei Sewell moves from right tackle to left tackle to replace Taylor Decker and is coming off a career-high 95.1 PFF grade last year. Tate Ratledge looked the part as a rookie at right guard, but Christian Mahogany struggled, and with Blake Miller set to start as a rookie, there are several concerns with this group. If Miller can hit the ground running, then they can be a top-10 unit when Mays returns, but Jared Goff could easily find himself under more pressure in 2026. 20. Cincinnati Bengals LT: Orlando Brown Jr. LG: Dylan Fairchild C: Ted Karras RG: Dalton Risner RT: Amarius Mims The Bengals’ offensive line was not a back-breakingly awful unit in the second half of the 2025 season. That was thanks to the emergence of rookie Dylan Fairchild at left guard and second-year right tackle Amarius Mims. Mims, in particular, took a huge stride forward in the second half of the year, with just one game with a PFF grade below 70.0 from Week 12 onward. 21. New York Jets LT: Olu Fashanu LG: Dylan Parham C: Josh Myers RG: Joe Tippmann RT: Armand Membou The Jets have one of the best emerging partnerships at offensive tackle in Fashanu and Membou, two first-round selections from the 2024 and 2025 NFL Drafts. Fashanu turned the corner as a pass blocker in the second half of the year, earning PFF pass-blocking grades of 74.7 or better in six of the final eight games. Membou earned PFF grades above 70.0 both in pass protection and as a run blocker, and while there are questions on the interior, this is a unit that could surprise in 2026 if they can get even solid play at guard and center. 22. Arizona Cardinals LT: Paris Johnson Jr. LG: Isaac Seumalo C: Hjalte Froholdt RG: Isaiah Adams RT: Elijah Wilkinson The Cardinals should be fine on the left side of the line, with left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. earning PFF pass-blocking grades above 77.0 in each of the past two seasons and the addition of Isaac Seumalo at left guard. The former Pittsburgh Steeler has earned a PFF grade above 65.0 in every season of his career in which he has played at least 600 snaps. The right side of the line is a bigger concern, with right guard Isaiah Adams earning PFF grades below 60.0 in each of his first two seasons in the league and Elijah Wilkinson’s career-high 65.5 PFF grade coming back in 2018. 23. New York Giants LT: Andrew Thomas LG: Jon Runyan C: John Michael Schmitz Jr. RG: Francis Mauigoa RT: Jermaine Eluemunor Andrew Thomas was arguably the Giants’ best player last year, earning a 90.3 PFF grade that tied his career high. His issue has been staying healthy, having missed significant time in both 2023 and 2024. They drafted Francis Mauigoa in the first round, and if he can hit the ground running, then the unit looks a lot stronger, but it’s a group that just might be another season away from making a bigger impact. 24. Baltimore Ravens LT: Ronnie Stanley LG: John Simpson C: Ethan Pocic RG: Olaivavega Ioane RT: Roger Rosengarten Overhauling both guard spots was a necessity for the Ravens, with the 55.2 combined PFF grade they got from their guards in 2025 ranking sixth worst in the league. Out are Andrew Vorhees , and in are John Simpson and Olaivavega Ioane. Both should be upgrades, but it’s important to temper expectations here. Simpson has just one season with a PFF grade above 60.0 in his career, while just one guard has earned a PFF grade above 80.0 as a rookie since 2018. The X-factor here is new offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, and while the unit should be better overall than it was a year ago, he could spark them closer to the middle of the pack. 25. Miami Dolphins LT: Patrick Paul LG: Kadyn Proctor C: Aaron Brewer RG: Jonah Savaiinaea RT: Austin Jackson Aaron Brewer has emerged as one of the best centers in football, and in Patrick Paul and Austin Jackson, they have a pair of tackles who earned PFF grades above 65.0. The concern is at guard, and as we just covered with Ioane, expectations should be tempered for a rookie like Kadyn Proctor. At the other guard spot, Jonah Savaiinaea’s 28.4 PFF grade in 2025 was the lowest among all starting offensive linemen in the league. 26. Carolina Panthers LT: Rasheed Walker LG: Damien Lewis C: Luke Fortner RG: Robert Hunt RT: Monroe Freeling The Panthers would have ranked inside the top 12 if they had their starting tackles, but they are without both Ikem Ekwonu and Taylor Moton , at least to start the year. They are fortunate to have backups they will feel pretty good about in Rasheed Walker, who has earned a PFF grade above 60.0 in each of his first three seasons in the league. They also have to be feeling positive about Monroe Freeling, but some growing pains should be expected for him in Year 1. 27. Houston Texans LT: Aireontae Ersery LG: Wyatt Teller C: Keylan Rutledge RG: Ed Ingram RT: Braden Smith There is some reason for optimism with this group, with left tackle Aireontae Ersery having some nice moments as a rookie and earning a 66.1 PFF pass-blocking grade in the process. His experience as a rookie should be valuable to his development, and he gets a veteran next to him in the form of Wyatt Teller in 2026. If Keylan Rutledge can have a solid rookie season, then this is a group that can climb into the top 20. 28. Green Bay Packers LT: Jordan Morgan LG: Aaron Banks C: Sean Rhyan RG: Anthony Belton RT: Zach Bako-Bewele The Packers’ offensive line could look far better by the end of the season, but right now, the only player I have confidence in having a strong season is right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele. He has yet to have a season with a PFF pass-blocking grade below 70.0 and has earned PFF grades above 80.0 in each of the past two seasons. The other four starters have just one season with a PFF grade above 65.0 between them, and the reality is that this group needs Jordan Morgan and Anthony Belton to take steps forward in their third and second years in the league, respectively. 29. Tennessee Titans LT: Dan Moore Jr. LG: Peter Skoronski C: Austin Schlottmann RG: Cordell Volson RT: JC Latham Peter Skoronski is one of the best guards in football and is continuing to get better, earning a career-high 79.0 PFF grade in 2025, while JC Latham has shown potential, improving his PFF grade from 61.8 as a rookie to 65.5 last year. There are big question marks at all three other spots on the line, though, with Dan Moore Jr. having just one season with a PFF grade above 65.0, Cordell Volson none above 60.0 and Austin Schlottmann never totaling more than 400 snaps in a single season. 30. Jacksonville Jaguars LT: Walker Little LG: Ezra Cleveland C: Robert Hainsey RG: Patrick Mekari RT: Anton Harrison This unit will rank higher once Cole Van Lanen gets back on the field, but the interior of the group is a major concern. Patrick Mekari has seen his PFF grade drop in each of the past two seasons, earning a PFF grade of just 51.8 last year, and is dealing with an injury himself, while center Robert Hainsey’s career-high 66.7 PFF grade came back in 2022. 31. Cleveland Browns LT: Spencer Fano LG: Zion Johnson C: Elgton Jenkins RG: Teven Jenkins RT: Tytus Howard The Browns are starting four new players on their offensive line this season, and there should be some hope for the future with the selection of left tackle Spencer Fano early in the 2025 NFL Draft. It will take time for him to develop, though, so expectations shouldn’t be too high for him as a rookie. Center Elgton Jenkins is the best player in this group for now and, with a PFF pass-blocking grade above 67.0 in each of his seven seasons in the NFL, should give them a strong presence in the middle of the line. 32. Washington Commanders LT: Brandon Coleman LG: Chris Paul C: Nick Allegretti RG: Sam Cosmi RT: Josh Conerly Jr. Before the injury to left tackle Laremy Tunsil , this was a group set to rank just inside the top 20, but the loss of Tunsil for a significant amount of time is a huge blow to the group. There will be an expectation of some improvement from Josh Conerly Jr. , and his 59.9 PFF grade in 2025 was fine for a rookie, but this is a unit that could really struggle if Tunsil misses the full season. McCarthy All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Kyler Murray named Minnesota Vikings’ starting quarterback over J.J. McCarthy By Mark Chichester Posted Aug 11, 2026 1:40 pm EDT Minnesota Vikings Kyler Murray wins Minnesota's quarterback competition: The Vikings named Murray their starter over J.J. McCarthy five months after signing the former No. 1 overall pick to a one-year contract. Murray regains fantasy football upside: Kevin O'Connell's offense and Justin Jefferson give Murray a path back to weekly starting status after he ranked among the top 12 fantasy quarterbacks in points per game in each of his first five seasons. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. The Minnesota Vikings have named Murray their starting quarterback over J.J. McCarthy , ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported Tuesday . The decision puts Murray atop the depth chart just five months after he signed a one-year contract with Minnesota, providing the former No. 1 overall pick with an opportunity to revitalize his career while giving the Vikings another chance to stabilize a position they have struggled with since Kirk Cousins left for Atlanta. Murray, entering his eighth NFL season, has never quite reached the heights typically associated with a No. 1 overall pick, but his play has generally remained above a respectable baseline. His lowest PFF grade came as a rookie in 2019 (64.2), while his career-best mark came in 2021 (82.9). Kyler Murray: PFF grades and rank since 2019 Season Snaps Offense Rank 2019 1,008 64.2 29 2020 1,102 82.8 13 2021 993 82.9 9 2022 718 67.2 25 2023 538 70.8 24 2024 1,065 82.1 11 2025 318 72.2 N/A Injuries have increasingly complicated that picture. Murray was limited to five starts in 2025 and has played a full season only once since 2021. Still, he earned a 72.2 PFF grade last season, ranking 21st among 43 qualifying quarterbacks. Last season, Murray completed 110 of 161 passes for 962 yards, six touchdowns and three interceptions across those five starts, recording four big-time throws and three turnover-worthy plays. His 1.4% turnover-worthy play rate trailed only Joe Burrow among qualifying quarterbacks, though his 2.3% big-time throw rate ranked 39th at the position. Accuracy remained a strength, as Murray delivered an accurate pass on 69.3% of his attempts, the best rate among qualifying quarterbacks. His ability to create with his legs also remained intact. Murray carried 29 times for 173 yards and a touchdown in 2025, averaging 6.0 yards per attempt and 3.10 yards after contact per attempt while forcing seven missed tackles. Six of those carries gained at least 10 yards. Wins Above Replacement Kyler Murray · QB -0.12 0.73 1.58 2.42 3.27 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 2019 · 0.88 WAR · Rank 26 of 73 at QB 2019 · 0.88 WAR · Rank 26 of 73 at QB 0.88 2020 · 2.14 WAR · Rank 13 of 83 at QB 2020 · 2.14 WAR · Rank 13 of 83 at QB 2.14 2021 · 2.92 WAR · Rank 11 of 85 at QB 2021 · 2.92 WAR · Rank 11 of 85 at QB 2.92 2022 · 0.82 WAR · Rank 29 of 86 at QB 2022 · 0.82 WAR · Rank 29 of 86 at QB 0.82 2023 · 0.71 WAR · Rank 26 of 85 at QB 2023 · 0.71 WAR · Rank 26 of 85 at QB 0.71 2024 · 0.80 WAR · Rank 12 of 69 at QB 2024 · 0.80 WAR · Rank 12 of 69 at QB 0.80 2025 · 0.55 WAR · Rank 33 of 82 at QB 2025 · 0.55 WAR · Rank 33 of 82 at QB 0.55 Player WAR Positional avg Select a season for WAR rank Avg QB (200+ snaps) That production is hardly an outlier. Murray has been one of the NFL’s most productive rushing quarterbacks since entering the league, totaling 535 carries, 3,202 rushing yards and 32 touchdowns across seven seasons. He has averaged 6.0 yards per carry, forced 59 missed tackles and produced 113 runs of 10-plus yards over that span. His best rushing season came in 2020, when he amassed 822 yards and 11 touchdowns on 133 carries while earning an 86.5 PFF rushing grade. And there is evidence that the high-end playmaking ability remains. As recently as the 2024 regular season, Murray ranked seventh among qualifying quarterbacks with 27 big-time throws and second with 7.3 yards per carry. Murray also excelled when simply asked to keep the offense on schedule. On throws that earned a 0 PFF grade — plays on which the quarterback is generally expected to execute the concept without doing anything exceptional, positively or negatively — Murray generated 0.028 EPA per attempt, fifth among qualifying quarterbacks in 2025. He completed 76.9% of those passes and averaged 5.1 yards per attempt. Click here to view Kyler Murray's profile in the 2026 PFF QB Annual The contrast with McCarthy is significant. McCarthy generated -0.200 EPA per attempt on zero-graded throws, ranking 35th among qualifying quarterbacks, while completing just 61.9% of his passes and averaging 4.4 yards per attempt. Murray's ability to execute the routine aspects of quarterback play at a much more efficient level provides another indication of what Minnesota could gain by putting him at the controls of Kevin O'Connell's offense. McCarthy did flash upside last season, generating the second-highest big-time throw rate among qualifying quarterbacks, but inconsistent mechanics and poor accuracy continued to undermine his play. He delivered an accurate pass on just 51.7% of his attempts, ranking 42nd among 43 qualifying quarterbacks, while his 60.1 PFF passing grade ranked 35th. The struggles weren't confined to difficult situations, either. McCarthy earned a 69.7 passing grade from a clean pocket, 37th among qualifiers, while his 45.5 passing grade under pressure ranked 24th. The fit offers reasons for optimism. O’Connell has coaxed productive quarterback play out of several starters during his Minnesota tenure, including Sam Darnold, who finished as a top-10 fantasy quarterback in 2024. Kirk Cousins also finished inside the top 10 in 2022 and ranked among the top 10 quarterbacks in fantasy points per game in 2023. Murray also gets another elite receiving option in Justin Jefferson. His best stretch in Arizona came while playing alongside DeAndre Hopkins from 2020 to 2022, with Murray finishing as fantasy’s overall QB2 in 2020 during Hopkins’ final All-Pro season. Murray finished among the top 12 fantasy quarterbacks in points per game in each of his first five NFL seasons before his production declined over the past two years. Now, with Jefferson at his disposal, an offensive line that could benefit from improved health and an O’Connell offense that has consistently produced fantasy-relevant quarterbacks, Murray has a legitimate path back to being a weekly starter in single-quarterback fantasy leagues. More importantly for Minnesota, he now has the opportunity to prove he can still be one on Sundays. records.new_body: Preseason legends: Who are the best preseason players in recent NFL history? All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Preseason legends: Who are the best preseason players in recent NFL history? By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 11, 2026 12:38 pm EDT Tyson Bagent has starred for the Bears : Chicago's backup quarterback continues to impress in August with a 91.1 preseason PFF passing grade. Cole Van Lanen turned a promising preseason into a career revitalization: Van Lanen earned a 77.5-plus overall PFF grade in three consecutive preseasons to become a core piece of the Jaguars ‘ offensive line. The PFF Early Bird Sale Is Here : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. There is no better annual reminder that football is back than convincing yourself an undrafted rookie with eight catches against third-string defenders is about to become your team’s next superstar. Every August, fans fall in love with players they had barely heard of a month earlier. Against largely vanilla opposing schemes, a backup quarterback can suddenly look like a franchise cornerstone, while a wide receiver destined for the bottom of the depth chart briefly becomes the hottest name on social media. One strong outing is all it takes for optimism to spiral, with fanbases convincing themselves they have unearthed the league’s next hidden gem. Sometimes that excitement proves completely justified. Victor Cruz remains the gold standard after announcing himself with a spectacular preseason before becoming an established NFL wide receiver. Far more often, though, preseason greatness exists in its own universe. Some players seem built specifically for August, producing momentary highlights before fading into supporting roles once the real football begins. Others carve out long NFL careers almost entirely because they consistently shine when roster spots are on the line. With another preseason now underway, we’re looking at some of the greatest August performers of the last decade. Quarterbacks By sheer volume, stalwart backup Brandon Allen leads the way with 2,579 preseason passing yards over the last decade. His stat line also illustrates why he has spent his career on the bench rather than as a viable starter, throwing nine touchdowns and 16 interceptions. Allen will likely get an opportunity to add to those totals this summer as he battles for a roster spot with the Giants. Patrick Mahomes sits atop the grading leaderboard with a 91.6 PFF preseason passing grade. That may come as a surprise considering how sparsely he has played in recent Augusts, but his overall sample size is larger than many would expect. Mahomes has appeared in 21 career preseason games, and no regular starting quarterback has taken more preseason dropbacks over the past decade than his 258. Right behind Mahomes is Tyson Bagent , whose 91.1 preseason passing grade has turned him into something of a cult hero among Chicago Bears fans. Bagent is the only quarterback over the last decade with at least 100 preseason pass attempts and zero turnover-worthy plays. That pristine record contrasts sharply with his regular-season opportunities, where he committed 11 turnover-worthy plays during a five-game stretch as a rookie and hasn’t seen much meaningful football since. Each preseason, he seems to rediscover the poise and efficiency that first put him on the radar as a top backup. Running Backs Among nearly 200 running backs with at least 50 preseason carries over the past decade, Jordan Mason owns the highest PFF rushing grade at 90.4. Unlike many names on this list, Mason translated his preseason production into a meaningful NFL role. After arriving as an undrafted free agent, he used successive impressive summers to earn the trust of San Francisco’s coaching staff before eventually establishing himself as a legitimate contributor. One player who could again feature in preseason headlines is Israel Abanikanda . Now with his fourth NFL franchise despite still being only 23 years old, Abanikanda continues to flash the explosiveness that made him a productive collegiate back. His 20 forced missed tackles are the most by any active player under 30 in preseason action over the last decade. If he receives another heavy workload this August, there is every chance he will strengthen his chance of a long-term home in the NFL. Wide Receivers Tight Ends Like Mahomes at quarterback, A.J. Green tops this position group despite never necessarily needing to prove anything in the preseason. His 89.8 PFF preseason receiving grade is the best among pass-catchers and serves as a testament to his work rate even when the stakes were low. The next names on the list are much less familiar outside their own fanbases. Veteran tight ends MyCole Pruitt and Tanner Hudson rank second and third with preseason receiving grades of 86.5 and 86.1, respectively. In particular, Hudson has become one of August’s most notable performers. His 676 preseason receiving yards and six touchdowns are both the highest totals recorded by any player over the last decade. Heading into another training camp with Cincinnati, he has an opportunity to extend that lead even further. Hudson has dropped just four of his 68 catchable preseason targets. Among younger players, Lil’Jordan Humphrey continues to be one of the league’s most productive preseason receivers. The Broncos wideout has accumulated 582 preseason receiving yards, the most of any active player under the age of 30. Offensive Line The offensive line is where the gap between preseason football and the regular season becomes most obvious. Some of the highest grades belong to players who were already stars and simply happened to play limited preseason snaps. Creed Humphrey has posted an 89.7 overall preseason grade, followed by Frank Ragnow at 88.5 and Kevin Zeitler at 87.7. However, the most interesting story belongs to Cole Van Lane n . Originally a sixth-round pick by Green Bay, Van Lanen endured being released during his first roster cutdown. Rather than disappearing from the league, he rebuilt his reputation through consistently excellent preseason performances. Now entering his fifth season with Jacksonville after signing a three-year extension, Van Lanen stands as the best example of how a productive summer can rejuvenate a football career. Defensive Linemen Edge Defenders Surprise, surprise. Myles Garrett owns the highest overall preseason grade among active front-seven defenders with at least 100 snaps, posting an outstanding 92.1 mark. Even in limited preseason action, one of the NFL’s greatest ever pass-rushers constantly looks like just that. Chicago Bears edge defender Austin Booker may be the next player to make the leap from preseason sensation to regular-season contributor. Still only 23 years old, Booker carries a 91.3 PFF preseason grade through his first two summers, fueled by 6.5 sacks and an exceptional 22.7% pressure rate. He should already have a rotational role in Chicago’s defense this season, but another productive August could push him firmly into the conversation for a full-time position. Veteran pass-rusher Trevis Gipson has quietly built one of the strongest preseason resumes of any active defender. Gipson has spent time with five different NFL franchises, and his 92.2 preseason pass-rushing grade demonstrates why teams keep bringing him in for another chance. He is the only active defender under 30 to eclipse 40 preseason pressures. Linebackers Defensive Backs Several of today’s established linebackers have tuned up for real football with dominant preseason performances. Frankie Luvu , Nakobe Dean , Malcolm Rodriguez , Drue Tranquill and Zack Baun have all produced career preseason grades above 85.0. Retired linebacker David Mayo stands alone as the preseason tackling king of the last decade. Across nine NFL seasons spent with four NFC franchises, Mayo is the only player to accumulate 100 preseason tackles since 2016. Among active players still in their twenties, safety Jeremy Reaves is a standout preseason contributor. Entering his ninth season in Washington, Reaves has experienced three different franchise names and precious little team success, yet every August, he seems to remind coaches exactly why he belongs on an NFL roster. Safety Tycen Anderson deserves special recognition for his coverage prowess. After spending the duration of his rookie contract in Cincinnati before moving to Denver this offseason, Anderson has allowed a passer rating of just 6.5 when targeted during preseason play. This can be explained by three interceptions, tied for the most among active players, and only four receptions allowed across more than 200 coverage snaps. records.new_body: The numbers behind Aaron Donald’s potential return to the NFL All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting The numbers behind Aaron Donald’s potential return to the NFL By Daire Carragher Posted Aug 11, 2026 12:26 pm EDT Aaron Donald is in his own tier of dominance: Donald recorded a 90.0-plus overall PFF grade in 10 straight seasons, becoming the only player ever to accomplish that. Donald would have plenty of help along the Rams' defensive line: Determining whether or not to double-team Donald or Myles Garrett is troubling enough, but Donald would also operate alongside a burgeoning star in Kobie Turner . The PFF Early Bird Sale Is Here : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. Sure-fire Hall of Fame defensive tackle Aaron Donald captured headlines when it was revealed that he officially worked out for the Rams in early August. Donald has made it clear that he will not return to football unless he feels he can still perform at a high level, but his comeback to the Rams appears increasingly plausible as the regular season approaches. If Donald does play again, it would likely be to contribute down the stretch. At 35 years old, he doesn’t need to withstand an 18-game season followed by a playoff run, nor does he need to travel to Melbourne, Australia, for the Rams’ season opener. The ideal scenario for both Donald and Los Angeles is likely for him to rejoin the team in some capacity between now and the Rams’ mid-November bye week before working toward seeing the field during the latter stages of the season. Donald was last seen on an NFL field at the end of the 2023 season. Thirteen sacks across his final two years showed signs of decline on paper for a player who averaged almost 15 sacks per season between 2018 and 2021. However, his underlying performances remained among the best in the sport, as evidenced by his 90.8 overall PFF grade in his final campaign. Donald remains the only player in PFF history to post 10 consecutive seasons with an overall PFF grade above 90.0. Despite not playing for two years, he still leads the NFL in total pressures over the past decade with 717. His 97 sacks during that span rank fourth, trailing only prospective teammate Myles Garrett , who leads the league with 126.5 sacks since entering the NFL. Aaron Donald: PFF grades (2014 to 2023) Season Snaps Defense Rank 2014 774 90.2 2 2015 984 92.9 1 2016 888 92.6 1 2017 935 94.4 1 2018 1197 94.8 1 2019 997 93.6 1 2020 968 94.2 1 2021 1268 93.5 1 2022 620 90.5 3 2023 921 90.8 2 Donald’s somewhat premature retirement meant we never saw him gradually decline into an average — or even merely above-average — player. With no real precedent to draw from, we can’t definitively rule out the possibility that he’s still one of the best interior pass-rushers in the world in 2026. If Donald does return, he’ll almost certainly have the strongest supporting cast of his career along the defensive line, highlighted by Garrett, a player of whom Donald has never had the luxury of lining up alongside, and vice versa. Throughout the final five years of his career, Donald was double-teamed on more than two-thirds of his pass-rushing snaps. That still didn’t stop him from producing some of the most dominant individual performances we’ve ever seen from an NFL defensive lineman. Likewise, Garrett has been the NFL’s most frequently double-teamed edge defender over the past two seasons. The nature of his alignment means he faces far fewer true double teams than Donald did on the interior, with most offenses instead relying on chipping tight ends to slow him down, often to little avail. If this duo does pair up at some point this season, my guess is that opponents’ game plans for Garrett won’t change too much. He’s in the prime of his career and has to be accounted for on every passing down. Donald’s presence shouldn’t alter that, at least not initially, until teams get a better sense of the level he’s operating at. If Donald returns and looks every bit the player he was before retiring, that’s when opposing offenses will start ringing the alarm bells. The Rams rushed four or more defenders on 98.5% of plays last season. Even against a standard four-man rush, double-teaming both future Hall of Famers would leave just four eligible receivers in the passing concept against seven coverage defenders, including a star the caliber of Trent McDuffie . How often would we actually see that, though? Will Donald have the conditioning to handle a heavy workload? We know he’s kept himself in phenomenal shape since leaving the league, but physical appearance and football conditioning are two entirely different things. The good news is that Donald was never a player who needed to come off the field. His final season saw him play 50 or more snaps in 13 of 17 games. For comparison, Los Angeles’ starting interior duo of Kobie Turner and Braden Fisk e surpassed the 50-snap threshold just seven times combined across 40 appearances last season. Turner and Fiske both return in 2026. So too does Poona Ford , who enjoyed a career year after bouncing around four teams in four seasons. Ford recorded a career-high 30 defensive stops against the run. Even beyond that trio, the Rams’ next three rotational interior defenders from last season — Tyler Davis , Ty Hamilton and Larrell Murchison — all return as well. This is essentially an unchanged interior defensive line group from what was already the second-highest-graded unit in the NFL last season. Turner shouldn’t be overlooked as an ideal running mate for Donald. Both are relatively undersized for the position, but on obvious passing downs — where you’d assume Donald would be deployed most often — this could be the best interior pass-rushing duo in football. through . --> Read more Read more PFF Interior Defender Rankings: The top 32 players ahead of the 2026 NFL season By Gordon McGuinness (opens in new tab) → Turner finished tied for second among interior defenders with 69 pressures, ranked seventh in sacks and sixth in PFF pass-rushing grade. Yet his impressive 12.7% pressure rate would still place as the second-lowest mark of Aaron Donald ’s career. He simply operated at a different level from the moment he entered the league. Among the four highest-graded pass-protecting offensive lines from last season, the Rams will face three of them in consecutive weeks between Weeks 3 and 5. Matchups against the Broncos, Eagles and Bills are among the most mouth-watering games of the early schedule, but they could easily come and go before Donald even puts his pads back on. Later in the season, two tantalizing matchups against the Seahawks in the space of three weeks could define the NFC West race. With both teams holding legitimate Super Bowl aspirations, there’s every chance they could meet three times within the span of a month once the postseason begins. No franchise has felt Donald’s wrath more than Seattle. The Seahawks were the reigning Super Bowl champions when the Rams selected Donald 13th overall in the 2014 NFL Draft. Since then, his 124 pressures and 17.5 sacks against Seahawks quarterbacks are both his highest totals against any opponent. So too is his 94.2 career PFF pass-rushing grade versus Seattle. However, in his only career meeting with Sam Darnold back in 2020, Darnold escaped all 10 of Donald’s pressures and led his then 0-13 New York Jets to their first victory of the season. Whether Donald ultimately returns or not, the fact this conversation is even happening speaks volumes. Most Hall of Famers are remembered for what they once were. Donald retired while still playing at an elite level, leaving open the possibility that one of the greatest defensive players in NFL history may still have something left to offer. records.new_body: 2026 NFL Season Preview: Strengths, concerns and breakout candidates for all 32 teams All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting 2026 NFL Season Preview: Strengths, concerns and breakout candidates for all 32 teams By Gordon McGuinness Posted Aug 11, 2026 10:42 am EDT All 32 teams are covered: PFF's 2026 NFL season preview hub links to a full breakdown of every team, including roster strengths, concerns, key additions and breakout candidates. The league looks dramatically different: Seattle enters as defending Super Bowl champion, while major offseason moves include Myles Garrett joining the Rams, Trey Hendrickson landing in Baltimore and A.J. Brown moving to New England. Quarterback storylines shape the season: Josh Allen, Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson remain central to AFC contenders, while Fernando Mendoza begins his career as the No. 1 overall pick in Las Vegas. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. The 2025 season ended with Mike Macdonald’s Seattle Seahawks lifting the Lombardi Trophy after a 14-3 campaign and three straight playoff wins, and with the New England Patriots completing one of the great single-season turnarounds — 4-13 to 14-3 and an AFC title — before falling at the final hurdle. The offseason that followed reshaped the league all over again: Myles Garrett is a Ram, Trey Hendrickson a Raven, A.J. Brown a Patriot and Mike Evans a 49er, while at least nine teams hired a new head coach and the Raiders took Fernando Mendoza first overall. Gordon McGuinness has broken down every roster in the league — the biggest strengths, the clearest concerns, the key additions and the players most likely to swing each season. Every 2026 team preview is linked below. Arizona Cardinals 2026 preview: Jeremiyah Love headlines new era Nine straight losses left the Arizona Cardinals with a 3-14 record, tied for the worst in the NFL. The collapse led to the firing of head coach Jonathan Gannon, with former Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator Mike LaFleur hired as his replacement. That was not the only major change, as the Cardinals also parted ways with quarterback Kyler Murray, ending the former No. 1 overall pick’s seven-year tenure in Arizona. Here is our 2026 preview of the Arizona Cardinals. Click here to read preview Atlanta Falcons 2026 preview: The quarterback competition takes center stage After a difficult start to the 2025 season left them at 4-9 through 13 games, the Atlanta Falcons won their final four contests to finish tied for the best record in the NFC South, ultimately placing third on tiebreakers. Atlanta responded with sweeping changes, hiring Kevin Stefanski as its new head coach and adding Tua Tagovailoa to create competition at quarterback. Here is our 2026 preview for the Atlanta Falcons. Click here to read preview Baltimore Ravens 2026 preview: Why Lamar Jackson and Trey Hendrickson fuel optimism The Baltimore Ravens endured a disappointing 2025 season, marred by injuries to quarterback Lamar Jackson before ultimately falling on Tyler Loop’s missed field goal on the final play of the season. They made sweeping changes this offseason, and optimism remains high as they head into 2026. Here’s our 2026 preview of the Baltimore Ravens. Click here to read preview Buffalo Bills 2026 preview: Joe Brady begins new era with the league’s best quarterback Josh Allen was the only one of the AFC’s “big four quarterbacks” to make the playoffs last season, so everything appeared to be in place for the Bills to finally get over the hump and reach the Super Bowl for the first time since the 1993 season. Instead, an overtime loss to the Broncos in Denver ended their season in the divisional round. Buffalo responded by moving on from head coach Sean McDermott and replacing him with Joe Brady. Here is our 2026 preview of the Buffalo Bills . Click here to read preview Carolina Panthers 2026 preview: Bryce Young enters pivotal year after NFC South title The Carolina Panthers lost their final two games of the 2025 regular season but still won the NFC South on a tiebreaker, returning to the playoffs for the first time since 2017. records.new_body: Las Vegas Raiders 2026 preview: Klint Kubiak takes over revamped roster All NFL - current Fantasy College NFL Draft DFS Betting Las Vegas Raiders 2026 preview: Klint Kubiak takes over revamped roster 3DE212A Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty (2) runs with the ball during the first half of an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs Sunday, Jan. 4, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/John Locher) By Gordon McGuinness Posted Aug 11, 2026 9:14 am EDT Las Vegas Raiders Fernando Mendoza is the quarterback of the future: The No. 1 overall pick earned a 90.7 PFF passing grade in his final college season, while Kirk Cousins gives Las Vegas the flexibility to let Mendoza develop. Ashton Jeanty is positioned for a Year 2 breakout: Jeanty produced 815 yards after contact as a rookie, and an improved offensive line could help him build on his 975 rushing yards. Last Chance! The PFF Early Bird Sale Ends Aug. 17 : Save 33% and get PFF+ for just $79.99, our lowest price of the year. through . --> Explore PFF Fantasy Tools EARLY BIRD SALE: SAVE 33% — the lowest price of the year (opens in new tab) The Las Vegas Raiders finished the 2025 season tied for the worst record in football at 3-14, but that gave them the No. 1 overall pick and another opportunity to find their franchise quarterback. They also hired Klint Kubiak as their new head coach after he helped the Seattle Seahawks win the Super Bowl as their offensive coordinator last season. Here’s our 2026 preview of the Las Vegas Raiders . Key Free Agency/Trade Additions Position Player 2025 PFF Grade WR Jalen Nailor 66.3 WR Dareke Young N/A G Spencer Burford 56.7 C Tyler Linderbaum 79.8 QB Kirk Cousins 76.0 FB Connor Heyward N/A DI Benito Jones 47.1 EDGE Kwity Paye 59.0 LB Quay Walker 46.0 LB Nakobe Dean 62.2 K Matt Gay 62.0 The addition of Kirk Cousins at quarterback means the Raiders don’t need to rush Fernando Mendoza into the starting lineup and can instead let him develop behind the veteran. After losing his starting job to Michael Penix Jr. in Atlanta ahead of the 2025 season, Cousins eventually returned to the lineup and earned a 75.0 PFF passing grade, ranking 14th among quarterbacks. The Raiders also made a major investment in the middle of their offensive line, making Tyler Linderbaum the highest-paid center in football. The former first-round pick has earned PFF grades between 74.6 and 79.9 in each of his four NFL seasons. His pass protection has been closer to average recently, with his 63.4 PFF pass-blocking grade ranking 21st at the position in 2025, but he remains an elite run blocker. His 83.2 PFF run-blocking grade last season ranked fourth among centers. 2026 NFL Draft Class Position Player 2025 PFF Grade QB Fernando Mendoza 91.6 DB Treydan Stukes 90.1 EDGE Keyron Crawford 76.3 G Trey Zuhn III 71.8 CB Jermod McCoy N/A HB Mike Washington Jr. 78.3 S Dalton Johnson 84.8 CB Hezekiah Masses 79.5 WR Malik Benson 73.0 DI Brandon Cleveland 72.1 Fernando Mendoza spent just one season at Indiana, but it ended with a national championship, a Heisman Trophy and his selection as the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. He earned a 90.7 PFF passing grade in his final college season, finishing the year with a 5.7% big-time throw rate and a 2.6% turnover-worthy play rate. The Raiders also stopped the slide of Tennessee cornerback Jermod McCoy. Once regarded as a potential top-10 pick, McCoy fell due to medical concerns after missing the entire 2025 season. His last season on the field was an impressive one, though, as he earned an 89.6 PFF coverage grade in 2024. McCoy saw 62 targets across 393 coverage snaps, allowing 31 receptions while combining for 10 interceptions and pass breakups. Reasons for optimism After a proposed trade to the Baltimore Ravens fell through, Maxx Crosby returns as the most important player on the Raiders’ defense. Crosby’s PFF grade has dipped below 80.0 in each of the past two seasons after three straight years above 90.0, but he remains one of the best all-around edge defenders in the NFL. He has earned PFF grades above 70.0 both as a pass rusher and run defender in five consecutive seasons. On offense, Brock Bowers continued to impress in his second NFL season. He missed five games due to injury but still ranked inside the top 10 among tight ends in both receiving yards and PFF receiving grade. Heading into Year 3, Bowers is firmly established as one of the best players at the position. The QB Annual Is Live Every qualifying quarterback. Every metric that matters. PFF grades, passing splits, EPA per dropback, clutch performance, interception luck and more — all in one interactive guide built on the same data trusted by all 32 NFL teams. Read the QB Annual (opens in new tab) Get PFF+ (opens in new tab) Reason for pessimism The Raiders have done a nice job adding talent at the skill positions in recent years, selecting tight end Brock Bowers and running back Ashton Jeanty in back-to-back NFL Drafts, but wide receiver remains a weakness. None of their returning wide receivers who saw at least 30 targets last season averaged more than 1.20 yards per route run. Their biggest addition at the position was Jalen Nailor, who averaged just 1.06 yards per route run last season. In fact, none of the wide receivers currently on the roster ranked better than 78th among the 111 players at the position with at least 30 targets in the regular season. That leaves 2025 second-round pick Jack Bech as perhaps their best hope for a breakout at the position. He showed flashes as a rookie but saw just 28 targets, giving him an opportunity to earn a much larger role in Year 2. Breakout Candidate It’s an easy choice, but the addition of Tyler Linderbaum at center gives Ashton Jeanty an excellent opportunity to take a step forward in Year 2. Jeanty was solid as a rookie, earning a 73.1 PFF rushing grade that ranked tied for 33rd at the position. However, the struggles of the offensive line contributed to him finishing just 18th with 975 rushing yards, despite his 815 yards after contact ranking eighth. With an improved offensive line in front of him and a better situation at quarterback, Jeanty should have an easier time producing at a higher level in his second season. Key roster battles How the Raiders’ defensive backfield takes shape will be something to watch during the preseason, with much potentially depending on where second-round pick Treydan Stukes fits best. Eric Stokes and Darien Porter are the likely starters on the outside, though Jermod McCoy could push for playing time if he hits the ground running. Taron Johnson is a natural fit in the slot. He earned a career-high 81.7 PFF coverage grade in 2023 and, while that mark has declined over the past two seasons, he has still graded above 60.0 in coverage in both years. Jeremy Chinn is best suited to playing in the box and is coming off a season in which he earned a 66.7 PFF grade. The biggest concern is at free safety, where Isaiah Pola-Mao’s 39.8 PFF grade in 2025 ranked 96th among the 97 safeties who played at least 300 snaps. That could create an opportunity for Stukes, though he played just 19 snaps at free safety last season, with most of his work coming in the slot or box. Given that free safety appears to be the weakest spot in the secondary, where the Raiders deploy Stukes during the preseason will be worth monitoring.
