records.new_body: Good NFL rookies have more college experience: PFF data explains the trend All NFL Fantasy College NFL Draft - current DFS Betting Good NFL rookies have more college experience: PFF data explains the trend By Bradley Locker Posted Jul 31, 2026 9:26 am EDT The rate of good rookies with high prior snap counts is growing: In 2025, 62.5% of high-graded rookies had played at least 1,750 snaps in college. An emphasis on seasoned mid-to-late-round picks: Recent newcomers like Kamren Kinchens , Jalen Coker and Rashid Shaheed have blossomed, in part due to their large college sample sizes. Still an imprecise science: Rookies with tons of experience don't always pan out right away, and those with fewer snaps can still star in their first years. As the Super Bowl winds down and the NFL offseason starts buzzing in mid-February, attention invariably turns to scouting for the NFL Draft. The ensuing two months help unearth uncut gems in the college class, sifting through players at every level — even to the point of prospect fatigue. As part of that evaluation process, specific adages and philosophies continue to come into discussion. Near the top of that list is what to make of prospects that are either older or have played more years/snaps in college. Those in favor of more seasoned players often tout athletes being more refined and “pro-ready,” having exposure to different systems, coaching styles and even processes of operation during games. On the other hand, detractors point to older players having fewer years to offer in the NFL, plus coming with potentially longer injury histories or more tread on the tires, especially at a position like running back. The debate about the sweet spot for prospect experience probably won’t subside anytime soon. But as the quest for finding players who can make an instant impact continues, there’s been a clear development. As PFF data underscores, more productive NFL rookies are benefiting from additional snaps at the collegiate level. For context, this research will lean on the number of collegiate snaps played, as opposed to the number of years in college. Although recent names have generated traction by appearing for even four schools, or by playing nearly seven seasons at the Division I level, that hasn’t always materialized into legitimate playing time at those stops. By contrast, snaps are a stronger indication of how much a player is actually seeing the field, no matter their number of years in school or path. Of the 20 highest-graded NFL rookies on both offense and defense to play a minimum of 250 snaps last season, 62.5% of them played at least 1,750 snaps in college. That included the highest-graded newcomer overall, Bills fifth-round pick Jackson Hawes (83.1), who played 1,955 snaps between Georgia Tech and Yale . Others meeting the criteria were Offensive Rookie of the Year Tetairoa McMillan — who saw 2,292 snaps over his three years at Arizona — the Saints’ Tyler Shough , the Giants’ Abdul Carter and the Seahawks’ Nick Emmanwori . If that figure feels high, it’s because it is. The number has climbed in each of the last four rookie classes, going from 40% in 2022 to 47.5% in 2023 to 52.2% in 2024 before peaking last season. In other words, the proportion of impressive first-year players with 1,750 or more career college snaps is only augmenting. Since 2022, some of the sport’s best players at their positions have gotten serious runway in the college level, a development that doesn’t feel like a coincidence. That extended time before the NFL has allowed young players to hit the ground running and quickly dominate. Notable recent NFL draftees with at least 1,800 college snaps Player Draft Class Overall PFF Grade College Snaps Brock Purdy 2022 91.2 3,148 Tyler Linderbaum 2022 86.9 2,317 Brock Bowers 2024 86.1 2,028 Quinyon Mitchell 2024 84.5 2,298 Will Anderson Jr. 2023 92.3 2,203 Devon Witherspoon 2023 90.8 2,334 Sauce Gardner 2022 91.1 2,110 Aidan Hutchinson 2022 93.1 1,891 Although the list above is largely comprised of first-round — and even top-10 — picks, the most revealing aspect of this research is that experience matters most for mid- or-late-round selections. Players taken in Round 3 or later naturally carry a much wider range of outcomes, but those with a bevy of college snaps have tended to grade higher in their first NFL season. Last season alone, the likes of Hawes, Cameron Skattebo , Nohl Williams , Craig Woodson , Xavier Watts and Josaiah Stewart earned at least a 71.0 overall PFF grade despite being taken in the third round or later. Each of those players met the college snap criteria to qualify, parlaying that time into not just NFL snaps but also quality performance. That sentiment has been true throughout the prior three years as well. Players like Jalen Coker , Kam Kinchens , Evan Williams , Tarheeb Still , Chamarri Conner , Rashid Shaheed , Cobie Durant and Reed Blankenship have enjoyed fruitful careers despite being mid-to-late round choices, in part by banking on their extensive college work. In terms of the nuances of this research, what’s compelling is that more good offensive rookies are meeting this higher college snap share. Positions like offensive line and receiver have particularly suggested that more seasoned prospects immediately yield superior first seasons. Recent first-round picks like Armand Membou , Joe Alt and Xavier Worthy fall into this category, as do names like Zach Frazier , Ozzy Trapilo , Tate Ratledge and Jayden Higgins . As franchises continue to refine their draft strategies, it appears that more fruits can be harvested right away by targeting prospects with a bigger sample of college snaps, especially on Day 2 and 3 of the draft. However, it’s not entirely that cut and dry. Simply playing a high volume of snaps in school doesn’t necessarily mean a player will turn in a plus rookie year. Just look at last year’s No. 1 overall pick Cam Ward, who ranked dead last among qualified passers in overall PFF grade despite accruing 4,005 snaps across Incarnate Word , Washington State and Miami (FL) . Rookies like Jonah Savaiinaea , Jahdae Barron , Barrett Carter and Brady Cook were also all substandard despite eclipsing at least 1,800 college snaps. Along similar lines, some tremendously talented players have not played a large number of snaps before getting to the NFL. Excluded from qualification were the likes of Puka Nacua , Kyle Hamilton , Bijan Robinson , Cooper DeJean , Jahmyr Gibbs and Carson Schwesinger , the latter of whom won Defensive Rookie of the Year despite playing only 806 snaps at UCLA . Consequently, players boasting elite natural skills can translate effectively and quickly without leveraging more experience, especially relative to peers. Another factor to consider in this exercise is the changing college football landscape. Rates have seemingly only increased for the number of players that not only play at more schools, but also for longer durations. That may help explain why last year’s highest-graded rookies consist of more well-traveled players, looming as a confounding factor. It will be fascinating to see how the NCAA’s updated five-year eligibility model, which removes redshirts and waivers, will affect this trend if at all. Determining rookie success is still a very inexact science. Player health, opportunity, schematic fit and coaching all matter tremendously in determining how much a newcomer will even play, let alone do so at a top-tier level. However, it’s evident that a larger share of good first-year NFL players leverage a larger body of work from their college days. Playing against better competition for longer before entering the league has clear benefits in helping players accelerate their own growth, which sets them up for success right away. This development bodes especially well for 2026 rookies like the 49ers ’ De’Zhaun Stribling, Cowboys ’ Caleb Downs, Lions ’ Blake Miller and Bills ’ Davison Igbinosun , who all played at least 2,450 snaps before being picked in April. records.new_body: Fantasy Football 2026: Veteran training camp status checks All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting Fantasy Football 2026: Veteran training camp status checks By Nic Bodiford Posted Jul 31, 2026 6:30 am EDT Watch Los Angeles Chargers receivers and tight ends : Two position groups face significant role changes in the new scheme. The Cardinals are sorting out their receiver pecking order : Arizona’s No. 1 wide receiver has not yet been determined. Terrange Ferguson could be primed for a bigger receiving role: The second-year tight end has reportedly worked as the Rams ’ No. 3 wideout. NFL training camps are now fully underway, with both rookies and veterans having reported across the league. While some NFL veterans are set to take on clear-cut roles, others enter fantasy-relevant training camp battles. The article below breaks down need-to-know information and recommended storylines to track in the coming weeks. Los Angeles Chargers wide receivers and tight ends As detailed in “ NFL Personnel Trends: How heavier groupings are shrinking the fantasy flex pool ,” new Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel creates a fantasy-friendly environment for his team’s top-two wide receivers by frequently using fullback-based personnel packages (20, 21 and 22 personnel). The tactic reduces the number of capable target-earners on the field, allowing the team’s best target-earners to hog opportunities. Chargers No. 1 wide receiver Ladd McConkey is a “ full go ” for training camp after successfully rehabbing the hamstring strain he suffered in spring practices. He has earned a 79.3 PFF receiving grade and a 20.4% target rate through two NFL seasons. Chargers No. 3 receiver Tre Harris enters his second NFL campaign and is reportedly set to be a “legitimate part of the passing offense” alongside McConkey and No. 2 wideout Quentin Johnston . Harris, 24, compiled a 14.4% target rate and a 66.6 PFF receiving grade as a 2025 rookie. Johnston, 24, has secured a 16.6% target rate and a 66.1 PFF receiving grade through three NFL seasons. If two, or all three, wide receivers must split fullback-set snaps, it reduces their weekly fantasy reliability. But if one wide receiver is largely limited to three-wide receiver sets, the other two will benefit. The Chargers’ tight end group faces a similar dynamic. Chargers general manager Joe Hortiz signed former Baltimore Ravens tight end Charlie Kolar to the 20th-highest positional contract in average annual value after 2025 rookie tight end Oronde Gadsden II ’s breakout. He then brought in former Cleveland Brown s tight end David Njoku on a cheap, one-year deal. If Gadsden, 23, can earn the starting role for 21 personnel (two running backs, one tight end and two wide receivers) and 11 personnel (one running back, one tight end and three wide receivers), he should return fantasy football TE1 value. As a rookie, Gadsden compiled a 16.9% target rate and a 71.1 PFF receiving grade while averaging 1.65 yards per route run (YPRR). Among 77 NFL tight ends with at least 990 offensive snaps from 2022-25, Kolar’s 66.2 PFF run-blocking grade ranks fifth, and his 73.5 PFF receiving grade placed 17th, though he garnered just 40 career targets. He boasts a 1.70 YPRR career average. Kolar will challenge for the No. 1 tight end role. Last season, Njoku earned a 61.6 PFF receiving grade, the second-worst of his career, and a career-worst 43.1 PFF run-blocking grade. He is a rotational player at best. Arizona Cardinals wide receivers The Arizona Cardinals are replacing their old X-receiver-centric passing offense with new head coach Mike LaFleur’s distributive scheme. LaFleur worked for or alongside Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay and/or San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan in 10 of the last 12 years. Cardinals X-receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. averaged 1.61 YPRR over the past two seasons while earning a 75.5 PFF receiving grade, while Cardinals Z-receiver Michael Wilson averaged 1.37 YPRR with a 73.1 PFF receiving grade during that span. Wilson averaged 2.46 YPRR while playing to an 85.9 PFF receiving grade during his Weeks 11-18 hot streak, in which he was the overall half-PPR WR2. While Harrison is the nominal No. 1 wide receiver, the top positional target-earner has not yet been established. Wilson could win this battle. WR Tetairoa McMillan , Carolina Panthers Carolina Panthers defending Offensive Rookie of the Year, wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan , missed “most” spring practices with a foot injury, his second such injury since December 2025. Fortunately, he recovered in time to take the field with his teammates on July 23, one day after veterans reported for camp. For context, McMillan dealt with three hamstring issues and a calf injury last season. Panthers head coach Dave Canales reportedly plans to double McMillan’s 15.5% slot rate from last year, “ if not more ,” partially due to third-round rookie wide receiver Chris Brazzell II’s potential premier abilities. Unfortunately, Brazzell’s Wednesday LCL sprain is expected to sideline him for the entire season, jeopardizing McMillan’s potential role alteration. Brazzell posted an 80.6 PFF receiving grade at Tennessee last year. McMillan averaged 1.84 YPRR with a 75.0 PFF receiving grade when lined up on the perimeter compared to 1.88 YPRR and an 82.1 PFF receiving grade when lined up in the slot. A natural second-year leap, coupled with his potential usage improvements, raise his ceiling for 2026. TE Terrance Ferguson , Los Angeles Rams Los Angeles Rams tight end Terrance Ferguson will reportedly operate as the team’s de facto No. 3 wide receiver after ranking fifth in average depth of target (aDot, 17.9) among 206 NFL skill-position players with at least 30 targets last season. He earned a 61.2 PFF receiving grade last year. Ferguson is a TE2 with explosive-pass-play upside. As outlined in “ NFL Personnel Trends: How heavier groupings are shrinking the fantasy flex pool ,” the Rams’ shallow pass-catching corps bodes positively for the team’s wide receivers. New England Patriots running backs New England Patriots starting running back Rhamondre Stevenson left practice early , just before the team’s final sprinting session on Tuesday. He was scheduled to speak with the media afterward, but did not show up. This scenario typically indicates an injury occurred; however, an illness is possible in this specific instance . Stevenson’s 77.2 PFF offense ranks tied for 15th among 35 NFL running backs with at least 180 offensive touches in 2025. With Stevenson sidelined by a toe injury in Weeks 9-11 last year, then-rookie running back TreVeyon Henderson finished as the half-PPR RB19, RB4 and RB4. He earned a 72.0 PFF rushing grade, a 56.0 PFF receiving grade and a 43.0 PFF pass-blocking grade during that span. He smartly spent spring practices refining his receiving and pass-protection skills. Stevenson’s departure could be a non-issue. Regardless, this battle is worth watching. records.new_body: Fantasy Football 2026: Rookie training camp status checks All NFL Fantasy - current College NFL Draft DFS Betting Fantasy Football 2026: Rookie training camp status checks By Nic Bodiford Posted Jul 31, 2026 6:15 am EDT Jeremiyah Love shouldn’t slip despite coaches’ comments : Love’s status as the current No. 2 running back creates a buy-low opportunity. Keep an eye on Cyrus Allen: The Chiefs fifth-round pick is opening eyes in training camp and could emerge as a real contributor. Caleb Douglas has a chance to shine fast : The Dolphins ’ wide receiver depth chart is wide open. NFL training camps are underway. Rookies typically report days before veterans, giving fantasy managers early indications as to which players are ahead of their 2026 NFL Draft counterparts. Although many rookies gradually become fantasy-relevant in-season, often as late as December, the groundwork is laid during the summer months, and early-season contributions are possible. The article below breaks down need-to-know information and recommended storylines to track in the coming weeks. RB Jeremiyah Love, Arizona Cardinals Arizona Cardinals training camp opened on July 22 for both rookies and veterans. Cardinals free-agent signee running back Tyler Allgeier is the first player up in team drills, while No. 3 overall pick Jeremiyah Love has rotated in behind him with the first-team offense. Old-school Cardinals offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett expressed excitement over backup running back James Conner ( ankle ), who is currently sitting out team drills, while downplaying Love’s status on the team. Meanwhile, presumed Cardinals No. 4 running back Trey Benson ’s social media activity could imply a desire to be traded. Love’s college career-best 93.1 PFF offense grade, earned in 2025, towers over Allgeier's (71.5 PFF offense grade), Conner's (63.7 PFF offense grade) and Benson’s (62.3 PFF offense grade) 2025 PFF offense grades, as does his fully guaranteed $53 million contract. Love’s career-high 93.7 PFF rushing grade and 72.6 PFF receiving grade closely trail current Las Vegas Raiders and former Boise State running back Ashton Jeanty ’s top college marks with a 96.6 PFF rushing grade and 91.6 PFF receiving grade. However, Love’s best ball consensus 3.02, RB13 ADP is far cheaper than Jeanty’s 2025 1.11, RB5 ADP. As Arizona attempts to spin Love’s first-team, backup involvement as a make-him-earn-it move, fantasy managers should continue drafting him at his current ADP, and pick him more aggressively if his ADP dips. RB Jadarian Price, Seattle Seahawks As detailed in “ 2026 NFL Draft: 3 early-down running backs for fantasy football ,” Seattle Seahawks No. 32 overall pick, running back Jadarian Price, is an undersized, yet talented rusher and decorated returner. He caught just 15-of-18 passes for 162 receiving yards and three receiving touchdowns via a 9.0% target rate while averaging just 0.81 yards per route run (YPRR) and earning a 61.5 PFF receiving grade. According to the Tacoma News Tribune’s Gregg Bell, the Seahawks are “ maximizing ” Price’s practice reps by having him play with the first-, second- and third-team offenses while frequently targeting him in passing game drills. Price may be able to return RB2 value as a run-centric committee leader. Passing game involvement would significantly increase his fantasy point-scoring potential. Track Price’s training camp development closely. RB Kaelon Black, San Francisco 49ers San Francisco 49ers second-year running back Jordan James operated as the No. 2 running back throughout spring practices. 49ers third-round rookie running back Kaelon Black rotated in behind him in the No. 3 role. This usage remained constant through the 49ers’ first training camp practice, and partway through the second, but James “didn't do much of anything for the second half of the session.” It is unclear whether his departure was injury-related, or whether the team wanted to give Black more reps. James, 22, received positive reports in training camp last year, but knee and finger injuries impacted his early-season availability. He logged 17 regular-season snaps and earned a 75.0 PFF rushing grade. Black is a 24-year-old rookie whose receiving production petered out after transferring from James Madison (2021-23) to Indiana (2024-25). During the Hoosiers’ College Football Playoff championship run, Black rushed 186 times for 1,034 rushing yards and 10 rushing touchdowns while averaging 0.16 missed tackles forced per rushing attempt, 3.5 yards after contact per rushing attempt and 5.6 yards per rushing attempt and earning an 85.1 PFF rushing grade. Monitor this training camp battle. WR Makai Lemon, Philadelphia Eagles Philadelphia Eagles first-round pick, wide receiver Makai Lemon ( hamstring ), said he will be “ 100.0% ” healthy when the team reports for training camp on July 28. Assuming the hamstring recovery was successful , Lemon will begin his quest to establish himself as the team’s No. 2 wide receiver. The 2025 Biletnikoff Award winner posted a 90.8 PFF offense grade last year. WR Cyrus Allen, Kansas City Chiefs Kansas City Chiefs fifth-round rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen generated dynasty-darling buzz in spring rookie drafts. He has stood out among Chiefs rookies, working with quarterback Patrick Mahomes since July 24, and received one-on-one coaching from head coach Andy Reid. Allen fared well at the 2026 Senior Bowl, with talent identifiers touting his separation skills. Internally, his route-running, explosiveness, ball skills, hands and smarts at Chiefs spring practices drew praise . Allen, 23, played for three different colleges. He posted career highs in target rate (25.3%), slot-target rate (22.3%), YPRR (2.42), catch rate (71.0%), missed tackles forced (eight), receptions (49) and receiving touchdowns (12) in his final college season at Cincinnati . His 715.2 PFF receiving grade from last year is also a career high. Allen must be rostered across all dynasty formats and could earn the Chiefs’ No. 4 wide receiver role in training camp. Ascending to the No. 3 role in-season is possible. WR Caleb Douglas, Miami Dolphins Miami Dolphins third-round rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas is a dark horse candidate to start for his new team this year. After two unproductive seasons at Florida , he transferred to Texas Tech , where he turned in two 90-plus-target seasons before declaring for the 2026 NFL Draft. Among 30 Power Four wide receivers with at least 150 targets from 2024-25, Douglas ties for fifth in targets (189), ranks 16th in receptions (113), sixth in receiving yards (1,730), ties for 10th in receiving touchdowns (13), ranks 25th in target rate (20.6%) and YPRR (1.88), first in deep-target rate (27.5%), ties for 17th in missed tackles forced (18), ranks 12th in yards after the catch per reception (5.7) and 26th in first downs per route run (0.08). Respectably, Douglas earned a 72.4 PFF receiving grade during that span. Volatile stable metrics are present, creating a risk-reward profile. He stands 6-foot-3.5, 206 pounds, possessing 4.39-second 40-yard-dash speed. Securing the Dolphins’ X-receiver role is possible. records.new_body: 2026 NFL Team Futures: Odds, Predictions Best Bets Skip to content Betting 2026 NFL Team Futures: Odds, Predictions & Best Bets By Josh Shepardson | 2026-08-19T13:04:34-04:00 Aug 19, 2026 | View Larger Image 2026 NFL Team Futures: Best Bets Denver Broncos to win the AFC West (+225) Jacksonville Jaguars Over 3.5 Division Wins (+140) Get More Player & Team Picks in Warren Sharp's Futures Package Warren Sharp's Futures Package has compiled a 98-55 (64%) record on non-longshot props over the last seven years. A $100 bettor is up $7,944 following Warren's futures since this package was created. Click here to learn more about our 2026 Futures Package! Best 2026 Team Futures Bet: Denver Broncos To Win The AFC West The Denver Broncos not only won the AFC West last year, but they were also the AFC’s No. 1 seed after going 14-3. Now, they’re priced behind the Kansas City Chiefs and the Los Angeles Chargers to win the division this year. There are valid reasons to believe the Broncos could take a step back. First, Denver won an NFL-high 11 one-score games and lost only two last season, resulting in an .846 winning percentage in one-score games, the best in the NFL. Regression is almost certain in one-score games. They went only 1-6 in one-score games in 2024. As another recent example, the Chiefs were an NFL-best 11-0 in one-score games in 2024 before falling to 1-9 in 2025. The Broncos should finish with much closer to a .500 record in one-score games in 2026, even if the pendulum doesn’t swing as extremely as it did for the Chiefs from 2024 to 2025. The Broncos were third in the percentage of one-score wins as a total of their wins in 2025 at 78.6%. Of course, regression in one-score games would hurt much less if the Broncos played in fewer than 13 of them. There were 288 one-score games in 2025, which amounts to an average of nine per team. Denver also routinely dug itself holes in 2025. They trailed in 15 games last year, and, as Warren Sharp pointed out in this year’s Sharp Football Preview , no team that has won even 11 games ever trailed in 15 games that season, let alone winning 14 as the 2025 Broncos did. They were a remarkable 12-3 in those 15 contests. They can’t continue to live that way if they want to repeat as the AFC West champions, but they trailed in fewer games (13) in 2024 than in 2025. As with regression in one-score games, it will hurt less for their record in games they trail in 2026 if they trail in fewer games. Another step forward from Bo Nix could help them win by larger margins and trail less often this year. As a rookie in 2024, Nix was tied for 17th in Expected Points Added (EPA) per play among 36 qualified quarterbacks before nudging up to 11th out of 33 qualified quarterbacks in 2025. The club traded for Jaylen Waddle , giving Nix a meaningful upgrade in his pass-catching corps. Sean Payton also ceded play-calling duties to new offensive coordinator Davis Webb . Webb has been the team’s QBs coach for the previous three years and was the passing game coordinator in 2025. Fortunately for the Broncos, Payton remains in the mix to reprise play-calling duties if things don’t go smoothly for Webb. The Broncos also have a top-flight defense, and Vance Joseph is still pushing the buttons as the team’s defensive coordinator. In 2025, Denver was third in points allowed per drive (1.62), first in yards allowed per play (4.5), second in yards allowed per game (278.2), third in pressure rate, and tied for seventh in EPA allowed per play. As good as the Broncos were on defense, they left meat on the bone. Denver was only tied for 26th in turnovers forced last year (14). The club lost John Franklin-Myers and P.J. Locke in free agency, but it remains a high-end defense, with our staff ranking its front seven and secondary fourth and second, respectively. The Chiefs and Chargers have their own nits to pick, and the Broncos have most of the nucleus of last year’s AFC No. 1 seed returning and a needle-mover joining their receiving corps. The AFC West should be highly competitive, but getting +225 odds on the defending AFC West Champion is appealing. Jacksonville handled its business in the division last year, splitting the season series against the Houston Texans and sweeping both the Tennessee Titans and the Indianapolis Colts. The Texans once again have a stacked defense and can challenge the Jaguars. The Colts and Titans have catching up to do. Encouragingly for Jacksonville’s 2026 outlook, Trevor Lawrence played better as last season went on. Among 34 qualified quarterbacks from Week 1 through Week 7, Lawrence was 26th in EPA per play. The Jaguars had their bye in Week 8. From Week 9 through Week 18, Lawrence was fifth in EPA per play, sandwiched between Josh Allen in fourth and a tie between Jordan Love and Jared Goff for sixth. The Jaguars also traded for Jakobi Meyers before Week 9, and Parker Washington emerged as an extremely efficient pass-catching weapon down the stretch. There are tangible changes that help explain Lawrence’s surge in EPA, not to mention his possibly becoming more comfortable with what was a new offense to him. If Lawrence’s improvements stick, he could be the best quarterback in the division. Daniel Jones was the division’s highest-ranked quarterback in EPA per play last year, ranking sixth among qualified quarterbacks, followed by C.J. Stroud in a tie for 12th. Jones is returning from a torn right Achilles tendon suffered in early December after playing at a previously unseen level of high-quality play, and Stroud ended the year on a sour note by playing dreadfully in the playoffs. As for Cam Ward , he was dead last in EPA per play among 33 qualified quarterbacks last season. Beyond continuity on the coaching staff and quarterback play, the defense is also coming off an above-average season. Jacksonville was tied for eighth in yards allowed per play (5.0), fifth in points allowed per drive (1.74), fifth in explosive play rate allowed, 19th in pressure rate, tied for 29th in sack rate, and second in turnovers forced (31). The Jaguars will likely regress in turnovers forced, but they can also log more sacks if more of their pressures are converted to sacks, even if their pressure rate doesn’t improve. Circling back to offense and taking a larger view than at the quarterback, they were an above-average group. The Jaguars were ninth in points per drive (2.35), sixth in points per game (27.9), 12th in success rate (42.3%), and tied for 14th in EPA per play. Jacksonville has the coaching staff and personnel in place to be an above-average team and a contender to win the division again this year, and the lookahead lines are favorable for backing Jacksonville to go over 3.5 wins in the AFC South. The Jaguars are favored against the Texans in London in Week 6, the Colts in Jacksonville in Week 8, the Titans in Tennessee in Week 10, and the Titans in Jacksonville in Week 12. Moreover, the Jaguars have a seven-day rest advantage against the Colts in Week 8, coming off their Week 7 bye, and a 4-day rest disadvantage against the Titans in Week 10. Jacksonville is an underdog in Week 15 in Houston and in Week 18 in Indianapolis. They have a 1-day rest disadvantage against the Texans in Week 18. Ultimately, if the Jaguars win all of their divisional games they’re favored in, they’d go over the 3.5 wins line. It’s also encouraging that one of the games they’re underdogs in is in Week 18, as motivation is all over the map in the final week of the regular season. Even if the Jaguars failed to split with the Texans, they could go over the line by sweeping the Titans and Colts again, and splitting with Houston would give them wiggle room to drop one of the contests against their other two AFC South foes. Moore — Most Regular Season Receiving Yards (+8000) Colston Loveland — Over 1000 Receiving Yards (+200) Fantasy football projections, like those done by Rich Hribar , can be a guide to help identify overvalued or undervalued players in the current betting markets. Using our projections, I will identify a couple of players at each position who we are higher on than the current market. We will also look at some longshot bets on teams that could significantly alter their strategy from previous seasons. Get More Player & Team Picks in Warren Sharp's Futures Package Warren Sharp's Futures Package has compiled a 98-55 (64%) record on non-longshot props over the last seven years. A $100 bettor is up $7,944 following Warren's futures since this package was created. Click here to learn more about our 2026 Futures Package! D.J. Moore 2026 Over/Under Prediction D.J. Moore is coming off two lackluster seasons by his standards, but a new environment and the opportunity to play with Josh Allen may have created the perfect recipe for an excellent buy-low opportunity. Moore has been seen smiling throughout training camp as he enters 2026 in a dramatically different situation after being traded from Chicago to Buffalo. Instead of playing in an environment where something was clearly not right personally and in a Ben Johnson offense where his target share declined significantly, Moore now gets to catch passes from a former MVP quarterback while reuniting with Joe Brady , his former offensive coordinator in Carolina. The biggest reason to bet Moore’s over is simple: Allen is without a doubt the best quarterback Moore has ever had passing him the ball. Moore has spent most of his career dealing with inconsistent quarterback situations, yet he has still exceeded 1,000 receiving yards in four seasons. He enters his ninth season averaging more than 1,000 receiving yards per season. Moore is also a huge upgrade at the wide receiver position for Allen. The Bills have not produced a 1,000-yard-wide receiver in either of the previous two seasons since Stefon Diggs ’ departure, while their average target depth ranked last in the NFL in 2025. Moore doesn't need an unreasonable target share to beat his season-long receiving-yardage line, but he should command a target share over 20% given the receiver depth in Buffalo. The Bills entered the 2024 season with a new slogan: Everybody Eats. Sean McDermott tried to spin that into a positive after the Bills parted ways with Diggs. However, targets are earned. The “Everybody Eats” slogan was admitting to everyone what was glaringly obvious: There wasn’t an alpha target earner on the roster. In an interview, Ian Rapoport talked about Moore as a breakout candidate for the upcoming fantasy season, but fantasy gamers should be aware that “the Buffalo Bills like to spread the ball around.” Again, this is a mythical statement and is a byproduct of a lackluster receiving room. Diggs was a member of the Buffalo Bills from 2020 to 2023. In those four years, he led all NFL receivers in receptions, was second in targets, and had 28.0% of the Bills' total team targets over that span. Before last season, Moore had four consecutive seasons in which he had over 26% of his team’s targets. In 2021, Brady’s final season as the Carolina Panthers offensive coordinator, Moore had 28.3% of the team's targets and 40.2% of the team’s total air yards. In that season, Moore caught passes from Cam Newton , Sam Darnold , and PJ Walker and still exceeded 1,150 receiving yards. The projections in the Sharp Football Analysis Draft Kit are bullish on Moore joining the Bills. Our projections have Moore projected for 83 receptions and more than 1,100 receiving yards, well over the season-long yardage prop. One of the biggest risks of betting season-long overs is injury. Moore has played every game in the past five seasons and has played 15 or more games in all eight seasons to start his career. Moore has played through injury in the past, which helps give him the opportunity to continue to accumulate volume over the full season. The market may be overreacting to Moore’s 2025 season and overconfident that his decline is age-related. In addition to our projections supporting the over, in the Wide Receiver Trends article, Rich Hribar highlighted that when searching for wide receivers to exceed expectations, one of the more common hits comes from players changing situations, making Moore a solid bet this season. Loveland was selected in the top 10 of the 2025 NFL Draft and entered the league with an elite tight end profile and skill set. Loveland started his rookie season slowly as he missed part of training camp with an injury and played a part-time role in the Bears offense in the opening months of the season. He opened his rookie season with just 5 receptions and 54 yards in the opening five games while he was still establishing himself within Ben Johnson ‘s offense and managing an injury. Loveland’s role and production accelerated dramatically as the season progressed. He finished the regular season and playoffs with four consecutive double-digit target games, including a 15-target game in the Bears' playoff victory against the Packers. The late-season production provides a much better indication of what Loveland could look like with a full-time role throughout the entire season. Loveland shared the field with rookie wide receiver Luther Burden for 173 passing plays and generated more targets, air yards, and receiving yards than the hyped second-year receiver. Both Loveland and Burden are projected for increasing roles in Year 2. However, Loveland may still be overlooked. Loveland led the Bears in receiving yards despite only being on the field for 63.8% of the team's dropbacks. With the Bears trading D.J. Moore and not investing much capital into a replacement, there is a significant opportunity for Loveland to increase his target share in an ascending offense. In the final five weeks of the regular season, the Bears had multiple tight ends on the field on 56.9% of the offensive plays. The increase of 13 personnel benefited Loveland the most as he averaged 3.34 yards per route and had 32.4% of the team's targets with three tight ends on the field. Johnson recently did an interview in which he stated that he wants the 2026 Bears to be the highest-scoring offense ever . The Bears have the seventh-most difficult strength of schedule in 2026, after the ninth-easiest last season. Injuries to Coby Bryant and Kyler Gordon are concerning for a defense which is not particularly deep with talent in the secondary, which could force the Bears into more shootouts, boosting Loveland’s ceiling. The Sharp Football Analysis projections have Loveland projected for 90 receptions and 1,068 receiving yards, which is not unreasonable given his late-season production. In the final game of the regular season and two playoff games, Loveland was targeted on 43.3%, 31.3%, and 37.0% of his routes. That is unsustainable, but it indicates that Loveland can push for a 22-25% target share through an entire season. Including the playoffs, Loveland averaged 9.9 air yards per target, which led all tight ends in the league, and gained 20 or more yards on 21.4% of his receptions. The ability to operate deeper down the field and create explosives means that a relatively modest increase in targets can produce substantial increases in yardage. Another important component in Loveland’s ascent is Caleb Williams . Williams registered an off-target throw on 15.9% of his passes targeted at the rookie tight end last season. Entering his third season in the NFL and second season with Johnson, Williams appears more comfortable running the offense than a year ago. Even a slight improvement in accuracy benefits Loveland. Given the way his role expanded throughout 2025, the 2026 season could be the year Loveland goes from promising rookie to legitimate NFL receiving weapon who is mentioned in the same sentence as Brock Bowers and Trey McBride when discussing the league’s high-upside tight ends. latest report… Jeremiyah Love Ankle Injury: Analysis & Return Timeline Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love is expected to miss the rest of the preseason after suffering a high ankle sprain in the team’s preseason opener over the weekend. Following the game, head coach Mike LaFleur told reporters that Love “could have returned” following his injury, but with this new diagnosis, Love’s availability for Week 1 is in question. The third-overall pick played 23 snaps during the first half, and his 14 touches were by far the most by any first-round pick this weekend. What makes this even more peculiar is the rest of the Cardinals were sent to the showers following the team’s first drive, but Love remained on the field for another 13 snaps before exiting with his injury. The Cardinals will turn to Tyler Allgeier to take over the bulk of the reps for the rest of the preseason while Love is out, but it will be worth monitoring if LaFleur’s over-usage of Love this weekend will cost him regular season reps. Luther Burden Groin Injury: Analysis & Return Timeline Bears WR Luther Burden is expected to miss the rest of training camp after suffering a strained groin in practice last week. Burden is still expected to have a bigger role in the offense after posting 600 yards in his rookie season. Chicago traded D.J. Moore to the Bills in the offseason to open up more reps for Burden opposite Rome Odunze . Long-time Lion Kalif Raymond could see more playing time if Burden’s absence extends into the regular season. Caleb Williams is no stranger to spreading the ball around; the Bears had four different players with over 600 receiving yards in 2025. However, Burden did lead the team with 10.8 yards per target last year and hauled in over 78% of his targets as a rookie. Raymond had a career-low 5.6 ADOT in 2025 and caught just 24 passes in 15 games last year. Tucker Kraft Knee Injury: Analysis & Return Timeline Good news in Green Bay as tight end Tucker Kraft joined his teammates on the field for team drills on Sunday for the first time since he tore his ACL last year. Kraft posted over 700 receiving yards in 2024 and was on pace for his first 1,000-yard campaign last year before a Week 9 injury ended his season. Entering the final year of his rookie contract, Kraft remains hopeful he can get a contract extension done with the Packers before the start of the season, but he told reporters that he expects to play limited snaps in the first half of 2026 as he recovers. Complicating issues is backup Luke Musgrave ’s health. He remains on the PUP list after suffering a neck injury during the team’s offseason workouts. That means Josh Whyle could be in for a snap increase at least early in the season. Packers tight ends were only targeted on 19.5% of the team’s passes in 2025. Jonathan Greenard Pec Injury: Analysis & Return Timeline Eagles new EDGE Jonathan Greenard was a surprise addition to the team’s PUP list on the first day of training camp. Despite the team saying it was a minor injury, it seems Greenard might not be a sure thing for Week 1 after all. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio told reporters this week that Greenard has been participating in team meetings but is still “a few weeks away” from joining his team on the practice field. If Greenard remains on the PUP list at the end of training camp, he will be forced to miss the first four games of the regular season. Since Greenard still counts against the Eagles’ 90-man roster during camp, it remains questionable why they would make the move if this was strictly a preseason injury. If Greenard does miss time, Jalyx Hunt and Nolan Smith will have a larger role on the edge, and Arnold Ebiketie could see an increase in snaps after coming over from the Falcons in free agency. Greenard suffered through an injury-riddled 2025, but signed a huge contract with the Eagles after they traded for him during the draft. Greenard posted back-to-back 12-sack seasons, but recorded just 3 in 12 games last year. What do those designations mean? By Warren Sharp | 2026-08-17T12:14:39-04:00 Aug 17, 2026 | View Larger Image While fans get excited about individual player performances in the preseason, we often learn a lot more about offensive scheme changes heading into the new season. With tons of new coaches and offenses trending toward heavier looks, 2026 shapes up as a year of major changes across the NFL , and we saw that in the first full week of preseason action. Which NFL Offenses Changed the Most in the 2026 Preseason? If the Colts do struggle, a distinct possibility according to betting markets, managing Taylor's workload becomes more likely down the stretch. Taylor turns 27 this season, and his age introduces a layer of risk as he has only played 17 games in two of his first five seasons. Should Taylor miss any time or the Colts struggle, reaching the required number of carries to eclipse 1,225 yards will be difficult. This is not a bet questioning Taylor’s talent or ability. It is a bet on volume reduction from 2025, which is a difficult season to replicate. records.new_body: Should Ben Johnson Actually Want the Highest Scoring Offense? Skip to content Analysis Should Ben Johnson Actually Want the Highest Scoring Offense? By Warren Sharp | 2026-08-17T11:21:38-04:00 Aug 13, 2026 | View Larger Image Ben Johnson says he wants the highest-scoring offense in league history, but perhaps he shouldn't. Scoring the most points and winning the Super Bowl have not usually gone hand in hand. Get Warren's Book for $34.99 Order Book Is Ben Johnson Right to Want the Highest Scoring Offense in History? In a profile about him appearing in The Athletic , Ben Johnson said: “I want to have the highest-scoring offense ever, which happens to be the 2013 Denver Broncos. I know how many points per game they scored [37.9], and I want to surpass them. I want shutouts. I want blowouts.” While Johnson wants to win a Super Bowl, he said his goals are actually beyond winning a Super Bowl: “Our goal is to win the Super Bowl, but I want more than that. The moon is the Super Bowl, but we’re shooting beyond that, for the stars. And I want these players to feel that each and every single day they come in.” While I admire the bravado and coach speak of trying to “out-talk” the rest of the NFL, who have their sights set on (simply) winning a Super Bowl, the question becomes: Is this even a good thing to want? Many would think it’s harmless and just said in good fun. I disagree. If this is how Johnson plans to coach the Bears, I assume he will be trying to run up the score when he can. I assume that means he’s going to be keeping in his starters deep into games, even if they are blowouts. I assume he’s going to try to ramp up the tempo. These are things you would have top of mind for every game as you’re planning out strategy in the week leading up to kickoff, and would be constantly thinking about throughout each game. If that is the case, I have concerns about the long-term ramifications. Let’s back up. The #1 goal each year should be to win a Super Bowl. Anything beyond that is gravy. To win a Super Bowl, you need to win as many regular season games as possible. You MUST secure that first-round bye in the playoffs (of which there is only one in each conference). The 17-game season that is the modern-day NFL is a war of attrition. More than ever before, whichever teams emerge healthiest have a big advantage in the playoffs. When you have the opportunity to lead in a blowout by 17 points in the fourth quarter, the smart move is to slow down and guarantee that you win while keeping your starters healthy and fresh, so they have the best edge the following week. That could mean running the ball more, reducing pace, pulling certain starters or anything else, so long as you don’t do it too early and risk blowing a lead. What it doesn’t mean is to continue to play the final five minutes when up 17 points like you played the first five minutes when the score is 0-0 and you’re working aggressively to build an insurmountable lead. Having a rest advantage over your next opponent is helpful, and it’s backed by data because the inverse is true. I went back to 2010 for this next analysis. When a team is off an overtime game and their opponent is not, those teams the following week are: 201-266 (43.0%) outright 208-246-13 (45.8%) against the spread And when you fix it to exclude overtime teams off a bye or playing an opponent who is off a short-week game, it’s even more pronounced: 168-224 (42.4%) outright 165-212-12 (43.8%) against the spread These teams who had to play longer (more minutes) than their next opponent MASSIVELY underachieve compared to expectations. If having to play longer in a game (the definition of overtime) hurts a team the next week, the opposite can’t hurt. Building a lead to be able to pull starters late certainly should give an advantage the following week. And if the goal is winning games, the goal should be to build that lead and pull starters, not keep them in to run up the score by expending energy that’s not necessary. But now let’s zoom out and look at the bigger picture. How have the highest-scoring teams in NFL history done in the postseason? I again went back to 2010 to dig in. Ben Johnson is correct: The highest-scoring team was the Denver Broncos with 606 points. They didn’t win the Super Bowl. In fact, there have been 22 teams that scored at least 500 points during the regular season since 2010. None of them won the Super Bowl. 0-22. ZERO! Then I went and just looked at the top two highest-scoring offenses each year since 2010. Of the 32 teams (2 per year, 16 years), only ONE won the Super Bowl. The 2022 Chiefs, who scored the most points of the 2022 season but still didn’t crack 500, let alone 606, were the only team. I went back just to break down the five highest-scoring teams since 2010: 606 points – 2013 Denver Broncos; Beat Chargers & Patriots; Lost Super Bowl XLVIII to Seahawks, 43-8 565 points – 2018 Kansas City Chiefs; Beat Colts in Divisional Round; Lost AFC Championship to Patriots, 37-31 (OT) 564 points – 2024 Detroit Lions; Lost Divisional Round to Commanders, 45-31 560 points – 2011 Green Bay Packers; Lost Divisional Round to Giants, 37-20 557 points – 2012 New England Patriots; Beat Texans in Divisional Round; Lost AFC Championship to Ravens, 28-13 Of the five highest-scoring teams, only one even made it to the Super Bowl. The bottom line here is the highest-scoring teams likely have great offenses. Great offenses win games, make the playoffs, and have a chance from there. But aiming to set the record for the most points scored in an NFL season is a deeply flawed and completely unnecessary objective. There has been no superior benefit to scoring a ton of points in a season. The 22 teams with 500+ points in a season since 2010 have zero Super Bowl rings. The ultimate goal should still be to win a Super Bowl. If you need to score a ton of points to support a bad defense en route to winning a Super Bowl, then you do what you need to do. But you don’t run up the score for no reason and stress your starters in the fourth quarters of blowouts simply because you’re trying to set a scoring record. It won’t help you win your very next game, which is the only way you’re going to earn a first-round bye. Given the fact that the Texans are favorites to win the AFC South and are buoyed by an elite defense, Montgomery could be trusted to protect leads on a team projected for favorable game scripts. Before splitting the backfield with Jahmyr Gibbs , who is currently the highest-paid running back in the league, Montgomery handled more than 200 carries in each of his first five NFL seasons. Montgomery has proven he can handle a large workload throughout his entire career. Xavier Hutchinson finished 2025 second on the team in wide receiver routes, and Christian Kirk ran 21 routes per game when healthy, ahead of Day 2 picks Jayden Higgins and Jaylin Noel . DeMeco Ryans has shown time and time again he trusts his elite defense and veterans on offense, which favors Montgomery. Woody Marks had an unremarkable season as a rookie, averaging 3.6 yards per carry, which provides runway for Montgomery to handle as much of the rushing work as possible. Rich Hribar points out in his running back tiers that Montgomery is a schematic fit for Nick Caley ’s man/gap rush attack. The Texans ranked second in the league in man/gap run rate last year. Montgomery had a 50% success rate and led all running backs in EPA per rush on man/gap runs. The offensive line is a concern, but the Texans overhauled the five-man unit that ranked 32nd in ESPN’s Run Block Win Rate last season. Even if the line does not improve, this is a bet based on volume over efficiency. There are strong signals for a 200-250 carry season, and I would not be shocked if Montgomery is among the leaders in rush attempts, pushing 280 carries if he remains healthy. records.new_body: 2026 NFL Betting Outlook: The Most Wide-Open Season in Years Skip to content Betting 2026 NFL Betting Outlook: The Most Wide-Open Season in Years By Warren Sharp | 2026-08-03T12:26:23-04:00 Aug 3, 2026 | View Larger Image The following is an excerpt from Warren Sharp's 2026 Football Preview . In addition to Warren's deep, detailed write-up on all 32 NFL teams, each chapter features page after page of full-color charts, stats, and heatmaps. Click here for a full FREE chapter from the 2026 Football Preview . I almost didn’t want the 2025 season to end because of how tremendously successful it was from a betting perspective But now that 2025 is in the rearview mirror, one thing about 2026 is clear: It’s WIDE OPEN and should be a crazy year. Think about who participated in the last few Super Bowls and their preseason odds. 2023 : +600 Chiefs beat the +900 49ers 2024 : +1200 Eagles beat the +500 Chiefs Before that, we had the +1000 Chiefs in 2022 and the +1200 Rams in 2021 take home the Lombardi. The longest odds were 12:1, and most often they were pitted against a team that was 10:1 or less. But in 2025? The +6000 Seahawks beat the +8000 Patriots. And in 2025, we saw perennial powers completely fade from contention. The Perfect Time to Bet on the NFL I already have a massive head start on 2026 thanks to the months of research I put into my preview book to outwork the competition. I feel great about the 2026 season and want you to join us, so I’m offering you the ability to join us at a massive discount. Use coupon code: SHARP175 and get up to $175 off any season-long package at Sharp Football Analysis! Click Here to Learn More About Our All-Access Betting Package! NFL Parity Over the five years from 2020 through 2024, the top-nine winningest teams, those with the best record, were the Chiefs, Bills, Packers, Ravens, Eagles, Bucs, Steelers, Cowboys, and Vikings. Last year, the Chiefs, Ravens, Bucs, Cowboys, and Vikings didn’t make the playoffs. Not only that, NONE of them even had a winning record in 2025. The Packers, Eagles, and Steelers didn’t win a playoff game. To sum it up: Five of the nine winningest teams over the prior half-decade had losing records in 2025, and eight of nine didn’t win a single playoff game. The only team that did win a playoff game was the Bills, who were the #2 most winningest team the prior five years. They wound up as a six-seed in the AFC and won exactly one playoff game, a Wild Card victory over the Jaguars, which they very easily could have lost. That’s ONE total playoff win among the nine winningest teams the prior five seasons. Absolutely remarkable. And in 2026, it seems like things are picking up where they left off in 2025. Some of the very best teams entering 2026 feel vulnerable. And those top-nine teams from the prior five years? Massive changes at the top for almost all of them. The best teams and their records since 2020 (pre-2025): 1. Chiefs (66-18) – replaced their offensive coordinator 2. Bills (61-22) – fired their head coach 3. Packers (54-30) – hired a new defensive coordinator 3. Ravens (54-30) – fired their head coach 5. Eagles (52-31-1) – fired their offensive coordinator 6. Bucs (51-33) – fired their offensive coordinator 7. Steelers (50-33-1) – hired a new head coach 8. Cowboys (49-35) – fired their defensive coordinator 8. Vikings (49-35) – no changes to top coaches The top of the 2026 landscape feels more open than ever, and that’s reflected in the odds. As we sit right now, there are 14 teams with odds of 20:1 or better to win the Super Bowl : Rams, Ravens, Bills, Seahawks, Chiefs, Eagles, Patriots, Chargers, Packers, Texans, Lions, 49ers, Broncos, and Bengals. Last year at this time, there were only five! Chiefs, Eagles, Bills, Ravens, and Lions. That is an amazing change in just one year. From five clear favorites in 2025 to 14 in 2026. Unprecedented Changes for the NFL in 2026 Uncertainty and change are the themes of the offseason. We have 10 new head coaches, 21 new offensive coordinators, and 16 new defensive coordinators. In a league with only 32 teams, we’re saying one-third have a new head coach, two-thirds have a new offensive coordinator, and half have a new defensive coordinator. That’s 47 new coaches at those positions overall. That’s the most turnover in coaching we’ve seen in years. Personally, I love it. I love it as a fan of progress and pivoting away from what isn’t delivering results. And I love it as a bettor, because with uncertainty comes opportunity. Think of it this way: pretend that every head coach, offensive coordinator, and defensive coordinator was entering their 10th straight season with the same team. The same 32 quarterbacks were starting for the 10th straight season, and the other 21 starters on offense and defense were unchanged as well. And pretend that no players ever were injured during the season. If that were the case, the sportsbooks would be pretty dialed into power ratings, spreads, player props, and more for the 2026 season. We, too, as bettors, would be dialed in. But we don’t initiate; they do. They set the line, and then we react. If their lines were so accurate because there were no unknowns, we would have no opportunities to find value, and thus, betting would be a true coin flip. Something done for pure entertainment, rather than because there is actually an edge and a way to generate profit. Fortunately, that’s not what we’re walking into in 2026. We’re walking into massive change from the coaching ranks, the likes of which we haven’t seen in recent memory. We’re walking into massive uncertainty at the top of the ranks among which teams will have the most success this year, the likes of which we haven’t seen in recent memory. This is a PERFECT time to be betting on the NFL if you actually are looking to generate profit, rather than flip coins for entertainment. This is when I’ve historically seen the most success, so I can’t wait to see how things unfold this season. In my 2026 NFL Preview , I shared predictions and thoughts on all 32 teams, their 32 quarterbacks, and their 32 play-callers, along with how I think their season will go. The edges come from understanding all 32 teams. This process simply works and has produced incredible results for readers and for me, personally, and I pass them along to clients: NFL Futures: 98-55 (64%) over seven years and produced a profit of +79.44 positions, meaning a $100 bettor is up $7,944 following them. In the last two years, a $100 bettor is up $3,144 on our futures. And I feel even more confident heading into 2026 than I did heading into 2025. Not only does this extensive research for the book pay off in season-long futures, but also immediately out of the gates heading into Week 1. Last year, we came out in Week 1 with a 33-23 (59%) record for +6.29 units and produced profit in 11 of the first 12 weeks of the season. In 2024, we came out of Week 1 with a 23-12 (65.7%) record for +8.14 units and produced profit in 8 of the first 9 weeks of the season. And the impact extends all season long. Last year, for the first time in my history, we introduced my “Best Bet of the Week.” Take a look at the results: ► 11-0 (100%) on 1.25+ unit bets ► 17-3 (85%) on our best bet of the week ► 19 out of 22 winning weeks (86%) A $100 bettor finished up $14,154 using my NFL service in 2025. In 2024, the results were just as record-breaking, as a $100 bettor finished up $15,636. Entering 2026, I’ve now produced profit in 19 of 20 seasons running Sharp Football Analysis. To reiterate some notes from that article that relate to passing production near the end zone since 2010: 67.1% of all passing touchdowns come from inside the red zone. In 2025, that rate was 69.1%. 43.8% of all passing touchdowns scored overall come from inside of the 10-yard line. In 2025, that rate was at 44.0%. 22.7% of all passing touchdowns scored overall come from inside the 5-yard line. In 2025, that rate was 23.8%. Over the past decade, a target from the 19-yard line has been worth 1.8 fantasy points on average. A target from the 10-yard line jumps up to 2.2 points on average. A target from the 5-yard line climbs to 2.8 points on average. A target in the actual end zone is worth 3.0 points on average. You get the drift. The closer you get to the end zone, the more valuable the opportunity is for fantasy points. records.new_body: Why the Seahawks Could Miss the Playoffs in 2026 Skip to content Betting Why the Seahawks Could Miss the Playoffs in 2026 By Warren Sharp | 2026-08-03T09:44:53-04:00 Aug 3, 2026 | View Larger Image It appears there is an infinite-money glitch many NFL fans are not taking advantage of, at least based on my recent appearance on The Herd with Colin Cowherd. At the very end of my 20-minute interview, when asked about the Seahawks, I expressed the possibility that the defending Super Bowl Champions are not a sure-fire, double-digit win team who can sleepwalk their way to the playoffs. I shared the possibility that a world exists in which Seattle is a fringe playoff team in 2026, a team that might make the playoffs but not easily and as a Wild Card team. The Seahawks currently have a 67% chance to make the playoffs according to the odds. By the reaction to my thoughts shared on the show, you would have assumed Seattle’s odds to make the playoffs were 99%. The current public consensus seems to be the defending Super Bowl Champions are a certainty to make the playoffs, and any option which expresses the possibility they find themselves fighting to punch their ticket in the final weeks of the season is unfounded. I don’t see it that way. While I’m not betting on Seattle to miss the playoffs, there are several reasons to believe the Seahawks could regress from their 14-3 record in 2026. Get Warren's Book for $34.99 Order Book Life After Klint Kubiak: Can the Offense Repeat? Let’s begin with the loss of OC Klint Kubiak . Kubiak entered the picture in 2025 and massively overhauled the way the offense operated. He turned it into something special enough to see the success it did. Let’s examine some of the changes he made in just one offseason, and compare the Seahawks offense in 2024 to Kubiak’s offense in 2025: 2024: #3 most 3+ WR sets 2025: #28 most 3+ WR sets They were OUTSTANDING out of 12 personnel, ranking #1 in yards per play. 2024: #28 most play action 2025: #8 most play action They were OUTSTANDING with play action, ranking #1 in yards per attempt. 2024: #25 most pre-snap motion 2025: #14 most pre-snap motion They were OUTSTANDING with pre-snap motion, ranking #6 in yards per play. These changes by Kubiak helped Seattle improve from #23 in EPA on first down in 2024 to #7 in 2025. And from #18 in yards per play in 2024 to #3 in 2025. That improvement in first-down efficiency allowed them to catch teams off guard early in games, jump out to leads, and outscore them by the #1 highest first-quarter margin in the NFL. They ranked #4 in first-quarter points, #7 in second-quarter points, and #2 in third-quarter points. Seattle outscored opponents by 55 points in the first quarter, #1 in the NFL, and by 118 points in the first half, #2. Through three quarters, their cumulative point margin was +183, the best in football. It is entirely reasonable to believe that a team whose offensive play-caller, the man who overhauled the offense and produced the #3 highest scoring offense in the NFL, would take some type of step backward after he left to be a head coach. Let’s keep in mind, the 2024 Seahawks, with many of the same players as 2025, scored a below-average 22.1 points per game (#18 in the NFL). The Run Game Concern And then there is the next biggest change for Seattle: their running game. Seattle had the #1 highest run rate in the NFL last year. They lost their RB1 this offseason when Kenneth Walker III signed with the Chiefs. Walker wasn’t just the RB1 for the Seahawks. He was their Super Bowl MVP, recording 161 scrimmage yards against the Patriots. His heir apparent, Zach Charbonnet , tore his ACL in the Divisional Round and will certainly miss time in 2026. Seattle now will turn to RB3 from 2025, George Holani , and first-round rookie Jadarian Price . Price is dynamic and talented, but his fumble rate ranked #3 highest in this RB class. He recorded the #2 worst pass protection grade of any RB in this class, and earned just a 9.9% target rate on routes, the #2 lowest in this class. He had just 15 total receptions in college. Until Charbonnet returns (and even after to a degree), this RB room has massive question marks as compared to 2025. On non-Walker runs last season, Seahawks RBs collectively ranked: #25 in yards per carry (3.9) #25 in explosive run rate (5.5%) #28 in stuff rate (22%) Subtracting Kubiak and Walker, with Charbonnet likely to miss the start of the season, is certainly a problem for a team that made so many improvements offensively in 2025, not simply by “playing better,” but thanks to all the tweaks made by the OC and by relying on the run game at the #1 highest rate in the NFL. Health Luck, One-Score Luck & Schedule Difficulty Seattle also had the good fortune last season of fielding the #3 healthiest roster in the NFL and delivering the #7 best win-rate in one-score games. While good teams win close games, close game variance can strike even the best teams, and certainly there is no way to know now whether Seattle will be a top three healthiest team by the end of the 2026 season. Lastly, I’ll just mention one caveat as it relates to one of the best defenses in the NFL, if not the single best, along with one of the best defensive coaches in the NFL, if not the single best. Over the entire regular season, these are the only healthy quarterbacks Seattle beat by more than one score (with the caveat that Jayden Daniels was not 100% entering the game he played and left the game with an injury): Week 2: Aaron Rodgers Week 3: Spencer Rattler Week 10: Jacoby Brissett Week 13: Max Brosmer Week 14: Kirk Cousins Week 17: Bryce Young Week 18: Brock Purdy With the exception of Brock Purdy ’s 49ers (13-3 win), the rest of this list that Seattle dispatched by more than one score was severely questionable. Don’t forget that in Week 15, Seattle barely beat 44-year-old Philip Rivers in his first NFL game played since retiring in 2020, winning by two points. The point is not to discredit Seattle’s obviously elite defense. It’s just to provide context to who they played and beat, and that the 2026 schedule of opposing QBs is not projected to be nearly as bad as it was in 2025. By my metrics, I project Seattle’s defense to play the #3 toughest schedule of opposing QBs and the #1 toughest overall schedule of offenses. And they’ll need to do so despite the losses of starters S Coby Bryant , CB Tariq Woolen , and EDGE Boye Mafe . None of these individual concerns are enough to say the Seahawks will struggle this season. Collectively, however, they present a reasonable case to imagine that Seattle might not assuredly win double-digit games and stamp a playoff ticket before the season has even started, which it seems like most Seahawks fans as well as NFL fans league-wide generally expect. Seattle still has an elite defense with an elite defensive coach, along with a quarterback, offensive line, and receiving corps that led them to 14 wins and a Super Bowl in 2025. But every year presents new problems to solve, new injuries to overcome, and it remains to be seen exactly how successful the Seahawks will be in 2026. While I don’t expect them to miss the playoffs, it’s more than reasonable to see a path in which they are battling for a Wild Card berth late in the season with many other fringe playoff teams. records.new_body: 2026 College Football Preview: Group of Six Conference Betting Subscribe Sign in 2026 College Football Preview: Group of Six Conference Betting A championship bet and at least one win total for each of the PAC-12, Mountain West, Sun Belt, American, MAC, and Conference USA THE WINDOW Aug 19, 2026 ∙ Paid 9 7 Share Subscribe Maybe the goal isn’t to get blown out by a Big Ten or SEC team, per se, but it is kind of a bummer that, nine times out of ten, that ends up being the case for the de facto champion of the smaller conferences. Last year, Tulane and James Madison both had a chance for a College Football Playoff stunner, but they trailed by a combined 51-9 at halftime to Ole Miss and Oregon, respectively. That’s not to besmirch the now “Group of Six” (with the reemergence of the PAC-12), but those results, and the wider dispersion of teams, flattened across six conferences, doesn’t help the cause for the small schools to get a second CFP participant going forward. Instead of two of the five (40%) G5 champions getting a playoff spot, it looks like just one-of-six (16.6%) will earn the honor. Fundamentally, it’s getting harder to make the Playoff, so, more than ever, the G6 teams need to focus on just winning their own league as the primary goal. What’s fun, is that accomplishment isn’t nearly the priority in the Power-4 — where in some cases, the powers that be seem content with abolishing conference title games entirely. Plus, with fewer teams per G6 conference, you get a more earnest depiction of who deserves to make the championship game, even to the point where the new PAC-12 is vibing out with what’s being called a “flex” week in Week 13. More fun: Whether we’re talking about futures, or game-to-game, the winning tickets cash the same as in the P4, and if we happen to stumble into undervalued or overvalued teams, the market tends to take a little longer to react. Average team ratings / SOS The Group of Six are in their own battle for a College Football Playoff spot, and with the addition of the new PAC-12, it’s important to understand the quality hierarchy among the second tier of college football. Sure enough, the PAC-12 plucked enough good teams from the Mountain West for their roster to have the best average rating, but it’s still below-average (50/100) nationally. PAC-12 teams play enough strong teams in the non-conference that there isn’t a huge downgrade for strength of schedule, unlike the other five leagues, whose general weakness, willingness to play FCS teams, and avoidance of Power-4 teams all adds up to a major downgrade relative to their season win totals. American Conference Odds from Bet365 No prohibitive favorite? THAT’s what we’re talking about! How much of Navy’s recent offensive success is predicated on the Midshipmen’s hybrid triple-option system, and what credit do graduated stars — Blake Horvath and Eli Heidenreich — get for a unit that led to a 21-5 record the last two seasons? UTSA gets the nod as No. 2, because Jeff Traylor hasn’t taken a bigger job, bringing back Owen McCown and a handful of key pieces to an electric offense (particularly at home). Estimated Market Rating Team ratings in grey for those without a Week 0/1 FBS matchup Many American Conference teams are opening the season with a cupcake, and almost none have a “Game of the Year” lookahead line to cross-reference with in order to estimate their rating in the betting market, starting with Navy . That said, how much more valuable is the knowledge that South Florida is a 12.5-point favorite at home to Florida International in Week 1? Maybe marginally more than North Texas’ status as 40-point underdog to Indiana. 🙄 The American is dotted with last year’s contenders — USF, Memphis, Tulane, North Texas — who’ve seen star head coaches leave for Power-4 schools (three in the SEC, and Oklahoma State). Brian Hartline is the most interesting replacement, coming over as a recruiting maven from Ohio State to South Florida . He’ll have to show that skillset as the Bulls are 113th nationally in returning production. His coaching hire acumen is in question after giving Tim Beck the offensive coordinator job. We’re definitely guessing on Army , a 6-6 team last season that played almost exclusively painfully close games, but the schedule is soft enough to warrant the juice on the over 7.5 wins. You can drown in the hopeful buzz surrounding teams with their head coach coming into his second full season: East Carolina , Florida Atlantic, and Tulsa. The Pirates have too much turnover to bank on eight wins. Possibly weird take — Florida Atlantic (5.5, -160) should get to six wins, but in doing so, will win as an underdog enough times to make it more worth our while to bet on the Owls from a game-to-game perspective. Caden Veltkamp had shoulder surgery to fix what ailed him last year in Zach Kittley’s second season, and the Owls’ boast the conference’s highest returning production rate with interesting transfers. FAU is an intriguing long-shot play, if everything comes together. The problem is, so is Tulsa , with their own second-year head coach, Tre Lamb, returning the second-most production. Oh, and K.C. Keeler’s also going into his second season, but there’s less buzz around Temple because the quarterback position isn’t settled in the same way. OH… AND… Scott Abell’s second season at Rice will at least have Jacurri Brown (Miami, UCF) operating a run-heavy offense that got the Owls to a Bowl game last year, but not much else. That there MIGHT be three teams worse than Rice this year, just shows the drop-off in the American. UAB is getting an automatic upgrade from Trent Dilfer, it’s just a matter of how much, but the super-low win totals down here will be decided by who wins a quasi-sub-tournament that includes a disaster of a program, Charlotte . out by a Big Ten or SEC team, per se, but it is kind of a bummer that, nine times out of ten, that ends up being the case for the de facto champion of the smaller conferences. Last year, Tulane and James Madison both had a chance for a College Football Playoff stunner, but they trailed by a combined 51-9 at halftime to Ole Miss and Oregon, respectively. That\u2019s not to besmirch the now \u201CGroup of Six\u201D (with the reemergence of the PAC-12), but those results, and the wider dispersion of teams, flattened across six conferences, doesn\u2019t help the cause for the small schools to get a second CFP participant going forward. Instead of two of the five (40%) G5 champions getting a playoff spot, it looks like just one-of-six (16.6%) will earn the honor. Fundamentally, it\u2019s getting harder to make the Playoff, so, more than ever, the G6 teams need to focus on just winning their own league as the primary goal. What\u2019s fun, is that accomplishment isn\u2019t nearly the priority in the Power-4 \u2014 where in some cases, the powers that be seem content with abolishing conference title games entirely. Plus, with fewer teams per G6 conference, you get a more earnest depiction of who deserves to make the championship game, even to the point where the new PAC-12 is vibing out with what\u2019s being called a \u201Cflex\u201D week in Week 13. More fun: Whether we\u2019re talking about futures, or game-to-game, the winning tickets cash the same as in the P4, and if we happen to stumble into undervalued or overvalued teams, the market tends to take a little longer to react. Average team ratings / SOS The Group of Six are in their own battle for a College Football Playoff spot, and with the addition of the new PAC-12, it\u2019s important to understand the quality hierarchy among the second tier of college football. Sure enough, the PAC-12 plucked enough good teams from the Mountain West for their roster to have the best average rating, but it\u2019s still below-average (50/100) nationally. PAC-12 teams play enough strong teams in the non-conference that there isn\u2019t a huge downgrade for strength of schedule, unlike the other five leagues, whose general weakness, willingness to play FCS teams, and avoidance of Power-4 teams all adds up to a major downgrade relative to their season win totals. American Conference Odds from Bet365 No prohibitive favorite? THAT\u2019s what we\u2019re talking about! How much of Navy\u2019s recent offensive success is predicated on the Midshipmen\u2019s hybrid triple-option system, and what credit do graduated stars \u2014 Blake Horvath and Eli Heidenreich \u2014 get for a unit that led to a 21-5 record the last two seasons? UTSA gets the nod as No. 2, because Jeff Traylor hasn\u2019t taken a bigger job, bringing back Owen McCown and a handful of key pieces to an electric offense (particularly at home). Estimated Market Rating Team ratings in grey for those without a Week 0/1 FBS matchup Many American Conference teams are opening the season with a cupcake, and almost none have a \u201CGame of the Year\u201D lookahead line to cross-reference with in order to estimate their rating in the betting market, starting with Navy . That said, how much more valuable is the knowledge that South Florida is a 12.5-point favorite at home to Florida International in Week 1? Maybe marginally more than North Texas\u2019 status as 40-point underdog to Indiana. \uD83D\uDE44 The American is dotted with last year\u2019s contenders \u2014 USF, Memphis, Tulane, North Texas \u2014 who\u2019ve seen star head coaches leave for Power-4 schools (three in the SEC, and Oklahoma State). Brian Hartline is the most interesting replacement, coming over as a recruiting maven from Ohio State to South Florida . He\u2019ll have to show that skillset as the Bulls are 113th nationally in returning production. His coaching hire acumen is in question after giving Tim Beck the offensive coordinator job. We\u2019re definitely guessing on Army , a 6-6 team last season that played almost exclusively painfully close games, but the schedule is soft enough to warrant the juice on the over 7.5 wins. You can drown in the hopeful buzz surrounding teams with their head coach coming into his second full season: East Carolina , Florida Atlantic, and Tulsa. The Pirates have too much turnover to bank on eight wins. Possibly weird take \u2014 Florida Atlantic (5.5, -160) should get to six wins, but in doing so, will win as an underdog enough times to make it more worth our while to bet on the Owls from a game-to-game perspective. Caden Veltkamp had shoulder surgery to fix what ailed him last year in Zach Kittley\u2019s second season, and the Owls\u2019 boast the conference\u2019s highest returning production rate with interesting transfers. FAU is an intriguing long-shot play, if everything comes together. The problem is, so is Tulsa , with their own second-year head coach, Tre Lamb, returning the second-most production. Oh, and K.C. Keeler\u2019s also going into his second season, but there\u2019s less buzz around Temple because the quarterback position isn\u2019t settled in the same way. OH\u2026 AND\u2026 Scott Abell\u2019s second season at Rice will at least have Jacurri Brown (Miami, UCF) operating a run-heavy offense that got the Owls to a Bowl game last year, but not much else. That there MIGHT be three teams worse than Rice this year, just shows the drop-off in the American. UAB is getting an automatic upgrade from Trent Dilfer, it\u2019s just a matter of how much, but the super-low win totals down here will be decided by who wins a quasi-sub-tournament that includes a disaster of a program, Charlotte . Sports asked for my take on the “Game of the Year” lookahead lines that are widely available on either DraftKings or FanDuel (and in some cases, both). So, we’ve got 12 bets to make for games played on Week 2 through 13: YAHOO!: CFB GOTY BETTING As it pertains to the fundamentals of betting, the root goal is to have a ticket that beats the market’s close — whether that’s for a game a few weeks from now, or late in the season. That would give us a better chance to win than the 53-57% rate we expect during the week of the game, because the more points we beat the market by, the better chance our ticket has of winning. Last year, we beat the market on nine of the 14 games in this article, and, in some cases, by a comically-large margin. But, football is football, so, while still profitable, the tickets themselves only went 7-6. With any luck, we should replicate that value in putting a dozen tickets in pocket now, while getting a fairer shake with commensurate results.
