records.new_body: 2026 College Football Preview: Betting the ACC Subscribe Sign in 2026 College Football Preview: Betting the ACC Three season win total bets, a GOTY to get now, and what’s old is new again with a title long shot? THE WINDOW Aug 13, 2026 ∙ Paid 8 7 Share Subscribe In the same way that, if you don’t play the lottery, you can’t win it, you can’t take advantage of an unusual, unpredictable, unprecedented turn of events, if you don’t take a swing on something like we did with Duke to win the ACC last year at 25-to-1. Given all that needed to happen to get that bet home, winning it was a fluke. WHO CARES? Duke facing, and beating, Virginia was so wonky, that the ACC felt compelled to change the tiebreaker rules for who makes the conference championship game (that’s been moved earlier on Championship Saturday to no longer compete with the Big Ten title game for eyeballs), but it’s too late — the winnings have long been in the accounts. It does mean that prohibitive, odds-on favorite, Miami, has an even better chance of getting to Charlotte THIS year. Plus, Duke versus Virginia last year, only further supports the idea that it’s the Hurricanes, and then a large gap between the rest of a league, whose teams carry an average estimated market rating (EMR) shy of 60, and whose strength of schedule only accounts for an 8% boost, on average. Conference odds Odds via Bet365 Miami is the odds-on favorite, since the only conceptually losable game comes outside of league-play, at Notre Dame, and the Canes also miss SMU and Louisville — the two teams they lost to last year — in the regular season. Plus, Mario Cristobal plundered the defending-champion Blue Devils, taking Darian Mensah and his favorite target Cooper Barkate. From there, it’s a wide selection of those who can either make an earnest leap up to clear-cut second-best ACC team, or do it with smoke-and-mirrors — a particularly soft slate as part of an imbalanced schedule. Of course, last year, Clemson was supposed to be the team that was fait accompli to make the title game (independent of their own tough non-conference matchups, vs. LSU, and at South Carolina), but the Tigers flopped hard. Either way, with so many candidates for the No. 2 slot, you can’t just rely on a cozy schedule, instead, needing a team also capable of making a leap, and priced in a way that suggests value. Team Rating Nationally From North Carolina ’s shoulder shrug-inducing nationally average rating of 50, up to SMU , there are 13 teams in the ACC within 13(.2) points of each other in betting lines. The Mustangs bring back Kevin Jennings for a third season, which might as well be 12 seasons in modern “college years.” However, while people are quick to point so many teams who blew various golden opportunities by getting upset, there’s not nearly enough shade being thrown at Rhett Lashlee, who lost at Cal (who’d just fired Justin Wilcox) in the regular season finale, missing out on the ACC title game (and a chance for back-to-back playoff berths). Lashlee’s dialled-back the transfer numbers, but a coordinator change interrupts some of the continuity we’d cite with Jennings. Even if you liked Jennings to realize the dream of SMU’s Heisman campaign for him, early-season trips to Tallahassee and Louisville could take him off the radar, and a late-season matchup with Notre Dame probably derail those hopes. After an electric bowl performance to cap the 2023 season, Miller Moss underwhelmed when given the keys to the USC offense in 2024, and Jeff Brohm couldn’t get much more out of Moss at Louisville last season. Maybe he’ll have more success with Ohio State transfer Lincoln Kienholz (who was edged by Julian Sayin for the starting job last year) and a rebuilt offensive line. A pair of good tailbacks named Brown (Isaac and Keyjuan) should help, while also taking advantage of the threat Kienholz brings with his legs as well. The issue for a possible win-total bet, is that the Cardinals face many of the ACC teams that we think may be underrated. Strangely, given the expected turnover from hiring James Franklin, Virginia Tech actually has the most returning production in the ACC (4th nationally), and as his want, Franklin’s non-conference schedule is pretty cozy, with just Maryland any kind of a threat. Franklin’s not a quick-turnaround artist though, finishing 6-6 in each of his first seasons at Vanderbilt and Penn State. The Hokies will likely have a conservative approach on offense, as OC Ty Howle and QB Ethan Grunkemeyer come with Franklin from PSU, which means Va-Tech likely wins the games they’re supposed to, and lose those they’re expected to. Your guess is as good as mine with what to expect from Florida State , as Mike Norvell could easily be fired before the end of the season, but if he’s right about Ashton Daniels (getting the most out of the quarterback even without the departed Gus Malzahn) maybe the Seminoles are worthy of a modest bump in market rating from 62 at the end of last season, to starting this season at 65. That’s not enough to make FSU an auto-fade, but there’s no reason to fully support the Noles with any kind of a futures play, either. It’s entirely possible that we’re betting against Virginia against the spread in every game this season. The market didn’t go crazy about the Cavaliers’ run to the conference title game last season (as the 31st-rated team by ESPN’s SP+), pushing Virginia up into the 60s. However, regression should be coming for a team that was built through the portal, hit with so many one-year players (including quarterback Chandler Morris), and are now trying to do it again. Virginia pulled wins out of the fire during a 4-game stretch (three in OT, 2-point win vs. Washington State). Being rated the same way heading into this season is making a lot of assumptions about a new portal class that features the well-travelled Beau Pribula, but the schedule looks pretty easy, as it’s actually led to a 10% rating downgrade for an ACC team with a 7.5-win total. With a modest increase from 57 to 61 in power rating for Pittsburgh , the market seems to think Pat Narduzzi found something with Mason Heintschel — a freshman who took over in October and lit up teams (FSU, Syracuse, Boston College, NC State, Stanford) at something of a low point. However, once the competition got more difficult (Notre Dame, Georgia Tech, Miami, East Carolina), it wasn’t as easy. Here’s the market rating for NC State at the end of the last two seasons, and the start of this coming season: 2024: 60/100 2025: 60/100 2026: 60/100 13 years of Dave Doeren, and we have a pretty good idea of what level the Wolfpack are expected to play at. There are two reasons to expect something more in Raleigh: CJ Bailey — arguably the best returning quarterback in the ACC (protected by stud left tackle transfer Jimarion McCrimon from ECU) A schedule without Miami, Clemson, SMU, and with Louisville at home With two winnable road games, as underdogs, in the first three weeks, backing the ‘Pack will be done early, and if that goes well, potentially often. Our premise for taking the flier on Duke last year, was that Manny Diaz was taking a buttoned-up defense from 2024 and using Mensah to even-out the balance with a better offense. Instead, while the offense was very good, the defense stunk. Walker Eget comes from San Jose State to replace Mensah, and he’s still got Nate Sheppard to give the ball to, but an internal succession plan on defense will have to be the thing that leads to the balance Diaz craves. A small downgrade in market rating seems appropriate, ahead of a wait-and-see approach. Five wins seems easy, but a sixth will have to come as a road underdog, and if that’s in the finale, it’s counter to a position we’ll have on another team. Georgia Tech made our outlier teams article because of the drop in their rating, but the Yellow Jackets are still decent favorite in the opener with Colorado, have an exciting duo in Alberto Mendoza and Justice Haynes in the backfield, and head coach Brent Key — the upset-maker. There’s just too many holes elsewhere, including two departed coordinators, to buy Tech’s over. Instead, we’ll look for good spots to back them as a ‘dog throughout the season. At the bottom the conference, North Carolina ’s rated as a perfectly-average team nationally, which is a bad thing for the Bill Belichick era, especially after the first lap of roster-building went so poorly that the Tar Heels are 103rd in returning production. GM Michael Lombardi was a literal joke this summer, the hiring of Bobby Petrino wreaks of cronyism, and tabbing Billy Edwards Jr. as the starting quarterback, is, at best, uninspiring. Oh, and the best thing about the Heels last season was Steve Belichick’s defense, but he’s on a medical leave away from the team. Unfortunately, everyone knows this, so outside of beating the market to TCU -6.5 in the season-opener, before it moved to -7.5, there’s no value in fading UNC. At least season-long. It feels a lot better at Stanford , but their rating is “good” enough that the only way to bet on the Cardinal is to fade them, except the market’s moved their way in Week 0 against Hawaii, indicating some bullishness on the Andrew Luck era — with Kavita Pritchard as head coach, (former Seahawks’) DC Kris Richard, and past Michigan starting quarterback Davis Warren in place. Lastly, they used to let Bill O’Brien coach an NFL team, and now he can’t sniff .500 in the ACC with Boston College . Capable quarterbacks — Thomas Castellanos and Dylan Lonergan — have gone away from the program. Instead, O’Brien looks to the FCS for a quarterback. Plus, for all the up-and-coming defensive minds looking for an ACC gig, O’Brien’s tabbed 62-year-old Ted Roof, who hasn’t coached a good defense in a decade-plus. season win total bets, a GOTY to get now, and what\u2019s old is new again with a title long shot?\",\"body_html\":\" Subscribe now In the same way that, if you don\u2019t play the lottery, you can\u2019t win it, you can\u2019t take advantage of an unusual, unpredictable, unprecedented turn of events, if you don\u2019t take a swing on something like we did with Duke to win the ACC last year at 25-to-1. Given all that needed to happen to get that bet home, winning it was a fluke. WHO CARES? Duke facing, and beating, Virginia was so wonky, that the ACC felt compelled to change the tiebreaker rules for who makes the conference championship game (that\u2019s been moved earlier on Championship Saturday to no longer compete with the Big Ten title game for eyeballs), but it\u2019s too late \u2014 the winnings have long been in the accounts. It does mean that prohibitive, odds-on favorite, Miami, has an even better chance of getting to Charlotte THIS year. Plus, Duke versus Virginia last year, only further supports the idea that it\u2019s the Hurricanes, and then a large gap between the rest of a league, whose teams carry an average estimated market rating (EMR) shy of 60, and whose strength of schedule only accounts for an 8% boost, on average. Conference odds Odds via Bet365 Miami is the odds-on favorite, since the only conceptually losable game comes outside of league-play, at Notre Dame, and the Canes also miss SMU and Louisville \u2014 the two teams they lost to last year \u2014 in the regular season. Plus, Mario Cristobal plundered the defending-champion Blue Devils, taking Darian Mensah and his favorite target Cooper Barkate. From there, it\u2019s a wide selection of those who can either make an earnest leap up to clear-cut second-best ACC team, or do it with smoke-and-mirrors \u2014 a particularly soft slate as part of an imbalanced schedule. Of course, last year, Clemson was supposed to be the team that was fait accompli to make the title game (independent of their own tough non-conference matchups, vs. LSU, and at South Carolina), but the Tigers flopped hard. Either way, with so many candidates for the No. 2 slot, you can\u2019t just rely on a cozy schedule, instead, needing a team also capable of making a leap, and priced in a way that suggests value. Team Rating Nationally From North Carolina \u2019s shoulder shrug-inducing nationally average rating of 50, up to SMU , there are 13 teams in the ACC within 13(.2) points of each other in betting lines. The Mustangs bring back Kevin Jennings for a third season, which might as well be 12 seasons in modern \u201Ccollege years.\u201D However, while people are quick to point so many teams who blew various golden opportunities by getting upset, there\u2019s not nearly enough shade being thrown at Rhett Lashlee, who lost at Cal (who\u2019d just fired Justin Wilcox) in the regular season finale, missing out on the ACC title game (and a chance for back-to-back playoff berths). Lashlee\u2019s dialled-back the transfer numbers, but a coordinator change interrupts some of the continuity we\u2019d cite with Jennings. Even if you liked Jennings to realize the dream of SMU\u2019s Heisman campaign for him, early-season trips to Tallahassee and Louisville could take him off the radar, and a late-season matchup with Notre Dame probably derail those hopes. After an electric bowl performance to cap the 2023 season, Miller Moss underwhelmed when given the keys to the USC offense in 2024, and Jeff Brohm couldn\u2019t get much more out of Moss at Louisville last season. Maybe he\u2019ll have more success with Ohio State transfer Lincoln Kienholz (who was edged by Julian Sayin for the starting job last year) and a rebuilt offensive line. A pair of good tailbacks named Brown (Isaac and Keyjuan) should help, while also taking advantage of the threat Kienholz brings with his legs as well. The issue for a possible win-total bet, is that the Cardinals face many of the ACC teams that we think may be underrated. Strangely, given the expected turnover from hiring James Franklin, Virginia Tech actually has the most returning production in the ACC (4th nationally), and as his want, Franklin\u2019s non-conference schedule is pretty cozy, with just Maryland any kind of a threat. Franklin\u2019s not a quick-turnaround artist though, finishing 6-6 in each of his first seasons at Vanderbilt and Penn State. The Hokies will likely have a conservative approach on offense, as OC Ty Howle and QB Ethan Grunkemeyer come with Franklin from PSU, which means Va-Tech likely wins the games they\u2019re supposed to, and lose those they\u2019re expected to. Your guess is as good as mine with what to expect from Florida State , as Mike Norvell could easily be fired before the end of the season, but if he\u2019s right about Ashton Daniels (getting the most out of the quarterback even without the departed Gus Malzahn) maybe the Seminoles are worthy of a modest bump in market rating from 62 at the end of last season, to starting this season at 65. That\u2019s not enough to make FSU an auto-fade, but there\u2019s no reason to fully support the Noles with any kind of a futures play, either. It\u2019s entirely possible that we\u2019re betting against Virginia against the spread in every game this season. The market didn\u2019t go crazy about the Cavaliers\u2019 run to the conference title game last season (as the 31st-rated team by ESPN\u2019s SP+), pushing Virginia up into the 60s. However, regression should be coming for a team that was built through the portal, hit with so many one-year players (including quarterback Chandler Morris), and are now trying to do it again. Virginia pulled wins out of the fire during a 4-game stretch (three in OT, 2-point win vs. Washington State). Being rated the same way heading into this season is making a lot of assumptions about a new portal class that features the well-travelled Beau Pribula, but the schedule looks pretty easy, as it\u2019s actually led to a 10% rating downgrade for an ACC team with a 7.5-win total. With a modest increase from 57 to 61 in power rating for Pittsburgh , the market seems to think Pat Narduzzi found something with Mason Heintschel \u2014 a freshman who took over in October and lit up teams (FSU, Syracuse, Boston College, NC State, Stanford) at something of a low point. However, once the competition got more difficult (Notre Dame, Georgia Tech, Miami, East Carolina), it wasn\u2019t as easy. Here\u2019s the market rating for NC State at the end of the last two seasons, and the start of this coming season: 2024: 60/100 2025: 60/100 2026: 60/100 13 years of Dave Doeren, and we have a pretty good idea of what level the Wolfpack are expected to play at. There are two reasons to expect something more in Raleigh: CJ Bailey \u2014 arguably the best returning quarterback in the ACC (protected by stud left tackle transfer Jimarion McCrimon from ECU) A schedule without Miami, Clemson, SMU, and with Louisville at home With two winnable road games, as underdogs, in the first three weeks, backing the \u2018Pack will be done early, and if that goes well, potentially often. Sports — Conference title future, three season-win total bets, and a Big Ten GOTY to buy now THE WINDOW Aug 12, 2026 6 6 Share Subscribe THE WINDOW is providing free subscribers sports betting content thanks to yahoo! sports this football season. The Big Ten is top-heavy, with a trio of teams making up Tier 1, and three more big-name programs making up Tier 2. While the champion came from 2 last year, there might some value on a similar-looking team to do it again this year. Why? Because unlike some years, there’s a TON of good matchups on the schedule this season. Free for Yahoo!, the Big Ten betting preview looks at those routes to the Big Ten Championship Game in Indianapolis, and why the middle class of the conference has THREE different regular season win total bets to make. BIG TEN BETTING PREVIEW (Y!) Of note, because of formatting differences compared to Yahoo!, we’ll add some of the missing pieces from our usual fare here. Including the Big Ten teams’ average market rating, and the average boost a team’s rating gets because of the difficulty of their strength of schedule (SOS): The average team in the Big Ten carries a power rating of 67.2 out of 100, which is helped by an average 17% boost thanks to an above-average schedule strength, and carried by highly-rated Ohio State, Oregon, Indiana, and, to a lesser extent, Michigan, USC, and Penn State. Conference odds Odds via Bet365 Bonus: “Game of the Year” value bet We’ll have one Game of the Year (GOTY) lookahead-line bet for each week from Week 2 to Week 13 for the free subscribers via Yahoo! Sports, but here’s another game-bet worth making, with an eye on getting the best number possible before kickoff. Indiana @ Michigan (+6, 52.5) Week 8 > The Hoosiers, as is their habit given a usually-breezy non-conference schedule, don’t play a game where they’ll be a single-digit favorite, let alone an underdog, until Week 7 when they’ll host a showdown with Ohio State, where they’ll put everything into gaining a game lead and the tiebreaker over the Buckeyes. At which point, they’ll either: Win, and find themselves in a letdown situation the following week for their visit to Ann Arbor Lose, and see their market rating dip to a point where they’re not going to be 6-point road favorites (and still be in a letdown situation), for their first high-level, true road game since going to Oregon last year, which the Hoosiers had a bye ahead of. Meanwhile, between now and Week 8, Michigan has a chance to get a big win or two when they host Oklahoma and Penn State. If Kyle Whittingham can keep the Wolverines defense at the level it’s been at the last couple seasons, and Jason Beck has tapped into the potential of 2025 top-recruit Bryce Underwood, then Michigan might not be a home underdog at all. If Kyle Whittingham can keep the Wolverines defense at the level it\u2019s been at the last couple seasons, and Jason Beck has tapped into the potential of 2025 top-recruit Bryce Underwood, then Michigan might not be a home underdog at all. records.new_body: 2026 College Football Preview: Betting the SEC Subscribe Sign in 2026 College Football Preview: Betting the SEC A bottom-to-top look, four regular season win totals, a GOTY bet, and a long-shot league winner THE WINDOW Aug 10, 2026 ∙ Paid 11 7 Share Subscribe The SEC and Big Ten have raised their game. Off the field. They’re not just bickering about which conference is better. They’re also taking things deep in the boardrooms; campaigning for a larger playoff (to include more of their teams, to make more money), and quietly threatening to separate from the NCAA entirely. On the field, the difference between the two leagues is that the bottom of the SEC is at least successfully trying to compete with the top of the league, instead of just saying curious , or delusional , things. Not to be outdone, one of just two teams under 60/100 in our estimated market ratings Kentucky , has a coach that seems irrationally confident (or is trying to cosplay Curt Cignetti) in what the lowest-ranked team in the conference will be able to do in Lexington. With Mississippi State being better than most anybody thought last season, and Vanderbilt — following their breakthrough by scoring one of the most sought-after quarterback recruits — it seems like everybody’s up compared to last year. The SEC’s conference stats — the teams’ average rank and the league’s average strength of schedule — reflect that: AVG. Rating: Out of /100 nationally, AVG. SOS: % above national-average Conference odds Odds via Bet365 If you’re a top program, a College Football Playoff regular, and you have a returning quarterback, you might have to wonder what you’d need to do not to be among the favorites to win your conference. Georgia and Texas (whose incumbent quarterback has a last name that rhymes with Shmanning) are atop the oddsboard in the SEC, and are also among the top of the league in returning production. Plus, the Longhorns made a series of splashes in the transfer market, scoring freak-show receiver Cam Coleman from Auburn, among others. In last year’s SEC preview , we made mention of the following: “In Year 2 of the 12-team playoff, after devaluing the conference championship by no longer giving the winner one of the top four seeds, we’re still exploring the possibility that a virtual lock for the CFP find themselves in a situation where winning the conference isn’t the priority it once was. ” Well, a year later, and the SEC Championship seems to be hanging by a thread. Last year, Alabama was dominated in the conference title game by Georgia, but then went on the road to Oklahoma and advanced to the Rose Bowl. A lack of urgency to qualify-for, and win, that extra game, complicates things in a way that doesn’t apply to most other futures markets — in college football or otherwise. Team Rating Nationally (Estimated market) rating: 0.5 = nationally average In Yahoo! Sports’ SEC preview , Corbie Craig took the Under 9.5 for Texas’s regular-season wins, citing (among other things) ESPN’s Bill Connelly having the Longhorns with a win projection of 8.6. Of note, as to why one might be fading the highly-rated ‘Horns, a defense that led the way for much of the season in Austin replaces coordinator Pete Kwiatkowski with Will Muschamp. However, I can’t get to that bet, given Texas doesn’t have Georgia or Alabama on their slate, and the Longhorns also get Ohio State at home this season. What is interesting, is that — using the lookahead “Game of the Year” lines as a cross-reference — Texas seems to carry a higher market rating earlier in the season, when it plays Ohio State and Oklahoma , than later on, when the Longhorns go to LSU and Texas A M . This might have more to do with an increase in home-field advantage later in the season, for places like Death Valley and College Station. The mission for Georgia this season, will be to crank up offensive explosiveness. Particularly, with Gunnar Stockton through the air. The Bulldogs are still super-talented and deep in the trenches, but the loss to Ole Miss in the CFP came with some alarmingly-bad in-game coaching decisions. Even should it lose in Tuscaloosa, or in the rematch to the rematch at Ole Miss, a 10-2 Georgia team should be back in the playoff, but would 7-2 in the conference even get the Dawgs into the SEC title game? You can throw a blanket over the next five teams — all rated around 80/100 in the betting market. For Texas A M, Oklahoma, Ole Miss, Alabama, and LSU, there’s room to jump up into title contention, but there’s one question for each that puts them on a second tier: Texas A M: Can Marcel Reed tighten things up, after a sloppy close to last season? Oklahoma: Is the assumption of good health for John Mateer the answer to OU’s offensive issues? Ole Miss: Can the Rebels keep up the level they ended last season at, with Trinidad Chambliss and Pete Golding? Alabama: Is there just a slow drift away from the Saban-era Crimson Tide? LSU: Are we sure Lane Kiffin wasn’t just the shiniest option for a handful of high-profile teams needing to find a vacancy? For their magical, post-Kiffin, run until the dying seconds of the Fiesta Bowl last season, Ole Miss never exceeded a low-80s market rating that they held through the previous two seasons of Kiffin’s tenure. Hence, the magic-ness of the run, as they were underdogs to both Georgia and Miami. With a pick’em-esque game that jumps off the page in Week 3, a win-total bet on the Rebels probably comes down that one game anyway. Our stance on LSU, is that we’ll get a good idea early on what we’re dealing with, as the Tigers take on Clemson, Texas A M, and the big trip to Ole Miss for Kiffin’s return to Oxford. Since there’s no reason to make assumptions about how they’ll finish the season (at Auburn, vs. Alabama, vs. Texas, and at Tennessee) via the futures market, we need not commit to an investment in Sam Leavitt’s health or Kiffin’s anything (including how he’ll mesh with incumbent defensive coordinator Blake Baker). Especially, at an EMR that’s in the low-80s, for a school that’s finished the last two seasons in the mid-to-low 60s. Post-Saban, Alabama’s finished the last two seasons with an EMR of around 80/100 — the new expectation from bettors and oddsmakers alike. Which should be a drag in T-town. 13 straight seasons of being power-rated in the top two via ESPN’s SP+ will create unmatchable expectations, and Alabama was barely in the top-20 last season, and has the lowest returning production of any of the SEC contenders, including Ryan Coleman-Williams, who dropped so many passes last season that he changed his name (adding the “Coleman”). However, a pretty comfy schedule is enough to dissuade us from an under bet. Florida , Tennessee , Auburn , and Missouri make up the league’s third tier, as two rebuild on the fly and two look to fill holes well enough to maintain their level. Medium-term, the Gators should be in good hands with Jon Sumrall, but, for this season, he’s putting a lot of trust in Buster Faulkner, hoping that his offensive coordinator hire is bringing the sound and the fury with Aaron Philo — his backup quarterback at Georgia Tech last year. Haynes King was doing a lot of the heavy-lifting in that offense. Laying a ton of points in the first week, and facing some bet-on teams when they get into the SEC slate, we’ll be fading the Gators week-by-week, rather than laying big juice on the win total. Missouri’s best player got shot this offseason . Which, you know, is kinda rough, but Ole Miss transfer, Austin Simmons, and new, well-travelled, offensive coordinator Chip Lindsey, might be the bigger question mark for Eli Drinkwitz. A Friday night game in Week 2 at Kansas will be worth watching closely to see who it all (*waves hands wildly*) looks for the Tigers. At the bottom of the league, Will Stein’s bravado will be tested in Lexington, but grabbing Kenny Minchey from Notre Dame makes the Wildcats an interesting underdog because of their theoretical backdoor-cover potential. That may be frequently necessary, as they have a top-10 SOS, and their rating isn’t bolstered by a large SOS boost the way Mississippi State (50% above national-average) and Arkansas (70% above national-average) are. The Bulldogs at least have mega-athlete, quarterback project, Kamario Taylor, returning to be the full-time starter for Jeff Lebby, who had Mississippi State competitive last year. Meanwhile, the Razorbacks hired Ryan Silverfield, whose biggest win at Memphis may have been… over Arkansas… and he’s tasked with choosing between KJ Jackson (holdover) and AJ Hill (brought from Memphis) at quarterback. bottom-to-top look, four regular season win totals, a GOTY bet, and a long-shot league winner\",\"body_html\":\" Subscribe now The SEC and Big Ten have raised their game. Off the field. They\u2019re not just bickering about which conference is better. They\u2019re also taking things deep in the boardrooms; campaigning for a larger playoff (to include more of their teams, to make more money), and quietly threatening to separate from the NCAA entirely. On the field, the difference between the two leagues is that the bottom of the SEC is at least successfully trying to compete with the top of the league, instead of just saying curious , or delusional , things. Not to be outdone, one of just two teams under 60/100 in our estimated market ratings Kentucky , has a coach that seems irrationally confident (or is trying to cosplay Curt Cignetti) in what the lowest-ranked team in the conference will be able to do in Lexington. With Mississippi State being better than most anybody thought last season, and Vanderbilt \u2014 following their breakthrough by scoring one of the most sought-after quarterback recruits \u2014 it seems like everybody\u2019s up compared to last year. The SEC\u2019s conference stats \u2014 the teams\u2019 average rank and the league\u2019s average strength of schedule \u2014 reflect that: AVG. Rating: Out of /100 nationally, AVG. SOS: % above national-average Conference odds Odds via Bet365 If you\u2019re a top program, a College Football Playoff regular, and you have a returning quarterback, you might have to wonder what you\u2019d need to do not to be among the favorites to win your conference. Georgia and Texas (whose incumbent quarterback has a last name that rhymes with Shmanning) are atop the oddsboard in the SEC, and are also among the top of the league in returning production. Plus, the Longhorns made a series of splashes in the transfer market, scoring freak-show receiver Cam Coleman from Auburn, among others. In last year\u2019s SEC preview , we made mention of the following: \u201CIn Year 2 of the 12-team playoff, after devaluing the conference championship by no longer giving the winner one of the top four seeds, we\u2019re still exploring the possibility that a virtual lock for the CFP find themselves in a situation where winning the conference isn\u2019t the priority it once was. \u201D Well, a year later, and the SEC Championship seems to be hanging by a thread. Last year, Alabama was dominated in the conference title game by Georgia, but then went on the road to Oklahoma and advanced to the Rose Bowl. A lack of urgency to qualify-for, and win, that extra game, complicates things in a way that doesn\u2019t apply to most other futures markets \u2014 in college football or otherwise. Team Rating Nationally (Estimated market) rating: 0.5 = nationally average In Yahoo! Sports\u2019 SEC preview , Corbie Craig took the Under 9.5 for Texas\u2019s regular-season wins, citing (among other things) ESPN\u2019s Bill Connelly having the Longhorns with a win projection of 8.6. Of note, as to why one might be fading the highly-rated \u2018Horns, a defense that led the way for much of the season in Austin replaces coordinator Pete Kwiatkowski with Will Muschamp. However, I can\u2019t get to that bet, given Texas doesn\u2019t have Georgia or Alabama on their slate, and the Longhorns also get Ohio State at home this season. What is interesting, is that \u2014 using the lookahead \u201CGame of the Year\u201D lines as a cross-reference \u2014 Texas seems to carry a higher market rating earlier in the season, when it plays Ohio State and Oklahoma , than later on, when the Longhorns go to LSU and Texas A M . This might have more to do with an increase in home-field advantage later in the season, for places like Death Valley and College Station. The mission for Georgia this season, will be to crank up offensive explosiveness. Particularly, with Gunnar Stockton through the air. The Bulldogs are still super-talented and deep in the trenches, but the loss to Ole Miss in the CFP came with some alarmingly-bad in-game coaching decisions. Even should it lose in Tuscaloosa, or in the rematch to the rematch at Ole Miss, a 10-2 Georgia team should be back in the playoff, but would 7-2 in the conference even get the Dawgs into the SEC title game? You can throw a blanket over the next five teams \u2014 all rated around 80/100 in the betting market. For Texas A M, Oklahoma, Ole Miss, Alabama, and LSU, there\u2019s room to jump up into title contention, but there\u2019s one question for each that puts them on a second tier: Texas A M: Can Marcel Reed tighten things up, after a sloppy close to last season? Oklahoma: Is the assumption of good health for John Mateer the answer to OU\u2019s offensive issues? Ole Miss: Can the Rebels keep up the level they ended last season at, with Trinidad Chambliss and Pete Golding? Alabama: Is there just a slow drift away from the Saban-era Crimson Tide? LSU: Are we sure Lane Kiffin wasn\u2019t just the shiniest option for a handful of high-profile teams needing to find a vacancy? For their magical, post-Kiffin, run until the dying seconds of the Fiesta Bowl last season, Ole Miss never exceeded a low-80s market rating that they held through the previous two seasons of Kiffin\u2019s tenure. Hence, the magic-ness of the run, as they were underdogs to both Georgia and Miami. With a pick\u2019em-esque game that jumps off the page in Week 3, a win-total bet on the Rebels probably comes down that one game anyway. Our stance on LSU, is that we\u2019ll get a good idea early on what we\u2019re dealing with, as the Tigers take on Clemson, Texas A M, and the big trip to Ole Miss for Kiffin\u2019s return to Oxford. Since there\u2019s no reason to make assumptions about how they\u2019ll finish the season (at Auburn, vs. Alabama, vs. Texas, and at Tennessee) via the futures market, we need not commit to an investment in Sam Leavitt\u2019s health or Kiffin\u2019s anything (including how he\u2019ll mesh with incumbent defensive coordinator Blake Baker). Especially, at an EMR that\u2019s in the low-80s, for a school that\u2019s finished the last two seasons in the mid-to-low 60s. Post-Saban, Alabama\u2019s finished the last two seasons with an EMR of around 80/100 \u2014 the new expectation from bettors and oddsmakers alike. Which should be a drag in T-town. 13 straight seasons of being power-rated in the top two via ESPN\u2019s SP+ will create unmatchable expectations, and Alabama was barely in the top-20 last

records.new_body: 2026 NFL Betting: Estimating every NFL teams’ power rating in the betting market Subscribe Sign in 2026 NFL Betting: Estimating every NFL teams’ power rating in the betting market Why it’s worth understanding offseason changes in how NFL teams are perceived before training camp THE WINDOW Jul 13, 2026 14 6 Share Subscribe The 2026 NFL season (and the 2026-‘27 betting season at THE WINDOW) begins… now! We are BACK, slowly building towards the start of football season — both pro and college — with our refresher on understanding the betting markets, and the specific status of each team as the betting market has progressively been shaped over the summer. Two things move betting markets: Action: Tangible things (injuries/suspensions, on-field results) that happen to change perception of the team(s) involved “Action”: A disproportionate amount of money gets bet on one side, and a sportsbook desires to balance their risk In early May, fresh off the NFL Draft, the action that happened was the league’s schedule release, making official when and where each team — who already had their list of opponents assigned — would play each other. Prior to this, oddsmakers had offered futures betting markets on the Super Bowl, AFC and NFC champion, divisions and regular-season win totals. In the two months since the slate was locked in, there has been an influx of granular data points on how each of the 32 teams are power-rated. Important: As discussed in our early look at NFL teams’ power ratings, this is the fundamental basis for our how all point spreads are built. Some sportsbooks have offered “Game of the Year” lines, but DraftKings has put up every game of the regular season for low-limit betting. As a result, bettors have had two months to pick away at those offerings, further shaping each team’s rating in the betting market (oddsmakers and bettors combined). While we may not want to submit an opinion via a bet now — tying up too much betting capital on games that are months away, at the very least, there’s been enough time to take this market information and apply it to our estimated market ratings ahead of the start of NFL training camps in the last week of July. 📢 Considering joining THE WINDOW’s Panes for the ‘26 season? From now until July 31st, membership is available at $120 annually. Just over $5 (USD) per the 22 weeks of football season from Week 1 of college football until the Super Bowl (plus, you get season-long bets in August, March Madness, and the Stanley Cup Playoffs!). Subscribe That’s the lowest price THE WINDOW has been, or will ever be, offered at. On August 1st, that price will go back to the standard $150 per year. For existing monthly subscribers on the initial $20/month membership, that doesn’t change, even as the monthly subscription has gone up with market inflation. However, those paying monthly CAN switch over to the discounted annual rate to save over $10/month. HOW TO CHANGE FROM MONTHLY TO ANNUAL How current point spreads project schedule strength For reference, here’s how are our estimated market ratings looked on May 11th , with only a slight consideration for schedule strength, mostly on how difficult each team’s division was projected to be: Now that we have more data about how the market feels about each team, cross-referencing each team with the various matchups they have and point spreads for more than just Week 1, we’ve learned more about each team’s non-division schedule, and are able to re-order all 32 teams accordingly. Updated market ratings (6/13/26) Here’s how the teams stack up as of mid-July: 🤓 Learn how to read the above chart: CLICK HERE 📝 Learn how to translate power ratings into point spreads: CLICK HERE Two months since the schedule release, NFL teams fall into three fundamental categories: No significant change to their estimated market power rating Change to their estimated market power rating due to micro information coming from their individual game point spreads (via DraftKings) Change to their estimated market power rating due to macro information — an overall move reflected in their regular season win total Either due to an obvious change in team outlook or bettors interest in betting the over or under Arizona Cardinals 🌵 No significant change, moving from 26 to 25 Atlanta Falcons 🦅 Dropped a quarter of a win in regular season win totals from 7.3 (7.5, +105) to 7.05 (7.5, +120) Baltimore Ravens 🐦‍⬛ No significant change, moving from 66 to 65 Buffalo Bills 🦬 Rise in rankings from 62 to 66 due to point spread data points, indicating a difficult schedule Carolina Panthers 😾 Big move in rankings from 38 to 45, reflecting both a rise in win total from 6.83 to 7.05 and point spread cross-referencing Chicago Bears 🐻 No significant change, moving from 59 to 60 Cincinnati Bengals 🐅 Drop in rating from 59 to 57 due to point spread data, but a rise in season win total from 9.98 (9.5, -130) to 10.21, indicative of an easier-than-expected schedule Cleveland Browns 🐶 Drop in rating from 35 to 31, stemming from both point spread data and a change in season win total from 5.98 to 5.78 Hmmmm, what could have happened on, say June 1, to have the market sour further on the Browns for the coming season? Dallas Cowboys ⭐️ Rise in rating from 54 to 58, despite a small downward adjustment in regular season win total, indicating a significantly easier non-division schedule than expected Denver Broncos 🐴 Drop from 60 to 57, reflective of a drop in season win total move from 9.98 to 9.58 Detroit Lions 🦁 Biggest drop, from 69 (and the top spot in May’s EMR) to 62, entirely reflective of the Lions’ soft non-division schedule and a high number of point spreads of over a touchdown Green Bay Packers 🧀 Small drop from 64 to 62, reflective of a drop in season win total from 10.21 to 9.98 Houston Texans 🤠 Up from 57 to 60, with a rise of a quarter-win in regular season win total as the over 9.5 has moved from -115 to -130 Indianapolis Colts 🐎 A drop in rating from 48 to 46 isn’t as significant as a drop in lined regular season win total of 8.27 down to 8.01 Jacksonville Jaguars 🐈‍⬛ No change in rating, but are the first listed of four teams to see the betting market shift from plus-money on the over (9.5) to juicing the over at a win total one win lower (8.5) Kansas City Chiefs 🪶 No change in rating Los Angeles Chargers ⚡️ Small change up from 60 to 62, but (like Jacksonville) a cosmetic change in regular season win total from 10.5 (+115 to the over) to 9.5 (-135 to the over) Los Angeles Rams 🐏 Big move up for the Super Bowl favorite from 68 to 74 — a significant starting point for the 2026-‘27 season — thanks to market’s interest in the addition of Myles Garrett, triggering a move from 11.2 projected wins to 12.1 Las Vegas Raiders 🏴‍☠️ No change in rating Miami Dolphins 🐬 Small rating increase from 25 to 28, pulling the Dolphins out of dead-last, though no change in regular season win total — a sign of respect for Miami’s schedule Minnesota Vikings😈 No change in rating New England Patriots🇺🇸 The third team with a cosmetic change to their regular season win total going from 10.06 to 9.98, but with a small increase in market rating after the A.J. Brown trade was made officially official New Orleans Saints ⚜️ No significant change, going from 43 to 42 New York Giants 🗽 Marginal increase in rating from 43 to 44 New York Jets ✈️ Like Dolphins, an increase in rating (31 to 35) comes without a change in regular season win total, out of respect for the opponents on the Jets’ schedule Philadelphia Eagles 🪽 No change in rating Pittsburgh Steelers🏗️ Small change to rating from 48 to 46 Seattle Seahawks🐦 Marginal change to rating from 68 to 67 San Francisco 49ers⛏️ The fourth team to see a cosmetic change in how their win total is presented, with a small decrease in rating from 62 to 61, which is only part of the reason the Rams are now -3.5 for Week 1’s neutral site matchup Tampa Bay Buccaneers⚔️ Increase in rating from 47 to 51 without a change in regular season win total, reflecting a difficult schedule (and, presumably, expected improvement of the NFC South as a whole) Tennessee Titans 🛡️ A win total drop from 6.6 to 6.4 is more significant than a rating drop from 39 to 38 Washington Commanders 🎖️ Small increase from 46 to 48, without a change to season win total What about home-field advantage (HFA)? After a season where home teams finished just four games above .500 straight up, or implied odds at just -102, standard home-field advantage appears to be set at just 1.5 points, after an average HFA of ~1.75. Early in the season, some consideration appears to be given to Miami for heat acclimation and Denver for elevation, giving each team 1.75 points of HFA. The Chargers (just one point), Rams, 49ers, Giants, Jets, Cardinals, seem to be getting docked at least a quarter point for a lack of intimidating or affecting home-field conditions. “Matt, why does this matter?” Between the time you read this and the kickoff to the NFL regular season on Wednesday, September 9, we’ll explore and have bets to make on the following futures markets: Team futures NFC Playoff Picture (Divisions, playoff yes/no, win totals) AFC Playoff Picture (Divisions, playoff yes/no, win totals) Player props Passing leaders: Yards and touchdowns Receiving leaders: Receptions, yards and touchdowns Rushing leaders: Yards and touchdowns Awards MVP Offensive Player of the Year Defensive Players of the Year Coach of the Year Offensive Rookie of the Year Defensive Rookie of the Year By the time Week 1 comes around, we’ll have an opinion about whether each team is overrated, underrated, or properly rated, and what their potential ceiling or floor is. Then, during the season, since we’ve established a root rating of what the market thinks of each team now, we can then compare how market opinion changes in a sample size of a few games should a team start hot or cold. That should create opportunities, where a point or two of value is created in the point spread market, despite nothing tangibly substantial happening to change the teams’ rating in the betting market. Which, it almost always does, in a shockingly short period of time. Looking forward to football season at THE WINDOW? Help us grow by liking (❤️) and/or restacking (🔄) this post. it\u2019s worth understanding offseason changes in how NFL teams are perceived before training camp\",\"body_html\":\" Subscribe now The 2026 NFL season (and the 2026-\u201827 betting season at THE WINDOW) begins\u2026 now! We are BACK, slowly building towards the start of football season \u2014 both pro and college \u2014 with our refresher on understanding the betting markets, and the specific status of each team as the betting market has progressively been shaped over the summer. Two things move betting markets: Action: Tangible things (injuries/suspensions, on-field results) that happen to change perception of the team(s) involved \u201CAction\u201D: A disproportionate amount of money gets bet on one side, and a sportsbook desires to balance their risk In early May, fresh off the NFL Draft, the action that happened was the league\u2019s schedule release, making official when and where each team \u2014 who already had their list of opponents assigned \u2014 would play each other. Prior to this, oddsmakers had offered futures betting markets on the Super Bowl, AFC and NFC champion, divisions and regular-season win totals. In the two months since the slate was locked in, there has been an influx of granular data points on how each of the 32 teams are power-rated. Important: As discussed in our early look at NFL teams\u2019 power ratings, this is the fundamental basis for our how all point spreads are built. Some sportsbooks have offered \u201CGame of the Year\u201D lines, but DraftKings has put up every game of the regular season for low-limit betting. As a result, bettors have had two months to pick away at those offerings, further shaping each team\u2019s rating in the betting market (oddsmakers and bettors combined). While we may not want to submit an opinion via a bet now \u2014 tying up too much betting capital on games that are months away, at the very least, there\u2019s been enough time to take this market information and apply it to our estimated market ratings ahead of the start of NFL training camps in the last week of July. \uD83D\uDCE2 Considering joining THE WINDOW\u2019s Panes for the \u201826 season? records.new_body: 2026 NFL Preseason Recap and Fantasy Football Notes: Week 1 - WalterFootball Skip to content Home 2026 NFL Preseason Recap and Fantasy Football Notes: Week 1 **** NOTES FOR EVERY GAME WILL BE UP AS SOON AS I WATCH THEM **** Follow me @walterfootball for updates. 2026 Preseason Notes: Week 1 2026 Fantasy Football Stock Pages: Week 1 Cowboys 17, Seahawks 7 Both the Cowboys and the Seahawks sat their starters in this game, but there was one extremely important development from a fantasy perspective. That would be that George Holani played extensively for the Seahawks. If Seattle considered Holani a major threat to Jadarian Price's workload, he likely would have sat with the other starters. However, he was given 12 carries in this game, which is an indication that he will not be playing very much in comparison to Price. The Seahawks started Drew Lock in this game, who eventually gave way to Jalen Milroe. The former third-round quarterback really struggled. He took a horrible sack and made some poor decisions. He ran well, but his passing has not come along in his development. The Cowboys, meanwhile, started Sam Howell, who was accurate in this game. Joe Milton eventually played the second half. Milton was able to zing some impressive throws in relief of Howell. On one occasion, he spun out of a sack and completed an 8-yard pass. Both quarterbacks threw touchdowns, coincidentally to the same player. The recipient of both Dallas touchdowns in this game was a rookie named Camden Brown. The undrafted player was able to wrestle the ball away from a defender on the first touchdown, and then he hauled in a one-handed catch on the second score. Brown had three receptions in total, and this all could have been a preseason fluke, but perhaps he'll emerge as a somewhat relevant player if he continues to make big plays like he did in this game. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Ravens 24, Eagles 7 There was only one fantasy-relevant player in this game, as both teams sat their starters. Rookie receiver Ja'Kobi Lane, who's enjoyed a terrific training camp, was able to catch three passes. He initially hauled in an 18-yard reception, and then he caught a pass in traffic and was able to run into the end zone. Baltimore's other rookie receiver, Elijah Sarratt, had a bigger night, although he did it more so with deeper backups. However, Sarratt was able to make a great diving catch at one point. Undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano played most of the game for the Ravens. He was accurate for the most part and looked pretty good for an undrafted player. Perhaps he can become a long-term backup at some point. Ravens rookie running back Adam Randall handled most of the workload for Baltimore in this contest. Randall had some nice runs, including his touchdown rush where he broke a tackle and was able to scamper into the end zone. Randall has good pass-protection skills, so perhaps he will be used at some point during the season. There's not much to say about the Eagles, who played mostly deep backups. Andy Dalton started but didn't play very much. Tanner McKee came in after that but wasn't effective at all, showing some indecisiveness in the pocket. The best quarterback for Philadelphia was Cole Payton, who was able to scramble for a first down and then hit a pass to eventually score a touchdown. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Vikings 13, Giants 10 Jaxson Dart was checked for concussions more than any player in the NFL last year, and that trend continued in the preseason opener. Dart was sacked on two occasions, and on the second one, a defender named Jay Ward destroyed him. Dart had to go into the medical blue tent later in the possession and missed one down. The good news is that Dart was able to return to action and immediately threw a touchdown pass to Malachi Fields. Dart's touchdown to Fields will look great, but the concern is that Dart continues to take brutal hit after brutal hit. If this trend continues, he will undoubtedly miss some action this year, making him a very risky fantasy selection in the middle rounds. Here were Dart's targets: Malachi Fields: 1 (1 end zone) Isaiah Likely: 2 Devin Singletary: 1 Tyrone Tracy: 1 Malachi Fields was the only Giants player to catch more than two passes in this game. He hauled in three balls in total, although only one came from Jaxson Dart. He made that one count, however, with a touchdown where he climbed the ladder and hauled in the pass over the defender. Fields' debut was great, and he continues to look like a terrific late-round sleeper. All three of the Giants' running backs rotated in this game. This is not a positive development for Cam Skattebo, though given that this was the preseason and Skattebo is coming off an injury, it's understandable that his touches would be limited in this game. However, the Giants' coaching staff nearly paid the price, as Tyrone Tracy Jr. was easily beaten in pass protection, resulting in one of the sacks that Dart took. By contrast, we didn't see much of the Vikings' starters. They played one drive, and Kyler Murray attempted three passes. Thanks to the running game, the Vikings were able to move into field goal position and score three points. Here were Murray's targets: Jordan Addison: 1 Max Bredeson: 1 Aaron Jones: 1 As for the Minnesota running game, Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason split the workload evenly. They basically rotated snaps. Jones was given the initial touch, and he broke a tackle to gain 15 yards. Mason, however, was also able to break a long run up the middle. Both Vikings runners looked great, albeit against what appears to be a very poor Giants run defense. The New York broadcast expressed extreme concern about the team's inability to stop the rush. NFL Preseason Announcers: This one stung from a betting perspective, as the Giants failed to cover by 1.5 points, with Minnesota covering as a -1.5 road favorite. John Harbaugh previously had terrific success in the preseason as the Ravens' head coach, but perhaps it was wrong to be very optimistic about Brandon Allen's chances of doing anything offensively. To be fair, however, the Giants got screwed late in the game. They had a big completion that was negated by offensive pass interference. Also, the Vikings initially went to Max Brosmer, but then went back to Carson Wentz to make sure that they'd win the game. Wentz predictably came up big with two third-down completions on the final drive, preventing the Giants from having a chance to win at the end. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Jaguars 24, Saints 20 Almost nothing was learned in this game. Both teams sat their starters, and even key backups didn't play. There were no fantasy-relevant players in this game, aside from perhaps Saints rookie tight end Oscar Delp. But he's more of a player who will be relevant in 2027 rather than this season, unless Juwan Johnson suffers an injury. Delp looked good, catching three passes for 10 yards and a touchdown. NFL Preseason Announcers: This was a very odd telecast. The broadcast missed the opening kickoff return that nearly went for a touchdown because the sideline reporter was talking to some old woman about how crime has decreased in New Orleans. Also, one of the broadcasters mentioned a very weird quote where he said, "Many in the NFL ranks were impressed with what Spencer Rattler did last year." Either those people were not watching him at all and pretending that they did, or they were knocked on their heads when they were small children. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Bills 29, Panthers 14 We had a good look at Buffalo's new offense in its brand-new stadium, as Josh Allen and the rest of the starters played two drives in their initial preseason game of 2026. The Bills scored on both possessions, nailing a field goal and then scoring a touchdown on those two drives. Allen began things by firing a 21-yard laser to Khalil Shakir, and later on, a deep pass of his to D.J. Moore set up a Keon Coleman receiving touchdown. The only negative that you could say about the Bills is that Allen was sacked twice, although one sack was negated by a penalty when a Carolina player grabbed Allen by the face mask. Still, this was concerning, even though the Panthers played their starting defense. Here were Allen's targets: Keon Coleman: 2 (1 end zone) D.J. Moore: 4 Khalil Shakir: 2 In addition to a new head coach and a brand-new stadium, the Bills also revealed their new No. 1 receiver, as D.J. Moore saw four targets, which was two more than any other Buffalo receiver had with Allen on the field. Moore looked great. He made a huge play after a short reception on the first drive and then hauled in a deep reception on the second possession. He grabbed his leg in what appeared to be discomfort after his final catch of the afternoon, and it looked bad at first glance, but it appears as though his shoe just fell off his foot. All indications are that he's okay. The Panthers also played their starters. In fact, Bryce Young was on the field for one more possession than Allen was. However, none of it was fruitful. The Panthers failed to score a single point while their starting offense was on the field. Young never had a chance. He was sacked on multiple occasions, as his worsened offensive line failed to block Buffalo's improved pass rush. He also had a pass batted at the line of scrimmage. There was an issue with NFL+ being unable to log people in, and there were many complaints made on X. You'd think that a multi-billion dollar operation wouldn't have any login issues, but that apparently is not the case. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Rams 20, Chiefs 12 Viewers of the Rams-Chiefs game were treated to a thrilling SEC battle between LSU and Alabama. Whoops, sorry, I got confused because Ty Simpson and Garrett Nussmeier battled each other in this initial preseason affair for the Rams and Chiefs. Both quarterbacks played the majority of the afternoon, which is a strategy that Aaron Glenn should have deployed with his rookie quarterback, Cade Klubnik. Beginning with Simpson, he was very impressive at times. Simpson threw a number of short passes, but he released the ball quickly and was very accurate. One of Simpson's better throws before the final drive was when he rolled out of the pocket and delivered a 23-yard strike to his receiver. He misfired badly on a short throw, but he rebounded with a nice 22-yard completion and then delivered strikes of 23 and 16 yards, ultimately throwing a 2-yard touchdown toward the end of the game to go up 20-9. Nussmeier, meanwhile, wasn't as impressive, but he still made some very good plays. On one occasion, he did a good job of buying time in the pocket to locate his receiver for a first down. He then made an impressive throw toward the sideline, and his receiver made a circus catch. It was reviewed, but replay showed that the pass was complete. Nussmeier didn't convert on a 94-yard touchdown, but he should have when he tossed a great bomb to his receiver, who dropped the ball. The Chiefs are set with their top two quarterbacks this year, but Nussmeier is easily the third quarterback on the roster, as he's miles ahead of Chris Oladokun. He looks like a potential No. 2 quarterback down the road. The Chiefs and Rams played their backups, but there were two young players who were absolutely worth noting. The first was Chiefs running back Emmett Johnson, who was their mid-round pick this year. Johnson had a great run of 12 yards where he deployed a terrific stiff-arm. He then made a nice cutback for a touchdown run, but that was negated by a penalty. After that, he showed great speed on a screen, but that was also nullified by a penalty. If you look at Johnson's stats, they'd be much better if it weren't for those two infractions. Later on, Johnson showed terrific power to convert a third-and-1, and then he carried defenders on a 12-yard gain. There's a good chance that Johnson ends up as the No. 2 running back on the roster because he is far more talented than Emari Demercado. The other young Chiefs player worth discussing is rookie receiver Cyrus Allen, who has made a big name for himself in training camp. Allen made a nice move to pick up a significant gain early on, but that was negated by offensive pass interference. Allen also made a leaping 10-yard catch to convert a third and eight. He looked good in this game, but it's still too early to say if he's a viable fantasy option. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Bears 34, Browns 10 The Bears' starters were nowhere to be seen in this game, while Cleveland had its starters on the field for the entire first half. Surely, the Browns' offense would have tons of success against Chicago's backups, right? That was not the case, though Deshaun Watson was able to engineer one scoring drive via some passes to rookie receiver KC Concepcion. Otherwise, the Browns did nothing offensively, as Watson saw tons of heat from Chicago's backup pass rush. On one occasion, he lost a fumble on a strip-sack. On another occasion, he had to skip a pass into the dirt toward Concepcion because he was under so much pressure. The Browns scored just 10 points on Chicago's backups in an embarrassing performance. Here were Watson's targets: Isaiah Bond: 1 Denzel Boston: 2 K.C. Concepcion: 4 Harold Fannin: 1 Jerry Jeudy: 2 Ahmani Marshall: 2 Dylan Sampson: 2 Blake Whiteheart: 1 Quinshon Judkins had no running room in this game. Watson handed him the ball on all three plays to begin the game, yet Judkins picked up only a grand total of eight yards on those carries. Cleveland's offensive line should be improved this season after the moves they made in the spring, but we saw no evidence of that in this game. The Browns went against Chicago's backups, and yet Judkins had no running room. The story for the Browns in this game, aside from their dysfunctional offense, was the play of the two rookie receivers. Denzel Boston caught the first pass, a gain of 17 yards, but KC Concepcion did everything after that. Concepcion handled the opening punt return, so I was concerned about his playing time, but he was on the field often with Watson. He saw more targets than anyone (4), and he showed some burst, especially on his yards after the catch on his touchdown score. Both project as quality sleepers in fantasy this year, despite the struggles of the rest of Cleveland's offense. Check out my 2026 Fantasy Football Sleepers page. Shedeur Sanders played the entire third quarter, and there were mixed results. He made decisions quicker than he did last year, and some of his incompletions were batted away. However, he threw a hideous interception where he sailed the ball way over his receiver's head. He didn't do enough to challenge Watson for the starting job. NFL Preseason Announcers: I spent most of this game being tiled by NFL+. I couldn't log in, and many others had the same issue. The NFL makes billions upon billions of dollars, and yet they couldn't figure out the log-in situation on their platform. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Broncos 27, Falcons 7 In an unusual event in the preseason, both teams played their starters in this game. However, the Broncos did not have Bo Nix, so they had Jarrett Stidham under center once more. Tua Tagovailoa, conversely, started for the Falcons and didn't have much of a chance against Denver's ferocious defense. Tagovailoa was constantly under pressure in this game, and it didn't help that he fumbled a shotgun snap and took a big loss on the opening series of the evening. All Tagovailoa did in this contest was toss checkdowns to Kyle Pitts. Here were Tagovailoa's targets: Kyle Pitts: 4 Even though Stidham started for the Broncos instead of Nix, that didn't stop Courtland Sutton from having an amazing game. Sutton hauled in a very deep pass where he landed inches shy of the goal line. The catch was good for 40 yards, but Sutton wasn't done. On the next possession, Sutton reeled in an amazing one-handed catch for 16 yards. It appears as though Sutton is highly motivated after the Broncos used a first-round pick to trade for Jaylen Waddle in a pre-draft deal. Waddle is going way earlier than Sutton in fantasy drafts, but they could have equal production this year. NFL Preseason Announcers: The Falcons announcer in this game was discussing a linebacker who used to play for Houston. In doing so, he mentioned the Texans' head coach as DeMarco Ryans instead of DeMeco Ryans. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Redskins 20, Dolphins 7 The Redskins did not play their starters in this game, while the Dolphins did for one possession, so I will discuss Miami's players first. Malik Willis led a touchdown drive to begin the game, going 4-of-5 and looking in command of his new offense. However, it must be noted that he was going against backups, so it's fair to be skeptical about Miami's performance. Here were Willis' targets: Caleb Douglas: 2 Malik Washington: 3 The star of Miami's offense, besides De'Von Achane, of course, was receiver Caleb Douglas. The third-round rookie saw two targets from Malik Willis, and he looked incredible on both of them. He appeared to catch the first pass, but upon replay review, it was apparent that he was barely out of bounds. The catch was terrific, so it would have made SportsCenter highlights had Douglas' one foot not been out of bounds. The second catch did make SportsCenter highlights, however. It was an incredible one-handed, back-shoulder catch to convert a third-and-5. The announcers in this game called Douglas a breakout star in training camp, and it appears to be true. Douglas, who was named the No. 1 receiver by his coaching staff, appears to be a terrific late-round fantasy sleeper. Miami's backup quarterbacks were awful in this game. Quinn Ewers entered the game and immediately made numerous mistakes, and then Cam Miller was even worse in the second half. If Malik Willis suffers an injury at some point, the Dolphins will be an automatic fade like the Jets were last year with Brady Cook. For those of you attempting to handcuff De'Von Achane and trying to figure out if you should go with Jaylen Wright or Ollie Gordon, the former was the immediate ball carrier after Achane left the game. Gordon entered the contest shortly afterward, so it appears as though Wright is the running back to own should Achane suffer an injury. However, it would most likely be a timeshare. There's not much to say about the Redskins, who played their backups. However, we saw a couple of rookie running backs who might be able to challenge Jacory Croskey-Merritt for the full-time early-down role. Kaytron Allen was the first running back on the field for the Redskins, and he had a great run with a strong burst of 16 yards. However, Robert Henry was the more impressive of the two backs. Henry, who played for UTSA, had some amazing carries where he was able to show off some terrific patience and set up some blocks to pick up significant gains. Henry had nearly half as many carries as Allen (23-12), and yet he nearly had as many rushing yards (85-75). The announcers ranted and raved about his potential, so perhaps he might be able to make the roster and eventually challenge for playing time. I'm not drafting him just yet, but he's a name to watch. NFL Preseason Announcers: The Redskins announcing team featured two old men, one of whom was confused most of the time. He kept complaining that the Dolphins were manhandling his team until he was told that the Dolphins were playing their starters. "Oh, they're playing starters?" he asked, as if he had never heard of any of the Miami players. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Buccaneers 24, Jets 16 One team played its starters in this game, and that would be the Jets. However, we did not see Geno Smith because he was nursing a minor injury. Fourth-round rookie Cade Klubnik started instead, and he had some nice moments mixed in with a couple of mistakes. One of Klubnik's initial errors was a weird underhanded toss to Breece Hall in the backfield, where it looked like the rookie quarterback panicked and delivered a horrible pass to Hall that was caught and taken for a loss. However, Klubnik rebounded with a laser to Garrett Wilson. Unfortunately, he took a loss on a scramble later on the drive instead of throwing the ball away. Klubnik looked fine except for those two mistakes. But the question must be asked: Why did he play just slightly longer than a quarter of action when he doesn't have any experience? Aaron Glenn is not a head coach who made quality decisions last year, and it appears as though he's still making mistakes. Klubnik is only a rookie, so he needs as much work as possible. Why have him on the field for just about 20 minutes of game action? He should have played for at least a half. While the Jets' starters played a drive, the Buccaneers' starters were nowhere to be seen. Baker Mayfield, Bucky Irving, and Emeka Egbuka did not play, though Egbuka is nursing an injury anyway. It's worth noting that the Buccaneers used Sean Tucker, whereas Irving and Kenneth Gainwell sat, so it appears as though the Buccaneers don't value Tucker as much as some late-round fantasy drafters believe they do. The one significant player who stood out for the Buccaneers was third-round rookie receiver Ted Hurst. Hurst saw six targets and caught just two of them, but he made those count. On the first reception, he made a nice juke move to pick up the first down. The second catch was an impressive diving reception. Hurst may see some action this year with Jalen McMillan injured and Egbuka's Week 1 status potentially in doubt. Follow me @walterfootball for updates. Cardinals 27, Raiders 14 While most teams played their backups in the initial week of the preseason, the Raiders and Cardinals both played their starters for a drive. However, all eyes were on one of the backups, as the No. 1 overall pick, Fernando Mendoza, made his NFL preseason debut. Mendoza's initial drive didn't amount to any points. However, he was able to convert a third-and-10 to Jack Bech along the sideline. The possession ended with no points because of a holding call and a Mike Washington drop. Mendoza's second possession was much more fruitful. He fired a laser to Malik Benson, threading the ball between three defenders for a gain of 15 yards. He then made a nice throw to Benson that was incomplete, but there was clear pass interference on the play. However, it wasn't called even though the defender clearly grabbed Benson's jersey. This didn't matter because Mendoza eventually found Bech for a touchdown. The Raiders didn't score any points on the third drive, as it was a three-and-out. Mendoza had to throw the ball away under pressure on third down. Mendoza, however, was able to lead his team into an opportunity to score points on the fourth drive when he went through his progressions quickly and found a receiver for a nice gain. He then moved the Raiders into field goal range, but the kick went wide right. This was a quality debut for Mendoza. He made some nice plays and didn't really make any mistakes. While we know that Kirk Cousins will start several games for the Raiders this year, it's clear that the team should be feeling very optimistic about Mendoza as the future. Both the first and the third overall picks in the 2026 NFL Draft played in this game. While Fernando Mendoza came off the bench, Jeremiyah Love actually started this game over Tyler Allgeier, which is a huge development. Another huge development is that Love was terrific in this contest, although that's not much of a surprise. On one run, he broke a tackle and showed off a spin move for a gain of 11 yards. On another rush, he made a great jump cut for a pickup of 10 yards. And then, on yet another terrific run, he hurdled a defender to gain 15 yards. It's extremely important to note that while Love started, Allgeier worked into the rotation, so it's not like the veteran didn't play. Love began the drive and was on the field for several snaps, and then Allgeier entered the game and played a few snaps after that. Love then returned and saw the same number of snaps before Allgeier entered once again. While we didn't see any goal-line opportunities, it's probably clear that Allgeier will be used in those situations. However, the fact that Love is already getting the first-team snaps over Allgeier speaks volumes, and Arizona clearly understands how talented he is. This night wasn't all positive for Love, however, because he suffered an ankle injury at some point during the second quarter. The good news is that head coach Mike LaFleur said that the injury wasn't very significant, but this situation will obviously need to be monitored. The other rookie running back in this game, Mike Washington, saw action once Ashton Jeanty departed after carrying the ball a few times with positive success. Washington had one of the highlights of the evening when he made a nice jump cut and used a great stiff-arm on a terrific 53-yard burst. Washington, however, dropped the ball on another play, so it wasn't a completely positive evening, but it was still a nice debut for the third-day rookie. We had a good look at both starting offenses in this game because both units went against the opposing starting defenses. Cousins had the first drive, where he completed all but one of his passes despite not having the services of Brock Bowers. He found his other tight end, Michael Mayer, for a touchdown. It was then Jacoby Brissett's turn, and he one-upped Cousins. Brissett completed all five of his passes, ultimately tossing a very accurate throw to Marvin Harrison Jr. for a touchdown, even though the defensive back had perfect coverage on the play. Brissett was just better than that, putting the ball where the Raiders defender didn't have a chance to break up the pass.
